paragraphs: In the noble copies of the Quran (mushafs), there are two kinds of Basmalah. The first is the Basmalah written at the beginning of the surahs, independent of the surah itself. The second is the Basmalah in the 30th verse of Surah an-Naml. There is no doubt that this Basmalah is a verse from the Quran, and this is certain by unanimous consensus of the scholars. However, whether the Basmalah at the beginning of surahs is part of the Quran is a disputed matter in the sciences of tafsir and usul (principles of Islamic jurisprudence). It is particularly related to the topics of faith, prayer (salah), and recitation (qira'ah).

Scholars such as Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri, 'Ata', and Ibn al-Mubarak stated that the Basmalah at the beginning of surahs is a verse of that surah. Imam al-Shafi'i and his students hold this view. According to them, the first of the seven verses of al-Fatihah is the Basmalah, and it is recited aloud in prayer. Imam Malik, on the other hand, relying on the tradition of the people of Medina, argues that the Basmalah at the beginning of surahs is not part of the Quran, but was written to separate the surahs and to seek blessing (tabarruk). For this reason, the Malikis do not recite the Basmalah in prayer. The Hanafis, however, accept that the Basmalah is an independent verse in its own right, but not an integral part of the surahs. Therefore, it was deemed appropriate to recite it silently in prayer.

The Basmalah ostensibly consists of four words: "Bismillahirrahmanirrahim". In reality, however, it consists of seven words. The preposition "bi" (with/by) is attached to an omitted (elliptical) verb, and this verb carries a meaning such as "I begin". The word "ism" (name) is the sign that allows a thing to be brought to mind. "Allah", on the other hand, is the proper name of the true Deity. The attributes "al-Rahman" and "al-Rahim" express the mercy of Allah. It is Sunnah to recite the Basmalah at the beginning of every important undertaking.

The supreme name "Allah" is the proper name of the Necessary Being whose existence is essential. This name encompasses within itself all attributes of perfection. Without accepting the existence and oneness of Allah, it is impossible to understand the universe. This name is the foundation of all sciences. Within human beings there is a latent feeling concerning Allah, and this feeling is stronger than all other emotions. The Quran was revealed to remind of and awaken this feeling.

The name "Allah" is different from generic words such as "Tanrı" (deity/god) or "Ilah". "Tanrı" is a common noun and can also be used for false deities. "Allah", on the other hand, is used only for the true Deity and has no plural form. For this reason, the name "Allah" cannot be fully translated into other languages. Süleyman Çelebi used the name "Allah" in his Mawlid and did not say "Tanrı". Similarly, the French word "dieu" corresponds to "Ilah", not "Allah".

It is known that the name Allah is Arabic and has been in use since the time of Ishmael (peace be upon him). In the Quran, too, it is recounted that when the polytheists were asked, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they replied, "Allah." Therefore, it is certain that this name belongs to the Arabic language. Although some claim that it was borrowed from Hebrew or Syriac, it cannot be proven that these languages antedate Arabic. Furthermore, the fact that words such as Israel and Gabriel (Jibril) are of foreign origin does not indicate that the word Allah is as well.

From a grammatical perspective, it has been debated whether the prefix "al-" at the beginning of the word Allah can be separated or not. According to one view, "al-" is an inseparable part of the word; the fact that the hamzah is not elided in the vocative case proves this. According to the other view, "al-" is the definite article, and the word is derived from "lah" or "ilah". The Kufan grammarians argued that it was formed by the contraction of "al-ilah"; scholars such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi adopted this view.

Other scholars, however, have stated that the word Allah is underived (murtajal) and is an inherently proper noun. According to Abu Hayyan and Imam al-Razi, the word has been from the very beginning an exclusive name belonging solely to Allah. The fact that the hamzah is not elided in the vocative case and that it is never applied to any other being is the most significant evidence of this. According to this view, the attribute of divinity is not derived from the name; rather, the name encompasses the attribute.

The name al-Rahman is likewise an attributive name unique solely to Allah. It means "the All-Merciful," yet this attribute has never been used for any other being. Grammatically, it is a predominant adjective (sifah ghalibah); it does not govern like a verb, and it is used in annexation (idafah). Al-Rahman cannot be translated; it can only be interpreted as "the Exceedingly Merciful." Al-Rahim, on the other hand, is an adjective and can also be used for entities other than Allah.

There is an important difference between al-Rahman and al-Rahim: the mercy of al-Rahman is general and necessary; it encompasses every being and is not contingent upon any condition. The mercy of al-Rahim, however, is specific and conditional; it belongs exclusively to the believers. That is why it has been said, "The Rahman of this world, the Rahim of the Hereafter." Were it not for the mercy of al-Rahman, created beings could not have been created; and were it not for the mercy of al-Rahim, effort and progress would not be possible.

The attributes al-Rahman and al-Rahim are distinct from each other; they are not repeated merely for emphasis. Al-Rahman is an eternal attribute of Allah and pertains to willing goodness at the inception; al-Rahim, on the other hand, is an active attribute pertaining to conferring goodness at the consummation. The mercy of al-Rahman is general, encompassing every created thing; the mercy of al-Rahim is more specific, an actual outpouring of grace. This distinction demonstrates that Allah's mercy is manifold, and there is no reason for despair for the believer.

The Basmalah ostensibly consists of a genitive construct (idafah) and two descriptive phrases (adjectival constructs), preceded by the preposition "ba". In reality, it is an abbreviated form of a hidden verbal sentence. The letter "ba" connects the action that the person pronouncing the Basmalah is about to perform (such as reading, writing, or eating) to the name of Allah. This hidden verb and subject are understood from the context of the discourse, and just as in Arabic, there are similar usages in Turkish as well.

Translating the Basmalah into Turkish is quite difficult. Various forms have been attempted, yet problems exist in each of them. Expressions such as "In the name of Rahman, Rahim Allah" either lead to a loss of meaning or arouse suspicions of the Trinity (tathlith). Therefore, it is most appropriate to pronounce the Basmalah as it is and reflect upon its meaning through tafsirs. It is necessary to remain faithful to the original and avoid defective translations.

The most important element in the Basmalah is the initial letter "ba". By means of this letter, a person connects the deed they are about to perform to the name of Allah. The "ba" conveys the meaning of either taking refuge and accompaniment, or seeking assistance (isti'anah). According to Sheikh Muhammad Abduh, the Basmalah signifies performing an act in the name of Allah, just as a judge delivers a verdict in the name of the sovereign. Although this interpretation holds true for specific offices, it cannot be applied to general usage.

The Basmalah is obligatory (fard) when writing the Quran (except for Surah at-Tawbah); it is likewise obligatory when slaughtering animals and hunting. In prayer, reciting it silently is Sunnah according to the Hanafis, and obligatory (fard) according to the Shafi'is. Beginning important affairs with the Basmalah is either recommended (mandub) or obligatory (wajib), depending on the significance of the act. In the hadiths, it is stated: "The Basmalah is the key to every book," and "Any important matter that does not begin with the Basmalah remains severed of blessing."

In short, the Basmalah is a unique maxim that summarizes the oneness of Allah, His mercy, and the relationship of servitude ('ubudiyyah). It is positioned at the beginning of every surah of the Quran and has become an established tradition for the entire Islamic Ummah. The Basmalah is the key to everything and holds infinite wisdom within it. The harmony and order among the verses of the Quran likewise demonstrate the miraculous nature (i'jaz) of this divine Word.

Human reason has been able to grasp the laws of attraction in the universe only in their material dimension. Yet in the realm of existence, there are also chemical, biological, spiritual, and social forces of attraction. The Quran presents a universal law of attraction that unites these different forces of attraction and encompasses every kind of existential relationship. In this law, we shall contemplate the absolute attraction of the creative Power, the bond between Allah and existence, and especially its manifestations in human relations.

The composition (nazm) of the Quran is a realm where scientific order and aesthetic order embrace each other. Its logical order is sounder than any compilation produced by science and art, and its literary beauties are more colorful and varied. The harmony between the clear verses (muhkamat) and the allegorical verses (mutashabihat) can only be seen in creation itself. As stated in Surah an-Nisa, verse 82, many contradictions should have been found in the Quran, yet none were found.

The order among the verses of the Quran is more distinct and profound than the order of celestial bodies. This order is both zahir (apparent) and batin (hidden). Its being apparent stems from its perfection, and its being hidden stems from its infinity. A poet expressed this state by saying: 'The virgin thoughts of the universe were shattered into pieces, yet the meanings of the Quran have still remained within the veil of protection.'

Above all, in order to be purified from heedlessness and whisperings of doubt, we must cling to the Basmalah by saying, 'I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.' Surah al-Fatihah begins with praise (hamd) to Allah and contains the following verses: Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful, and Sovereign of the Day of Recompense. You alone we worship, and from You alone we seek help. Guide us to the straight path—the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked anger or of those who are astray.

Between the Basmalah and al-Fatihah, there are strong ties in terms of antecedent context (sibaq) and the flow of discourse (siyaq). The Basmalah consists of seven words: four independent words and three names of Allah. Al-Fatihah, on the other hand, consists of seven verses, four fundamental statements, and three pause points. In response to the appeal of mercy in the Basmalah, al-Fatihah is an expression of gratitude. Al-Fatihah is the explanation of the Basmalah and the manifestation of its meanings.

According to what is stated in a Hadith Qudsi, Surah al-Fatihah has been divided equally between Allah and the servant. The first three verses belong to Allah, and the last three verses belong to the servant; the verse in the middle, 'You alone we worship, and from You alone we seek help,' is between the two. This balance reflects justice, which is the foundation of the cosmic order. At the same time, it points to a social reality such as the consensus (ijma') of the Ummah being a legal proof.

Hamd is praise situated between madih (general commendation) and shukr (gratitude), rendered in response to a voluntary good. Madih can also be made to inanimate beings, whereas hamd is directed only toward an entity possessing will and following an act of goodness. While shukr is in return for a blessing that has reached one, hamd can also be offered for a good that has not yet materialized. Hamd and shukr are always grounded in truth and are moral; madih, however, often remains mere falsehood. The Prophet commanded hamd and forbade excessive praise.

When hamd and shukr are compared, the aspect of respect and valuation in hamd weighs heavier. For hamd is praise rendered even if the bestowed blessing has not reached the person; in this respect, it is more sincere and directed toward the truth. Furthermore, hamd encompasses virtues such as sharing the joy of those who have attained blessings and regarding that which has not yet arrived as having arrived. For this reason, the most perfect form of shukr is hamd offered with the tongue. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Hamd is the head of gratitude. Whoever does not praise Allah has not thanked Him.'

Hamd encompasses all verbal praises, remembrances (dhikr), and expressions of respect made with the tongue. When one says 'Praise be to Allah (hamd olsun)', the feeling of happiness and bliss experienced in the face of a good deed or bestowal worthy of all these respects is proclaimed. This means both praising the author of that goodness and rejoicing in that happiness. Hamd is a moral virtue, like proclaiming the blessing and eradicating ingratitude. From the standpoint of humanity, happiness can be summarized in two words: tana'um (being in blessing and abundance) and in'am (bestowing blessings). Happiness lies not in prosperity itself, but in its being felt and appreciated. Hamd is precisely the verbal expression of this feeling.

The stations of hamd are respectively as follows: Hamidiyyah (praising), Mahmudiyyah (being praiseworthy), Hamidiyyah and Mahmudiyyah, Mahmudiyyah and Hamidiyyah. At the highest station, one of the divine manifestations belonging to Allah is seen. At this station, Allah's beautiful names such as al-Hamid and al-Mahmud manifest. Furthermore, Ahmad and Muhammad, among the blessed names of the Prophet (peace be upon him), also point to this station. Maqam al-Mahmud (the Praiseworthy Station) is the highest station of intercession promised to the Prophet. At this station, 'Liwa al-Hamd' (the Banner of Praise) will be handed to him, and his Ummah will gather under this banner. The conclusion of the prayers of the people of Paradise will also be: 'Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'

Al-Fatihah, beginning with 'Alhamdulillah', teaches us these happinesses and goals of maturity. The letter 'lam' in the phrase 'Alhamdulillah' carries the meanings of belonging, entitlement, and ownership. The sentence means: 'The reality of praise, in all its varieties and degrees, is exclusive to Allah, is Allah's right, and is Allah's possession.' This nominal sentence expresses continuous and perpetual praise. There is no other nominal sentence in al-Fatihah; the other sentences are verbal sentences and explain this nominal sentence.

'Rabb al-Alamin' is an attribute of Allah. Because 'Alamin' is a plural designating beings endowed with intellect, it means 'the Lord of all realms, and especially the realms of intelligent beings.' This expression points to the wisdom behind the revelation of the Quran. The word 'Rabb' derives from the verbal root meaning to nurture and rear (tarbiyah) and is a name given to the one who nurtures. It expresses hyperbolic emphasis; that is, it signifies a flawless nurturer possessing everything necessary for upbringing. It also conveys the meanings of owner and master. However, 'Rabb' cannot be used alone for anyone other than Allah.

The tarbiyah (nurturing) of the Rabb is to bring a thing step by step to maturity. Throughout the worlds, the laws of nurture and maturation are visible at every moment. This state demonstrates Allah's infinite power. When the Lord of the worlds is mentioned, one contemplates the law of nurture in the universe. Some philosophers failed to see this law, claiming that the universe was created all at once or had existed from eternity. Yet observation and intellect demonstrate that everything comes into being gradually, develops, and then ceases to be. The formation of the human being is also an example of this process.

Creation, nurture, and selection in the universe constitute a divine order and are the work of Allah's absolute perfection. In recent years, science and philosophy have accepted the existence of the law of evolution/development (takamul) in nature. However, some do not attribute this evolution to Allah, but ascribe it to a blind and unconscious nature. Yet science is based on the law of causality. The principle that 'nothing comes from nothing' states that every originated thing has a cause. Naturalism contradicts this law. There is harmony and proportionality between cause and effect. For this reason, scientists who accept evolution in nature are compelled to conceive of Allah in His infinite perfection.

For example, a grain of wheat falls into the soil and yields a hundred grains. This is an increase in quantity. If this increase is attributed solely to the nature of the first grain, it becomes a logical fallacy like '1=100'. Yet at the culmination of every development, there is a maturity that arrives from outside. This is development attained through nurture (tarbiyah). The rule 'the complete does not arise from the deficient; the deficient arises from the complete' applies. Therefore, science and philosophy accept the existence and perfection of Allah. Naturalists, contradicting their own theories, still do not abandon the notion of nurture, whereas without Allah's nurture, these claims remain groundless.

The word 'âlem' (world/realm) is a noun of instrument meaning an instrument of knowledge, and its plural form, 'âlemîn', is a plural used for rational beings. Its usage with the definite article 'lâm' as 'el-âlemîn' encompasses the entire universe and all of its parts. Employing a plural designating rational beings within this generality demonstrates that they are held superior and points to the significance of rational beings in understanding the Lord of the worlds.

Every entity in the universe is a sign pointing to the existence and Lordship (Rububiyyah) of Allah. This indication begins with a brief sign at first glance, then deepens through detailed reflection. The connection between human perceptions and physical things necessitates the existence of Allah. Even while perceiving our own existence, we are compelled to acknowledge Allah, Who encompasses us and the external world; otherwise, we cannot verify any reality.

The attributes of Rahmân and Rahîm express the mercy of Allah. Allah's mercy is not an emotional impression like human compassion, but consists of essential (dhati) and active (fi'li) attributes. Rahmân indicates the will to create and bestow existence, whereas Rahîm signifies the act of bestowing blessings and doing good. These two attributes denote that Allah's mercy is both all-encompassing and specific.

The mercy of the Rahmân reaches all beings equally as they emerge from non-existence into existence. The mercy of the Rahîm, on the other hand, is directed toward beings endowed with free will, administering reward and punishment according to their choices. This is a requirement of Allah's justice and wisdom. While associating partners with Allah (shirk) and rebellion render the continuation of existence impossible, monotheism (tawhid) preserves the balance of mercy.

While acting with partial free will (iradah juz'iyyah), man should not fall into the error of regarding this will as absolute. Allah is both the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden. In the present time, just as in the past, everything is in His hand of power. Man's aspect of helplessness bears witness to Allah's power, while his aspect of choice bears witness to His will. This balance condemns man neither to determinism (jabr) nor to absolute freedom; rather, through Allah's mercy, it holds responsibility and freedom together.

In this section, while explaining the expression "Mâliki yevmiddîn", Elmalılı emphasizes that man is not in the position of giving reward and punishment, but of receiving them. It is stated that Allah is the true owner of all dominion, and that temporary authorities in this world are merely borrowed. His sovereignty is an absolute ownership encompassing the heavens, the earths, and all realms.

The concept of "Yevmiddîn" is examined: it is stated that the word "dîn" in Arabic carries meanings such as retribution, reckoning, judgment, obedience, and sacred law (sharia), and that it does not directly mean the Day of Resurrection. It is noted that, in addition to being understood here as the day of retribution, it is also interpreted in the familiar sense of religion. What is meant is the final day when every deed will be recompensed, that is, the Day of the Hereafter. It is explained that the word "day" denotes absolute time, and that the days of the Hereafter are expressed with different measures compared to worldly days.

It is explained that "yevmiddîn" points to the Day of Resurrection, but is not the resurrection itself. It is emphasized that the Day of Resurrection encompasses stages such as resurrection, gathering (hashr), reckoning, the scale (mizan), and the traverse (sirat), and that the phrase "yevmiddîn" reinforces encouragement and warning by highlighting the day of retribution, which is the final of these stages. For this reason, it is stated that the expression "the Day of Din" should not be translated simply as "the Day of Resurrection" or "the Day of Reckoning," but rather that it conveys a stronger meaning.

The definition of religion (din) is provided: Religion is a divine system that guides rational beings toward goodness by their own free will. It is explained that this definition encompasses both true religion and false religions. The prerequisite of religion is intellect and free will, whereas religiosity requires knowledge and love. The difference between religion and religiosity is like the difference between divine law and human effort. The fruit of religion consists of deeds that are inherently good; goodness is done because it is good in the sight of Allah.

The distinguishing characteristic of the true religion is that it is based on voluntary obedience, not compulsion. There is no compulsion in religion; man must choose goodness through his free will. Doing good solely for self-interest is not genuine religiosity; what is essential is to do good for the sake of Allah's pleasure. The law of Allah is known through revelation and prophethood; intellect and transmitted tradition work together at this point. In Islam, the authoritative sources are the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogical reasoning (qiyas).

Finally, it is stated that the true religion will be verified through the fulfillment of its promises, and that Islamic history bears witness to this. It is expressed that today's utilitarian mentality diminishes the influence of the true religion, yet the reality of the Day of Din serves as a warning against such trends. Elmalılı interprets the expression "Mâliki yevmiddîn" both in the sense of the day of retribution and the day of religion in the well-known sense, suggesting that it be translated as "Master of the Day of Din." Furthermore, the recitation variants are addressed, explaining the subtle nuance between the readings "Melik" and "Mâlik".

Ownership (malikiyyah) is the private right of disposal that a person possesses over wealth and property for their own benefit. Authority, on the other hand, is the power of sovereignty. In reality, both belong to Allah, the Lord of the worlds. The property and authority possessed by human beings, however, are temporary and held in trust. Nonetheless, in this world, human selfishness and pride rely on this temporary property and authority. The happiness of life depends on the provision of private property and social order. Neither extreme socialism nor extreme individualism is beneficial for humanity. Both must be in balance.

The phrase "mâliki yevmiddin" in the verse conveys that on that day no one will be able to help anyone else and that true dominion belongs to Allah alone. This warning is terrifying for those who rely on their temporary possessions in this world. However, this verse does not impart despair; for on that day, by the mercy of Allah, believers will receive their share of bliss, while disbelievers will be deprived. The two recitations, "Mâlik" and "melik", emphasize this warning separately in terms of individual ownership and social ownership.

The first three verses of al-Fatihah constitute a proposition consisting of one premise and five proofs. Praise belongs exclusively to Allah, because He is worthy of it by virtue of His Essence and His attributes. He deserves it by His Essence because He is Allah. He deserves it by His attributes because He is the Lord of the worlds, the Rahmân, the Rahîm, and the Master of the Day of Din. Addressing mankind, these verses remind them of Allah's power and mercy, directing them to worship Him alone.

The expression "İyyâke na'budü" declares that servitude and worship must be directed to Allah alone. Worship is a specific act of obedience expressing drawing near to Allah based on intention. Every act of worship is a drawing near, but not every drawing near is an act of worship. Deeds performed without intention are not considered acts of worship. For this reason, intention is a prerequisite in acts of worship such as prayer, fasting, and zakat. The essence of worship is complete submission and humility before Allah.

The human soul experiences a continuous ebb and flow between hope and fear. When hope is present, activity increases; when fear is present, either transgression or despair arises. When man realizes his helplessness, he turns to Allah, the sole source of all hopes and fears. This turning is indeed the beginning of the feeling of worship. However, humans often fall into polytheism (shirk) by attaching this sentiment to transient things. True worship is devotion rendered exclusively to Allah, bringing peace to the heart.

When the Prophet (peace be upon him) passed away, Umar denied the event, but Abu Bakr calmed the Companions by reciting verse 3/144 of Surah Al 'Imran. He said, "If you worship Muhammad, he has died; but if you worship Allah, He never dies." This event demonstrates how wrong it is for people to attach themselves to transient beings. A believer is like a fresh crop; as the wind blows, it bends, but it rises again. A disbeliever is like a pine tree; once it is brought down, it cannot rise again.

Worship requires hope and fear to unite in a single source. A person finds peace when directing all their fears and hopes toward Allah. The pride of the ego may object, thinking that worship is humiliation. In truth, real elevation is possible only through submitting to Allah. Arrogance and pride are an illness for which worship is the remedy. The servant must be able to say, "I did not exist, Allah brought me into being; I would sacrifice everything in His path." This is the very submission taught by the Fatihah.

The expression "İyyâke nesteîn" emphasizes that help must be sought from Allah alone. The servant knows that they cannot worship by their own power and asks for help from Allah. This seeking of help is essential for the continuation of worship. By combining servitude and the plea for help with these two sentences, the Fatihah forms the foundation of a Muslim's life.

In the statement "You alone we worship and from You alone we ask for help," "asking for help" (nestaîn) can be understood in three ways: asking for help in a general sense, asking for help in every matter, or asking for help in a specific matter based on a particular contextual indication. Although the third possibility might come to mind due to the context of worship, the statement's orientation toward tawhid by means of abbreviation and specification necessitates asking for general help. Help is of two kinds: necessary help (things without which the action cannot occur, such as power and intellect) and unnecessary help (things that facilitate the task). In the science of jurisprudence (usul), this division is known by the names kudret-i mümekkine (enabling power) and kudret-i müyessire (facilitating power).

This verse shows us that all help belongs to Allah, but the willing is ours. This willing is termed partial free will (juz'i iradah) or acquisition (kasb). The actions a person performs with their own will express the sum of the connection between a desirer (the human being) and a Creator (Allah). Creation depends not only on the immediate proximate cause, but on the coming together of all causes. For example, like the operation of a machine: the machine is the locus of the work, the machinist is the one who wills, and the Creator is Allah. These three levels are an evident reality. One should neither presume man to be a soulless machine like the Jabriyyah, nor consider man a creator like Allah.

The expression "You alone we worship and from You alone we ask for help" bears the character of a covenant (ahd) between Allah and His servants. This covenant possesses a collective rather than an individual dimension; for the plural form is used as "we worship" and "we ask for help." This points to the virtue of congregational worship and aims at the formation of a collective spirit. This collective spirit develops through directing love and fear toward Allah alone, transforming into a universal feeling of brotherhood. Indeed, Islam is this great collective spirit itself.

The first person to realize this covenant in the fullest sense was the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). In his solitude in the Cave of Hira, he possessed a collective conscience that represented all of humanity, and he received this covenant from Allah and conveyed it to his Ummah. By adhering to his Sunnah, the Islamic community was able to truly utter this covenant of servitude and established an exemplary state in the world. If one were to say "I worship You alone" while reciting the Fatihah in prayer, the prayer would be invalidated; because Allah wills to make a covenant with a collective conscience, not an individual one.

This verse expresses both the oneness of Allah (tawhid) and the unity of servitude. The phrase "You alone we worship" contains the testimony of tawhid and rejects all forms of polytheism (shirk). Here, there are two types of obligation: individual obligation (fard al-ayn, belonging to each individual) and collective obligation (fard al-kifayah, belonging to the community). However, in this verse, without erasing the personal meaning, each individual uttering this statement on behalf of the community is understood as an individual obligation. In this manner, Islam unites the consciences of both the individual and society at a single point, elevating them to the most perfect rank of tawhid.

In his commentary on Surah al-Fatihah, Elmalılı Hamdi Yazır addresses the belief of shirk in detail. He divides those who associate partners with Allah into various categories: corporeal partners (such as idols, trees, animals, and humans), simple bodies (the Magians who worship fire), celestial bodies (the Sabians who worship the sun, moon, and stars), and non-corporeal partners (such as spiritual entities, angels, and the belief in two deities). All such beliefs are shirk and contradict the oneness of Allah.

Yazır especially criticizes the belief in two deities (Thanawiyyah) and emphasizes its logical inconsistency. He points out that two separate primary principles cannot establish an order, that this would necessitate a third common ground, and that it ultimately leads to the doctrine of the Trinity in Christianity. He states that humanity deviated from the belief in one God and plunged into various forms of shirk, but Islam corrected these deviations with true tawhid. In this context, he states that the address "yâ eyyuhellezîne âmenû" in Surah al-Fatihah is an evidence rejecting shirk.

Yazır then proceeds to the supplication "ihdinâ sırâtal mustakîm". He emphasizes that this supplication is an explanation of the expression "nesteîn" (we ask for help) and that the most important help from Allah is guidance (hidayah). He lists four kinds of guidance: granting material and spiritual faculties, showing the proofs that distinguish truth from falsehood, sending prophets and scriptures, and the unveiling (kashf) and inspiration (ilham) granted specifically to the saints (awliya). He notes that guidance is direction toward goodness, and that its use for evil actions is metaphorical.

Yazır analyzes the expression "sırât-ı mustakîm". He explains that the word "sırât" means a busy, broad way, and that "mustakîm" means completely straight with no crookedness whatsoever. He states that these two words combine to express the path of truth, the community (millah) of Islam. He touches upon the different recitations (qira'at) of "sırât" in Arabic and draws attention to the wisdom behind the word selections in the Quran. In addition, he distinguishes between the physical and spiritual dimensions of the concept of "path."

Finally, Yazır interprets the expression "sırâtallezîne en'amte aleyhim". He states that "in'am" means bestowing blessings and that Allah's blessings cannot be counted. He explains that the word "ni'mah" (blessing) originally means tasting pleasure, and that blessings are divided into worldly and otherworldly. By briefly explaining the concepts of "mağdûb" (those who have incurred wrath) and "dâllîn" (those who have gone astray), he emphasizes that the straight path is far removed from these two forms of deviance.

Blessings are divided into two: divinely bestowed (wahbi) and acquired through effort (kasbi). These are also divided into spiritual and corporeal subcategories. Among spiritual blessings are the breathing of the spirit, intellect, and intelligence; corporeal blessings include the body and its organs. Acquired blessings, on the other hand, are things like purifying the soul, knowledge, good character, wealth, and status. Blessings of the Hereafter consist of attaining Allah's pleasure and finding peace in Paradise. However, the end of worldly blessings can sometimes turn into disaster; the true blessing consists of the sound blessings that serve as a means to happiness in the Hereafter.

There are two views regarding the interpretation of the expression 'En'amte aleyhim': The first is the meaning 'You bestowed favor upon them,' that is, You made them felicitous, without presupposing any direct object. The second is 'You bestowed that path upon them as a blessing' by assuming an implied direct object (mef'ul). The author of al-Kashshaf preferred the first, while al-Tabari preferred the second. According to Elmalılı, the most correct approach is to understand this expression as 'metonymy for bestowing the straight path as a blessing'; thus, the blessing of the path (sirat) acquires a meaning that encompasses all blessings.

The blessing of the path is the greatest blessing, because obtaining the path to any blessing ensures continuous access to that blessing. For this reason, praying 'Guide us to the straight path' has been taught in the Fatihah; this is superior to asking for specific blessings. When the straight path is found, all paths of blessings are reached, and blessings become continuous. This is also why the Fatihah is called 'ta'lim-i mesele' (instruction on how to supplicate).

Those upon whom favor has been bestowed are the prophets, the steadfast affirmers of truth (siddiqin), the martyrs, and the righteous. Surah an-Nisa 4:69 explains this in the most comprehensive manner. The most perfect example is the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his noble Companions. The success and happiness they attained in history have not been witnessed in any other community. For this reason, the expression 'those upon whom You have bestowed favor' specifically refers to the path of the Prophet Muhammad and his Companions.

It is disputed whether the word 'gayri' is an adjective (sifat) or an apposition (bedel). While al-Kashshaf and Qadi Baydawi state that it can be a bedel, Abu al-Su'ud rejects this and maintains that it is a sifat. Elmalılı also adopts Abu al-Su'ud's view: 'Gayri' is an adjective and indicates that those upon whom favor has been bestowed are those who are far from wrath and misguidance. Thus, true blessing also includes being saved from wrath and misguidance, which is precisely what Islam is.

Wrath is Allah's will to punish; misguidance (dalalah) is deviating from the right path. In the Quran, wrath is generally attributed to the Jews, and misguidance to the Christians. Although this encompasses other disbelievers as well, they are mentioned as the most prominent examples. In a hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet also stated: 'The Jews are those who incurred wrath, and the Christians are the astray.' However, the generality of the ayah must be preserved, and it should not be restricted solely to these two groups.

The hadith of 'Adi b. Hatim supports this tafsir. According to the narration, the Prophet stated that the Jews are the 'magdubi aleyhim' and the Christians are the 'dallin'. This is an important explanation in the exegesis of the Fatihah. Nevertheless, some commentators have stated that it is more appropriate to preserve the general meaning of the ayah and accept the Jews and Christians as illustrative examples.

There are hadiths stating that the expressions 'magdubi aleyhim' and 'dallin' in the Fatihah refer to the Jews and Christians, yet the meaning of the ayah is not limited to them alone. Since these hadiths are not mutawatir (mass-transmitted), restricting the ayah is objectionable. There are two forms of interpretation: In the first, the Jews and Christians are intended merely as textual referents, whereas in the second, this distinction is demonstrated more comprehensively by way of meaning and implication. Elmalılı finds the second interpretation more in keeping with the style of the Quran.

In the time of the Messenger of Allah, the Jews, out of love for the world and selfishness, had corrupted the Torah and, by acting unjustly toward the prophets, had incurred Allah's wrath. Having lost their political freedom, they were dispersed and involved with secret societies. Although they possessed an illuminating scripture in the past, at that time they had become a community whose interior did not match their exterior, striving to suppress the truth.

The Christians, on the other hand, were a great empire at that time as the heirs of Rome and masters of Constantinople (Istanbul). Outwardly, they seemed to have attained blessings, but in reality they were in danger. Entrenched in the belief in a Trinity of deities, having halted intellectual progress, leaving the law to the whims of the clergy, and disregarding human rights, this misguidance had made them candidates for decline in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. Allah sent the religion of Islam, free from these perils.

Surah al-Fatihah describes the knowledge of Allah and the creation of the universe at its beginning, the principles of the religion of Islam in its middle, and the straight path in its final three verses. With the expression 'not the path of those who have incurred wrath, nor of those who are astray,' it determines the boundary of the true path. This boundary is the safe and straight path that leads to the blessings of Allah. The surah summarizes this meaning with the 'Basmalah' at its beginning.

The religion of Islam is a true path established by history and experience. Our Prophet and his Companions attained immense blessings by walking upon this path. Because the Quran and the Sunnah have been preserved without corruption, the reality of Islam has not changed. The decline of contemporary Muslims stems not from the religion itself, but from their failure to practice it properly. As people attempt to adapt the law of the Truth to themselves, distress increases; the solution is to persevere upon the straight path.

Saying 'Amin' at the end of the Fatihah is a Sunnah. 'Amin' means 'accept' and is not part of the Quran. Our Prophet commanded the congregation to say 'amin' when the imam says 'veleddallin', informing that the angels also say 'amin' and that whoever's utterance coincides with theirs will have their sins forgiven. It is appropriate for both the imam and the congregation to say it silently.

There is a difference of opinion among scholars as to whether the disjointed letters (huruf al-muqatta'at) found at the beginning of surahs are considered verses (ayahs) or not. While the Kufan scholars count these letters as independent verses, the Basran scholars do not accept any of them as a verse. This disagreement stems from the fact that verses are determined by divine decree (tawqifi) rather than analogy (qiyasi), and it is similar to variations in recitation (qira'ah). The first of the disputed verses of Surah al-Baqarah is "Alif Lam Mim".

Although "Alif Lam Mim" appears as a single word in writing, it is pronounced as three distinct letters when recited. These letters are the names of the alphabetical letters that form the fundamental building blocks of language. Each letter signifies a sound and the written form of that sound. On their own, these letters are meaningless sounds, but by coming together, they form words and meanings. This situation brings to mind two different modes of reading and interpreting: the standard alphabet (alifba) or the numerical alphabet (abjad).

Exegetes (mufassirun) are divided into two main views regarding the meaning of these letters: According to the first view, Allah challenges the Arabs with these letters, emphasizing that they cannot produce the like of the Quran, which is composed of the very basic letters of the language they speak. Proponents of this view have also stated that "Alif Lam Mim" is a name of the surah or of the Quran. According to the second view, these letters serve as abbreviations or ciphers, pointing to specific meanings. For example, each letter could be the initial letter of a name or carry a numerical value according to abjad calculation. A third view combines both approaches, arguing that the letters possess both exoteric (zahir) and esoteric (batin) meanings.

The profound meaning of these letters takes a person on an intellectual journey leading from sounds to words, from words to meanings, from meanings to existence, and ultimately to Allah's knowledge. At the end of this journey, one must admit their helplessness and say, "Allahu a'lam" (Allah knows best). It is in this respect that the disjointed letters are among the allegorical verses (mutashabihat); that is, they are not devoid of meaning, but rather an expression whose full depth human intellect cannot completely comprehend because they are so rich in meaning.

One of the wisdoms behind the use of these letters at the beginning of surahs is to draw attention and evoke astonishment. According to narration, while the polytheists tried to prevent the recitation of the Quran by making noise, they began to listen in astonishment upon hearing these letters and thus benefited from the Quran. For this reason, these letters should especially be recorded as a reason for revelation (sabab al-nuzul). As for the absence of these letters at the beginning of al-Fatihah, it is because the primary aim of al-Fatihah is clear guidance and instruction.

In terms of grammatical inflection (i'rab), the names "Alif Lam Mim" have no grammatical inflection because they are words enumerated one by one. Nevertheless, they can be regarded as a subject-predicate (mubtada'-khabar) construction or as the direct object (maf'ul) of a verb. The sounds of these letters are divine sounds possessing distinctive qualities known only to the Prophet (peace be upon him), having resonated in his ear in a special way during revelation. These sounds have also been regarded as a name for the Quran or the surah.

The expression "That is the Book," which follows these letters, introduces the Quran revealed with these extraordinary sounds. Here, the word "book" denotes both the wording (composition/nazm) and the meaning together. The Quran does not consist merely of meaning; rather, this unique composition that Allah revealed to our Prophet (peace be upon him) is a book that is both recited and written. Among Muslims, when "the book" is mentioned, the Noble Quran is the first thing that comes to mind.

At the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah, Elmalılı emphasizes that the Quran is a book in which there is no doubt (rayb). Rayb encompasses not only doubt, but also ill suspicion and accusation. With this verse, Allah has removed both intellectual and moral doubt, demonstrating the perfection of the book. Addressing the Prophet (peace be upon him), it was communicated that he should have no anxiety in this regard, and his trustworthiness in both receiving and conveying the revelation was confirmed.

Those who doubt the truth of the Quran fall into two categories: either stubborn disbelievers combined with ignorance, or hypocrites who have made doubt a habitual disposition in everything. Their doubts are entirely baseless and unjustified. Subsequent verses (such as al-Baqarah 2:23 and al-An'am 6:93) will defend and substantiate this matter in greater detail.

In terms of theology (kalam) and philosophy, this beginning points to epistemology (theory of knowledge). In Islamic creed (aqa'id), the principle 'the realities of things are firmly established' refutes the Sophists (skeptics). The Quran is the greatest remedy against both theoretical and moral skepticism. The greatest ailment of humanity is doubt, and by eliminating it, the Quran demonstrates the true path.

The Book is guidance for the God-fearing (muttaqun). Guidance (hidayah) is used in two senses: showing the way and conveying one to the destination. The Quran's guidance is related to direction and counsel (irshad); whereas granting success (tawfiq) is an act of Allah. The Quran was sent down as a general guidance for everyone, yet benefiting from it depends on human will and the capacity for piety (taqwa). The God-fearing are those who possess the capacity for self-restraint and caution, and they are the ones who will receive the true share of guidance.

Piety (taqwa/ittiqa) has three degrees: the first is to believe by shunning polytheism (shirk); the second is to avoid major sins and fulfill obligatory duties (fara'id); the third is to attain complete devotion by detaching the heart from everything that distracts it from Allah. This final degree is the lofty rank attained also by the prophets. Taqwa is not merely a negative abstinence, but also an active embrace of righteous deeds. The guidance of the Quran encompasses all of these degrees.

The first four verses of Surah al-Baqarah are like the answer to the prayer 'Guide us' in al-Fatihah. Through four harmonious sentences, these verses articulate the Quran's eternality, its truths, its epistemic character, and its objective of guidance. Ascending from three letters to three names, and from there to three concise sentences, this composition is a beautiful example of the harmony within the Quran.

One of the attributes of the God-fearing is belief in the unseen (ghayb). Ghayb is the realm that cannot be seen yet is real. Everything we perceive with our senses is, in fact, a manifestation of unseen movements. As Imam al-Ghazali also stated, things like light and sound are not separate external entities, but occurrences created at the moment of contact with our senses. Reality is grasped through intellect and inner insight (basirah).

Allah Almighty is not the absolute unseen; He is the source of all things seen and unseen. He will be seen with the eyes in the Hereafter, yet He cannot be fully comprehended. This is the creed of the Ahl al-Sunnah. The vision of Allah will occur transcendent of direction and spatial location, nor will seeing Him constitute total comprehension.

The word 'ghayb' mentioned in the Quran means not only that which is unseen, but also that which has not yet been seen. We Muslims believe in the unseen that is supported by evidence and aligned with reason. For example, the past and the future are invisible today, but the future may be seen tomorrow. Belief in Allah, the angels, and the Hereafter is likewise; there are rational and traditional proofs for their existence.

The world is like a narrow isthmus between the past and the future. At present, man perceives only the events passing through this isthmus. Yet there are also realms of the unseen in the past and the future. Beyond these lies a supreme power that encompasses all things. Thus, the God-fearing (those mindful of Allah) believe in the Lord of these seen and unseen realms.

There are two types of the unseen: The first consists of unseen realities for which there is no evidence and which are known only to Allah. The second consists of unseen realities for which evidence exists, which are intended by the verse's statement, 'they believe in the unseen.' These are the articles of faith, such as Allah, the Hereafter, the angels, the prophets, and the scriptures. This faith is attained sometimes through intuitive discernment and experiential unveiling (kashf), and sometimes through rational proofs.

The word ghayb (the unseen) derives from the root ghaybah (absence from sight). Gha'ib (absent), on the other hand, refers to that which is not present, neither appearing to you nor seeing you. Ghayb, however, cannot be seen, yet it sees. When ghayb is applied to Allah, it is because He cannot be seen, yet He sees all things.

In lexical terms, faith (iman) means 'to feel secure' and 'to affirm'. As a religious term, it is to affirm with the heart and declare with the tongue the oneness of Allah, the prophethood of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and the definitive knowledge he brought. The most concise expression of this faith is the declaration of faith (kalimah al-tawhid), while its broader expression is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, divine decree (qadar), and resurrection after death.

Islamic scholars have advanced differing views regarding the nature of faith. According to the Kharijites and the Mu'tazilites, faith consists of heart, tongue, and deed. According to the Karramiyyah, it is solely declaration with the tongue. The Ash'arites take affirmation of the heart as the essential basis and make declaration with the tongue a requisite condition. The Hanafis, however, define faith as affirmation of the heart and declaration with the tongue; they regard deeds not as an integral part of faith, but as its fruit.

According to Imam al-A'zam Abu Hanifa, faith is declaration with the tongue and affirmation of the heart. Mere verbal declaration would have necessitated accepting the faith of the hypocrites; mere knowledge, on the other hand, would have necessitated accepting the faith of the People of the Book. Yet Allah has revealed that the hypocrites are liars and that the People of the Book did not believe despite knowing the truth. As for deeds, they are separate from faith; they serve the perfection of faith. A Muslim cannot conceal his faith unless under compulsion; however, in situations of mortal danger, he may practice precautionary dissimulation (taqiyyah).

The foremost attribute of the god-fearing (muttaqin), who guard against disobeying Allah, is that they establish prayer. That is, not merely performing the prayer, but establishing it uprightly, fulfilling its conditions, observing it with reverence (khushu'), and maintaining it steadfastly. This serves as a reminder that prayer is the pillar of religion. When performed in congregation, prayer is like a column that sustains society.

The benefits of prayer are innumerable: purity, strength of heart, the ordering of time, and social rectification, among others. In particular, prostration shatters arrogance and instills humility in a person. Prayer is an ascension (mi'raj) that lifts the believer from human frailties and elevates him toward Allah.

The word salah signifies supplication and physical movement (moving the haunches). In Islam, prayer is a comprehensive act of worship performed with the heart, tongue, and body, possessing specific conditions and essential pillars. It has been detailed in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh) along with its obligations (fard), necessary duties (wajib), sunnah practices, and other rulings.

The god-fearing do not confine themselves to bodily acts of worship alone; they also spend from their wealth. Provision (rizq) encompasses everything from which benefit is derived, while spending (infaq) means expending in the path of Allah. At the forefront of this stands zakah. Zakah is the bridge of Islam and the foremost representative of financial acts of worship.

Zakah bridges the chasm between the rich and the poor, establishing bonds of love and brotherhood in society. When giving zakah, a Muslim regards himself as a distributor appointed by Allah. In this way, prayer and zakah, as the primary practices of faith, form the essence of all other acts of worship.

The god-fearing believe both in what has been revealed to you (the Quran) and in the scriptures revealed before you. This necessitates faith in all of Allah's prophets. Islam stands as a witness over all heavenly religions and confirms previous scriptures. In this respect, Islam is a universal and comprehensive religion.

While most past religions granted no right of existence to anyone outside themselves, Islam approaches everyone with tolerance. In our times, humanity suffers under the claim of asserting dominance over truth. Salvation, however, is possible only by submitting to the absolute sovereignty of the True Lord (al-Haqq). Indeed, the heart of Islam moves with this broad conscience and faith.

Those who will possess certain knowledge regarding the Hereafter are exclusively the god-fearing who possess this expansive faith. The conjectures about the Hereafter held by those who believe in some prophets and reject others, such as the Jews and Christians, can never attain the degree of certainty (yaqin). For the Hereafter is among the matters of the unseen (ghayb) and can only be known through the truthful reports of the prophets sent by Allah. The one who completed this report is the final Prophet, Muhammad (peace be upon him). The belief in the Hereafter of those who believe in past prophets but do not believe in the final Prophet and the scripture and Sacred Law revealed to him likewise does not conform to truth. Such corrupted beliefs can only be rectified through faith in the proclamations of Muhammad (peace be upon him), whereby true and certain knowledge of the Hereafter is attained.

The life of the Hereafter is entirely distinct from the life of this world, and the scientific laws of this world are not suitable for grasping all of its subtleties. The blessings of the Hereafter are eternal and devoid of sorrow; while some resemble those of this world, there are also things that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. Knowing the reality of the Hereafter depends upon knowing the foundation of truth. Science and knowledge demonstrate that the Hereafter is not a rationally absurd impossibility, that today has a tomorrow, and that we must prepare for it. Yet what that tomorrow will be like is known only to Allah, and can only be reported by the prophets who are granted knowledge of the unseen.

'Iqan (certainty / yaqin) means definitive knowledge that conforms to reality and is unadulterated by doubt. Certainty has degrees: mathematical and logical knowledge is certain and necessary; empirical sciences (such as chemistry and physics), though not necessary, are certain. However, particular opinions derived through erroneous deductions from these sciences are not certain. Certainty is not confined merely to necessary and intuitive knowledge; what is witnessed, experienced, transmitted via mass corroboration (tawatur), and arrived at through sound deductive reasoning also yields certainty. Our firm conviction regarding Allah's power must never be abandoned while pursuing the sciences, nor should necessary certainties be sacrificed for the sake of ordinary certainties. Everything is possible by Allah's leave; in order not to be bewildered when confronted with the emergence of things previously deemed impossible, we must hold firmly to the principles of definitive faith.

'Muflihun' derives from the root falah; it means cleaving through obstacles to attain deliverance and achieve what is desired—that is, those who attain salvation. Here, through the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) 'hum', it is understood that muflihun is designated exclusively for the god-fearing who abide upon guidance. That is to say, salvation belongs solely to those who fear Allah, believe, and perform righteous deeds. For those who believe yet abandon acts of worship, their salvation is neither complete nor perfect; nevertheless, on account of their faith, one does not despair of Allah's mercy. This verse shows that salvation (falah) depends on guidance (hidayah), and guidance depends on mindfulness of Allah (taqwa); this dependency is not an inevitable causal relationship of necessity, but a manifestation of Allah's grace and mercy.

Lexically, kufr (disbelief) means to cover a blessing—that is, ingratitude. In religion, it is the antithesis of faith (iman) and entails denying, rejecting, or failing to affirm that which must be believed. Disbelief may be of the heart, verbal, or practical. Practical disbelief consists of committing acts incompatible with faith, such as worshipping idols or insulting the Quran. The abandonment of deeds, on the other hand, is of two types: partial abandonment (occasional omission) may not constitute disbelief; however, completely abandoning deeds or making the neglect of prayer a habit can constitute disbelief. Faith requires indivisible wholeness; when a part of it is rejected, disbelief occurs. There is no middle ground between faith and disbelief; a person is either a believer or a disbeliever.

Allah has sealed the hearts and hearing of those who disbelieve, and over their eyes is a veil. This sealing (khatm) signifies that they will not accept guidance. 'Khatm' means to seal and solidify something or to bring it to an end. This verse announces that those who persist in disbelief will no longer find the right path and will suffer a tremendous punishment. While the preceding verses describe guidance and salvation for the God-fearing (muttaqin), here the condition of the disbelievers is explained by way of contrast.

The concept of the heart carries both physical and spiritual meanings. The physical heart is the pinecone-shaped piece of flesh located in the chest that enables blood circulation. The spiritual heart, on the other hand, is the center of consciousness, conscience, feeling, and thought. In the Quran and Islamic sciences, when the heart is mentioned, it is generally this second meaning that is intended. Faith, disbelief, and knowing Allah are related to this heart. Sealed hearts are the hearts of those who cannot perceive the truth and are trapped in their own desires.

Allah has sealed the hearts and hearing of those whose disbelief has become manifest, and placed a veil over their eyes. Therefore, whether you warn them or do not warn them, they will not believe. In the verse, hearts and eyes are mentioned in the plural, whereas hearing is brought in the singular. The reason for this is an indication that in faith, the paths of reflection and sight are many, while the path of hearing is singular (the center of prophethood). These people are now deprived of all three means of knowledge required to comprehend the truth: heart and intellect, sound senses, and hearing the report.

The sealing of the heart occurs when sins become a habit. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When a sin is committed for the first time, a black spot forms on the heart. If the person repents and turns to Allah, the heart becomes polished. When the sin is repeated, the stain increases and eventually covers the entire heart.' This is indeed the seal mentioned in the verse. This seal is a second nature acquired through the servant's own earning. Its creation belongs to Allah, yet it does not come to pass without the servant's earning. This point explains the secret of the matter of morality and upbringing.

These verses also shed light on the subject of predestination and compulsion. Allah's eternal knowledge does not compel a person. Although Allah knew that the disbelievers would not believe, He held them responsible for having faith. For, by virtue of their initial creation, they had the capacity to believe. However, after acquiring the habit of disbelief, they become incapable of doing so. This responsibility is according to the initial creation. There is no compulsion here; according to the Ahl al-Sunnah, the creation of actions belongs to Allah, while their acquisition belongs to the servant.

The occasion of revelation for these verses is the Jews and hypocrites in Medina. Among the Jews, just as there were those who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, there were also those who persisted in obstinacy. The hypocrites, on the other hand, were certain individuals from the Aws and Khazraj tribes, whose leader was Abdullah ibn Ubayy. They were outwardly Muslim while harboring hostility within. For this reason, the verses at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah introduce three groups of people: believers, disbelievers, and hypocrites.

The hypocrites say, 'We have believed in Allah and the Last Day,' though they do not believe. They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they deceive none but themselves. In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased their disease. When it is said to them, 'Do not cause corruption on the earth,' they say, 'We are only peacemakers.' In truth, they are the very corruptors themselves. When they are asked to believe as the believers have believed, they say, 'Shall we believe as those fools have believed?' In truth, they themselves are the fools, but they do not know.

When the hypocrites meet the believers, they say, 'We believe,' but when they are alone with their devils (their disbelieving friends), they say, 'We are with you; we were only mocking them.' Allah mocks them and gives them respite to wander blindly in their transgression. They have purchased error in exchange for guidance; their transaction has brought no profit, nor have they been guided. Their situation is like that of someone who kindles a fire: just as it illuminates his surroundings, Allah takes away their light and leaves them in darkness. Or they are like those caught in a rainstorm pouring from the sky, accompanied by darkness, thunder, and lightning; they thrust their fingers into their ears in terror of the thunderbolts. Allah encompasses them at every moment. Had He willed, He could have completely taken away their hearing and sight.

Consciousness (shu'ur) in human beings is of two kinds: overt feeling and covert feeling. Overt feeling relates to the external senses, while covert feeling relates to conscience. Conscience is a kind of 'consciousness of consciousness.' Intellect, however, begins behind consciousness and deals with its prior state, its posterior state, and its inner reality. Consciousness is an instantaneous and simple state of unity, whereas the intellect engages in the synthesis and analysis of this consciousness. In the hearts of the hypocrites, there is an unprecedented spiritual disease.

This disease is that of disbelief, doubt, and hypocrisy. The hypocrites doubt everything, even themselves. They imagine truth and reality to consist solely of themselves. For this reason, they regard deceit and trickery as a mark of superiority. Yet this disease is curable; however, they do not hold fast to the true religion and doubt it as well.

Allah Almighty has increased this disease. For they rejected the truth brought by the prophet and became obstinate. Because of this, Allah firmly entrenched the disease in their hearts and increased it more and more. For that reason, they began resorting to trickery against Allah and the believers. In the Hereafter, this disease will cause them a most painful punishment.

When it is said to the hypocrites, 'Do not cause corruption on the earth,' they say, 'We are only reformers.' In truth, they are the very corruptors themselves, but they are not aware of it. They mistake the corruption they commit for reform. Furthermore, when it is said, 'Believe as these people have believed,' they refuse to accept equality, saying, 'Shall we believe as those fools have believed?'

Whereas in reality, they themselves are the fools (sufaha'), yet they do not know it. The hypocrites consider faith foolishness and look down upon the believers. Yet knowledge is a matter of certainty (yaqin); it is attained not through doubt, but through true faith. They, however, are filled with doubt from beginning to end, and for this reason possess neither consciousness nor knowledge.

When the hypocrites meet the believers, they flatter them saying, 'We believe,' but when they meet secretly with their devils (devils among humans and jinn), they say, 'We are with you; we are only mocking them.' According to a narration, when Abdullah ibn Ubayy saw Abu Bakr, Umar, and Ali, he praised them and then told his companions, 'This is how we ward off the fools'; whereupon this verse was revealed. The verse exposes the inner reality of the hypocrites and the covert forces behind them (the polytheist leaders and Jewish rabbis).

The word shaytan (devil) is a generic noun used for evil, obstinate beings that exceed all bounds in transgression. It has categories such as human devils, animal devils, and jinn devils. According to Sibawayh, it derives from the meaning of 'remoteness' (remote from truth), while according to another view, it means 'burned' or 'futile.' The human devil is visible, but his deviltry is hidden; the jinn devil, however, is a completely concealed evil force. The devils mentioned in the verse, in addition to the leaders of the hypocrites, are the polytheist leaders and Jewish scholars.

Allah mocks the hypocrites; this mockery takes the form of sentencing them in this world to suffer inner torment while being treated as Muslims, and in the Hereafter to be disgraced in the lowest depths of the Fire. Divine mockery is a humiliation, yet it embodies justice; Allah turns them into a laughingstock by leaving them unchecked in their transgression. This verse was revealed to calm the agitation of the believers and to teach patience.

The hypocrites have purchased misguidance in exchange for guidance (the right path); this trade of theirs has brought no profit. For guidance is the capital of all capitals; to lose it and acquire error is to destroy both capital and profit. In contrast to the righteous, this verse shows the end of the hypocrites and emphasizes the importance of adhering to the law of honesty in trade. The two parables that follow were revealed to explain this state better.

The first parable: The state of the hypocrites resembles a man who kindles a fire; when the fire illuminates his surroundings, Allah takes away their light of sight and leaves them in darkness. They become deaf, dumb, and blind; they can never find the right path again. This symbolizes the blindness of the hypocrites' inner sight in the face of the illumination of the Prophet's call.

The second parable: The hypocrites are like people caught in a downpour falling from the sky. Within the rain are darkness, thunder, and lightning. Out of fear of death, they thrust their fingers into their ears. Allah encompasses the disbelievers from every side. This parable describes the dread and flight that the warnings and glad tidings of the Quran evoke in the hypocrites.

The state of the hypocrites is likened to a rainstorm laden with thunder and lightning. They thrust their fingers into their ears for fear of death, fleeing from the thunderclaps. Yet Allah encompasses the disbelievers on all sides; there is no escaping His punishment. The One Who must truly be feared is Allah, and true duty lies in obeying His commands.

Thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts are actually three distinct manifestations of a single phenomenon. According to the religious explanation, there is an angel who drives the clouds, called 'ra'd' (thunder). This angel glorifies Allah, and as he shouts, he casts fire from his mouth; lightning is thus these whips of fire, and the thunderbolt is his strike. All of these occurrences simply consist of executing Allah's command.

Natural sciences also explain these phenomena through electrical discharge. When positively and negatively charged clouds come together, lightning and thunder are produced. These explanations do not contradict the angelic force described by religion; on the contrary, they demonstrate the existence of a motive force. Both explanations essentially point to the same reality: Allah's power.

Whenever lightning flashes, the hypocrites walk in its light, but when darkness descends upon them, they stand completely still. Had Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight as well. For Allah is capable of all things. Power (qudrah) is the ability to choose and execute; unlike blind force, it does not imply necessity or compulsion. Allah does whatever He wills, and nothing can incapacitate Him.

These verses lay bare the indecision and hypocrisy of the hypocrites. They appear as though they want to benefit from Islam, but at the moment of danger, they flee. Yet true salvation lies in having faith in Allah and submitting to Him. A human being can be protected from Allah's punishment only by serving Him. Plugging one's ears after the lightning has struck is of no use; precautions must be taken beforehand.

After explaining the classes of people and their capacities for guidance at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah, Allah addresses all of mankind in the 21st verse and issues His first command: Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, that you may be protected. This command emphasizes the foundations of tawhid (divine oneness) and worship, which are the bedrock of Islam. Worship is a requirement of creation and an expression of gratitude; however, without Allah's grace, protection cannot be guaranteed—it can only be hoped for.

In the 22nd verse, Allah's blessings are enumerated: the earth as a couch, the sky as a canopy, rain, and provision. All of these blessings are manifestations of Allah's mercy. While people know all this, they must not set up rivals to Allah, nor accept partners alongside Him. The word 'andad' shows that everything equated with Allah is in truth fabricated and false.

In the 23rd verse, a challenge is issued to those who doubt: If you are in doubt that the Quran has come from Allah, produce a surah like it. This is the 'tahaddi' (challenge), which is the greatest miracle of the Prophet's prophethood. The peerless eloquence and content of the Quran constitute a miracle such that no human being could ever produce its like, and this fact has been established by experience across the centuries.

In the 24th verse, the outcome of this challenge is declared: If you cannot produce it—and you never will—then beware of the Fire of Hell whose fuel is men and stones. This fire has been prepared for the disbelievers. The word 'hijarah' mentioned in the verse may refer to idols as well as substances such as coal. This demonstrates the scientific aspect of the Quran.

In the 25th verse, glad tidings are given to those who believe and perform righteous deeds: for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow. There, they will say that the fruits offered to them resemble those of the world, but in truth they are far superior. The blessings in Paradise are the recompense for righteous deeds performed in this world, and they are eternal. Addressed to the Prophet, it is commanded that he proclaim this glad tiding.

While describing the blessings of Paradise, pure spouses are mentioned. In these spouses, none of the worldly impurities exist; neither physical impurities such as menstruation and postpartum bleeding, nor moral defects such as immorality and discord are to be found. The Islamic land in this world should also be like such a paradise, yet the essential difference is this: the worldly homeland is transient and can be lost, whereas the Paradise of the Hereafter is eternal, and those who enter it will never depart. All glad tidings and bliss reside in this eternity.

Some object to the mention of provision and women in these glad tidings; however, the pleasures of the Hereafter are not identical to those of this world, but vastly superior. The use of parables—that is, examples—in the Quran is also full of wisdom. Allah does not shy away from presenting a mosquito as an example. Those who believe know that these parables are the truth from their Lord; those who disbelieve mock, saying, 'What did Allah intend by this example?' Allah misguides many by these examples and guides many aright; yet those He misguides are only the defiantly disobedient (fasiqun).

The defiantly disobedient (fasiqun) are those who break Allah's covenant, sever kinship ties, and spread corruption on earth. In the lexicon, fisq means 'to depart' or 'to step out'; in religious terminology, it denotes departing from obedience to Allah by committing major sins. Fisq has three degrees: committing sins occasionally, committing them persistently, and committing them without regarding the sin as abhorrent. This third degree is disbelief (kufr). The defiantly disobedient in this verse are mentioned with their straying that amounts to disbelief.

How can you be ungrateful to Allah? When you were dead, He brought you to life; then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life again, and finally to Him you will be returned. In these two verses, the purpose of life, the worth of man, and Allah's grace are summarized. Whatever is on the earth was created entirely for you. Then Allah directed Himself to the heaven and fashioned them into seven heavens. In the face of these blessings, what a grave error disbelief and denial are!

Allah created everything on the earth for human beings to benefit from and made them inherently permissible. However, the lives, honor, and property of people are not permissible to one another; violating them is a major sin. Humans were created not for one another, but to worship Allah. For this reason, a person cannot even dispose of his own life as he pleases. The legal maxim in Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh) that 'the default status of things is permissibility' is derived from this verse.

Allah did not create man merely as a being who would live on the earth and benefit from the things upon it. He also allotted man a share from the heavens, and even made alterations across the seven heavens for this purpose. For this reason, man is not a creature belonging solely to the earth; if he feels constricted on earth, he is permitted to benefit from the heavens. For this, his soul must first experience celestial feelings and come to know Allah. Those who drown in earthly lusts and animalistic baseness, however, are deprived of this elevation.

The mention in the Quran of the ordering of the heavens after the creation of the earth is a sequence in terms of narrative order, not in terms of time. Human perception takes man as its center; it first recognizes the earth that is close, and then the heaven. For this reason, this sequence is followed in the verses. There are two main views regarding the 'seven heavens': One orders the seven layers of heaven from an astronomical perspective starting from the earth up to the planets; the other states that the physical heaven is the first heaven, beyond which lie six more spiritual heavens. These spiritual heavens pertain to the angels and divine commands.

After these explanations, Allah informs the angels that He will create a vicegerent (khalifah) on the earth. 'Khalifah' means a deputy who succeeds someone and exercises authority on their behalf. The angels ask, 'Will You place therein one who will cause corruption and shed blood?' This question is not an objection, but an inquiry to understand the underlying wisdom. Furthermore, the angels recall that they glorify and sanctify Allah. Allah, however, replies, 'Indeed, I know that which you do not know.'

Thereafter, Allah teaches Adam all the names, shows them to the angels, and says, 'Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful.' The angels say, 'Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us.' When Adam informs them of their names, Allah reminds the angels that He knows the unseen. Then, the angels are commanded to prostrate before Adam; all of them prostrate except Iblis. Iblis behaves arrogantly and disbelieves. Adam and his wife are settled in Paradise, yet Satan deceives them, causing their expulsion from Paradise. Allah opens the gate of repentance and accepts Adam's repentance. Humanity descends to earth in mutual enmity, and those who follow the guidance that comes from Allah attain salvation.

This narrative encompasses many beginnings: the beginning of human reproduction, religion, knowledge, language, duty and brotherhood, and law. It is emphasized that there is no original sin in human nature, and that sin and enmity occur subsequently through external factors. It recounts Satan's enmity toward man, and that man can struggle against this enmity by embracing and remaining true to his own innate disposition. The importance of repentance and man's high potential are recalled. Man was created as a product of the earth and the heavens, indeed as a grand microcosm; the means for all his happiness have been prepared. Man must now shake himself free from this base life, remember the blessings, attain the heights of his soul, and prepare for the Hereafter.

There are important explanations from Elmalılı's tafsir regarding the duties of the angels and their roles in the realm of existence. The angels, who express the diffusion of Allah's act of creation from unity into multiplicity, are messengers who convey divine commands, as well as beings who actively bring strength and assistance. No event in the universe occurs without an angel; for this reason, not even a drop of rain falls without an angel. Angels should be conceived of as constructive principles.

Philosophers and theologians (mutakallimun) have expressed different views regarding the nature of angels. According to the first view, angels are subtle bodies pertaining to the ether, possessing the power to change shape. The second view states that they are immaterial substances, resembling the human soul yet being more perfect. In the hadiths narrated from the Prophet (peace be upon him), the multitude of angels and the vast manifestations of Allah's power are described; so much so that up to the seventh heaven, each layer contains many times more angels than the previous ones.

When Allah informed the angels that He would create a vicegerent on earth, the angels asked: 'Will You place therein one who will cause corruption and shed blood?'
