They expressed that they glorify and sanctify Allah. The Lord's response was: 'Indeed, I know that which you do not know.' This response indicates that there are aspects regarding the wisdom and reasons for the vicegerency (khilafah) of which the angels are unaware.

Allah taught Adam all the names. There are various interpretations regarding what these names were. According to some, they are the names of all beings (human, animal, mountain, sea, etc.); according to others, the names of the angels; and according to still others, the names of Adam's descendants. Adam's learning of the names demonstrates how vital language and the attribute of speech (kalam) are for the vicegerency. The most prominent characteristic distinguishing man from other beings is this linguistic faculty.

When the angels were unable to know the names taught to Adam, they admitted their inability and said, 'Subhanaka, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us.' Thereupon, Allah commanded Adam to inform them of those names, and Adam recited the names one by one. This demonstrated that Adam was worthy of the vicegerency and that the attributes of knowledge and speech were decisive in this regard.

The commentary also dwells on the origin of the name 'Adam'. Some scholars have stated that this name is not Arabic, but rather means 'earth' or 'soil' in Hebrew or Syriac. In Arabic, it is stated to be a diptote (ghayr munsarif) because it is used as a proper noun. These explanations emphasize the significance of Adam's personality and his place in human history.

Elmalılı explains the linguistic origin of the name Adam. He notes that the word Adam is used as a common noun in Arabic, and that it also appears in similar forms in Hebrew and Syriac. It is also related in some sources that Adam was called by different names in different languages. The most accurate view is that the name Adam is a word belonging to the primordial language of humanity.

Allah commands the angels to prostrate before Adam. The angels immediately prostrate, with the exception of Iblis. Iblis, however, displays arrogance and disobeys the command. In reality, Iblis is of the jinn and among the disbelievers. His disbelief is not merely disobedience, but at the same time a disdain for Allah's command and a presumption of his own superiority.

Prostration (sajdah) is the highest degree of humility and reverence. The angels' prostration to Adam was not an act of worship toward Adam, but obedience to Allah's command and an act of service to the station of vicegerency. Through this prostration, the angels were tasked with assisting Adam. Human beings, as the children of Adam, have undertaken this very same duty of vicegerency.

Allah commands Adam and his wife to dwell in Paradise and eat and drink freely therein as they please, but not to approach a specific tree. This prohibition delineates man's boundaries. What the tree was is not explained in the Quran; there are reports that it was wheat, grape, or fig. What is important is that this prohibition was instituted as a test and for servitude.

Satan causes them to be expelled from Paradise by deceiving them into eating from this tree. Thereupon, Allah informs them to descend to the earth and that they will live as enemies to one another. Yet, a temporary enjoyment on earth is also ordained. This descent marks the beginning of human history.

Adam realizes his mistake and repents by receiving certain words from his Lord. Allah accepts his repentance and shows His mercy. Repentance (tawbah) means turning back from the state of sin to one's primordial nature (fitrah). Allah is the Accepter of Repentance, the Merciful.

Allah does not revoke the command to descend to the earth, but He promises to send guidance from Himself. Whoever follows this guidance, there shall be no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve. And whoever denies Allah's verses, they will abide in the Fire eternally. This is the beginning of humanity's journey of vicegerency (khilafah).

The address at the end of the story of Adam encompasses all of humanity. Adam and Eve, along with their offspring, represent an entire genus. The descent to the earth took place in multiplicity, and since we existed in the loins of Adam as an idea, we are included in this address. Human beings are fundamentally brethren, and this story emphasizes the common origin of humanity.

In this context, Elmalılı also touches upon the subject of creation and evolution. He maintains that the theory of evolution has not been scientifically proven, and that humans were created directly by Allah, not from apes. All humans are descendants of Adam and are brethren. The exact time of Adam's descent to the earth is not certain; it may have occurred hundreds of thousands of years ago. These views are the explanations presented in Elmalılı's tafsir.

Following this story, Almighty Allah directs a specific address to the Children of Israel, who are the People of the Book. In verse 40, it is stated: "O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and fulfill your covenant with Me so that I will fulfill My covenant with you, and fear only Me." This favor is the scripture and prophethood given to them, as well as believing in the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), who was heralded in the Torah. Their covenant was to follow the final prophet who was to be sent.

In verse 41, they are commanded to believe in the Quran which confirms the Torah in their possession, not to be the first to disbelieve in it, and not to exchange Allah's verses for a small worldly gain. In verse 42, they are forbidden from mixing truth with falsehood and concealing it, and from knowingly confounding truth with falsehood. This verse prohibits fraud in knowledge and action, distortion (tahrif), and presenting falsehood as truth.

In verse 43, they are commanded to establish prayer, give zakah, and bow with those who bow (the Muslim congregation). Ruku (bowing) is an act of worship specific to Islamic prayer, pointing to the importance of the congregation. In verse 44, they are rebuked for commanding people to do good while forgetting themselves. This addresses scholars and leaders in particular; counseling others while not practicing it oneself is a great contradiction. In a hadith narrated in al-Bukhari and Muslim, it is reported that on the Day of Resurrection, such a person will be turned around in Hellfire.

In verse 45, it is commanded to seek help from Allah through patience and prayer. Patience is the key to every distress, while prayer provides spiritual and physical discipline. Fasting also accustoms one to patience. These acts of worship deliver man from hardship and serve as a means to divine assistance. Patience and prayer protect a person from evils such as lying, deception, and concealing the truth.

Patience and prayer are the ways of seeking Allah's help. This is not difficult except for those who possess humility (khushu')—that is, the reverent who know that they will meet their Lord and return to Him. They possess this awareness through certainty (yaqin) or preponderant conviction, and through this, patience and prayer bring them delight.

O Children of Israel! Remember My favor that I bestowed upon you and that I favored you over the worlds. And beware of a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will a ransom be taken, nor will they be helped. This warning is directed especially at the disbelievers and emphasizes that intercession is invalid without Allah's permission.

The first favor: We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh. They were subjecting you to the worst of torment, slaughtering your sons and letting your women live. In that was a tremendous trial from your Lord. The expression 'people of Pharaoh' indicates that the primary responsibility for the oppression belonged to those who followed him.

The second favor: We parted the sea and delivered you, and drowned the people of Pharaoh in the water. The third favor: We made an appointment with Moses (Musa) for forty nights, yet you took the calf for worship in his absence and became wrongdoers. Then We pardoned you, so that you might give thanks.

The fourth favor: We gave Moses the scripture and the criterion (furqan). The fifth favor: Moses said to you, 'Slay your selves'; this was better for your repentance, and Allah accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepter of Repentance, the Merciful. This event describes the eradication of the corruption of the calf and the application of the criterion.

The sixth favor: You said, 'We will never believe you until we see Allah openly,' so the thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on. Then We revived you after your death so that you might give thanks.

In this section, it is recounted that the affliction of the thunderbolt befell the Children of Israel when they demanded to see Allah openly from Prophet Moses, after which they were revived. Although this incident occurred not to the entire people but to the chosen seventy men, it was attributed to the whole people because responsibility was collective. This demonstrates that in divine law, in matters such as communal obligations (fard al-kifayah), the community is more important than the individual. This attitude of refusing to believe without seeing Allah is a great disbelief and ingratitude. This incident contains an important lesson regarding the states of ascent and decline of human beings.

Among the favors recalled thereafter are the shading of clouds over them in the wilderness of Tih and the sending down of manna and quails. Although they were told, 'Eat of the good provisions,' they showed ingratitude by hoarding and storing them up, and for this reason the blessing ceased. Later, the command was given: 'Enter this city, enter through the gate prostrating and say, "hittah" (forgive our sins), and We will forgive your transgressions.' However, the wrongdoers altered the word, saying another word instead of 'hittah,' and because of this, a foul torment was sent down upon them.

One of these favors was the gushing forth of twelve springs when Moses struck the rock with his staff. This miracle ensured that water was provided separately to the twelve tribes of the Children of Israel. The incident demonstrates the importance of acting in accordance with the divine command following supplication. Allah creates means, and for this reason, when a physical effort such as striking the rock with a staff was combined with spiritual supplication, the miracle occurred. From this, it is understood that one must supplicate to Allah from the heart and resort to the means that are inspired.

Later, the Children of Israel stated that they were tired of a single kind of food and demanded vegetables, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions. Moses said to them, 'Do you wish to exchange what is superior for what is inferior? Go down to a town, and you will find what you want.' This request of theirs was rooted in a vile desire, such as longing for slavery in Egypt. Because of this, the stamp of humiliation and misery was struck upon them, and they incurred the wrath of Allah. The reason for this was that they disbelieved in the verses of Allah and killed the prophets unjustly.

Lastly, it is stated that whoever among the believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians truly believes in Allah and the Last Day and works righteousness, they will have their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear upon them, nor will they grieve. Here, it is emphasized that after Prophet Muhammad was sent as a prophet, true faith also encompasses believing in him. Since even those who believed in previous prophets were obligated to believe in the coming prophet, this verse indicates that they, too, must believe in the final prophet.

The Quran divides the concept of faith (iman) into outward and true. The prophethood of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is historically self-evident; denying it is a contradiction. In the verse, it is stated that whoever truly believes in Allah and the Last Day and works righteousness—including Jews, Christians, and Sabians—there shall be no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve. Although outward faith is sufficient for the formation of the Islamic community, true salvation is tied to complete faith and righteous deeds.

The word Yahudi (Jew) is derived in Arabic from repenting or from the name Judah. Nasara (Christians) traces back to Nazareth, the hometown of Jesus, or to tanasur, meaning mutual assistance. Sabi'in (Sabians), on the other hand, means those who change their religion, referring to groups that worship angels or stars.

A covenant was taken from the Children of Israel to hold firmly to the scripture by raising Mount Tur above them. Yet they turned back on their word. Those among them who violated the Sabbath were struck by Allah's wrath and transformed into apes. This incident is recounted as a lesson and an admonition for past and future generations. Commentators are divided into two views on whether this transformation was physical or spiritual.

Moses informed his people that Allah commanded them to slaughter a cow. Making a mockery of this, his people repeatedly questioned the cow's attributes. Allah stated that it was a cow neither old nor young, bright yellow, unyoked to the plow, and unblemished. Eventually, they found and slaughtered it, though they had almost failed to do so.

The Children of Israel had killed a man and cast the blame upon one another. Allah commanded them to strike the dead man with a piece of the slaughtered cow; the dead man came back to life and revealed his killer. Afterward, their hearts hardened, becoming like stone or even harder; yet from stones rivers gush forth, and some fall down out of the fear of Allah. Allah is not unaware of what they do. This story is a miracle demonstrating that resurrection after death is possible.

Addressing the Children of Israel, Allah informs that despite all these miracles, their hearts hardened, becoming like stone or even harder. Yet from some stones rivers gush forth, some split open and water seeps out, and some fall down out of the fear of Allah. But their hearts remain utterly unaffected by revelation. Allah is not unaware of what they do.

The believers hoped that these hard-hearted people would come to faith. In truth, a faction of them would hear the Word of Allah and knowingly distort it after having understood it. When they met the believers, they would say, 'We believe,' but when they were alone among themselves, they would reproach one another, saying: 'Do you disclose to them the truths that Allah has revealed to you so that they may use them as an argument against you? Have you no sense?' Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they disclose?

A portion of the Children of Israel are unlettered; they do not know the scripture, indulging only in wishful thinking and living in conjecture. Woe, then, to those who write the book with their own hands and then say, 'This is from Allah,' to fabricate a lie for a petty worldly gain. Woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for the guilt they have earned!

The Jews said, 'The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days.' Elmalılı transmits various narrations regarding these numbered days: such as forty days, seven days, or seven thousand years. They utter against Allah things of which they have no knowledge. In truth, whoever commits an evil deed and is encompassed by their sin, they are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein eternally. As for those who believe and perform righteous deeds, they are the companions of Paradise, abiding therein eternally. This is the definitive promise of Allah.

Remember when We took a covenant (misaq) from the Children of Israel: You shall not worship anyone except Allah; you shall show kindness to parents, relatives, orphans, and the poor; speak good words to people; establish prayer; and give zakah. Then you turned away, except for a few among you. And remember when We took another covenant: You shall not shed each other's blood, nor expel one another from your homes. You affirmed this and you were witnesses. Yet you are the very ones who kill yourselves, expel a faction of your own from their homes, and support one another against them in enmity and wrongdoing; but if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, even though expelling them was forbidden to you. Do you, then, believe in part of the scripture and disbelieve in part? The recompense for this is nothing but disgrace in this worldly life, and on the Day of Resurrection, the most severe punishment. Allah is not unaware of what you do.

These are the ones who have bought the worldly life at the price of the Hereafter. For this reason, their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be helped. And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, followed him up with messengers, gave Jesus, the son of Mary, clear signs, and supported him with the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus). Will you, then, whenever a messenger comes to you with an order that your souls do not desire, act arrogantly, rejecting some and killing others?

Bayyinah means an evidence that is clear in itself and leaves no need for any other explanation. The miracles of the prophets are evidence of this kind. The bayyinat of Jesus are his miracles that clearly demonstrate his prophethood. The name 'Isa (Jesus) derives from the Syriac 'Isho'; Maryam (Mary), on the other hand, means 'servant' in Syriac.
The explicit mention of Jesus among the prophets after Moses is because the religion of Jesus abrogated certain rulings in the Torah and constituted a distinct religion.

The concept of spirit (ruh) is addressed from three primary perspectives: spirit as the origin of motion, spirit as the source of life, and spirit as the source of perception. Motion, life, and perception are the essential attributes of the spirit. The spirit is an entity opposed to matter, imparting life, motion, and perception to living beings.

Commentators have put forward different views regarding the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus): the Spirit of Allah, the Greatest Name of Allah, the Gospel, or Gabriel. According to the most sound view, the Holy Spirit is Gabriel. Jesus was specifically supported with this spirit because Gabriel accompanied him ever since his mother's pregnancy.

The Jews mocked the invitation of our Prophet (peace be upon him) by saying, 'Our hearts are wrapped.' Allah cursed them for their disbelief. Previously, however, they had been awaiting the arrival of a prophet heralded in the Torah and praying for victory through him against the polytheists. Yet when the prophet they were waiting for arrived, they denied him out of envy and selfishness. For this reason, they incurred the wrath of Allah.

While the Jews were waiting for the end-times prophet foretold in the Torah and asserting that they would prevail through him, they denied him out of envy when that prophet arrived. Through this denial, they both deserved the former wrath and incurred a new wrath upon themselves. They were also debased by rendering void the ruling of their own scripture.

When it is said to them, 'Believe in what Allah has revealed,' they say, 'We believe only in what was revealed to us.' Yet the Quran confirms the Torah that is with them. They are asked: If you were truly believers, why did you slay the prophets of Allah before?

Moses came to you with clear proofs, then after him you worshipped the calf. We took a covenant from you by raising Mount Tur above you, and you said, 'We heard and disobeyed.' How vile are the things your faith commands you to do, that you kill prophets and disbelieve in your scripture!

Say: If the home of the Hereafter belongs to you and you are truthful in this claim, then wish for death. Yet they will never wish for it, because of the sins their hands have committed. You will find them the greediest of people for life; even greedier than the polytheists. The desire for a long life will not save them from punishment.

The meaning the Jews assign to the expression 'the abode of the Hereafter' is the ideal of establishing an earthly state. This belief of theirs is contradictory, because without believing in the true Hereafter, no sacrifice can be made for such a cause. Their fleeing from death demonstrates that these claims of theirs are false.

As for the hostility toward Gabriel, some Jews harbor enmity toward him, saying 'he brings war and violence.' Yet it is he who brought down the Quran. Allah declares that whoever is an enemy to Gabriel and Michael is a disbeliever, and that He is likewise their enemy.

The Jews harbored enmity by claiming that Allah had commanded Gabriel to deliver the prophethood to them, but that Gabriel had brought it to Muhammad (peace be upon him) instead. However, the verse informs that the true reason for this enmity is that the Quran was revealed into the heart of Muhammad (peace be upon him), and that this took place by Allah's permission. Furthermore, the Quran confirms the previous scriptures and is a source of guidance and glad tidings for the believers; therefore, harboring hostility toward Gabriel is hostility toward Allah and His scriptures.

The word "Jibril" is composed in Hebrew of "jebr" (servant) and "il" (God/Allah), meaning "Abdullah" (servant of Allah). Some commentators, however, give it the meaning of "Allah's omnipotence (jabarut)" (His majesty). In Arabic, it is recited with different variant readings (qira'at), such as Jabra'il, Jabre'il, Jabril, and Jibril. This name conveys the certainty and irresistibility of revelatory knowledge. Mentioning the angel in this manner also defines his duty: a source of knowledge possessing cognitive and practical necessity that no power can obstruct.

In the verse, it is proclaimed: "Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel—it is he who brought the Quran down upon your heart by Allah's permission." This is a warning; for Gabriel brings the Quran, which confirms the previous scriptures and provides guidance and glad tidings to the believers. Consequently, enmity toward Gabriel is regarded as enmity toward Allah, His scriptures, and His messengers. Allah, too, is an enemy to the disbelievers; their being granted respite is not a blessing, but an affliction. However, if they repent and believe, they will partake in guidance and glad tidings.

The expression "upon your heart" conveys that the revelation completely encompasses and envelops the heart. Indeed, when revelation descended, it left a heavy impact upon the Prophet (peace be upon him), to such an extent that he endured great hardship, even sweating on a cold day. This demonstrates that divine knowledge is necessary and definitive. Moreover, the expression "upon your heart" (ala qalbik) rather than "upon you" (alayk) emphasizes that the speech was uttered not by the Messenger of Allah, but by Allah Himself.

In verse 99, Allah declares that He has revealed clear verses, and that none will reject them except the defiantly disobedient (fasiq). In verse 100, it is stated that whenever they enter into a covenant, a party among them breaks it, and most of them do not believe. In verse 101, it is related that when a messenger came to them confirming the scripture they already possessed, a party of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs.

In verse 102, it is stated that they followed what the devils fabricated concerning the kingdom of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic. They also conveyed to students what had been revealed in Babylon to the two angels named Harut and Marut; yet the angels would warn, "We are only a test, so do not practice magic and become disbelievers." The magicians would learn from them that by which they cause separation between a man and his wife, yet they could not harm anyone with it except by Allah's permission. They acquired that which harmed them and brought them no share in the Hereafter. Had they only believed and been mindful of Allah, the reward from Allah would have been far better.

Linguistically, magic (sihr) means a subtle matter whose cause is hidden. In the religious sense, it is presenting truth as falsehood and falsehood as truth, illusion, and deception. The types of magic include methods such as talismans, exerting influence through spiritual force, and enlisting the aid of the jinn. However, the core issue is the relationship between magic and disbelief (kufr); teaching and practicing magic alienates one from faith. The verse underscores that those who engage in magic have no share in the Hereafter.

Types of magic are divided into four: deceiving the eye (illusion/conjuring), sleight of hand performed with mechanical devices, magic produced with chemical substances, and captivating the heart (suggestion) along with calumny (gossip and discord). These are gathered under two fundamental principles: that which is sheer falsehood and deception, and that which is more or less the abuse of truth. Magic cannot be described as entirely unreal in every instance; some of it is mingled with reality. To indicate these two categories, the verse uses first the term "magic" and subsequently "that which was revealed to Harut and Marut."

In the narrative of Harut and Marut, what was sent down to them was not actually magic, but knowledge susceptible to misuse. When teaching, they would caution, "We are but a trial, so do not fall into disbelief." The devils, however, taught it as magic and led people into disbelief. Elmalılı takes the particle "ma" in the verse not as a negative particle, but as a relative pronoun (mawzul), and notes that this aligns with the context of the verse. This knowledge was also imparted to the people of Babylon by way of inspiration, but was transformed into magic through its misuse.

The Babylonians fell into disbelief by attributing the celestial and terrestrial forces they learned from Harut and Marut to the stars. Later, the devils instigated discord against the rule of Solomon (peace be upon him) using this knowledge. The Jews, too, learned these magical practices and did things to cause separation between a husband and his wife. Yet they can cause no harm except by Allah's permission; true causal efficacy belongs to Allah alone. Those who are deceived by magic have no share in the Hereafter.

Addressing the believers: Do not say 'Ra'ina', but say 'Unzurna' and listen attentively. The Jews used this word as an insult. Furthermore, the expression 'ra'ina' carries a connotation of uncouthness and gives the false impression of mutual regard. Yet proper etiquette toward the prophet is not to watch over him, but to submit to his oversight. Believers must distance themselves from animalistic conceptions and embrace humane stewardship. This verse teaches the foundation of leadership (imamah) and social order.

The disbelievers do not wish for any good to be sent down to you from your Lord. Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills. As for the abrogation (naskh) of verses, Allah brings what is better or similar to them. Abrogation is not contrary to Allah's power; to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Do not interrogate your messenger as Moses was questioned before. Whoever exchanges faith for disbelief has strayed from the straight path.

In verse 106 of Surah al-Baqarah, it is declared that Allah may repeal the ruling of certain verses and bring what is better or similar in their place. This is termed abrogation (naskh). Naskh is the subsequent introduction of another evidence in place of a legal ruling (shar'i ruling). This modification signifies that, according to divine knowledge, the term of the ruling has ended; it does not denote any deficiency in Allah's knowledge or power. Abrogation does not occur in eternal matters such as the tenets of faith, but in temporary rulings such as commands and prohibitions. There are also textual variant readings (qira'at) of the verse: in some readings it is recited as 'nunsikh' (We abrogate), while in others as 'nunsi' (We cause to be forgotten). These variants enrich the meaning.

In verse 107, it is emphasized that Allah has power over all things and that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. The Possessor of this infinite power may alter whichever ruling He wills, whenever He wills. In verse 108, believers are reminded not to make extraordinary demands of their messenger, as was demanded of Moses (peace be upon him). Whoever exchanges faith for disbelief has strayed from the right path.

Verse 109 conveys that many of the People of the Book wish to turn the believers back from their faith out of envy, even after the truth has become clearly evident to them. The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse was that after the Battle of Uhud, certain Jews provoked Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman and Ammar ibn Yasir, attempting to turn them away from their religion. The believers are commanded to forgive and overlook these individuals until Allah's command comes.

In verse 110, establishing prayer properly and giving zakah are commanded. Moreover, whatever good a person sends forth for their own soul will find its reward with Allah. Allah sees all that is done, and no good deed will go unrewarded.

In verse 111, it is reported that the Jews and Christians claim that no one will enter Paradise except themselves. This is merely their wishful thinking. They are demanded to produce proof to substantiate this claim. There is also a variant in the recitation (qira'ah) of the verse read as 'umniyyah', which indicates that they are merely engaged in vain desires.

Verse 112 explains the true path to entering Paradise: Whoever submits their face completely to Allah while being a doer of good, their reward is with their Lord. There will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve. Here, the expression 'face' represents the entirety of a person's being. Islam signifies submission and peace (salamah), while ihsan is to worship Allah as though one sees Him. These two concepts constitute the essence of the religion.

In verse 113, it is reported that the Jews say, 'The Christians have nothing to stand on,' and the Christians say, 'The Jews have nothing to stand on.' Yet both groups read the scripture. The occasion of revelation for this verse was a dispute between the Christians of Najran and the Jews of Medina. Both sides fundamentally reject one another. Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. This verse warns believers against such disputes and directs them toward sincerity (ikhlas).

While constantly reading the same scripture, the Jews and Christians said to one another, "They have nothing to stand on." Those who possess no knowledge said the same thing. Muslims must not act like this; they should not categorically dismiss others, but rather base their words on evidence and debate in the best manner. Allah will judge their disputes on the Day of Resurrection.

In verse 114, it is stated that none is more unjust than those who prevent the mention of Allah's name in His mosques and strive for their ruin. Such wrongdoers should not enter them except in fear. For them is disgrace in this world, and for them is a great punishment in the Hereafter. The occasion of revelation of the verse relates to the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House in Jerusalem); the Romans and Byzantine Christians perpetrated this injustice, and it later passed into the hands of the Muslims. This serves as an admonition for Muslims today as well.

In verse 115, it is declared that both the east and the west belong to Allah; so wherever you turn, there is the face of Allah. Allah's mercy is all-encompassing, and He knows all things. A mosque is not strictly required for prayer; in case of necessity, any direction can serve as the qiblah. This verse also points to the change of the qiblah and provides ease for Muslims.

In verses 116–118, those who say that Allah has taken a child are condemned. The Jews said, "Ezra (Uzayr) is the son of Allah," the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and the polytheists said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Allah is the Originator of the heavens and the earth; when He decrees a matter, He merely says to it, "Be!" and it is. Those without knowledge said, "Why does Allah not speak to us, or why does a sign not come to us?" Yet those before them had said the same thing. Allah has made the signs clear for people who possess certainty.

In verses 119–121, it is stated that the Prophet was sent with the truth as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner, and that he is not responsible for the companions of the Hellfire. The Jews and the Christians will never be pleased until the Prophet follows their religion (millah). The guidance of Allah is the only true guidance. If one were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come through revelation, one would find neither protector nor helper against Allah. Those who recite the Book as it ought to be recited believe in it; those who disbelieve in it are the losers.

When explaining the concept of "millah" (religious path/community), Elmalılı Hamdi Yazır defines it as the path around which a community gathers and upon which it walks. This path consists of the principles and course being followed. Millah is not the society itself, but the prevailing principles to which that society adheres. Judaism and Christianity are each a millah, yet they are religions that have deviated from the true path and been corrupted by following whims and desires. Allah strictly warned His Prophet against following such false paths.

In verse 121, mention is made of the People of the Book. Those who recite the Book given by Allah as it ought to be recited read it distinctly, with reverence, and by comprehending its meaning. These are the ones who truly believe in the scripture and become genuine People of the Book. Whoever disbelieves in the scripture or alters it is among the losers. This verse encompasses figures like Abdullah ibn Salam, who recited the Torah properly and subsequently embraced Islam, as well as the forty individuals who arrived from Abyssinia.

In verses 122–123, the Children of Israel are addressed: they are asked to remember the blessings and favor bestowed upon them. Furthermore, they are commanded to guard against a Day when no soul will avail another, no ransom will be accepted, and no intercession will benefit. This is a warning issued for the third time.

In verse 124, the trial of Abraham (Ibrahim) is recounted. His Lord tested him with certain commands, and when Abraham fulfilled them, Allah declared that He would make him a leader (imam) for mankind. Abraham pleaded that leaders be made from his offspring as well, but Allah stated that His covenant does not include the wrongdoers. This verse serves as evidence that an oppressor is not worthy of leadership and that anyone lacking justice must be removed from this station. It is emphasized that due to the transgressions of the Children of Israel, leadership departed from them and passed to the lineage of Ishmael (Ismail).

In verse 125, it is recalled that the Kaaba was made a place of return (and reward) and security for mankind. It is commanded that the Station of Abraham (Maqam Ibrahim) be taken as a place of prayer, and that the Kaaba be kept pure for those who circumambulate, those who stay in devotion (i'tikaf), and those who bow and prostrate in prayer. This also hints at the change of the qiblah. The covenant entrusted to Abraham and Ishmael was to attend with utmost care to the purity of this House.

Verse 126 contains the supplication of Abraham. He asked that Mecca be made a secure city and that its people who believe be provided with fruits. Allah, however, made known that He would also provide for the disbelievers in this world, but would drive them to the torment of the Fire in the Hereafter. This shows that even prophets can err in their independent judgment (ijtihad), but Allah corrects their mistakes. Sustenance, unlike spiritual leadership (imamah), is not a blessing restricted solely to believers.

As Abraham and his son Ishmael were raising the foundations of the Kaaba, they prayed: 'Our Lord, accept this service from us. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.' They also beseeched: 'Make us submissive (Muslim) to You, and from our descendants make a community submissive to You; show us our rites of worship, and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepter of Repentance, the Merciful.'

Abraham and Ishmael prayed, 'Our Lord, send among our descendants a messenger who will recite to them Your verses, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise.' This supplication points to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), as no other prophet came from the lineage of Ishmael. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'I am the supplication of my father Abraham, the glad tidings of my brother Jesus, and the vision of my mother.'

Whoever turns away from the religion of Abraham is only one who degrades himself into debasement. According to narration, Abdullah ibn Salam invited his nephews to Islam; one of them believed, while the other did not. Allah made known that He chose Abraham and that he was His friend. Abraham submitted completely to his Lord and turned to Him as an upright monotheist (hanif).

Abraham and Jacob enjoined their sons: 'Allah has chosen this religion for you, so do not die except as Muslims.' On his deathbed, Jacob asked his sons: 'What will you worship after me?' They replied: 'We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—one God—and to Him we submit.'

The fact that Jacob's sons said 'our fathers Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac' indicates that the sons of Ishmael were also their brothers. In the Torah, it was stated through the tongue of Moses: 'I will send a prophet from among your brothers.' This prophet is the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), who descends from the line of Ishmael. There are many glad tidings concerning him in both the Torah and the Gospel.

In the Torah, it was foretold that Ishmael's hand would be above all and that someone would appear from Mount Paran; in the Psalms (Zabur), that a prophet bearing a divine law would be sent; and in the Gospel, that the Paraclete (Faraqlit) would come. All of these verses confirm the prophethood of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). After these proofs, Allah declared: 'That was a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be questioned about what they used to do.'

These verses emphasize that past communities bear their own responsibility, while we are accountable for our own deeds. Prophets like Abraham and Jacob were a community; they have passed away. What they earned belongs to them, and what we have earned belongs to us. Boasting of lineage and ancestry is of no avail; everyone will be held to account for their own striving. Our Prophet (peace be upon him) also said to the Banu Hashim: 'Do not come to me merely with your lineage.'

The Jews and the Christians say, 'Be Jews or Christians, so that you may be guided.' Say to them: 'No, rather we follow the religion of Abraham, as an upright monotheist (hanif); he was not of the polytheists.' We believe in Allah, in what has been revealed to us, in what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Descendants, in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and to all the prophets; we make no distinction between any of them, and to Allah we are submitted.

If they believe as you have believed, they will have found the right path; but if they turn away, they are in dissension. Allah is sufficient for you. Allah's dye (sibghah) is the best; and we worship Him. It is not the artificial dye that Christians call baptism, but innate faith (fitrah) that is the dye of Allah.

Do you dispute with us concerning Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds, and we are sincerely devoted to Him. Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Descendants were Jews or Christians? Say: 'Do you know better, or does Allah?' And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony from Allah? Allah is not unaware of what you do.

In these verses, there are several warnings: Do not boast of past ancestors; everyone is responsible for their own deeds. The abrogation of rulings (naskh) is possible; this is a foundation of the science of jurisprudence (fiqh). Do not blindly imitate predecessors; distinguish truth from falsehood. These principles are reiterated and reinforced in this section of Surah al-Baqarah.

Some foolish people among mankind will say, 'What has turned them away from their qiblah that they were facing?' Say: 'To Allah belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path.' Thus We have made you a middle community (wasat) so that you may be witnesses over mankind and the Messenger may be a witness over you. Our changing the former qiblah was only to distinguish those who follow the Messenger from those who turn back on their heels; and indeed, it was burdensome except for those whom Allah has guided.

We see you turning your face toward the heaven; now We will surely turn you to a qiblah that will please you. Turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram; wherever you may be, turn your faces toward it. Those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord. Even if you were to bring them every kind of proof, they still would not follow your qiblah; nor should you follow their qiblah. Besides, they do not follow each other's qiblah either. If you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would certainly be among the wrongdoers.

In these verses, while some scholars of recitation (qira'ah) read with the letter 'ya', others read it differently. In terms of meaning, Allah bears witness that Abraham and the other prophets were neither Jews nor Christians. O Muhammad, say to them: 'Do you know better, or does Allah?' Allah knows that they were upright monotheists (hanif) and Muslims. Yet you knowingly deny this truth. Who could be more unjust than one who conceals a truthful testimony? Allah has declared that the wrongdoers will not attain His covenant. Past communities have passed away; what they earned belongs to them, and what you have earned belongs to you. You are not responsible for what they used to do.

Commentators of the Quran note that there are several important warnings in this verse: First, rather than boasting of the virtues of past ancestors, everyone will be called to account for their own deeds. Second, it is possible for rulings prescribed for past communities to change; indeed, rulings change with the changing of times. This is among the flexible principles of Islam, ensuring its endurance until the Day of Resurrection. Third, those who wish to walk the path of the prophets must not blindly imitate their predecessors, but must act by distinguishing truth from falsehood, for everyone is responsible for what they themselves have done.

Regarding the change of the qiblah, some foolish people will say, 'What has turned them away from their qiblah?' Say to them: 'To Allah belong the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path.' Here lies an answer to the supplication in Surah al-Fatihah. This new way is a straight path (sirat al-mustaqim) that is more beautiful than the previous one and leads to safety and salvation. This guidance depends entirely on the will of Allah; the servant's striving comes only after this bestowal of grace. Nor is prophethood attained through personal effort.

Allah has made you a middle community (wasat) so that you may be witnesses over mankind and the Prophet may be a witness over you. A witness is one who is just and speaks the truth. In order to become such an exemplary community, Muslims have been guided to a new straight path (sirat al-mustaqim) under the guidance of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The consensus (ijma') of this community serves as evidence for the truth. However, this distinction depends on living in accordance with the Book and the Sunnah. Otherwise, they are doomed to become satellites of other nations.

While our Prophet (peace be upon him) used to perform the prayer facing the Kaaba in Mecca, after the migration (hijrah) to Medina, he turned toward Jerusalem. Later, the command to turn back to the Kaaba arrived. Regarding this change, Allah stated that He saw his face turning toward the heaven and that He would turn him to a qiblah with which he would be pleased. Turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram now. Wherever you may be, turn toward that direction. The People of the Book know that this is a truth from their Lord. Allah is not unaware of what they do.

O Muhammad, even if you were to bring the People of the Book every kind of proof, they would not follow your qiblah, nor will you follow their qiblah. They do not follow each other's qiblah either. If you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would surely be among the wrongdoers. The scholars of the People of the Book recognize the Prophet just as they recognize their own sons; yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth. The address in the third person (gha'ib) in this verse conveys the sense of an objective testimony.

The People of the Book recognized the final prophet as 'that prophet' due to the descriptions recounted in the Torah. Before the clear verses and miracles brought by the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), their scholars had no doubt left; they knew him as conclusively as they knew their own children. However, this knowledge is not sufficient for faith. For faith, alongside knowledge in the heart, obedience and open affirmation are also required. Because they disbelieved despite knowing, they became among the disbelievers who knowingly concealed the truth.

Addressing the Prophet, Allah states: 'The truth is from your Lord, so never be among the doubters.' This address also warns the ummah and particularly reinforces the matter of the qiblah. The qiblah is the primary physical manifestation ensuring the spiritual unity of an ummah. There cannot be an ummah without a qiblah. Because the Kaaba was the qiblah of Abraham, it is worthy of being the most comprehensive direction of unity. Even though the orientation of each community toward the Kaaba differs, they all gather at a single center.

Every community has a direction to which it turns. The believers, too, should race in good deeds by turning toward the Kaaba. The purpose of the qiblah is to embark upon a race for good deeds with orderly unity. Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together. He is capable of all things. Turn your faces toward the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) in prayer; this command is the truth from your Lord. Allah is not unaware of what you do.

The command regarding the qiblah was repeated so that people would have no argument against you. The People of the Book and the polytheists are left unable to raise objections concerning the change of the qiblah. Yet the wrongdoers still speak out, but their words are invalid. Do not fear them, but fear Allah. This command is so that He may complete His favor upon you and that you may be guided. The completion of the favor is to die upon Islam and enter Paradise.

Allah sent a messenger from among yourselves. He recites His verses to you, purifies you, teaches you the Book and wisdom, and teaches you what you did not know. This is a tremendous favor. Making the Kaaba the qiblah is also for the completion of this favor. For this, you have two duties: remember Me, and I will remember you; give thanks to Me, and do not be ungrateful. Remembrance (dhikr) occurs through the tongue, heart, and body. Gratitude (shukr) is also expressed through these means. The beginning of servitude is remembrance, and its culmination is gratitude.

O you who believe! Seek help through patience and prayer. Allah is with those who are patient. Patience is the beginning of every success. Prayer, on the other hand, is the greatest strengthener of faith and a means of drawing near to Allah. Do not say of those who are killed in the cause of Allah, 'They are dead'; rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive it. We will surely test you with something of fear, hunger, and loss of wealth, lives, and crops. And give glad tidings to the patient.

When an affliction strikes them, they say, 'To Allah we belong, and to Him we shall return.' Upon them are forgiveness and mercy from their Lord. And it is they who are rightly guided. Patience and prayer are the most important means of drawing divine assistance. Allah's being with the patient is a great honor He bestows upon them.

Believers, seek help from Allah through patience and prayer. Do not call those slain in the cause of Allah 'dead'; they are not dead, but alive. However, you cannot perceive their life. This is a spiritual life. As narrated from Hasan al-Basri, the provisions of the martyrs are presented to their souls. This verse is an indication that the soul remains conscious after death. The majority of the Companions and the Successors (tabi'un) hold this view. The specific mention of the martyrs here is to make known their exalted station. The life of the Hereafter, however, is broader; matters such as resurrection after death and the realm of the isthmus (barzakh) will be explained in due course.

Allah will test you with something of fear, hunger, and a loss of wealth, lives, and crops. These tribulations are a taste in this world to lead toward the immense blessings of the Hereafter. Give glad tidings to the patient; in times of affliction, they say, 'İnnâ lillâhi ve innâ ileyhi râciûn' (Truly to Allah we belong, and truly to Him we shall return). These words mean surrendering one's wealth and life to Allah, and being content with whatever He wills to do. Moreover, they express faith that we will not perish through death but will return to Allah, as well as the hope of being well-pleased with Him. This station is referred to as 'al-nafs al-radiyah' (the content soul) and 'al-nafs al-mardiyyah' (the soul well-pleasing to Him).

The soul (nafs) rises successively through the levels of first 'ammarah' (inciting to evil), then 'lawwamah' (self-reproaching), then 'mutma'innah' (tranquil), then 'radiyah' (content), and finally 'mardiyyah' (well-pleasing to Allah). The address in Surah al-Fajr, 'O tranquil soul! Return to your Lord,' conveys this. The return is not spatial; Allah the Exalted is transcendent beyond space. This return is an acknowledgment of our soul coming to an end, an acknowledgment of enduring, or a state between annihilation and everlasting existence. In truth, our existence exists through Allah's knowledge, and we endure through His eternity. In the Hereafter, we will be resurrected in a new creation.

Some philosophers viewed the Hereafter solely as the soul remaining immortal, but this is erroneous. The soul is a mystery from Allah's command, but our endurance is through Allah's eternity. The statement 'We belong to Allah, and to Him we shall return' is a reality not confined merely to the soul or the body, but beyond both. The Hereafter occurs through the resurrection after the life of the isthmus (barzakh). This return is an attainment of Allah's grace or His wrath, and it takes place through subsisting in Allah (baqa bi'llah). Hope and fear must rest upon this foundation.

Safa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. There is no sin upon whoever performs Hajj or Umrah to walk (sa'y) between them. This verse was revealed because Muslims hesitated due to the presence of idols there during the pre-Islamic period of ignorance (Jahiliyyah). Our Prophet (peace be upon him) performed this circumambulation and commanded the sa'y. In the Hanafi school of law, this sa'y is regarded as obligatory (wajib). It is based on the commemoration of Hagar, the wife of Abraham (peace be upon him), running between Safa and Marwah while suffering from thirst. This demonstrates the importance of seeking refuge in Allah and exercising patience in moments of distress. Voluntary good deeds also carry immense reward; in a sacred hadith (hadith qudsi), it is stated that the believer draws near to Allah through voluntary deeds.

Those who conceal the clear proofs and verses of guidance that Allah has sent down, after He has made them clear to the people, are cursed by Allah and cursed by all who can curse. Except those who repent, reform their condition, and make the truth clear; they will be forgiven. As for those who disbelieve in Our verses and die as disbelievers, they shall remain under an eternal curse, and their punishment will not be lightened. This ruling is general; it encompasses anyone who conceals a religious truth. Abu Hurayrah stated that he narrated hadiths relying upon these verses.

In this section, after attention is drawn once again to the story of Adam (peace be upon him), the condition of those who repent is described. Those who repented and reformed their condition made the truths known. This shows that repentance is tied to the reward of declaration and disclosure, which is the opposite of the sin of concealment. Every sin has a repentance specific to itself; concealing a manifest truth is disbelief, whereas faith is declaring the truth. In verse 161, it is stated that those who do not believe in the manifest proofs and guidance sent down by Allah, along with all the prophets and scriptures, the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him), and the Quran, but persist in disbelief and die as disbelievers, are the cursed ones.

In verse 162, it is stated that the curse of Allah, the angels, and all humanity is upon them, that they will abide under the curse eternally, and that their punishment will not be lightened. Since all disbelief is the concealment of a truth, this verse encompasses everyone other than those excepted through repentance in the previous verse. Furthermore, this verse establishes a more general ruling of condemnation by also including those who, even if they articulated the truth with their tongues or pens, did not believe in their hearts and died in disbelief.

In verse 163, monotheism (tawhid) is emphasized: 'Your God is surely one God. There is no god but Him. He is the Most Compassionate (al-Rahman), the Most Merciful (al-Rahim).' This verse calls people to abandon disbelief and discord and enter the fold of monotheism. The oneness of Allah is unique in His essence and His attributes; there is no true god besides Him. The pronoun 'Huwa' is counted among the greatest names that indicate His essence, while the name 'Allah' signifies the totality of His essence and attributes. He is both al-Rahman and al-Rahim; all mercy belongs to Him.

The polytheists had demanded a physical miracle from the Prophet (peace be upon him), such as turning Mount Safa into gold. Thereupon, Allah Almighty revealed verse 164, declaring that in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ships that sail through the sea, the sending down of rain to revive the dead earth, the dispersing of living creatures, the shifting of the winds, and the clouds, there are many signs (ayat) for people of understanding. These signs are greater, more beneficial, and more enduring proofs than the miracle that was demanded.

The signs described in this verse are clear proofs for a people who use their reason. Intellect (aql) is a spiritual light that serves to understand things that cannot be perceived through the senses. Reasoning is moving from effect to cause or from cause to effect by grasping the law of causality between causes and effects. There are various kinds of intellect: reflective thought (fikr), intuition (hads), heard/learned intellect (aql-i masmu'), and sacred intellect (qudsi aql). The highest rank is the 'first intellect' (aql-i awwal), which is the light of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The Quran encourages people to exercise their intellect, and through this path, it teaches reaching the existence, oneness, and mercy of Allah.

In verses 165–167, it is stated that among people are those who take equals besides Allah, loving them as they should love Allah, whereas the love of believers for Allah is stronger. On the Day of Resurrection, those who were followed will disown those who followed them, and all ties will be severed. The followers will say, 'If only we had another turn in the world, so that we might disown them as they have disowned us.' Allah will show them their deeds as regrets, and they will never emerge from the Fire. These verses explain that excessively loving things other than Allah is polytheism (shirk), resulting in eternal punishment.

Love for Allah and love for the Prophet are the completion of faith. A believer loves Allah, and loves the Prophet for His sake. Mingling anyone other than Allah into the intention during prayer is disbelief (kufr). One only prays on behalf of the Prophet or righteous servants; one does not ask anything from them. Loving them as one loves Allah, offering sacrifices in their name, or invoking their names like 'Bismillah' is polytheism. Such superstitions emerge in ignorant eras when religious knowledge has weakened.

The unity of existence (wahdat al-wujud) requires understanding the distinction between saying 'There is no existent being other than Allah' and saying 'Every existent being is Allah.' The first means regarding the existence of the universe as a shadow and illusion and acknowledging that real existence belongs to Allah. The second means accepting multiplicity and attributing divinity to everything, which is polytheism. This is the false doctrine known as pantheism. The monotheism of Islam is the principle of 'There is no god but Allah'; it should not be understood as 'There is no existence other than Him.'

Certain extremist groups, such as Wahhabism, have considered reverence for prophets and righteous servants to be polytheism. Yet loving and showing reverence for the sake of Allah is not polytheism. Visiting graves should be done in accordance with the Sunnah, and it should serve as a reminder of death. Praying for the deceased and wishing goodness for them is not loving them as one loves Allah. It is necessary to avoid extremism; neither neglecting them nor idolizing them is correct.

The believers' love for Allah is continuous; they turn to Allah under all circumstances. Polytheists, on the other hand, remember Allah in times of distress and return to their idols once relieved. Their love is fragmented and fickle. Those who believe direct all their love toward Allah and love created beings for the sake of Allah. They also love their leaders solely for the pleasure of Allah. Otherwise, they cannot escape wrongdoing and polytheism.

When it is said in the Quran, 'Follow what Allah has revealed,' some say, 'We follow what we found our forefathers upon.' This is blind imitation (taqlid). Even if their forefathers lacked knowledge and were misguided, following them defies reason. What is right is to follow Allah's proof. Imitation without knowledge and proof is following Satan. The condition of such disbelievers is like that of animals that only hear a call and cry without understanding.

O you who believe! Eat of the lawful and pure provisions given to you, and be grateful to Allah. Allah has forbidden you only carrion (dead meat), blood, the flesh of swine, and that which is slaughtered in the name of other than Allah. But in cases of necessity, without exceeding rights and without surpassing the measure of necessity, there is no sin in eating. Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

In the verses, the importance of eating lawful and pure foods and expressing gratitude to Allah is emphasized first. It is stated that those who show ingratitude for blessings cannot be freed from physical and spiritual impurity. Quranic commentators explain that the command 'eat' signifies permissibility (mubah), whereas the command 'be grateful' signifies obligation (wajib). It is noted that the act of eating has degrees such as obligatory (fard), recommended (mandub), permissible (mubah), and forbidden (haram): eating enough to prevent death is obligatory, eating to gain strength for worship is recommended, eating until fully satisfied is permissible, and eating beyond that is forbidden.

The things forbidden by Allah are: carrion (dead meat), flowing blood, the flesh of swine, and animals slaughtered in the name of other than Allah. 'Ihlal' stems from the polytheists raising their voices in the name of their idols during slaughter; over time it acquired the general meaning of slaughter. In cases of necessity, there is a dispensation (rukhsah) to consume these forbidden items, provided that one does not infringe upon another's right and restricts the intake to the amount necessary to avert death. The legal maxims 'Necessities make forbidden things permissible' and 'Necessity is measured by its extent' are derived from these verses.

Verses 174–176 condemn those who conceal the Book revealed by Allah to obtain worldly gain. They are as if filling their bellies with fire; on the Day of Resurrection, Allah will not speak to them nor purify them, and for them is a painful punishment. They have exchanged guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. Those who differ over the Book (such as those who believe in the Torah and the Gospel but reject the Quran) are in deep schism far from the truth. The verse emphasizes that true unity among people is possible only through belief in the true Book.

In verse 177, true righteousness (birr) is defined: It is not turning one's face toward the east or the west, but believing in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets; giving wealth out of love for Him to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, beggars, and for freeing captives; establishing prayer and paying zakah; fulfilling promises when made; and being patient in poverty, illness, and during warfare. It is these who are the truthful and it is these who are the righteous. The verse encompasses all the noble virtues of humanity.

In verses 178–179, legal retribution (qisas—life for life) is made obligatory: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, the woman for the woman. However, if the guardian of the slain forgives or accepts blood money (diyah), retribution is dropped; it is then necessary to act according to custom and pay the blood money with fairness. This is an alleviation and a mercy. Whoever transgresses after the pardon shall have a painful punishment. There is life in retribution, O people of understanding! The verse abolishes the inequalities of pre-Islamic ignorance (Jahiliyyah) and establishes equality in the security of life. Retribution is only applied in intentional killing; accidental killing is subject to a different ruling. There are differing views among legal schools (madhhabs) on whether a free person can be executed in retribution for a slave, or a man for a woman; the Hanafis apply retribution based on the principle of the inherent equality of human life.

In Surah al-Baqarah, verse 178, while the ruling of retribution (qisas) is explained, the matters of pardon and blood money (diyah) are also addressed. Accordingly, if the guardian (heir) of the slain person pardons the killer unconditionally (in an absolute manner) without stipulating any conditions, he must abide by this pardon and not demand blood money or anything else in return. If the pardon is granted in exchange for a specified amount of blood money or other property, it becomes obligatory (wajib) upon the killer to accept this compensation and pay it in a fair and proper manner. This regulation aims to establish justice between the parties and prevent blood feuds.

The expression 'from his brother' mentioned in the verse refers to the guardian, that is, the heir of the slain person. Describing the killer here as the brother of the victim's guardian is in the context of brotherhood in religion or a shared homeland. This characterization indicates that the lives and the rights to life of all individuals in Islamic society—whether free or slave, female or male, Muslim or dhimmi (non-Muslim subject)—are fraternally inviolable and sacrosanct. At the same time, it carries a profound human, moral, and social meaning that encourages the guardian to pardon.

If the guardian of the slain person decides to pardon, he should act with this consciousness of brotherhood, not go to excess in demanding blood money, and make his demand in accordance with recognized customary fairness (ma'ruf). The killer, recognizing the value of this pardon, must also pay his debt handsomely and without causing hardship. This ruling is a lightening and a mercy from your Lord. Whoever transgresses the limit after this ruling (for instance, by killing the murderer after having pardoned him), for him there is retribution in this world and a painful punishment in the Hereafter. The primary ruling is retribution; pardon and blood money, however, are a facilitation and a mercy.

The wisdom behind the legitimacy of retribution is emphasized by the verse, 'There is life for you in retribution, O people of understanding!' Retribution serves to preserve life both by deterring prospective killers and by ensuring the security of life in society. This aphorism is more eloquent and comprehensive than similar sayings in Arabic literature, because it clearly expresses that retribution is not aimed at killing, but on the contrary, at preserving life. Were it not for retribution, pardon would also have no meaning.

In verses 180–182, the subject of bequests (wasiyyah) is addressed. When someone is afflicted with a terminal illness, if they are to leave behind wealth (khayr), making a bequest to parents and close relatives in a recognized, proper manner (ma'ruf) is prescribed as a duty and an obligation upon those who fear Allah. Whoever alters this bequest after hearing it, the sin of it falls solely upon them. However, if someone fears a mistake or sin on the part of the testator and reconciles between the parties, there is no blame upon him. Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.

Scholars have differed as to whether the command of bequest in this verse was abrogated (naskh) by the verses of inheritance. According to the majority, a bequest to a relative who is an heir was abrogated, whereas a bequest to a relative who is not an heir, while not obligatory, is recommended (mustahabb). A group of scholars (such as Hasan al-Basri and Tawus) contend that a bequest to a relative who is not an heir is still obligatory. In conclusion, making a bequest to a non-inheriting relative is at least recommended (mandub) and is permissible within one-third of the estate.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani claimed that there is no abrogation (naskh) in the Quran. However, he was not consistent in this view and ultimately had to concede that the inheritance verses partially abrogated the bequest verse. Rather than calling this 'abrogation', he termed it 'specification' (takhsis). Yet specification is made between two proofs whose dates of revelation are unknown, whereas it is certain that the inheritance verses were revealed later. In this case, the operation carried out is not specification but partial abrogation, which is the opinion of a minority school of thought.

Great scholars such as al-Jassas have fiercely criticized those who deny abrogation in the Quran. According to them, both the predecessors (Salaf) and successors (Khalaf) of the Ummah accepted abrogation and entertained no doubt regarding it. Rejecting abrogation is akin to rejecting the Quran's general ('amm), specific (khass), clear (muhkam), and allegorical (mutashabih) verses. Such a claim is a form of fanaticism put forward by individuals devoid of sound knowledge, leading to a distortion of religious rulings.

In conclusion, Abu Muslim is the only person among Muslim scholars to deny abrogation. Even according to his view, it is not possible to act upon the bequest verse on its own. The ruling in this verse was entirely abrogated by the inheritance verses. However, other indications in the verse may be acted upon within the principles of jurisprudence (usul). For instance, there is no abrogation in verses 181–182 concerning the alteration of a bequest; these rulings remain valid.

Allah warned those who alter a bequest, stating that doing so is a grave sin. However, if a bequest has deviated from the truth and entails injustice, rectifying it is permissible. In that case, if someone reconciles the parties and turns the bequest toward justice, he commits no sin, for Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful. This permission is a concession (rukhsah), not a source of reward (thawab). Fulfilling a bequest, on the other hand, is a tremendous responsibility.

Next, Allah declares that He has made the act of fasting obligatory. Fasting is an act of worship that was also prescribed for previous communities, serving to discipline the servants of Allah. It is proclaimed to the believers: 'Fasting is prescribed for you so that you may attain protection (and piety).' Fasting curbs the desires of the lower self (nafs), teaches patience, and leads to God-consciousness (taqwa). Through this act of worship, a person is freed from enslavement to worldly pleasures and draws closer to Allah.

Fasting has been made obligatory only for a designated number of days. Those who are ill or on a journey make up the missed days later. Those who can fast only with extreme difficulty pay a ransom (fidyah). Increasing the ransom is good, but fasting is more virtuous. The legal definition of fasting in the Sharia is to abstain with intention from food, drink, and sexual intercourse from the break of dawn (imsak) until sunset. The measure of travel that qualifies for the journey dispensation is a three-day distance of normal walking; modern conveyances are also evaluated according to their customary status.

In this section, the commentary on the verses of Surah al-Baqarah concerning fasting continues. First, the meaning of the word "yutîkûne" is addressed. This word means not simply 'to be capable of,' but rather 'to endure with difficulty, to have one's strength depleted.' Therefore, the verse was revealed not concerning those who lack the capability to fast altogether, but regarding those who experience extreme difficulty in fasting or cannot endure it at all. These individuals are chronically ill persons with no hope of recovery and the elderly of advanced age.

The variant recitations (qira'at) of the verse are also addressed. In the recitations of Nafi', Abu Ja'far, and Ibn 'Amir, the word "fidyah" is used in the sense of 'feeding a poor person.' The amount of the fidyah is determined by legal standards: half a sa' of wheat, or one sa' of other foodstuffs. This measure also forms the basis for the charity of Fitr (sadaqat al-fitr) and expiations (kaffarat).

Commentators have differed regarding whom the verse addresses. According to one view, following the concession regarding the sick and the traveler, the verse encompasses those who are similar to them but lack the possibility of making up missed days. According to another view, the verse granted a choice to those who were healthy and resident, but this ruling was later abrogated by the verse 'Whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it.' Imam Malik, on the other hand, interpreted the verse as referring to those who have an outstanding debt from a past Ramadan and lack the capacity to make it up.

According to the preferred view, the verse is not abrogated. Many Companions, foremost among them Ibn Abbas, stated that the verse concerns very elderly men and women and that its ruling remains in effect. The Hanafi school is also of this opinion. Accordingly, those who can barely endure fasting in terms of both performance and making up missed fasts pay a ransom (fidyah). This ransom is legislated because fasting is an impossibility for them.

Then, the passage moves to verse 185. In this verse, the month of Ramadan is described, and it is emphasized as the month in which the Quran was revealed. The literal and technical meanings of the word "shahr" (month) are explained. It is discussed whether the word Ramadan is one of the names of Allah or merely the name of a month. Furthermore, views regarding the derivation of the name Ramadan are addressed: it is reported that it is called by this name because it is a month that cleanses sins.

There are various opinions regarding the origin of the word Ramadan. According to the majority, it comes from "ramad" (ramaz)—that is, the scorching of stones from the intense heat of the sun. The reason this month is named Ramadan is either the heat of hunger and thirst endured during fasting, or that fasting burns away sins. According to another view, the Arabs anciently named the months according to the seasons, and since this month coincided with intense heat, it was called Ramadan. Others say that Ramadan is derived from "ramad" in the sense of whetting and sharpening weapons, and that the Arabs prepared for battle in this month. It has also been narrated that the name Ramadan is among the beautiful names of Allah. In short, Ramadan carries meanings such as cleansing, burning, and sharpness.

In a hadith, it was stated regarding the month of Ramadan: "Its beginning is mercy, its middle is forgiveness, and its end is salvation from the Fire." The most blessed night of this month is the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr), and the Quran began to be revealed on this night. The word Quran is read in two ways: with a hamzah, derived from "qira'ah" (recitation), and without a hamzah, from the root "qarn" (conjoining). Imam al-Shafi'i stated that its form without a hamzah is not derived from another word, like the Torah and the Gospel, but is a proper name for the Book of Allah.

It is disputed whether the phrase "a fixed number of days" refers to Ramadan or to earlier fasts. According to Qatadah and 'Ata', this refers to the initial fast—that is, three days of every month or the Day of Ashura—after which Ramadan was made obligatory. However, according to the majority of scholars, the initial fast was established by the Sunnah, while the fast of Ramadan began with the verse "Fasting is prescribed for you." The intent of "a fixed number of days" is also Ramadan. The revelation of the Quran in the month of Ramadan has been interpreted in three ways: it was sent down all at once to the worldly heaven and then revealed piecemeal; it began to be revealed in this month; or it was stated as praise for this month.

The word "shuhud" (witnessing) mentioned in the verse has three different meanings: first, being resident during the month of Ramadan; second, knowing the month with certainty; and third, sighting the crescent moon. Accordingly, whoever witnesses Ramadan must fast. The hadiths regarding the sighting of the crescent moon are as follows: "Do not begin fasting until you see the crescent moon. If it is overcast, complete the month to thirty." Sighting the crescent moon at the beginning of Ramadan is essential. When the sky is clear, if only a few people see it while others do not, the testimony of these individuals is deemed refuted. In overcast weather, however, the testimony of a single person is sufficient. According to the Hanafis, one upright witness is required for Ramadan, and two upright witnesses are required for Eid.

Scholars hold differing views regarding the determination of the crescent moon through calculation. Astronomical calculation is not based on sighting the crescent moon; therefore, it has not been accepted as a legal (shar'i) criterion. Moreover, calculation is not known to everyone, which contradicts the Islamic principle of ease. For this reason, the beginning of fasting has remained tied to sighting the crescent moon. However, if in our day the obligation of searching for the crescent moon is neglected, it may be possible to benefit from astronomical calculation. Nevertheless, Muslims should not forget the duty of observing the crescent moon.

Fasting is obligatory upon every accountable (mukallaf) believer. Those who are ill or traveling may refrain from fasting during Ramadan and make up for it later. This is a concession (rukhsah), not a strict obligation ('azimah). For the elderly and the sick who have no hope of recovery, fidya is given. Allah desires ease, not hardship. These rulings were laid down to complete the number of days of the Ramadan fast and to give thanks to Allah. Through fasting, the soul is disciplined, patience is learned, and happiness in the Hereafter is attained.

In the prescription of the Ramadan fast, a fixed number of days was taken as the basis. Although the sighting of the month is an overarching cause, the detailed cause is each individual day. For this reason, fasting was first made obligatory as a fixed number of days, and the month served as its clarification. The expression "so that you may complete the number" linked the month to the number of days. Consequently, whoever breaks the fast for a few days during Ramadan is not required to make up the entire month, but only the days they did not fast. Likewise, for those whose status of accountability changes during Ramadan (such as those reaching puberty or those embarking on a journey), the ruling is shaped accordingly.

Following the fast, the command to glorify Allah with takbir is emphasized. Takbir means magnifying Allah, and it occurs in three ways: through belief with the heart, affirmation with words, and worship through deeds. The takbir in this verse is an expression of completing the count of Ramadan and reaching Eid. For this takbir, recited with the words "Allahu Akbar," it is commendable (mustahabb) to utter it silently when the crescent of Shawwal is sighted, and it is Sunnah to utter it aloud while going to the Eid prayer. According to the preferred view in the Hanafi school, none of these takbirs is obligatory (wajib).

The scope of the takbir in the verse also includes the Eid prayer and the takbirs recited therein. The expression "so that you may give thanks" indicates that the joy of Eid should be observed as an occasion of gratitude. Thus, the act of worship through fasting is brought in line with the command "eat and give thanks." Furthermore, in these sentences there are proofs that refute the Jabriyyah sect.

In verse 186, when His servants ask about Him, Allah Almighty responds by saying, "I am near; I answer the call of the caller when he calls upon Me." This nearness is not a spatial nearness, but rather signifies answering supplication swiftly. The verse refutes the naturalists, who regard Allah as a blind force, and those who deny the origin of divine decree. There is also a warning for those who assume Allah to be distant and shout in their supplications; humility is essential when supplicating.

The doubts raised regarding supplication are answered. That divine decree has already been determined does not render supplication unnecessary, for supplication is itself among the causes decreed in destiny. Allah's knowledge encompasses all things, yet supplication is a demonstration of servitude.
