A person both submits with contentment to the divine decree and makes supplication; these two states are not contradictory. Supplication is the essence of worship, and this verse, following the command of fasting, reinforces the importance of the fast.

The nearness of Allah is a profound subject debated by philosophers and theologians. In the words of al-Razi, Allah is nearer to the essence of every contingent being than that essence's own existence. This means that just as there can be no existence without Allah, there can also be no logic without Allah. The statement in the verse saying "I am near" rather than "My servants are near to Me" indicates that nearness originates from Allah, not from the servant. When the person who supplicates detaches from everything other than Allah, they have truly supplicated and attained Allah's nearness.

The occasion of revelation for the verse on fasting is as follows: The early Muslims could eat, drink, and be intimate with their spouses in the evening only until they performed the night prayer ('isha) or fell asleep. One night, after 'isha, Umar was intimate with his wife, felt remorse, and presented the matter to the Prophet. Thereupon, verse 187 of al-Baqarah was revealed. With this verse, it was made lawful to be intimate with spouses during the nights of fasting, and permission was given to eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct from the black thread. In addition, the analogy was drawn that spouses are a garment for one another.

The word "rafath" (refes) in this ayah signifies sexual intercourse. Allah, wishing ease for the Ummah, excluded the night from fasting and made sexual intercourse lawful. The command of "mubasharah" also indicates permissibility. However, the expression "seek what Allah has decreed for you" points out that the purpose of intimacy should be offspring. The white thread is the true dawn (al-fajr al-sadiq); the time of imsak begins with its rising. The false dawn (al-fajr al-kadhib), on the other hand, is the deceptive dawn and is not the criterion for beginning the fast.

The ayah is also evidence that the fast of one who enters the morning in a state of major ritual impurity (janabah) is valid. Because when sexual intercourse is permitted at night, postponing the ritual bath (ghusl) until morning also becomes permissible. The obligatory components (fard) of fasting are three: time, intention, and abstention (imsak). The time is from the break of dawn until the setting of the sun. Intention is required. Fasting is not only abstaining from eating, drinking, and sexual intercourse, but at the same time guarding organs such as the tongue, eyes, and ears from sin. Nevertheless, the obligatory imsak applies only to eating, drinking, and sexual intercourse. The others are recommended (mandub).

While in a state of i'tikaf (seclusion) in mosques, sexual intercourse with spouses is forbidden. I'tikaf is staying in a mosque with the intention of worship. In the legal (shar'i) i'tikaf, fasting is a condition, and for this reason, it must last at least one day. Our Prophet (peace be upon him) regularly observed i'tikaf during the last ten days of Ramadan. I'tikaf is an emphasized Sunnah (sunnah al-mu'akkadah); it is not obligatory (wajib). However, continually abandoning it is not viewed favorably.

In ayah 188 of al-Baqarah, consuming wealth through wrongful means is prohibited. This encompasses situations such as bribery and unlawful gain. Wealth becomes unlawful (haram) either due to a quality inherent to it (for example, a poisonous or prohibited animal) or due to a flaw in the method of acquiring it. After undergoing self-discipline through fasting, believers should not unjustly reach for the property of others. Bribing judges leads to consuming property unjustly. Societies that abide by right and justice find peace.

There are narrations concerning the occasion of revelation of this ayah. In one of them, in a land dispute between Abdan al-Hadrami and Imru' al-Qays, when the Messenger of Allah proposed an oath, Imru' al-Qays heard the ayah and relinquished his claim. In another narration, two disputants came for judgment, and the Prophet said: "I am only a human being; I judge according to your arguments. Whomever I judge in favor of regarding his brother's right, I have only given him a piece of fire," whereupon the parties wept and relinquished their claims.

Ayah 189 of al-Baqarah answers the question asked about the new moons (crescents): The new moons are measurements of time for the people and for Hajj. During the Age of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah), they considered it righteousness to enter houses from the back door while in ihram. Islam corrected this misconception, declaring that true righteousness is to possess piety (taqwa). Believers should enter their houses through their doors and be mindful of Allah. This ayah both points to the importance of the crescent in determining the times of worship and rejects superstitious customs.

One day, while in ihram, the Messenger of Allah entered through the gate of a ruined vineyard, and a man, seeing him, followed behind him. When the man was reminded that he was in ihram, he said, 'I am content with your Sunnah; you entered, so I entered.' This incident, together with a question regarding the crescents, became the occasion for the revelation of the ayah, and such awkward customs of the Jahiliyyah were abolished. In response, it was stated: The crescents are measurements of time for the people and for Hajj. Thanks to the phases of the moon, the number of years and the reckoning of time are known; this is also explained in Surahs Yunus and al-Isra.

There are many religious and worldly benefits in reckoning time by lunar months. The religious ones are: acts of worship such as the Ramadan fast, Hajj, the waiting period (iddah) of death, the iddah of menopause, and vows. The worldly ones are matters such as debts, rents, promises, and the gestation period. The changing of the moon in crescent phases is more convenient for reckoning time than the sun; through its relationship to night and day, the reckoning of the week has also been adapted to it. In addition, the transformation of the moon is proof that celestial bodies also undergo change and can perish. In this respect, the moon is an important sign illustrating Allah's power and unity.

After this explanation, righteousness is not entering houses from their rears; rather, righteousness is that of one who fears Allah and protects himself. That is, the people of piety (taqwa) are those who believe and do good deeds. Asking the Prophet about the astronomical causes of the crescent is treating him like an astronomer and straining revelation unnecessarily. What truly ought to be done is to abandon Jahiliyyah customs and turn to Allah with piety. Enter houses through their doors, begin affairs from the proper way, and do not occupy yourselves with unnecessary questions.

With ayah 190 comes the command to fight: Fight in the way of Allah those who fight against you, but do not commit unjust aggression. Muslims were initially forbidden from fighting; then, with this ayah, permission was granted for defensive fighting. Although some narrations state that the first ayah on fighting is the verse of permission in Surah al-Hajj, the majority hold the view that this ayah is the first command to fight. This command is a previously promised permission and fulfilled the good tidings in previous scriptures that the final prophet would wage jihad with the sword.

Whether this ayah was abrogated (mansukh) by subsequent ayahs is disputed. According to one view, the ayah is solely for defense and was abrogated by the command of total warfare in Surah at-Tawbah. According to the other view, the ayah is decisive (muhkam) because it encompasses both defense and offense, and subsequent ayahs are explanatory. Al-Raghib says: First, leniency was commanded, then permission to fight was given, and then came the command to fight against those who turn away from the truth. This is a requirement of gradual policy.

Europeans spread two contradictory ideas regarding Islam: the first is portraying it as aggressive by claiming that Islam spread by the sword; the second is aiming to disarm it by asserting that war in Islam is exclusively defensive. Both views are incorrect. The truth is that in Islam, both defense and, when necessary, offense in the way of Allah are legitimate. However, every war must be in the way of Allah, and unjust aggression and excess are forbidden. These ayahs regulated fighting in the Sacred Precinct (Haram) and during the sacred months, aiming to remove obstacles to visiting the Kaaba following the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.

Ayah 191 says: kill them wherever you overtake them, and expel them from wherever they expelled you. Fitnah (persecution/discord) is more severe than killing. Fitnah deprives a person of religion and worldly life; therefore, fighting is necessary to eradicate fitnah. Do not fight them near al-Masjid al-Haram unless they fight you there; but if they fight you, retaliate. These rulings warn believers against fitnah and encourage becoming a ghazi or a martyr in the way of Allah.

It is not permissible to kill by way of aggression within the sanctuary (haram) of the Kaaba and Mecca the Blessed (Makkah al-Mukarramah). The primary duty is solely to expel them. However, whoever kills there is killed. In fact, if someone commits a murder within Mecca and takes refuge in the sanctuary of the Kaaba, it is still not permissible to kill him there; he is taken out and legal retribution (qisas) is carried out. The verses, "And remember when We made the House a place of return for people and a sanctuary secure [from any enemy aggression]" (Al-Baqarah, 2/125) and "Whoever enters it is safe [from any violation]" (Al 'Imran, 3/97) support this ruling. However, whoever commits murder within the Sacred Sanctuary (al-Haram al-Sharif) is killed there; this command specifies (takhsis) the preceding part. It is stated in "Ahkam al-Qur'an" that: since there can be no abrogating (nasikh) and abrogated (mansukh) elements within a single address, and both the unity of recitation and the order of revelation indicate that these two verses were revealed in a single address, and with no authentic transmission to the contrary existing, just as the expression 'Kill them wherever you find them' does not abrogate the ruling of what precedes it but rather explains it, likewise this prohibition does not abrogate the entirety of the command 'Kill them,' but specifies it. Furthermore, this prohibition has not been abrogated by any command; it is definitive (muhkam).

When the expression in verse 192, "If they cease [their disbelief], then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful," is evaluated together with the stipulation "Expel them from wherever they have expelled you," it is understood that this verse does not concern the People of the Book, but is specific to the Arab polytheists. While submission with the poll-tax (jizya) is acceptable from the People of the Book, the Arab polytheists are bound either to accept Islam or face the sword. In verse 193, it is stated: "Fight them until there is no fitnah (polytheism and discord) and religion is entirely for Allah." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I have been commanded to fight these people until they say 'La ilaha illallah.' When they say it, they protect their lives from me." While others could safeguard their blood with jizya, this permission was not granted to the Arab polytheists. If they desist from disbelief and accept Islam, then there is no hostility except against the oppressors.

In verse 194, the issue of the sacred month is addressed: "The sacred month is for the sacred month, and for violations there is legal retribution (qisas)." This means: whoever attacks you and violates something of your sanctity and inviolability, retaliate against them to the same extent they attacked you. "The retribution for an evil deed is an evil one like it" (Ash-Shura, 42/40). The one who initiates evil is more unjust; retaliation is not transgression, but the punishment for transgression. Retribution (qisas) expresses responding in kind. In accordance with this general rule, the sacred month is likewise exchanged for the same sacred month. In the year of Hudaybiyyah, in the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah, the enemies violated the sanctity of the sacred month by hurling stones and arrows at the Muslims; you, too, by retaliating in kind, do not refrain from fighting in the same month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. As the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of the verse, it is mentioned that the polytheists plotted to alter the treaty during the sacred month, or that the Quraysh turned the Messenger of Allah back from Mecca in the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. In any case, these verses were revealed in the year of the fulfilled 'umrah (the 7th year of the Hijrah). Although the "custom of the sacred months" was later abrogated unconditionally, the general rulings regarding retaliating in kind remain in force.

In verse 195, spending in the way of Allah (infaq) is commanded: "And spend in the way of Allah and do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands." The occasion of revelation of this verse was to serve as a reminder that abandoning jihad is a peril. According to a narration, during a campaign against Constantinople in the Umayyad era, when a Muslim charged at the enemy in the fortress, the crowd said, "He is throwing himself into destruction." Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, however, stated that this verse was revealed concerning the Ansar who said, "Let us stay with our properties and occupy ourselves with putting them in order," and he pointed out that throwing oneself into destruction was abandoning jihad. There are also different interpretations of the verse, such as wasting one's wealth through extravagance and perishing, or rushing into battle in a way that has no impact on the enemy. As Imam Muhammad stated in his "Siyar al-Kabir," a single person charging against a thousand people is permissible if there is hope of survival or breaking the enemy, but otherwise it is reprehensible (makruh). In any case, causing one's own death without any benefit to the religion or the believers is not appropriate; yet if there is a benefit for the faith, it is an honorable station.

Verse 196 brings the rulings concerning Hajj and 'umrah: "And complete the Hajj and 'umrah for Allah. But if you are prevented, then [send] what can be obtained with ease of sacrificial animals..." This verse was also revealed during the year of the fulfilled 'umrah. The definitions, pillars (arkan), conditions, obligations (wajibat), sunnahs, and prohibitions of Hajj and 'umrah are explained in detail in books of jurisprudence (fiqh). The obligation of Hajj primarily indicates through this verse that completing a Hajj and 'umrah once begun is obligatory; its fundamental obligation, however, was established later with Al 'Imran 97. The wisdom of Hajj encompasses numerous religious and worldly benefits; it is the greatest act of worship that practically manifests social unity. Hajj and 'umrah also carry the meaning of jihad. The verse also legislated the tamattu' and qiran forms of Hajj and made the sacrifice obligatory. There are three types of Hajj: ifrad, tamattu', and qiran.

The completion of Hajj and 'umrah is commanded. Since the completion of supererogatory (nafl) acts of worship once begun is obligatory, this command does not yet constitute definitive evidence that Hajj and 'umrah are fundamentally obligatory. The scholars differed on whether 'umrah is obligatory (wajib): Aisha, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Hasan al-Basri, and Imam al-Shafi'i held that 'umrah is obligatory; Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and al-Sha'bi stated that it is supererogatory. In the Hanafi school, 'umrah is not separately obligatory (fard); if begun as a voluntary act, completing it becomes obligatory (wajib).

Ihsar is being prevented from fulfilling the pillars of Hajj or 'umrah after entering ihram. Obstacles such as an enemy, illness, or disability are considered ihsar. A person subjected to ihsar sends a sacrificial animal to the Sanctuary (Haram) in order to exit ihram, and once the presumption that the sacrifice has been slaughtered is formed, they may shave their head and exit ihram. According to the Hanafis, the sacrifice must be slaughtered within the Haram; al-Shafi'i and Malik stated that the sacrifice may be slaughtered at the place of prevention (ihsar), yet authentic narrations indicate that the Prophet (peace be upon him) slaughtered his sacrifice in the Haram.

If it becomes necessary to shave the head while in ihram due to an ailment such as lice or wounds on the head, one chooses as a ransom (fidyah) between fasting for three days, feeding six poor persons, or sacrificing a sheep. This ruling applies not only to ihsar, but to any situation of illness and affliction. In addition, other prohibitions of ihram, such as wearing stitched garments or using perfume, similarly fall under concession (rukhsah) through a ransom.

Those who perform the tamattu' and qiran forms of Hajj—that is, those who combine 'umrah and Hajj—are obligated to slaughter a sacrificial animal that can be obtained with ease. According to al-Shafi'i, this sacrifice is to compensate for a deficiency, and its owner may not eat from it; according to the Hanafis, it is a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and its owner may eat from it. Those who cannot find a sacrificial animal fast for ten days: three days during Hajj and seven days after returning. This ruling applies to those who do not reside around the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram)—that is, the pilgrims coming from beyond the miqat (afaqis).

Hajj is during well-known months: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. Whoever intends to perform Hajj during these months must refrain from sexual relations, committing sins, and disputing during Hajj. Taking provisions has been commanded, and it has been declared that the best provision is God-consciousness (taqwa). Taqwa provides protection from evil and is the most important preparation for both journeys (this worldly life and the Hereafter).

Remember Allah at Muzdalifah after descending from Arafat. During the Age of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah), the Quraysh, considering themselves superior, would not go up to Arafat and would make the standing (waqfah) only at Muzdalifah. With this verse, everyone was commanded to come from Arafat, emphasizing equality. Whoever does not perform the standing at Arafat on the Day of Arafah has not attained the Hajj.

When you have completed your rites of Hajj, remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance. Among people are those who pray only for this world, and they have no share in the Hereafter; while others say, "Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." For these, there is a share of what they have earned. Allah is swift in reckoning.

According to Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, happiness has three levels: pertaining to the soul, pertaining to the body, and external. Happiness pertaining to the soul is related to knowledge and good character; that pertaining to the body is related to health and beauty; and external happiness is related to wealth and status. Those who say, "Give to us in this world" may ask for any of these aspects. However, if knowledge and morality are sought for worldly gain, they become worldly; and those who do not believe in the Hereafter ask only for this world.

The prayer of the believers is as follows: "Our Lord! Give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." Hasana (good/blessing) is every blessing that brings joy to a person's soul, body, or circumstances. There is a distinction between hasan, hasana, and husna: while hasan is used for both concrete entities and abstract meanings, hasana is used for spiritual matters, and husna is used exclusively in spiritual contexts. People of intellect and insight, considering both the beginning and the end, ask for goodness in both this world and the Hereafter.

People are of three kinds: some desire only this world, some desire both this world and the Hereafter, and some sacrifice their lives for the pleasure of Allah. Allah grants a share to each according to their desire; He is swift in reckoning. The phrase "those" encompasses both groups; indeed, as stated in Surah ash-Shura, whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, their harvest is increased, and whoever desires the harvest of this world, they are given of it, but they have no share in the Hereafter.

The numbered days are the days of tashriq, which are the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth days of Dhu al-Hijjah. Remembering Allah with takbir during these days has been commanded. The Day of Arafah and the day of Eid are also days of remembrance. Stoning the devil and reciting takbir after Hajj are among the significant acts of worship of these days. Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) would recite takbir in his tent and on the road, and the people would follow him. The command "Remember Allah during the numbered days" refers to the takbirs of tashriq.

Among people are those who utter pleasing words regarding the life of this world and call Allah to witness what is in their hearts, yet in reality they are the fiercest of adversaries. They cause corruption in the land and destroy crops and cattle. When it is said to them, "Fear Allah," pride drives them to further sin. Hell is sufficient for them; what an evil resting place! These verses were revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, yet they encompass all hypocrites.

In contrast, among people are those who give their lives seeking the pleasure of Allah. These are Allah's distinguished servants; they endure hardships for the sake of religion and worship, and they strive (perform jihad). They pass from the pleased soul (nafs al-radiyyah) to the pleasing soul (nafs al-mardiyyah). Allah is compassionate to His servants and enjoins piety upon them. However, there are also those who, out of satanic arrogance, mistake their own whims for the pleasure of Allah; for this reason, the condition of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah should be compared with that of the Kharijites.

O you who believe! Enter into peace and security in complete submission, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. For Satan is an open enemy to you. Islam means submitting to Allah and entering into peace. A Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand others are safe. If you deviate from peace after clear proofs have come to you, know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.

You will not enter Paradise without being tested by hardships as were the nations before you. Such poverty and afflictions befell them that the messenger and those with him said, "When is the help of Allah?" Behold, the help of Allah is near.

In his commentary on verse 213 of Surah al-Baqarah, Elmalılı states that the expression 'Mankind was one community' in the verse indicates that humanity was initially united, that they subsequently fell into disagreement, and that Allah sent prophets. This meaning is supported by the context preceding and following the verse, as well as by Surah Yunus, verse 19, and the recitation (qira'ah) of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. The first human beings lived as a single community starting from Adam, and differences arose later.

According to the majority of tafsir scholars, this 'single community' was upon truth and monotheism (tawhid). By their very creation, they were inclined toward unity; polytheism (shirk) and disbelief (kufr) emerged only later. Proponents of this view narrated that this unity lasted for ten centuries from Adam to Noah, or that it consisted solely of Adam, Eve, and their offspring. The fundamental point is that tawhid is an eternal principle embedded in human innate nature (fitrah).

Some scholars, such as Ikrimah and Qatadah, asserted that this single community was upon disbelief and falsehood. However, this view faces three objections: it would imply that the prophets were sent to create division, it contradicts the fact that Adam was both a prophet and a father, and it does not accord with the social meaning of the word 'ummah' (community). These objections render the majority opinion more coherent.

According to a third view attributed to al-Maturidi, the earliest humans lived in a natural state, devoid of any divine law (shari'ah) and legal responsibility. When disputes arose with population growth, prophets were sent. This view has been criticized because it deprives 'ummah' of its social meaning and contradicts the reality that humans are inherently social by nature. The prohibition given to Adam, 'do not approach this tree,' shows that responsibility existed from the very beginning.

Qadi Abd al-Jabbar of the Mu'tazilah stated that prior to the prophets, people were a community governed by rational laws. Another group of scholars refrained from passing judgment on this matter, deferring the knowledge to Allah, while some limited the 'single community' to the peoples of Abraham and Moses (Musa). After pointing out the weaknesses of these views, Elmalılı emphasizes that the first view is more sound and concludes that the verse directs humanity toward monotheism and peace through the prophethood of Muhammad.

Allah proclaims: O community of Muhammad! Did you think that you would enter Paradise merely by believing, without experiencing the afflictions and hardships that befell the communities before you? Those communities were shaken to such an extent that their prophet and the believers with him were brought to say, 'When is the help of Allah?' Know well that the help of Allah is certainly near. As long as you do not deviate from faith and guidance, you will attain that help. This verse was revealed in Medina due to the hostility of the Jews or because of the Battle of Uhud or the Battle of the Trench. By the course of history, this community will also encounter the hardships endured by previous nations, but those who are patient will succeed. The era of the Prophet will be the foundation for all standards; transgression will subsequently reappear, but through patience and effort, the partisans of truth will attain divine help, witness truth prevail, and establish universal peace.

In verse 215: "O Muhammad! They ask you where they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents, close relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah knows it." This verse was revealed upon the question of Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who was martyred in the Battle of Uhud. The priority of spending is first on parents, then close relatives, then orphans, the poor, and travelers. It becomes obligatory according to the degree of kinship. Allah also knows any other good deeds and will reward them.

In verse 216: "Fighting is ordained for you, though you dislike it. It may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you; and it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you. Allah knows, and you know not." Fighting is an obligation that establishes general peace and unifies the truth. Sometimes it is an individual obligation (fard al-ayn), and sometimes a collective obligation (fard al-kifayah). Liking and disliking is an emotion; goodness and badness depend on outcomes. Allah informs [us of this] through His Book and historical examples. Since human history is filled with transgression and division, war is an inevitable necessity. Because Allah knows that the good of those committed to the truth lies in their protection, He made fighting an obligation. Martyrdom, victory, and spoils of war will be good.

In verse 217: "O Muhammad! They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is a great sin; but keeping [people] from the path of Allah, disbelief in Him, preventing access to al-Masjid al-Haram, and expelling its people from it are greater sins. Persecution (fitnah) is worse than killing. They will fight you if they can to turn you away from your religion. Whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies as a disbeliever, their deeds will become worthless; they are the companions of the Fire, remaining there eternally." This verse was revealed regarding the raid that Abdullah ibn Jahsh carried out against a Quraysh caravan at Nakhlah. It was the month of Rajab at that time, and fighting had taken place during the sacred month. The Muslims hesitated, but the verse made it known that persecution is greater.

In verse 218: "Indeed, those who have believed, those who have emigrated, and those who have striven in the cause of Allah hope for Allah's mercy. Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful." In verse 219: "O Muhammad! They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is a great sin and some benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit. They also ask you what they should spend; say: The surplus (that which exceeds necessity). Thus Allah clarifies the verses to you so that you may reflect." This verse was revealed upon the question of Umar and Mu'adh. The prohibition of wine came gradually; first it was declared a great sin through this verse, then approaching prayer while intoxicated was forbidden with an-Nisa 4:43, and finally it was rendered strictly forbidden with al-Ma'idah 5:90–91. Although the word 'khamr' is a specific name for grape wine, it generally encompasses everything that causes intoxication. According to Imam Malik and al-Shafi'i, every kind of intoxicant is forbidden and not even a single drop is permissible. While Imam Abu Hanifah stated that grape wine is forbidden in its essence, and other intoxicants are forbidden due to their intoxicating property—such that drinking a small quantity might be permissible—the preferred view is that whatever intoxicates in large amounts, a small amount of it is also forbidden. Gambling is likewise forbidden; lottery-type games such as the divining arrows (azlam) of the Jahiliyyah period are also gambling. In summary, this verse declares that wine and gambling are great sins; their benefits are temporary, while their harms are lasting.

Acquire wealth through lawful (halal) earnings, not through illegitimate ways such as gambling. After providing for the needs of yourself and the family members you are obligated to support, spend the surplus in charitable causes. Allah makes His verses that explain His legal rulings known to you so that you may reflect and act accordingly.

These verses contain rulings for both this world and the Hereafter. The religion of Islam encompasses both realms. In this context, they ask you about the situation of orphans. According to narration, when the verse concerning orphans in Surah an-Nisa was revealed, people became hesitant to associate with orphans. Thereupon, this verse was revealed: Improving the affairs of orphans is better than neglecting them. If you live together with them, they are your brothers in faith. Allah knows the corruptor from the rectifier. Had He willed, He could have put you in hardship; approach orphans with the intention of betterment through the strength He has provided.

Do not marry polytheist women until they believe. A believing bondwoman is better than a polytheist woman, even if she pleases you. And do not marry believing women to polytheist men; a believing slave is better than a polytheist man. Polytheists call you to the Fire, while Allah invites to Paradise and forgiveness. "Polytheist" (mushrik) here encompasses both open idolaters and those of the People of the Book who distort monotheism (tawhid). However, with the verse in Surah al-Ma'idah, permission was granted to marry women from the People of the Book; but giving believing women in marriage to men from the People of the Book is strictly forbidden.

They ask you about women's menstruation. Say: It is a harm. Stay away from women while they are in this state, and do not have sexual relations until they are cleansed. When they have cleansed themselves, approach them from where Allah has commanded you. Indeed, Allah loves those who repent and those who purify themselves. Women are a tilth for you; so go to your tilth however you wish, but prepare ahead for yourselves. Fear Allah and know that you will meet Him.

Do not make Allah an obstacle in your oaths against doing good, acting righteously, and making peace between people. Allah does not hold you accountable for unintentional empty oaths, but He holds you accountable for deliberate false oaths made by your hearts. Those who swear not to approach their wives shall wait four months; if they return, Allah is Forgiving, and if they decide upon divorce, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing. Divorced women shall wait for three menstrual cycles; their husbands have more right to take them back during this period if they desire reconciliation. Divorce is twice; then either retaining in honor or releasing in good will. After the third divorce, a woman is not lawful to her former husband until she marries another husband. These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them.

An inadvertent oath (laghw) is one lacking intent and resolve, where a person swears based on their conviction and then realizes they were mistaken. Imam al-Shafi'i also includes among inadvertent oaths words uttered for emphasis without any intention of swearing, such as "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah." The intent of not holding accountable in this verse refers to accountability in the Hereafter, not expiation (kaffarah) in this world. Allah does not hold one accountable for oaths made without knowing and assumed to be true; however, He holds one accountable for oaths sworn falsely and deliberately with the earning of the heart, which is called a false oath that plunges one into sin (yamin al-ghamus) and has no expiation.

For men who practice ila, that is, swear not to have sexual intercourse with their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. If they return during this period by breaking their oath (fay'), they are forgiven through expiation. If they do not return, they are considered to have resolved upon divorce. The early scholars (Salaf) differed on this matter: Ibn Abbas and a group stated that an irrevocable divorce (ba'in talaq) takes place at the end of four months, while a narration from Ali and Ibn Umar indicates that once the period expires, the husband is detained and compelled either to return or to divorce. The third view states that a revocable divorce (raj'i talaq) occurs at the end of four months. The Hanafis adopted the first view, while the Shafi'is and Malikis adopted the second view.

Divorced women shall wait for three menstrual cycles or periods of purity (quru'). The word 'quru'' means both menstruation and the period of purity. The Hanafis, relying on hadiths transmitted from Aisha and Ibn Umar, interpreted this as menstruation. Women may not conceal the menstruation or pregnancy that Allah has created in their wombs. Their husbands have a greater right to take them back during the waiting period ('iddah) if they have divorced them with a revocable divorce (raj'i talaq). Men have a degree over women; this is because they bear the burdens of the family and provide maintenance.

Divorce (talaq) is twice. After the second divorce, one must either retain the wife with kindness or release her with grace. It is not lawful to take back the dower (mahr) or anything else. However, if it is feared that the husband and wife will not be able to observe the bounds of Allah, it is permissible for the woman to seek divorce in exchange for compensation (khul'). This becomes an irrevocable divorce (ba'in talaq). According to a narration, Jamila sought khul' because she did not love her husband Thabit ibn Qays. These rulings are the bounds of Allah; whoever transgresses them, they are the wrongdoers.

After the third divorce, the woman is not lawful for her first husband until she marries another husband. This prohibition continues until the woman genuinely marries another man and consummates the marriage with him. Allah permitted up to three divorces and arranged this as a trial period. When the waiting periods of divorced women come to an end, it is commanded either to retain them with kindness or release them. It is forbidden to take the verses of Allah in mockery. Furthermore, guardians may not prevent divorced women from remarrying their former husbands; this is better and purer.

Mothers suckle their children for two full years. The father is obligated to provide food and clothing for the nursing mother. No mother or father should be subjected to harm on account of their child. The parents may decide to wean the child through mutual consultation. It is also permissible to entrust the child to another wet nurse. In all these rulings, one must fear Allah and know that He sees all things.

Allah Almighty commanded that mothers suckle their children for two full years. This period is for those who wish to complete the nursing. The father of the child is obligated to provide for the mother's food and clothing within his means. No one is burdened beyond their capacity. Neither mother nor father should be made to suffer harm on account of the child. If the father has passed away, this maintenance obligation falls upon the heir.

If the mother and father decide on weaning before two years through mutual consultation and with regard for the child's well-being, there is no sin upon them in this regard. However, if it is done without the consent of one of the parties, it becomes a sin. If the father wishes to hire a wet nurse for his child, he has the right to do so, provided he pays the fee according to customary practice. Allah is aware of all that you do.

Women whose husbands pass away observe a waiting period ('iddah) of four months and ten days. During this period, they may not marry, adorn themselves, or present themselves to suitors. When the waiting period ends, there is no sin upon them, as they may present themselves to suitors to marry in a lawful manner. The duration of the waiting period for death, unlike the waiting period for divorce, is equal for every woman, and this is based on a divine wisdom.

You may hint indirectly at your desire to marry women observing the waiting period for bereavement. However, it is not permissible to make secret agreements or promise intercourse. Do not resolve on the marriage contract until the waiting period has reached its term. Allah knows what is in your hearts, so beware of what is forbidden. Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Forbearing.

There is no sin upon you if you divorce a woman whose dower (mahr) has not been specified and with whom marriage has not yet been consummated. However, you must provide for her a compensatory gift (mut'ah) according to your means. If you have specified a mahr and divorce her before consummation, it is your duty to pay half of the mahr. Either the woman or the husband may waive this right; for the man to give more is closer to righteousness (taqwa). Do not forget graciousness between you.

Maintain the prayers, especially the middle prayer (the afternoon prayer, 'Asr), and stand before Allah in devotion and humility. Even in a state of fear, perform the prayer on foot or while mounted. When you are safe, perform the prayer as usual. There are differing opinions as to which prayer is the middle prayer; the strongest narration indicates that it is the 'Asr prayer.

There are various opinions regarding the middle prayer. While some stated that it is the 'Asr (afternoon) prayer, some indicated that it is the Friday prayer, and others that it is the Fajr (dawn) prayer. The Prophet's (peace be upon him) hadith, 'They diverted us from the middle prayer,' points to the 'Asr prayer. However, which prayer is the middle prayer has not acquired certainty; this uncertainty is intended to ensure that care is given to all prayers.

According to one view, the middle prayer was designated as the 'Asr prayer, but later this designation was lifted. Therefore, the soundest view is that any of the five daily prayers could be the middle prayer. Whichever prayer is the most challenging for a person is the middle prayer for them.

Allah commanded: Guard the prayers, especially the middle prayer. In times of fear, the prayer may be performed on foot or while mounted, depending on the circumstances. In states of extreme fear, it is permissible to pray by gesturing (ima). When security is attained, prayers must be performed in full.

Men who pass away are obligated to leave provision for their wives for one year. However, this ruling was subsequently abrogated by the inheritance verses. Divorced women are also granted a provision (mut'ah) according to customary practice. This is a duty upon those who fear Allah.

Many people abandoned their homes out of fear of death, yet Allah said to them, 'Die,' and then brought them back to life. This shows that there is no escape from Allah's decree and that He has power to do whatever He wills. The believers must fight in the way of Allah and lend Him a goodly loan.

After Moses (Musa), the Children of Israel asked one of their prophets for a commander to wage war. Saul (Talut) was chosen as their commander. There were those who looked down on him due to his lack of wealth and lineage. The sign of Saul was the Ark (tabut) that the angels would bring. The small group that passed the test of the river gained victory over Goliath (Calut) by Allah's permission. David (Dawud) killed Goliath, and Allah granted him kingship and prophethood.

The Children of Israel objected to their prophet regarding Saul's becoming king, saying: 'We are more worthy of kingship than he is, and he has not been given wealth.' The prophet informed them that Allah had chosen him and granted him an abundance of knowledge and physical stature. What matters in kingship is not lineage, but merit and Allah's choice. Allah gives His kingdom to whom He wills; He knows all things and is all-encompassing in mercy.

The sign of Saul's kingship was the arrival of the lost Ark (Tabut). This Ark was a chest containing sacred relics left by the family of Moses and Aaron (Harun), and a tranquility and reassurance (sakinah). The sakinah was a spiritual support and a sign of victory for the Children of Israel. The arrival of the Ark was clear proof of the legitimacy of Saul's kingship.

When Saul set out with his army, he tested his soldiers with a river, saying: 'Whoever drinks from this water is not of me, except the one who scoops up a handful.' Most of the soldiers disobeyed the order and drank from the river, and only a few remained with Saul. The thirst of those who drank only increased, and they had no strength left to fight. Thereupon, Saul and the believers with him prayed to Allah for patience and victory against Goliath and his army.

As a result of supplication, with Allah's permission, the enemy was routed and David killed Goliath. Allah granted David kingdom, wisdom, and prophethood. This story demonstrates that a small group, through faith and patience, can achieve great victories. Furthermore, it recounts that Allah maintains the order of the earth by repelling some people by means of others. The legitimacy of war is to prevent corruption and establish justice.

Next, the degrees of the prophets are described: Allah favored some prophets over others. He spoke to Moses, gave clear miracles to Jesus, and supported him with the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus). The highest station, although not explicitly stated, belongs to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). When discussing the superiority of prophets, one must avoid excess and negligence (ifrat and tafrit).

In Ayat al-Kursi, Allah's oneness, life, self-subsistence (Qayyumiyyah), and the all-encompassing nature of His knowledge are emphasized. Then it is stated, 'There is no compulsion in religion'; because right guidance has become distinct from error. Whoever rejects taghut and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold that never breaks.

The superiorities and degrees of the prophets are divine gifts from Allah, not inherent attributes existing in their own persons. Prophethood is a deputation to convey and fulfill the divine commands. They are subsumed in the divine command; they cannot unconditionally do whatever they wish. Absolute will belongs to Allah.

Had Allah willed, the communities after the prophets would not have shed each other's blood. In particular, Jesus' counsel, 'Turn the other cheek to the one who slaps your cheek,' forbids even retaliating against aggression. Yet despite this, discord and wars took place. This means that a divine command does not eliminate the possibility of acting contrary to it; a legislative command (amr taklifi) is not a creative, compelling will (iradah takwiniyyah).

Allah did not will for discord to be absolutely nonexistent. The degrees of the prophets and the diversity of nations are by His will. Just as the command of Tawhid did not completely prevent discord, neither did it eliminate the possibility of opposition. It is precisely for this reason that jihad was made obligatory as a practical, active proof of the truth; it is meant to prevent disbelief and aggression.

In verse 254, those who believe in Allah and His messengers are commanded to spend from their wealth in the way of Allah. On the Day of Resurrection, neither bargaining, nor friendship, nor intercession will be of benefit. One must make preparation by giving zakah and charity before that day arrives. Those who disbelieve are wrongdoers; they do not heed abstract proofs, stopping only when confronted with a practical obstacle.

Ayat al-Kursi is a magnificent verse that introduces Allah in the most beautiful manner. There is no deity except Allah; He is the Ever-Living (al-Hayy) and the Self-Sustaining (al-Qayyum). Neither slumber nor heedlessness overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them. His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth, and guarding them does not tire Him. He is the Most High, the Most Great.

In the lexicon, kursi means that which is sat upon, a throne, a seat of knowledge, and similar meanings. Allah's Kursi expresses His dominion and the reign of His knowledge. Commentators have stated that the Kursi is a vast body beneath the Throne (Arsh) that encompasses the heavens and the earth. However, it is not possible to determine its true nature. What is essential is that Allah encompasses all things, and nothing can encompass Him.

The hadiths concerning the Kursi and the Throne (Arsh) explain by way of analogy that the Kursi is not the eighth heaven or the sphere of the fixed stars, but rather a ring that is vast in comparison to the heavens and the earth, yet small in comparison to the Throne. Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, in his commentary on al-Fatihah, addresses the Kursi through theories of space and the Throne through theories of time. While absolute space encompasses the heavens and the earth, all spatial extensions fit into a single moment of time, and this circle of circumstance remains like a small ring in a vast desert. There are also narrations regarding the spiritual values of the Kursi and the Throne; while their essence is included within the boundary of the Throne, this stems not from the Kursi being corporeal, but from it being a stage for the manifestation of spiritual forces.

There are different views regarding the Kursi: First, Kursi means dominion, power, and sovereignty; for divinity is manifested only through power and creation. Second, Allah's Kursi means His knowledge; this view is narrated from Ibn Abbas and preferred by many commentators such as Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. Third, the purpose is solely to convey Allah's majesty and greatness; just as He designated the Kaaba as His house and made the Black Stone (al-Hajar al-Aswad) a place to be kissed, He addressed humanity in ways with which they are familiar. Just as corporeality is not intended in these analogies, the purpose in the Throne and the Kursi is likewise to convey Allah's majesty and greatness.

Although it is certain that a Kursi in its known physical sense is not meant, it is obligatory to believe that Allah has a Kursi. That it involves a concept more or less related to physical form does not necessitate attributing corporeality to Allah. The attribution of the Kursi to Allah is not an 'attribution of sitting,' but an 'attribution of Lordship' (rububiyyah). As understood from the verse, Allah's Kursi is something that covers all of the heavens and the earth and encompasses all physical bodies. We believe in its existence and understand that we cannot know its true reality. We conceive of the Kursi as a locus for the manifestation of absolute knowledge and dominion, and we recognize with certainty that all bodies remain within it and that the One Who exercises authority over it is a Being far exalted above being a physical body.

What is settled here is not Allah, but the totality of bodies termed the heavens and the earth. Above this is the Throne (Arsh), which encompasses the extension of time, the realm of intellects and souls, and is surrounded by the angels brought near (al-muqarrabun); this realm is beyond space and carries no meaning of corporeality. Allah Almighty is not within the Throne, but is above it with the attribute of Rahmaniyyah (All-Mercifulness); this being above is a transcendence that has nothing to do with physical space. Allah's encompassment is in terms of mercy and knowledge. The Kursi is a locus of manifestation for this knowledge and mercy toward our realm. Neither the relationship of the Kursi nor that of the Throne to Allah is in the nature of occupying space; rather, it is a relationship of Lordship through manifestations such as dominion and governance.

In verse 256, it is stated: 'There is no compulsion in religion.' This means that compulsion—just as in religion—does not exist in anything within Islam. The subject matter of religion is not involuntary actions, but voluntary actions. Just as belief through compulsion is impossible, an action performed under compulsion is not an act of worship, for 'Actions are judged only by intentions.' All demands of religion must be fulfilled without compulsion, with good will and consent. A person must accept Islam by their own consent; even if the faith of one who believes under compulsion were valid, it would be deficient. The occasion of revelation for the verse occurred when some of the Ansar wished to force their children away from their religions; while this concerned the People of the Book, it carries a general ruling.

The purpose of jihad is to protect people from compulsion and to elevate the word of Allah by making the true religion prevail. Jihad is not compulsion, but a contest and a test. In the land of Islam, compulsion is forbidden; everyone is free in their religion. Polytheists and the People of the Book can all live with their freedom of religion. However, regarding the Arab polytheists, there is the command, 'Fight them until there is no more fitnah (persecution/discord)'; this is not in the sense of denying them religious freedom, but is a special situation. The view that the verse has been abrogated is weak; it is more widely accepted that it either applies specifically to the People of the Book or retains its general ruling.

The ruling that 'there is no compulsion in religion' is general, and it covers the period after the right way of Islam has become distinct from error. However, this verse must be considered alongside later verses, such as the command to fight. If there were a contradiction between them, the later would abrogate the earlier; yet it is not certain that this verse was revealed later. Therefore, they may explain and specify one another. Consequently, there is no compulsion within the sphere of Islam's legal rulings; warfare and punishments for crimes fall outside this scope. Furthermore, this ruling remains valid as long as discord (fitnah) is not eliminated and followers of other religions living in the land of Islam do not breach their allegiance.

Taghut derives from the root 'tughyan' (transgression) and refers to anything that is rebellious against Allah and worshipped. Beings such as humans, Satan, idols, and stone altars can be taghut. However, prophets such as Jesus and Ezra are not taghut, because they never consented to polytheism (shirk). The first condition of Tawhid is to reject taghut. In other words, the statement 'there is no deity except Allah' first requires rejecting taghuts. Whoever then believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold.

Allah is the ally of those who believe; He brings them out from depths of darkness into the light. Darknesses are many, whereas light is one, and that is the light of Allah. As for those who disbelieve, their allies are the taghuts; they pull them from light into darknesses. These disbelievers will abide eternally in Hell along with their taghuts. A person who does not believe in Allah cannot escape the harassment of taghuts, even if he denies them, and in the end, he is doomed to fall under their sway.

The debate between Abraham (peace be upon him) and Nimrod shows how a believer should act against taghut. When Abraham was describing his Lord, he said, 'He gives life and causes death.' Nimrod replied, 'I too give life and cause death,' killing one of two men and releasing the other. Thereupon Abraham said, 'Allah brings up the sun from the east, so bring it up from the west,' and Nimrod was confounded. This shows that Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people, and how a believer can defeat taghut with the help of Allah.

A man passed by a town that was fallen into ruin and said, 'How will Allah bring this back to life after its death?' Thereupon, Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then revived him and asked how long he had remained. The man said, 'A day or less.' Allah showed him that he had remained for a hundred years, that his food and drink had not spoiled, while his donkey had decayed. Then He commanded him to look at the bones; He brought them together and clothed them with flesh. Thus, the man realized that Allah is competent over all things.

Abraham (peace be upon him) said, 'My Lord! Show me how You give life to the dead.' Allah said, 'Have you not believed?' Abraham said, 'I have believed, but I ask so that my heart may be completely reassured.' Thereupon, Allah commanded him to take four birds and tame them to himself, then cut them into pieces, place parts of them on each mountain peak, and call the birds. The birds came running to him. This is an evidence demonstrating Allah's power to bring the dead to life.

In this section, the commentary regarding the 259th verse of Surah al-Baqarah is addressed. The verse relates that once a person passed by an entirely deserted village whose roofs had caved in and walls had collapsed, and said, 'How will Allah bring this back to life after its death?' The commentators have put forward different views regarding who this person was: some stated that he was Ezra, while others mentioned Jeremiah, a servant of Lot, or another prophet. The location of the village has also been interpreted in different ways; the most famous view is that it was Jerusalem. This event is cited as an example of Allah's power to revive the dead.

The person's words, 'How will Allah bring this back to life?' may carry different meanings: it could be an expectant anticipation of revival with hope, an admission of human helplessness, or an expression of utter despair. The commentators are of the opinion that this statement was not an absolute denial, but rather a slip of the tongue resulting from a believer's sorrow. For despair is disbelief; however, in moments of extreme grief and helplessness, even prophets may experience a temporary lapse of hope. In such situations, divine help arrives immediately, though it is sometimes deferred in order to discipline the person.

Allah caused that person to die, left him dead for a hundred years, and then revived him. Upon reviving him, He asked, 'How long did you remain?' and the man answered, 'A day or part of a day.' This response shows that personal consciousness continues even after death. Then Allah showed that his food and drink had not spoiled, and demonstrated how the bones of his donkey were joined together and clothed with flesh. This is a living example of resurrection from death. The person reinforced his faith by saying, 'I know that Allah has power over all things.'

In the second part, the supplication of Abraham, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead,' is addressed. When Allah asked, 'Do you not believe?' Abraham answered, 'I have believed, but I ask so that my heart may be completely reassured.' Thereupon, Allah commanded him to take four birds and become thoroughly familiar with them, then divide them into parts, place a piece on each mountain peak, and then call them. The birds, by Allah's leave, came to life and came to Abraham. This is a miracle concerning Allah's power to give life.

These two stories emphasize that Allah is the Almighty (al-Aziz) and the All-Wise (al-Hakim). That is, He is both all-powerful over everything and performs His actions with wisdom, linking them to specific causes. Remaining bound to causes does not indicate any incapacity on His part; on the contrary, it is a requirement of His wisdom. The act of giving life occurs sometimes directly in a miraculous manner, and sometimes through a chain of known causes. This signifies the simultaneous manifestation of Allah's attributes of might and wisdom.

Finally, the message these verses give to believers is this: True life and resurrection depend on Allah's will. Whoever has full faith in His power emerges from darkness into light; he finds hope and peace. Abraham's request for 'his heart to be reassured' is the desire to reinforce faith through direct observation. Allah may bestow this station upon whichever of His servants He wills. This is precisely why the verses conclude with the ruling that 'Allah has power over all things.'

While discussing the subject of resurrection and giving life, Elmalılı emphasizes that Allah's power is far greater than the capacity of human memory and mind. Even a person's recollection of something forgotten is an example of giving life. Allah's giving of life, however, is far swifter than this. The miracle of Abraham reviving the birds shows that Allah is the Giver of Life (al-Muhyi) and that everything comes into being by His command 'Be.' In this context, spending in the way of Allah is likewise a means of revival and blessing.

In the 261st verse, the state of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is likened to a grain: that grain produces seven ears, in each ear there are a hundred grains, thus seven hundred grains are obtained from a single grain. Allah multiplies further for whom He wills. This example explains that the reward of spending in Allah's cause (infaq) is multiplied manifold. Although the expression 'fî sebîlillah' generally denotes expenses made for jihad, this verse applies broadly to every kind of charity and spending. Allah's mercy is vast, and He is All-Knowing.

In verses 262–264, the conditions for the acceptance of spending (infaq) are explained: Reminding others of one's charity with reproach and causing injury nullifies it. Allah does not accept expenditures made hypocritically by the disbelievers. Believers must not deprive themselves of reward by likening their charity to the ostentation of the disbelievers through reproach and injury. Kind speech and forgiving shortcomings are better than charity followed by injury. Allah is free of all need, Most Forbearing (Halim).

In verses 265–266, two parables are given: The first is that the condition of those who spend seeking Allah's pleasure and strengthening their own souls is like a beautiful garden on a high hill; a heavy downpour doubles its fruit. The second is the example of someone who has grown old with dependent children and loses their garden to a fiery whirlwind. This conveys that the reward of faith and righteous deeds is Paradise, whereas ostentation and reproach will destroy these blessings.

In verses 267–274, the details of what to spend from and how to spend are set forth: One must spend from the good things earned and from the best of what the earth produces. Satan threatens with poverty, while Allah promises of His bounty. Whoever is granted wisdom has been granted great good. Charities may be given openly or secretly; giving secretly is better and serves as an expiation for sins. The bashful poor who have dedicated themselves to the cause of Allah might not be widely known; they must be recognized by their features. Those who spend night and day, secretly and openly, have their reward with their Lord; there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

Allah commands the believers to spend from the finest of what they have earned and from what We have brought forth from the earth. They are instructed not to attempt to give foul and worthless things that they themselves would never accept without closing their eyes to them. This command underscores that infaq must be made from that which is purest and most valuable.

This verse corrects two misconceptions regarding spending. The first is considering wealth merely as the product of labor while neglecting natural resources. The second is regarding capital as the absolute cause of gain and treating labor as worthless. In truth, real capital is the richness of the earth and the bounty of creation. Money is accumulated labor; even when viewed as capital, it is labor by origin. For this reason, spending from the finest earnings has been commanded.

Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to stinginess and shameful deeds. Allah, however, promises you forgiveness and bounty. Allah's bounty is vast, and He is All-Knowing. He grants multiplied returns in this world and the Hereafter to those who spend. Therefore, one must not be swayed by Satan's whisperings, but rather rely on Allah's promise.

Allah grants wisdom to whom He wills. Whoever is granted wisdom has attained abundant good. Wisdom has many definitions: hitting the mark in speech and deed, the harmony of knowledge and action, grasping the inner reality of created things, understanding Allah's command, and the like. Wisdom is both a divine gift and a virtue that can be acquired through personal endeavor.

The highest station of wisdom is prophethood. Every prophet is wise (hakim), but not every wise person is a prophet. Attaining wisdom requires a pure intellect and a pure heart. Those who succumb to lusts and satanic whisperings remain deprived of wisdom. This verse encourages the believers to spend from their finest wealth and to seek wisdom.

Wisdom rests upon the firm order established by Allah, namely Sunnatullah. Within this order, everything is firmly linked together. Human wisdom consists in understanding this divine order, acting in conformity with it, and producing works beneficial to others. According to Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, Allah's wisdom is creating what serves the benefit of His servants; human wisdom is doing things that benefit others. However, humans must not fall into the delusion of mistaking their own discoveries and inventions for the primary cause.

There are numerous definitions of wisdom. One is placing everything in its proper place. This holds true for both divine wisdom and human wisdom. Another definition is that wisdom is turning toward good and righteous deeds. Likewise, in governance, a human striving to emulate the Supreme Creator according to human capacity is also wisdom. Moreover, the definition expressed as 'adopting the character of Allah' points to the magnificent character of the Prophet and is identified with the morality of the Quran.

Wisdom is the union of knowledge and action. Merely getting stuck in theoretical knowledge is not wisdom, but philosophizing. Beneficial knowledge must be sought, and useless knowledge avoided. Knowledge without action is futile, and action without knowledge cannot be wisdom. Wisdom is therefore the integrated whole of sound knowledge and righteous conduct. The method of Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh) is likewise grounded upon the progression from knowledge to servanthood. The universe is a book of wisdom, and the Quran is the expression of this wisdom in divine speech.

Wisdom also possesses a dimension belonging to the heart. Conscience is the soul's realization of itself, and the heart is the focal point of this unity. The divine states of contraction (qabd) and expansion (bast) relate to the tightening and broadening of the heart. A healthy life depends on the balanced continuation of these two states. Wisdom lies in the balance struck between despair and hope, between fear and hope, and in the steadfastness of this harmony.

In the Quran, wisdom is interpreted in four ways: the admonitions of the Quran, understanding and knowledge, prophethood, and the subtle secrets of the Quran. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi states that all of these signify knowledge. In addition, wisdom denotes knowledge of the abrogating and the abrogated (nasikh and mansukh), the clear and the ambiguous (muhkam and mutashabih), piety (taqwa) in religion, and reverent awe (khashyah). In the end, wisdom is knowledge that leads to beneficial action, beneficial action grounded in knowledge, or soundness in both knowledge and action. The phrase 'abundant good' points to the consummate wisdom born of the union of knowledge and deed.

Allah's bounty and mercy are immensely vast; however, none understand this except the people of wisdom who act upon their knowledge and reflect deeply. Every expenditure made and every vow pledged in the way of Allah or in the way of Satan is known to Allah, and He will recompense it. The wrongdoers have no helpers; those who commit injustice have primarily wronged themselves. Allah's wise order will one day seize and punish them.

The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Allah. Love of Allah and fear of Him reside together; as nearness increases, fear increases as well. For this reason, Allah first stated, 'None will grasp it except people of deep discernment,' then, 'Indeed, Allah knows it,' and followed this with a three-tiered warning: 'There will be no helpers for the wrongdoers.'

When asked whether charities should be given openly or in secret, Allah made known that giving openly is commendable, but giving secretly is better and conceals sins. The word sadaqah denotes truthfulness and perfection. Differing views exist as to whether the charities in the verse refer to the obligatory or the voluntary; the preferred position is that it is more virtuous to give obligatory zakat openly and voluntary charities in secret.

Giving voluntary charities in secret keeps one distant from ostentation, preserves the dignity of the poor, prevents seeking fame and imposing obligation, and multiplies the reward many times over. However, giving openly may be more virtuous if it encourages others. As for obligatory zakat, it ought to be given openly in order to comply with the command and dispel suspicion.

Allah guides whom He wills; you are only a warner. Whatever good you spend is for your own benefit. For this reason, you may also give voluntary charity to the polytheist poor. Obligatory charities, however, are for the poor who are constrained in the way of Allah, unable to engage in trade or travel, appear modest, and do not beg; these are individuals who, like the People of the Bench (Ashab al-Suffah), are devoted to sacred knowledge and worship.

It is narrated from Abdullah b. Abbas that one day our Prophet (peace be upon him) saw the condition of the People of the Suffah (Ashab al-Suffah), noticed their poverty and hardship, and gave them glad tidings. It is narrated that the verse was revealed upon this incident. The ruling of the verse is general; it encompasses all Muslims who devote themselves for the sake of Allah to paths such as jihad, knowledge, or service, who possess no wealth or property, or who have no time to earn a livelihood. Such people are the foremost priority for charity and spending (infaq). Furthermore, those who perform any act of kindness or generosity should not forget that Allah knows it and will reward it.

Those who spend their wealth night and day, secretly and openly, have a great reward with their Lord; there is no fear for them, nor shall they grieve. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) gave forty thousand dinars in charity night and day, secretly and openly, and Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) likewise distributed his four silver dirhams in the same manner. Our Prophet (peace be upon him) asked Ali, "Why did you do this?" and he replied, "In order to be worthy of my Lord's promise." Although there are different narrations regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse, according to al-Razi, the best view is that the verse was revealed to encourage anyone who gives charity for all times and circumstances.

Being able to spend night and day, secretly and openly, is the most perfect form of spending (infaq). By accelerating the circulation of wealth, this prevents hoarding and black-marketeering. The individual economy and the general economy are intertwined; when social order deteriorates, the responsibility of the wealthy among the people of faith increases. However, the verse does not command spending all of one's wealth; in the verse (al-Baqarah 2/219), it is commanded to give "that which is beyond your needs." In obligatory charities, the minimum threshold (nisab) must be taken into account, while in voluntary charities, the preservation of capital should be observed. The admonition in Surah al-Isra, "Do not tie your hand to your neck, nor stretch it out entirely and become wasteful," also demonstrates this balance.

According to what is narrated from Qatadah, our Prophet (peace be upon him) said, "Those who amass great wealth are vile," and when the Companions asked about exceptions, he said, "Except those who spend of their wealth to their right, to their left, in front of them, and behind them." The verse encourages measured spending that is free from excess. Spending everything is not a requirement; however, total spending, as Ali did, is also permissible. The absolute meaning of the verse should be applied according to needs, times, and individuals. There is no waste in goodness, but spending that leads a person to regret is objectionable. The influence of the social environment is significant in this matter; in an environment hostile to virtuous conduct, the benevolent face great difficulties.

In the continuation of the verse, usury/interest (riba) is forbidden. Riba literally means excess; in the language of the Sharia, it is an excess in a bilateral contract that remains without a countervalue. The riba widespread among the Arabs of the pre-Islamic era of ignorance (Jahiliyyah) was stipulating an excess payment based on the term of deferral when lending. Allah has made trade lawful and forbidden interest. Those who consume interest will stand like someone beaten by Satan. Whoever desists from interest, their past sins are forgiven; those who return to it are companions of the Fire. Allah blesses charities with increase and destroys interest. Those who believe, do righteous deeds, establish prayer, and pay zakat have their rewards. Believers are commanded to fear Allah and abandon what remains of interest; otherwise, it is declared that war will be waged against them by Allah and His Messenger. If the debtor is in hardship, granting him respite, or even forgiving the debt as charity, is better. On the Day of Resurrection, everyone will be compensated in full for what they have earned.

Riba literally means excess and increase. In the Sharia, it refers to the excess taken on debts—that is, interest. This excess applied to all debts other than interest-free benevolent loans (qard al-hasan) is called riba. Just as in cash transactions, the deferral markup in deferred credit sales (nasi'ah) is also riba. For the six commodities mentioned in the famous hadith (wheat, barley, dates, salt, gold, and silver), an immediate hand-to-hand exchange of the same kind and equal quantity was stipulated, and any excess was deemed riba. Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) stated that riba has obscure forms, and that transactions such as salam (forward sale: paying upfront for future delivery of goods) in animal trading could also be judged as riba.

Riba is more of a societal disease than an individual trouble. It spreads rapidly in impoverished societies and brings society under its sway. At the advent of Islam, thanks to the Muhammadan grace, this development came about within twenty years, and the scourge of riba was wiped away from society. A commerce free of riba was put into practice.

Tafsir scholars have enumerated the reasons why riba was declared forbidden. First, riba is taking a person's property without a countervalue. Second, riba keeps people away from genuinely working, earning, and engaging in production. Third, usury causes kindness and mutual assistance among people in the form of 'benevolent loans' (qard al-hasan) to be cut off. Fourth, considering riba permissible grants the rich the opportunity to extract excess wealth from the poor and destitute, which contradicts Allah's mercy. Fifth, the primary reason for riba being forbidden is that it is established by divine textual decree (nass); even if we do not fully know its underlying wisdom, we must recognize that it is forbidden.

In many respects, riba derails right and justice. Allah gradually diminishes and ultimately destroys riba, which is thought to increase wealth; in contrast, He blesses and multiplies charities, which are thought to decrease wealth. While riba devours like a worm the lives that would produce wealth, charities become reward, life, and blessing. Allah does not love those who are confirmed disbelievers and deeply sinful, persisting regarding lawful and unlawful; He loves those who repent.

Those who believe, do righteous deeds, establish prayer, and pay zakat have their reward with their Lord; there is no fear for them, nor shall they grieve. O you who believe! Fear Allah, and leave what remains of riba. If you do not, know that you will be subjected to a war from Allah and His Messenger. Allah has cursed both the one who consumes riba and the one who pays it. If you repent, your principal is yours; you will neither wrong nor be wronged.

Various occasions of revelation have been narrated for this verse. Four brothers from the Thaqif tribe, after becoming Muslims, demanded their interest receivables from the Banu Mughirah, and the Prophet sent this verse. In addition, the date trade between Abbas and Uthman b. Affan, as well as the joint usurious partnership between Abbas and Khalid b. al-Walid, are also cited as reasons. During the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet declared that all riba from the era of ignorance was null and void, and the first riba he abolished was that of Abbas, son of Abd al-Muttalib. Contracts made in the abode of war (dar al-harb) are not annulled from their foundation after entering Islam, but they are not permitted to continue.

Those who carry out riba transactions in the Abode of Islam (Dar al-Islam), whether out of denial of religion or with sinful intent, are confronted with war from Allah and His Messenger. If the debtor is destitute, he must be granted time; forgiving the debt as charity is even better. O you who believe! Fear the Day when you will be returned to Allah; everyone will be paid what they have earned, and they will not be wronged. This verse is the very last verse revealed of the Holy Quran; it warns of death and the Day of Resurrection.

The discourse has transitioned from the subject of spending (infaq) to the rulings on trade and riba, and from there to the rulings on debt. Since debt is a matter upheld by human dignity, Allah has taken it under His own eternal covenant and linked it to the sense of God-consciousness (taqwa), which is the greatest sanction. However, so that piety does not hinder lawful earnings, it has been stated that debts must be recorded in written documents.

In verse 282, it is commanded that when entering into a debt transaction for a specified term, it must be written down. A scribe who knows how to write should not refuse to write as Allah has taught him. The debtor should dictate, and fearing Allah, his Lord, he should not diminish anything from the right. If the debtor is feeble-minded, a minor, or unable to dictate, his guardian should dictate truthfully. Two men should be present as witnesses; if two men are not available, then one man and two women may witness, so that if one of them forgets, the other may remind her. Witnesses should not refuse when they are called upon, and scribes should not weary of writing down the debt, whether it is small or large, until its term. This is more equitable in the sight of Allah, sounder for testimony, and more conducive to avoiding doubt. However, in immediate on-the-spot transactions, there is no harm in not writing it down. In buying and selling, witnesses should still be taken, and neither the scribe nor the witness should be harmed.

Regarding the testimony of women, the verse stipulates two women in place of one man. The reason for this is that the likelihood of forgetting is greater in women. In a woman's nature, emotionality predominates, which increases susceptibility to influence and forgetting. Moreover, a woman's sense of modesty is strong, and it is not suitable for her to be involved with external commercial affairs. For this reason, the burden of testimony was placed upon two women so that they might remind one another. However, in matters that women know exclusively among themselves, the testimony of a single woman is also valid.

In verse 283, it is stated that if you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe, taking a pledge will serve in place of a written document. A pledge is also permissible while resident, but it is not recommended when writing is possible. If you trust one another, there is no need to take a pledge; the one who is trusted must fulfill the trust. Concealing testimony burdens the heart with guilt and is among the major sins. Allah knows everything.

In verse 284, it is stated that whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth belongs to Allah. Whether you disclose what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. Allah is capable of all things. Following the previous rulings on debt and testimony, this verse reminds that everything is within the knowledge of Allah and that people are also held accountable for their intentions.

There are two narrations regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse: one was revealed concerning concealing testimony and speaking the truth, and the other concerning believers taking disbelievers as allies and imitating them. Whatever is in the heavens and on the earth belongs to Allah; nothing remains hidden from His knowledge. Whether you disclose what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it.
