This verse encompasses all kinds of voluntary and involuntary feelings, thoughts, intentions, and memories within you. However, the context of the verse pertains to evils such as concealing testimony; good deeds seem to be outside this. Moreover, feelings that have firmly settled within you are taken as the basis; fleeting ones are not included. Likewise, voluntary actions are called to account, whereas involuntary ones depend on Allah's will. Ultimately, people must avoid every evil, whether open or hidden, and make good deeds a habit. Allah is capable of all things; He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.

Returning to the general address at the beginning of the surah, this verse carries the significance of a renewed look at Ayat al-Kursi. While demonstrating the severe punishment for concealing testimony—which is a sin of the heart—it also summarizes the verses, proofs, responsibilities, and rulings within the surah. In particular, it connects faith in the Hereafter to knowing Allah and to His attributes of knowledge, will, and power. These three verses (285-286) are referred to as 'khawatim Surat al-Baqarah' (the concluding verses of Surah al-Baqarah); the first returns to the fifteen verses concerning the disbelievers and hypocrites, while the last two harmonize with the believers and the God-fearing at the beginning of the surah. In this way, it is determined in whom the faith and attributes mentioned at the beginning are actually found.

The Prophet believed in all that was revealed to him from his Lord, and the believers believed in Allah, His angels, His books, and His messengers. They said, 'We make no distinction between any of Allah's messengers; we hear and obey. Grant us Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return.' This verse encompasses all the articles of faith and emphasizes making no distinction among the messengers. According to a narration, when the verse 'whether you disclose what is within yourselves or conceal it' was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Companions; the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) commanded them to say, 'we hear and obey.' Thereupon, Allah relieved them by revealing the verse stating that He will not burden a soul beyond its capacity.

Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. Every good a person earns is for himself, and every evil he commits is against himself. This verse summarizes the fundamental principle of divine obligation: responsibility is proportional to a person's capacity. Allah desires ease for His servants, not hardship. There are subtle distinctions between the words 'kasb' and 'iktisab'; according to some scholars, kasb is to attain by hitting the mark, whereas iktisab is absolute exertion. According to the first view, good deeds are in a person's favor, and bad deeds are against him. According to the second view, working in accordance with proper procedure is beneficial, while striving blindly is harmful. According to the third view, earning for others is in one's favor, while earning only for oneself is against one. According to the fourth view, enabling others to earn is in one's favor, while living off someone else's earnings is against one.

Because the believers accepted Allah's commands with graceful obedience, believed in the Hereafter, and sought forgiveness, they were rewarded with this verse. Allah's obligation is not beyond the capacity of His servants; rather, it provides them with mercy and ease. In addition to obligatory duties, there is also encouragement for supererogatory acts of worship and good deeds. In conclusion, if anyone does good, it is to his own benefit, and if he does evil, it is to his own detriment. This principle applies both in this world and the Hereafter. The justice and mercy of Allah require that He does not burden His servants beyond their capacity; otherwise, this would be a punishment. With this wisdom, servants must submit by saying 'we hear and obey' and seek forgiveness from Allah.

Allah gave this response in answer to the supplication of the believers who said, 'We hear, we obey the command, our Lord, we seek Your forgiveness, and to You alone is the return.' These verses show that Allah's speech manifests not only with His Messenger, but also with the community that believes in him, in the form of a conversation and intimate supplication. Through this style, believers find themselves in direct conversation with Allah, and this is expressed as an immense blessing. Those who attain this honor will also be granted the permission to make requests of Allah.

With this answer, Allah explains the subtlety of obligation and gives the good tidings that no burden beyond their capacity will be placed upon them. At the same time, He indirectly indicates that an obligation beyond one's capacity would have been possible. By explaining the value of earning and that blessing corresponds to hardship, He encourages good deeds that have not been made obligatory. This response also encompasses the content of the sacred hadith, 'My servant continues to draw near to Me with supererogatory acts of worship,' and concludes with a prayer.

"Our Lord! Do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake." Forgetting and making a mistake are of two kinds: in one, a person is excused, while in the other, they are not. For example, one who sees an impurity and forgets to clean it before praying is not excused; however, if they did not see it, they are excused. Likewise, one who shoots at game without considering that a person might be present is not excused. Nor is someone excused who fails to learn religious commandments and does not review them to avoid forgetting. Therefore, the expression "...beyond what they have the capacity for" does not encompass all mistakes and instances of forgetfulness; those within one's control do not relieve one of accountability. Evil deeds committed by mistake are as harmful as poison, and before Allah their consequence does not change. For this reason, believers are obligated to avoid forgetfulness and mistakes as much as possible.

"Our Lord! Do not place upon us a heavy burden as You placed upon those before us." Do not subject us to strict rulings and harsh covenants as were imposed upon the Children of Israel. According to tafsir scholars, the Jews were under such obligations as fifty daily prayers, a tax of one-fourth of their wealth, cutting away garments tainted with impurity, capital punishments, and slaying themselves. Believers prayed to be preserved from these hardships, and Allah removed them through the verse in Surah al-A'raf.

"Our Lord! Lay not on us that which we have no power to bear." This prayer is made despite the promise of ease in the preceding verse, because the word capacity can also be used in the sense of endurance, which carries the possibility of pressure. Moreover, an obligation may not be the result of a divine command, but may come through the oppression of transgressors. While believers ask to be protected from every unbearable burden, they know that disbelievers will face unjust burdens and that this is a manifestation of divine justice. Hearts are between two fingers of Allah; supplication is made in order not to deviate from the right path and not to suffer intolerable afflictions.

Pardon our sins and grant us forgiveness! Treat us with Your mercy, for You are our Protector. Help us against the community of disbelievers and grant us victory. It is reported that when the Prophet (peace be upon him) prayed with these supplications, Allah stated, "Indeed, I have done so." Surah Al Imran will begin as an answer to this prayer for help and victory.

Great virtues regarding the last two verses of Surah al-Baqarah have been reported in hadiths. Narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "Whoever recites these two verses from Surah al-Baqarah at night, they will suffice him." In a hadith from Abu Dharr: "Allah concluded Surah al-Baqarah with two verses that are from a treasure beneath the Throne. Learn them and teach them to your children, for they are prayer (salah), supplication, and Quran." Umar and Ali would not sleep without reciting these verses. It is also narrated that Gabriel instructed the Prophet (peace be upon him) to say "amin" at the end of these verses.

The letters "Alif, Lam, Mim" at the beginning of Surah Al-Imran possess a remarkable recitation. These letters are generally recited with a fathah on the second mim and by connecting them to the majestic name of Allah; however, in the recitation of Abu Ja'far, there is a pause (sakt). Linguists and exegetes have put forward various views regarding this recitation. In terms of meaning, a special quality is considered to exist in the combination of the states of connection (wasl) and stopping (waqf) here: this state virtually represents a concise symbol of Ayat al-Kursi. Indeed, the fact that Surah al-Baqarah is referred to as 'Surat al-Kursi' and that Ayat al-Kursi is the greatest verse supports this interpretation.

At the beginning of the surah, Allah's oneness and unique sublimity are emphasized. He is al-Hayy and al-Qayyum; that is, He is the Ever-Living, immortal, and the Sustainer and Governor of all things. No being other than Him can be a deity. For this reason, accepting Jesus or anyone else as a deity is disbelief (kufr). This fundamental belief also serves as an example in the surah that ambiguous verses (mutashabih) must be understood by referring to clear, decisive verses (muhkam). In this way, believers are protected from straying.

The Quran confirms previously revealed scriptures such as the Torah and the Gospel. However, a correct understanding of these books depends on believing in the Quran and the prophethood of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The Quran is a Furqan (Criterion) that verifies the accounts and laws of previous prophets, while at the same time completing them. For this reason, it is not possible to truly understand the previous scriptures without confirming the Quran.

By sending down the Furqan, Allah distinguished truth from falsehood and showed the right path. Those who reject His verses, especially those who attack tawhid (divine oneness) and the infallibility ('ismah) of the prophets, are destined for a severe punishment. Allah is al-Aziz (the Almighty), the Lord of retribution. He may grant respite for a time to those who trample upon the truth, but in the end He ruins them. This is a requirement of His might.

Forgiveness is meaningful only for the one who has the power to punish. Allah forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. The Christians' depiction of Allah as a helpless father who sacrifices his son is contrary to His majesty. Allah neither begets nor is He begotten; He is One and in need of nothing. The belief in a triune god (the Trinity) is false and leads man into deviation. True salvation lies in adhering to the belief in tawhid.

For people to accept committing sin as an inherent necessity of creation, and then to claim that this sin cannot be forgiven, is in reality to deny Allah's forgiveness and omnipotence. This mindset means abolishing the supreme authority that inflicts punishment and placing the penalty for their own sins upon Allah. It is precisely this conception that lies at the foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity in Christianity.

The doctrine of the Trinity is an enigma arising from the denial or conflation of the attributes of Allah, the true Deity. Jesus never invited people to such a belief. His miracles were evidence of his prophethood; yet later, these miracles were shrouded in mystery, and the expression "father" in the Gospel was stripped of its metaphorical meaning and interpreted as a literal father. This distortion was formalized through secret meetings and the Council of Nicaea, becoming the fundamental dogma of Christianity.

The Quran sets forth the manifest truths regarding Allah's essence and attributes that are established by both reason and transmitted evidence (naql). It refutes these false beliefs and subtly critiques the transgressing attitudes of Christians toward Allah. The Quran demonstrates that all these deviations converge under the concept of disbelief (kufr). At the same time, it confirms the previous scriptures and states that it corresponds to their uncorrupted originals.

Allah's retribution is neither ignorant nor treacherous; it is entirely for wisdom and might. Those who seek to demean the truth will ultimately suffer defeat. Allah's retribution is harmonious with His justice and mercy, for He is al-Hayy and al-Qayyum. Forgiveness is meaningful only for those who possess the power to take retribution. Allah shows mercy to whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.

The Quran is a criterion (furqan) that distinguishes truth from falsehood. Allah sent down this Book in truth and justice, to confirm what came before it. The previous scriptures, the Torah and the Gospel, were also for guidance to humankind. The Quran shows that the prophethood of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was not a novelty, but that he was a prophet foretold by previous prophets as well.

Allah's knowledge encompasses all things. Nothing in the earth or the heavens is hidden from Him. He shapes you in the wombs as He wills and fashions you into whatever form He desires. This is a manifestation of His unique power and wisdom.

Allah is the Creator, the Fashioner, and the Bestower of existence in the most beautiful manner upon all things. The physical and spiritual forms within you are works brought into being by His will. When you reflect upon the formation of the fetus, you realize how many branches of knowledge it is related to, and that yet undiscovered divine sciences (ulum al-ladunniyyah) also play a role in this process. Every human being, including Jesus, was fashioned by Allah in the womb. Thus, when Allah is mentioned, one must contemplate these creative and fashioning attributes of His.

The knowledge of Allah, who is al-Khaliq al-Musawwir (the Creator and Fashioner), encompasses all things; the unseen (ghayb) and the seen (shahadah) are equal before Him. False beliefs such as the doctrine of the Trinity cannot remain hidden from Him either. He is not a blind or aimless creator; all knowledge originates from Him. The prophets and Jesus conveyed tidings of the unseen only through His teaching.

The power of this Creator and Fashioner is infinite. The order called nature is the product of His continuous agency, while miracles are His non-routine and unique agency. The laws of nature are subject to His divine power, not its master. The shaping of prime matter is renewed at every moment, and every new form emerges directly through the power of Allah.

The Creator and Fashioner possesses entirely free will in creation; He is under no compulsion. The diverse forms in the wombs are the work of His will. The laws of nature are not necessary, but contingent laws. Heredity is likewise not a necessity, but a state contingent upon Allah's will. The issue of original sin should also be evaluated within this framework; Allah can forgive sins if He so wills.

The verses of the Quran are of two categories: decisive (muhkam) and allegorical (mutashabih). Decisive verses are those whose meaning is clear and established; they are the foundation of the Book. Allegorical verses, on the other hand, are those that can bear multiple meanings and are ambiguous. These are understood by referring to the decisive verses. It is not correct to take allegorical verses as the basis and interpret decisive ones through them; this would render the entirety of the Book allegorical.

Quranic verses are divided into two categories: muhkam (clear and definitive in meaning) and mutashabih (allegorical, bearing multiple meanings). Muhkam verses constitute the foundation of the Book and must be followed. Mutashabih verses, on the other hand, may be ambiguous either in terms of wording (unusual words, concise or elongated expressions), or in terms of meaning (subjects beyond human comprehension, such as Allah's attributes and the Hereafter), or in terms of both. While certain types of mutashabih require approaches such as investigation, reflection, and awaiting an explanatory interpretation, with respect to the truly ambiguous verses, pausing and submitting to Allah is essential. None knows the ultimate interpretation (ta'wil) of allegorical verses except Allah.

Those in whose hearts is perversity pursue ambiguous (mutashabih) verses in order to cause discord and cast doubt among people, interpreting them according to their own desires. Whereas those scholars firmly grounded in knowledge say: 'We believe in this Book; all of it is from our Lord.' They believe in all the clear (muhkam) and ambiguous verses, can distinguish truth from falsehood, and, seeking refuge in Allah, pray as follows: 'Our Lord! Do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us mercy from Yourself. Truly, You are the Bestower.'

The letter 'waw' in the phrase 'those firmly grounded in knowledge (al-rasikhun fi al-ilm)' mentioned in the verse can be read in two ways: If it is taken as istinaf (the resumption of a new sentence), none knows the interpretation (ta'wil) of the ambiguous except Allah, and the scholars merely say, 'We believe.' If it is taken as conjunction (atf), it means that Allah and the scholars firmly grounded in knowledge know its interpretation. Both views have been narrated from the Companions. This disagreement indicates that the interpretation of the ambiguous cannot be known in every aspect, but a portion of it can be known by scholars. For this reason, the ambiguous is divided into three categories: that which only Allah knows (such as the time of the Hour), that which is possible for humans to know (such as rare expressions), and that which is specific to scholars.

The Jews and the Christians misinterpreted ambiguous verses, attributing a son to Allah or attempting to calculate the time of the Day of Judgment through abjad calculation (gematria). This stems from the perversity in their hearts. Yet Allah's promise is true, and the disbelievers will be punished just like the people of Pharaoh. The believers, on the other hand, attain victory with Allah's help despite being few in number, as was the case in the Battle of Badr. Allah supports those who fight in His cause, and this is a clear lesson for those who can see.

In the life of this world, things such as women, sons, gold, silver, horses, cattle, and crops have been made alluring and pleasing to people. These are the transient worldly benefits. Yet true beauty and the blessings of eternal life reside with Allah. Man must avoid becoming excessively attached to these worldly blessings and turn toward that which is enduring in the presence of Allah.

The word "qanatir" is the plural of qintar. The qintar is the largest unit of weight and was used in different forms across various eras and peoples. This expression was used to describe excessive fondness for the appetizing things of this world.

Love for these lustful desires drags man into every evil. Yet they are transient and base. Man's true objective ought to be the blessings that are with Allah. The life of this world is a means for the Hereafter, and to harbor love for these means while abandoning the true objective is sheer foolishness.

As stated in verses 15-17, there are gardens (paradises), purified spouses, and Allah's pleasure for the servants who are mindful of Allah. These are far better than the transient pleasures of the world. These blessings are reserved for those servants who are patient, truthful, devoutly obedient with reverent awe, spend in charity, and seek forgiveness before dawn.

Taqwa (piety) is not mere empty words; Allah knows the inward and outward states of His servants. Believers who have faith, ask for the forgiveness of their sins, implore protection from torment, and adopt the aforementioned virtuous qualities as their nature will attain the finest outcome and Allah's good pleasure.

In verse 18, Allah, the angels, and those endowed with knowledge have testified that there is no god but Allah. This testimony is borne upholding justice and equity. Allah's testimony occurs through His declaration of His oneness, His creation of proofs, and His making it known to those endowed with knowledge. The foundation of all certainty (yaqin) is the knowledge and testimony of the Exalted Truth (al-Haqq Ta'ala) concerning Himself and His oneness.

In verse 19, it is declared that the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam. Those who were given the Scripture differed only after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual envy and transgression. Those who deny Allah's verses should know that Allah is swift in reckoning. The religion of Islam is founded upon the belief in Tawhid (monotheism) and demands submission to Allah.

According to a narration, two Christian scholars came to Medina, and after getting to know the Prophet (peace be upon him), they asked about the greatest testimony, whereupon this verse was revealed. The concept of religion (din) signifies attaining salvation through obedience and commitment. Islam, on the other hand, means entering into peace, submission, and safety. True Tawhid is to believe in Allah, the pre-eternal and everlasting God who has no partner, and to testify solely to Him. In the sight of Allah, religion is only Islam, which is built upon this Tawhid.

In this section, Elmalılı emphasizes that Islam is the only true religion. He states that the angels and those endowed with knowledge testify to the oneness of Allah, and that seeking a religion other than this is disbelief. He explains that the disagreements of the People of the Book arose out of rebellion and enmity even after knowledge had come to them, and that those who reject Islam will face Allah's swift reckoning. He then proceeds to the occasion of revelation, explaining verse 20, which addresses submission to Allah. He conveys that the Prophet said, 'I and those who follow me have submitted to Allah,' that he must convey Islam to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered, and that his responsibility regarding those who turn away is merely to convey the message.

In verses 21-22, the glad tidings of a painful punishment are given to those who deny Allah's verses, kill the prophets unjustly, and slay those who enjoin justice. It is reported that all their deeds have come to naught in this world and the Hereafter, and that they will have no helpers. Elmalılı explains that these verses encompass Jews, Christians, and other disbelievers, and that they will be subjected to such punishment as a result of their denial and oppression.

In verses 23-25, it is recounted that those who were given a portion of the Scripture turned away when invited to the Book of Allah to arbitrate between them. It is noted that the reason for this was their claim, 'The Fire will not touch us except for a numbered few days.' Elmalılı explains that this assertion deluded them, that on the Day of Resurrection everyone will be recompensed in full for what they have done, and he portrays the terror of that day.

Verses 26-27 declare that Allah is the Owner of all sovereignty, granting it to whom He wills and stripping it from whom He wills, merging the night into the day and the day into the night, bringing forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living, and providing sustenance to whom He wills without measure. Elmalılı recounts the occasion of revelation of these verses: during the Battle of the Trench, while striking a boulder, the sparks produced by the three blows of the Prophet (peace be upon him) pointed to the conquests of Persia, the Byzantine Empire, and Sana'a, and this promise was mocked by the hypocrites. Furthermore, hadiths concerning the virtues of these verses are cited, stating that reciting these verses brings great rewards.

In verses 28-30, believers are forbidden from taking disbelievers as allies; it is stated that whoever does so has severed ties with Allah, with an exception made for the state of taqiyyah (precautionary protection). Elmalılı lists four different occasions of revelation for this verse: the Jews attempting to influence the believers, Companions like Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah showing affection toward the Meccans, the hypocrites spying, and 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit's friendship with the Jews. It is emphasized that believers must refrain from befriending disbelievers, though they may resort to taqiyyah when compelled to do so. Finally, it is recalled that Allah is most compassionate to His servants, and that He is the One who ought truly to be feared.

In verses 31–32, it is stated that the sign of loving Allah is following the Prophet. Elmalılı explains that true love consists of obeying the beloved and seeking his pleasure; therefore, those who love Allah must follow the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). In response to the hypocrites' claim that 'Muhammad wants people to obey him,' it is stated that following the Prophet is in reality obedience to Allah, because he was sent as Allah's Messenger. It is recalled that those who rebel against Allah and His Messenger are disbelievers, and that Allah does not love the disbelievers. It is emphasized that the Christians' deification of Jesus and the Jews' rejection of other prophets actually had nothing to do with love for Allah, and that they acted in this way because they followed their own egos and personal desires.

Disbelief is of two kinds: loving by associating partners with Allah (shirk) and loving for the sake of Allah (tawhid). The Christians' love for Jesus is shirk because they idolized him instead of Allah. Yet what is sought is 'loving for the sake of Allah.' For this reason, Allah commanded following the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by stating, 'Follow me so that Allah will love you.' This following is obedience to Allah, because the Prophet conveys on behalf of Allah.

For true belief in tawhid, the testimony 'Lâ ilâhe illallah' is not sufficient on its own; 'Muhammedün Resulullah' must also be added. Otherwise, false beliefs may arise, such as Allah incarnating (hulul) into a servant—as the Christians attribute to Jesus—or wahdat al-wujud. In Islam, these two testimonies are united. Those who obey Allah and His Messenger attain Allah's love and mercy.

Prophethood is based on the divine law of selection (istifa). Istifa means selecting and taking the purest and most unadulterated essence of something. Through this law, Allah has made the prophets superior to other people. The exegetes (mufassirun) have explained istifa in two ways: first, that Allah made them the purest of His creation; second, that He purified them from blameworthy traits and endowed them with noble qualities. Both meanings complement each other.

The law of istifa is also seen in nature. There is an evolution (development) among minerals, plants, and animals. However, this evolution does not happen on its own; it depends on the will of a Creator. In natural science, there are two opposing theories: the first says that all beings originate from a single root, and the second says that each species reproduces from its own seed. This contradiction shows that creation takes place through a divine power.

In verses 33–34, Allah announces that He chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of Imran above all the worlds. These distinguished lineages continued as offspring one from another. Jesus is from the family of Imran, while the Prophet Muhammad is from the family of Abraham. The law of istifa shows that the prophets are superior to other people and that this superiority is passed down from generation to generation.

Prophethood is not an ordinary characteristic of the human species, but a divine grace that Allah bestows upon the most perfect individuals He has chosen (istifa). This selection took the form of a chain continuing from generation to generation and progressing by degrees toward greater perfection. There are great differences among people in terms of intellect, ability, and character; these differences are so diverse that each could be considered a distinct species. It is to individuals possessing these distinguished intellects that prophethood is granted. Allah created humanity from nothing and, through selection upon selection (istifa upon istifa), chose prophets. The most perfect example of this greatest selection is the prophethood of the Prophet Muhammad. Prophets are superior to other people in both bodily and spiritual faculties; for instance, they can see distant things, see behind veils, and hear sounds that others cannot hear. On this subject, Islamic philosophers have noted that the holy soul (al-nafs al-qudsiyyah) of the prophets is qualitatively different from that of ordinary people.

Almighty Allah chose Adam from among other beings at the time of creation and created him upon a pure, unblemished nature (fitrah). It is not an obligatory law that human beings must be born from human beings; Adam, the first human, was not born of a human. Later, Allah granted the development of spiritual faculties to certain individuals from Adam's offspring, choosing Noah, and then Abraham. From Abraham two branches diverged: Ishmael was the forerunner to the advent of the Prophet Muhammad, while Isaac was the beginning of prophethood and dominion leading up to the Family of Imran (Al-i Imran). The word 'al' means closeness to a person and being bound to him in school of thought. Here, Al-i Imran has two possibilities, encompassing Imran the father of Moses and Aaron, and Imran the father of Mary. The second is more probable. Having understood this secret of istifa, let us now move on to the story of Mary and Jesus.

Hannah, the wife of Imran, dedicated the child in her womb to Allah in complete devotion and prayed for it to be accepted. When she gave birth to a female child, she said, 'My Lord, I have given birth to a female; and the male is not like the female. I have named her Mary, and I commit her and her offspring to Your protection from Satan the outcast.' Her Lord accepted Mary with gracious acceptance, caused her to grow like a good plant, and placed her in the care of Zechariah. Whenever Zechariah entered the sanctuary (mihrab), he found new sustenance with Mary, and she would say that it was from Allah. After her father died, Mary was raised in this manner with special care from Allah.

One day, Zechariah prayed to his Lord in the sanctuary, asking Him to grant him good offspring. While he was standing in prayer, the angels called out to him: 'Allah gives you good tidings of John (Yahya), confirming a word from Allah (Jesus), noble, chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous.' Zechariah asked how this could be, mentioning his old age and that his wife was barren, and Allah informed him that He does whatever He wills. Zechariah asked for a sign, and Allah commanded that he not speak to people for three days except by gestures, and that he glorify Him much. John was the first to confirm Jesus; this confirmation began while in the mother's womb. For John's birth, too, was contrary to the ordinary course of nature and bears witness in reality that Allah can do whatever He wills.

The angels said to Mary: 'O Mary! Allah has chosen you, purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds. Stand devoutly before your Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow.' In accordance with this divine selection, Mary occupied herself with worship, stood devoutly before her Lord, performed prayer, and was with the congregation. Allah revealed these accounts of the unseen to the Prophet Muhammad. The angels gave Mary the glad tidings of Jesus: 'Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name will be the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, honored in this world and the Hereafter, and of those brought near to Allah. He will speak to people in the cradle and in maturity, and will be of the righteous.' Mary asked how she could have a child when no man had touched her, and Allah said, 'Even so, Allah creates what He wills; when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be!" and it is.'

Allah taught Jesus the Book (writing), wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel. Jesus was sent as a messenger to the Children of Israel and brought the following miracles: he fashioned a bird out of clay, and when he breathed into it, it became a bird; he healed the blind from birth and the leper; he raised the dead; and he informed them of what they ate and stored in their houses. All of this took place by Allah's leave. Jesus came confirming the Torah that was before him and making lawful some of what had been forbidden. He said, 'Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him; this is the straight path.' The call of Jesus consisted entirely of tawhid (monotheism); he did not deify himself, but called solely to the worship of Allah.

Jesus is 'a word from Allah'; this indicates that his creation was extraordinary and that he is a creation of Allah. However, he is not the entirety of the words, but merely one of them; he is not the son of Allah, but the son of Mary. The Christians' claims of the Trinity are false. That Jesus is 'among those brought near to Allah' is not a partnership in divinity, but merely an elevated rank. Jesus speaking in the cradle and in adulthood demonstrates that he was created in time and underwent change, which refutes the claim of divinity. The religion Jesus brought was Islam; just like the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), he commanded submission to Allah and worshipping Him alone. In summary, the meaning of the word of Jesus consists of the word of tawhid (kalimat al-tawhid).

The Prophet Jesus (peace be upon him) was a prophet sent as a word and a spirit from Allah. Just as he confirmed the prophets before him, he also gave glad tidings of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) who was to come after him. When he perceived the disbelief of the Children of Israel, he sought helpers for himself in the cause of Allah. The disciples supported him, saying, 'We are the helpers of Allah. We have believed in Allah, and we are Muslims (those who submit).'

The disciples reinforced their faith and submission with a supplication: 'Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and we have followed the messenger, so register us among the witnesses.' With this prayer, they intended not only the testimony of Jesus, but the testimony of all the prophets and especially the community (ummah) of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Spiritually, the disciples were counted among the ummah of Muhammad.

The Children of Israel devised secret plots to kill the Prophet Jesus (peace be upon him) and eliminate the religion of tawhid. However, Allah foiled their plot. Allah's plan was a punishment against their ill intentions and an act of grace. This plan did not permit Jesus to be killed; rather, it raised him up.

Allah addressed the Prophet Jesus (peace be upon him), saying: 'I will take you, raise you up to Myself, and purify you from those who disbelieve.' There are different interpretations regarding the word 'wafat' (taking / causing to die). According to some, Jesus was not killed, but was raised alive to the heavens and will return to the world before the Day of Resurrection. This is the continuation of a soul in the life of the Isthmus (barzakh). According to another interpretation, Jesus' soul was taken and his body was raised. The most well-known view is that Jesus did not die and will pass away near the Day of Resurrection.

For those who disbelieve, there is a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, while those who believe and do righteous deeds will receive their rewards in full. Allah does not love the wrongdoers. These verses are from the wise Quran. Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is as the likeness of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him, 'Be!' and he was. This demonstrates Allah's power of creation and that Jesus possesses no divinity.

This section begins with the verses revealed after the Christian delegation of Najran claimed that the Prophet Jesus (peace be upon him) was God, citing his birth without a father as justification. Allah Almighty gave them the example of the Prophet Adam: Adam was also created from dust without a father or a mother, yet he is neither God nor the son of God. Thus, Jesus is just like Adam. This verse both provides a clear response to the Christians and indirectly addresses the Jews and other deniers. Tafsir scholars have unanimously agreed that the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse was the debate with the delegation of Najran.

The case of the Prophet Jesus (peace be upon him) is characterized in the Quran as an allegorical or ambiguous (mutashabih) expression. Mutashabih means that which is not self-explanatory and can only be understood by referring it back to a clear, definitive (muhkam) verse. Here, the creation of Jesus is explained by drawing an analogy to the creation of Adam. Adam is a definitive example created without a father and without a mother. Jesus was also born of Mary without a father; in this respect, he resembles Adam. People of understanding do not deny allegorical occurrences; rather, they seek to understand them by referring them back to definitive examples. This is the methodology of those deeply rooted in knowledge.

From the perspective of natural sciences as well, the fatherless birth of the Prophet Jesus (peace be upon him) is not impossible. In nature, there exists the phenomenon called atavism (reversion), where a trait traces back to distant ancestors. Moreover, the human germ-cell (nutfah) does not always have to come from a male; by divine intervention, Mary's womb was receptive to the formation of the seed. This is a manifestation of Allah's power. To deny it would be to deny man's own creation and Allah's omnipotence over all things. Indeed, the creation of Adam from dust is likewise the work of that same divine power.

Following the debate, if the Christians persisted in obstinacy and insisted that the Prophet Jesus (peace be upon him) is God or the son of God, Allah Almighty commanded His Prophet to perform mubahalah (invoking a mutual curse). In verse 61 of Surah Al 'Imran, both sides were asked to summon their sons, their women, and themselves, and pray for the curse of Allah to be upon the liars. The delegation of Najran feared this proposition, made an agreement, accepted paying the jizya, and came under the protection of the Islamic state. This is an important ruling in terms of making the truth manifest and silencing falsehood.

Finally, Allah Almighty invites the People of the Book to a common word: that we worship none but Allah, associate nothing with Him, and do not take one another as lords besides Allah. This call occurs in verse 64 of Surah Al 'Imran. This is the very call of Islam to tawhid. The Christians taking the Prophet Jesus (peace be upon him) as a lord was in fact deifying him, whereas Jesus is also a servant and messenger of Allah. This common word secures the unity of humanity and true freedom. Only those who serve none other than Allah attain salvation in this way.

When the People of the Book argued about Abraham, they attempted to consider him a Jew or a Christian. Yet Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; rather, he was an upright Muslim who affirmed the oneness of Allah (hanif), and was not of the polytheists. The closest of people to him are those who followed him, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and those who believe. Allah is the protector of the believers.

A group among the People of the Book wished to lead the believers astray. They said, 'Believe in what was revealed to the believers at the beginning of the day, and reject it at its end.' They advised not to trust anyone who does not follow their religion. Allah grants His bounty to whom He wills, and His mercy is vast.

Some among the People of the Book uphold trusts, while others act treacherously. The reason for their treachery is their claim: 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered.' Yet Allah loves those who fulfill their pledge and guard against evil. Those who sell their covenant with Allah for a meager price will have no share in the Hereafter.

A group among the People of the Book twist their tongues to present what is not from the Book as though it were from the Book, saying, 'This is from Allah.' Yet they utter a lie. Allah took a covenant from the prophets that they would believe in and aid whatever messenger came to them after them. Whoever turns away after this covenant, it is they who are the transgressors.

Those who seek other than Allah's religion seek in vain. Whatever is in the heavens and on earth has submitted to Him. The prophets call people to the worship of Allah, not to themselves. Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, his religion will not be accepted, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers. The repentance of those who believe and then disbelieve will not be accepted unless death overtakes them.

Attaining true righteousness (birr) is not possible unless you spend in the way of Allah from what you love. Faith and knowledge are not sufficient; righteous deeds and spending in charity (infaq) are also required. Allah knows everything that is spent and gives its reward. Birr is that intended benefit which leads to goodness; faith is the foundation of religion, and birr is its ultimate goal.

The Jews claimed that the things made unlawful for the Children of Israel had been unlawful since Noah and Abraham. However, before the Torah, foods were lawful except for what Jacob had forbidden for himself. The Torah abrogated rulings by making unlawful certain things that had previously been lawful. The Kaaba is the first sanctuary established for mankind, and performing the pilgrimage (hajj) is an obligation for those who have the means.

A Jew named Shammās ibn Qays sought to sow discord between the tribes of Aws and Khazraj by provoking them. However, our Prophet was informed of the situation and warned them, and they reconciled. Thereupon, Allah revealed verses warning the People of the Book and cautioning the believers against following them: O you who believe! Fear Allah as He deserves to be feared, and do not die except as Muslims. Hold firmly to the rope of Allah and do not fall into division. Remember Allah's favor upon you: when you were enemies, He united your hearts and saved you from the edge of a pit of fire.

The phrase "hablullah" (the rope of Allah) mentioned in verse 103 means the evidence and means that serve as a path to reaching Allah. This has been interpreted with meanings such as the Quran, the congregation, sincerity (ikhlas), and Islam. In a hadith, our Prophet (peace be upon him) stated that the rope of Allah is the Quran. The verse commands holding firmly to the rope of Allah collectively as a congregation. This emphasizes the unity and solidarity of the Islamic community.

In verse 104, it is commanded that there be a group among you that calls to goodness, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. This group is called an "ummah" and constitutes leadership (imamah). The duty of enjoining good and forbidding wrong is a collective obligation (fard al-kifayah) upon all Muslims; that is, if a portion of them fulfills it, the others are absolved of responsibility. However, if a specific group is formed for this task, it becomes an individual obligation (fard al-'ayn) upon them. Those who perform this duty attain salvation.

Verses 105–109 warn against being like those who split into factions and fell into discord after clear proofs had come to them. On the Day of Resurrection, some faces will turn white and some will turn black. While those whose faces turn black will suffer punishment for disbelieving after having believed, those whose faces turn white will abide eternally in Allah's mercy. These verses remind that Allah does not do any injustice and that everything in the heavens and on earth belongs to Him.

In verses 110–112, Muslims are described as the best nation brought forth for mankind. They enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah. Most of the People of the Book are transgressors; they cannot harm Muslims except for causing slight annoyance. The stamp of humiliation and destitution has been struck upon them; only those who take refuge in the rope of Allah and a covenant with people can be saved from this abasement. This is because they disbelieved in Allah's verses and killed the prophets without right.

Verses 113–115 state that the People of the Book are not all the same, and that among them is a community standing firm in righteousness. They recite the verses of Allah through the hours of the night prostrating, believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and race in good deeds. They are among the righteous, and the good deeds they perform will not go unrewarded. There are various narrations regarding the occasion of revelation of these verses; they may have been revealed concerning those among the People of the Book who became Muslims or concerning Christians, or they were revealed to praise the believers.

Verses 116–120 state that the wealth and children of the disbelievers will not benefit them at all, and that what they spend will go to waste just like a scorching wind destroying crops. Believers should not take confidants from outside their own ranks, for they constantly desire evil and conceal their hatred and enmity. While the believers love them, they do not love Muslims. When good touches the Muslims, it grieves them, and when evil befalls them, they rejoice at it. If the Muslims remain patient and fear Allah as He ought to be feared, their plots will not harm them. These verses describe the situation of the hypocrites and polytheists, particularly before the Battle of Uhud.

Verses 121–129 recall the Battle of Uhud. Early in the morning, our Prophet had deployed the believers at their battle stations. Two groups among you were on the verge of losing heart, yet Allah was their guardian. At Badr, although they were few and weak, they achieved victory with Allah's help. Our Prophet had given good tidings that if they remained patient and guarded themselves, they would be aided with three thousand, or even five thousand, angels. Help comes only from Allah. This help was meant to cut off a portion of the disbelievers or to disgrace them. Even our Prophet holds no authority over the matter; everything depends on Allah's will. Everything in the heavens and on earth belongs to Allah; He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.

Unless by Allah's command, even the Prophet cannot do anything against the disbelievers, nor can he even invoke a curse upon them. In the Battle of Uhud, the Messenger of Allah wished to curse the disbelievers, whereupon this verse was revealed. Everything depends on Allah's command. Allah either crushes whomever He wills, as happened at Badr, or disgraces them, or grants them repentance, or punishes them severely. The reason for this punishment is that the disbelievers are wrongdoers. Whatever is in the heavens and on earth belongs to Allah; He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. The believers must trust in Allah's command, be patient, and remain steadfast in piety.

O you who believe! Do not consume interest (usury) doubled and multiplied; fear Allah so that you may attain salvation. Guard yourselves against the Fire prepared for the disbelievers. Obey Allah and the Messenger so that you may be shown mercy. These verses emphasize the importance of avoiding interest for internal reform. Doubled and multiplied interest is the interest added to the principal. Exegetes state that this prohibition makes interest categorically unlawful. This verse was revealed to recall the event of Uhud. Even though the verses in Surah al-Baqarah were revealed later, it is certain that interest is unlawful.

Hasten to the forgiveness of your Lord and to a Paradise as vast as the heavens and the earth! This Paradise is prepared for those who fear Allah as He deserves. They spend for the sake of Allah in prosperity and adversity, swallow their anger, and pardon people. When they commit a shameful deed or wrong themselves, they remember Allah and immediately ask for forgiveness, and they do not knowingly persist in committing sin. Their reward is forgiveness from their Lord and gardens beneath which rivers flow. How excellent is the reward of those who strive!

In this verse, it is stated that the width of Paradise is as vast as the heavens and the earth. According to Ibn Abbas and the majority of scholars, when the heavens and the earth are spread out and joined together, they serve as the measure of Paradise's width, while its length is known only to Allah. This indicates that Paradise is greater than the heavens. It is narrated that the envoy of Heraclius asked our Prophet: 'If Paradise is this vast, where is Hell?' to which the Messenger of Allah replied: 'When daytime comes, where does the night go?' Paradise has been prepared for the righteous (al-muttaqun), and their distinctive qualities are: spending in prosperity and adversity, overcoming anger, pardoning others, repenting immediately upon committing a sin, and not persisting in it.

Many nations have passed away before you. Travel throughout the earth and see what was the end of the deniers. This Quran is a clear explanation for humanity, a guide and an admonition for those mindful of Allah. Do not falter, and do not grieve; you are superior if you are truly believers. If a wound touched you at Uhud, a similar wound had touched that people at Badr. We alternate these days among people so that Allah may distinguish the believers, take martyrs from among them, and eliminate the disbelievers. Allah does not love the wrongdoers.

Or did you think that you would enter Paradise before Allah made evident those of you who strive and those who are patient? You certainly used to long for death before encountering it; now you have seen it, yet you stand gazing at it. Muhammad is no more than a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Whoever turns back does not harm Allah in the least. Allah will reward the grateful. No soul can die except by Allah’s leave, at a predetermined appointed time. Whoever desires the reward of this world, We give him of it, and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We give him of it. And We will reward the grateful.

There is no harm in desiring martyrdom. However, the true purpose is to attain the rank of martyrdom in the cause of the Truth and to reach the true life promised by Allah. In the Battle of Uhud, Anas ibn al-Nadr offered courage by saying, 'If Muhammad has died, his Lord does not die; fight for the cause for which he fought,' and fought until he fell as a martyr.

When the rumor spread during the battle that 'Muhammad has been killed,' many Muslims were shaken. Some fled, while others sat down and waited. Thereupon, the verse was revealed: 'Muhammad is no more than a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?' This verse draws attention to the incidents of apostasy that would arise after the death of the Prophet.

‘Inqilab ‘ala al-‘aqib’ means turning back on one’s heels. Here, it is a metaphor for fleeing from battle or apostatizing from the religion. The verse rebukes them, saying, 'Will you turn back from your religion?' It is emphasized that prophets are not permanent, but the religion is permanent. The Prophet Muhammad will pass away just like the other prophets, but you must remain steadfast and safeguard your religion.

No soul can die without Allah's permission. Whether in bed or in battle, death is Allah's decree. For this reason, duty must not be abandoned out of fear of death. Whoever desires the reward of this world is given it, and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter is also given it. The grateful are those who remain steadfast in Allah’s blessings and obey Him.

O you who believe! If you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back to your former religion and you will suffer loss. Allah will help you and cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists. The polytheists will be struck with fear because they associate partners with Allah without any authority.

Allah had fulfilled His promise to you and routed the enemy. However, you did not show patience, you disobeyed the command, and you disputed over the spoils of war. When the archers abandoned their posts despite the Prophet's command, Allah turned victory away from you. This was a test, and Allah forgave you.

On that day, as you were fleeing, the Prophet was calling to you from behind. Allah brought upon you sorrow upon sorrow. Then, He sent down upon you a slumber of security. The hypocrites, on the other hand, were saying, 'Had we had any say in this matter, we would not have been killed.' Allah did this to test the believers and to purify their hearts, and then He forgave them. By the mercy of Allah, the Prophet dealt with them gently and consulted them in their affairs. Allah loves those who put their trust in Him.

After that grief, Allah granted security and slumber to the believers. One cannot sleep in the midst of intense fear; being able to sleep shows that there is tranquility in the heart. It is narrated that as the polytheists were departing from Uhud, they threatened, 'We will return.' The Muslims were anxious that the enemy might turn back and attack or raid Medina, and they waited beneath their shields ready for battle. In this moment of fear and grief, Allah granted security, and they began to doze off. Al-Zubayr and Abu Talhah described what relief this slumber brought. This sleep was no ordinary sleep; it was a divine aid. A similar slumber had occurred at Badr as well (al-Anfal 8:11). In this event, there were two groups: the believers and the hypocrites. Because the believers firmly believed that Allah would aid His religion, they knew that this affliction would not lead to complete eradication. Thus, despite their fears, their sense of security was not lost, and they were able to fall asleep and find tranquility.

Another group was concerned only with themselves. They were the hypocrites; they doubted the prophethood of the Prophet and had joined the battle only out of a desire for spoils or rebellion. Many of them had fled in the beginning along with Abdullah ibn Ubayy, while some had remained behind. When the course of the battle changed, they first rejoiced as if taking revenge, but later their fear intensified. With the mindset of the Days of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah), they harbored ill thoughts of Allah, saying, 'Had Muhammad been a true prophet, Allah would not have given the disbelievers power over him like this.' By saying, 'Do we have any share in this matter?' they harbored a political aim or grudge. Allah declared that everything is in His hands, saying: 'Say: Indeed, the matter belongs entirely to Allah.'

The hypocrites were concealing something within themselves, saying, 'If there had been anything for us in that promised victory, we would not have been killed here.' With these words, they were denying the Prophet's promise and objecting to their opinions not being accepted in the consultation (shura). Yet the Messenger of Allah had invited them to consultation, and the majority had decided to go out to battle. Their saying now, 'if we had had any say,' was a distortion of the truth. Allah answered them thus: 'Even if you had been inside your homes, those decreed to be killed would have gone out to the places of their death.' It is impossible to alter Allah's decree. Allah did this to bring forth the sincerity and hypocrisy within you, and to purge what is hidden in the hearts. Allah knows well what is in the breasts.

Those of you who turned back on the day the two armies met were caused to slip by Satan because of some of their sins. Even so, Allah pardoned their sins, for Allah is indeed All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing. There are various narrations concerning the number of those who stood firm or fled on that day. Some fled as far as Medina, where women rebuked them and threw dust upon them. While reciting this verse in his sermon, Umar said, 'On the day of Uhud we were routed, and I climbed up the mountain.' It is narrated that those who stood firm were fourteen men: from the Emigrants (Muhajirun), Abu Bakr, Ali, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Talhah, Abu Ubaydah, and al-Zubayr; and from the Helpers (Ansar), Hubab, Abu Dujanah, Asim, Harith, Sahl, Usayd, and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. Eight of them had pledged to fight unto death with the Messenger of Allah.

O believers, do not be like the disbelievers who say regarding their brothers, 'Had they been with us, they would not have died.' This utterance is so that Allah may make that thought a deep regret in their hearts. It is Allah who gives life and causes death; He takes life whether on a journey or at home. Believers must place their trust only in Allah. If you are slain or die in the way of Allah, Allah's forgiveness and mercy are certainly better than what the disbelievers hoard. In the end, you will all be gathered back to Allah.

O Muhammad! By the mercy of Allah, you were gentle with them. If you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you. Forgive them, ask Allah's forgiveness for them, and consult them in matters. And when you have decided, place your trust in Allah. Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him. Consultation (mushawara) means seeking opinion. Although the scholars differed as to whether this command is obligatory (fard) or recommended (mandub), it appears outwardly to be obligatory. In matters where revelation had not descended, the Prophet also exercised personal legal reasoning (ijtihad) and found strength through consultation. The Messenger of Allah stated, 'Allah and His Messenger have no need of consultation, but it is a mercy for this community.' A community that consults does not stray from the right path.

If Allah helps you, none can overcome you. But if He forsakes you, who is there to help you after Him? Let the believers place their trust in Allah alone. Relying on Allah (tawakkul) means resorting to the causes while binding the heart to Allah. The archers had excused their rushing for the spoils of war by saying, 'We feared that the Messenger of Allah would not distribute them.'

In this section, the issue of treachery regarding the spoils of war (ghulul) is addressed first. Ghulul means secretly stealing from the spoils of war or betraying a trust; misappropriating public property also falls under this scope. Our Prophet (peace be upon him) counted ghulul among the major sins and narrated many hadiths regarding it. Subsequently, in verses 162–163, it is emphasized that the Prophet who pursues the pleasure of Allah and the person who acts treacherously and incurs the wrath of Allah are not equal, and that everyone will be ranked according to their deeds.

In verse 164, it is reminded that Allah bestowed a great favor upon the believers by sending them a prophet from among themselves. This prophet recites Allah's verses to them, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom, whereas they were previously in clear astrayness. In verse 165, the calamity that befell the Muslims at the Battle of Uhud is questioned: Having inflicted twice as much upon the enemy at Badr, where did this come from now? The answer is: This is from yourselves; that is, it is due to your own faults such as disobeying orders and falling prey to greed for the spoils of war. Allah is capable of all things.

In verses 166–167, it is explained that the calamity that befell them on the day the two armies met was by Allah's leave. Its wisdom was to identify the believers and distinguish the hypocrites. When it was said to the hypocrites, 'Come, fight in the way of Allah or defend yourselves,' they said, 'If we had known there would be fighting, we would have followed you.' Yet on that day they were closer to disbelief than to faith, uttering with their mouths what was not in their hearts.

In verse 168, it is stated that the hypocrites, who fled the battle and stayed behind, said of their martyred brothers, 'Had they listened to us, they would not have been killed.' Say to them: 'Avert death from yourselves if you are truthful.' Verses 169–171 explain that those who are slain in the way of Allah (the martyrs) must not be thought of as dead; rather, they are provided for in the presence of their Lord, rejoicing in the bounty of Allah, and conveying the glad tidings that there will be no fear for those left behind. These verses were revealed concerning the martyrs of Uhud.

Verses 172–174 pertain to the Expedition of Hamra al-Asad, praising the believers who responded to the call of Allah and His Messenger even after sustaining injuries. When people said to them, 'The enemy has gathered an army against you, so fear them,' this only increased their faith, and they said, 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is an excellent trustee.' Consequently, they returned with the bounty of Allah, having suffered no harm. In verses 175–179, it is declared that one should not fear the allies of Satan, that those who race into disbelief should not cause grief, that a painful punishment awaits those who trade faith for disbelief, that the respite granted to the disbelievers is only to let them increase in sin, and that Allah will not leave the believers in the state they are in until He separates the vile from the good.

Allah Almighty does not leave sincere believers in a mixed state; He arranges means to distinguish the vile from the good. Yet He does not disclose the unseen to you, but informs the messengers He chooses. O believers, believe in Allah and His messengers, and be mindful of Him, for there is a great reward. In this verse, it is heralded that the hypocrites will be disgraced in this world, and glad tidings of a magnificent reward are given to the believers. In the subsequent verse 180, it is proclaimed that the inheritance of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone, and that those who are stingy with this fleeting wealth commit a grave sin. Here, inheritance is a divine law, serving as preparation for the inheritance verses in Surah an-Nisa.

In verse 181, it is stated that Allah heard the words of those who said, 'Allah is poor and we are rich.' According to narration, Abu Bakr slapped the Jewish scholar Phinehas for saying this, and Phinehas denied it. Allah confirmed Abu Bakr and revealed this verse. It is also narrated that the Jews said, 'Is your Lord poor that He asks for a loan?' Allah declares that He will record these words of theirs, along with their killing of the prophets unjustly, and will say, 'Taste the burning torment!' This recording signifies the logging of deeds or that retribution will not be neglected. The crime of slaying prophets is attributed to the character of Judaism and demonstrates that their disbelief was not genuine skepticism.

In verse 183, it is related that the Jews said, 'We will not believe in any prophet until he brings us an offering consumed by fire.' Our Prophet is commanded to reply: 'Messengers came to you before me with clear proofs and with that which you mentioned. Why then did you kill them if you are truthful?' This demonstrates that their claims were mere fabrications and that they had no intention of believing. In verse 184, it is reminded that the rejection of prophets is the established practice of Allah (sunnatullah), and the Messenger of Allah is comforted.

In verse 185, it is declared that every soul shall taste death, and that rewards will be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has indeed attained salvation. The worldly life is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion. This verse has given rise to diverse interpretations regarding the eternity of the soul. While some maintain that the soul does not die, the majority of scholars state that it is an exception to the general ruling. Death and resurrection constitute the bedrock of faith in the Hereafter. The full recompense for worldly deeds is rendered upon the Resurrection; the provision of this world is nothing but deceptive pleasure.

In verse 186, it is conveyed that the believers will surely be tested in their possessions and their lives, and that they will hear hurtful words from those who were given the Scripture before them and from the polytheists. Patience and piety are among the matters requiring great resolve. In verse 187, it is recalled that Allah took a covenant from the People of the Book to make their scriptures known and not conceal them, yet they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a trifling worldly gain. This serves as a warning that encompasses Muslims as well.

In verses 188–189, it is emphasized that those who exult in what they have done and love to be praised for what they have not done will never escape the punishment; to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and He is capable of all things.

In verses 190–194, it is explained that in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, there are signs for people of understanding; that they remember Allah and reflect in every state, and pray, "Our Lord! You have not created this in vain; protect us from the punishment of Hellfire." In these prayers, they ask for the forgiveness of sins, to be among the righteous, and not to be disgraced on the Day of Resurrection.

In verse 195, it is stated that Allah responded to these prayers: that He will not cause the deed of any worker among them, whether male or female, to be lost; that He will remit the sins of those who emigrated, were driven out of their homes, suffered harm, fought, and were killed, and will admit them into Gardens. In verses 196–200, it is emphasized that the prosperity of the disbelievers is deceptive; that for the believers there are eternal gardens and a reward far better with Allah; that among the People of the Scripture there are also those who believe; and finally, that patience, steadfastness, standing guard, and piety (taqwa) are the means of salvation.

Allah declares that the People of the Scripture, who were given the Torah and the Gospel, gave their pledge to explain these scriptures to the people and not conceal anything. In particular, heralding the final prophet, Muhammad (peace be upon him), and spreading the knowledge confirming his prophethood was their greatest duty. But they broke this covenant and cast the scripture behind their backs.

The scholars of the People of the Scripture did not fulfill the pledge Allah had taken from them; they concealed the truth and persecuted the Prophet. In return, they took a small worldly gain. No matter how great this price may be, it is trivial compared to the reward of the Hereafter. Muslims must not fall into this state either; they must declare the truth with patience, piety (taqwa), and loyalty, and exalt the Word of Allah.

Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they have not done will escape punishment. Although this verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites, its ruling encompasses everyone who engages in such conduct. Pride and conceit lead a person to forget Allah and distort the truth. When these two conditions combine, a painful punishment is deserved.

In the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, there are indeed many signs for people of pure understanding. When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) recited this verse, he wept profusely and said, "Woe to the one who recites it and does not reflect upon it!" This verse encourages contemplation of the power and wisdom of Allah.

Those possessing complete understanding (ulu'l-elbab) remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying down. They reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth and say, "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You, protect us from the punishment of the Fire." This reflection leads them to faith and to turning toward Allah.

In their prayers, they say, "Our Lord, a caller called to faith, so we believed. Forgive us our sins, and take us among the righteous. Grant us what You promised through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection." And Allah accepts their prayers and declares that He will not allow their good deeds to be in vain.

Let not the movement of the disbelievers throughout the lands deceive you. This is but a brief enjoyment; their ultimate destination is Hell. However, among the People of the Scripture there are those who believe in Allah, in what has been revealed to you, and in what was revealed to them. They are humble, and they do not sell the signs of Allah for a small price. It is they whose reward is with their Lord.

In short, O you who believe, do not panic, be patient. Patience is of three degrees: patience in adversity, patience in obedience, and patience against sin. Strive to outdo the enemies of Allah in patience. Furthermore, engage in murabatah—that is, remain bound to one another, attend diligently to duty, be prepared for war, and keep watch on the borders.

Ribat is perseverance in the cause of Allah. Originally, it is derived from tying horses; it means tying one's horse against the enemy and keeping watch. Those who keep guard in the border towns of Islam are called murabit. Today, murabits are soldiers under arms in the cause of Allah, keeping guard in barracks and outposts.

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: "Guarding an outpost for a single day in the cause of Allah is better than the world and all that is in it." Also in a hadith: "Whoever dies as a murabit in the cause of Allah, his good deed continues, his provision is granted, he is safe from tribulations, and Allah will resurrect him secure from fear." A prayer in an outpost is equivalent to two million prayers. Narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar: "Ribat is more virtuous than jihad, because it protects the blood of Muslims."

Do these things, fear Allah as He ought to be feared, and refrain from disobeying His commands so that you may attain salvation and achieve your desires. This is the answer to the prayer at the end of Surah al-Baqarah: "Grant us victory over the disbelieving people!"

Here Surah Al 'Imran ends, and the Zahrawayn (al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran) meet at a point of convergence. Next, Surah an-Nisa begins in order to provide divine upbringing, explain human creation and brotherhood, elucidate the rights and duties concerning family life, and complete religious education.

Surah an-Nisa begins by addressing humanity and deals with important matters such as women, orphans, marriage, and inheritance. In the first verse, emphasizing that human beings were created from a single soul, it is commanded to be mindful of Allah and beware of disobeying Him. While this draws attention to the brotherhood of humanity and the unity of creation, it also reminds that the rights of kinship must be observed.

The evidence of creation is emphasized; attributing everything to nature is incorrect, because nature cannot explain the emergence of female from male. By Allah's power, Adam was created from earth, and Eve was created from Adam. Marriage and the multiplication of progeny are encouraged; this is a divine discipline and a duty of servanthood.

The creation of Adam and Eve is explained through the hadith regarding creation from the rib. This shows the distinct natures of man and woman and the harmony between them. The concept of 'rahim' (kinship) is emphasized; observing the rights of relatives and maintaining family ties holds great importance in the sight of Allah. Numerous hadiths are narrated on this subject.

The preservation and protection of orphans' property is commanded. Mixing the property of orphans with one's own or consuming it unjustly is a grave sin. The word 'orphan' (yatim), in addition to children whose fathers have died, also encompasses widowed women. It is demanded that orphans be treated with justice and that their property be handed over to them fully and on time.

The verse regarding polygyny states that if one fears acting unjustly when marrying orphan girls, one may marry other women of one's choice, two, three, or four, but that justice is a strict condition. If justice cannot be maintained, one must be content with a single woman or a bondwoman. According to the tafsir of Aisha, this verse was revealed to prevent guardians from committing injustice against their orphan wards.

There are various narrations regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse. According to a narration from Ibn Abbas, during the pre-Islamic period of ignorance (Jahiliyyah), men would marry orphan girls out of greed for their wealth and would not observe their rights. With this verse, Allah Almighty commanded that those who fear acting unjustly toward the wealth of orphans must also observe justice in marrying women and marry no more than four. This is, at the same time, a restriction on marrying more than one woman.

Another narration comes from Hasan al-Basri: Guardians would marry orphan girls for their wealth, mistreat them, and wait for their deaths. This verse prohibited them from this attitude. Furthermore, according to a narration from Ikrima, a man would marry a large number of women, and when his wealth was exhausted, he would turn to the wealth of orphans. For this reason, marrying more than four women was prohibited.

Some commentators interpreted the occasion of revelation of the verse differently. According to Mujahid, it means: "If you fear committing injustice regarding orphans, fear committing unlawful sexual intercourse (zina) as well." Emphasizing the moral dimension of the verse, this interpretation states that the permission to marry more than one woman is a safeguard against zina. Aisha's narration, on the other hand, indicates the clearest reason: Guardians would prevent beautiful or wealthy orphan girls from marrying others, offer them an unfair, low mahr (dower), and cause them harm. The verse prohibited this practice.

The ruling of the verse is the prohibition of marrying more than four women. However, although some Zahiris claimed that the sum of these numbers is nine, this view contradicts scholarly consensus (ijma). On the other hand, the Rafidis went to extremes by asserting that there is no limitation whatsoever. What is correct is that the maximum number permitted by the verse is four. Those who fear that they cannot maintain justice must be content with a single woman.

In the subsequent verses, it is commanded that women be given their mahr graciously as a gift. It is enjoined not to surrender wealth to those of weak judgment (safihs), but rather to provide for their maintenance from it and speak to them with kind words. Orphans must be tested until they reach the age of marriage and demonstrate sound judgment (rushd), and only then should their property be handed over to them. Guardians must not squander orphans' property; if a guardian is wealthy, he should abstain from it entirely, and if he is poor, he may consume of it within lawful and reasonable limits.

Regarding the rulings of inheritance, it is declared that men and women have a designated share in what parents and close relatives leave behind. This verse abolished the custom of the pre-Islamic period of ignorance (Jahiliyyah) that denied inheritance to women and children. Revealed upon the complaint of a woman named Umm Kuhla, this verse establishes that inheritance does not belong exclusively to men. Subsequently, the amounts of the prescribed shares (fara'id) are explained in detail.

If relatives, orphans, and the needy are present during the division of inheritance, it is recommended to give them something from it and speak to them kindly. In addition, those who fear leaving weak children behind them are urged to show the same sensitivity toward orphans. A stern warning is given that those who unjustly consume the property of orphans are only filling their bellies with fire and will enter Hell. Following these warnings, people avoided intermingling with orphans, but this fear was alleviated by a subsequent verse in Surah al-Baqarah.

Allah commands you concerning your children regarding the division of inheritance: for the male, a share equal to that of two females; if there are only daughters numbering more than two, they receive two-thirds of the estate; if there is only one daughter, her share is half. For the parents of the deceased, each receives a sixth of the estate if the deceased left children; if he left no children and his parents are his heirs, his mother receives a third; if he left siblings, his mother receives a sixth. These shares are applied after the payment of any bequests and debts. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

The inheritance of spouses: if she has no child, half of the wife's estate belongs to the husband, and if she has a child, one-fourth. From the husband's estate, if he has no child, one-fourth belongs to the wife, and if he has a child, one-eighth. If there are siblings who inherit through kalalah (having left neither ascendants nor descendants), a single brother or sister receives a sixth; if they are more than that, they share equally in one-third. All shares are distributed after the payment of any bequests and debts. Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing.

These two verses regulate the system of inheritance: the first addresses those with direct lineage, such as children and parents, while the second addresses indirect ties, such as spouses and kalalah (collateral heirs). During the Jahiliyyah, inheritance was based on combatant men and contractual alliances; women and children could not inherit. Islam initially continued this system with additional grounds such as the Hijrah and brotherly pacts, and later, through al-Anfal 75, retained only the grounds of kinship (nasab), marriage, and wala' (the bond of emancipation).

The occasion of revelation of the inheritance verse: When Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' was martyred, he left behind two daughters, a wife, and a brother. When the brother took the entire estate, the wife complained to the Prophet (peace be upon him). Thereupon, this verse was revealed and the first division of inheritance was carried out: two-thirds was given to the daughters, one-eighth to the mother, and the remainder to the brother. This initiated a momentous transformation, establishing women and children as legal heirs and recognizing marriage as a legal basis for inheritance.

The wisdom behind a male receiving the share of two females: The financial burden of maintenance (nafaqah) in the family falls upon the man; a man spends on both himself and his wife, whereas a woman spends only on herself. For this reason, the man's share is larger. Furthermore, a woman's financial liability is generally less than that of a man; this distinction is also observed in matters such as blood money (diyah). Islam observes justice by ensuring this balance. According to an explanation narrated from Ja'far al-Sadiq, this rule is rooted in the wisdom of creation and is an eternal law of divine justice.
