Details regarding the inheritance of children: An only son receives the entire inheritance; in mixed genders, a male receives twice the share of a female. The share of two daughters is two-thirds (except for Ibn Abbas, who states that it is half). If there are children, the father and mother each receive one-sixth; if there are no children, the mother receives one-third and the father takes the remainder. If there are siblings, the mother's share drops to one-sixth. All shares are distributed after debts and bequests; bequests come after debts (as Ali pointed out).

Kalalah: This refers to kinship outside of ascendants and descendants; it comes into play when the deceased leaves neither children nor parents. The siblings meant in this verse are maternal siblings; for this reason, they receive equal shares. The rulings concerning other siblings will appear at the end of the surah. The concept of kalalah was debated among the Companions; while Abu Bakr stated that it refers to relatives other than parents and children, Umar indicated that it meant leaving no offspring.

In the verse of inheritance, Allah Almighty commanded that bequests and debts be settled in a manner that does not harm the heirs. The Prophet (peace be upon him) stated, 'There is no bequest for an heir,' indicating that this ruling was abrogated by the inheritance verses. A bequest cannot exceed one-third of the estate; anything beyond that is subject to the permission of the heirs. Falsely acknowledging a debt during a deathbed illness is also deemed causing harm to the heirs, and such debts are not paid from the inheritance.

The limits ordained by Allah: Whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be admitted into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Whoever disobeys and transgresses the limits will be cast into Hell, facing a humiliating punishment. It was commanded that four witnesses be brought against women guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, and once the offense was established, that they be confined to their homes until death; however, this ruling was abrogated by the verse of flogging in Surah an-Nur. It was also ordained that male and female offenders be subjected to reprimand and distress, which was subsequently transformed into the prescribed legal punishment.

The repentance acceptable to Allah is only that of those who commit sin in ignorance and promptly repent. The repentance of those who say 'I have repented' at the moment of death, or those who die as disbelievers, is invalid. As for the condition of those who persist in sin and repent shortly before the death agony, it is subject to Allah's will. A believer's repentance at the final breath may be valid, yet this has not been definitively promised.

It is unlawful to inherit women against their will or to coerce them in order to recover part of the bridal gift (mahr) given to them, unless they commit open indecency. You must live with women in kindness; even if you dislike them, Allah may have placed much good in them. When divorcing a wife to marry another, the mahr given to the former must not be reclaimed. Marrying women whom one's fathers had married in the pre-Islamic era of ignorance (Jahiliyyah) is strictly prohibited.

Allah has forbidden you to marry the following women: your mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, nieces (daughters of brothers and sisters), foster mothers, foster sisters, mothers-in-law, stepdaughters from wives with whom you have consummated the marriage, the wives of your own biological sons, and two sisters joined in marriage at the same time. Those prohibited through fosterage are the same as those prohibited through blood relations. Marrying free married women is also forbidden, except for female captives of war. Marriage was instituted for the purpose of chastity and reproduction; temporary marriage (mut'ah) contracted solely for pleasure is impermissible.

In verse 25, it is stated that those lacking the financial means to marry free believing women may marry believing slave women with the permission of their masters. It is stipulated that these slave women must be chaste, neither engaging in unlawful intercourse nor taking secret paramours. If they commit illicit intercourse after marriage, they are subject to half the punishment prescribed for free women. While Imam al-Shafi'i regarded this situation as forbidden, Imam al-A'zam considered it disliked (makruh). Marrying a slave woman is presented as an alternative for those who fear falling into sin; nevertheless, exercising patience is better.

In verses 26–28, Allah's purpose in establishing these rulings is made clear: to teach you what you did not know, to guide you to the ways of those before you, and to accept your repentance. Furthermore, it is highlighted that those who follow their lusts seek to divert people far from the straight path, whereas Allah desires to lighten your burdens. Man is reminded that he was created weak, and it is affirmed that Islam is a religion of ease. These verses serve as an answer to the supplication in Surah al-Fatihah, 'Guide us to the straight path.'

In verse 29, the believers are instructed not to consume one another's wealth unjustly, while trade conducted by mutual consent is declared lawful. The term 'batil' (falsehood/vanity) encompasses all unlawful means of acquisition and expenditure, such as theft, breach of trust, usury (riba), and gambling. Trade is explicitly mentioned because it represents the primary and most prevalent lawful basis of ownership. In addition, it is emphasized that the requirement of mutual consent must be respected in commercial transactions.

Again in verse 29, the expression 'do not kill yourselves' bears multiple meanings: committing suicide, exhausting one's soul with unbearable hardship, causing one's own death through crime, or placing oneself in danger. It also prohibits taking one another's lives. Unjustly devouring wealth, hoarding, and illicit profiteering can likewise bring about people's deaths. Out of Allah's mercy, such unlawful acts have been forbidden, while lawful trade has been granted freely.

In verse 30, it is stated that whoever commits these transgressions out of injustice and enmity will be cast into the fire of Hell. That is effortless for Allah. Following this, in verse 31, glad tidings are given that those who avoid the major sins will have their minor faults expiated and will be admitted into an honorable station. In verse 32, people are reminded not to covet that by which Allah has favored some over others, for each has a portion of what they have earned. In verse 33, heirs are designated, and the instruction is given to distribute the shares to those with whom oaths of allegiance were made.

In the 31st verse, Allah proclaims that He will pardon the minor sins of those who refrain from major sins and will admit them into a pleasant dwelling, Paradise. This is a manifestation of Allah's mercy. In the recitation of Nafi' and Abu Ja'far, reading the letter 'mim' with a fatha, it bears the meaning 'We will enter you into an honorable, delightful place of hospitality.' In this context, it is emphasized that one must not covet the rank of another and must avoid envy and malice, as these inevitably lead to major sins.

In the 32nd verse, coveting the blessings that Allah has granted more abundantly to some over others is forbidden. Such longings signify envy, malice, and discontent with Allah's decree. Men have a share of what they have earned, and women have a share of what they have earned; each receives the reward of their own striving. The true obligation is not to desire another's portion, but to labor using the capacities bestowed by Allah and to ask of Him. Concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, it is narrated that Umm Salamah voiced a desire for women to receive shares of inheritance equal to those of men.

In the 33rd verse, the rules of inheritance are summarized: for every man and woman, there is an appointed share left by parents, close kin, and those bound by solemn covenants. This is a grace from Allah, and no one has been left solely to their own earning. Therefore, do not covet one another's portions and do not consume wealth unjustly; surely Allah is a witness over all things.

In the 34th verse, it is affirmed that men are caretakers and guardians (qawwamun) over women. This position rests upon two foundations: Allah having favored some above others in creation, and men providing support from their wealth. In instances of women's rebellious discord (nushuz), a progression of measures is outlined: first exhortation, then separating beds, and finally striking lightly. The occasion of revelation was an incident in which Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' struck his wife; while the Prophet (peace be upon him) initially intended to grant equal retaliation (qisas), this verse was revealed, underscoring the man's authority over the woman.

In verse 35, in the event of discord, it is commanded that an arbitrator be sent from each of the two families. There is disagreement regarding the authority of the arbitrators; some say they have the authority to separate, while others say they can only reconcile. The verse shows that the primary objective is reconciliation; Allah reconciles between those who seek reconciliation with good intentions. The disobedience of men will be addressed later in verse 128.

In verses 36–41, ten important duties are listed: worshiping Allah, being good to parents, and doing good to relatives, orphans, the needy, the near neighbor and the distant neighbor, the companion, the traveler, and slaves. Allah does not love those who are arrogant, stingy, and enjoin stinginess upon others. The occasion of revelation of these verses is that certain Jews advised the Ansar not to spend their wealth on the Emigrants (Muhajirun). Furthermore, it is stated that on the Day of Resurrection a witness will be brought from every community and the prophets will testify.

In verses 42–43, it is explained that on the Day of Resurrection the disbelievers will desire to be swallowed up by the earth, yet they will not be able to conceal anything. Next comes the prohibition against approaching prayer: prayer cannot be performed while intoxicated or in a state of major ritual impurity (junub), unless one is passing through on a journey, without taking a full ritual bath (ghusl). If one is ill or traveling and cannot find water, dry ablution (tayammum) is permissible. The words 'junub', 'gha'it', and 'lamastum' are explained; there is a difference of opinion between the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools regarding the nullification of ablution by touch.

The word tayammum means "to intend," and intention is part of the essence of this act of worship. "Sa'id" means the earth's surface; it encompasses stone and soil. For this reason, even if soil does not stick to the hands, tayammum with a stone is permissible. However, Imam al-Shafi'i stated that at least a little soil must cling to the hands. "Tayyib" means pure and clean; therefore, it must not be impure or doubtful. Cleanliness is so important in Islam that when water cannot be found, one must form the intention, direct one's heart toward purification, and wipe the face and hands up to the elbows with clean earth. This demonstrates that both physical and spiritual purification are united. Allah is Pardoning and has granted a concession for tayammum.

In verses 44–46, the Jews who were given a portion of the Scripture are criticized. They distort words from their original meanings and, twisting their tongues, say, "We hear and disobey," "Listen, may you not hear," and "ra'ina" (look at us). Yet, had they said, "We hear and obey," "Listen," and "look upon us," it would have been better for them. Allah cursed them on account of their disbelief. Distortion (tahrif) occurs in three ways: altering words, misinterpreting them, and uttering statements deceptively. These verses reveal their disrespect toward the Prophet and their obstinacy.

In verse 47, Allah calls the People of the Book to believe in the Quran, which confirms the Torah in their hands. Otherwise, their faces will be effaced and turned backward, or they will be cursed just as the Sabbath-breakers were cursed. In verse 48, it is stated that Allah will never forgive associating partners with Him, but He will forgive other sins for whomsoever He wills. This identifies associating partners with Allah (shirk) as the greatest sin. The claims of the Jews, such as "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved," are rejected.

Verses 49–55 describe those who claim purity for themselves and the Jewish leaders who regarded the idolaters as superior to the believers. Huyayy b. Akhtab and Ka'b b. al-Ashraf allied with Quraysh, prostrated before idols, and disparaged the Muslims. Verses 51–55 emphasize that they believed in idolatry and taghut (false deities/tyranny), and that they are those whom Allah has cursed. In verses 56–57, it is stated that as for the disbelievers who deny the verses, whenever their skins are roasted through in Hell, their skins will be renewed; whereas those who believe and perform righteous deeds will abide eternally in Gardens beneath which rivers flow, blessed with purified spouses and dense shade.

Verse 58 is a very important verse in which Allah commands returning trusts to their rightful owners and judging between people with justice. Trust (amanah) means trustworthiness; it is of three kinds: toward Allah, toward people, and toward oneself. This verse was revealed concerning a well-known incident during the conquest of Mecca regarding the return of the key of the Kaaba to Uthman b. Talha. One must comply with Allah's commands and avoid betrayal and injustice.

In verse 59, believers are commanded to obey Allah and the Prophet, and to obey those in authority among them. However, this obedience is not unconditional; one does not obey someone who commands sin. The qualification "among you" indicates that obedience to non-believing rulers is not obligatory. While believers should not revolt, they must not obey in matters that involve disobedience to Allah. Regarding this, our Prophet stated: "A Muslim is obligated to listen and obey, whether he likes it or dislikes it, except when commanded to commit a sin; if commanded to sin, there is no obedience."

In verse 83 of Surah an-Nisa, it is commanded that news of security or fear should not be spread immediately, but instead brought to the Prophet and those in authority. This indicates the existence of scholars and jurists who have the capacity to derive rulings from the verses. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi explains that these people of authority are the "ahl al-hall wal-aqd" (those qualified to bind and loosen), that is, the people of consensus (ijma), and that their agreement represents the community (ummah), forming an evidence after the Quran and Sunnah. Regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse, it is narrated that during a detachment under the command of Khalid b. al-Walid, Ammar b. Yasir granted protection (aman) to a man, leading to a dispute with Khalid. The Prophet (peace be upon him) accepted Ammar's protection, but reminded him not to give pledges on his own against his commander again.

Believers are commanded to refer any dispute that arises among them to Allah and His Messenger. This means not judging solely according to one's own desires, and turning not to other authorities, but first to Allah and the Prophet. In Islam, rulings are of four types: those explicitly stated in the Quran, those stated in the Sunnah, those established by consensus (ijma), and those derived through sound analogical reasoning (qiyas). Qiyas is the deduction of a ruling in issues not clarified in the sacred texts (nass) by seeking similarity and the effective cause (illah). Although the Zahiri school rejects qiyas, it is in fact impossible to resolve disputes without qiyas. In the event of disagreement, recourse is made to the consultation (shura) of the authorities and ultimately to the ruler, which is itself obedience to Allah's command.

The verses draw attention to the hypocrites who claim that they believe: they wish to resort to taghut (the transgressing Satan who does not fear Allah). Yet they were commanded to reject taghut. According to a narration, a hypocrite and a Jew had a dispute; the Jew wanted to go to the Prophet (peace be upon him), while the hypocrite wanted to go to the leader of the Jews, Ka'b b. al-Ashraf. When Umar heard that the hypocrite was not satisfied with the judgment of the Messenger of Allah, he killed him, and this act was praised in the sight of Allah. Thus, this incident demonstrates that resorting to the court of taghut is disbelief, and that true faith requires complete submission to the judgment of the Prophet.

Those who obey Allah and the Messenger will be together with the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. Following this comes the command to fight directed to the believers: all kinds of precautions must be taken against the enemy, and they should mobilize either in small detachments or all together. However, those among them who drag their feet rejoice if a calamity befalls them, and if a victory is won, they express regret saying, "If only I had been with them." The truly sincere fight in the cause of Allah, selling the life of this world for the Hereafter; whether they are killed or achieve victory, they will receive a great reward. The legitimacy of war is to rescue the oppressed and weak men, women, and children. Believers fight in the cause of Allah, while disbelievers fight in the cause of the taghut (false deities); indeed, the plot of Satan is weak.

Those who were once restrained from fighting and commanded to establish prayer and give zakah began to fear people as they would fear Allah when fighting was made obligatory upon them. The enjoyment of this world is brief, and the Hereafter is far better for the righteous. Death will reach you wherever you may be; even if you are in fortified towers, you cannot escape. Good is from Allah, while evil is from one's own self. Words such as "subat" (a troop of more than ten people) and "fatil" (the thin thread in the groove of a date stone, signifying an infinitesimal amount) are explained. Obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah; you have not been sent as a keeper over those who turn away. The hypocrites outwardly say "we obey," yet when night falls, they conspire other things. The Quran should be pondered; had it been from other than Allah, they would surely have found many contradictions in it.

As narrated in this section, when the Prophet (peace be upon him) arrived in Medina, there was initially abundance and affordability. However, when the obstinacy of the Jews and the hypocrisy of the hypocrites surfaced during the call to Islam, famine and high prices set in. This situation was a trial also witnessed in communities to which earlier prophets had been sent. The hypocrites and the Jews attributed these afflictions to the Prophet, saying, 'This man brings misfortune; since he arrived, crops have dwindled and prices have soared.' These verses were revealed precisely in response to their slanders. The phrasing of the verse encompasses not only this specific incident, but also general circumstances such as victory or defeat in war.

In the continuation of the verse, it is proclaimed: 'Say: Whatever good comes to you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from your own self.' This statement emphasizes that everything occurs by the decree of Allah, yet evils afflict humans on account of their own faults or sins. A person should recognize all good as coming from Allah, and ascribe evil to oneself. Regarding the question of destiny (qadar), this verse accepts neither strict fatalism (jabr) nor absolute autonomy; it teaches a balance between the two. The will of Allah encompasses all things, yet human responsibility remains intact.

After stating that obeying our Prophet is obeying Allah, it is recounted how the hypocrites secretly hatch plans of defiance. Outwardly they say, 'at your command,' yet as soon as they leave your presence, they conspire by night to do the exact opposite of what they told you. Allah knows and records whatever they conceal. What falls upon our Prophet is solely conveying the message; he is not tasked with being their guardian. For this reason, the believers must rely upon Allah in every matter and pay no heed to the schemes of the hypocrites.

As proof that the Quran is the word of Allah, it is underscored that it contains no contradiction or inconsistency whatsoever. Had it originated from other than Allah, they would have found many discrepancies and contradictions within it. On the contrary, the Quran is in perfect harmony, both in its historical reports and in its legal rulings. As for the apparent differences between verses, they are arranged with divine wisdom according to changing times and circumstances. For this reason, believers should contemplate the Quran and realize that it originates from the presence of Allah.

The believers are instructed not to spread rumors the moment they hear them, but to consult the Prophet and those in authority first. In this manner, the accuracy of the report and its suitability for the public interest must be examined. Those possessing the capacity for istinbat (deduction), that is, ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), can derive the proper judgment regarding such events. This verse also teaches that uninformed individuals must refer matters to scholars. Moreover, Umar's investigating the rumor that the Prophet had divorced his wives and uncovering the truth is among the reasons for the revelation of this verse.

The command to fight in the cause of Allah serves as a reminder that an individual is responsible for his own soul. The Prophet (peace be upon him) was resolute in marching out to battle even if he were left entirely alone at the Battle of Badr Minor (Badr al-Sughra). The believers must be urged to battle, for Allah will surely restrain the might of the disbelievers. Whoever engages in a good intercession (mediation) partakes in its reward, and whoever engages in an evil intercession bears a share of its burden. For this reason, believers should mediate for good and strictly avoid mediating for evil.

The etiquette of greeting is likewise taught here: when you are greeted with a greeting, return it with one that is better, or return it equally. In Islam, the greeting of peace (salam) is a supplication for safety and well-being in both this world and the Hereafter. The greetings of the pre-Islamic period of ignorance (Jahiliyyah), such as 'May God grant you a long life,' are deficient; the authentic greeting consists of wishing peace and security. This verse also points toward being prepared for peace after war. Muslims should reciprocate accordingly whenever enemies lean toward peace.

Detailed explanations are provided regarding offering and returning the greeting of salam. Salam is among the beautiful names of Allah, and in twelve instances in the Quran, Allah greets the believers. Returning a greeting is a collective obligation (fard al-kifayah). In situations such as listening to a sermon (khutbah), reciting the Quran, or teaching sacred knowledge, greetings are not answered. It is Sunnah for the one walking to greet the one sitting, the rider to greet the pedestrian, the younger to greet the elder, and the smaller group to greet the larger group. That the person giving the greeting should not raise his voice excessively has been narrated from Imam al-A'zam (Abu Hanifah). A given greeting must be returned at least in kind, and kindness must not be left unreciprocated.

It is affirmed that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that He will gather everyone together on the Day of Resurrection (verse 87). Our being divided into two factions concerning the hypocrites is reproached; Allah has cast them back because of the sins they earned. It is impossible to guide the one whom Allah has left to stray (verse 88).

The hypocrites wish that you too would fall into disbelief; they must not be taken as allies until they emigrate in the cause of Allah, and if they turn away from emigration, they must be seized and killed wherever they are found (verse 89). However, those who seek refuge with a people with whom you have a treaty, or those who remain neutral, fighting neither you nor their own people, are exempt from this ruling. Had Allah willed, He could have given them power over you; if they offer you peace, attacking them is impermissible (verse 90). There are also others who seek to be secure from both you and their own people, yet whenever they are lured back into discord (fitnah), they plunge headlong into it; if they do not withdraw from you nor offer you peace, they must be seized and slain (verse 91).

If a believer kills another believer by mistake, as an expiation (kaffarah) he must emancipate a believing slave and pay blood money (diyah) to the family of the deceased, unless the family charitably foregoes it. If the slain person was a believer but belonged to a people hostile to you, only the emancipation of a slave is required; if he belonged to a people with whom you maintain a treaty, both blood money and expiation are incumbent. Whoever cannot find a slave to free must fast for two consecutive months (verse 92). As for the penalty for one who intentionally murders a believer, it is eternal Hellfire; Allah is wrathful with him, has cursed him, and has prepared a tremendous punishment for him (verse 93).

When setting out for jihad in the cause of Allah, thorough investigation must be made to distinguish the believer from the disbeliever. To anyone who offers a greeting of peace or surrenders, one must not say, 'You are not a believer,' in order to pursue worldly gain. With Allah there are abundant spoils. You too were like that before, and Allah bestowed His favor upon you. Therefore, investigate thoroughly and do not act hastily. Allah is well aware of what you do (verse 94).

In this section, certain incidents encountered by the believers during war are recounted. For example, a Companion named Mirdas, despite having accepted Islam, was killed by Usamah ibn Zayd; the Prophet (peace be upon him) was deeply grieved by this and rebuked Usamah, saying, "How could you kill him when he had said lâilâhe illallah?" Similarly, Muhallam ibn Jussamah, who killed 'Amir ibn al-Adbat, met with the same reaction and passed away shortly thereafter following the Prophet's supplication against him. These incidents demonstrate that a person who professes to be a Muslim must not be killed immediately and that intentions must be left to Allah.

Even if a person who declares that they have entered Islam is insincere, this declaration must prevent them from being killed. Indeed, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad questioned the Prophet regarding a similar situation, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Do not kill him! For if you kill him, he will be in your position after you kill him, and you will be in his position before he uttered the word he said." These hadiths emphasize that even in war, killing someone who professes to be a Muslim is a grave sin, and that unless one cuts open their heart, their faith cannot be questioned.

Following these incidents, verses 95–96 of Surah an-Nisa were revealed. In these verses, it is stated that those who remain behind from battle without a legitimate excuse and those who strive (jihad) in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives are not equal. Allah has favored the mujahideen over those who sit back by a degree and promised them a great reward. However, Paradise has been promised to both groups. The concept of 'excuse' encompasses physical impediments such as illness, blindness, and lameness, or the lack of necessary provisions for battle. These verses indicate that jihad is a collective obligation (fard al-kifayah) and that not everyone bears the same degree of responsibility.

Verses 97–100 address those Muslims who did not emigrate and remained under oppression. As the angels take the souls of those who wrong themselves, they ask them, "What was your state?" and they reply, "We were oppressed in the land." The angels reject their excuse, saying, "Was Allah's earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?" However, men, women, and children who are truly helpless and destitute are exempt from this ruling; it is hoped that Allah will pardon them. Emigration (hijrah) is, when necessary, a form of jihad, and an individual must depart from a place where they cannot practice their religion.

In verse 100, it is proclaimed that whoever leaves their home emigrating in the cause of Allah and then dies along the way, their reward is incumbent upon Allah. This underscores the significance of intention and effort. As in the case of Jundub ibn Damrah, whoever sets out with the intention of emigration and passes away on the way receives a reward as though they had reached their destination. This verse dispels the apprehensions holding Muslims back from emigration and recalls Allah's forgiveness.

Verses 101–104 explain how prayer is to be observed during travel and in states of fear. When traveling upon the earth, there is no blame in shortening the prayer if harm from the disbelievers is feared. When the Prophet (peace be upon him) led his Companions in prayer during battle, one group would stand in prayer carrying their weapons while the other group stood guard; then the groups would alternate. In instances of rain or illness, it is permissible to lay down weapons, yet vigilance must not be abandoned. Once fear has subsided, prayer is performed in full. One must not show slackness in pursuing the enemy, must bear the suffering they cause with patience, and must place hope in Allah.

These verses demonstrate that even in arduous circumstances such as war and emigration, acts of worship must not be neglected, yet dispensations are provided according to circumstances. Furthermore, the sincerity of intention and the imperative of trust in Allah are emphasized, aiming to embolden the believers concerning both jihad and emigration. In every circumstance, Allah knows the condition of His servants and shows them mercy.

According to Hanafi scholars, shortening the prayer during travel is performing the obligatory prayer in its original two-rak'ah form; for when prayer was initially made obligatory, it was ordained as two rak'ahs during travel, and was subsequently expanded to four rak'ahs when resident. Therefore, the "shortening" mentioned in the verse pertains to quality/manner, encompassing conditions such as praying by gesture (ima') or while walking in times of fear.

The manner of performing the fear prayer (salat al-khawf): The imam divides the congregation into two groups; while one group prays, the other keeps watch against the enemy. After the first group completes one rak'ah, they yield their place to the second group, who then pray the second rak'ah behind the imam. Each group then completes their remaining rak'ah independently. In this manner, everyone performs two rak'ahs.

In the verse, it is commanded to keep weapons at hand and remain vigilant so that the enemy cannot launch a surprise raid. The incident of Ghawrath ibn al-Harith recounts the Prophet's rescue through Allah's help under such circumstances. This incident shows that taking precautions and placing trust in Allah must be undertaken together.

Prayer has been made obligatory at designated times. Allah has appointed five states in the rising and setting of the sun as markers for these times: noon, afternoon, evening, night, and dawn. These times have been compared to the stages of human life; each time serves as an occasion for gratitude and servitude to Allah.

When the battle concludes and a secure atmosphere is established, prayers must be performed in full or those that were missed must be made up. Furthermore, weakness must not be exhibited against the enemy, bearing in mind that they too suffer pain; nevertheless, one must never deviate from justice, and the rights of the disbelievers must be respected.

The occasion of revelation for verses 105–115 is the incident of Banu Ubayriq. An individual named Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq falsely accused a Jewish man of theft; however, when the truth became evident, Allah admonished the Prophet not to defend the treacherous. These verses emphasize that one must never be an advocate for the treacherous and that justice must be administered equally to all.

Verses 106–108 articulate the gravity of judicial authority and the solemnity of the responsibility borne by judges, witnesses, and advocates. While Allah Almighty protects the Prophet from error—stemming from his inclination to defend Tu'mah on the basis of outward Islam and the entreaties of his clan—He indicates that for a judge to rule in favor of a traitor, even unwittingly by being deceived by apparent pretexts, constitutes a shortcoming. For this reason, refraining from defending the treacherous and seeking Allah's forgiveness is enjoined. Allah is Forgiving (Ghafur) and Merciful (Rahim) toward those who seek His pardon. This warning conveys a severe admonition and an urge to repentance directed at those who knowingly support traitors, those who instigate injustice out of self-interest or partisanship, and judges who follow their own personal opinion and desires.

Betraying oneself is a person's deceiving oneself and exposing oneself to punishment by committing sins. Siding with a traitor is likewise a betrayal of one's own self. Allah does not love anyone who is sinful and treacherous. In this expression, there is a warning against persistence and habitual sin, as well as an encouragement toward repentance. Furthermore, some of those who betray themselves utter words with which Allah is not pleased, and while doing so, they have no fear of Allah, seeking only to hide from people. The word 'tabyit' means to deliberate and scheme by night, or to craft speech like a poetic verse (bayt). These individuals secretly concoct evil schemes, make decisions contrary to Allah's pleasure, and seek to deceive people. Yet Allah encompasses all things and will fully requite what they do.

In verse 109, addressing those who defend the traitors, it is said: "Here you are—you are the ones who argued on their behalf in the life of this world; but who will defend them on the Day of Resurrection?" Through this defense in the world, not only do they fail to save them, but by partaking in their guilt, they betray their own selves. In verses 110–111, whoever commits an evil deed or wrongs himself and then asks Allah for forgiveness will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful. However, whoever commits a sin earns it only against his own soul, and bears its harmful consequences himself. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

In verse 112, it is stated that whoever commits an error or a sin and then casts it upon an innocent person has burdened himself with slander and a manifest sin. There are three different views regarding the distinction between 'khati'ah' (error) and 'ithm' (sin): first, khati'ah is a minor sin, while ithm is a major sin. Second, khati'ah is a minor sin whose effect remains confined to the doer, whereas ithm is a transitive sin that wrongs another person. Third, khati'ah is that which is improper to do whether committed deliberately or inadvertently, whereas ithm is that which is committed intentionally. Slander is itself a major sin; shifting one's own sin onto someone else is to add the sin of slander onto that sin. Therefore, it is necessary to avoid such conduct, to repent, and to seek forgiveness and make amends with the wronged party.

In verse 113, it is stated that had it not been for Allah's grace and His mercy, a faction of the traitors would have sought to mislead the Prophet. Although the kin of Tu'mah knew he was a thief, they came to the Prophet asking him to defend him and to pin the theft on a Jewish man. Yet they were only leading themselves astray. Allah revealed the Book and wisdom to the Prophet and taught him secrets he did not know. This is a tremendous grace protecting him from error both outwardly and inwardly. In verse 114, it is stated that there is no good in most of their secret counsels, except for those conducted for three purposes: charity, kindness, or reconciliation between people. These three terms encompass all righteous deeds: procuring benefit (charity / sadaqah), averting harm (reconciliation / islah), and spiritual benefit (righteous conduct / ma'ruf). For whoever does these seeking the pleasure of Allah, there is a great reward.

In verse 115, it is stated that whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows a path other than that of the believers, will be left to what he has chosen and cast into Hell. This verse was revealed concerning Tu'mah, who fled to Mecca and apostatized after his treachery was exposed. 'Shiqaq' means to break away and enter into defiant opposition. The way of the believers is the path of tawhid (monotheism) and the sound religion. Opposing the Messenger of Allah means straying from the path of the believers, and this demonstrates that adhering to the consensus of the Ummah (ijma' al-ummah) is obligatory. In verse 116, it is reiterated that Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him (shirk), but forgives anything less than that for whom He wills. Shirk is both a monstrous fabrication and a profound deviation. The shirk of the People of the Book is predominantly based on fabrication, whereas that of others is predominantly based on ignorance. Neither will be forgiven unless one repents.

In verse 117, it is stated that those who associate partners with Allah invoke none besides Him except female entities (inath). Most of their idols had female names and female shapes. In the polytheists' conception of god, the image of woman is predominant; they view their deities not as active, authoritative beings, but as female entities that yield to them. Through the deception of Satan, this deviance extends even to the worship of woman. Actual women, on the other hand, are degraded by this conception. The polytheists' supplication is a form of worship in which affection and hope predominate. Gods of fear, on the other hand, are generally male, and worship of them takes the form of groveling flattery.

In verses 118–120, it is recounted that the defiant Satan was cursed by Allah and swore that he would take a designated portion of His servants, mislead them, fill them with false desires, command them to slit the ears of livestock, and command them to alter Allah's creation. What is meant here is every kind of deviance brought about through the whisperings of Satan: such as making women resemble men and men resemble women, using bodily organs outside their purpose of creation, and declaring the lawful to be unlawful and the unlawful to be lawful. These five declarations of Satan constitute the head of shirk and the fountainhead of deviance.

In this section, mention is first made of the deceptive promises of Satan, who turns people away from truth and goodness. Satan is an accursed being who rebelled against Allah's command. Those who take him as an ally are enticed by his promises and deluded by false pride. Yet all of Satan's promises are nothing but an illusion that will only bring disappointment to humanity. The ultimate destination of those who follow Satan in this manner is Hell, from which there is no escape. However, those who repent and turn away from shirk retain the hope of forgiveness.

In contrast, for those who believe and perform righteous deeds, Gardens beneath which rivers flow have been promised. This promise is Allah's absolute pledge, and who is more truthful in speech than Allah? Paradise cannot be attained through the wishful thinking of the Muslims nor through that of the People of the Book. Each person can attain Allah's mercy only by doing good and guarding against evil. Not even the slightest injustice will be done, and everyone will receive the complete recompense for their deeds.

The best religion in the sight of Allah is that of one who surrenders his whole being to Allah, does good, and follows the way of Abraham (Ibrahim) as a hanif (an upright monotheist). For Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend (khalil). This friendship is an exalted station attained through Abraham's devotion and sacrifices for Allah. Those who follow his path also partake of this friendship. This religion is Islam, and there is none better than it.

It is mistaken for Christians to regard the expression 'son of God' as a badge of honor and to claim on that basis that Christianity is superior. Ascribing a son to Allah is associating partners with Him and constitutes a grave slander. Furthermore, a master's son is not necessarily superior to his servant; the son of Noah is an example of this. True superiority lies in friendship with Allah and servitude to Him. Even the Gospel itself corroborates this truth.

Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth belongs to Allah. He encompasses all things. Neither the friendship of Abraham nor the curse of Satan lies outside Allah's dominion. Everyone is subject to Allah's authority and decree. Man must exercise his free will in accordance with Allah's commands, judge with justice, and seek His good pleasure in every matter. This is the purpose of creation and the reason for the sending of the scriptures.

Following these explanations, answers are given to rulings (fatwas) requested concerning women. Matters such as withholding the inheritance rights of orphan girls and being unwilling to marry them are addressed. Allah commands acting with justice in these affairs. Asking the Prophet for a ruling is intended to ascertain the correct judgment in difficult issues. A mufti must be qualified and trustworthy.

If a woman fears ill-treatment or estrangement from her husband, there is no blame upon them in making peace between themselves through reconciliation. Reconciliation is better than separation. Souls are inclined to selfishness; however, living together amicably and guarding against discord is pleasing in the sight of Allah. An agreement can be reached through the woman relinquishing some of her rights or the man making a sacrifice.

Full justice between wives in terms of love is not possible, for the heart is not subject to one's will. However, equality must be observed in material rights such as maintenance and overnight stays. It is not permissible to incline completely toward one wife and leave the other suspended. If injustice is avoided and things are rectified, Allah is All-Forgiving.

If the husband and wife decide to separate as a result of disagreement, Allah will enrich each of them out of His vast bounty, leaving them in no need of the other. Separation must be with the mutual consent of both parties; coercion or injustice is a sin. Allah is the Owner of whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth; everything is in need of Him, while He is in need of nothing.

Allah has commanded both the previous communities and the Muslims to fear Him. Let those who disbelieve know that whatever is in the heavens and on the earth belongs to Allah. He is worthy of all praise and does not need the worship of His servants. People's disbelief causes Him no harm, nor does their gratitude bring Him any benefit. He merely protects His servants out of His mercy and guides them to the right path.

Allah Almighty informs that, if He wills, He can eliminate you and bring another people in your place. Upon the revelation of this ayah, it is narrated that the Messenger of Allah tapped the back of Salman al-Farsi and said, 'They are his people.' Whoever desires the reward of this world should know that the reward of both this world and the Hereafter is with Allah; the wise person should ask for both rewards or prioritize the Hereafter. Allah knows intentions and repays everyone according to their intention.

O you who believe! Stand firmly for justice, bearing witness for Allah alone, even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or your close relatives. Whether rich or poor, Allah is closer to both of them than you are. Do not follow the desire of your soul and deviate from justice. If you distort your testimony or refuse to give it, Allah is fully aware of what you do.

Believe in Allah, His Messenger, the Book He sent down to His Messenger, and the scriptures sent down before. Whoever denies Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day has fallen into deep misguidance. Those who believe, then disbelieve, then believe again, then disbelieve, and then increase in disbelief—Allah will neither forgive them nor guide them to the right path. There is a painful punishment for the hypocrites; they take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers, whereas all honor and glory belong entirely to Allah.

Allah has already revealed to you in the Book that when you hear His verses being denied and ridiculed, you must not sit with those disbelievers unless they engage in another topic; otherwise, you will be just like them. Indeed, Allah will gather all the hypocrites and disbelievers together in Hell. The hypocrites keep watch over you; if a victory comes to you, they say, 'Were we not with you?' but if the disbelievers achieve a victory, they say, 'Did we not gain advantage over you and protect you from the believers?' Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and He will never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers.

The hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, yet Allah will turn their plots back upon them. When they stand up for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off, and they remember Allah but little. They waver between disbelief and faith, belonging neither to the believers nor to the disbelievers. Whoever Allah leaves to stray, no way of salvation can be found for him. O you who believe! Do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers; otherwise, you will give Allah a clear proof against yourselves. The hypocrites are in the lowest depth of Hell, and you will find no helper for them. Except those who repent, make amends, hold firmly to Allah, and are sincere in their religion—they will be with the believers. Allah will grant a great reward.

Allah does not like offensive speech to be uttered openly, except by one who has been wronged. Whether you reveal a good deed or conceal it, or pardon an evil, Allah is All-Forgiving and Omnipotent. Those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers desire to differentiate between them by believing in some and disbelieving in others. They are the true disbelievers; a humiliating punishment has been prepared for them. As for those who believe in Allah and His messengers and make no distinction between any of them, Allah will soon grant them their rewards. Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

There are those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, those who separate Allah from His messenger in faith, and those who accept some messengers and reject others. The Jews and Christians belong to this last group. This verse demonstrates that there is no middle path between faith and disbelief; rejecting one prophet is equivalent to rejecting them all, and rejecting all of them is equivalent to denying Allah. For this reason, Allah has prepared a humiliating punishment for all disbelievers.
As for those who believe in Allah and His messengers and make no distinction between any of them, Allah will give them their rewards and forgive their sins. This promise is for the believers.

The People of the Book asked our Prophet to bring down a book to them from heaven. Yet they had asked Moses (Musa) for something even greater, saying, 'Show us Allah openly.' Because of their wrongdoing, they were struck by lightning; then they worshipped the calf. Allah pardoned them and gave Moses a clear proof.

Allah raised Mount Tur over them to take their pledge, commanded them to enter the gate prostrating, told them not to violate the Sabbath, and took a firm covenant from them. Yet they broke their pledge, rejected the verses, killed the prophets, and said, 'Our hearts are wrapped.' For this reason, Allah sealed their hearts.

The Jews were cursed on account of their disbelief in Jesus and their uttering a monstrous slander against Mary, as well as their saying, 'We killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah.' Yet they neither killed him nor crucified him, but it was made to appear so to them. Those who differ over this matter are in doubt about it. Allah raised Jesus up to Himself.

Every one of the People of the Book will surely believe in Jesus before his death. On the Day of Resurrection, Jesus will be a witness against them. Because of the wrongdoing of the Jews, their taking of usury, and their consuming people's wealth wrongfully, Allah forbade them the wholesome things that had previously been lawful to them, and prepared a painful punishment for the disbelievers.

Those among the People of the Book who are well-grounded in knowledge and the believers believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you. They establish prayer, give zakat, and believe in Allah and the Last Day. For them, there is a great reward.

Allah has revealed to you just as He revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. He also revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Descendants, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, Solomon, and David. He sent messengers as bringers of good tidings and warners so that mankind would have no excuse before Allah. Allah bears witness to what He has revealed to you. Those who disbelieve and hinder others from the path of Allah have strayed into deep misguidance. Allah will neither forgive them nor guide them to the right path; they will abide in Hell forever.

Revelation (wahy) is of several kinds: seeing Gabriel (Jibril) and hearing the speech, hearing a voice from behind a veil, breathing into the heart, inspiration (ilham), subjugation (taskhir), and by means of true dreams. Literally, wahy is a swift and hidden communication. In its general sense, it can apply to anyone; however, as a technical term, it refers to the special communication from Allah to the prophets. This special revelation imparts definitive knowledge, and prophethood begins only with such revelation.

Allah revealed to many prophets after Noah: Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the descendants, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, Solomon, and He gave the Psalms (Zabur) to David. None of these prophets had a book sent down all at once, as claimed by the People of the Book. The Psalms is a book containing no legal rulings, consisting solely of wisdom, admonition, and praise.

Prophets do not consist solely of those who are known. Allah sent many more messengers whose names were mentioned as well as those whose names were not mentioned. For this reason, the claim that prophets emerged only from Palestine and its surrounding regions is invalid. Allah's choice is based on divine wisdom; this circumstance should not be regarded as strange, just like characteristics in other matters. The exact number of prophets is not known; only those necessary for faith have been made known.

Allah addressed Moses (Musa) directly with speech from behind a veil, which is the highest rank of revelation. Other prophets were also inspired at various levels. That prophets received revelation in different ways casts no doubt upon their truthfulness. The gradual descent of the Quran also rests on a divine wisdom; for the People of the Book to demand a book brought down all at once from heaven is baseless.

Allah Himself bears witness to the Quran He sent down to His Messenger; the angels also bear witness. This is a miracle sent down with divine knowledge. Those who disbelieve in it and obstruct people from the path of Allah are in deep misguidance. It is not possible for them to be forgiven or guided to the right path; they shall abide in Hell forever.

O people! The Messenger has brought you the truth from your Lord; believe in him for your own good. O People of the Book! Do not go to extremes in your religion and do not say anything about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is the messenger of Allah, His word conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him. Do not say, 'Allah is three'; that is better for you. Allah is One, exalted above having a child; to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.

Jesus does not disdain from being a servant to Allah, nor do the angels. Whoever shows arrogance against servitude, Allah will gather everyone before Him; He will grant those who believe and do good deeds their reward in full and more, while He will punish those who act arrogantly with a severe torment. Allah is sufficient to set the affairs of His servants right; seeking a guardian other than Him is futile.

There has come to you from your Lord a clear proof (Muhammad) and a manifest light (the Quran). Those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him, He will admit them into His mercy and grace, and guide them to a straight path.

They ask you for a legal ruling concerning the inheritance of a kalalah (a person who leaves behind neither parent nor child). Say: Allah gives you a ruling as follows: If a person dies without children and has a sister, half of his estate belongs to her. If a sister dies and has a brother, the brother inherits from her. If there are two sisters, two-thirds belongs to them. If the siblings are a mixture of male and female, the male's share is equal to the share of two females. Allah makes this clear to you lest you go astray; and He is All-Knowing of everything.

Just as when a brother dies, if a sister dies leaving behind neither child nor father, the brother inherits her entire estate. But if the sister has a son or a father, the brother cannot inherit; if she has a daughter, he cannot take the whole estate, but takes what remains.

Under the same conditions, if there are two or more sisters, their prescribed share is two-thirds of the estate. If there is a remainder, it is given to the 'asabah (agnatic/paternal relatives); if there are none, it reverts to the sisters by way of radd (reversion).
If the surviving siblings are a mixture of male and female, the male is given a share equal to the share of two females. Allah explains these rulings to you lest you go astray.

The Basran scholars interpreted the expression 'lest you go astray' in this explanation as 'disliking that you should go astray,' whereas the Kufan scholars interpreted it as 'so that you do not go astray.' In our dialect, saying 'lest you err' carries the same meaning; that is, if it is not explained, you would err. However, presuming an implicit negative particle is better than presuming a conditional clause.

This verse is an answer to a request for a legal ruling that begins with the phrase 'They ask you for a ruling,' and serves as a preparation for the explanations in Surah al-Ma'idah. Allah knows all things; knowing your circumstances concerning life and death, He has made clear the rulings that are for your benefit. You, too, should learn them and walk on the straight path.

This surah encompasses eighteen obligatory duties. According to what Abu Hayyan recorded, the students of the famous al-Kindi, the first philosopher of the Arabs, said to him, 'O philosopher, compose something for us equal to this Quran.' He replied, 'Very well, I will not produce an equivalent for all of it, but I will make something similar to a part of it,' and worked for days. Then he came forth and said: 'By Allah, neither we nor anyone else has the power to do this. I opened the Mushaf, and Surah al-Ma'idah appeared before me; I looked, and it enjoined fidelity (keeping one's word), prohibited backsliding, made a general analysis, then made an exception, and subsequently gave news of His power and wisdom, fitting all of this into two lines. No one could express this without writing volumes.'

'Uqud is the plural of 'aqd. 'Aqd means a documented contract; it is likened to a bond and knot that firmly ties one thing to another. In the dictionary, it means to bind tightly and to knot. Transferred from this meaning, a person's adoption of something, or binding oneself or another by compelling the other to silence, is called an 'aqd (contract/covenant). 'I'tiqad' (creed/conviction) also derives from this. Not every contract relies on offer and acceptance; in some, an agreement is formed merely through consent. Vows and oaths regarding the future are of this kind. 'Ahd' (covenant), on the other hand, means preserving and watching over something from state to state; documents required to be thus observed are called 'ahd'. Although 'ahd' and 'aqd' appear synonymous, 'aqd' conveys a greater sense of consolidation. 'Wafa' and 'ifa' mean fulfilling the requirements of the covenant and contract. Here, 'al-'uqud' encompasses all contracts: the legal obligations Allah has imposed upon His servants, the vows and oaths servants bind themselves to of their own accord, trusts and transactions made among people, and even treaties made with the people of war (harb), protected non-Muslim subjects (dhimmah), and others. From this, the following legal principle is deduced: The presumption in contracts is validity, unless evidence to annul them has been established.

O you who believe, fulfill all the contracts to which you are bound. Faith (iman) is a contract; by this contract, you entered into covenants with Allah. Then, you make other contracts and bind yourselves of your own accord, among yourselves, or among people. Fulfill, then, all these contracts. In short, this is the root of the religion, the verdict of faith, and the command of Allah. In harmony with the name of the surah, the explanation begins first with the means of livelihood: Various animals have been made lawful for you, except those whose unlawfulness is recited or will follow below. You cannot consider hunting lawful while you are in the state of ihram; however, you may eat from animals slaughtered by those who are not in ihram. This lawfulness and unlawfulness are divine covenants. Being able to eat the meat of an animal slaughtered by someone else is the fruit of a contract between you, such as purchase or gift. The game that is forbidden while in ihram is land game, not sea game.

'Bahimah' means any animal that lacks intellect. What is made lawful here is not animals (baha'im) in an absolute sense, but four-legged animals living on land and in the sea. 'An'am' refers to domestic livestock such as camels, cattle, sheep, and goats. Solid-hoofed animals such as horses, mules, and donkeys are not included in an'am. The compound 'bahimat al-an'am' either functions as an explicative genitive (idafat bayaniyyah) meaning 'the animals known as an'am'—in which case game animals such as gazelles and deer also become lawful—or as a comparative genitive (idafat lamiyyah tashbihiyyah) meaning 'animals that are like an'am', rendering wild animals that resemble livestock in chewing the cud and lacking canine teeth lawful. Under either interpretation, bahimat al-an'am does not include marine animals.

The following have been made unlawful for you: 1. Maytah (carrion, that is, what dies without being slaughtered). 2. Blood (spilled blood is impure and unlawful). 3. Swineflesh (the pig itself is impure). 4. That over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked at the time of slaughter (for instance, that slaughtered in the name of al-Lat and al-'Uzza). These are fundamental. Those following them fall religiously under their scope. During the Jahiliyyah period, although some did not eat carrion, they ate the following, which are essentially of the nature of carrion: 5. The suffocated (that which died from suffocation in any way). 6. The beaten (that which died from a blow). 7. The fallen (that which died by falling from a height). 8. The gored (that which was gored or butted). 9. That partially eaten by a wild beast (that which was destroyed by a predatory animal). Since the blood of these five was not drained by slaughter, they are entirely carrion and unlawful.

Allah has forbidden carrion, blood, swineflesh, animals slaughtered in the name of other than Allah, the suffocated, the beaten, the fallen from above, the gored, and animals partially eaten by wild beasts. However, if these animals are reached before dying and are properly slaughtered according to the prescribed rules, they become lawful. Quran commentators have put forward differing opinions regarding the scope of this exception. While some stated that the exception applies only to that partially eaten by a wild beast, the majority stated that it encompasses all of them, from the suffocated to that partially eaten by a wild beast. In any event, this exception does not encompass things that cannot be slaughtered, such as carrion, blood, and swine.

In Islam, slaughter carried out according to the prescribed rules is called 'tazkiyah'. Tazkiyah is terminating the animal's life by slitting its throat and draining its blood. The place of slaughter is from the base of the neck to beneath the jaw. There are four vessels that must be cut: the windpipe, the esophagus, and the two jugular veins. According to the Hanafi school, at least three of these must be severed. The slaughter instrument must be sharp, and the animal must not be tormented. It is a condition that the slaughterer be a Muslim or from the People of the Book and pronounce the Basmalah.

Animals slaughtered on stone altars (nusub) are also unlawful. During the Jahiliyyah period, slaughters were performed for idols or in front of them. In addition, seeking fortunes with divining arrows (azlam)—that is, fortune-telling and gambling—has also been prohibited. All these prohibitions are characterized as departing from obedience to Allah and transgression (fisq). Believers must strictly stay away from them.

These verses were revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage on the day of Arafah at the time of Friday prayer: 'Today I have perfected for you your religion, completed My favor upon you, and chosen for you Islam as your religion.' With this verse, it was announced that the religion was completed and that the possibility of abrogation (naskh) no longer remained. The Companions rejoiced greatly at this verse; however, Abu Bakr wept, understanding that the death of the Messenger of Allah was drawing near.

Nonetheless, in a state of dire necessity (the danger of dying of hunger), a person may eat from forbidden things, provided they do not transgress the limits and do not usurp another's right. Allah is Forgiving, Merciful. As stated in the preceding verses, this exception is valid only for the moment of necessity.

When the Companions asked what had been made lawful for them, the Messenger of Allah was commanded to proclaim: 'Lawful to you are good and wholesome things. Eat of what the hunting animals you have trained as Allah taught you catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it.' Furthermore, the food of the People of the Book is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. Chaste women among the believing women and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you are lawful for you, provided that you pay their dowries in an honorable manner. Whoever rejects faith, their deeds come to naught, and in the Hereafter they will be among the losers.

According to what Ka'b narrated, Gabriel (peace be upon him) would not enter a house in which there was a dog. Thereupon, the Prophet (peace be upon him) ordered the killing of dogs and assigned Abu Rafi' to this task. When the dogs in Medina were killed, the Companions came and asked, 'What has been made lawful for us?' The Messenger of Allah remained silent, and then this ayah was revealed. In another narration, when 'Adi ibn Hatim and Zayd al-Khayl asked about hunting with dogs and falcons, this verse was revealed once again. Although different narrations indicate that the ayah was revealed before or after the verse of prohibition, both cases are consistent with the context of the discourse.

In this ayah, 'tayyibat' (wholesome things) were made lawful. Tayyibat are clean and good things that sound human nature finds pleasant. The taste of those with bad habits is not taken into account. The original principle regarding things is permissibility, but khaba'ith (foul things) are excluded from this generality. This is a major principle in determining the lawful and the unlawful. While the pre-Islamic Arabs of Jahiliyyah ate filthy things such as carrion, they would arbitrarily forbid certain animals to themselves out of mere delusion. By declaring that wholesome things are lawful, this verse abolished those customs.

Jawarih means predatory hunting animals. Mukallib means training these animals for hunting. If a trained dog or bird of prey wounds and kills the prey, and the animal is already dead by the time the hunter reaches it, wounding takes the place of slaughtering and the game becomes lawful. However, if the animal eats from the prey it killed, this means it caught it for itself, and it is not eaten. It must be released while pronouncing the Basmalah. There are different opinions on this matter; according to the Hanafi school, the fact that a bird of prey ate from it does not preclude its lawfulness.

The food of the People of the Book is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. The word 'ta'am' (food) has generally been interpreted as slaughtered meat, because regarding foods like bread, there is no difference between the People of the Book and others; the difference lies in slaughtered meat and game. What the People of the Book slaughter is eaten as long as they do not slaughter it in the name of anyone other than Allah. However, if you hear that they slaughtered it in the name of the Messiah, it is not permissible to eat it. Furthermore, it is lawful for you to marry chaste, free women from among the People of the Book by giving them their dowry. As for Muslim women marrying men from the People of the Book, it is never permissible.

In the continuation of the ayah comes the command of wudu (ablution). When you rise for prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. If you are in a state of major ritual impurity (junub), purify yourselves. If you cannot find water, perform tayammum (dry ablution). This verse was revealed when water could not be found during the expedition in which Aisha's necklace was lost. There is disagreement regarding whether the feet should be washed or wiped due to a difference in recitation. The majority considers washing to be obligatory, and the Sunnah also supports this. Wiping is performed over leather socks.

O you who believe! When you rise for prayer—that is, when you intend to perform prayer—wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. Prayer is not valid without this purification. This is called 'tuhur' (purification) or 'wudu' (ablution). The obligatory acts of ablution are four: three washings and one wiping. Imam al-Shafi'i also considered intention and proper order to be obligatory, making them six; Ahmad ibn Hanbal added rinsing the inside of the mouth and nose as well, stating there are eight obligations. Among the Hanafis, intention, order, rinsing the mouth, and sniffing water into the nose are Sunnah. Although the outward wording of the verse might seem to require a separate ablution for every prayer, the majority does not hold this view. Our Prophet performed five daily prayers with a single ablution, which demonstrated its permissibility. Furthermore, there is consensus that the ayah should be understood as 'when you rise for prayer while you do not have ablution.' In wiping the head, the letter 'ba' is used; from this, the Hanafis deduced the meaning of passing the hand over the head, holding that the obligatory amount of wiping is one-fourth of the head, whereas Malik and Ahmad ibn Hanbal deemed the entire head obligatory, and al-Shafi'i considered the touch of a single finger sufficient.

Washing means letting water flow completely over the limb. Rubbing is not a condition. Ablution is purification from hadath (ritual impurity); it is different from purification from najasah (physical filth). In ablution, physical impurity must be removed beforehand. Washing once is sufficient for fulfilling the obligation, while washing twice or three times is Sunnah. Wiping, on the other hand, means touching something and passing the hand over it; its obligatory element is contact. Wiping the head is the touching of the wet hand to the required amount. Repeating the wipe is not Sunnah, though the hair may be smoothed down gently. If you are in a state of janabah—that is, if seminal fluid has been emitted or sexual intercourse has taken place—you must perform ghusl and wash thoroughly from head to toe. Rinsing the mouth and sniffing water into the nose, which are Sunnah in ablution, are obligatory in ghusl.

If you are ill, on a journey, have relieved yourselves, or have touched women, and you cannot find water, then perform tayammum with clean earth. Make your intention and wipe over your faces and forearms. Tayammum takes the place of wudu or ghusl when water cannot be found or cannot be used. In the verse, it is stipulated that 'sa'id' (the earth) be clean; something must be wiped from the hands onto the face and arms. While according to the Hanafis merely touching the earth with the hand is sufficient, according to the Shafi'is something must definitely be transferred from the hand to the face and arms. The debate over whether tayammum is permissible on stone, marble, and minerals originates from this point.

With these commands of purification, Allah does not intend to place difficulty upon you, but rather He intends to purify you from material and spiritual filth and complete His favor upon you, so that you may be grateful. There is no hardship in religion; the wisdom behind ablution, ghusl, and tayammum is both physical and spiritual purification. Gratitude increases blessing, and the increase of blessing becomes a cause for gratitude. Here, the completion of favor is an indication of the blessings of the Hereafter alongside the blessings of this world. The greatest blessing is the consciousness of gratitude. Those who attain the pleasure of Allah are those who give thanks.

Remember Allah's favor upon you and His covenant (mithaq) that He made with you. This covenant is the moment you said, 'We hear and we obey.' It is the primordial covenant established at the creation of Adam and encompasses the obedience and pledge of allegiance of all believers to the Prophet. Mujahid linked this covenant to the statement 'Am I not your Lord?' in verse 172 of Surah al-A'raf, whereas al-Suddi linked it to rational and legal evidences. In short, do not forget the pledge of servanthood, give thanks for the blessing of Islam, and fulfill your covenants. Allah knows the secrets within your breasts; therefore, give importance to both outward and inward purification.

O you who believe! Be steadfast for Allah as witnesses to justice. And let not the hatred of a people drive you to injustice. Justice is nearer to righteousness (taqwa). Fear Allah; indeed, Allah is well aware of what you do. Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward. As for those who disbelieve and deny the verses, they are the companions of the Hellfire. This ayah, unlike its counterpart in Surah an-Nisa, emphasizes observing justice even in the state of hostility. There, domestic affairs come to the fore, whereas here, foreign relations come to prominence. Believers should rely on Allah alone.

Remember Allah's favor: when a people intended to stretch out their hands against you, but Allah withheld their hands from you. This refers to the assassination attempt by the Jews of Banu Nadir against our Prophet, or generally the thwarting of the attacks of the polytheists. Believers should place their trust in Allah (tawakkul) and rely on nothing else. The consequence of breaching agreements is evil; the example of the Children of Israel points to this. Allah had taken a covenant from them and sent twelve overseers (naqib) from among them. It was promised that if they established prayer, gave zakah, believed in the messengers, supported them, and lent a goodly loan in the way of Allah, their sins would be expiated and they would be admitted into gardens of Paradise.

Yet the Children of Israel broke their pledge; therefore Allah cursed them and hardened their hearts. They would distort words from their contexts and forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of. Except for a few among them, treachery is constantly witnessed from them. Even so, pardon them and overlook [their misdeeds], for Allah loves those who do good. Those who said, "We are Christians," also forgot much of what they had been reminded of, and enmity and hatred were cast among them until the Day of Resurrection. Allah will inform them of what they used to do.

Because the Children of Israel broke the covenant, Allah cursed them and hardened their hearts. They displaced words from their contexts and altered the Torah. They forgot a significant portion of what they had been reminded of. They commit acts of treachery against our Prophet, though those among them who believe are an exception. Allah commanded forgiveness and overlooking; this is a general pardon, showing that not every act of treachery must be punished. The subsequent verses on warfare did not abrogate this pardon, but merely clarified it.

A pledge had also been taken from the Christians, but they too forgot a significant portion of the reminders given to them, especially abandoning tawhid (monotheism) and belief in the final Prophet. Thereupon, Allah cast enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection. They made a craft of the evils they committed, and they will receive the recompense for it in the Hereafter.

O People of the Book! Our Messenger Muhammad has come to you, clarifying much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and overlooking much. There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book (the Quran). Through this Book, Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace and brings them out of darkness into light. This address invites the Jews and Christians to the right path and exposes the truths they had concealed.

Those who said, "Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary," have surely disbelieved. Yet if Allah wished to destroy the Messiah, his mother, and everyone on the earth, no one could prevent Him. To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He creates whatever He wills. The Jews and the Christians said, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved ones." Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are human beings among those He has created.

Our Messenger has come to you after an interval between the messengers, lest you should say, "No bearer of good tidings and no warner has come to us." Now, a bearer of good tidings and a warner has indeed come to you. And Allah is capable of all things.

The Christians' assertion that "Allah is the Messiah" stems from their doctrine of the Trinity. Although some commentators have stated that this verse was revealed concerning specific sects (such as the Jacobites, Chaldeans, etc.), this belief is generally an innovation (bid'ah) embraced by the majority of Christians. The disputes over whether there is one nature or two natures in the Messiah also reflect various aspects of this deviation.

Following the Council of Nicaea, official Christian doctrine took shape, Arius and his followers were excommunicated, and the Trinity was accepted. This council obscured the truth and left an enigma of misguidance for subsequent generations. In reality, the Spirit of Truth (Paraclete) foretold in earlier scriptures arrived with Muhammad (peace be upon him), but the Christians denied it.

In his commentary on verse 72 of Surah al-Ma'idah, Elmalılı examines the major denominations of Christianity and their understanding of the Trinity. He notes that there are three major sects—namely the Melkites (Catholic and Orthodox), Nestorianism, and Jacobitism (Monophysite)—and that among them, the Melkites are the most widespread. He summarizes the emergence of these sects from the earliest councils onward, along with the condemnation of movements such as Arianism, Macedonianism, and Nestorianism.

Nestorianism contends that there are two persons (divine and human) in Jesus, and that what was born of Mary was solely human. By contrast, Jacobitism (Monophysites) claims that there is only a single nature (divine) in Jesus and that the divine swallowed up the human. The historical spread of these sects and their conflicts with one another are recounted, with particular emphasis on the Jacobite presence in Egypt, Abyssinia, and Syria.

Protestantism, on the other hand, emerged later, opposing the Pope and accepting the Holy Bible as the sole authority. Yet Protestants do not differ from Catholics regarding the Trinity and the divinity of the Messiah. The differences between them center on points such as prioritizing faith over works, permitting clerical marriage, and vigorously adopting the doctrine of predestination. Elmalılı considers it a contradiction that Protestants claim to value reason while blindly accepting irrational dogmas such as the Trinity.

In conclusion, all Christian sects (except for the Arians) accept the doctrine of the Trinity and the divinity of the Messiah. However, they disagree on whether a human nature exists in the Messiah alongside the divine nature. While the Monophysites say, "The Messiah is Allah," the others converge on saying, "Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary." Thus, the verse rejects this latter statement, declaring that those who say, "Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary," are disbelievers.

In the continuation of the verse, it is emphasized that if Allah willed to destroy the Messiah, his mother, and all those on earth, no one could prevent it. Proceeding from this, the transience and helplessness of the Messiah and other beings are demonstrated. The Divine, however, is exalted above all transience and possesses absolute power. For this reason, neither the Messiah nor any other being can be identified with Allah or become a partner to Him. With this explanation, Elmalılı refutes both the Christian claim of the Trinity and pantheistic concepts such as wahdat al-wujud (unity of existence).

Allah creates as He wills; His creation is not in the manner of breaking off a part from Himself or emanation (sudur). No being separates from Him, is born of Him, or originates from Him. The creation of Jesus without a mother is also an example of this power and does not indicate his divinity. If Allah wills, He creates from an origin, and if He wills, without an origin. Just as He created Adam from dust, Eve from Adam, and Jesus from Mary, every creation occurs by His own will.

Miracles such as Jesus creating a bird with his hands and raising the dead do not demonstrate his divinity, but rather Allah's power. Had Allah not willed it, Jesus could not have done these things.
