Allah is capable of all things; created beings do not diminish His power in the least, but are rather His handiwork. All beings are subject to Allah; their power is relative, while true power belongs to Allah. Therefore, those who say, "Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary," are disbelievers.

The Jews and the Christians considered themselves privileged, saying, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved ones." According to Ibn Abbas, the original reason for this statement was the response given by the Jews to the call of the Prophet (peace be upon him). The Christians, on the other hand, meant their affiliation with the Messiah. Even if this expression was initially used as a metaphor, it was later adopted as a literal truth, and at the Council of Nicaea, the view of begottenness was reinforced with the phrase "from the essence of the Father." Through this claim, they deemed themselves exempt from accountability and aimed to establish dominion over others.

In response to them, Allah stated: "You are merely human beings like other people; you are His servants. Allah punishes you for your sins; He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. Whatever you may be, you cannot escape being created beings." Allah's dominion encompasses everything in the heavens and the earth; no creature holds a special standing before Him. Everyone will arrive in His presence and be held to account.

O People of the Book! Our Messenger Muhammad (peace be upon him) has come to you during a period of cessation (fatrah) when the succession of messengers had ceased. He explains the truth to you so that in the Hereafter you may not say, "No bearer of good tidings or warner came to us." Allah has power over all things. Believe in this Prophet and obey him; attain the forgiveness of your sins. Today, you cannot deny the coming of this Prophet, whose arrival was foretold in the Torah and the Gospel.

Moses (Musa) said to his people: "Remember Allah's favor upon you when He raised prophets from among you, made you kings (or free people), and gave you what He had not given to anyone else in the worlds." Foremost among these blessings was their liberation from bondage in Egypt and their attainment of freedom. According to some exegetes, the expression "kings" means "free people." This freedom signifies the possession of personal and political rights.

Moses continued: "O my people! Enter the holy land which Allah has destined for you, and do not turn back, or you will turn about as losers." But the Children of Israel said: "There is a tyrannical people there; we will never enter it until they depart from it." Two men who feared Allah said: "Enter upon them through the gate, and you will prevail; and put your trust in Allah." But the people disobeyed, saying: "Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting right here." Thereupon Moses prayed: "My Lord! I have power over none except myself and my brother; so separate us from this defiantly disobedient (fasiq) people." And Allah decreed: "Then indeed, that holy land is forbidden to them for forty years; they shall wander bewildered through the earth."

The "Holy Land" (al-Ard al-Muqaddasah) refers to Jerusalem and the blessed territories surrounding it. Although there are various narrations concerning the boundaries of this place, al-Tabari states that the most accurate approach is simply to suffice with saying the "holy land." However, this region does not fall outside the area between the Euphrates and al-Arish.

When the people of Moses were commanded to enter the holy land promised to them, they rejected this command, saying that there was a tyrannical and mighty people there. They said, "We will never enter it until they leave it," making this condition an impossibility. This was an act of defiance against Allah and the prophet, and was akin to an excuse of the kind "until a camel goes through the eye of a needle."

In connection with this event, the exegetes recount what happened to the twelve spies sent by the Children of Israel. Having seen that the tyrants were enormous and formidable, these spies became terrified, and upon their return, they spread the news and discouraged the people from fighting. Only Joshua, the brave companion of Moses, and Caleb, his son-in-law, trusted in Allah and stated that the task would be easy.

The story of "Og, son of Anak" (Uj ibn Unuq) is narrated as a fable describing the might of the tyrannical people. In this fable, it is told that Og was a giant three thousand three hundred and thirty-three cubits tall and three thousand years old. However, such accounts are in reality allegories symbolizing the collapse of a state. The Quran summarizes these legends with the expression "a tyrannical people" and teaches how to distinguish truth from fantasy.

In the face of the people's stubbornness, Moses prayed: "O my Lord! I have power over none except myself and my brother; so separate us from this defiantly disobedient people." Because of this rebellion, Allah forbade the holy land to them for forty years; throughout this period, they would wander bewildered and landless in the Desert of Tih. This was a punishment for those who abused their freedom.

Narrations differ as to whether Moses and Aaron remained in Tih throughout the forty years. Some say that they did not suffer torment in Tih, but rather educated the Children of Israel and raised a new generation. According to the widespread narration, Moses and Aaron passed away in Tih, and subsequently Joshua became a prophet and conquered the holy land along with the new generation.

Following this narrative, the story of the two sons of Adam (Cain and Abel), which corresponds to the state of the Children of Israel, is recounted. Each of them offered a sacrifice; one was accepted, while the other was not. The one whose sacrifice was not accepted swore to kill his brother. The other said, "Allah only accepts from those who fear Him," adding that he would not kill him, but rather preferred that his brother bear his sin along with his own and end up in Hell.

Yielding to his own desires (nafs), Cain killed his brother and became one of the losers. While he did not know what to do with the corpse, Allah sent a raven scratching the ground to show him how to bury it. Cain was filled with regret. This story emphasizes the evil of envy and murder.

It was because of this incident that the following decree was ordained for the Children of Israel: whoever kills a soul—unless for a soul or for corruption done in the land—it is as if he had killed all of mankind; and whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved all of mankind. This illustrates the sanctity of human life and the gravity of the sin of unlawful killing.

In this section, the link between the preceding narrative and the decrees given to the Children of Israel is addressed. Some scholars (such as al-Hasan and al-Dahhak) thought that the recounted murder took place among the Children of Israel and that the rulings were therefore specific to them. However, the majority holds that the story took place between the two sons of Adam, and that these decrees were revealed because of the universal message conveyed by the narrative. This message is that murder is an enormous crime and that emotions such as envy and selfishness drag man into catastrophe. It was precisely because this disposition was prominent among the Children of Israel that more severe rulings (retaliation [qisas] and capital punishment) were made obligatory for them.

The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption throughout the land is determined, according to the gravity of the crime, as execution, crucifixion, the cutting off of hands and feet on opposite sides, or exile. Various narrations are reported regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse, foremost among them the story of the people of Uraynah. The majority of jurists state that this ruling applies to highway robbers and encompasses both the disbeliever and the transgressing (fasiq) Muslim. The expression "waging war against Allah" is metaphorical; it signifies disobeying the commands of Allah or attacking the believers.

It is disputed whether the particle "or" among the penalties indicates an option or a distribution based on the offense. The majority (jumhur) maintains that the punishments are graded according to the severity of the crime and that the judge does not have the discretion to choose. However, the possibility of a choice aimed at mitigating the punishment cannot be entirely dismissed. Indeed, Imam al-Shafi'i interpreted the penalty of exile in two ways: continuous pursuit for those who have not been caught, and imprisonment for those who merely made threats. Imam al-A'zam (Abu Hanifah), on the other hand, understood exile as imprisonment and stated that banishing someone to another land is objectionable.

In the continuation of the verse, it is stated that those who repent before they are captured are exempt from the punishment. However, personal rights (retaliation, compensation for property) are not dropped; victims or their heirs may pursue their claims. This repentance drops the right of Allah, but does not drop the rights of fellow humans. Then, in the 35th verse, the believers are commanded to have God-consciousness (taqwa), seek a means of approach (wasilah) to Allah, and engage in jihad. A means of approach refers to every kind of righteous deed and intention that draws one closer to Allah; this is attained through supererogatory acts of worship, good character, and striving for Allah's pleasure. Seeking a means of approach is an element that complements faith and piety.

In verses 36–37, it is explained that even if the disbelievers wished to offer everything on earth as a ransom to be saved from the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them, and they will remain in eternal torment. This serves as a warning for the believers. In verses 38–39, the ruling of amputating the hand is established as the punishment for theft. Theft is defined as taking someone else's property in secret, and for the penalty to be applied, the property must reach a specific value and be taken from a secure place of custody. Glad tidings are given that those who repent and mend their ways will be forgiven.

Elmalılı details the necessary conditions for the execution of the penalty for theft. He states that for the act of theft to incur the prescribed legal punishment (hadd), the property must reach a specific threshold (nisab) and be kept in a secured place (hirz). He relates the views of different schools of jurisprudence: while the Zahiris and Kharijites impose the punishment for any theft, whether small or great, the Hanafis stipulate the conditions of nisab and hirz. In addition, he draws attention to the principle that prescribed penalties are averted by doubts; circumstances such as doubt regarding permissibility (shubhat al-ibahah), doubt regarding entitlement (shubhat al-haqq), and doubt arising from dire necessity (shubhat al-idtirar) waive the hadd. Umar's suspension of the penalty for theft during the year of famine is cited as an example of this application of doubt.

He explains that there are differing juridical opinions regarding the amount of nisab, such as a quarter of a dinar, three dirhams, or ten dirhams. While Imam al-A'zam (Abu Hanifah) stipulates ten dirhams, al-Shafi'i considers a quarter of a dinar sufficient. Elmalılı argues that the threshold of nisab may change over time, maintaining that this amount can be updated in light of price differences between gold and silver and to eliminate any doubt arising from necessity. He emphasizes that the penalty is not merely retribution, but also a deterrent punishment (nakal) from Allah; amputating the thief's hand purifies both the individual and society from corruption.

In the commentary on verse 39, it is stated that Allah is forgiving if the thief repents. It is debated whether the punishment is dropped if repentance occurs before the sentence is executed. The majority (the Hanafis) hold that it is not dropped unless the owner of the stolen property forgives, whereas al-Shafi'i maintains that it is dropped. Drawing from the phrase 'and amends his conduct,' Elmalılı explains that showing good conduct after repentance and reimbursing the stolen property are necessary; however, if the penalty of amputation has already been carried out, financial restitution is not required.

In verse 40, it is recalled that the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and that He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills. In verse 41, addressing the Prophet, it is stated that those who race into disbelief (the hypocrites and the Jews) should not grieve him. Their characteristics are listed: they listen eagerly to falsehood, distort words from their proper contexts, and listen on behalf of another group who have not come to you. If Allah intends to put someone to trial (fitnah), no one can avail them against Allah in the least. For them is disgrace in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a tremendous punishment.

As the occasion of revelation, it is recounted that the Jews distorted the punishment of stoning (rajm) and appealed to the Prophet. Although stoning was commanded in the Torah for adulterers, Jewish scholars altered this punishment, mitigating it to forty lashes and blackening the face. The Prophet uncovered the truth by administering an oath to Abdullah ibn Suriya and executed the sentence of stoning. Furthermore, the disparity in blood money (diyah) between the Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayzah is also among the reasons for the revelation of these verses.

In the commentary on verses 41–43, the habit of the Jews and hypocrites of listening to falsehood and consuming illicit gain (suht) is addressed. Suht encompasses all kinds of unlawful earnings, such as bribery, the wages of prostitution, and the price of wine. It is conveyed that the Prophet is free to judge between them or abstain, but if he judges, he must judge with justice. There are differing opinions as to whether this discretion was abrogated: while some say it is obligatory for a Muslim judge to adjudicate between non-Muslims who apply to him, others maintain that he remains free to choose. Ultimately, it is emphasized that those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed are the disbelievers, the wrongdoers, or the defiantly disobedient (fasiqun).

Allah Almighty criticizes the Jews for seeking your arbitration while they possess the Torah, and then turning away from the judgment delivered. This conduct of theirs shows that they do not truly believe in the Torah or in Allah's judgment. For had they truly believed, they would have been content with the ruling found in their own scripture. In truth, they merely follow their desires. Therefore, you should not grieve over their disbelief.

The Torah was revealed as guidance and light. The prophets and their successors—the rabbaniyyun (godly scholars devoted to knowledge and worship) and the ahbar (Jewish scholars)—judged by this scripture. A rabbani is one who nurtures people with knowledge, educating them first with fundamental matters. The ahbar are prominent scholars who write down and record knowledge. They are charged with preserving the Book of Allah. This preservation takes place both by feeling it in their hearts and teaching it with their tongues, and by abiding by its rulings and putting them into practice. Allah commands, 'Do not fear the people, but fear Me, and do not sell My verses for a small price.' Whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed—it is they who are the disbelievers.

The rulings of legal retribution (qisas) are prescribed in the Torah: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and for wounds is legal retribution. Qisas is founded on the principle of exact equivalence and equality, such as a life for a life or an eye for an eye. However, in cases of wounds where equivalence is not possible, qisas is not applied; instead, arsh (stipulated compensation) or hukumah al-'adl (equitable indemnification assessed by experts) is paid. Retribution is primarily a human right (haqq al-'abd); the wronged party may forgive. Forgiving serves as an expiation for that person.

'There is life for you in legal retribution, O people of understanding!' (Al-Baqarah 2:179). Retribution was ordained not to kill, but to protect life. Executing a murderer means saving an innocent life. Under this powerful manifestation of justice, forgiving is an even greater virtue. 'Whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved all of mankind.' (Al-Ma'idah 5:32). Thus, this ruling is a guidance and a light, comprising justice on one side and benevolence on the other.

Let the people of the Gospel also judge by what Allah has revealed. Jesus was sent as a prophet confirming the Torah, and the Gospel was given to him. In the Gospel too, there is guidance and light. Whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed—it is they who are the defiantly disobedient (fasiqun). Disbelief (kufr) arises from rejecting the divine ruling; wrongdoing (zulm) from placing a matter where it does not belong; and defiance (fisq) from departing from the truth. These three descriptions vary according to the degree and nature of turning away from the ruling.

And unto you (O Muhammad!) We revealed the Book in truth, confirming the scriptures that came before it and as a guardian (muhaymin) over them. Muhaymin signifies one who watches over, protects, bears witness, and is trustworthy. The Quran preserves the true rulings in the Torah and the Gospel and rectifies those that were corrupted. From now on, no ruling that does not receive its confirmation can be acted upon. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires. Unto each community We have appointed a law (shir'ah, a specific path) and an open way (minhaj, a clear method). Shir'ah consists of secondary rulings that vary according to times and circumstances, whereas minhaj consists of immutable, primary principles. The universal foundations shared by all prophets constitute the minhaj, while the rulings specific to each of them constitute the shir'ah.

Had Allah willed, He would have made you a single community. However, He willed to test you through the different legal paths He gave you. So race toward good deeds. Unto Allah is the return of you all, and He will inform you concerning that wherein you used to differ.

In verse 49, our Prophet (peace be upon him) is commanded to judge by the true Book revealed by Allah and not to follow their desires. According to a narration, the Jews came seeking a ruling in their own favor in order to lure our Prophet into discord, but this verse was revealed. Here, attention is drawn to the fact that those who do not accept Allah's judgment commit a grave, hidden sin. Furthermore, it is emphasized that this sin will certainly be punished in this world, and that judges must judge with truth and justice.

In verse 50, those who abandon the judgment of Allah and seek the judgment of Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance) are condemned. The judgment of Jahiliyyah entails evils such as injustice, sycophancy, malice, and inequality. Yet, there is no judgment better than the judgment of Allah. It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning a murder incident between the Banu Nadir and the Banu Qurayzah, where our Prophet judged with equality, but the Banu Nadir were dissatisfied with this and demanded the custom of Jahiliyyah.

In verses 51-53, the believers are commanded not to take Jews and Christians as allies. They are allies of one another; whoever takes them as allies is one of them. The hypocrites, in whose hearts is a disease, rush among them out of fear of a misfortune. According to a narration, 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy declared that he would not sever his alliance with the Jews, whereupon these verses were revealed. In the end, it is announced that the deeds of these hypocrites will come to naught.

In verses 54-56, it is stated that whoever apostatizes from their religion, Allah will replace them with a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, and dignified and firm against the disbelievers. This community strives in the cause of Allah and does not fear the blame of any blamer. This is the grace of Allah. In the commentary of the verse, various views are transmitted regarding who this community might be: such as Abu Bakr and his companions, the people of Yemen, or the Persians. Furthermore, it is emphasized that the true ally is only Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.

In verses 57-63, it is commanded not to take as allies those among the People of the Book and the disbelievers who treat religion as a matter of ridicule and amusement. When they are called to prayer, they mock it. Our Prophet is directed to ask the People of the Book whether their resentment toward them is solely because they believe in Allah and what has been revealed. Then, those who incurred Allah's curse and wrath, and were turned into apes and pigs, and those who worshiped false deities (taghut) are described. The hypocrites' claims of faith are refuted, and it is stated that most of the People of the Book race with one another in sin, hostility, and consuming illicit gain. Their rabbis and scholars ought to have forbidden them.

In verses 64-66, the statement of the Jews that 'Allah's hand is tied' is condemned. On the contrary, Allah's hands are outstretched. Enmity and hatred have been cast among them until the Day of Resurrection. Had the People of the Book believed and been mindful of Allah, their sins would have been pardoned and they would have been admitted into the gardens of bliss. Had they observed the Torah and the Gospel, they would have eaten of blessings from above them and from beneath their feet. Among them is a moderate group, but most of them do evil.

In verses 67-69, our Prophet is commanded to convey what has been revealed to him; otherwise, he will not have fulfilled his prophetic mission. Allah will protect him from the people. 'O People of the Book! You have no standing until you observe the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to you.' Then, whoever among the believers, the Jews, the Sabians, and the Christians believes in Allah and the Last Day and performs righteous deeds, there will be no fear upon them, nor will they grieve.

In verses 70-75, it is recalled that a covenant was taken from the Children of Israel and messengers were sent to them, but they denied some and killed others. They thought there would be no trial, so they grew blind and deaf. Those who said, 'Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,' and 'Allah is the third of three,' have certainly disbelieved. Yet the Messiah had commanded them to worship Allah. Let them repent and seek His forgiveness. Jesus, son of Mary, is only a messenger; his mother was a woman of truth; they both used to eat food. Despite the verses being made clear to them, they still turn away.

Here, it is explained that if a nation fails to appreciate the blessing of Islam, Allah will replace it with another nation. Historically, the Arabs, then the Persians, and then the Turks undertook this service. If the Turks are also ungrateful, another community will take their place. Allah will send many more communities until the Day of Resurrection.

In verse 55, it is stated that the protector and ally (wali) of the believers is only Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. Those believers who establish prayer and give zakah. There are various narrations concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse: according to one narration, Ali gave his ring to a beggar while in bowing (ruku'), whereupon this verse was revealed. However, this does not mean that the verse is exclusive to Ali; it encompasses all believers in general.

In verses 56-58, it is emphasized that the party of Allah (Hizbullah) will be triumphant, and that those who ridicule religion must not be taken as allies. In particular, the disbelievers who mock the call to prayer (the adhan) must not be taken as allies. Concerning the occasion of revelation of these verses, it is related that a Christian who mocked the adhan perished in a fire.

In verses 59-60, a reply is given to the People of the Book: 'Do you resent us only because we believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us?' Then, mention is made of those whom Allah cursed, who incurred His wrath, who were transformed into apes and pigs, and who worshiped false deities (taghut). This announces the state of those who are in an even worse condition than the People of the Book. 'Maskh' (metamorphosis) may be spiritual, or it may encompass both physical form and moral character.

In verses 61-63, the condition of the hypocrites is described: they say 'We believe,' but they enter as disbelievers and leave as such. Most of them race with one another in sin, transgression, and consuming illicit gain. While the rabbis (rabbaniyyun) and scholars should have forbidden them, they do not forbid them, and this is indeed a vile practice. The most severe rebuke is found in this verse.

In verse 64, the statement of the Jews, 'Allah's hand is tied,' is cited. This implies that Allah is stingy or powerless. Yet both of Allah's hands are outstretched; He bestows as He wills. This utterance is the Jews attributing their own stinginess to Allah. The phrase in the verse, 'May their hands be tied and may they be cursed for what they said,' is either an invocation against them or an announcement of its consequence.

This statement of the Jews is based on a flawed conception regarding Allah's power and will. Yet Allah is absolute in power and supreme in generosity. The word 'hand' is used figuratively in language; it does not denote a physical hand. While the early scholars (Salaf) accepted such allegorical verses (mutashabihat) without interpretation, later theologians (mutakallimun) provided rational interpretations (ta'wil). In our own language, the idiom 'open-handed' is used to express generosity.

The word 'yad' (hand) attributed to Allah the Exalted carries several meanings in Arabic: power and might, possession, assistance, and special designation. As in the saying 'One hand is above another,' the meaning of power is widely used. When it is said, 'This land is in so-and-so's hand (yad),' ownership is intended. The expression 'I made this with my own hand' conveys that special care and attention were devoted to it. According to most scholars, the word 'yad' used in reference to Allah signifies power or favor. Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, however, regards it as an attribute subsisting in the Divine Essence, distinct from power. Nevertheless, it must be remembered that 'yad' here is a metaphorical reply to the Jews' claim that 'Allah's hand is tied.' The dual expression 'two hands' serves emphasis and intensification; if we wish, it may also be interpreted as one being an open hand (mercy) and the other a closed hand (wrath).

The Jews attributed tight-fistedness to Allah by saying, "Allah's hand is tied." The Quran refutes this statement of theirs and proclaims that both of Allah's hands are outstretched, bestowing as He wills. Because of their stubbornness, this disbelief of theirs will only increase their transgression. Allah has cast enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection. Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it. He does not love those who spread corruption and He punishes them. Yet, if they believe and guard against evil, He will expiate their sins and admit them into the Gardens of Delight.

If the People of the Book had properly observed the Torah, the Gospel, and what was sent down to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet—that is, they would have attained abundance from every direction. There are seven different interpretations of this expression: general abundance, rain from the sky and produce from the earth, fruits of the trees and cultivated crops, unearned grants and blessings earned through labor, public benefits provided by the state and private enterprise, the happiness of Muslims at the moment of victory, and the depiction of the blessings of the Hereafter. However, they did not do this. Among them is a moderate (muqtasid) community, but they are few. The majority of them commit corruption.

There are two views regarding the moderate community (ummah muqtasidah): The first is that they are those who believed from among the People of the Book, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and the Negus (Najashi). The second is that they are those who, although they did not believe, are not obstinate, but rather moderate and impartial. The preferred view is the second one. Our Prophet was commanded to convey all that was revealed to him, and it was made known that Allah would protect him from the people. According to narration, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) stated upon this command that his fear had completely vanished. It was requested that the People of the Book be told: "You stand on nothing until you observe the Torah, the Gospel, and all that was revealed to you."

In the noble ayah, the believers, the Jews, the Sabians, and the Christians are mentioned, and it is stated: "Whoever truly believes in Allah and the Last Day and works righteousness, no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve." This indicates that all these groups will attain salvation on the condition of faith. However, this cannot occur through merely outward faith; true faith and righteous deeds are required together. The ayah also serves as a warning to believers: being outwardly Muslim is not sufficient for salvation. Furthermore, in terms of worldly rulings, there is equality between Muslims and non-Muslims, but salvation in the Hereafter depends upon true faith.

Some orientalists have claimed that there is abrogation (naskh) between ayah 62 of Surah al-Baqarah and ayah 69 of Surah al-Ma'idah. This is not correct. Between the two ayahs there is only a difference in grammatical inflection (i'rab); the meaning and ruling are identical. Both ayahs invite the People of the Book and other groups to faith and promise salvation to those who believe. The interpretations of French orientalists on this matter are politically motivated and aimed at misrepresenting Islam's concept of tolerance. Muslim jurists (mujtahids) did not say that these ayahs were abrogated; on the contrary, they stated that they corroborate each other.

In this section, Elmalılı primarily emphasizes that no Islamic scholar, whether classical or contemporary, has stated or thought that the two ayahs in Surah al-Ma'idah (ayah 69 and the accompanying verses) are abrogated. He notes that the fundamentals of faith and creed—for example, the principle that those who believe in Allah and the Last Day and perform righteous deeds will experience neither fear nor grief—are an eternal truth, and that no religion can be a true religion without accepting this principle. Abrogation is possible only in subsidiary rulings (furu'), that is, in practical matters that change according to time and place; abrogation is not permissible in such fundamental tenets of belief.

Elmalılı characterizes the claim by some Western (particularly French) writers—that Muslim jurists abrogated the first of the ayahs in question with the second—as an outright slander. He states that this claim is the product of both ignorance and malicious intent. For abrogation requires the presence of two contradictory rulings; however, in these ayahs the ruling is identical, with a difference only in the naming of the enumerated groups. Furthermore, he adds that Muslim scholars are in consensus on this matter, whereas those who cast slander upon them are mired in political bigotry.

The author explains that the religion of Islam contains both constant (usul) and variable (furu') rulings. He states that the verbal and practical Sunnah of the Prophet (peace be upon him) also encompasses rulings that vary according to circumstances, but that these variable rulings are not contrary to fundamental principles. He stresses that the two ayahs in Surah al-Ma'idah belong to the constant principles and cannot be interpreted according to environmental conditions. Furthermore, he indicates that these ayahs must be evaluated together with the preceding and succeeding verses; otherwise, it will lead to misunderstandings.

Elmalılı provides the etymology of the word 'Sabi'in' (Sabians). He explains that it derives from the root 's-b-e' in Arabic, meaning one who departs from one religion into another. He touches upon the variations in recitation (qira'ah), noting that Nafi' and Abu Ja'far recited it without a hamzah. He explains that the literal meaning of the word is 'one who departs from a well-known religion to another,' which is why 'Sabi'in' refers to those outside the religions of Islam, Judaism, and Christianity. In addition, he adds that the word is the name of a specific religion or sect, whose adherents are called 'Sabi'i' or 'Sabi'.

He conveys various opinions regarding who the Sabians were: According to some, they were a group who claimed adherence to the religion of the prophets Noah or Enoch (Idris), but over time drifted toward star worship and idolatry. He notes that Sabianism was influenced by ancient Syriac and Chaldean traditions, and that during the Abbasid era, several scholars emerged from this group. He describes their acts of worship as including seven daily prayers, thirty days of fasting, pilgrimage, and festivals, noting that in terms of intention and reverence (khushu'), their prayer resembled the Muslim prayer.

Lastly, Elmalılı sets forth the fundamental distinction between Hanifism (the monotheistic faith of Tawhid) and Sabianism. He stresses that the Hanifs did not accept the mediation of either spiritual or corporeal beings to draw near to Allah, worshipping Allah directly. The Sabians, on the other hand, in an effort to take spiritual entities as intermediaries, eventually deviated into the worship of stars and idols, thereby falling into polytheism (shirk). Through this comparison, he demonstrates Islam's pure creed of Tawhid and its superiority over other faiths.

In describing the belief system of the Sabians, Elmalılı first conveys their views concerning spiritual beings (ruhaniyyun). According to them, the Creator of the universe is Allah, but He cannot be reached directly; rather, there are spiritual beings who serve as intermediaries. These spiritual beings, like angels, are incorporeal entities that obey Allah's command, and humans hope to attain closeness to Allah by drawing near to them.

The influence of these spiritual beings has three aspects: in terms of essence (jawhar), action (fi'l), and state (hal). In their essence, they are free from matter; in their action, they act as intermediaries in creation and governance; and in their state, they are in perpetual remembrance (dhikr) of Allah and worship. It is believed that these spiritual beings hold influence over the stars, celestial bodies, and natural phenomena.

The Sabians were divided into various groups around this belief: Ashab al-Hayakil (worshipers of statues), Ashab al-Ashkhas (worshipers of concrete idols), the Hizbaniyyah (a pantheistic group maintaining that Allah manifests in human individuals), and the Hiribbaniyyah (a more moderate group remaining devoted to the prophets). Each group adopted different practices as a method of reaching spiritual beings.

The Hanifs, on the other hand, opposed these beliefs. Prophets such as Abraham (peace be upon him) counseled worshiping Allah alone and associating no partners with Him. Elmalılı summarizes the view of the Hanifs as follows: Spiritual beings and the stars are proofs of Allah's power; one must not worship them, but turn toward their Creator. Man's elevation is possible only through monotheism (tawhid).

Whether the Sabians are People of the Book is disputed. Imam al-A'zam considered certain Sabians (those who followed Yahya ibn Zakariyya) to be People of the Book, stating that what they slaughter may be eaten and their women may be married. However, the Imameyn (Abu Yusuf and Muhammad) and other scholars stated that the Sabians who worship stars are polytheists (mushrikun) and cannot be considered People of the Book. Elmalılı emphasizes that mentioning the Sabians separately from the Jews and Christians in the Quran indicates that they are not People of the Book.

In his commentary on verse 69 of Surah al-Ma'idah, Elmalılı draws attention to the expression 'Sabi'in' mentioned in the verse. According to him, the Johannites (Christians of Saint John), one of the Christian sects, are also included in the 'Sabi'in' group, and therefore the 'Sabi'in' in the verse refers to a branch of the Christians. At this point, he criticizes some translators for treating the 'Sabi'in' as a separate group and states that this leads to misunderstandings. Emphasizing that Islam is the highest degree of Hanifism, Elmalılı states that everyone must accept this religion.

The essence of the 69th verse is this: Whosoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and performs righteous deeds—whether Muslim, Jew, Christian, or Sabian—there shall be no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve. This ruling is universal and always valid. Faith is to accept everything coming from Allah, while faith in the hereafter is to affirm the Day of Reckoning. Righteous deeds consist of obeying Allah's commands and prohibitions, doing good, and abstaining from evil. Whoever possesses these conditions attains salvation.

In verses 70–71, the covenant taken from the Children of Israel is recalled. Allah sent them prophets, but whenever they encountered commands that were difficult for their desires, they denied some of the prophets and killed others. They thought that no affliction would befall them, so they became blind and deaf. Then they repented, and Allah accepted their repentance. Yet again, most of them became blind and deaf. This shows that they did not fulfill the condition of faith and righteous deeds.

In verses 72–73, the beliefs of the Christians are criticized. Those who say, 'Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary,' have disbelieved. Yet the Messiah called the Children of Israel to worship Allah alone and forbade polytheism (shirk). Those who say, 'Allah is the third of three,' have also certainly disbelieved. Elmalılı explains that in terms of Arabic grammar, this expression means 'the third of three,' not 'one of three.' The Christian belief in the Trinity consists of accepting three deities and considering Allah the third among them, which is blatant polytheism.

In verse 74, it is reported that there is a painful punishment for those who do not renounce these words and repent. As for Allah, He is Most Forgiving and Most Merciful (Ghafur and Rahim); He forgives those who repent. In verse 75, it is emphasized that the Messiah was merely a prophet, before whom many prophets had passed away. His mother Mary was a woman of truth (siddiqah). They both ate food—that is, they had human needs. This is clear proof that they could not be deities. Moreover, the fact that the Messiah had peers and counterparts shows that he was not a deity, but a prophet.

In verse 76, the meaninglessness of worshiping things besides Allah that can neither benefit nor harm them is expressed. Allah hears and knows all things. Helpless beings, however, can never be deities. This verse warns both Christians and idolaters.

Allah warns the People of the Book against unjustly exceeding the limits in their religion. Excess in religion is of two kinds: Justified excess is investigating the truths of the religion and meticulously implementing its rulings, which is praised. Unjust excess, on the other hand, is exceeding the limits of truth by deviating into falsehood. The Christians fell into excess by deifying the Messiah, while the Jews did so by denying his prophethood. At the foundation of this extremism lies the blind imitation of predecessors and following the desires of the soul. The distinguishing feature between faith and disbelief is the difference between servitude to Allah, Who is the Truth, and servitude to the desire of the soul.

Those who disbelieved from among the Children of Israel were cursed by the tongue of David and Jesus, the son of Mary. This curse was because of their rebellion and their transgressions against the truth. David's curse was directed at those who violated the Sabbath prohibition, while Jesus's curse was directed at those who were ungrateful after the miracle of the heavenly table. They did not prevent one another from the evil they committed; how vile was what they used to do. Many of the People of the Book take the disbelievers as allies. Allah has become angry with them and has prepared an eternal punishment for them. If they had believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed, they would not have taken the disbelievers as allies; but most of them have transgressed.

The most severe of people in animosity toward the believers are the Jews and the polytheists. The hostility of the Jews is greater because of their worldly ambition, hardness of heart, and stubbornness against the Truth. In contrast, those who say, 'We are Christians,' are closer in affection to the believers. The reason for this is that among them are priests and monks, and they are not arrogant. Priests occupy themselves with knowledge and worship, while monks renounce the world out of fear of the hereafter. These qualities make them more inclined to accept the truth.

When they hear the Quran revealed to the Prophet, the eyes of the Christians who realize that it is the truth overflow with tears, and they say, 'O our Lord, we have believed, so record us among the witnesses.' They hope that Allah will admit them into Paradise along with the righteous. Because of these sincere words, Allah rewards them with gardens beneath which rivers flow. Those who disbelieve and deny the verses are the companions of Hellfire. The Negus and his companions are among those who were the occasion for the revelation of these verses.

Addressing the believers, it is commanded that they not declare forbidden the good things that Allah has made lawful, and that they not exceed the limits. Allah does not love those who exceed the limits. They must eat from the lawful and pure provisions and fear Allah. They are not held accountable for unintentional oaths, but there is an expiation for breaking deliberate oaths: feeding ten poor persons, or clothing them, or freeing a slave; whoever is unable to afford this must fast for three days. They are asked to guard their oaths and be grateful for Allah's verses.

Do not consider unlawful the good and wholesome things that Allah has made lawful for you. Do not abandon what is lawful by going to extremes like past nations. According to narration, a group of Companions, deeply moved by the Prophet's warnings concerning the Day of Judgment, gathered at the house of Uthman ibn Maz'un and decided to fast continuously, abstain from meat and fat, stay away from women, and renounce the world. When the Prophet heard about this, he told them that their own selves had a right over them, that he himself prayed and slept, fasted and broke his fast, ate meat and fat, and approached women, saying: 'Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.' It was upon this incident that these verses were revealed. A believer loves what is pleasant and wholesome, yet lives in accordance with Allah's command.

The command not to consider what is lawful as unlawful gives rise to a dilemma regarding oaths: If a person swears an oath to make something lawful forbidden to himself, if he breaks his oath, he acts contrary to the command 'fulfill your contracts'; if he keeps his oath, he acts contrary to the command 'do not consider lawful things as unlawful.' To resolve this problem, Allah Almighty made known that oaths are divided into two categories: unintentional oaths (laghw, sworn vainly and not regarded as a contract) and binding oaths (mun'aqidah, made deliberately and regarded as a contract). We are not held accountable for unintentional oaths, but binding oaths are considered contracts, and if broken, expiation (kaffarah) is required. The expiation is to feed ten poor persons for a day, or to clothe them, or to free a slave; whoever lacks the means must fast for three days. There are differing views between Imam Abu Hanifah and Imam al-Shafi'i regarding the exact amount of expiation. If breaking the oath is more beneficial, it is permissible to break it by offering expiation.

In the noble verse, intoxicants, gambling, altars/idols (erected stones), and divining arrows are characterized as an abomination of Satan's handiwork, and avoiding them is commanded. Satan desires only to sow enmity and hatred among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. Therefore, obey Allah and obey the Prophet, and beware of evil. But if you turn away, know that the duty of the Prophet is only to deliver the message clearly. This verse is the third and final verse regarding the prohibition of intoxicants. In the preceding verses, it had been stated that intoxicants are a grave sin and that one must not approach prayer while intoxicated.

After the verse prohibiting intoxicants was revealed, the Companions asked about the condition of those who had passed away previously having consumed intoxicants. Thereupon, the following verse was revealed: There is no sin upon those who believe and perform righteous deeds for what they consumed in the past, so long as they fear Allah, remain steadfast in faith, continue doing righteous deeds, then again fear Allah and do good. In this verse, piety (taqwa) is mentioned in three degrees, ultimately reaching the station of spiritual excellence (ihsan). This signifies taqwa across the past, present, and future; the relationship of a person with their own self, with fellow people, and with Allah; and the initial, intermediate, and final stages.

Allah Almighty made known that He would test the believers by forbidding hunting while in the state of ihram. In the year of Hudaybiyyah, game animals approached so close to the believers that they could be caught by hand or spear. This was a test to distinguish those who fear Allah from those who do not. Whoever hunts despite this prohibition must pay an expiation by sending a sacrificial animal equivalent to the game they killed to the Kaaba, or by feeding the poor, or by fasting. Marine game, however, is lawful for one in ihram. Allah made the Kaaba, the sacred months, the sacrificial offering, and the garlanded animals a means of order for humankind. These are so that you may know that Allah knows all things. The duty of the Prophet is only to deliver the message; Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal. Say: The bad and the good are not equal, even though the abundance of the bad may impress you. Fear Allah, O people of understanding, so that you may attain salvation.

O you who believe! Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram. Whoever hunts and kills deliberately—that is, knowing that they are in ihram and that hunting is forbidden—must slaughter an equivalent sacrificial animal (camel, cattle, or sheep/goat) as a penalty for the game killed. This equivalence is determined by the appraisal of two just persons. The sacrificial animal is sent to the Kaaba. If one chooses, it is also permissible to feed the poor or to fast in lieu of this penalty. This penalty offers options so that the offender may taste the consequence of their deed. Those who hunt forgetfully or by mistake are also subject to this penalty; this is the opinion of many scholars. According to the Hanafi and Maliki schools, the hunted animal is treated as carrion and cannot be eaten; al-Shafi'i, however, states that if it was slaughtered, it may be eaten.

The game of the sea and its food have been made lawful for you, both while in ihram and during normal times. Both travelers and non-travelers may benefit from it. Land game, however, is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram. There is no harm in eating what has been hunted by someone not in ihram, provided you did not signal or command it to be hunted. Seafood, fish, and the like are always lawful. Relying on the hadith 'Its water is pure and its dead are lawful,' al-Shafi'i asserts that all marine animals are lawful, whereas the majority restrict this to fish. Even fish that die naturally in the sea are not eaten. This verse was revealed concerning the Banu Mudlij, who inquired about fish stranded on the shore. The word 'sea' (bahr) also encompasses large bodies of water such as rivers and lakes. In short, land hunting is forbidden in ihram and within the Sacred Precinct (Haram), while sea hunting is lawful under all circumstances. Fear Allah, and remember that unto Him you will be gathered.

Allah made the Kaaba, the sacred month, the sacrificial offerings, and the garlands means of sustaining the religious and worldly affairs of humankind. These demonstrate that Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise. Even if we cannot fully comprehend the underlying wisdom of these acts of worship, we must perform them as commanded. Allah's punishment is severe, yet He is also Forgiving and Merciful. Therefore, we should both fear Him and hope for His mercy.

The duty of the Prophet is only to convey the message; and he has fulfilled it. You no longer have any right to make excuses or demand other things from him. Say: The foul and the pure, the evil and the good are not equal, even though the abundance of the evil might impress you. People of understanding should prefer what is pure and good, not what is merely plentiful. Lawful earning, even if little, is far better than that which is plentiful yet forbidden. Those who associate partners with Allah consider legitimate their invented practices such as bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah, and ham; whereas Allah never commanded these. They merely imitate their forefathers. When it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Prophet,' they say, 'We follow the way of our forefathers.' Yet their forefathers possessed no knowledge and were not guided.

O you who believe! Take care of yourselves. If you are rightly guided, those who go astray cannot harm you. This does not mean that everyone should only look out for their own concerns; on the contrary, enjoining good and forbidding evil is a requirement of this verse. First, a person must rectify oneself, and then influence society. Narrated from Abu Bakr: If people see an evil and do not change it, Allah will afflict them all with punishment. In the end, to Allah you will all return, and you will receive the recompense for what you used to do.

Witnessing at the time of making a bequest (wasiyyah) is important. Two just persons from among you, or if death approaches while traveling, two non-Muslims may act as witnesses. If you suspect them, you detain them after the prayer and make them swear by Allah: "We will not sell our oath for any price, nor will we conceal the testimony of Allah; otherwise, we would surely be sinners." If it becomes apparent that they were lying, two others from the deceased's next of kin step forward and swear an oath truer than the oath of the former ones. This regulation ensures that witnesses tell the truth. Fear Allah; He does not guide the defiantly disobedient.

In this section, it is explained that if a Muslim cannot find witnesses while making a bequest on a journey, he may take two people from among non-Muslims (the People of the Book or others) as witnesses. Scholars such as Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and Mujahid hold this view. However, this testimony is permissible only when traveling abroad and when no Muslim witness can be found. Abu Musa encountered such a case in Kufa and accepted their testimony after administering an oath to the witnesses.

It is disputed whether the ruling of this verse was abrogated (naskh) by the debt verse in Surah al-Baqarah (2/282). Some scholars state that because the debt verse stipulates that witnesses must be Muslim, this verse is abrogated (mansukh). Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, however, rejects this abrogation with six proofs: the expression 'others from outside your group' in the verse, the stipulation of travel, the administering of oaths, the reason for revelation (sabab al-nuzul), the consensus of the Companions, and the principle of necessity (darurah). According to him, the testimony of non-believers is permissible in cases of necessity, and this ruling remains valid.

If suspicion arises that the witnesses are lying, they are made to take an oath. According to most mujtahids, administering an oath to a witness is not legitimate, yet this verse shows that it is permissible in cases of suspicion. If the treachery of the witnesses becomes apparent, two individuals from the party whose rights were violated are brought forward in their place and take an oath. This ruling also applies to executors who carry out the will; once their breach of trust is established, they are dismissed from their duty.

In verse 108, it is stated that administering an oath in this manner is more likely to ensure that witnesses provide proper testimony or fear the consequences of lying. In verse 109, it is reported that on the Day Allah gathers the messengers, He will ask them how their communities responded, and the messengers will reply, 'We have no knowledge; surely You are the Knower of the unseen.' This recalls the great reckoning in the Hereafter and warns and instills fear in the believers.

In verses 110–111, the blessings bestowed upon Jesus are enumerated: being supported with Gabriel, speaking in the cradle and in maturity, being taught the Book and wisdom, fashioning a bird out of clay and breathing life into it, healing the blind and the leper, raising the dead, and being protected from the Children of Israel. It is also recounted that it was revealed to the disciples to believe, and they said, 'We have believed, and bear witness that we are Muslims.' This points to the miracles of Jesus and the sincerity of the disciples.

In verses 112–115, the disciples ask, 'Can your Lord send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?' Jesus warns them, 'Fear Allah, if you are believers.' The disciples explain their purpose: they wish to eat from it, to have their hearts reassured, and to witness to its truth. Jesus prays, 'O Allah, send down to us a table from heaven to be a recurring feast for us, for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You.' Allah announces that He will send it down, but whoever disbelieves afterward will be subjected to an unprecedented punishment. Commentators note that there are differing narrations as to whether this table actually descended or not.

In the final section of Surah al-Ma'idah, various narrations concerning the request of the people of Jesus for the table to be sent down are related. According to the first narration, upon the prayer of Jesus, a red table spread descended containing food such as fish, vegetables, and bread. Jesus pleaded with Allah that this bounty might be a mercy. When some of those who ate from the table later rebelled, they were transformed into apes and swine. Christians made the Sunday on which this event occurred a feast day.

In the second narration, the table descended every other day for forty days, and whenever the poor and the sick ate from it, they grew wealthy or were healed. However, when Allah commanded that the table be designated for the poor rather than the rich, the people fell into dispute, and eighty-three individuals were transformed into apes and swine. According to a third narration, when the people realized the danger of such a miracle and sought forgiveness (istighfar), the table did not descend.

Qadi al-Baydawi, after citing these narrations, states that some Sufis interpreted the table as the realities of knowledge. According to him, this story points to the danger of an individual making a request unsuited to their spiritual station. The table of Jesus is an instructive lesson when compared to the table of Islam granted to Muslims: the greater the blessing, the more severe the punishment for disbelief.

Following these reminders come the verses in which Allah questions Jesus: 'Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two deities besides Allah"?' Jesus declares that he said no such thing and that he commanded them only to worship Allah. He explains that he was a witness over them as long as he remained among them, but after Allah caused him to die (took him up), Allah alone was the Watcher over them.

The response of Jesus is an exemplary model of total submission and proper etiquette (adab). He glorifies Allah and affirms that he would never utter words unbefitting of him. Bowing before Allah's absolute will, he says, 'If You punish them, they are indeed Your servants; and if You forgive them, You indeed are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.' These verses refute the Christian doctrine of the Trinity and emphasize that Jesus is merely a servant.

After this questioning, Allah gives glad tidings of the Day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. On that Day, they will abide eternally in gardens beneath which rivers flow; Allah will be pleased with them, and they will be pleased with Him. That is the supreme triumph. To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and He is capable of all things.

The conclusion of the surah calls the believers to Allah's pleasure and to steadfast truthfulness. No blessing in this world is as precious as Allah's pleasure. Muslims must not break their covenants as the Jews and Christians did, but must uphold uprightness solely for the pleasure of Allah. Surah al-Ma'idah concludes with the words 'Praise be to Allah' and continues with Surah al-An'am.

Praise belongs to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, and made darkness and light. His sovereignty and dominion encompass not only the subsequent states of beings, but also creating and bringing them into existence. The expressions of praise that occur at the beginning of five surahs in the Quran are explanations of the general praise in al-Fatihah from various perspectives.

In this verse, the verb 'khalq' (creation) is used for the heavens and the earth, while 'ja'l' (making/appointing) is used for darkness and light. While 'khalq' carries the meaning of bringing something into existence out of nothing and ordaining it, 'ja'l' is more general and involves relating something to another thing or transforming it—such as 'making the night a time for rest.'

The creation of darkness and light is in respect of their being opposite phenomena that succeed one another. This does not indicate the existence of two separate deities as the Magians claim; on the contrary, these are secondary and relative phenomena. The fact that 'zulumat' (darkness) appears in the plural while 'nur' (light) is singular points to the difference between shirk (polytheism) and tawhid (monotheism). Furthermore, these concepts are also used metaphorically in spiritual meanings, such as disbelief and faith, or ignorance and knowledge.

Allah initially created human beings from clay. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi states that every human being indirectly originates from clay because nourishment is derived from the soil. However, according to the well-known tafsir, this refers to the creation of Adam. The creation of human beings from semen is also from a base fluid, yet the origin of semen ultimately traces back to the soil.

Modern science bases the origin of life on the cell. It is impossible for the cell to arise on its own (spontaneous generation); this necessitates the existence of a divine Creator. Pasteur's experiments also demonstrated that living beings reproduce only through seeds of their own kind. The creation of the first cell from earthly matter is proof of Allah's power.

There is an appointed term (lifespan) for every human being. Two appointed terms are mentioned in this verse: one is the term that is decreed (which actually takes place), and the other is the term determined in Allah's presence (the specified term, ajal musamma). This second term is the Day of Resurrection and Reckoning. Some commentators have interpreted these two terms differently; however, the correct view is the distinction between the appointed time of death and the appointed time of the Hereafter.

Allah is the only deity worshipped in the heavens and on the earth; He knows what is secret and what is open. The disbelievers turn away from the verses/signs of their Lord and deny the truth (the Quran). However, news of what they used to ridicule will surely come to them.

When narrating the destruction of previous nations, Allah Almighty uses the word 'qarn'. Qarn signifies a community living in a particular epoch. Peoples such as 'Ad and Thamud were destroyed because of their sins despite the immense power and blessings granted to them. This demonstrates that sins are a significant factor in bringing about a nation's appointed end. If Allah wills, He can destroy you in a similar manner and bring forth others in your place.

The polytheists demanded of the Prophet Muhammad that a tangible book be sent down. However, Allah stated that even if such a miracle were to come, they would say, 'This is nothing but obvious magic.' The verse revealed upon this demand of Abdullah b. Abi Umayyah shows that those who persist in denial will reject even the clearest proofs. Their true intention is not to believe in the truth.

The polytheists demanded that an angel be sent down, saying, 'Why was an angel not sent down to him?!' But Allah declared that in such a case the matter would be settled, and that they would be unable to bear seeing an angel and would perish. For the original form of angels is terrifying beyond human endurance. Even the prophets could rarely see angels in their original form. For this reason, Allah sent His prophets as human beings.

If the messenger had been an angel, We would have sent him in human form. Even then, the polytheists would have continued to deny him, saying, 'You are just a human being like us.' Indeed, previous messengers were also ridiculed, and in the end, punishment encompassed those who mocked. Therefore, the Prophet Muhammad was commanded to travel through the land and see the end of those who denied the truth.

Allah declares that whatever is in the heavens and on the earth belongs to Him. He has prescribed mercy upon Himself. That is, He has made mercy His attribute; His mercy takes precedence over His wrath. He will gather everyone on the Day of Resurrection; yet those who have ruined their own souls (the disbelievers) do not believe in this. Whatever rests in the night and the day belongs to Him; He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.

The Prophet Muhammad is instructed not to take any ally other than Allah. Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth; He feeds, but is not fed. The Prophet was commanded to be the first of those who submit to Islam and was told not to be of the polytheists. If he were to disobey, he feared the torment of a mighty Day. Whoever is spared from the torment on that Day has truly attained mercy. If Allah afflicts you with harm, none can remove it but He; and if He bestows good upon you, He has power over all things. He is the Supreme over His servants, the All-Wise, the All-Aware.

The word 'Fatir' means to cleave or originate something for the first time. The creation of the heavens and the earth was such that non-existence was cleaved open and existence emerged. Fitrah is the initial state of creation, while nature (tabi'ah) is the harmony in the continuation of this state. Allah both creates the innate dispositions (fitrahs) and provides the necessary provisions for their continuation.

The polytheists demanded of the Prophet Muhammad that he produce a witness to his prophethood. Allah declared that He Himself is the greatest witness. The Quran was revealed to warn both the people of Mecca and everyone who comes after. The Prophet bears witness to the oneness of Allah and is free from what they associate with Him. Those who were given the Scripture (Jews and Christians) recognize the Prophet just as they recognize their own children; yet a group among them knowingly denies it. Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His verses/signs? On that Day, the polytheists will lie, saying, 'By our Lord, we were not polytheists,' and the idols they fabricated will vanish from them.

Without Allah's testimony, nothing can testify to its own existence. The existence and knowledge of everything rely on Allah's knowledge. Even the testimony in one's conscience is in fact a reflection of Allah's testimony. For this reason, certain knowledge can only be attained through Allah's testimony. Prophethood is likewise a special testimony and command of Allah; the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him) is established through the testimony that Allah placed in his heart.

What was fundamental to Muhammad (peace be upon him) was not self-confidence, but trust in Allah. He would say, 'I commit my affair to Allah,' and always relied upon Allah. To rely on one's ego (nafs) is to fail to recognize Allah and to make oneself a deity. This state of the Prophet is proof of his prophethood. Contrary to the claim of the Italian historian, the Prophet did not rely on himself, but placed his trust in Allah (tawakkul).

The hearts of those who listen to the Quran are veiled; these veils prevent them from understanding it. They describe the Quran as 'tales of the ancients.' Figures like Abu Sufyan, Walid, and Nadr listened to the Prophet, but did not accept the truth because of the barriers over their hearts. These barriers are formed through a person's own evil choices and persist by Allah's leave.

While the word 'asatir' originally meant 'written things', over time it came to be used in the sense of 'legends, tales'. Those who characterized the Quran as 'asatir al-awwalin' viewed it not as a divine book, but as tales of the ancients. Yet the Quran is a miracle that conveys truths. This characterization stems from the corruption of their hearts.

When the disbelievers witness the punishment of the Fire, they feel regret and wish to return to the world. However, this regret does not stem from genuine faith, but from desperation. Even if they were returned to the world, they would commit the very same wrongdoing again. The wrongdoers who fabricate lies against Allah and deny His verses can never attain salvation. The life of the Hereafter is far better than the life of this world; one who possesses reason chooses the Hereafter.

In these verses, Allah Almighty declares that while the disbelievers deny the resurrection after death and the Day of Judgment, when they find themselves in distress they show remorse, yet if they were sent back they would do the very same things, and they are liars in these words of theirs. In this world, they found themselves in distress many times and showed remorse, but at the very first opportunity they returned to their former evil ways. When cast into the Fire in the Hereafter, they will say, 'Oh, would that we were sent back, so that we would not deny the verses of our Lord and would be among the believers!' Yet this remorse is not sincere; for they are only perturbed when the evil deeds they previously concealed are cast in their faces. Otherwise, if they were sent back, they would again do the very things they were forbidden from doing.

Disbelief and rebellion have become such an ingrained disposition for them that they can neither turn back nor be turned back. When they are brought before their Lord, Allah will say to them, 'Was this resurrection after death not real?' and they will reply, 'Yes, by our Lord, it was real.' Allah will say, 'Then taste the punishment, because you used to deny it.' Those who denied the meeting with Allah have suffered loss. Loss (khusran) is the forfeit of immense reward and everlasting bliss. Burden (wizr) and liability (wabal) are the weight of major sins. Humans have been granted intellect, senses, and faculties so that with them they may attain the realities of the afterlife; if one uses them merely for worldly pleasures, at the end of life they will suffer an irreparable loss.

The life of this world is nothing but amusement and play. Its fleeting pleasures mean nothing to those who contemplate death. The abode of the Hereafter, however, is better for those mindful of Allah (taqwa); for it is enduring and eternal. Allah invites people to reflect by saying, 'Will you not reason?' Because the disbelievers assume worldly life to be the sole reality, they plunge into heedlessness, chase after diversion, and deny the verses of Allah.

As a consolation to the Messenger of Allah, it is stated: 'Do not let their words grieve you; for in truth, they do not deny you, but rather they reject the verses of Allah.' Polytheists such as Abu Jahl and al-Harith ibn 'Amir admitted that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was truthful, yet out of obstinacy they did not believe. This stems from their denial of Allah and His power. The messengers before you were also denied and persecuted, yet they remained patient. The help of Allah came to them, and His promises never change. Indeed, some of the news of the messengers has already come to you.

If the turning away of the disbelievers weighs heavily upon you, then even if you could find a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign, what good would it do? Had Allah willed, He would have gathered them all upon guidance. So do not be among the ignorant! Only those who listen accept the call. As for the dead, Allah resurrects them, and then to Him they are returned. The polytheists said, 'Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?' Say, 'Indeed, Allah is fully capable of sending down a sign, but most of them do not know.' Just as they fail to benefit from the verses that have been sent down, they would not benefit from a new miracle either.

The animals that walk upon the earth and the birds that fly with their wings are communities like you. We have not neglected anything in the Book; then they will all be gathered before their Lord. Those who deny Our verses are deaf and dumb, lingering in darkness. Allah leads astray whom He wills, and places whom He wills upon a straight path. Say, 'Tell me: if the punishment of Allah should come upon you or the Hour should arrive, would you call upon anyone other than Allah? Answer, if you are truthful!'

In moments of distress and dire necessity, the disbelievers, by virtue of their innate nature (fitrah), pray to Allah alone and forget all others besides Him. If Allah wills, He removes that distress, whereupon they revert once again to their former polytheism. This state of affairs demonstrates that man turns sincerely to Allah in times of hardship, yet becomes ungrateful once ease is attained.

Messengers were also sent to earlier communities, and when they rejected them, they were afflicted with hardship and distress. In this way, they were expected to supplicate humbly and repent. However, they grew obstinate and hardened their hearts; and Satan made what they did appear pleasing to them. In the end, when they forgot the warnings, Allah opened the gates of everything to them, and amidst abundance and prosperity they became arrogant and fell into heedlessness. Just as they were rejoicing and relishing their pleasures, they were seized suddenly by the punishment and plunged into despair. Thus, the root of the people who committed wrongdoing was cut off; and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

The Messenger of Allah is commanded to say to the polytheists: 'Tell me: if Allah were to take away your hearing and your sight and seal your hearts, what deity other than Allah could restore them to you?' The verses are explained in varied ways, yet they still turn away. Ask again: 'If the punishment of Allah should come upon you suddenly or openly, would anyone be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?'

Messengers are sent only as bearers of glad tidings and as warners. Whoever believes and performs righteous deeds, there shall be no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve. As for those who deny Our verses, they will be afflicted with punishment because of the wickedness they committed. The Messenger does nothing except follow what is revealed to him; the treasures of Allah are not in his possession, nor does he know the unseen (ghayb), nor is he an angel. He only warns with the Quran those who fear being gathered before their Lord.

Do not dismiss from your presence those who worship their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. You are not responsible for their reckoning in the least, nor are they responsible for yours. If you dismiss them, you will be among the wrongdoers. Thus We have tested people through one another, so that they say, 'Has Allah favored these among us?' Does Allah not best know those who are grateful? When those who believe in Our verses come to you, greet them with peace; your Lord has prescribed mercy upon Himself: whoever among you does evil out of ignorance and then repents and amends, He is indeed Forgiving, Merciful. Thus do We explain the verses in detail, so that the way of the criminals may become manifest.

According to the narration, when the notables of Quraysh saw poor Muslims such as Suhayb, Bilal, 'Ammar, and Salman alongside the Prophet (peace be upon him), they said, 'Are we to follow behind these people? Drive them away from your presence so that we may speak with you.' The Messenger of Allah replied, 'I will not drive the believers away.' Umar said, 'Why not try it and see what happens?' Upon their insistence, this verse was revealed. Later, the verse in Surah al-Kahf was revealed: 'And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening,' and the Prophet (peace be upon him) never separated them from his side, saying, 'Life is with you, and death is with you.'

In the 53rd verse, it is explained that Allah tests people by means of one another by blessing the poor and weak with faith and sincerity. Those seized by arrogance and pride say, 'Did Allah prefer these over us?' This trial exposes the attitudes of those who pride themselves on wealth and status toward poor and weak believers. Those who abandon their pride and repent succeed, whereas those who persist in obstinacy lose. In this way, the underlying wisdom behind the prohibition of driving away the believers is elucidated.

In verses 54-55, it is given as glad tidings that peace should be conveyed to those who believe in Our verses, that your Lord has prescribed mercy upon Himself, and that whoever commits evil out of ignorance and then repents and reforms will be forgiven. Allah explains the verses in this way so that the path of the criminals may become clearly evident.

In verses 56-59, the Prophet is informed that he is forbidden to worship anything other than Allah and that he will not follow their desires. It is said, 'I am upon clear proof from my Lord, yet you have denied it. The punishment you seek to hasten is not in my hands; the judgment belongs only to Allah.' With Him are the keys of the unseen; in the land and the sea, He knows the falling of a leaf, the grain in the darkness of the earth, and everything wet and dry, in a clear book (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

In verses 60-62, it is explained that Allah puts people to sleep at night (takes their souls), knows what they do by day, and then raises and awakens them. When the moment of death arrives, Our messengers take the soul, and then they are returned to their true Master (Mawla). The judgment belongs to Him, and He is the swiftest of reckoners. Here, an analogy is drawn between sleep and death; waking up each night is evidence for the resurrection in the Hereafter.

In verses 63-65, it is stated that it is Allah who delivers them from the darknesses of the land and the sea, yet even though people implore Him and promise to be grateful, they still associate partners with Him. Allah has the power to send punishment from above (celestial disasters) and from beneath (terrestrial disasters), and to divide people into sects and make them taste the violence of one another. The verses are explained in this way so that they may understand.

In verses 66-67, it is stated that although the people denied the Quran, it is the truth, and for every news there is a determined time. The Prophet is not a guardian over them, but merely a messenger.

In verses 68-70, it is commanded: when you see those who engage in idle mockery of Our verses, turn away from them, and do not sit with the wrongdoers. Leave those who take their religion as play and amusement and are deceived by the worldly life; but remind with the Quran so that no soul is surrendered to ruin for what it has earned, for it has no protector or intercessor besides Allah. For those who disbelieve, there will be a boiling drink and a painful punishment.

In verses 71-73, it is stated that turning away from beseeching things besides Allah that can neither benefit nor harm is required, and that turning back from the right path is like becoming someone bewildered whom devils have led astray. Allah's way is the only right path; we have been commanded to establish prayer and fear Allah. It is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth; whenever He says to a thing 'Be,' it is. On the day the Trumpet (Sur) is blown, the sovereignty belongs to Him; He knows the unseen and the witnessed.

In this section, the struggle of Abraham (Ibrahim) with his people is recounted. Allah proves the belief in Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) by first exposing the overt deviance of idol worshippers, and then the theoretical deviance of star worshippers. Abraham tells his father Azar that worshipping idols is manifest misguidance. Allah shows Abraham the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, granting him firm conviction.

Abraham sees a star in the darkness of the night and says, 'This is my Lord'; when the star sets, he says, 'I do not love those that set,' explaining that a star cannot be a deity. He then observes the moon and the sun in turn, and seeing that they also set, he proclaims the belief in Tawhid, saying, 'I have turned my face toward the One who created the heavens and the earth, and I am not of the polytheists.' This event demonstrates that without Allah's guidance, man can fall into misguidance.

His people begin to argue with Abraham. Abraham says, 'Allah has guided me to the right path; why do you argue with me concerning Him? I do not fear those you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something. You do not fear associating partners with Allah, so why should I fear?' and adds: 'Those who believe and do not mix their faith with injustice—they are the ones who are in security, and they are rightly guided.'

Following these proofs given to Abraham, Allah exalts him. He then enumerates prophets such as Noah, David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John, Jesus, Elijah, Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot. These are the chosen servants whom Allah guided.
