Even if the Meccan polytheists disbelieve in these prophets, Allah will bring forth another people who will not deny them. Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is also commanded to follow the path of these prophets.

The polytheists display great ignorance by saying, 'Allah has not sent down anything to human beings.' Yet the Torah given to Moses is light and guidance for people. They, however, turn the Torah into separate sheets of paper, disclosing some of it and concealing most of it. They do not accept that Allah has sent down scripture. When 'Allah' is mentioned to them, they continue to amuse themselves with idle talk.

This Book (the Quran) is a blessed book revealed to confirm the scriptures that came before it and to warn the people of Mecca and all humanity around it. Those who believe in the Hereafter believe in this Book and remain steadfast in their prayers. The wisdom behind the revelation of the Quran is not exclusive to the Arabs; while the expression 'Umm al-Qura' points to Mecca as the center, the phrase 'and those around it' targets all of mankind.

Those who did not appraise Allah with true appraisal denied divine revelation by saying, 'Allah has not sent down anything to human beings.' Among those who uttered this statement was Malik ibn al-Sayf, the chief rabbi of the Jews of Medina. When the Messenger of Allah spoke with him and questioned him by adjuring him by the Torah, Malik grew angry and made this statement. The Jews subsequently deposed him from leadership and replaced him with Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. This event has been narrated as the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of the verse.

Who could be more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah, or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' when nothing has been revealed to him, or claims, 'I will reveal the like of what Allah has sent down'? If only you could see their state while in the agonies of death! The angels stretch forth their hands, saying: 'Surrender your souls. Today you will be recompensed with a humiliating punishment because you used to say wrongful things against Allah and acted arrogantly toward His verses.' On that day, they come all alone just as they were first created, leaving behind everything they possessed; and the partners they trusted in have vanished from them.

Undoubtedly, it is Allah who cleaves the grain and the fruit-stone. He brings forth the living from the dead, and He is the bringer forth of the dead from the living. Such is Allah; how then are you turned away? It is He who cleaves the darkness to bring forth the dawn. He made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for calculating time. That is the determination of Allah, the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing. A seed or a stone splits beneath the earth and sprouts; this is a clear proof of Allah's power.

It is He who created the stars for you so that you may guide yourselves by them through the darknesses of the land and the sea. Indeed, We have explained the verses in detail for a people who know. It is He who created you from a single soul; then there is for you a place of dwelling and a place of repository. It is He who sends down water from the sky; with it He brings forth vegetation of every kind, and from that plant He brings forth green foliage, from which He produces grains clustered over one another, clusters of date palms, vineyards, and groves of olives and pomegranates. Look at their fruits when they bear fruit and ripen! Surely in these are lessons for a people who believe. All these signs of creation demonstrate Allah's oneness and power.

They also made the jinn partners with Allah, even though He created them. Without any knowledge, they fabricated sons and daughters for Him. Exalted and transcendent is His glory far above the attributes they ascribe. He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth out of nothing. How could He have a child when He has no spouse? He is the Creator of all things, and He is the Knower of all things.

Allah created human beings from a single soul, placing some in a place of settlement (settled in the womb) and some in a repository (still in the loins). This difference demonstrates the diversity and variation of creation. The emergence of many different beings from a single source runs contrary to the uniform law of nature, and this is possible only through the power of the Creator. This state of affairs is an evident artistry that points to Allah's existence, knowledge, and power.

These verses have been explained for those who possess fiqh—that is, people endowed with subtle and profound understanding. For objective proofs are known through subjective proofs. A person's knowing oneself is an essential condition for understanding these verses. Explanations given to those who do not know their own souls are in vain. Those with deep insight grasp the principle in these verses and become privy to the secrets of creation.

Allah sent down water from the sky, and with it He brought forth the vegetation of everything. From it He produced greenery, closely clustered grains (ears of grain), date clusters, vineyards, and fruits such as olives and pomegranates that are both similar and diverse. People ought to understand Allah's power by observing the development of these plants from their unripe state to their ripening. These are manifest proofs for people who believe.

Each of the mentioned fruits has distinct benefits. The date serves as a staple food; grapes are the sultan of fruits; oil is extracted from olives; and the pomegranate, with its hard rind, inner membranes, seeds, and sweet juice, brings contraries together. This diversity and harmony are clear examples of Allah's art of creation.

Despite all these proofs, people associated the jinn as partners with Allah. The concept of jinn encompasses angels, devils, and unseen beings. Some worshipped angels, while others attributed good and evil to two separate deities. Dualist beliefs, such as the Zoroastrians (Majus), fell into shirk by attributing good to Allah and evil to Satan or Ahriman. In truth, both good and evil exist by Allah's creation; there is no creator or deity besides Him.

In this verse, it is recounted that those who associate partners with Allah took partners from among the jinn. The polytheists worshipped the jinn by considering them partners with Allah, whereas it is Allah who created the jinn as well. This shows that associating the created with the Creator is immense ignorance and injustice. Moreover, this associating of partners encompasses not only idol worship, but also the worship of hidden things such as unseen forces and powers of nature.

Some polytheists attributed sons and daughters to Allah. The Arab polytheists considered the angels to be daughters of Allah, the Zoroastrians regarded Hormizd and Ahriman as sons, the Jews accepted Ezra (Uzayr) as the son of Allah, and the Christians accepted the Messiah as the son of Allah. All of these claims rest on no knowledge whatsoever and are nothing but slander. Allah is transcendent above them; His Essence is far removed from imperfections such as partnership and having children.

How could Allah have a child when He is the incomparable Originator of the heavens and the earth? He has no spouse, and a child requires a mother. Yet it is impossible for Allah to have a spouse. Birth and giving birth can only be conceived among created beings; such attributes are inconceivable for the Creator. Allah is the Creator of all things and is in need of nothing.

Ibda' means creating without a preexisting model. The heavens and the earth were created in this manner. Allah is the unique Creator who brings everything into existence out of nothing. His creation does not depend on matter or form. Material causes come after Allah's creation. He creates as He wills, and nothing can be equal to Him. Allah's knowledge encompasses all things; He knows everything.

Such is Allah, your Lord. There is no god but He, the Creator of all things. Therefore, worship Him alone and put your trust in Him. He is the Trustee (Wakil) over all things. Eyes cannot perceive Him, but He perceives all eyes. He is the Subtle (al-Latif), the All-Aware (al-Khabir). After these explanations, the truth has now become evident: whoever sees the truth does so to his own benefit, and whoever acts blindly does so to his own detriment.

Allah Almighty informs that eyes cannot perceive Him, yet He perceives all things. Basirah (insight) means seeing with the eye of the heart and attaining true knowledge. Whoever looks with insight and believes does so to his own benefit, and whoever acts blindly does so to his own detriment. Real blindness is not blindness of the eyes, but blindness of the heart. Allah does not protect those who turn blind to proofs of insight; He leaves them in darkness.

Allah explains the verses in diverse ways so that the disbelievers may say, 'You have studied.' Yet these verses are sources of insight for people of knowledge. The Prophet is commanded to follow what is revealed to him from his Lord and pay no heed to the polytheists. Had Allah willed, He could have compelled them to faith, but because He did not so will, they remained polytheists. The Prophet is not a guardian over them.

Believers must not insult those whom the polytheists worship, lest they revile Allah out of ignorance. To each community their deeds have been made alluring. In the end, the return is to Allah. The polytheists swear that if a miracle comes to them, they will surely believe. Say: Miracles are only with Allah. Allah turns their hearts and their eyes; just as they did not believe at first, so too will they not believe.

Even if angels were sent down to them, the dead spoke to them, and all things were gathered and brought before them, they would not believe unless Allah willed. And thus We have appointed for every prophet enemies—human and jinn devils. They whisper gilded speech to one another in order to deceive. This is so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline toward such speech, be pleased with it, and continue committing the offenses they commit.

When Allah has sent down the Book fully explained, it is not right to seek a judge other than Him. The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice; there is no one who can alter His words. If you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the way of Allah; for they follow nothing but conjecture and they do nothing but guess. Your Lord knows best who is guided on the right path.

Allah has sent down to you a Book fully explained in such a way that leaves no need for other miracles, and He has made His judgment definitive. The miracle of this Book is clearer, more comprehensive, and more enduring than other miracles. For instance, while the miracle of the splitting of the moon was a transient and indirect proof, the Quran expresses the same truth clearly and perpetually. For this reason, while Allah's judgment stands, it is not right to incline toward the gilded words of devils and seek another judge.

Just as the Quraysh polytheists turned to soothsayers in their disputes, they also proposed to the Messenger of Allah that he choose an arbiter from among the Jewish or Christian scholars. Allah, however, rejects this proposal by stating: "Shall I seek a judge other than Allah?" For the Quran is entirely truthful in its accounts and completely just in its rulings; there is no power that can change it. Allah hears every word and knows every intention, which is why His judgment can neither be overturned nor escaped.

If you obey the majority of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the path of Allah. For they follow conjecture and their own desires; they do not rely on knowledge. They claim that Allah has revealed nothing, associate partners with Him, and determine what is lawful (halal) and unlawful (haram) according to their whims. Yet Allah knows best who is rightly guided and who strays from the path.

If you believe in the verses of Allah, eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned. Allah has explained to you what is forbidden to you, except in cases of necessity. Many mislead people without knowledge. Abandon open sin and secret sin; those who earn sin will receive their punishment. Do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for this is transgression (fisq). The devils inspire their allies; if you obey them, you will surely become polytheists.

Scholars have expressed differing opinions regarding the ruling of the Basmalah in slaughter. Ata stated that the Basmalah is a condition for all kinds of food, but the majority (jumhur) hold the view that this ruling applies only to animals to be slaughtered. If the Basmalah is deliberately omitted, the meat is not eaten; if omitted forgetfully, it may be eaten. According to Imam al-A'zam, if it is deliberately omitted, it is not eaten; if forgotten, it is eaten. Imam Shafi'i, on the other hand, stated that if the one slaughtering is a Muslim or of the People of the Book, what is slaughtered without the Basmalah is lawful (halal). The command in the verses expresses remembering Allah in an absolute sense; the Basmalah is Sunnah.

One whom We brought to life with guidance when he was dead, and to whom We gave a light with which to walk among people, is not like one who remains in darkness and cannot emerge from it. Thus, what they did has been made pleasing to the disbelievers. In every land, We made its prominent figures criminals so that they might plot deceit therein; yet they only bring evil upon themselves. When a verse comes to them, they say, "We will not believe unless we too are given prophethood." Allah knows best to whom He will give prophethood. Humiliation and severe punishment will reach the criminals.

Whomever Allah wills to guide, He opens his chest to Islam; and whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his chest tight and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky. This is the straight path of your Lord. We have explained the verses for a people who take heed. For them is the abode of peace with their Lord; and Allah is their ally because of the good deeds they used to do.

Allah opens the heart of the one He wills to guide to Islam and places such a light in his heart that his chest expands and finds relief through faith and obedience. When the Prophet (peace be upon him) was asked about the sign of this opening, he said, 'Turning toward the home of eternity, turning away from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it arrives.' And whomever Allah wills to lead astray, He constricts his chest, suffocating him as if he were climbing into the sky; thus the torment and defilement of disbelief are placed upon him. This path is the straight path of your Lord, and all signs have been explained in the Quran for those who reflect.

On the day Allah gathers humans and jinn, He says to the jinn, 'O company of jinn! You have led many humans astray.' Those among humans who were allies of the jinn will say, 'Our Lord! We benefited from one another, and we have reached our appointed term that You set for us.' Allah will say, 'Your dwelling place is the Fire, where you will abide eternally, except as Allah wills.' Surely your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing. Thus We make the wrongdoers allies of one another because of the sins they used to earn.

When Allah says, 'O company of jinn and humans! Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting My verses to you and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?' they will say, 'We bear witness against ourselves.' The worldly life deceived them, and they bore witness against themselves that they were disbelievers. In this scene, the human allies of the jinn attempt to excuse the jinn by assuming responsibility, yet all of them deserve the same sin and punishment.

The polytheists used to allocate a share for Allah from the crops and livestock He created, and also a share for their partners (idols). What belonged to their partners would not reach Allah, whereas what belonged to Allah would reach their partners. Likewise, their partners made the killing of their children appear pleasing to many of the polytheists; they wanted them both to ruin themselves and to confuse and corrupt their religion. Had Allah willed, they would not have done so. So leave them with what they fabricate.

The polytheists said, according to their own claims, 'These livestock and crops are forbidden; none may eat of them except whom we will.' They prohibited riding on the backs of some animals, and slaughtered others without mentioning the name of Allah. As for what was in the wombs of the livestock, they said, 'It is lawful only for our males and forbidden to our females; but if it is born dead, then they all share in it.' All of these were rulings made by fabricating lies against Allah. Allah has caused those who killed their children out of ignorance and forbade the lawful sustenance to suffer loss; they have strayed from the right path.

Allah created gardens, both trellised and untrellised, date palms, crops, olives, and pomegranates. Eat of their fruit when they bear fruit, give its due (its zakat and charity) on the day of harvest, and do not be wasteful. Of the livestock, He created those that carry burdens and those used for furnishings. Eat of the sustenance that Allah has provided, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. He created eight pairs: sheep, goats, camels, and cattle. Who can be more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah regarding prohibitions? In what was revealed to our Prophet, the only things made forbidden are carrion, spilled blood, the flesh of swine, and animals slaughtered in the name of other than Allah. Whoever is forced by necessity, without transgressing or exceeding limits, may eat of them. Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful. For the Jews, animals with claws and certain fats were made forbidden. Say to the polytheists: their claim that 'Had Allah willed, we would not have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything' is the word of those before them. The most decisive argument belongs to Allah; had He willed, He would have guided you all. Do not follow the whims of those who deny My verses and do not believe in the Hereafter.

The Arab polytheists used to declare certain animals forbidden by inventing lies against Allah. When the rulings of Islam began to be revealed, they entered into a dispute with the Messenger of Allah. According to a narration, their orator, Malik ibn Awf, came to the Messenger of Allah and said, 'You are making certain things lawful.' The Messenger of Allah asked, 'You made things forbidden without basis; where did you get the idea to forbid them when the eight pairs created by Allah are lawful?' When Malik was unable to answer, he fell silent. Thereupon, Allah explained the eight pairs He created and made lawful.

The expression 'eight pairs' mentioned in the verse means four pairs—male and female—of sheep, goat, camel, and cattle species, that is, eight individuals. In these verses, a methodology regarding declaring things forbidden is demonstrated: first, eight pairs are enumerated, then grouped into four species; subsequently, attributes that might potentially be considered grounds for prohibition—such as being male, being female, or being in the womb—are specified in detail, and it is proven that none of these has any relevance to prohibition. This is the finest example of the method called 'takhrij and tanqih al-manat' (derivation and refinement of the ratio legis) in Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh). However, this rational method alone is not sufficient; the effective cause (illah) must be based upon an established foundation, which can only be established through revelation.

Thereupon it is stated: Say, I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to someone who would eat it, except carrion, spilled blood, the flesh of swine—for it is impure—and animals slaughtered in the name of other than Allah are forbidden. The concept of impurity (rijs) is not limited to external appearance alone; things that are spiritually impure, such as alcohol, are also forbidden. Moreover, 'transgression' (fisq)—that is, what is slaughtered by invoking a name other than Allah—is also forbidden. One who is compelled by necessity, without violating the rights of others and without exceeding the required amount, may eat of them. These prohibitions can be extended on grounds such as aggression and excessiveness; indeed, predatory beasts and impure insects have also been forbidden on these principles.

Earlier, We also forbade every animal with claws to the Jews. The term claw (zufur) encompasses various animals such as camels, horses, and beasts of prey; however, cattle and sheep are outside this scope. Furthermore, We forbade the internal fats of cattle and sheep to them, except for the fats adhering to the back, the entrails, or mixed with bone (such as tail fat), which were not forbidden. This prohibition was a punishment due to the aggression of the Jews. Allah speaks the truth; this prohibition came about because of their wrongdoing.

The polytheists use destiny as an excuse, saying, 'If Allah had willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.' However, while Allah's will encompasses everything, this does not mean that what they did was right. Allah decrees sin, but does not approve of it; He has given human beings freedom of choice and responsibility. Past nations also denied their prophets and in the end tasted the punishment. Therefore, these polytheists will suffer the same fate. Allah's mercy is vast, but the sinners will sooner or later meet their punishment.

The polytheists were trying to defend themselves by saying, "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything." Yet this claim of theirs is based not on knowledge, but merely on conjecture and delusion. By perpetuating the lies and slander inherited from their forefathers, they fabricate lies against Allah. Following their own whims and desires, they distort the truth and ignore the proofs of Allah. In reality, they are only lying and deceiving themselves.

O Muhammad! Say: The most decisive and conclusive proof belongs to Allah. Allah has created countless signs in the heavens and the earth, provided lessons from past communities, given you intellect and will, and sent scriptures and prophets. Although this claim of yours is an attempt to defend yourselves by using Allah's will, it is actually a proof entirely against you. For by saying, "If Allah had willed, we could not have done it," you confess that you cannot oppose His will, but then with this confession you attempt to justify your polytheism (shirk). This is a contradiction and in fact proves tawhid (monotheism).

O Muhammad! Say to the polytheists: Bring forth your witnesses who will testify that Allah made this forbidden. If they come and testify, "Allah forbade these," do not testify with them. Do not follow the desires of those who deny Our verses, who do not believe in the Hereafter, and who associate partners with Allah. Their testimony is nothing other than false testimony. This verse, returning to the beginning of the surah, emphasizes the truth of tawhid and prophethood.

Say: Come, let me recite what your Lord has forbidden to you: Do not associate anything with Him. Treat parents with kindness. Do not kill your children out of fear of poverty; We provide sustenance for you and for them. Do not approach immoralities, whether open or secret. Do not take a life that Allah has made sacred, except by right. These are what Allah has enjoined upon you. Also, do not approach the property of an orphan, except in the fairest manner. Give full measure and weight with justice; We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity. Whenever you speak, be just, even if it concerns a close relative. Fulfill the covenant of Allah. These are what He has enjoined upon you so that you may take heed.

And this is My straight path, so follow it. Do not follow other paths that will separate you from the path of Allah. Allah has enjoined these upon you so that you may be mindful. These verses resemble the Ten Commandments in the Torah and are decisive rulings common to all divine laws. Whoever obeys these commands and avoids the prohibitions attains salvation; whoever turns away from them falls into misguidance. The path of the Prophet is the path of tawhid; uniting on this path is a divine strength. Those who fall into division will be ruined.

Allah Almighty informs that He gave the Torah to Moses (Musa) and that this scripture was a guidance and mercy explaining all things. Then, it is emphasized that this Quran is also a blessed scripture, that it must be followed, and that one must fear Allah. The Quran was sent down to eliminate excuses and pretexts such as that the previous scriptures were sent down to only two communities (Jews and Christians) while we were unaware, or that had a scripture been given to us, we would have been better guided.

The fact that this scripture was sent down in Arabic also invalidates excuses such as the Arab society's illiteracy. For every community that hears that the book has been revealed is obligated to learn it and spread it. On the Day of Resurrection, such excuses will not be accepted.

The disbelievers wait for the angels, your Lord, or some of His signs (portents) to come. However, on the day when the signs of your Lord arrive, faith on that day will not benefit anyone who did not believe before or who did not earn any good through their faith. Elmalılı explains here that there are two kinds of signs: one consists of signs foretelling future events (faith must be placed in these), and the other consists of signs where events actually occur, at which point faith is of no benefit. He details the prerequisite of prior faith and earning good for faith to be accepted, and touches upon the view of the Mu'tazilah.

In verse 159, it is stated that the Prophet has no relation to those who divided their religion and broke up into sects. Among these groups, polytheists, Jews, Christians, and even those who broke away from the Muslims can be counted. Our Prophet reported that his ummah would split into seventy-three sects, and that only one would be saved. In verse 160, it is stated that whoever brings a good deed will receive tenfold reward, while whoever brings an evil deed will be penalized only with its equal. This is a manifestation of Allah's justice and grace. The punishment for disbelief (kufr) is eternal, because disbelief is an eternal evil.

In verses 161–163, our Prophet is commanded to say that he has been guided to a straight path, the upright (hanif) religion of Abraham, that his prayer, his acts of worship, his life, and his death are for Allah, the Lord of the worlds, that He has no partner, and that he is the first of the Muslims. Finally, in verses 164–165, it is emphasized that while Allah is the Lord of all things, seeking a Lord other than Him is meaningless, that whatever each person earns belongs to them alone, and that no one will bear the burden of another. Allah has made human beings successors upon the earth and tests them through the blessings He has bestowed upon them.

With His decree, "Indeed, I will place a vicegerent upon the earth" (al-Baqarah, 2:30), Almighty Allah also granted this ummah the high station and honor He gave to Adam, making them successors upon the earth. This responsibility and trust have been placed upon humankind.

Allah has raised some people above others by degrees in attributes such as intellect, knowledge, honor, rank, wealth, and provision. The purpose of this is to test human beings, to distinguish those who use the granted blessings properly and show gratitude from those who do not, and to select those who do the best deeds.

This world is a realm of trial and competition. Today's condition is the result of the past trial, and tomorrow's condition will be the result of today's trial. The Ummah of Muhammad is in a test not only among its own individuals, but also alongside the nations that came before it, and must take heed from them and win the race.

The variation in degrees is a requirement of this test and competition. For this reason, those who are at the top may fall, and those who are below may rise. The danger and responsibility of those occupying higher ranks are heavier. Therefore, one should not take pride in high worldly status and rank, but should strive as is due.

O Muhammad! Your Lord's punishment is swift. To the disbelievers and rebels who do not fulfill the due of the blessings He has bestowed and do not show gratitude—no matter how high a station they may hold—your Lord brings about their affliction at whichever moment He wills. Everything that is to come is near. Along with this, Allah is All-Forgiving and Most Merciful; He overlooks the shortcomings of those who are grateful and obedient, and brings them into His mercy.

If the time when this surah was revealed in Mecca and the subsequent stages of Islamic history are considered, it becomes evident how many miracles concerning the future this verse contains, and that this still continues. With the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) being sent as a messenger, a new era in human life opened that would surpass past communities as well.
Surah al-An'am ends here. Now, let us listen to Surah al-A'raf, which explains how the appointment as successors and the trial mentioned in this verse have unfolded since the past.

Surah al-A'raf begins with the disjointed letters (huruf al-muqatta'at). There are various interpretations regarding the meaning of these letters. According to a narration from Ibn Abbas, they mean 'Allah knows and explains.' Al-Suddi, on the other hand, stated that it is an abbreviation of the name 'the Fashioner' (al-Musawwir). However, commentators of the Quran point out that such interpretations are not reliable since they do not rest upon definitive evidence. These letters indicate that the surah contains allegorical (mutashabih) verses and that certain truths lie beyond human comprehension.

In the surah, it is said: 'O community of Muhammad! Follow the Book sent down to you from your Lord, and do not take protectors and helpers besides Him.' Do not follow any word or deed contrary to the Book. How many a city there was whose people were suddenly overtaken by Our punishment while they were in heedlessness! This is recalled as the earthly end of those who do not follow the Book.

On the Day of Resurrection, questions will be put both to the communities to whom prophets were sent and to the prophets themselves. This questioning will take the form of rebuke and holding to account. Since the sins of the guilty will be evident from their faces, they will not be questioned individually about them, but rather how they responded to the conveyance of the prophets' messages will be interrogated. Allah knows all things, and nothing is hidden from Him.

The weighing on that Day is the truth. Everyone's deeds will be weighed; those whose good deeds outweigh their evil deeds will attain salvation, while those whose scales are light will have ruined themselves. This is the consequence of their wronging Allah's verses and denying them.

Allah established you on the earth and provided you with means of livelihood. Despite this, how little gratitude you show! Then He created you, fashioned you, and commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam. All the angels prostrated except Iblis. Iblis grew arrogant, saying, 'I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay,' and refused to prostrate.

Allah said to Iblis: 'Then descend from here, for it is not for you to be arrogant here. Get out; you are indeed among the degraded.' Iblis asked for respite until the Day people are resurrected. Allah granted him respite. Iblis said: 'Because You have led me astray, I will surely lie in wait for them on Your straight path; I will approach them from before them and behind them, from their right and from their left, and You will not find most of them grateful.'

Allah said: 'Get out of here, disgraced and expelled. I will surely fill Hell with all of those who follow you.' He then commanded Adam and his wife to dwell in Paradise, to eat from wherever they pleased, but not to approach this tree, lest they become of the wrongdoers. Satan whispered to them in order to deceive them, saying: 'Your Lord has only forbidden you this tree lest you become angels or become immortal.' He swore to them that he was giving them sincere counsel. Thus, he deceived them, and they tasted of the tree. When their private parts became visible to them, they began to cover themselves with the leaves of Paradise. Their Lord called out to them: 'Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is an open enemy to you?'

Adam and his wife repented, saying: 'Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.' Allah said: 'Descend, being enemies to one another. On earth you will have a dwelling place and livelihood for a time. There you shall live, there you shall die, and from there you shall be brought forth resurrected.'

Iblis's refusal to prostrate stemmed from arrogance and a flawed analogy (qiyas). In saying 'I am better than him,' he took the substance of creation as his measure, while failing to take into account the spirit, form, and purpose decreed by Allah. This is the consequence of materialism and personal pride. Iblis did not deny Allah, nor did he deny resurrection after death; rather, he fell into disbelief by refusing to obey the command and by disputing it. This event serves as a warning and a means of trial for humanity.

Upon being granted respite by Allah, instead of being grateful and repenting, Iblis swore that he would attack people from every direction to mislead them. He said that he would come at them from their front, from behind them, from their right, and from their left, and that He would not find most of them grateful. Thereupon, Allah expelled him from Paradise as banished and degraded, announcing that He would fill Hell with him and whoever follows him.

Allah did not expel Iblis immediately, but questioned him; yet when he responded with arrogance and obstinacy, he was cast down from his station. While Iblis had the chance to regret and reform, he grew utterly defiant instead and resolved to commit evil eternally. It was then that he was completely expelled by Allah and condemned to eternal punishment along with those who follow him. The fall of Iblis in this trial that began with the creation of Adam is an admonition and lesson for humankind so that they do not fall into the same error.

When Adam and Eve (Hawwa) were placed in Paradise, they were permitted to eat and drink as they wished, but were forbidden to approach a specific tree. This prohibition showed that they were not entirely devoid of responsibility and that this tree was a realm of trial. Satan whispered to them in order to expose their private parts, deceiving them by saying that if they ate from this tree, they would become angels or abide eternally. Tricked by Satan, who swore that he only desired their good, Adam and Eve ate from the forbidden tree, and immediately their private parts were exposed.

Realizing their mistake, Adam and Eve immediately repented and pleaded with Allah: 'Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; if You do not forgive us and show mercy to us, we will surely be among the losers.' Allah accepted their repentance, yet sent them down to earth. In this narrative, while Adam's five qualities (admitting his mistake, feeling remorse, blaming oneself, repentance, and never despairing of mercy) brought him felicity, Iblis's contrary actions (refusing to admit his mistake, feeling no remorse, not blaming himself, attributing the fault to Allah, and despairing of mercy) brought him wretchedness.

Allah sent down to the Children of Adam clothing to cover their private parts and as an adornment. But the garment of piety (taqwa) is best. Let not Satan deceive you just as he had your parents expelled from Paradise; for he and his tribe see you from where you cannot see them. When hypocrites commit evil, they say: 'We found our fathers doing this, and Allah has commanded it of us.' Say: 'Allah does not command indecency; do you say against Allah that which you do not know?'

Allah enjoins justice; direct your faces toward Him at every place of worship (masjid) and call upon Him, making religion purely sincere for Him alone. As He originated you, so will you return to Him. A group He guided, and a group deserved straying; for they took devils as allies instead of Allah and thought they were rightly guided. For every nation there is a term; when it arrives, they can neither delay it by an hour nor advance it.

Allah commands that fine clothing be worn when going to the mosques, and that one eat and drink but not be wasteful. Wastefulness (israf) entails declaring the unlawful as lawful, making the lawful unlawful, or going to excess in eating, drinking, and adornment. Allah does not love the wasteful. As the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse, it is narrated that in the pre-Islamic period of ignorance (jahiliyyah), there was the custom of performing circumambulation (tawaf) naked, and the Banu Amir used to torment themselves by eating very little during the days of pilgrimage (Hajj). When the Muslims also wished to act likewise, this verse was revealed. In this verse, the principles of preserving health, which constitutes half of medicine, are summarized.

No one can forbid the adornments and wholesome provisions that Allah has produced for His servants. This verse is evidence that the default ruling regarding clothing and food is permissibility. Prohibition applies only to what Allah has explicitly forbidden. Allah has forbidden immoralities (both open and secret), sin, wrongful rebellion, associating partners with Him for which He has sent down no authority, and speaking about Allah without knowledge. Polytheism is sheer ignorance consisting of nothing other than following Satan without evidence.

For every community there is an appointed term (a time of destruction). When that appointed term arrives, it can neither be delayed nor advanced. This means that the disbelievers and the rebellious are not punished immediately but are granted respite, yet in the end they will certainly meet their punishment. Believers must not be deceived by this respite, but should repent immediately and adhere firmly to Allah's commands.

Those who deny Our verses and act arrogantly against them are those for whom the gates of heaven will not be opened, nor will they enter Paradise. They can only enter Paradise when a camel passes through the eye of a needle; this is a proverb expressing impossibility. The disbelievers will have beds and coverings of fire in Hell. As for the believers, they will enter Paradise, rancor will be removed from their hearts, rivers will flow beneath them, and they will praise Allah.

Between the people of Paradise and the people of Hell there is a veil, and on the Heights (al-A'raf) are those who recognize both sides by their marks. They greet the people of Paradise with peace, being those who have not yet entered it though they ardently desire to enter. The people of Hell will plead with the people of Paradise for water and provision, but this has been forbidden to the disbelievers. Because they took their religion as amusement and play, and the life of this world deceived them, they will be forgotten in the Hereafter.

There are two primary views regarding the people of al-A'raf. According to the first, they are a monotheistic group whose deeds fell short and whose good deeds and misdeeds weighed equally in the Scale (mizan). They remain for a time between Paradise and Hell, after which Allah passes judgment concerning them. According to the second view, they are figures of high rank, such as prophets, martyrs, the righteous, and scholars. Under the first view, the people of al-A'raf are those who have not yet entered Paradise but desire to enter, and the people of Paradise say to them, 'Peace be upon you.' Under the second view, this situation describes the state of the people of Paradise before they enter it, and the people of al-A'raf give them glad tidings of peace and safety.

What is described in verses 48–51 is the calling out by the people of al-A'raf to individuals they recognize by their marks. These were disbelievers such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and their like. They used to say, 'Is Allah going to admit people like Salman and 'Ammar into Paradise while throwing us into Hell?' These are the very ones to whom the people of al-A'raf cry out, 'Neither your gathering nor your arrogance has availed you anything.' And those whom they point to, asking, 'Are these the ones?', are believers such as Salman and 'Ammar.

In verses 52–53, it is stated that Allah brought them a Book that He detailed based on knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe. The disbelievers, however, await its interpretation (ta'wil)—that is, its ultimate outcome and the realization of the news it conveyed. Ta'wil means bringing something to its conclusion. In order to believe in the Hereafter, they wait for the Day of Resurrection to arrive. When that Day comes, they will say, 'The messengers of our Lord certainly brought the truth,' and they will seek intercessors or wish to return to the worldly life, but this will be of no benefit to them.

In verse 54, it is stated that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself above the Throne (istiwa' 'ala al-'Arsh). The expression 'six days' does not mean known days like worldly days, but denotes periods or spans of time. These timeframes may be shorter or longer than a known day. For instance, it is indicated in verses that a single day may last a thousand years or fifty thousand years. The true nature of these six days is allegorical (mutashabih), yet it is certain that the universe is not eternal (qadim), that it was created stage by stage, and that it is under the dominion of Allah.

In verses 55–58, it is commanded to supplicate to Allah in humility and secret, that He does not love transgressors, and that corruption should not be caused on earth. Allah, who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy, bears heavy clouds, drives them to a dry land, sends down rain, and brings forth all kinds of crops. In this manner the dead will also be brought forth. The vegetation of a good land emerges by the permission of its Lord, whereas from the bad land nothing comes forth except stunted, useless growth. Thus are the verses explained for a people who are grateful.

There are two main views regarding istiwa' and the Throne (al-'Arsh). According to the school of the early righteous predecessors (the Salaf), one believes in the attribute of Allah's istiwa' over the Throne while entrusting its modality (kayfiyyah) to Allah's knowledge. Later scholars (al-muta'akhkhirun), however, adopted figurative interpretation (ta'wil), understanding istiwa' as signifying Allah's majesty and sovereignty. The Throne is an exalted entity that encompasses the entire universe; whether it is a physical body (jism) is debated. Istiwa' must be understood in a manner befitting Allah, free from attributes such as place and direction.

When explaining the phrase 'then He established His dominion over the Throne' in Surah al-A'raf, verse 54, Elmalılı Hamdi Yazır states that the concept of 'istiwa'' in Arabic is a metonymy (kinayah) for complete ownership and the orderly execution of affairs. This expression conveys the penetration of Allah's power and the unfolding of His will through His continuous command over His creation and His implementation of orderly decrees. Hasan al-Basri expressed this as 'He assumed mastery over His affair.' The word 'then' (thumma) indicates that at the initial moments of creation there was not yet an orderly continuity, whereas istiwa' can be conceived with the commencement of this order.

In the second interpretation, istiwa' is taken to mean 'istila',' that is, triumph and dominion. According to this, after creation Allah held everything under His power and mastery. This meaning is related to the expression 'He encompasses all things' in Surah as-Sajdah, verse 54. Although Ibn al-'Arabi did not accept this meaning, it was countered with the poet's line: 'Bishr conquered (istawla 'ala) Iraq without a sword and without shedding blood.'

In the third interpretation, the Throne is taken to mean the realm and dominion, while istiwa' is taken to mean mastery (istila'). This interpretation offers three benefits: first, it draws special attention to the meaning of istiwa'; second, it serves as a reminder of Allah's supreme authority over human sovereignties; third, it emphasizes Allah's sublime and absolute perfection not only in His active attributes, but in all His essential attributes. Furthermore, from this perspective, the delay implied by the word 'then' does not pertain to time between creation and istiwa', but rather to the rank of textual exposition.

According to a fourth interpretation, 'He established Himself over the Throne' means that everything is equal in relation to Allah. That is, Allah is not like physical bodies that move from one place to another; those in the heavens and those on the earth are at an equal distance to Him. This is an understanding that eliminates the limitations of place and distance. However, this should not be interpreted as meaning that istiwa' itself signifies equality; rather, the intent is an essential or relational attribute that entails equality. This meaning can be illustrated by the example of a geometric center, yet in Allah's divine relation, no distinction of distance can be conceived.

All these interpretations are intended to prevent the word istiwa' from being understood in physical senses such as sitting or leaning. To imagine Allah sitting upon a throne or leaning against a place is, both rationally and religiously, gross ignorance. The soundest path is to follow the school of the majority of the Salaf and say, 'Allah created the heavens and the earth, then He established Himself over the Throne in the sense He intended.' However, this does not mean that the verse contains no comprehensible meaning, for the continuation of the verse concerning the covering of the night and the day elucidates this istiwa'.

In the continuation of the verse, the expression 'He wraps the night over the day, which pursues it incessantly' displays one of the broadest manifestations of istiwa. Allah drapes the night over the day; in the moment of this draping, the light of the day turns into darkness, and darkness into light. This transformation continues in a ceaseless alternation and proclaims Allah's sovereignty. The mutual draping of night and day in this manner demonstrates the existence of a will superior to their natures.

The chasing of night and day after one another is expressed with spiritual words such as 'talab' (pursuit) and 'hathith' (prompting/swiftly). This describes both an objective and a subjective state. Although the hasty pursuit of the day may appear like a pursuit of the sun, contrary to this pursuit, the night is brought and the day is vanquished. This shows that Allah has subjected the sun, the moon, and the stars to His command. None of them is an originator or a determiner on its own; all of them are subject to Allah's command.

All creation and command belong to Allah. Created beings are His dominion, and the decrees that govern them are also His. Bodies and physical forms, matter and shape are His invention; the force and spirit that animate them are His effect. Nothing can exist without being grounded in His origination, nor can there be any command that does not conform to His command. The expression 'Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command' summarizes this truth.

Next, with the attribute 'Lord of the worlds', the superiority of beings possessed of intellect over other realms and the fact that Allah's greatness transcends the intellect are recalled. In their journey of knowing Allah, those endowed with intellect should neither neglect the value of their reason nor overestimate reason and imagine that sovereignty belongs to it. They should neither become fixated solely on external manifestations and see the sun as clearer than its Lord, nor turn entirely inward and suppose their Lord to be within themselves. Sovereignty belongs neither to the realm of the sun and the moon nor to the realm of intellects; it belongs to the Truth Most High (Haqq Ta'ala) above both.

Allah Almighty commands His servants to supplicate to Him with humility and in secret. Here, in the recitation of 'Asim according to the transmission of Abu Bakr Shu'bah, there is also a reading that means 'with a kind of fear.' That is to say, first know your place and recognize your Lord; His greatness, majesty, and authority of creation and command belong exclusively to Him. You are in need of Him at every moment and are under His decree. Then know that you are permitted and indeed commanded to pray directly to Him. In your supplication, you should be neither reckless nor loud and clamorous; you must implore secretly with complete reverence and sincerity. For Allah does not love the transgressors. Those who exceed the limits in supplication and lose moderation in their prayers are deprived of His love.

Supplication is the lesser entreating the Greater with earnestness for one's need. For this reason, a state of entreaty, sincerity, and earnestness is essential in prayer. Shouting and clamoring crosses the boundary from sincerity into ostentation. In an authentic hadith, our Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'You are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; rather, you are calling upon Allah, Who is All-Hearing and near.' Transgressing in supplication is like asking for supernatural feats (miracles), asking for the rank of prophethood, or asking for things that are sinful. When Abdullah ibn Mughaffal heard his son pray, 'O Allah, when I enter Paradise, I ask You for the white palace on its right side,' he warned him and related that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'There will be a people who will transgress in supplication.' When supplicating, one must be balanced between fear and hope.

Do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set in order. Allah created the earth, established its order, settled you upon it, and provided sustenance. Your responsibility is either to improve it or to corrupt it. Let the goal of your desires be tawhid (monotheism), faith, obedience, justice, and righteousness. Seek to build, not to destroy; pursue goodness, not corruption. A person should reflect upon the catastrophe of being deprived of the things they need and avoid every form of mischief-making. When praying, be in a state of both fear and hope; fear and hope are like two wings on the spiritual path. Those who maintain this balance become among the muhsinun (the doers of good) who have attained the station of ihsan. Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.

Allah sends winds as heralds of glad tidings of His mercy. According to recitation variants, it is read as 'nashirat' or 'nushr'. These winds stir the stagnant air when it is about to rain, making motion the precursor to blessing. Wind is of eight kinds: four are punishment, and four are mercy. The winds of mercy are the nashirat, the mubashshirat, the mursalat, and the dhariyat. The movement of the winds is a divine dispensation. Indeed, they lift and carry heavy clouds. This is also noteworthy from the standpoint of physical science; heavy water droplets are borne by the buoyant force of air. This situation is an analogy for the resurrection of the dead. Allah sends down water upon a dead land and brings forth fruits with it; in like manner will the dead be raised.

A good land brings forth its vegetation richly by the permission of its Lord, while that which is bad yields only with difficulty and is useless. This is a parable for mankind. Prophets and divine messages are a mercy like rain. Human beings, too, are like the soil, divided into two categories: the good and the bad. The good benefit from the prophets, take heed, believe, and produce righteous deeds. The wicked, on the other hand, deny the blessings and remain deprived. Thus do We explain the verses in diverse ways for a people who give thanks.

Noah (Nuh) was sent as a prophet to his people. He told them to worship Allah and said that he feared for them the punishment of a tremendous day. The notables of the people accused him of clear misguidance. Noah declared that he was a messenger sent by the Lord of the worlds and that there was no misguidance in him. They denied him; so We saved Noah and those with him in the ark, and drowned those who denied Our verses. Then, to the people of 'Ad, We sent their brother Hud. He, too, called them to tawhid (monotheism). His people accused him of foolishness and lying. Hud reminded them of Allah's blessings and warned them of punishment. When they insisted on not abandoning the idols of their forefathers, the punishment came, and those who believed were saved.

And to the people of Thamud, We sent their brother Salih. He brought the she-camel of Allah as a miracle and told them not to harm her. Those who grew arrogant among the people transgressed the command of their Lord by slaughtering the she-camel; then the earthquake seized them and destroyed them. Afterwards, We sent the prophet Lot (Lut). His people were committing a grave obscenity by leaving women and turning to men. They sought to expel Lot and his followers. We saved Lot and his family, while his wife remained with the disbelievers. We rained down upon them a rain of punishment. And to Midian (Madyan), We sent Shu'ayb. He forbade cheating in measure and weight and causing corruption on the earth. A part of his people believed, while another part sat on every road threatening and hindering people from the way of Allah. Shu'ayb told them to await Allah's judgment. These stories clarify historical truths that had been corrupted before the revelation of the Quran and provide an admonition for humanity.

Elmalılı Hamdi Yazır addresses the purpose behind the narration of Quranic stories and the accounts transmitted by commentators concerning them. He states that some commentators, especially earlier ones, transmitted narrations circulating prior to the Quran, thereby demonstrating how the Quran corrected the corruptions within those narrations. However, he notes that those lacking expertise in tafsir perceived these transmissions as the very essence of the stories, straying from the path of Quranic truth, and seeking religion in bizarre interpretations outside the Sunnah. In response to them, he expresses that pure naturalists dismissed these accounts as 'fables of the ancients' or attributed them entirely to nature. The Quran, on the other hand, emphasizes that the truth lies between these two extremes and conveys the stories in the most beautiful manner. He indicates that these stories must be read with careful attention to the essence of each prophet's call, their method of conveying the message, their debates with their people, the outcomes of faith and disbelief, and shared values. He affirms that all causes of downfall and destruction stem from failing to heed the command of the Truth (al-Haqq), failing to appreciate the leaders sent by Allah, and ingratitude. He adds that the true religion is not a human-made social institution, but a divine establishment, and that the capacity of every nation for life and happiness is in harmony with the glory of the Creator.

Against the preaching of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), the arrogant notables among his people threaten to either expel him and the believers from their land or force them to return to their religion. Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) replies that returning to their religion after Allah had delivered them from disbelief would be fabricating a lie against Allah, and that this would not be possible unless Allah so willed. He states that they rely upon Allah and prays for Him to judge between them with justice. The disbelievers among the people, however, declare that those who follow Shu'ayb will surely be in ruin. Then the dreadful earthquake seizes them, and they are left fallen prone upon their knees in their dwellings. Those who denied Shu'ayb became as though they had never prospered there. Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) turns away from them, declaring that he had conveyed the truths sent by his Lord and had advised them, asking how he could now grieve over a disbelieving people. Elmalılı explains the word 'jusum' (cüsûm): it means collapsing and clinging to the ground chest-first while grasping both legs with the hands, just as a hare or bird sleeps. That is, they stumbled and fell prone upon their faces in their homeland such that not a trace of movement remained in them. He also notes that Shu'ayb felt sorrow over the destruction of his people, but, recognizing that they were not worthy of grief, severed his spiritual concern, neither gloating over their fate nor finding it permissible to lament for them.

To explain that the nations uprooted by this severe punishment deserved such an outcome, and to present a concise summary of the cautionary lessons from these five stories before moving to the sixth, the following verses were revealed: 'We never sent a prophet to any town but We seized its people with poverty and hardship so that they might humble themselves. Then We exchanged their suffering for good (prosperity), until they multiplied and said: 'Our fathers too were touched by hardship and joy.' So We seized them suddenly while they were unaware.' In his commentary on these verses, Elmalılı explains that the people of every town to which a prophet was sent were first afflicted with poverty and illness, and then granted abundance and health, thereby being tested with both bitter and sweet circumstances. This continued until they multiplied—that is, increased in wealth and population. By saying, 'Our fathers too were touched by hardship and joy,' they failed to recognize that these conditions stemmed from Allah's discipline, regarding them instead as natural and inevitable occurrences. It was then that We seized them suddenly. Whether the seizure being sudden means the destruction occurred instantaneously or unfolded over a period makes no difference; what matters is vigilance before the seizure begins.

Continuing: 'And if the people of those towns had believed and feared (Allah's punishment), We would certainly have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn.' Elmalılı notes that in this verse, faith and piety (taqwa) bring blessings, whereas denial leads to punishment. In the verses that follow, it is questioned whether the people of the towns felt secure that punishment would not come upon them while they slept at night or played in the forenoon. It is emphasized that none feel secure from Allah's plan (makr) except the people who are in loss. Elmalılı explains that the expression 'Allah's plan' is a metaphor signifying that He punishes His servants gradually and from an unexpected quarter. Furthermore, it is stated that it has become clear to those who inherit the earth after its previous inhabitants that if He had willed, He could have afflicted them too for their sins, but He seals their hearts so they do not hear the truth. Thus are some of the news of those cities narrated; their messengers had brought them clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in the truths they had previously denied. Thus does Allah seal the hearts of the disbelievers. We did not find most of them keeping their word; rather, We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient.

The story of Moses (Musa) is recounted in greater detail than the others because his miracles were more potent and the ignorance and tyranny of his people were more pervasive. Elmalılı dwells in detail on the meaning of the word 'mala'' (mele'). 'Mala'' denotes a council or assembly united on a common opinion, whose form and appearance fill the eyes, and whose stature and importance captivate hearts. In modern terms, this corresponds to 'high society' or the ruling elite. This council gathered around Pharaoh represented the entirety of the people. Moses was sent with signs to Pharaoh and this council of his. They, however, wronged those signs, treating them as lies and rejecting them. Moses came to Pharaoh and said, 'I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds; it is an obligation upon me to speak nothing concerning Allah except the truth. I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord; so send the Children of Israel with me.' Pharaoh demanded a miracle, saying, 'If you are of the truthful, then bring it forth!' Moses threw down his staff, and it became an enormous serpent. According to narration, when the serpent began slithering toward Pharaoh, Pharaoh grew terrified and pleaded, whereupon Moses took hold of it. Elmalılı explains that this transformation was not an overturning of essential reality, but rather a change in the form of the staff's matter, or the placement of the serpent's form in the mind in its stead. When Moses drew forth his hand from his bosom, it turned radiant white, shining brightly. These two miracles are manifestations of Allah's wrath and mercy.

The council (mala') of Pharaoh said, 'This is surely a very knowledgeable sorcerer; he wants to drive you out of your land. What do you instruct?' Elmalılı notes that the phrase 'what do you instruct?' is remarkably striking; this indicates that the governing authority of Pharaoh's regime rested in the hands of this consultative council. Furthermore, the statement 'He wants to drive you out of your land' suggests that the council was composed of the native population of Egypt. Some Quranic commentators have even posited that the matter was submitted to a public referendum. Elmalılı emphasizes that Pharaoh temporarily set aside his claim to divinity here, displaying a hypocritical humility by asking 'what do you instruct?', which represents a prominent example of Pharaoh's own sorcery. Moreover, his demand for a miracle from Moses indicates that Pharaoh was already aware that truthful prophets had come in the past and brought miracles.

Pharaoh's consultative council did not immediately launch an attack against the miracles of Moses (Musa), but instead proposed holding a contest. They said to him, "Stall Moses and his brother for a while, send heralds to the cities, and gather all the skilled magicians." This proposal demonstrates that mutual consultation (mushawarah and istisharah) is beneficial in bringing the truth to light. It also indicates that Aaron (Harun) was alongside Moses.

The assembled magicians put on a great display of magic, bewitching the eyes of the people and presenting terrifying illusions. They cast down thick ropes and staffs, making the valley appear full of snakes. According to narration, this was an optical illusion accomplished with hollow pieces of wood and leather filled with mercury, which moved when heated. However, Allah revealed to Moses to cast down his staff, and the staff swallowed all of their fabrications. Thus, the truth became manifest and falsehood vanished.

Faced with this event, the magicians, knowing the true limits of sorcery, realized that this was a divine miracle and immediately fell down in prostration, accepting faith. They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron." This demonstrates the value of knowledge and expertise: even expertise in the craft of magic enabled them to distinguish a miracle from sorcery. This shows what great benefits expertise in the doctrine of tawhid (the oneness of God) can offer humanity.

Pharaoh was humiliated by the magicians' embracing faith and concocted an intrigue to mislead public opinion. Rebuking them, he said: "Did you believe in him before I gave you permission? This is surely a plot; you conspired with Moses in the city to drive out its people from Egypt." Yet the reality was the sincere faith of the magicians in the face of the overwhelming power of the miracle. Pharaoh attempted to exploit patriotic sentiments to portray Moses and the believers as enemies.

Scholars have stated that these verses are among the greatest proofs regarding the virtue of knowledge. Because the magicians understood the essence of sorcery, they immediately realized that Moses' staff was not magic. Had they been ignorant, they might have fallen into doubt, thinking, "Perhaps he simply knows magic better than we do." Instead, they believed without hesitation. This shows that specialization in any field is an important means for recognizing the truth.

Some who wish to deny the reality of the miracles mentioned in the verses have interpreted them as metaphors and allegories. However, this stems from being entrenched in naturalistic assumptions and thereby denying miracles. Yet once reason verifies the authenticity of a transmitted report, if it is conveyed as an extraordinary occurrence, reason should not judge it merely by its own conventional standards, but investigate its intrinsic possibility. The power of Allah is limitless; He can do whatever He wills. To claim that extraordinary events are impossible is also contrary to the scientific mindset, for science does not deny rare occurrences; it merely generalizes.

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi relates that there are three views regarding whether a departure from customary norms (khariq al-adah) is possible: the Ahl al-Sunnah generally regard it as possible; naturalist philosophers deem it impossible; and the Mu'tazilah accept part of it as possible and part as impossible. Naturalists claim that acknowledging extraordinary occurrences invalidates scientific causality. However, this claim is inconsistent, because whether without a cause or through causes, the possibility of extraordinary events is inevitable in every case. Allah, the All-Knowing and All-Powerful, creates whatever He wills.

In modern philosophy, the certainty of natural sciences has been debated, and Kant's view has been presented as a middle path. According to Kant, because the laws of nature are derived from experience, they are not strictly necessary but merely report what has occurred. This view is compatible with the approach of Muslim theologians (mutakallimun).

The possibility of miracles is no more extraordinary than the creation and destruction of the universe. Customary events (adah) fall within our certain knowledge, yet the possibility of the contrary is likewise within our knowledge. For example, that a snake comes from another snake is certain, but its creation from something else is also entirely possible.

Events in the universe operate through the balance of two opposing harmonies: positive and negative. All recognition and differentiation occur by virtue of a departure from the customary (an extraordinary occurrence). Miracles are also of these distinguishing characteristics and constitute a divine custom (adah ilahiyyah). They are known not through pure reason and analogy, but through observation and transmitted reports.

Some deny miracles by saying, "We are more advanced than the ancients; we can do what they could not do." This is an obstinate attitude that harms science and progress. They fail to see the variability of nature and that it begins anew with fresh creation at every moment. For example, it is normal for a staff to decay and change over time; for that same transformation to happen instantaneously is by no means impossible.

The Quran draws attention to normal customs, but it does not deny miracles. One must not place limits on Allah's power. In verse 7:54, it is emphasized that both creation and command belong to Allah. The stories of the prophets should be understood through the exemplar of this initial creation; the hearts of those who deny are sealed.

The laws of nature are formed through observation, experimentation, and generalization, but they are not absolute. Our knowledge concerning causes is incomplete and relative. For something to be deemed impossible, a genuine logical contradiction is required. For example, instantaneous creation—much like an electric current suddenly dropping to zero—is possible. Rigid naturalists fail to see these possibilities and fall into pessimism.

Pharaoh, assuming Moses' miracle was sorcery, gathered the magicians. When the magicians were defeated, they embraced faith. Pharaoh threatened them, saying, "I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides and crucify you." The magicians replied, "Indeed, to our Lord we will return," and remained steadfast in their faith. They declared that Pharaoh was seeking revenge against them solely because they had believed.

The magicians pointed out that death is inevitable, that martyrdom is a reward, and that Pharaoh himself would also die. They prayed to Allah for patience and to die as Muslims. This event made it absolute that the miracle was not magic. Some scholars state that the magicians were martyred, and the flow of the verses supports this.

The notables among Pharaoh's people incited him against Moses and the Children of Israel. They said, "If you leave them, they will cause corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods." Here, the term 'gods' refers to the deities that Pharaoh approved of and permitted. In reality, Pharaoh considered himself the supreme lord.

Pharaoh was gripped by immense fear in the face of Moses' staff miracle. To conceal this fear and boost his men's morale, without even uttering Moses' name, he attempted to dispel their anxieties by claiming, 'We will kill the male children of the Children of Israel and spare their women; indeed, we hold overwhelming dominance over them.' In fact, he was so terrified of Moses that he did not even dare utter his name. Through these words, he implied that Moses' strength derived from his people, claiming he could crush and destroy them.

When Moses saw that his people were thrown into panic by Pharaoh's threats, he gave them two commands and two glad tidings: Seek help from Allah and be patient. For the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as an inheritance to whom He wills of His servants. The favorable outcome belongs to the righteous who fear Allah. If you too protect yourselves (through piety), the ultimate outcome will be yours. With these words, he sought to reassure his people.

The Children of Israel, however, complained despite the comfort offered by Moses (Musa), saying, 'We were suffering persecution before you came to us, and we are still suffering after you have come.' These words reflected both the pain felt under Pharaoh's oppression and a longing for deliverance. Moses gave them glad tidings, saying, 'Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy, make you successors in the land, and see how you act.'

To warn Pharaoh and his people, Allah afflicted them with years of famine and hardship. Whenever good came to them, they said, 'This is our due,' but when evil befell them, they blamed Moses and those with him as an evil omen. Thereupon, Allah sent upon them distinct signs such as the flood, locusts, pests, frogs, and blood. Each time, they pleaded with Moses and promised that they would believe, but as soon as the punishment was lifted, they broke their word.

In the end, Allah took retribution upon them and drowned them all in the sea. They deserved this punishment because they denied His verses and were heedless of them. As for the Children of Israel who had been oppressed and despised, He made them heirs to the blessed eastern and western parts of the land. Your Lord's gracious promise to them was fulfilled because of their patience. And He destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had constructed and erected.

After the Children of Israel crossed the sea, they came upon a people devoted to idols and said to Moses, 'Make for us a god just as they have gods.' Moses rebuked them for their ignorance, replying, 'Indeed, the religion these people follow is doomed to destruction, and what they do is futile. Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, when He has favored you above all the worlds?'

When Allah delivered the Children of Israel from the oppression of Pharaoh, He put them through a great trial. Pharaoh was inflicting the worst torment upon them by slaughtering their sons and sparing their daughters.

When the Children of Israel encountered a people worshipping idols, they asked Moses to make similar idols for them. Moses told them that they were acting out of ignorance and reminded them that the religion of the idolaters was false and that Allah had favored them above all the worlds.
Moses emphasized to his people that seeking a deity other than Allah was ingratitude. Reminding them of their deliverance from Pharaoh, he stated that they ought to be grateful for these blessings.

Moses was appointed thirty nights, and ten nights were added to them, completing forty nights. Leaving his brother Aaron (Harun) as his deputy over his people, Moses went to the appointment set by Allah. During this period, purification was attained through fasting and worship.

At the appointed time, Moses was blessed with the speech of Allah. However, upon his desire to see Allah, he was told, "You will never see Me"; and when Allah manifested His glory to the mountain, it crumbled to dust, and Moses fell unconscious. When he recovered, he repented and declared that he was the first of the believers.

Allah wrote for Moses on the Tablets concerning all things, commanding him to adhere firmly to them and instructing his people to take the best of them. Furthermore, it was conveyed that those who behave arrogantly on earth would be turned away from His verses, and that the deeds of those who deny the verses and the Hereafter would come to nothing.

In Moses' absence, the Children of Israel fashioned a statue of a calf from ornaments that made a lowing sound, and they worshipped it. When they were stricken with remorse and felt deep regret, they said, "If our Lord does not have mercy upon us, we shall surely be among the losers." When Moses returned angry and grieved, he put down the Tablets and questioned his brother Aaron. Aaron explained that the people deemed him weak and almost killed him. Moses prayed to Allah to forgive him and his brother. It was revealed that those who worshipped the calf would face wrath and humiliation, but those who repented would be forgiven. Then Moses took up the Tablets; inscribed upon them were guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord.

In verse 151, Aaron (peace be upon him) defends himself in an eloquent manner to appease the anger of his brother Moses, explaining that he is innocent. Moses then asks Allah's forgiveness first for himself and then for his brother; this indicates that Aaron too was in need of seeking forgiveness (istighfar).

In verse 152, it is stated that those who took the calf as a deity will suffer humiliation in this world and divine wrath in the Hereafter. As for the punishment of al-Samiri, it was the affliction of 'do not touch'. This punishment serves as a general warning for those who invent lies against Allah and is not exclusive to the Children of Israel.

In verse 153, it is emphasized that for those who commit evil deeds and then repent and believe, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. The door of repentance is open and Allah fulfills His promise; this stands as a source of hope alongside the warnings in the preceding verses.

In verse 154, when Moses' anger subsides, he takes up the Tablets again. In these Tablets are guidance and mercy; however, this is for those who fear Allah. The taking up of the Tablets became possible once Moses had calmed down.

In verse 155, Moses chooses seventy men from his people and takes them to Mount Sinai (Tur-i Sina) for repentance at the appointed time. However, when they say they will not believe until they see Allah, they are seized by a violent earthquake. Moses states that this is a trial and asks Allah for forgiveness.

In verse 156, Moses asks for good in this world and the Hereafter. Allah declares that His punishment strikes whom He wills, while His mercy encompasses all things. Yet this mercy is specifically ordained for those who possess piety (taqwa), give zakah, and believe in His verses. This demonstrates that mercy will subsequently be specified for them.

In verse 157, the characteristics of the unlettered Prophet (al-nabiyy al-ummi) are described: he enjoins good, forbids evil, makes lawful what is wholesome, and prohibits what is foul. He relieves them of their heavy burdens and the shackles that bound them. This Prophet is found written in the Torah and the Gospel and is recognized by his attributes.

Those who believe in that Prophet, honor him, support him, and follow the light sent down with him are the ones who attain salvation. This mercy is addressed not only to the Children of Israel, but to all of humanity, and has been decreed for the ummah of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).

Allah the Almighty conveys that in the story of Moses, the premises of mercy and punishment are distinguished from one another, and with the prophethood of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), mercy has become a universal principle. Mercy is now open not merely to a single people, but to all mankind. Indeed, it has been revealed: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah!" (az-Zumar 39:53). Moses (peace be upon him), at the appointed time and place (miqat) on Mount Sinai, requested this dispensation of mercy for himself and his people, but Allah declared that this would only be possible by following the Prophet of the end times and his law (Shari'ah). Thus, the story of Moses points toward the coming Prophet of mercy.

At this point, there is a manifestation of the divine istiwa mentioned in the verse: "Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days and then established Himself over the Throne" (al-A'raf, 7:54). As stated in the noble hadith: "Time has revolved back to its shape on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth." With the era of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), an entirely new epoch of history commenced, and the dispensations of previous prophets merged within this universal order. The descriptions in the Torah and the Gospel likewise corroborate this reality, demonstrating that Moses was a prophet sent solely to the Children of Israel, preparing them for the Prophet who was to come.

For this reason, Allah Almighty commands the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as follows: "Say: O mankind! Indeed, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all. To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. There is no deity except Him. He gives life and causes death. So believe in Allah and His unlettered Prophet—who believes in Allah and all His words—and follow him so that you may be guided."
