(Al-A'raf, 7/158) This verse clearly proclaims that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was sent to all of humanity. The claims of the Jews that "Muhammad was sent only to the Arabs" are groundless and consist merely of distorting the Torah.

Then Allah informs that among the people of Moses (Musa) there was a community that guided to the right path: "And among the people of Moses is a community which guides by truth and by it establishes justice." (Al-A'raf, 7/159) They were people who followed the truth and judged with justice. Allah divided them into twelve tribes and gave a separate spring to each of them. He also made clouds a shade over them and sent down manna and quails. Yet they showed ingratitude for these blessings and wronged themselves. Afterwards, Allah commanded them to settle in a town and say 'hittah' (forgiveness), but the wrongdoers among them altered this word to say 'hintah' (wheat). Thereupon, Allah sent down a punishment from heaven upon them.

Allah reminds the Children of Israel of what befell the town by the seashore. The people of that town were violating the Sabbath prohibition and fishing. On the Sabbath, the fish would come in shoals, whereas on other days they would not come. A group among them said to those who warned against this evil, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah will destroy?" Those who warned replied, "To be an excuse before your Lord and so that perhaps they may avoid evil." Ultimately, when that people forgot the admonitions, those who warned were saved, while the wrongdoers were subjected to a severe punishment. When they exceeded all bounds in what was forbidden, it was said to them, "Be despised apes!"

Allah informs that until the Day of Resurrection, He will send against the Children of Israel those who will inflict upon them the worst punishment. Indeed, by sending Nebuchadnezzar (Buhtunnasr) against them, He ruined their state and condemned them to heavy taxes. Nonetheless, Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful. Then He dispersed them across the earth in fragments, dividing them into different communities, righteous and wicked. There are good among them, and there are bad. He tested them with blessings and tribulations so that perhaps they might return to the truth.

Afterwards, there succeeded a corrupt generation who inherited the Book (the Torah). Saying, "We will surely be forgiven anyway," they coveted worldly goods and took bribes. Yet the covenant had been taken from them that they would say nothing about Allah except the truth, and they had read and studied the Book. Allah emphasizes that the home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Him, and proclaims that the reward of those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer will not be lost.

In verses 169–170, mention is made of a corrupt generation that succeeded the Children of Israel. They inherited the Torah, read it, and attained the position of passing judgment. However, they did not hold fast to the Book; they used it for their own interests. In exchange for worldly gain, they would alter the truth, hope that their sins would be forgiven, and when the same gain presented itself again, they would take it once more. Yet a pledge had been taken from them to abide by the rulings in the Book. The home of the Hereafter is better for the righteous. As for those who hold fast to the Book and perform prayer, they will not lose their reward.

In verse 171, those who did not hold firmly to the Book given to the Children of Israel are reminded of Mount Sinai (Tur) being raised over them as if it were a canopy, about to fall upon them. Allah commanded them: 'Hold firmly to what We have given you and remember what is in it so that you may be protected.' This was a covenant taken under compulsion. The raising of the mountain shows Allah's power and the consequence of defying His command. People should obey the truth willingly, without having to be forced to submit. Natural phenomena are also signs of Allah's power and warn mankind.

In verses 172–174, it is related that Allah brought forth their descendants from the Children of Adam, made them bear witness against themselves, and asked, 'Am I not your Lord?' to which they replied, 'Yes, we testify.' This was so that on the Day of Resurrection they could not say, 'We were unaware of this.' There are two views regarding the nature of this covenant (mithaq): First, that it is an allegory (tamthil); Allah created human beings with an innate disposition (fitrah) inclined toward monotheism (tawhid), enabling them to recognize Him through intellect and proofs. Second, that it is an actual event; a covenant concluded in the realm of souls. Yet both views emphasize that the capacity to recognize Allah exists in the creation of man and that he must remain faithful to this covenant. This covenant is a primordial pact and forms the foundation of human responsibility.

In verses 175–176, the story is told of a man who, although given verses/signs, stripped them away and followed Satan. Had Allah willed, He would have elevated him, but he clung to the earth. His condition is like that of a dog: whether you drive it away or leave it alone, it lolls out its tongue and pants. This is the parable of the people who deny the verses/signs. This story is recounted so that a lesson may be drawn.

In verses 177–181, it is declared how wretched the condition of those who deny the verses/signs is, that whoever Allah guides is rightly guided, and whoever He leaves to stray is in ruin. It is stated that many of the jinn and mankind were created for Hell, because although they have hearts, eyes, and ears, they do not use them, and they are even lower than cattle. The most beautiful names belong to Allah; so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate regarding His names. Likewise, among mankind there is a community that guides to the truth and establishes justice.

In this section, the covenant (mithaq) that Allah took from human beings is dwelt upon. This covenant is an inherent commitment that human beings bring with them from creation. The progeny taken from the loins of Adam acknowledged their own existence and the oneness of their Lord. This commitment exists in the innate disposition (fitrah) of every human being and becomes conscious upon reaching puberty. While some state that this covenant was taken in the realm of souls, others say it takes place upon reaching puberty. What is fundamental, however, is that every person feels this commitment within themselves and bears responsibility.

There are different views regarding the covenant (mithaq). According to one view, this commitment begins when the progeny is taken from the father's loins and is completed through the stages passed in the mother's womb. Puberty is the time of the actual execution of this commitment. Another view contends that the covenant is taken upon reaching puberty. The expressions "ahdh" (taking) and "ishhad" (making testify) in the verse indicate the moment when a person begins to gain self-awareness. Both interpretations form the foundation of man's accountability before Allah.

By reminding them of this covenant, Allah prevented people from putting forward excuses on the Day of Resurrection, such as "we were unaware of this" or "our forefathers associated partners with Allah, and we were only descendants after them." Every individual is responsible for their own commitment, and the sin of forefathers cannot be placed upon another. This explanation rejects blind imitation and the evasion of responsibility.

Then, the story of a person who, despite having been given verses, stripped himself of them and followed Satan is related. Following worldly love and his desires, this person debased himself and remained in continuous distress, like the panting of a dog. This story represents the state of those who deny the verses. For those who plunge into debasement, it is the same whether they are warned or not.

Those who deny Allah's verses are drawn step by step toward their downfall through istidraj (gradual enticement to ruin) from a place they do not know. Istidraj is a person assuming blessings are in their favor, whereas in reality they cause an increase in their punishment. This is a severe trap. Furthermore, the polytheists are criticized for not reflecting that there is no madness in the prophet, for not looking into the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, and for not realizing that their appointed time has drawn near. As for the timing of the Day of Judgment, it is known only with Allah.

In verse 187, the polytheists ask the Prophet (peace be upon him) when the Day of Judgment will take place. According to two separate narrations, in one it was the Jews and in the other the Quraysh who asked this question. Allah informs that knowledge of the Hour's time belongs solely to Him, that it will come suddenly, and that most people do not know this. These questions are asked as though with the impression that the Prophet must certainly know it, yet the answer is clear: that knowledge is with Allah.

In verse 188, the Prophet (peace be upon him) expresses that he possesses no power to bring benefit or harm to himself, but can only do as much as Allah wills. Had he known the unseen (ghayb), he would have done more good and no harm would have touched him. He is only a warner and a bearer of glad tidings. Here, it is emphasized that knowledge and power are distinct things; knowing the unseen does not entail divine lordship.

In verses 189–190, it is related that man was created from a single soul and that his mate was created from it. This soul is Adam, and his mate is Eve. When the couple come together, the woman bears a light burden and becomes pregnant. As childbirth approaches, they pray to Allah for a righteous child. But when Allah grants them a righteous child, they begin to associate partners with Him concerning this blessing. This shows that polytheism (shirk) emerged later. Most people forget this truth and follow the way of their forefathers.

In verses 191–195, it is stated that the idols associated as partners with Allah cannot create anything, are themselves created, and can help neither themselves nor those who worship them. If you call them to the right path, they do not hear; calling them and remaining silent are equal. What the polytheists worship are servants just like themselves. They do not have feet to walk with, hands to grasp with, eyes to see with, or ears to hear with. The Prophet (peace be upon him) is told that the polytheists and their partners may set traps, but he is under Allah's protection.

In verses 196–198, it is emphasized that the guardian (wali—helper and protector) of the Prophet (peace be upon him) is Allah. Allah is the One Who sent down the Book, and He protects His righteous servants. Those worshipped besides Allah, however, can neither help you nor themselves. If you call them to guidance, they do not hear; you see them looking at you, yet they do not see. In fact, in addition to the idols, these verses also encompass the leaders of the polytheists; they, too, do not hear or see in any real sense.

In verse 199, the Prophet (peace be upon him) is commanded to treat with pardon, to enjoin customary good (urf), and to turn away from the ignorant. 'Urf' refers to necessary and beneficial deeds that people recognize and accept as good. However, not every custom is urf; invalid traditions are not enjoined. Enjoining urf requires that the commanded deed be recognized good (maruf—good and beneficial). Here, it is recalled that the fundamental principles of Islam were first explained and then commanded.

In verses 200–206, it is commanded to seek refuge in Allah whenever a whisper comes from Satan. Those who fear Allah pause and reflect at the moment of whisper, retaining their insight. The brethren of the devils, on the other hand, persist in error. When a verse is not brought to the Prophet (peace be upon him), the polytheists say, 'Why did you not piece it together?'; he replies that he only follows revelation. The Quran is insights from the Lord, a guidance, and a mercy. When the Quran is recited, one should remain silent and listen, and Allah should be remembered morning and evening. The angels also prostrate before Allah and do not behave arrogantly.

Verse 199 puts forward a broad principle covering areas such as morality, law, and governance. According to this principle, one must turn away from the ignorant and not respond in kind to their foolish words. Serving as an interpretation of this verse, it is stated in a hadith qudsi: 'The highest of virtues is that you seek out the one who cuts you off, bestow favors upon the one who deprives you, and forgive the one who wrongs you.' According to narration, when this verse was revealed, our Prophet (peace be upon him) asked, 'How can this be when wrath has occurred?', whereupon verse 200 was revealed.

In verses 200–201, it is commanded to immediately seek refuge in Allah in the event of an instigation from Satan. Allah hears and knows; seeking refuge inwardly in the heart is also sufficient. The God-fearing (muttaqin), even when the slightest phantom from Satan touches them, pause to think, remember, and take heed. While this verse is an address to the Messenger of Allah, it is a general warning to all believers.

In verses 202–203, those who are brothers to the devils (devils among humans and jinn) are described. They assist one another in temptation and cannot desist from evil. When you do not bring a verse to the Prophet, they malign his prophethood by saying, 'So you couldn't put it together, eh?' The Messenger of Allah [was told]: Say, 'I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord.' This Quran is insights from your Lord, a guidance, and a mercy.

In verse 204, when the Quran is recited, listening to it and remaining silent is commanded, so that mercy may be attained. This command applies in prayer, in the sermon (khutbah), or in any gathering. Listening and remaining silent are made conditional upon recitation (qira'ah). Recitation is the audible reading by an intelligent person aimed at comprehension. For this reason, the sound coming from a gramophone or radio is not recitation, but an echo; listening to it is not obligatory (wajib).

While listening to the Quran played on a gramophone is not obligatory, it should not be thought of as though not listening to it were obligatory. For even if it is not a complete recitation, it is similar to recitation, and disrespect is not permissible. Even though playing the Quran in an unworthy place is a sin, if it has been played, listening to it earns reward. In such a case, a Muslim should not show disrespect and, if possible, should remove it to a suitable place.

In verse 205, our Prophet (peace be upon him) and his community are commanded to remember their Lord within the soul and inwardly. This remembrance (dhikr) must be done with humility and fear, imploringly, in heart and mind, quietly, morning and evening. One must not be among the heedless, must keep the heart awake, and must continue remembering Allah. Remembrance should be in such a way that it does not hinder sound reflection.

There is a wondrous relationship between the soul and the body in human beings. The effect in the soul reflects upon the body, and the effect in the body reflects upon the soul. For example, when one imagines something sour, the mouth waters. When remembrance with the tongue becomes a habit, an impression is formed in the realm of imagination, a light rises from the soul, and this light is reflected back onto the tongue. This mutual interaction is endless; the journey of gnosis (marifah) progresses toward the pleasure of the Truth (al-Haqq), its vessel being the self (nafs) and its rudder remembrance (dhikr). Heedlessness is absolute danger.

In verse 206, those in the presence of your Lord (the angels) do not show arrogance in worshipping Him; they glorify and praise Him, and they prostrate. When this verse is recited, performing the prostration of recitation (tilawah) is prescribed. As narrated from our Prophet (peace be upon him): 'When the son of Adam recites the verse of prostration and prostrates, Satan withdraws weeping and says, "Woe to me; I was commanded to prostrate and I rebelled, so for me is the Fire."' Through this remembrance and prostration, a path is opened from al-A'raf to Paradise.

They ask you about the spoils of war (anfal). Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger. That is, the authority to rule concerning the spoils belongs solely to Allah and the Prophet; no one else has a say or approval. So fear Allah, settle disputes among yourselves, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are truly believers.

True believers are those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited, and who put their trust solely in their Lord. They perform the prayer properly and spend out of what We have provided for them. It is they who are the true believers; for them are high ranks with their Lord, forgiveness, and a generous provision.

When your Lord brought you out of your home for the truth, a group of the believers were reluctant. Even after the truth had become clear, they were arguing with you as if they were being driven toward death. Allah had promised you one of the two parties: either the caravan or the Quraysh army. You wished for the unarmed, weaker caravan, whereas Allah willed to establish the truth with His words and to cut off the root of the disbelievers.

Remember when you implored your Lord for help, and He answered your prayer: 'I am helping you with a thousand angels following one another.' Allah made this only as glad tidings and that your hearts might find peace. Victory comes only from Allah. He granted you security by casting slumber over you, sent down rain from the sky to purify you and to remove the whispers of Satan from you, to strengthen your hearts, and to make your footing firm.

Your Lord revealed to the angels: 'I am with you, so give steadfastness to the believers. I will cast terror into the hearts of the disbelievers, so strike above their necks and strike every fingertip of theirs.' That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger. And whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, let him know that Allah is severe in punishment. Taste this, then; and for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire.

O you who believe! When you encounter the disbelievers marching together for battle, do not turn your backs to them. Whoever turns his back on that day, unless maneuvering for battle or joining another company, incurs the wrath of Allah, and his abode is Hell. It was not you who killed them, but Allah killed them. And when you threw, it was not you who threw, but Allah who threw. This was to test the believers with a good test. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

In these verses, it is described how, prior to the Battle of Badr, the polytheists asked Allah for victory (fath), yet the outcome turned against them. Clinging to the covering of the Kaaba, the polytheists had prayed for Him to help whichever of the two armies was superior. Their prayer was answered, but because their condition was not sound, the result turned in favor of the believers. In fact, this verse shows that the cause of the battle was the aggressive stance of the polytheists. If they abandon this desire—that is, if they cease opposing Allah and His Messenger—it is better for them. But if they return to the thought of war, Allah too will return, and their host, no matter how numerous, will be of no avail. Allah is with the believers, yet this companionship is not unconditional; it depends on complete faith and the fulfillment of necessary conditions.

Then the believers are addressed: Obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you hear. Do not be like those who say 'we hear' while they do not hear. For the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the mute who do not understand and do not reflect. What is meant here are those who have ears yet do not hear the truth, have tongues yet do not speak the truth, and have minds yet do not comprehend the truth. Such people are lower than harmful beasts in human form. One who is born deaf cannot speak because speech is learned through hearing. However, the deafness and muteness here pertain to senses deliberately closed against the truth; there is nothing of good in these people.

If Allah had recognized any good in them, He would surely have made them hear, but they did not listen to the voice of truth; thus there is no good in them. Even if Allah had made them hear, they would still have turned away and not benefited from what they heard. Here, one cannot say, 'Why did Allah not compel them?' because the matter pertains to will and partial choice (juz'i ikhtiyar); compulsion does not enter this realm. These people heed nothing other than compulsion, so do not be like them.

O you who believe! Respond to Allah and the Messenger when the Prophet calls you to that which gives you life. This call is an invitation that brings you out from a state akin to death into a free and eternal life. Allah intervenes between a person and his heart, and you will surely be gathered unto Him. And guard against a tribulation (fitnah) that does not afflict only those among you who do wrong; it spreads and encompasses everyone. This tribulation arises from sins such as showing laxity in commanding good and forbidding evil. Like the act of someone drilling a hole in the bottom of a ship, this tribulation affects everyone aboard. Allah's punishment is severe; therefore protect yourselves from tribulation. Remember when you were a few, deemed weak and oppressed in the land, fearing that the people would abduct you. Allah gave you shelter, strengthened you with His aid, and provided you with pure sustenance so that you might be grateful.

O you who believe! Do not betray Allah and the Messenger, lest you knowingly betray your own trusts. Your wealth and your children are nothing but a means of trial; and with Allah is a great reward. If you are mindful of Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan—an insight distinguishing truth from falsehood), expiate your bad deeds, and forgive you. Allah is the Possessor of great bounty. This 'furqan' makes you a radiant and enlightened community, like the dawn breaking in the darkness of night, covers your faults, and elevates your honor.

Remember when the disbelievers plotted against you to restrain you, kill you, or expel you; Allah countered their plotting with the best of plots (the permission for the Hijrah). The polytheists gathered at Dar al-Nadwah and made plans to imprison, banish, or kill the Prophet (peace be upon him). At the proposal of Abu Jahl, they decided to choose a young man from every tribe to kill him collectively. When Gabriel informed him of the situation, our Prophet had Ali lie in his bed and took refuge in the cave with Abu Bakr. When they raided in the morning, they were astonished to see Ali.

When the verses were recited to them, these disbelievers said, 'We have heard; if we wished, we could say the like of this; these are nothing but legends of the ancients.' They even challenged, 'O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or bring upon us a painful punishment.' Yet Allah was not going to punish them while you were among them, nor does He punish them while they seek forgiveness (istighfar). But now they prevent people from the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), whereas only the righteous and God-fearing (al-muttaqun) are worthy of its custodianship. Their prayer at the Kaaba is nothing but whistling and clapping of hands. So taste the punishment because of your disbelief. Those who spend their wealth to hinder others from the path of Allah will continue to spend it; then it will become a source of regret for them, and they will be overcome. The disbelievers will be gathered and driven into Hell. Allah will separate the vile from the pure, heap the vile one upon another, and cast them all into Hell. Say to them: If they desist, what is past will be forgiven them; but if they return to rebellion, the precedent of earlier nations (sunnatullah) has already been established for them.

The polytheists devised all kinds of plots against the Prophet. Allah, in turn, countered their plots and foiled their plans. He gave them hope for a time and kept them occupied, and then, rendering all their efforts fruitless, He facilitated the Prophet's emigration (hijrah). At Badr as well, He misled them by making the Muslims appear few in their eyes; thus, Allah's scheming (makr) was intended to nullify the scheming of the schemers and punish them. The action of Allah is far removed from deception and trickery; His scheme serves to thwart the plotting of the plotters and bring about good. This expression is an instance of mushakalah (figurative correspondence), and scheming in the literal sense cannot be attributed to Allah.

Polytheists such as Nadr ibn al-Harith denied the Quran when they heard it, saying, "These are tales of the ancients." They even challenged, "If this is indeed the truth from Allah, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring upon us a painful punishment." However, Allah did not punish them immediately because the Prophet was among them and there were those among them who repented and sought forgiveness (istighfar). The Prophet was the very embodiment of mercy; punishment would not be sent down upon a place where he was present. Furthermore, as long as there were people repenting and seeking forgiveness, punishment would not come. This is Allah's established way (sunnah).

The polytheists were barring people from al-Masjid al-Haram. Yet, they were not the guardians of al-Masjid al-Haram; its guardians are none but the righteous (muttaqin). What they performed beside the House of Allah in the name of prayer and worship was nothing more than whistling and clapping hands. In this manner, they amused themselves under the pretense of worshipping, and by making noise, they disturbed the peace of the Prophet. That they were not punished despite this was because the Prophet and those who repented were among them; it was not because they did not deserve punishment.

The disbelievers were spending their wealth to turn people away from the path of Allah. At Badr, they made a particular effort toward this. But in the end, this wealth will become a source of anguish and regret for them; it will go to waste, and ultimately they will be defeated and driven to Hell. Allah will thereby separate the wicked from the good, pile them all together, and heap them into Hell. It is they who are the true losers. Say to them, O Prophet: if they desist, what is past will be forgiven them; but if they return to fighting, they will perish in accordance with the precedent of the earlier peoples.

Allah commanded fighting until fitnah (persecution and discord) is eliminated and religion belongs entirely to Allah. If the enemy desists, Allah sees what they do; if they do not desist, Allah is your protector. As for the spoils of war, know this: one-fifth of whatever spoils you take belongs to Allah, the Prophet, his relatives, orphans, the needy (miskin), and the stranded traveler. The remaining four-fifths are distributed among the warriors. This was revealed after the Battle of Badr. On that day, Allah aided the believers, granting them victory with a small force against a numerous enemy. The Prophet saw the enemy as few in a dream, which increased the courage of the believers. By causing both sides to see each other as few, Allah brought about the victory He had decreed. This is a miracle demonstrating that all matters are returned to Allah.

O you who believe, when you encounter an enemy force in battle, stand firm and remember Allah much. This provides morale and leads to victory and divine reward. Even battle must not keep you from remembering Allah; for ultimately, all matters return to Him.

In the Battle of Badr, Allah brought about a wondrous victory by making both sides appear few and weak in each other's eyes. The believers took courage seeing the enemy as few, while the disbelievers initially underestimated the believers, and once the battle began, saw them as twice their own number. This is a miracle of Allah's power.

Believers must not dispute with one another; otherwise, they will fall into fear and lose their strength. Allah is with those who are patient. Do not go out to battle insolently and ostentatiously like the polytheists; Allah encompasses all that they do.

Satan made their deeds attractive to the polytheists and said, "No one can overcome you today, and I am your protector." But when the two sides came in sight of each other, he fled and said, "I have nothing to do with you; I fear Allah." This demonstrates the ultimate outcome of arrogance and falsehood.

The hypocrites and those with disease in their hearts said of the believers, "Their religion has deluded them." Yet whoever puts their trust in Allah, Allah is sufficient for them. Even if the believers are few in number, they prevail with the help of Allah.

The angels take the souls of the disbelievers, striking their faces and their backs, and saying, "Taste the punishment of the Blazing Fire." This is the consequence of the sins their own hands have earned; Allah is never unjust to His servants.

Allah does not alter a blessing He has bestowed upon a people unless they change what is in themselves. Pharaoh and earlier peoples were destroyed because they denied the verses and signs. This is a divine law.

In the sight of Allah, the worst of living creatures are those who persist in disbelief and repeatedly break their treaties. If you encounter them in war, punish them in such a way as to make an example of them for those behind them. If you fear treachery from a people, inform them openly that the treaty is terminated; indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous.

The disbelievers cannot escape or frustrate Allah. Prepare against them whatever force and warhorses you can muster. This will deter the enemies, and whatever you spend in the way of Allah will be paid back to you in full.

If the enemy inclines toward peace, you too incline toward peace and put your trust in Allah. He supports you with His help and with the believers. It is Allah who joined the hearts of the believers; even if you had spent everything on earth, you could not have united their hearts.

Allah Almighty informs that the disbelievers should not think they have escaped or outstripped the truth. They can never frustrate Allah, the Prophet, or the people of truth and justice. Those who break their covenants cannot escape the punishment for their betrayal; they will certainly be seized. This warning recalls the state of the traitors mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah, verse 13: because they broke their pledge, they were cursed and their hearts were hardened.

The believers are commanded to prepare against the enemy whatever force and tethered horses they can muster. This preparation is intended to deter and subdue both the polytheists of Mecca and other enemies whom they do not know. Whatever is spent in the way of Allah will be repaid in full, and no injustice will be done. Just as in the example of the two vineyards in Surah al-Kahf, verse 33, deeds will not go to waste.

If the enemy inclines toward peace, the believers should also incline toward peace. The primary objective is not war, but peace. Trust should be placed in Allah, and there should be no fear of schemes and deception. If the enemy intends to deceive, the help of Allah is sufficient. Indeed, Allah supported the Prophet with His aid and with the believers, and He bound their hearts together. While there was formerly enmity between the tribes of Aws and Khazraj, they became brothers through Islam.

Allah is sufficient for the Prophet and the believers who follow him. While the believers were being encouraged to jihad, it was initially declared that twenty steadfast individuals could overcome two hundred disbelievers. Later, however, this burden was lightened; knowing there was weakness, it was stated that one hundred steadfast individuals could overcome two hundred, and a thousand could overcome two thousand. Allah is with those who are patient.

It is not fitting for any prophet to take captives until he has achieved a decisive victory and thoroughly subdued the enemy in the land. While taking captives and demanding ransom at Badr meant desiring worldly goods, Allah wills the Hereafter. Had there not been a prior decree from Allah, a severe punishment would have struck on account of taking this ransom. Yet Allah is Forgiving and Merciful; henceforth, the spoils of war may be consumed as lawful and good.

The captives should be told that if Allah finds any good in their hearts, He will grant them something better than what was taken from them and will forgive their sins. According to the narration of Abbas, he became a Muslim when he disclosed to the Prophet the gold he had secretly entrusted to his wife. If the captives act treacherously, they are doomed to be crushed, for they have already betrayed Allah before. Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise.

Those who believed, emigrated, and strove with their wealth and lives, along with those who sheltered and aided them, are allies of one another. As for the believers who have not yet emigrated, there is no bond of guardianship with them until they emigrate; however, if they seek help in matters of religion, assistance must be extended, provided it is not against a people with whom you have a treaty. The disbelievers are also allies of one another; if the believers do not ally with and support one another as well, discord will spread across the earth. Those who emigrate later are also from you; yet ties of kinship have greater priority in the Book of Allah.

During the Battle of Badr, Abbas was also among the captives. He had twenty uqiyyahs (eight hundred dirhams) of gold with him, which he had brought to feed the polytheist soldiers. Abbas claimed that he had already accepted Islam beforehand, but had joined the battle under compulsion. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said that if what he said was true, Allah would grant him his reward, but outward appearances were against them. After paying the ransom, Abbas asked for the return of the gold, but the Prophet refused, saying, "Do you ask for what you took to use against us? No, by no means."

The Prophet ordered Abbas to also pay the ransom for his two nephews, Aqil and Nawfal. When Abbas said, "You have reduced me to a state where I will have to beg from the Quraysh," the Messenger of Allah reminded him of the gold he had secretly entrusted to his wife Umm al-Fadl when departing Mecca: "Where is that gold?" Abbas asked in astonishment, "How do you know?" When the Prophet said, "My Lord informed me," Abbas immediately recited the testimony of faith and believed with sincere conviction.

Abbas later said: "Allah gave me something better in place of that gold. Now I have twenty enslaved servants, the least of whom conducts business in partnership with twenty thousand. Moreover, Allah bestowed Zamzam upon me, in exchange for which I would not take all the wealth of Mecca. From now on, I continually look forward to the forgiveness of my Lord."

In the 72nd verse, it is stated that the believing Emigrants (Muhajirun) and Helpers (Ansar) are guardians and allies of one another. They inherit from one another and manage each other's affairs. As for the believers who have not yet emigrated, there is no right of guardianship until they emigrate. However, if they seek help concerning religion, it is an obligation to assist them, provided it is not against a people with whom you have a treaty.

In the 73rd verse, it is emphasized that the disbelievers are allies of one another, and that neither guardianship nor inheritance exists between a believer and a disbeliever. Difference of religion and difference of abodes preclude inheritance. If these principles are not observed, great discord and corruption will prevail on earth. Believers are divided into the Emigrants (Muhajirun), the Helpers (Ansar), and other Muslims, and the principles of mutual solidarity among them are established.

In the 74th verse, those who believed, emigrated, strove in the cause of Allah, and demonstrated patience and endurance, together with the Helpers (Ansar) who sheltered and aided them, are described as true believers. For them is forgiveness and an honorable provision. The expression here, 'those are the true believers in all truth,' is a relative specification in comparison to those who did not emigrate.

In the 75th verse, it is stated that those who believe and emigrate hereafter and participate in striving alongside you are also of you. However, from now on, blood relatives are closer to one another in inheritance according to the Book of Allah. The provisions regarding inheritance previously established under the brotherhood pact between the Emigrants (Muhajirun) and the Helpers (Ansar) were abrogated. According to the soundest view, this ruling took effect after Hudaybiyyah. Allah knows all things.

The first verse of Surah at-Tawbah begins with the concept of 'bara'ah' (disavowal/immunity). In the dictionary, bara'ah means to be freed from something and to distance oneself from it. Here, however, as a political and legal term, it signifies the termination of a treaty and the end of non-aggression. The verse announces that this is an ultimatum from Allah and His Messenger to the polytheists with whom they had made a treaty.

In the second verse, the polytheists are granted permission to travel freely throughout the land for four months. This period is a respite for them to make their preparations. However, at the end of this period, they are reminded that they cannot frustrate Allah and that the disbelievers will be disgraced and humiliated. The view that the beginning of these four months was the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah is the predominant one.

The third verse describes the proclamation made on the day of the Greater Pilgrimage (Hajj al-Akbar). This proclamation announces that Allah and His Messenger are disassociated from the polytheists. The expression 'Hajj al-Akbar' has been interpreted differently; some say it is the Day of Arafah, while others say it is the first day of the Feast of Sacrifice (Eid al-Adha). What is essential is that this proclamation was an announcement made to all mankind.

The fourth verse states that the polytheists who remained faithful to their treaties are an exception. These are those who observed the terms and did not cause harm to the Muslims. It is commanded that they be granted respite until the end of their treaty's term. Allah loves those who are mindful of Him (al-muttaqin), and fulfilling one's covenant is part of taqwa (God-consciousness).

The fifth verse commands that after the sacred months have passed, the polytheists be killed wherever they are found, taken captive, and ambushed on their ways. However, if they repent, establish prayer, and pay zakah, their way is to be cleared. This offers the polytheists the choice of either death and captivity or entering Islam. Torture and mutilation (muthla) are forbidden in war.

The sixth verse commands that if one of the polytheists asks for asylum (aman), asylum must be granted to him and he must be given the opportunity to hear the word of Allah. This shows that even warfare has an aspect of mercy.

In the 6th verse of Surah at-Tawbah, Allah commands that if one of the polytheists asks for asylum seeking to listen to the word of Allah, asylum must be granted to him. Upon a polytheist coming to Ali and asking about this verse, although the interpretation was made that the verse only covers those who come for a religious need, the verse actually contains an unqualified expression of asking for asylum. In this case, the person granting asylum must do so taking into account that the other party will have the opportunity to listen to the word of Allah. Granting asylum to those who come for the purpose of listening is obligatory (wajib), whereas for those who come for worldly needs, depending on the situation, it may be permissible or not obligatory.

One of the conclusions drawn from this verse is that if a disbeliever wishes to learn the proofs of faith, it is obligatory (wajib) upon Muslims to explain these proofs to him. Furthermore, according to the scholars of jurisprudence (fiqh), if an enemy belligerent (harbi) enters the abode of Islam (Dar al-Islam) having received asylum for a legitimate legal purpose or for trade—even if he enters with a doubtful asylum granted by a child or an insane person—he must be protected. Envoys and ambassadors, on the other hand, inherently possess asylum. Even if the person who has been granted asylum does not believe after hearing the word of Allah, the safety of his life and property is ensured, and he is escorted safely to his homeland.

Is this proclamation an injustice against the polytheists with whom treaties were made? Verses 7–10 explain this: The polytheists cannot have a covenant in the sight of Allah and His Messenger, except those who made a treaty near the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) and remained faithful to their covenant. As long as they are true to you, be true to them. However, when the polytheists find an opportunity, they observe neither ties of kinship nor oaths; they try to please you with their tongues, but their hearts refuse. They sell the signs of Allah for a small worldly gain and hinder people from the path of Allah. Regarding a believer, they observe neither oath nor covenant; it is they who are the real transgressors.

In the 11th verse, if these polytheists repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, then they are your brothers in religion. The verses are explained in detail for a people who know. In the 12th verse, if they break their oaths after their treaty and revile your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief. For their oaths mean nothing to them; perhaps then they will desist. That is to say, war must be waged against those who break their oaths and insult religion.

In verses 13–16, the believers are encouraged to fight against those who broke their oaths, plotted to expel the Prophet from his homeland, and initiated the first attack. Do not fear them; rather, fear Allah. The wisdoms behind fighting are as follows: Allah will punish them by your hands, disgrace them, grant you victory over them, bring relief to the hearts of the believers, and remove the rage from their hearts. Allah grants repentance to whom He wills. The believers must know that they will not be left to themselves without striving (jihad) as those who take no protector or confidant other than Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.

In these verses, the command to fight has five objectives: punishment, humiliating the enemy, helping the believers, bringing relief to the hearts of the oppressed believers, and dispelling malice and rage. Fighting must not be viewed merely as killing and destruction, but as an instrument of divine punishment; and the believers, while fulfilling this duty, must avoid unjust torment.

The objective of war is not merely to punish or belittle the enemy. The primary objective is to attain Allah's help and His good pleasure. This dispels the malice and rage in hearts and brings peace. In the verse, these five fundamental principles are listed: punishing the enemy, devastating them, bringing serenity to hearts, removing rage, and attaining divine help. All of these require that warfare be founded upon faith and sincerity (ikhlas). Furthermore, repentance, which is the ultimate goal of fighting, is emphasized: Allah grants repentance to whom He wills. This repentance can take the form of disbelievers turning to faith, as well as believers being purified from their sins. Allah granting repentance to whom He wills indicates that not everyone will benefit from this blessing. Conditions such as prosperity and hardship affect people's dispositions differently; some become arrogant in prosperity, while others take heed in hardship. This, too, depends on the will of Allah.

In the 16th verse, the following question is posed to the believers: 'Or did you think that you would be left alone?' Did you think that Allah would leave you without testing you, before He knows those among you who strive (jihad) and who take no intimate friend other than Allah, His Messenger, and the believers? Allah is fully aware of what you do; He will distinguish between those who strive and those who do not. The condition of the hypocrites and the sincere strivers (mujahidin) will be made manifest, and they will be requited accordingly.

In the 17th verse, it is declared that the polytheists cannot maintain the mosques of Allah. For while they bear witness against themselves to their own disbelief, their deeds have become worthless, and in the Fire they will abide eternally. The services rendered by the polytheists to the Kaaba are not considered genuine maintenance without faith. True maintenance consists of the physical upkeep of the building and the presence of a large congregation, while spiritual maintenance is possible through worship, remembrance (dhikr), and seeking knowledge within it solely for the sake of Allah. These services of the polytheists actually harm the spirit of the mosque.

In the 18th verse, it is stated that the mosques of Allah can only be maintained by those who possess four characteristics: belief in Allah and the Last Day, establishing prayer, giving zakah, and fearing none except Allah. These qualities must be combined so that mosques are rightly maintained and prosper. For the spiritual maintenance of mosques is only possible through sincere believers. Those who possess these characteristics are the rightly guided ones.

In verses 19–20, providing water to pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) cannot be held equal to the deed of those who believe and strive (jihad) in the cause of Allah. These services of the polytheists cannot be compared with faith and striving; they are not equal in the sight of Allah. Those who believe, emigrate, and strive with their lives and their wealth hold the greatest rank in the sight of Allah. It is they who are the triumphant. This superiority is also emphasized in Surah an-Nisa. In the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), it is narrated that these verses were revealed when the polytheists asked the Jews, 'Are we more virtuous, or Muhammad and his companions?'

Verses 21–22 report that these strivers (mujahideen) are given glad tidings of mercy and pleasure from their Lord, and of gardens (Paradise) containing everlasting bliss. That Paradise is eternal, and the greatest reward is with Allah.

In this section, it is emphasized that those who believe, emigrate, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah possess the greatest rank in the sight of Allah. It is stated that they are the ones who attain salvation, and that this salvation is certain and absolute. Furthermore, the superiority of those who strive over those occupied with other acts of worship and service is supported by verses in Surah an-Nisa.

Regarding the occasion of revelation of the verses, it is narrated that the polytheists boasted about deeds such as providing water (siqayah) to pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque, and asked the Jews whether they or the Prophet Muhammad and his companions were more virtuous. It is also related that the verses were revealed upon al-Abbas preferring to perform these services rather than emigrating, and that the Prophet (peace be upon him) told him to continue the duty of providing water.

In verses 23–24, the believers are commanded not to take their fathers and brothers as allies (awliya) if they choose disbelief. A warning is given that if worldly loves such as family, wealth, and commerce are held above the love of Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His cause, this constitutes defiance and transgression (fisq), and Allah will not guide such a rebellious people. These verses teach that believers must establish their priorities and, when necessary, be able to renounce even those they love most.

In verses 25–26, the Battle of Hunayn is described. Even though the Muslims were numerous in number, in order to show that they could not achieve success without Allah's help, they were first put to rout; then Allah sent down His tranquility (sakinah) and aided them with invisible armies, bringing them to victory. This event is an important lesson showing that victory comes solely from Allah and that relying on numerical superiority is wrong.

In verse 27, it is stated that following the Battle of Hunayn, many people repented and became Muslims. The Prophet's (peace be upon him) release of the captives and returning their property was a result of this repentance. While the verse emphasizes that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, it also shows that even past animosities can be forgiven.

In verse 28, it is stated that the polytheists are impure and that they are henceforth forbidden from approaching the Sacred Mosque. Upon the Muslims' concern over a potential decline in pilgrimage and trade revenues, this prohibition is reinforced with Allah's promise to enrich them as He wills. The verse teaches that Muslims must not abandon religious rulings out of economic concerns.

In verse 28, Allah the Almighty declares that the polytheists are impure. This impurity is a spiritual impurity stemming from the belief of polytheism (shirk). For this reason, starting from the ninth year of the Hijrah, polytheists were forbidden from approaching the Sacred Mosque. There are differing opinions among the legal schools (madhhabs) regarding the scope of this ban: according to the Hanafis, the ban applies only to the Hajj; according to the Shafi'is, to the entire Sacred Precinct (Haram area); and according to the Malikis, to all mosques. The believers should not fear experiencing financial hardship because of this ban, for Allah will enrich them out of His bounty.

In verse 29, fighting is commanded against those among the People of the Book who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day, who do not consider unlawful what Allah and His Messenger have made unlawful, and who do not adopt the religion of truth. This fighting is to continue until they pay the poll tax (jizyah) willingly by their own hand while being subdued. The expression 'an yadin' means that the jizyah is paid out of hand, with submission, without delay, and directly by the hand of the payer. While jizyah is specific to the People of the Book, it is established by hadith that Zoroastrians (Majus) are also subject to the same ruling. Whether jizyah may be taken from the Arab polytheists, however, is a matter of dispute among the legal schools.

In verse 30, it is stated that the Jews said, 'Ezra (Uzayr) is the son of Allah,' while the Christians said, 'The Messiah is the son of Allah.' These words are baseless claims fabricated by their own mouths, imitating the blasphemous assertions of those who disbelieved before them. May Allah destroy those who utter such words; how deluded they are from the truth!

In verse 31, it is related that the People of the Book took their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah. This means that they accepted that their clergy had the authority to legislate what is lawful and unlawful, and followed their words while abandoning the rulings of Allah. Affirming them when they declared lawful what Allah had made unlawful, or unlawful what Allah had made lawful, amounted to worshiping them. Indeed, when the Companion 'Adi ibn Hatim heard this verse, the Messenger of Allah explained it to him in this manner.

In verses 32–33, it is stated that the disbelievers wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah refuses except to perfect His light. Allah has sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that this religion may prevail over all religions, even though the polytheists dislike it. These verses give glad tidings that Islam will ultimately triumph and prevail over all other religions.

These narrations show that calling someone 'lord' is not a prerequisite for taking them as a lord. Obeying someone without regard to whether it contradicts Allah's command, and unquestioningly accepting their orders, means taking them as a lord and worshiping them. The Jews and Christians took their scholars and clergymen as lords by obeying them in matters that ran contrary to Allah's command. This constitutes taking lords 'besides Allah' and is polytheism (shirk). However, obedience that is in conformity with Allah's command is part of obedience to Allah and is legitimate.

Obedience to scholars is contingent upon the condition that knowledge is given its due right and that it is in goodness (ma'ruf). Giving knowledge its due right means following the truth and seeking the pleasure of Allah. Those who strive to make truth appear falsehood and falsehood appear truth are tyrants (taghut). Granting scholars the authority to legislate while disregarding Allah's commands is to take them as lords. The Jews and Christians attributed such lordship to their rabbis and monks, claiming that they were infallible and believing that they had the authority to alter religious rulings. It is this that the verse criticizes.

Allah wills to perfect His light, even though the disbelievers detest it. They attempt to extinguish Allah's light with their mouths. Yet Allah will surely make His light shine brightly, exalt the religion of monotheism (tawhid), and make Islam triumphant. It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth. This religion is Islam, which upholds the truth in all things. Allah will cause this religion to prevail over all other religions, making it manifest even though the polytheists dislike it. This is a fulfilled promise: Islam is supreme, and nothing surpasses it.

O you who believe! Indeed, many of the Jewish rabbis and Christian monks unjustly consume the wealth of people and hinder from the way of Allah. Give tidings of a painful punishment to those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah. On that Day, these hoarded treasures will be heated in the fire of Hell, and their foreheads, sides, and backs will be branded with them; and it will be said, 'This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard!' This is a warning to those who amass wealth and do not give its zakat.

Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve. Four of them are sacred months. That is the correct religion. So do not wrong yourselves in these months. And fight against the polytheists collectively just as they fight against you collectively. Allah is with the righteous. 'Nasi'' (postponing a sacred month) is only an increase in disbelief. With it, the disbelievers deem a month lawful one year and unlawful another year, so that they conform to the number of months Allah has made sacred. Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.

Observing Allah's sacred months is an important obligation for the believers. However, the polytheists do not recognize the sanctity of these months, and whenever they find an opportunity, they launch attacks even at Arafat. For this reason, in order to preserve the sanctity of the sacred months, which is the most sacred of all inviolabilities, one must not allow other sanctities to be violated. Otherwise, one would be wronging oneself. The verse in Surah al-Baqarah, "Do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands" (2/195), points to this situation. The purpose here is to prevent the polytheists from exploiting these months as they did in the Pre-Islamic Period of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah).

Just as the polytheists fight against you collectively, fight against them collectively as well. This command is not bound by time or place; it states that fighting must be undertaken whenever necessary, regardless of which month it is. The concept of the sacred months eliminated the absolute prohibition of warfare that existed in the Jahiliyyah era. For unjust killing that is not done for the sake of Allah is always forbidden, whereas jihad in the way of Allah is an act of worship that must be performed in every season. The verses "Wherever you encounter them" (al-Baqarah 2/191) and "Wherever you find them" (at-Tawbah 9/5) emphasize this matter.

The prohibition of fighting during the sacred months remains valid unless one is subjected to an enemy attack. If the enemy launches the first attack, fighting for defensive purposes is permissible. This prohibition should not be understood as an instruction not to wrong yourselves by initially deeming warfare permissible. On the contrary, abandoning jihad during the sacred months and giving the enemy an advantage means exposing oneself to danger. Therefore, the verse indicates that jihad is necessary in order to protect the sanctity of the sacred months.

The practice of "nasi'" (postponement) mentioned in the verse is nothing but an increase in disbelief. The word nasi' literally means to postpone, to delay. The Arabs altered their calendar, which was based on lunar months, shifted the positions of the sacred months, and considered a month lawful at times and unlawful at others. This practice was intended to breach the prohibition of warfare and to adjust the pilgrimage season according to their own interests. By adding one month every two years, they would completely erase an entire year every twenty-five years.

Nasi' is not a custom unique to the Arabs; any kind of calendar manipulation carried out for similar purposes constitutes disbelief. Postponing or advancing times in order to make lawful what Allah has forbidden corrupts religious fundamentals. For this reason, the verse informs us that nasi' causes an increase in disbelief and leads the disbelievers into misguidance.

The polytheists try to conform to the number of months established by Allah by regarding the same month as lawful one year and unlawful another year. However, this is merely their arbitrary discretion. In reality, the sacred months are fixed as determined by Allah and cannot be altered. These manipulations are similar to how the Jews and Christians shifted their religious days by switching from a lunar calendar to a solar calendar. Any form of nasi' prevents acts of worship from being performed on time and violates religious sanctities.

In conclusion, the practice of nasi' is nothing other than going to extremes in disbelief. Showing reverence for Allah's sacred months is an obligation upon the believers. Warfare can be conducted at any time, but only for defense against enemy attack. Preserving the sanctity of the sacred months is possible by observing what is right and obeying Allah's commands. Allah is with the righteous and helps them.

The system of nasi' (postponing months) practiced during the Jahiliyyah era did not merely consist of delaying a single month. This practice led to shifting all of the sacred months and violating the sanctities established by Allah. The purpose was to violate religious rulings in order to secure worldly gains such as warfare or trade. This situation was characterized as a compounded form of disbelief, and it was emphasized that deeming Allah's prohibitions lawful is a grave deviance.

Verses 38–41 of Surah at-Tawbah were revealed during the Expedition of Tabuk, which took place in the ninth year of the Hijrah. At that time, due to hardships such as intense heat, scarcity, and the ripening of fruits, some believers were sluggish in going out for jihad. Allah rebuked them, declaring that preferring the transient pleasures of the worldly life over the Hereafter is a grave error. A warning was issued that jihad is an obligation and that failing to comply with this command would lead to a painful punishment.

In verse 40, it is recalled that if the believers do not help the Prophet, Allah will certainly help him. The incident that took place in the Cave of Thawr during the Hijrah is cited as an example: Our Prophet (peace be upon him), with only Abu Bakr by his side, reassured him by saying, "Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us," and Allah protected him by sending down tranquility upon him and supporting him with unseen hosts. The word of the disbelievers was debased, while the word of Allah remained supreme.

In verse 41, believers are commanded to mobilize "whether light or heavily equipped." This indicates that every believer must participate in jihad according to their own circumstances. Jihad is carried out with both wealth and life; it is a sacrifice made against one's comfort and possessions. Recognizing that this sacrifice is good requires knowledge and insight. Every effort spent in the way of Allah is counted as participating in the battle itself.

In verses 42–45, the attitude of the hypocrites who did not participate in jihad is criticized. If the expedition had offered immediate gains and an easy journey, they would have joined. However, when faced with hardship, they lagged behind, and later they will swear oaths to make excuses. Allah knows that they are liars. True believers, on the other hand, never ask for permission to stay behind from jihad; their hearts are filled with faith in Allah and the Last Day.

In verses 46–47, it is stated that if the hypocrites had been sincere, they would have made preparations for battle. However, because Allah disliked their going forth, He held them back, and it was said, 'Remain with those who sit back.' Had they gone out with you, they would only have increased you in corruption and sown discord among you. Among you are those who would listen to them, and Allah is most knowing of the wrongdoers.

In this section, the profound meanings of Allah's address to our Prophet (peace be upon him), "May Allah pardon you," are examined. Beyond being an ordinary tidings of pardon, this expression points to the Prophet's exalted responsibility and his role as an exemplar for the ummah. The Prophet is held accountable not for any sin, but even for a momentary lapse of mindfulness in the presence of Allah; this form of address emphasizes his human nature, thus protecting the believers from an excess similar to the Christians' extreme devotion to Jesus.

The verses indicate that believers should not ask for permission regarding jihad, because true faith requires not evading jihad, but participating in it whole-heartedly. In contrast, those asking for permission are in reality hypocrites who do not believe in Allah and the Hereafter, and whose hearts are filled with doubt. This behavior of theirs contradicts their claim of faith and reinforces the likelihood of their dishonesty.

Although the Prophet's immediate granting of permission to those who asked for it may seem like an error contrary to divine wisdom, it was actually an irregularity stemming from his excessive tolerance and optimism. Allah did not want these hypocrites to take part in the battle, for their presence would have introduced corruption and discord into the army. Therefore, by holding them back in their places, He protected the Muslims.

The characteristic traits of the hypocrites are described: when good touches the Muslims, they are grieved, and when misfortune befalls them, they rejoice. They boast, claiming to have taken precautions according to their own lights. However, the Muslim knows that whatever befalls them is by Allah's decree, and relies solely on Him.

Tawakkul (reliance upon Allah) is not the abandonment of duty, but rather leaving the outcome to Him while carrying out Allah's commands. For the believer, there are two good outcomes: victory or martyrdom. For the hypocrites, however, a punishment is anticipated either from Allah or at the hands of the Muslims. Their spending (infaq) is not accepted because they do not believe; and their wealth and children are nothing other than a source of torment in this world.

The hypocrites' spending will not be accepted, whether they spend willingly or unwillingly. For they have disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, perform the prayer lazily, and spend reluctantly. Because they do not believe in their hearts, these acts of worship feel burdensome to them, and they perform them purely for show. For this reason, their wealth and children are not a blessing for them, but a cause of torment in the worldly life; and they perish as disbelievers.

The hypocrites swear that they are of you, yet they are not of you; their hearts fail them out of fear. If they could find a place of refuge or a cave, they would flee thither headlong. They slander you concerning the distribution of charities (sadaqat); if they are given from it, they are pleased, and if they are not given, they become angry. Yet, had they been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and said, 'Allah is sufficient for us,' it would have been far better for them.

Charities (zakah) are allocated to eight categories: the poor, the needy, those employed to collect zakah, those whose hearts are to be reconciled to Islam, slaves, debtors, those in the cause of Allah, and the stranded travelers. Allah has ordained this as an obligation. Sadaqah is a right given for the sake of Allah, carrying the condition of transferring ownership (tamlik), and given to the needy. Zakah is the right of the poor from the wealth of the rich.

Those whose hearts are to be reconciled (al-mu'allafat al-qulub) refers to the share given in the early period of Islam to certain disbelievers or weak Muslims to strengthen the Muslims. However, Umar stated that this practice was discontinued once the Muslims grew strong, and Abu Bakr did not object to this. The Hanafi and Maliki schools of thought hold the view that this share has lapsed. According to the Shafi'i school, however, it may be reinstated in case of need.

The other categories are: slaves (al-riqab) to be emancipated; debtors (al-gharimin) unable to pay their debts; those in the cause of Allah (fi sabilillah), specifically those striving in jihad, as well as the poor undertaking the pilgrimage (hajj) and the pursuit of knowledge; and stranded travelers (ibn al-sabil). Scholars unanimously state that the most significant portion of 'in the cause of Allah' constitutes the mujahideen. Zakah can only be given to one of these eight categories; it cannot be spent on the wealthy or on other charitable causes.

Regarding spending in the cause of Allah (fi sabilillah), it has been debated whether aid given to the mujahideen can count toward obligatory charities such as zakah. According to Elmalılı, the expression 'fi sabilillah' in the verse directly refers to those engaged in jihad; other types of charitable works are valid only in the case of supererogatory charities. Obligatory charities like zakah may only be spent on the equipment and supplies that the mujahideen require in jihad. These expenditures may also be made by delivering them not directly to the mujahideen in person, but to the commander; this is a matter of ijtihad. All eight categories of charities are based on poverty and need; the collectors ('amilun) and those whose hearts are to be reconciled receive it not as charity, but as wages or for the purpose of aiding Islam.

In the 61st verse, it is described that the hypocrites harmed the Prophet and said, 'He is an ear [listening to everything that is said].' According to the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), a hypocrite named Julas b. Suwayd said, 'We say whatever we wish, then deny it in his presence and swear an oath, and he believes us.' Elmalılı notes that the Arabs refer to a naive person as an 'ear.' This attitude of the Messenger of Allah is not naivety, but a mercy to the believers; he believes in Allah and trusts the words of the believers. The verse draws attention to the difference between faith and assent through the prepositions 'ba' and 'lam'. A painful punishment awaits those who distress the Prophet.

In verses 64-66, it is reported that the hypocrites feared the revelation of a surah that would expose what was in their hearts, yet they mocked and made excuses. They say, 'We were only joking'; whereas Allah responds, 'Was it at Allah, His verses, and His Messenger that you were mocking?' After claiming to believe, they openly displayed their disbelief; although some of them may be forgiven, those who persist will be subjected to punishment. These verses lay bare the evil intentions and insincerity of the hypocrites.

In verses 67-70, it is explained that the hypocrite men and women resemble one another; they enjoin what is wrong, forbid what is right, and withhold from spending in the cause of Allah. Because they forgot Allah, Allah also forgot them; they are the defiantly disobedient (fasiq). Hell has been promised to them eternally. The news of earlier peoples (the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Abraham, and Midian) reached them; nor was it that they were wronged, but rather they wronged themselves.

Verses 71-72 state that the believers are allies and protectors of one another; they enjoin what is good, forbid what is evil, establish prayer, and give zakah. Allah has promised them gardens beneath which rivers flow and pleasant dwellings in the Gardens of Eden ('Adn). The good pleasure of Allah (ridwan), however, is greater than all these blessings. According to a narration, when the people of Paradise attain Allah's good pleasure, they will realize that this blessing is the greatest of all.

In verses 73-80, the Prophet is commanded to strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and to be stern with them. Even though the hypocrites swear that they did not say anything bad, they uttered the word of disbelief and reverted to disbelief after embracing Islam. Despite having been enriched through Allah's bounty, they sought revenge. If they repent, it is better for them; if they do not, there is torment in this world and the Hereafter. Some of them made a covenant with Allah, but they broke their pledge, acted stingily, and lied; consequently, hypocrisy has settled in their hearts until the Day of Resurrection. Allah knows their secrets. Those who mocked the believers who gave voluntary contributions were made a laughingstock and subjected to a painful punishment. It will not benefit them if the Prophet asks forgiveness for them, because they have disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger.

Allah knows the secrets and private whispers concealed by the hypocrites. He is the Knower of all the unseen. The hypocrites who mock those among the believers who give extra charity voluntarily and those who can find nothing to give beyond their bare efforts have, in truth, only made fools of themselves. A painful punishment awaits them. As for the Prophet, whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness—even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will not forgive them. For they have disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger. Allah does not guide such a rebellious crowd of transgressors (fasiqun).

Jihad against the hypocrites is conducted through evidence and proofs; warfare is merely one form of it. Julas b. Suwayd spoke evil words regarding the Prophet (peace be upon him) and then swore an oath denying it, but Allah revealed a verse proving him a liar. Fifteen men from among the hypocrites set an ambush on the return from Tabuk to kill the Prophet (peace be upon him), but they fled upon Hudhayfah's warning. Allah knows their true inner state and thwarts their secret schemes.

Tha'labah b. Hatib asked the Prophet (peace be upon him) for wealth; the Prophet said that a little wealth was better for him, but when Tha'labah insisted, he prayed for him and his wealth multiplied. Afterwards, he abstained from giving zakah, which is why the Prophet said of him, 'Woe to him!' and refused to accept his charity. This incident shows the consequence of breaking a pledge and how hypocrisy takes root in the heart. Allah instills a hypocrisy that will endure until the Day of Resurrection in the hearts of those who break their promises.

The believers giving voluntary charity (nafilah) is praised. 'Abd al-Rahman b. 'Awf brought half of his wealth as charity, while 'Asim b. 'Adiyy brought one of the two sa's of dates he had earned from a night's labor. The hypocrites accused them of showing off, but Allah disgraced them. Tatawwu' refers to non-obligatory acts of worship and is virtuous, provided one does not go to excess in giving charity.

The Prophet sought forgiveness seventy times for 'Abdullah b. Ubayy, yet Allah informed him that He would not forgive him. For he disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger. A crowd of transgressors cannot attain guidance. The hypocrites who remained behind from the battle were pleased with staying behind and said, 'Do not go forth to battle in this heat.' It is said to them that the fire of Hell is far hotter. Henceforth, no expedition will be undertaken with them, their funeral prayers will not be performed when they die, and no one will stand at their graves. Allah wills that they be punished in this world by means of their wealth and their children.

Following the hypocrites of Medina, the condition of the desert Arabs (Bedouins) is recounted. Some of the Bedouins remained behind from battle under the pretext of excuses, while the outright liars simply stayed put. There is no sin upon the weak, the sick, and those who can find nothing to spend. However, those who requested permission to stay behind despite being wealthy are condemned. They will fabricate excuses to those returning from the expedition, but they will not be believed. The Bedouins are more severe in disbelief and hypocrisy; some of them regard spending in the way of Allah (infaq) as an onerous penalty, while others, believing in Allah and the Last Day, look for good. Allah admits the sincere into His mercy.

The foremost pioneers among the Emigrants and the Helpers (al-sabiqun al-awwalun) and those who followed them in good deeds have earned Allah's pleasure. Gardens beneath which rivers flow have been prepared for them. These are the ones who attain the supreme triumph. There are hypocrites among the surrounding Bedouins and the people of Medina; only Allah knows them. They will be punished twice, and then they will be driven into a tremendous punishment. The repentance of those who acknowledge their sins and mix righteous deeds with evil ones is accepted. Charity is taken from their wealth so that they are purified and cleansed, and that they may find tranquility through the prayers of the Prophet. Allah is the One Who accepts repentance and takes charity.

The believers are told that their deeds will be observed by Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. The forgiveness of some of those who did not participate in the expedition is deferred to Allah's decree. There are also those who erected a mosque to cause harm, foster disbelief, and create division among the Muslims. They swear, 'We intended nothing but good,' yet Allah bears witness that they are liars.

In this section, mention is made of the Mosque of Harm (al-Masjid al-Dirar), which the hypocrites built to inflict harm, bolster disbelief, and sow division among the believers. Allah commands His Prophet never to pray in this mosque. The mosque founded on piety from the very first day (the Quba Mosque or the Prophet's Mosque), on the other hand, is far more worthy to pray in. In that mosque are men who love to purify themselves from sins and strive to be thoroughly cleansed; and Allah loves those who purify themselves. The building of the hypocrites will remain a knot of hypocrisy in their hearts until their hearts are torn to pieces.

Among the Bedouin Arabs surrounding Medina and the people of Medina itself, there are also hypocrites. They have gone so far in hypocrisy and attained such skill in concealing their secrets and practicing dissimulation (taqiyyah) that without revelation, even the Prophet would not know them. Allah will punish them twice: once with the punishment of this world and once with the punishment of the grave, and thereafter they will be cast into the tremendous punishment of Hell.

Furthermore, a group among the hypocrites admitted their sins, showed remorse, and mixed righteous deeds with bad ones. They punished themselves by tying themselves to the pillars of the mosque and begged Allah for forgiveness. Upon this verse, the Prophet was commanded to take charity from their wealth, thereby ensuring that they were purified and cleansed. Scholars have expressed different opinions as to whether this charity was the obligatory zakah or a specific charity taken as an expiation (kaffarah) for sins. However, the verse has been cited as evidence that zakah must be collected by the head of state.

For another group, judgment was deferred (murji'ah). These were Ka'b b. Malik, Murarah b. al-Rabi', and Hilal b. Umayyah, who had participated in the Battle of Badr and were delayed in repenting. The Prophet forbade speaking to them, and people fell into conflicting thoughts concerning them. Allah would either punish them or accept their repentance. This was a matter resting upon Allah's wisdom.

Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for Paradise. They fight in the way of Allah; they kill and are killed. This is a promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran. And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah? Rejoice, then, in this bargain for the believers! The believers are those who repent, who worship, who praise Him, who fast, who bow down and prostrate, who enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil, and who keep the limits set by Allah. So give good tidings of the supreme triumph to them.

Allah declares that He has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in order to grant them Paradise in return. Although this is expressed in the manner of a transaction contract, in reality, everything belongs to Allah. Allah encourages His servants to spend the life and wealth He has granted them for His sake alone, and promises eternal Paradise to those who do so. This is a tremendous grace and bounty from Allah. Complying with this contract, the believers sacrifice their lives and their wealth in the way of Allah; they kill and are killed. This promise is affirmed in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran. Allah does not break His promise; therefore, the believers should rejoice over this transaction and give glad tidings to one another.

The characteristics of these believers are enumerated: They are those who repent, those who worship, those who praise, those who journey (those who fast), those who bow, those who prostrate, those who enjoin good, those who forbid evil, and those who preserve the bounds of Allah. Fasting is described as journeying because fasting distances a person from carnal desires and takes them on a spiritual journey. Furthermore, fasting is a spiritual discipline and serves as a means for an individual to explore their inner world. The believers possessing these noble qualities makes them worthy of the divine promise.

Allah has forbidden the Prophet and the believers from seeking forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they are relatives, once it has become certain that they are the companions of the Hellfire.
