Those you associate as partners have created nothing upon the earth. Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease to exist. He is Forbearing and Forgiving.

The disbelievers had sworn that if a warner came to them, they would surely be rightly guided. But when the prophet came, this only increased their aversion. They acted arrogantly on earth and devised evil plots. Yet evil plots engulf only their own makers. You will find no change in the Sunnah of Allah.

Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how the end was for those before them? They were mightier in strength. There is nothing that can frustrate Allah. If Allah were to immediately seize people for the sins they have committed, He would not leave a single living creature on the face of the earth. But He defers them until an appointed term. When their appointed time arrives, He does what is necessary. Allah is All-Seeing of His servants.

There are various views regarding the letters Yā-Sīn at the beginning of the surah. According to the majority, this is the name of the surah. According to some, it is an oath, and according to others, it is among the names of Allah. According to one narration, it is one of the names of the Prophet (peace be upon him) and means "O human" or "O master." Following these letters, the expression "By the wise Qur'an" emphasizes the truth of the Prophet's messengerhood. Such powerful affirmations are intended to console and reassure the Prophet in the face of the disbelievers' fierce opposition.

It is stated that the Prophet is on a straight path, and that this path is the Sharia of Islam. The purpose of the Qur'an's revelation is to warn a people whose forefathers were not warned and who are in heedlessness. This people is the Arab society, because no prophet had been sent to them before. The Qur'an addresses both all of humanity and specifically the Arabs.

The expression "Already has the word of punishment proven true against most of them" announces that, like previous communities, most of this people will not believe. This word of punishment points to the divine decree in Surah as-Sajdah meaning "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and humans together." This judgment is for those who remain obstinate after the arrival of a prophet.

It is described that shackles (aghlal) are placed around the necks of those who will not believe, reaching up to their chins, and that barriers are set before them and behind them. According to most scholars, these expressions are metaphorical; they depict a person becoming a captive to habits of disbelief and sin, unable to perceive the truth. Because of these barriers, they do not believe even if they are warned.

The one who will benefit from the warning is he who follows the Qur'an and fears the Most Merciful in the unseen (ghayb)—that is, who reveres Allah with sincere devotion. For such people, there is great forgiveness and an honorable reward. Allah declares that He will resurrect the dead, that He records the traces of deeds of good and evil left behind, and that everything is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). This is the fundamental wisdom behind warning and giving glad tidings.

Allah gives the people of a city (Antioch) as an example to the Prophet. Two prophets were sent there first, and then a third was sent to reinforce them, but the people denied them and accused them of bringing an ill omen. The prophets stated that they were only obligated to convey the message clearly. From the farthest part of the city, a man (Habib an-Najjar) came running and called upon his people to follow the messengers.

This man emphasized that the prophets ask for no payment and that they are rightly guided. He stated that he must worship Allah who created him, and that taking deities besides Him is clear misguidance. He declared, "Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me," and was martyred. Upon entering Paradise, he wished that his people could only know of this bliss.

Following that man, Allah did not send down an army from the heavens upon the people; a single blast (sayhah) destroyed them. This shows the ultimate end of disbelieving societies. Alas for the servants! There did not come to them a prophet except that they mocked him. How many generations before them have been destroyed, and all of them will be brought together before Him for reckoning.

Almighty Allah demonstrates His power by reviving the dead earth and producing from it various plants, grains, date-palm groves, and grapevines. People eat of these fruits, yet they forget that these are Allah's bestowal and fail to show gratitude. Gratitude consists of acknowledging the blessing with the tongue as coming from Allah, believing this in the heart, and obeying Allah with the physical limbs.

The alternation of night and day, the sun running its course in a determined orbit, and the moon passing through phases until it returns like an old dried date stalk are proofs of Allah's power. It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each floats in an orbit.

Just as Allah carried mankind in Noah's ark, He also protects them in the mother's womb. Had He willed, He could have drowned them, but out of His mercy He grants them life for an appointed time. Despite this, when the disbelievers are told to fear the punishment before them and behind them, they turn away; when asked to spend on the poor, they scoff and ask, 'When will this promise be?' They await nothing but a single cry that will seize them while they are still disputing, unable even to make a bequest.

When the Horn is blown, they will emerge from their graves and hasten to their Lord, saying, 'Woe to us! Who has raised us? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth.' With a single cry, all are gathered. On that Day, no soul will be wronged in the least, and everyone will be recompensed for what they did. The people of Paradise, together with their spouses, recline on couches in the shade; fruits and whatever they ask for belong to them. A greeting of 'Peace' is conveyed to them as a word from a Merciful Lord. To the criminals, however, it is said: 'Stand apart today,' and they are reminded not to worship Satan.

Had Allah willed, He could have blinded the eyes of the disbelievers or transfixed them in their places; however, He has deferred their punishment to the Hereafter. He causes the human being to decline in strength with old age, which demonstrates His power. Poetry was not taught to the Prophet; the Qur'an is an admonition and a clear book. Forgetting that he was created from a drop of fluid, man asks who will give life to decayed bones. Allah declares that the One who brought them into being the first time will revive them, that He produces fire from the green tree, and that the One who created the heavens and the earth is capable of creating their likeness. When He wills a thing to be, He merely says to it, 'Be!' and it is. Exalted is the glory of Allah, in whose hand is the dominion over all things, and to Him you will all be returned.
The Qur'an is nothing other than a reminder (dhikr), an admonition and guidance from Allah, and a clear book. It is the Word of Allah to be recited in acts of worship and in places of worship.

In verse 70, this warning is given to warn and awaken those who are alive, and so that the decree of punishment may prove true against those who persist in disbelief. Just as happened to many before them, the decree of punishment has become binding upon them as well.

In verses 71–76, a reality that the heedless fail to perceive is described: We created livestock for them from what Our hands have made—that is, from blessings We created directly Ourselves. There are many subtleties in this reminder, which the discerning taste of those who read it will appreciate.

The occasion of revelation for verses 77–79 is as follows: Ubayy ibn Khalaf brought a decayed bone to the Prophet (peace be upon him) and asked, 'Can Allah bring this to life?' The Prophet (peace be upon him) replied, 'Yes, He will resurrect you as well and cast you into the Fire.' This verse emphasizes that man fails to consider that We created him from a drop of fluid, and that Allah is All-Knowing of every manner of creation.

In verse 80, it is described that Allah made fire for you from the green tree. The well-known examples are the markh and 'afar trees; while still green, they produce fire through friction. Commentators of tafsir have pointed out that what is meant here is not the wood of the tree, but the heat generated by friction, which also alludes to electricity.
Verses 81–82: Is not Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, able to create the like of them? Indeed, He is capable. His command, when He intends a thing, is only to say to it, 'Be!' and it is.

Verse 83: Glorify Allah, in whose hand is the dominion over all things. To Him you shall all be returned. Those who return with faith and willingly, like Habib an-Najjar, are forgiven; those who are returned by force suffer their punishment. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that the virtues of Surah Ya-Sin were revealed on account of this verse.

At the beginning of Surah as-Saffat, Allah swears by the angels lined up in ranks, those who drive forcefully, and those who recite the remembrance, emphasizing that your God is truly One. These oaths point to the importance of organized effort in Islam, such as community, jihad, and the pursuit of knowledge.

The lowest heaven has been adorned with stars and protected from every rebellious devil. The devils cannot listen to the exalted assembly, and those who attempt to eavesdrop are pursued by a piercing flame. This describes the material and spiritual defeat of those who remain heedless of divine revelation.

On the Day of Resurrection, the wrongdoers, their companions, and what they used to worship will be gathered and driven to Hell. There, they will blame one another: while the leaders say, 'You were not believers anyway,' the common people will reply, 'It was you who led us astray.' Ultimately, everyone will face retribution for what they have done.

For the people of Paradise, however, there are fruits, rivers, and noble companions. When one of them sees his worldly friend in Hell, he realizes that he was saved solely through the grace of Allah. The tree of Zaqqum, on the other hand, is the food of the dwellers of Hell; its shoots are as hideous as the heads of devils.

The prayer of Prophet Noah (Nuh) was answered; he and his family were saved from the deluge, and his lineage was perpetuated. A salutation of peace and an honorable reputation were preserved for him among later generations. Abraham (Ibrahim) was likewise among those who followed in his footsteps, turning to his Lord with a pure and sound heart.

Abraham shattered the idols and confronted his people, proclaiming that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. When they sought to cast him into the fire, Allah granted him aid; later, Abraham was tested with the sacrifice of his son Ishmael (Ismail). When both submitted, Allah ransomed him with a momentous sacrifice and characterized this event as a manifest trial. Afterward, the glad tidings of Isaac (Ishak) were given.

Allah bestowed blessings upon Abraham, as well as upon Ishmael—the forbearing son—and upon Isaac. This blessing signified the multiplication and continuity of the progeny of both sons. Yet there is a crucial point here: from both lineages arose both righteous individuals and those who wronged their own souls. Thus, the piety of ancestors does not guarantee the righteousness of their descendants; wrongdoers emerged from the lineage of Abraham, just as idolaters emerged from the lineage of Noah. This underscores the primacy of personal faith and righteous deeds over ancestral lineage.

Next, the story of Moses (Musa) and Aaron (Harun) is recounted. Allah favored them with blessings, delivered them and their people from immense distress, supported them, and made them victorious. He bestowed upon them the Scripture (Torah) and guided them to the straight path. An honorable memory was left for them among later generations, and it was said, "Peace be upon Moses and Aaron." This demonstrates that the doers of good will be rewarded and that they were among Allah's believing servants.

Elijah (Ilyas) was also among the dispatched messengers. He exhorted his people not to worship the idol named Ba'l instead of Allah, yet they rejected him. A salutation of peace was likewise preserved for Elijah among subsequent generations. The Prophet Lot (Lut) is also mentioned; Allah saved him and his family, while annihilating the rest, except for an elderly woman who remained behind. It is noted that the Quraysh, traveling to Syria (Sham) for trade, passed by the ruins of Lot's people, serving as a cautionary lesson for them to take heed.

The story of Prophet Jonah (Yunus) contains profound lessons. Departed in anger with his people without divine leave, he fled aboard a laden ship; subsequently, lots were cast, he was cast into the sea, and was swallowed by a great fish. Within the belly of the fish, his prayer—"There is no deity except You; exalted are You! Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers"—was accepted, and he was brought forth onto an open shore. A gourd-bearing plant was made to grow over him, and he was then sent back to a community of a hundred thousand or more. His people believed and were granted worldly sustenance for a time.

Addressing the polytheists, the question "Are the daughters for your Lord, while the sons are for them?" censures their attribution of female offspring to Allah. While they regarded the angels as Allah's daughters, they themselves loathed having daughters. Furthermore, they fabricated a kinship between Allah and the jinn. Yet both the jinn and the angels know that these liars will be hauled into Hell. Exalted is Allah far above their claims. His sincere servants, however, never engage in such association (shirk). The polytheists and what they worship can only mislead those who are destined for Hell; they cannot lead the sincere servants astray.

The polytheists claim, "If only we had possessed a scripture like earlier peoples, we would have been sincere servants." Yet when the Quran came to them, they disbelieved in it. In time, they will realize their fate. Allah has promised that He will aid His messengers and that His hosts will prevail. For this reason, the Prophet is commanded to turn away from them for an appointed time and observe what befalls them. The surah concludes by declaring the Lord far above the attributes ascribed to Him by the polytheists, extending peace upon the messengers, and offering all praise to Allah, the Lord of all the worlds.

It is narrated that when Abu Talib fell ill, the Quraysh came and complained that the Messenger of Allah was speaking ill of their idols. Abu Talib called for his nephew. When our Prophet proposed to them that they say "lâ ilâhe illallah", the disbelievers jumped up in agitation and said, "Has he made the gods into one single god? This is truly an astonishing thing!" Thus, the first seven verses of Surah Sad were revealed concerning this event.

The letter "Sâd" at the beginning of the surah is among the disjointed/mutashabih letters (huruf al-muqatta'at). It has been said that this is a challenge, the name of the surah, or that it points to meanings such as truthfulness. In addition, it carries the meaning of "sadâ" (the reverberating echo of a sound); in this case, it may be a command to respond to the Qur'an. In some narrations, it is stated that this letter is the name of a sea beneath the Throne of Allah.

The word "dhikr" (remembrance/zikir) here can bear three meanings: honor and glory, counsel and reminder, and explaining the requirements of the religion. The response to this oath has been elided; however, its meaning is the truthfulness of the Prophet and the certainty of the arrival of the promised punishment. The disbelievers, on the other hand, are entrenched in pride and discord; they do not accept tawhid (the oneness of Allah). They say, "We have not heard of this in the latest religion (millet-i ahire)"; this is an indication that, like the latter community (the Christians), they too accepted the Trinity.

The disbelievers, jealous of the revelation of the Qur'an, objected by saying, "Has this reminder been sent down to him from among us?" They are a mere remnant, like the routed confederate armies of the past. These verses point to the Quraysh's defeat at Badr. In what follows, it is recounted that the disbelievers mockingly demanded the punishment be hastened. Patience is counseled to the Prophet, and he is asked to remember David (Davud), a powerful servant.

David (peace be upon him) was a strong prophet who remembered and praised Allah abundantly. The mountains and birds would glorify Allah alongside him. Allah had granted him wisdom and the ability to distinguish truth from falsehood. One day, two litigants climbed over the wall into his prayer chamber (mihrab) and presented a dispute regarding oppression between them. David warned the wrongdoer, and realizing that he was being tested, he immediately repented and fell down in prostration. Allah forgave him and granted him nearness to Himself. Thereupon, it was proclaimed: "O David! We have made you a viceregent upon the earth; so judge with truth, and do not follow whim and desire."

The heavens, the earth, and what is between them were not created in vain. The presumption of the disbelievers is the contrary. Those who believe and perform righteous deeds cannot be held equal to the corrupters. The Qur'an is a blessed book; it was sent down so that its verses might be pondered and that people of understanding might take heed.

Solomon (peace be upon him) was also an excellent servant; he glorified Allah abundantly and constantly turned to Him. One late afternoon, thoroughbred horses were displayed before him. He stated that his love for horses was out of the remembrance of his Lord. Then he stroked the legs and necks of the horses. Solomon was tested; a lifeless body was placed upon his throne. He then repented and asked Allah for a dominion uniquely his own. Allah placed the wind, the devils (those who build and dive), and others under his command. This was a bounty from Allah.

Job (peace be upon him) should also be remembered. At one time, he pleaded to his Lord, saying that Satan had afflicted him with distress and torment. Allah commanded him to strike the ground with his foot; from there, cool water emerged for bathing and drinking. His family was restored to him, along with the like of them in addition. Furthermore, he was told to take a bundle in his hand and strike his wife with it so as not to break his oath. Job was a patient and excellent servant; he was ever turning to Allah.

The word "dighth" (dığs) mentioned in this section of Surah Sad means a bundle or a handful of twigs. According to the narration, Job had sworn to strike his wife with a hundred lashes; Allah granted him the concession (rukhsah) to strike with a gathered bundle. This concession is known in Islamic jurisprudence as the "Jobian concession" (Eyyub ruhsatı). According to Elmalılı, this indication may also point to the necessity of establishing a community.

Next, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are commemorated. They are described as "possessors of hands and vision"; that is, they were potent in righteous deeds and sound knowledge. Through a pure quality, they attained mindfulness of the Hereafter and were devoted, sincere servants. In addition, Ishmael, Elisha, and Dhul-Kifl are mentioned; all of them are among the very best. Ishmael is highlighted separately; Elisha was the successor of Elijah and was granted prophethood; and Dhul-Kifl, as the son of Job, called people to the oneness of Allah (tawhid) in the region of Damascus (Sham).

These verses serve as an admonition. For the righteous, there is a beautiful destination: the Gardens of Eden ('Adn). There, every gate is open, and diverse fruits and matchless drinks are offered. By their side are companions of equal age whose gazes are restrained solely to their spouses. This is the provision promised for the Day of Reckoning, and it will never be depleted.

For the transgressors, however, there is Hell and a wretched resting place. There, they taste boiling fluid and foul pus (ghassaq). Ghassaq, as the opposite of scalding water (hamim), is an intensely cold and foul-smelling drink. Moreover, diverse torments of similar pairs are presented to them. A dispute breaks out between the leaders and their followers; the leaders say to those who follow behind, "No welcome for you!" and they reply, "Nay, it is you who have no welcome, for you brought Hell upon us!" Then they pray against them: "O our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, double their punishment manifold!" Furthermore, remembering how they used to ridicule the poor believers in the world, they are astonished when they do not see them in Hell. This dispute will surely come to pass.

Our Prophet (peace be upon him) is addressed thus: "Say: I am only a warner. There is no god but Allah, the One, the All-Dominant." This is momentous news, yet people turn away from it. The Prophet had no knowledge of the dispute among the exalted assembly of angels (al-mala' al-a'la), but he was informed through revelation. This dispute relates to the statement mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah: "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption?" The secret of the dispute in the exalted assembly concerns the expiation of sins and the attainment of high ranks.

Allah tells the angels that He is going to create a human being from clay. After fashioning and proportioning him, He commands them to prostrate before him once He has breathed into him of His spirit. The angels all prostrate together, but Iblis behaves arrogantly, refuses to prostrate, and becomes one of the disbelievers. Allah asks: "What prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My own hands?" Iblis replies, "I am better than him; You created me from fire, and You created him from clay." Thereupon, Allah banishes Iblis from Paradise and proclaims that His curse is upon him until an appointed time. Iblis asks for respite to mislead mankind, though he concedes that sincere servants will be exempt from this. Allah then declares that He will surely fill Hell with Iblis and all those who follow him.

It is said to the Prophet that he asks for no payment in return for the Qur'an and imposes nothing of his own accord. The Qur'an is an admonition for all the worlds. Everyone will surely come to know its news after a time, in this world or in the Hereafter.

The revelation of this Book is from Allah. It is emphasized that He possesses almighty power and wisdom. The attribute 'al-Aziz' signifies that Allah is never vanquished and has no partner. These two attributes highlight that the Quran is a mighty and wise book, and they prepare the way for the theme of tawhid (the oneness of God).

Pure religion belongs to Allah alone. Those who associate partners with Him claim that they worship idols, angels, or noble servants such as Jesus only so that 'they may bring us closer to Allah.' Yet this is baseless; worship must be rendered to Allah alone. Glad tidings are for those who avoid the Taghut (false deities) and turn to Allah.

Allah has sent down the best of speech as a harmonious book consistent within itself and paired. The skins of those who hear it shiver, and then soften with the remembrance of Allah. This is Allah's guidance; He guides with it whom He wills, and whomever He leaves to stray, no one can guide.

Allah presents a parable: A man belongs to many quarreling partners, while another belongs entirely to one person and is at peace. Can the two ever be equal? Praise belongs to Allah, yet most of them do not know. Both the Prophet and other people are mortal; on the Day of Resurrection, you will dispute in the presence of your Lord.

The righteous (muttaqun) who bring the truth and confirm it will have whatever they desire with their Lord. Allah will overlook even their worst deeds and reward them according to the best of what they did. Allah is sufficient for His servant; none other than Him should be feared.

Allah takes the souls at the time of their death and during their sleep. He retains those for whom He has decreed death, and releases the others until a specified term. Indeed, in this are signs for those who reflect. In death and sleep, the soul is in Allah's hands; this points to the resurrection and the return to Allah.

Intercession belongs entirely to Allah. No one can intercede without His permission. When Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of the disbelievers shrink with aversion, but when others are mentioned, their faces brighten. O My servants! Do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed, He forgives all sins. Repent and turn to your Lord before the punishment comes.

The word 'yamin' means right hand, and it also conveys the meanings of strength and taking an oath. Here it can be interpreted as strength or an oath. As in the verse, "On that Day We will roll up the sky like the rolling up of scrolls for writings" (al-Anbiya, 21/104), a covenant has been made to roll up the sky. According to a narration from Aisha in Sahih Muslim, it was reported that during this time people will be upon the Sirat (the bridge).

In describing the Day of Resurrection, the blowing of the Trumpet (Sur) is recounted. Here there are two blowings: the first is the destructive 'nafkh al-sa'iq' (the blast of swooning), and the second is the raising 'nafkh al-qiyam' (the blast of resurrection). Although the word 'qiyamah' derives from the meaning of 'qiyam' (rising/standing) in the second blast, it also encompasses the first as its beginning; therefore, the breaking of the Hour signifies the greatest devastation.

In verses 69-70: Sa'iq refers to swooning and dying as if struck by a thunderbolt. Following this, the earth is made radiant. This is the gathering place of the Mahshar, which will be transformed in accordance with the expression in Surah Ibrahim, verse 48: "On the Day the earth will be replaced with another earth." In a hadith, it is reported that people will be gathered upon a white ground. Regarding this place, which will be illuminated by the light of the Lord, Ibn Abbas stated that it is not the light of the sun and the moon, but another light that Allah will create. The Book (the record of deeds) is laid open, and the prophets and witnesses are brought forward.

Verses 71-72: Those who disbelieved are driven into Hell in groups. Its gates are opened, and its keepers say to them: 'Did there not come to you messengers from among yourselves reciting to you My verses and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?' They say, 'Yes, they did.' But the decree of punishment has been realized against the disbelievers. It is said to them: 'Enter the gates of Hell to abide eternally therein.' How wretched is the abode of the arrogant!

Verses 73-74: Those who feared their Lord are led to Paradise in groups. Its gates are opened, and its keepers say: 'Peace be upon you; you have done well! Enter it to abide eternally.' And they say: 'Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the land of Paradise; we dwell wherever we please in Paradise.' How excellent is the reward of those who perform good deeds!

Verse 75: You will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying their Lord with praise. Judgment is executed among the people with truth, and it is proclaimed: 'Praise be to Allah, the Lord of the worlds.'

The letters 'Ha Mim' at the beginning of Surah al-Mu'min, according to some scholars, indicate the names ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, or serve as an oath by these names. It has also been narrated that these letters were recited as 'Ar-Rahman'. The letters 'Ha Mim' have also been interpreted as the beginning of Hamd (praise) and the middle of the name Muhammad, and it has been said to mean 'O Muhammad'. However, the majority stated that these are names of the Quran or of the surahs, and therefore, bearing characteristics such as 'alamiyyah' (proper noun) and 'ta'nith' (femininity), they are diptote (ghayr munsarif).

The angels who carry the Throne (Hamalat al-Arsh) are archangels, and their number is stated to be eight in Surah al-Haqqah. In some narrations, there is also the view that they are four today and will be eight on the Day of Resurrection. Furthermore, there are angels who surround the Throne; these are called 'Kerubiyyun' (Cherubim). Kerubiyyun means the angels closest to Allah, and according to some, they are only the angels who carry the Throne. Ibn Sina, on the other hand, stated that the Kerubiyyun angels are the commanders of the highest sphere, while the angels who carry the Throne are the Amilun (active) angels.

On the Day of Resurrection, it will be cried out to the disbelievers: 'Allah's hatred toward you is greater than your hatred toward yourselves; for when you were called to faith, you used to disbelieve.' They will say: 'Our Lord! You made us die twice and gave us life twice. Now we have recognized our sins. Is there, then, any way out?' In response, it will be said: 'This punishment is upon you for this reason: when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when partners were associated with Him, you believed. So the judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Most Great.'

Allah is the One Who shows His signs and sends down provision for you from the heaven. Yet none understands this except those who turn to Him with heart and mind. So call upon Allah, dedicating religion purely to Him, even if the disbelievers dislike it. Allah is the Exalter of ranks, the Lord of the Throne. He sends down the spirit (the angel) by His command upon whomever He wills, to warn of the terror of the Day of Meeting. On that Day, it will be asked: 'Whose is the dominion this Day?' In response, it will be said: 'It belongs to Allah, the One, the Subduer.' On that Day, every soul will be recompensed for what it earned, and there will be no injustice.

A believer from Pharaoh's family who concealed his faith opposed those who wished to kill Moses (Musa), saying: 'Will you kill a man merely because he says, "My Lord is Allah," when he has come to you with clear proofs from your Lord? If he is a liar, his lie will be against him; but if he is truthful, some of that with which he threatens you will strike you.' Warning his people, this individual reminded them that the life of this world is only a temporary enjoyment and that the Hereafter is the enduring abode, calling them to salvation. Pharaoh, paying no heed to these admonitions, wished to build a tower and reach the pathways of the heavens to look upon the God of Moses, but his plot came to naught.
While the believer was calling his people to salvation, they were calling him to the Fire. This appeal demonstrated that standing up against Pharaoh was both legitimate and necessary for salvation.

Allah protected that believer from the plots of Pharaoh's family. Pharaoh and his troops suffered an evil punishment in this world. In the life of the grave as well, they are exposed to the Fire morning and evening and tormented, and on the Day of Resurrection, they will be cast into the severest punishment.

Allah helps His messengers and those who believe, both in this world and in the Hereafter. On that Day, offering excuses will not benefit the wrongdoers; upon them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode. Moses was given guidance, and the Children of Israel were made to inherit the Torah. The Prophet was commanded patience, seeking forgiveness, and glorification.

Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any proof have in their breasts nothing but an arrogance that they will never attain. Regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse, there are two narrations: the polytheists of Quraysh, or the Jews awaiting the Dajjal. Both groups denied the truth out of their arrogance.

The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of humankind. The blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are those who believe and do righteous deeds equal with the evildoer. The Hour will certainly come. Allah has said, 'Call upon Me; I will respond to you.' Those who are too proud to worship Him will enter Hell.

Their faith at the moment they saw Allah's wrath did not benefit them. This is the established law of Allah regarding His servants. It is at this point that the disbelievers were lost in ruin. That is to say, repentance and faith shown when the punishment arrives do not save a person; because for faith to be accepted, one must believe in the unseen and submit before witnessing the punishment.

These verses aim to remind of Allah's blessings and to encourage travel. Specifically, the creation of riding beasts provides humans with both transportation and other benefits. This reminder serves as a preparation for the call in verse 82 below: 'Have they not traveled through the earth and observed?'

When the messengers came to them with clear proofs and miracles, the disbelievers relied 'in the name of knowledge' on the knowledge, crafts, and philosophy they possessed. Because of this reliance, they persisted in refusing to acknowledge the clear signs brought by the messengers.

Accepting their own intellect and accumulated knowledge as absolute truth, they belittled the divine message. However, the miracles of the messengers and the clear signs they conveyed are present in every era, but the arrogant do not wish to see them.

Here, people are urged to see the end of past communities and take heed. Traveling through the earth and observing the fate of those who disbelieved serves as a warning and a lesson for those who believe.

The opening verses of Surah Fussilat state that the Quran is a book whose verses have been clearly explained in detail (tafsil). The polytheists refused to listen to the Prophet, asserting that their hearts were veiled and their ears were heavy. According to a narration, Abu Jahl placed a curtain between himself and the Prophet; however, the following day seventy people came asking him to explain Islam, and they embraced Islam.

In the verse concerning the creation of the earth in two days, the word 'yawm' denotes time in an absolute sense. While some commentators interpret these two days as the separation of the earth from the heaven and the leveling of the earth, others maintain that they point to the turning of the seasons. Within four days, the mountains, blessings, and sustenance were ordained. These four days, together with the preceding two days, constitute six days, which aligns with the six days of creation mentioned in other verses.

The creation of the heaven while it was smoke and the command given to the earth and the heaven to 'come, willingly or unwillingly,' signifies their obedience. This command is to be understood as natural laws submitting to the divine will. The heavens were arranged into seven tiers in two days, and the nearest heaven was adorned with stars and safeguarded. Thereafter, the polytheists are warned through the reminder of the destruction of the peoples of 'Ad and Thamud.

On the Day of Resurrection, the ears, eyes, and skins of the disbelievers will bear witness against them. Their skins will say that Allah made them speak. The disbelievers committed sins assuming that Allah would not know. Companions from among the devils were set over them, and these companions made their evil deeds seem fair to them. Thus, the decree of punishment was fulfilled against them.

The disbelievers attempted to drown out the Quran by making noise while it was being recited. Allah will make them taste a severe punishment and will requite them for the worst of their deeds. As for those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, telling them not to fear and giving them the glad tidings of Paradise. The angels are their allies in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. This is hospitality from Allah, the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.

Who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah, performs righteous deeds, and says, 'I am of the Muslims'? Evil must be repelled in the best possible manner so that even enmity may turn into friendship. None attain this maturity except those who show patience. The night and the day, the sun and the moon are signs of Allah's existence. Prostration must be made only to Allah, who created them. Just as Allah brings the dead earth back to life, He will likewise resurrect the dead.

Those who deny the Quran when it comes to them will surely suffer their punishment. It is a profoundly precious book; falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it. It has been revealed by Allah, the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy. Nothing is said to our Prophet except what was said to the messengers before him. Your Lord is the possessor of both forgiveness and painful punishment. In response to those who object to the Quran being in Arabic, it is stated that even if it had been revealed in a foreign tongue, they would still have objected. The Quran is guidance and healing for those who believe; for those who disbelieve, there is a heaviness in their ears, and it is blindness to them. It is as if they are being called from a distant place and do not hear.

Inviting to Allah is the most beautiful of speech. There are two conditions for this invitation: the inviter must himself perform righteous deeds and be a Muslim in true sincerity. The one who invites must say, 'I am of the Muslims,' call to good, and ensure that their deeds are in harmony with their call. Evil and good are not equal; the finest invitation is to repay evil with good. When this is done, even enmity becomes like a close relative. This disposition is granted only to those who are patient and possess a great portion of good. If a prompting from Satan should arise, one must immediately seek refuge in Allah.

The night and the day, the sun and the moon are among the proofs of Allah's existence and power. Prostration should not be made to them, but rather to Allah who created them. There are juridical rulings concerning the verse of prostration (sajdah): while Imam al-Shafi'i states that prostration should be performed at verse 41:37, according to Imam al-A'zam Abu Hanifa, it is performed at 41:38. The revival of the earth with rain after drought also demonstrates Allah's power; it is proof that He will also revive the dead.

Those who deviate (ilhad) regarding Our verses—that is, those who stray from righteousness, disbelieve, and distort—will be cast into the Fire. These are the ones who deny the Quran. The Quran is an unassailable (aziz) and praiseworthy (hamid) book; falsehood cannot approach it. Nothing was said to our Prophet except what had been said to the prophets before him. The disbelievers criticized the Quran for being in Arabic. Yet the Quran is guidance and healing for those who believe, whereas the disbelievers cannot benefit from it.

Moses was also given the Torah, and dispute arose concerning it. Had a prior word not gone forth from your Lord delaying the punishment, judgment would have been decreed between them immediately. They are in grave doubt concerning the Quran. Whoever does good does so for the benefit of their own soul, and whoever does evil does so against it. Your Lord is never unjust to His servants.

Knowledge of the Hour belongs exclusively to Allah. No being besides Him possesses this knowledge. On that Day, when Allah questions them concerning the partners they associated with Him, they will say, 'None of us bears witness to that.' The things they used to worship previously will vanish from them, and they will find no place of escape. Man never tires of asking for good, but when evil touches him, he falls into despair. When he is made to taste mercy, he becomes arrogant and denies the Hereafter. Allah will surely inform the disbelievers of what they did and will make them taste a heavy punishment. When favor is bestowed upon man, he turns away; but when evil touches him, he prays profusely. Ask our Prophet: If the Quran has indeed come from Allah and yet you have denied it, who could be further astray?

We will show the disbelievers Our signs both on the horizons and within their own souls until it becomes completely manifest that the Quran is the truth. It is sufficient that your Lord is a witness over all things. Indeed, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord. Yet Allah encompasses all things in His knowledge and power. They cannot escape His punishment. Meeting Allah is true and inevitable.

Elmalılı states that the letters "Hâ-mîm" at the beginning of the surah are two separate names, and that this surah is considered separated in order to harmonize with the other "Hâ-mîm" surahs. Next, he says that the use of the present tense for the verb "reveals" indicates Allah's customary way of revelation (wahy) and points to the modes of revelation to be explained at the end of this surah (42:51). According to the author of al-Kashshaf, the meanings in this surah were revealed in their exact essence to you and to the prophets before you; for in them there is a great warning and favor for the servants.

The expression "The heavens are almost breaking apart from above them" describes the majesty of Allah. In the presence of His sublime majesty, the heavens tremble as if they might split open from above them. According to al-Zamakhshari, this is because Allah's exaltation is above the heavens. Next, it is stated that the angels seek forgiveness for those on the earth; this may be general, or, when specified for the believers, it carries the meaning of intercession (shafa'ah).

In verses 9–10, it is emphasized that the judgment of whatever you differ over belongs to Allah. The Messenger says, "That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn." Here, Elmalılı notes that the judgment will be delivered on the Day of Resurrection and that Allah will distinguish the rightful from the wrongful.

In verse 11, it is explained that Allah created the heavens and the earth, created for human beings spouses from among their own kind and pairs from the livestock, thereby providing reproduction. The expression "There is nothing like unto Him" is a metonymy (kinayah) emphasizing that Allah has no equal. Elmalılı points out that this expression carries the same meaning as saying "There is nothing like Allah," yet the metonymy is far more emphatic. Explaining the concept of mumathalah (resemblance), he adds that Allah's attributes are not like those found in human beings, and that He is the Eternal, All-Encompassing Hearer and Seer.

In verse 12, it is explained that the keys (treasures) of the heavens and the earth belong to Allah, and that He expands and restricts provision for whom He wills. Elmalılı states that this circumstance exists through the wisdom of the All-Knowing Allah, and that there is good both in the expansion and in the restriction of provision. This verse also points to the relationship between legal rulings (shar'i rulings) and knowledge.

In verse 13, it is stated that Allah has ordained as a law for you the religion (tawhid and righteousness) that He enjoined upon Noah (Nuh), and similarly what He enjoined upon Abraham (Ibrahim), Moses (Musa), and Jesus ('Isa), which He revealed to Muhammad. The command "Establish the religion and do not become divided therein" is the common message of all the prophets. Defining religion, Elmalılı states that it is a path through which voluntary actions are tied to a consequence, grounded in tawhid (monotheism) and obedience. Quoting Muhyiddin Ibn 'Arabi, he explains that establishing the religion is possible through the community (jama'ah), whereas division grants an opportunity to the enemy.

In verse 14, it is stated that the reason those who fell into division after knowledge had come to them was "baghy" (insolence, rivalry, or envy). Elmalılı explains that knowledge alone is not sufficient, and that religious discipline is necessary to suppress the evil inclinations of the soul (nafs). Had it not been for a prior word from Allah postponing the punishment, judgment would have been rendered immediately. Then, it is added that those who were made to inherit the Scripture are also in disquieting doubt.

In verse 15, the Messenger is commanded to invite people to tawhid, to remain upright, and not to follow the whims of the people. Saying, "I believe in whatever book Allah has sent down," the Messenger is tasked with judging with justice. Elmalılı emphasizes that the statement "our deeds are ours and your deeds are yours" leaves no room for dispute, and that the return of all is to Allah. In verse 16, it is explained that the arguments of those who dispute concerning Allah's religion after it has been accepted are invalid before their Lord, and upon them is wrath and severe punishment.

In verses 17–19, it is stated that the Book and the Balance were sent down with the truth, that the Hour might be near, that those who disbelieve seek to hasten it, whereas those who believe fear it and know that it is the truth. Elmalılı states that those who dispute concerning the Hour are in deep misguidance. In verse 19, it is emphasized that Allah is Most Subtle and Kind (Latif) to His servants and gives provision to whom He wills; it is expressed that this favor is a promise to those who believe.

In verses 20–23, it is explained that whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, his harvest will be increased, while whoever desires the harvest of the world, something of it will be given to him, but he will have no share in the Hereafter. Furthermore, it is stated that they have no partners who could legitimate what Allah has not permitted, and that for the wrongdoers there is a painful punishment. It is related that on the Day of Resurrection, while the wrongdoers tremble in fear, those who believe and do righteous deeds will be in the gardens of Paradise, and that this is the great favor. The Messenger is instructed not to ask for any reward for conveying the message other than love among kinfolk.

In verses 24–26, it is recounted that the polytheists said of the Messenger, "He has invented a lie against Allah," whereas if Allah willed, He could seal his heart, and that He eliminates falsehood and establishes the truth. It is emphasized that Allah accepts repentance, pardons misdeeds, and knows what is done. It is added that the repentance of those who believe and do righteous deeds is accepted, while for the disbelievers there is a severe punishment.

In verses 27–29, it is stated that if Allah were to extend provision abundantly, His servants would commit tyranny, and for this reason He sends it down in the measure He wills. Sending down the rain after they have despaired and spreading His mercy everywhere are proofs of Allah's power. The creation of the heavens, the earth, and the living creatures is also among the proofs of His power, and He is fully capable of gathering them whenever He wills.

Elmalılı explains that the word "harth" means sowing crops, tilling, and yield, and that in this verse it is used for deeds and rewards. Whoever intends the reward of the Hereafter, Allah increases his harvest; and whoever desires only worldly gain, he is given of this world as much as is decreed, but he has no share in the Hereafter. This ruling is also confirmed by the hadith on intention: everyone receives a reward according to their intention, and the same act yields different outcomes with different intentions.

In verse 21, it is questioned whether the polytheists have partners who legitimate things that Allah has not permitted. These partners are devils or idols. Nothing can be legitimated without the permission of Allah. The word "fasl" (decisive decree) refers to the postponement of the judgment or punishment between the believers and the disbelievers until an appointed time. A painful punishment will surely come upon the wrongdoers.

On the Day of Resurrection, while the wrongdoers tremble in fear of the punishment for the injustices they committed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will be in the finest meadows of Paradise (rawdah). "Rawdah" refers to the most delightful areas of lush, well-watered gardens. There, the believers attain whatever they desire in the presence of their Lord; this great favor is manifold superior to worldly blessings.

Our Prophet does not ask for a reward in return for his proclamation; he only asks for love due to kinship or love for the sake of closeness (qurbah) to Allah. According to Ibn Abbas, this means saying to the Quraysh, "at least respect my kinship." Whoever acquires a good deed (hasanah), Allah grants him even more goodness; for He is Most Forgiving (Ghafur) and Most Appreciative (Shakur).

The polytheists claim that the Prophet invented a lie against Allah; yet if Allah willed, He could seal his heart as well. Allah eliminates falsehood and establishes the truth through His words. He accepts the repentance of those who repent. The living creatures dispersed throughout the heavens and the earth are among His signs (ayat). Allah is fully capable of gathering them all whenever He wills.

The misfortunes that befall a person are due to the sins their own hands have earned, yet Allah forgives much. It is impossible to frustrate Allah; besides Him, there is neither protector nor helper. The ships sailing like mountains upon the sea are also proof of His power. If He wills, He stills the wind, leaving the ships motionless; if He wills, He destroys them on account of sins. Those who dispute concerning the verses should know that they have no place of refuge.

The life of this world is a fleeting enjoyment; what is enduring are the blessings in the presence of Allah. Those who believe and put their trust in their Lord avoid major sins (kaba'ir) and indecencies (fawahish), and when they are angry, they forgive. They respond to the call of their Lord, establish prayer, conduct their affairs by mutual consultation (shura) among themselves, and spend out of the provision given to them. When subjected to oppression, they unite and defend their rights; and this is an obligation within the scope of communal duty (fard al-kifayah).

The recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it; yet whoever pardons, their reward rests with Allah. There is no blame on someone who is wronged and defends their right; the real blame is directed at those who oppress people and commit insolence on the earth without right. Patience and forgiveness are among the matters requiring great resolve.

Allah speaks to a human being only in three ways: through revelation (inspiration to the heart), from behind a veil (by causing them to hear, as with Moses [Musa]), or by sending an angelic messenger. The revelation that comes through Gabriel is of the highest degree. The prophets convey the revelation they receive through these means to humanity.

In this section, the ways in which Allah sends revelation to His prophets are addressed. As stated in verse 42:51, Allah speaks to a human being in only three ways: either through direct revelation, from behind a veil, or by sending an angelic messenger. These three forms summarize all possible types of revelation. In his tafsir of this verse, Elmalılı also touches upon the lexical meaning of the concept of revelation (wahy), citing from al-Alusi that Imam Abu Abd Allah Taymi al-Isbahani stated that 'the essence of wahy is conveying, and inspiration, gesturing, and writing are also considered forms of revelation.' According to Raghib's Mufradat, however, the root essence of wahy is a swift sign, and it is used because it encompasses swiftness.

Although revelation (wahy) lexically derives from a triliteral verb, in the Quran it generally appears in the quadriliteral 'if'al' form. The word 'iyha' means both to reveal and to cause to reveal. Here, direct revelation is called 'wahy', while that which occurs through a messenger is termed 'iyha'. Allah has not spoken to any prophet in any way other than these three forms and does not speak to humans face to face; for He is exalted above all. Rather, by His wisdom, He speaks through wahy or iyha. Shaykh Abd al-Wahhab al-Sha'rani's statements regarding this verse are also noteworthy: what prevents one from hearing Allah's speech is the level of human nature; when the servant rises above this, Allah speaks to him as He speaks to spirits. Human nature means being entangled in affairs that hinder one from reaching the station of the spirit. To those at the level of human nature, Allah speaks through worldly things and manifests Himself in them.

Among the forms of revelation, the strongest is when the angel appears to the prophet and conveys the message. Because this serves as a witnessing between both the sender and the recipient, it is more corroborative in imparting knowledge. Revelation came to the prophets mostly in this manner. Another form is speaking from behind a veil, which is like Moses hearing the speech of Allah. The third form occurs by way of direct inspiration into the heart. The hadith of the Messenger of Allah, 'The Holy Spirit breathed into my heart,' is an example of this. In addition, inspiration, subjugation (taskhir, making subservient), and dreams also fall within the scope of revelation. Indeed, Allah inspired the honeybee and revealed to the mother of Moses. The Prophet said: 'Revelation has ceased; only glad tidings (mubashshirat) remain, and that is the dream of a believer.'

Revelation is not merely a subjective emotional phenomenon; on the contrary, it possesses the quality of being a certainty of knowledge ('ilm al-yaqin) and even perceptual certainty ('ayn al-yaqin) that receives tidings from the Truth and takes place beyond the self, making things known. These three faculties (eye, ear, heart) constitute the nature of revelation. This is also consistent with the verse at the beginning of the surah: 'Thus He reveals to you, and to those before you.' Elmalılı notes here that the Quran revealed to the Messenger of Allah is a spiritual life principle, akin to the principle of knowledge and will. The Prophet did not previously know what the book was; he learned the requirements of faith only through revelation. For among the conditions of faith, reason alone is not sufficient, and there are matters that must be acquired through revelation.

As for the portion of revelation that reaches the saints (awliya) other than prophets, it is inspiration (ilham). However, this inspiration consists only of subtle secrets extending from the specific spirits of the angels; it is not the angel itself. The angel does not bring down revelation to anyone other than prophets and does not command with a divine decree. For the Sharia is complete, and only glad tidings (mubashshirat, joyous inspirations) remain. These inspirations may come from Allah to the servant directly or through an intermediary. The intermediary belongs to prophethood. The saints can only see the angel outside the state of delivering revelation; they do not see the angel at the moment of revelation. For this reason, the saints cannot attain the rank of prophethood. As al-Sha'rani also emphasized, 'The inspiration of anyone other than prophets is not a source of knowledge for the general public.' This is an established principle accepted in Islamic creed ('aqa'id) and legal methodology (usul).

In the continuation of the verse, Elmalılı conveys the following meaning: 'And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command.' That is, We revealed the Quran. Previously, you did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was. But We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed, you (O Muhammad) surely guide to the straight path, that is, the path of Allah. This path is the straight and upright way that has no crookedness or deviation, coming from Allah and leading to Allah.

This verse describes the greatness of the path of Allah and the way to attain every desire. As a concluding word, it is emphasized that whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth belongs to Allah.

Everything is the property of Allah; the right of disposal and judgment belong solely to Him. For this reason, everything should be asked of Him, and should be asked within the bounds of His will, His Sharia, and His law.
Even if some things are temporarily under the authority of individuals or societies, in the end all affairs return and reach Allah alone. Temporary controls cease, and judgment remains with Allah.

Therefore, those who follow a path other than Allah's and worship others ultimately become bewildered and wretched. Those who keep to the path of Allah, however, attain every desire, achieving forgiveness and the pleasure of Allah.
Surah ash-Shura concludes here. Following it, in the same spirit, comes Surah az-Zukhruf. With the prayer of our Prophet: 'O Allah! Make us among those whom You have guided to Your straight path.'

At the beginning of the surah, the letters "Ha-Mim" and the oath sworn by the clear Book demonstrate that the Quran needs no other proof to prove itself. The origin of the Book, the Preserved Tablet (Lawh al-Mahfuz) or Allah's knowledge, is exalted and full of wisdom. Despite the transgression of the polytheists, Allah reminds that He will not abandon the warning, that He also sent prophets to earlier nations, and that they were destroyed.

The confession of the polytheists when asked that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth demonstrates His power. Just as Allah revives the dead earth, it is stated that they will also be brought forth into a new life through the Quran. Allah, who created all the pairs, teaches them to mount their riding beasts and give thanks; the importance of supplication (du'a) and glorification (tasbih) during travel is emphasized.

The polytheists ascribe a portion of His servants to Allah (through incarnation [hulul], offspring, or association of partners). Yet, not considering everything created by Allah as belonging to Him and associating partners with Him is ingratitude. Then, the claim that Allah has taken daughters is rejected; their regarding the angels as female and their fatalistic excuses are criticized. Their blind imitation of their fathers' religion is condemned, and Abraham's heritage of monotheism (tawhid) is recalled.

In response to the Quraysh's assertion that the Quran ought to have been sent down to a great man from the two cities, it is declared that it is Allah who distributes mercy, that worldly wealth is transient, and that the Hereafter is for the righteous. A devil is assigned to whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful (al-Rahman); on the Day of Resurrection, friends become enemies.

The sending of Moses (Musa) to Pharaoh and his miracles are recounted; Pharaoh's arrogance and the obedience of his people cause their destruction. This narrative serves as a comfort to the Prophet and a warning to the Quraysh. Then, the example of Jesus is presented; it is emphasized that he is not a deity, but a servant and a prophet. The fact that Jesus is a sign of the Hour is stated, and the command to follow his path is given.

In the final section of the surah, the promise of Paradise to the righteous, the punishment of Hell for the criminals, and the matter of intercession (shafa'ah) are addressed. It is stated that Allah knows everything, that idols cannot intercede, and that only those who knowingly bear witness to the truth can intercede. The polytheists are criticized for acknowledging Allah's role as the Creator and yet still turning away from the truth.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) submitted to his Lord that his people did not believe, and Allah informed him to pay no heed to them for now and to turn away saying, 'Peace be upon you,' for they will soon come to know.

On the Day of Resurrection, it will be said addressing the righteous servants: 'Today there is no fear for you.' They will be received with joy on their faces, and hospitality will be served to them in golden platters in Paradise. Therein is whatever souls desire and eyes delight in, and they will abide therein eternally.

The criminals, however, are in the torment of Hell. They cry out, 'O Malik,' asking their Lord to put an end to them. But they are told that they are to remain permanently and that there is no salvation through death. For they did not love the truth sent to them in the worldly life.
Allah questions whether the polytheists have devised a firm plot against the Prophet. Yet He hears their secret talks, and beside them are angels recording everything. Allah's plot is firmer.

For the sake of the Prophet's supplication, 'O Lord,' it is emphasized that the Most Merciful has no offspring. The polytheists do not believe. Finally, the Prophet is commanded to pay no heed to them and to pass them by with peace; they will soon come to know. With this warning, Surah az-Zukhruf ends and Surah ad-Dukhan begins.

The letters "Hâ-mîm" at the beginning of the surah are a concise symbol of the divine mercy of the Rahman (the All-Merciful) manifested in the soul of Muhammad. Then, an oath is sworn by the clear book. While this book could be the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), in view of the pronoun, it is more fitting that it refers to the Quran.

It is reported that the Quran was sent down on a blessed night. According to most tafsir scholars, this night is the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr); Ikrima and some others state that it is the night of mid-Sha'ban (Laylat al-Bara'ah). It is stated that on this night every wise matter is distinguished, and provisions, lifespans, and other decrees are recorded. Reconciling the two views, it is expressed that the descent of the Quran in its entirety (inzal) took place on the night of Bara'ah, while its gradual descent (tanzil) began on the Night of Decree.

There are two interpretations regarding the smoke (dukhan): First, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, is the smoke seen during the years of severe famine; second is the smoke that will envelop the sky as a sign of the Day of Judgment. This smoke will have an effect resembling a cold on believers, and an intoxicating effect on disbelievers. Both interpretations are deemed suitable to the context of the verse.

Allah cites the destruction of Pharaoh's people as an example. He reminds that He delivered the Children of Israel from humiliating punishment, knowingly favored them above the worlds, and granted them signs (miracles). Then, it is recounted that the disbelievers of Mecca denied the Hereafter, saying, "There is nothing beyond our first death."

In response to the denial of the disbelievers, it is recalled that the people of Tubba' and those before them were destroyed. It is emphasized that the heavens and the earth were not created in play, and that the day of distinguishing truth from falsehood will come. On that day, a friend will be of no benefit to a friend, and none shall be saved except those upon whom Allah has mercy.

It is recounted that the tree of Zaqqum is the food of the sinners, boiling in bellies like scalding water. The righteous (muttaqin), on the other hand, will be in gardens, by springs, in garments of silk and accompanied by houris; they will taste no death there except the first death. This is a great bounty from your Lord.

At the end of the surah, it is stated that the Quran has been made easy in the Arabic language in the hope that they might take heed. The Prophet is commanded to wait for what will befall them; for they too are waiting.

Surah al-Jathiyah begins with the verse, "The revelation of this Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise." This emphasizes that the Quran was sent down by Allah and that He is all-conquering and the Possessor of wisdom. Then it is stated that there are numerous signs (proofs) in the heavens and the earth for the believers. These signs point to Allah's existence, might, and power; the believers must examine them and take heed.

In the creation of man and in the animals, there are also signs for people of assured faith. The creation, diversity, and reproduction of animals demonstrate Allah's power. The alternation of night and day, the sending down of rain to revive the earth, and the directing of the winds are also lessons for a people who understand. These signs point to the Hereafter and the resurrection after death.

Woe to those who hear the verses of Allah and then persist in arrogance! These verses were revealed concerning the likes of Abu Jahl. It is then explained that Allah has subjected the sea to your service so that ships may sail upon it and that you may seek His bounty. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth has all been placed at the service of humanity as a grace from Allah; this requires giving thanks.

The believers are told to forgive those who do not look forward to the days of Allah's retribution. Everyone will be recompensed for what they have earned. The Children of Israel were given the Scripture, judgment, and prophethood; they were provided with wholesome sustenance and favored over the worlds. However, they fell into discord only after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual rivalry. Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection.

Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was placed upon a clear path (shariah) in matters of religion; he must follow it and not follow the desires of those who do not know. The wrongdoers are allies of one another, whereas Allah is the Protector of the righteous (al-muttaqun). The Quran is a light, guidance, and mercy for mankind. Do those who commit evil deeds think that they will be treated like those who believe and do righteous deeds? How ill they judge!

Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth; everyone will be recompensed for what they have done, and they will not be wronged. There is no one who can guide the person who takes their own desire as their god, whom Allah has led astray based on His knowledge, and whose hearing and heart He has sealed, and over whose sight He has placed a veil. The polytheists say, "There is nothing beyond this worldly life of ours; time alone destroys us." Yet they have no knowledge of this; they do nothing but conjecture.

When the verses are recited to them clearly, the polytheists say, "Bring back our forefathers if you are truthful." Say: "Allah gives you life, then causes you to die, and then gathers you together on the Day of Resurrection. But most people do not know."

To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. On the Day of Resurrection, those who follow falsehood will be the losers. You will see every community kneeling; each will be summoned to its record. Those who believe and do righteous deeds will enter into mercy; as for the disbelievers, they will be reminded that His verses were recited to them, but they acted arrogantly and denied the Resurrection. The evil of the deeds they committed will become apparent to them, and they will abide in the Fire forever.

Praise be to Allah, Lord of the heavens, Lord of the earth, and Lord of the worlds. All greatness and sovereignty in the heavens and the earth belong to Him. He is the Almighty (all-conquering) and the All-Wise (the Possessor of absolute judgment and wisdom).

The word 'sa'ah' (the Hour), which refers to the day the Resurrection will occur, is a portion of time according to al-Raghib's explanation. It was given this name by comparison to the Resurrection. Knowledge of when the Resurrection will take place belongs to Allah alone. There are two interpretations of this word: The first is Allah's swift reckoning. The second is that those who witness the Resurrection will think they had remained in the world for only an evening or the morning thereof.

The concept of the Hour is divided into three categories: The major hour is the resurrection of people for the reckoning. The middle hour is the death of the people of an entire generation. The minor hour is a person's own death. Every individual's death is their personal resurrection. Indeed, it has been said, 'Whoever dies, their resurrection has already come to pass.' However, the Hour mentioned in this verse refers to the general Resurrection.

The word 'jathiyah' in the verse 'And you will see every community kneeling (jathiyah)' has been interpreted in two ways. The first means kneeling, which expresses respect and a composed posture. The second means a gathered congregation. The intent is the gathering before Allah for the reckoning.

What is emphasized in these verses is Allah's absolute sovereignty in the heavens and the earth, the certainty of the Day of Resurrection, and the gathering of all nations before His presence for the reckoning on that day. While explaining these concepts, Elmalılı cited various interpretations, yet did not pass a definitive judgment.

The concepts of bid'a and bid'at refer to unprecedented new things. With the verse, 'Say: I am not the first of the messengers,' the Prophet (peace be upon him) states that he did not introduce an innovation different from those before him, but rather followed their path. Furthermore, a witness from the Children of Israel saw the likeness of Prophet Muhammad in the Torah and believed. It is narrated that this witness was Abdullah ibn Salam, though some say it was Moses (Musa). There is a difference of opinion as to whether the verse is Makki or Madani.

In verse 11, it is reported that the disbelievers belittled the believers, saying, 'If there were any good in Islam, they would not have preceded us to it,' and then would say, 'This is an ancient lie.' These words were spoken by both the polytheists and the Jews. Most of the believers were poor people like Ammar, Suhayb, and Bilal; by disparaging them, they sought to belittle Islam.

In verse 12, it is emphasized that before the Quran, the Torah, the book of Moses, was a guide and a mercy. The Quran, on the other hand, is a book revealed in Arabic, confirming the previous scriptures, warning the wrongdoers, and giving glad tidings to the doers of good. In verses 13-14, it is stated that there will be no fear or grief for those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and remain steadfast, and that they are the companions of Paradise.

In verse 15, Allah enjoins man to do good to his parents. The hardships endured by the mother are described: the period of pregnancy and weaning is thirty months. This period is interpreted as six months of pregnancy and two years of nursing. An incident that took place between Umar and Ali indicates that the minimum duration of pregnancy is six months. When a person reaches the age of forty, he prays to give thanks to Allah, to perform righteous deeds, and for the rectification of his offspring. This supplication was revealed concerning Abu Bakr.

In verse 16, glad tidings are given that the best of what these righteous people have done will be accepted and their misdeeds will be overlooked. The expression 'the best' encompasses acts of obedience such as the recommended (mandub) and the obligatory (wajib). In the counsel Abu Bakr gave to Umar, it is explained that Allah has rights by night and by day, and that the heaviness of the Scale (mizan) depends on following the truth.

In verses 17-18, a contrasting example is presented: a person who says 'Fie upon you' to his parents and denies the resurrection. His parents, seeking refuge in Allah, call him to faith, but he says, 'This is nothing but legends of the ancients.' Such are those among the communities of jinn and men that passed away before them against whom the decree of punishment has been realized; they are the ruined. In verses 19-20, it is stated that everyone has ranks according to what they have done, and that because the disbelievers indulged in the pleasure of good things in this world, they will face a humiliating punishment in the Hereafter.

In verse 20, it is explained that the disbelievers who exhausted their good things in the life of this world will receive no reward in the Hereafter. It is narrated that upon this verse, Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) did not become attached to worldly pleasures, wishing to preserve his good deeds for the Hereafter. Furthermore, the poverty of the People of the Bench (Ahl al-Suffah) is related, along with the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) stating that their condition was better for them in the world.

In verses 21-23, it is recounted that Hud (peace be upon him), the prophet of the people of 'Ad, warned his people in the region of al-Ahqaf. Ahqaf means curved sand dunes and points to the frailty of their land despite the might of the people of 'Ad. Hud told them not to worship anything other than Allah and stated that he feared for them the punishment of a tremendous day.

In verses 24-25, it is related that the punishment approached in the form of a cloud; the people rejoiced, thinking it was a rain cloud, but it was a wind bearing a painful punishment. The wind demolished everything and destroyed them. Narrated from Ibn Abbas, it is stated that the wind submerged the people in a torrent of sand for seven nights and eight days, ultimately casting them into the sea. Hud and the believers were spared.

In verses 26-28, it is emphasized that the faculties Allah bestowed upon the people of 'Ad (hearing, sight, intellect/hearts) availed them nothing because they rejected the signs of Allah. The destroyed lands around them (such as Ma'rib, Thamud, and Sodom) are cited as examples. It is explained that the deities they had taken besides Allah did not help them; on the contrary, they vanished from them.

In verses 29-32, it is related that a group of jinn was directed to the Prophet (peace be upon him) to listen to the Quran. After listening to the Quran, these jinn returned to their people and called them to faith. They said that the scripture revealed after Moses guided to the right path, that those who respond to Allah's caller will be forgiven, and that those who do not respond cannot escape Allah.

In verses 33-35, it is stated that Allah, Who is able to give life to the dead, did not grow weary with creating the heavens and the earth. It is reported that on the day the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire, they will confess the truth. The Prophet is commanded to be patient just as the messengers of steadfast resolve (ulu al-'azm) were patient. It is stated that when they witness the punishment of the Hereafter, the time they remained in the world will seem short to them, and that none will be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient (fasiqun).

Allah renders worthless the deeds of those who disbelieve and avert people from the path of Allah. In contrast, for those who believe, perform righteous deeds, and believe in what has been revealed to Muhammad, He pardons their sins and rectifies their state. The fundamental difference between these two groups is that the disbelievers follow falsehood, while the believers follow the truth from their Lord. Thus does Allah present their examples to people.

When you encounter the disbelievers in battle, strike their necks. Once you have overcome their strength, bind the captives securely. Thereafter, either release them freely or take ransom. This ayah offers options to the leader regarding captives: executing them, enslaving them, releasing them for ransom, or setting them free without compensation. However, the scholars differed on this matter; while some state that this ruling was abrogated by the verses in Surah at-Tawbah, others maintain that it is definitive (muhkam). According to al-Tabari, both verses are valid, and the leader has discretion.

The deeds of those slain in the path of Allah will not be in vain. Allah guides them, rectifies their state, and admits them into Paradise. Paradise has been made known to them in this world and adorned with sweet fragrances. If the believers help Allah (by upholding His commands and serving His religion), Allah will also help them and make their feet firm.

As for the disbelievers, ruin awaits them and their deeds will come to nothing. That is because they disliked what Allah revealed. Have they not traveled through the earth and seen the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them. The same fate applies to these disbelievers as well. Allah is the protector and helper of the believers, whereas the disbelievers have no protector.

Allah admits those who believe and perform righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. The disbelievers, on the other hand, eat and drink like cattle in this world, and their destination is the Fire. How many cities far stronger than the city that drove you out have been destroyed! Is one who relies on clear evidence from his Lord like one whose evil deeds are made appealing to him and who follows his own desires?

The description of the Paradise promised to the righteous: In it are rivers of incorruptible water, rivers of milk whose taste never changes, rivers of wine delicious to those who drink it, and rivers of purified honey.

Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Those who disbelieve indulge in worldly pleasures, eating and drinking like cattle, and their final destination is the Fire. While there are all kinds of fruits and forgiveness from their Lord in Paradise for the believers, the disbelievers are made to drink boiling water that tears their bowels to pieces. These two groups are not alike at all.

The representation of the Paradise promised to the righteous is as follows: In it are rivers of incorruptible water, milk whose taste never alters, delicious and non-intoxicating wine, and pure, filtered honey. Moreover, there are all kinds of fruits and forgiveness from their Lord. This forgiveness has been interpreted as never reminding them of their sins, or as bounty and good pleasure. While the people of Paradise abide eternally amid these blessings, the people of Hell will be tormented with boiling water.

The hypocrites come to the gathering of the Messenger of Allah and listen to his words, yet they treat them lightly. When they depart from his presence, they ask the knowledgeable Companions mockingly, "What did he just say?" Allah has sealed their hearts; they follow their whims and desires. As for those who are guided, Allah increases their guidance and inspires them with piety. The portents of the Hour have come; they will not believe until the punishment comes upon them suddenly.

O Muhammad! Know that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. Ask forgiveness both for your own sin and for the believing men and believing women. Allah knows your movements and your place of rest. This is a conclusion to the explanations given since the beginning of the surah. This seeking of forgiveness (istighfar) will find its response in the upcoming Surah al-Fath.

The believers used to wish for a surah about jihad to be revealed. Yet when a definitive surah was revealed mentioning fighting, the hypocrites with sickness in their hearts look at you with faint glances out of fear of death. Yet death is more fitting for them than living. Their duty was obedience and speaking righteous words. Once the matter was determined, showing loyalty would have been better for them.
