To those who turned back to disbelief after the right path had become clear to them, Satan made their evils seem appealing and lured them with false hopes. That is because they said to those who disliked what Allah revealed, "We will obey you in some matters." Allah knows what they conceal. How terrible will their state be when the angels take their souls, striking their faces and their backs! This is because they pursued what displeased Allah and disliked His good pleasure; thus Allah rendered their deeds worthless.

Allah will surely test you until He makes evident those among you who strive in jihad and those who are patient. Those who disbelieve, bar others from the path of Allah, and oppose the Prophet can cause no harm to Allah; Allah will render their deeds worthless. O you who believe! Obey Allah and obey the Prophet, and do not render your deeds vain. Those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers, Allah will never forgive them.

Do not falter and call for peace when you have the upper hand; Allah is with you, and He will not deprive you of the reward of your deeds. The worldly life is only play and amusement. If you believe and are conscious of Allah, He will grant you your rewards and will not ask you for all your wealth. Had He demanded it, you would have shown stinginess, and your rancor would have been exposed. You are being called to spend in the way of Allah; whoever is stingy harms only himself. Allah is rich (free of all needs), and you are poor. If you turn away, Allah will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you.

The revelation of Surah al-Fath is narrated in a hadith transmitted from Umar: While on an expedition with the Prophet (peace be upon him), he asked a question three times, and when he received no answer, he grew concerned. Then he heard a voice, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Tonight a surah was revealed to me that is dearer to me than the world and all that is in it: "Truly, We have granted you a clear victory."' This surah was revealed after the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, somewhere between Mecca and Medina.

The surah has 29 verses, 560 words, and 2,430 letters. Its rhyme-letter (the common final letter of the verses) is 'nun'. Its connection to the preceding surah, Surah Muhammad, is clear: in the former, repentance and seeking forgiveness were commanded, while here forgiveness is proclaimed; that one concluded with a warning of replacement, whereas this one begins with the glad tidings of victory.

The word 'victory' in verse 1 refers, according to most commentators, to the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. This treaty ensured the recognition of the Muslims as a state and opened the door to subsequent conquests. The purpose of the Prophet (peace be upon him) in this expedition was not war but umrah; however, upon encountering the polytheists, peace was made, and this became an instrument for the spread of Islam.

In verses 2–3, the wisdom behind the victory is explained in four points: Allah forgiving the past and future sins of the Prophet, completing His favor upon him, guiding him to a straight path, and aiding him with a mighty victory. Here, according to most commentators, the expression 'sin' refers to instances such as the Prophet occasionally choosing the less optimal alternative in his independent judgment (ijtihad); furthermore, this forgiveness also signifies the easing of the hardships encountered in the Prophet's mission of messengership.

In verse 4, the concept of 'tranquility' (sakinah) is addressed. Tranquility is the inner peace and reassurance that descends upon the heart; it is sent down into the hearts of the believers so that they may add faith to their faith. This tranquility is one of the hosts of Allah, and by bringing peace to the believers, it prepares them for great victories. Allah is the Master of the hosts of the heavens and the earth; He knows all things and governs with wisdom.

In verses 5–7, two more reasons of wisdom behind this victory are mentioned: admitting believing men and women into gardens and overlooking their misdeeds, and subjecting to punishment the hypocrites and polytheists who harbor evil thoughts about Allah. This punishment is the consequence of their evil thoughts. To Allah belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth; He is Almighty and All-Wise.

In verses 8–10, the duty of the Prophet is explained as a witness, a bearer of glad tidings, and a warner. The believers must believe in Allah and His Messenger, honor and support Him, and glorify Him morning and evening. Furthermore, the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) made to the Prophet was in reality made to Allah; whoever breaks this pledge breaks it only to his own detriment, while whoever fulfills it will receive an immense reward.

Verses 11–14 describe the excuses and true nature of the Bedouins who did not join the expedition of Hudaybiyyah. They will say, 'Our wealth and our families kept us occupied, so ask forgiveness for us.' Yet they say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. Allah informs them that they assumed the Prophet and the believers would never return, and for this reason they deserved destruction. For whoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger, Hell has been prepared.

In verses 15–17, those who stayed behind from the battle are criticized for wanting to join only for the spoils of war and attempting to alter the word of Allah. They are informed that they will be called to fight against a people of great might: if they obey, there will be a fair reward, but if not, a painful punishment. Those with valid excuses (the blind, the lame, and the sick) are not held accountable; whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will enter Paradise, while those who turn away will suffer punishment.

The Bedouins who stayed behind from the battle will say, when you set out to take the spoils, 'Allow us to follow you.' They wish to change the word of Allah. Allah has promised the spoils to those who were present at Hudaybiyyah. Say to them: 'You shall never follow us. Thus has Allah declared beforehand.' Then they will say, 'No, you envy us.' In truth, they understand little of the reality.

Say to those Bedouins who remained behind: 'You will be called to fight against a people of great might.' It has been narrated that this people refers to Banu Hanifah, the Persians, or the Byzantines. These opinions are given by way of example, not limitation.

There is no blame upon the blind, the lame, or the sick for not going to war. They have valid excuses. If they wish and are able to go, that is also permissible. Indeed, Ibn Umm Maktum took part in the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah despite being blind.

Certainly, Allah was well pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree at Hudaybiyyah. He knew what was in their hearts, sent down reassurance upon them, and rewarded them with a near victory (Khaybar). He also promised them abundant spoils of war. Allah has promised you abundant spoils that you will capture, granted this to you promptly, and restrained the hands of the people from you.

If the disbelievers had fought against you, they would surely have turned their backs and fled. Such is the established way of Allah, and you will find no change in His way. It is He who held back your hands after making you victorious over them in the heart of Mecca. For there were believing men and women there whom you did not yet know; Allah prevented fighting so that you would not trample them. Had they been separated, We would surely have subjected those who disbelieved to a painful punishment.

Those who disbelieved had harbored in their hearts the fanatical zeal of the pre-Islamic days of ignorance (jahiliyyah). Thereupon Allah sent down His tranquility and reassurance upon His Messenger and the believers, and bound them to the word of piety (taqwa), for they were well entitled to it and worthy of it. And Allah is Knower of all things.

Umar was troubled by the peace treaty and objected to the Prophet (peace be upon him), but Abu Bakr calmed him, saying that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) was upon the truth and that his promise would certainly be fulfilled. Against the pagan zeal of ignorance displayed by the polytheists, Allah Almighty sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and the believers, soothing them and keeping them firm upon the word of piety (taqwa).

There are differing views regarding the word of piety (kalimat al-taqwa): according to some, it is the word of monotheism (tawhid) and the declaration of faith (shahadah); according to others, it is loyalty to the peace treaty and fidelity to the pledge. Because the believers were more deserving and worthy of this word than anyone else, Allah kept them steadfast upon it.

Allah has fulfilled the vision of His Prophet in truth. The believers will enter the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) in security, with their heads shaved or hair shortened. However, this will occur when Allah wills. The condition 'if Allah wills' (insha'Allah) indicates that the fulfillment of the promise depends on the will of Allah and that there may be those among them who will pass away before then. Prior to this, Allah granted an imminent victory, such as the peace of Hudaybiyyah and the conquest of Khaybar.

Allah has sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth. This religion shall prevail over all other religions. This superiority is both in terms of evidence and knowledge, as well as actual victory. And Allah is sufficient as a witness.

Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the Messenger of Allah. Those who are with him are firm against the disbelievers and compassionate among themselves. They are constantly bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty and good pleasure from Allah. On their faces are marks from the traces of prostration. Their description is likewise given in the Torah and the Gospel: they are like a seed that puts forth its shoot, strengthens it, and delights the sowers. In this manner, Allah increases and strengthens the believers, enraging the disbelievers through them. To those who believe and do righteous deeds, He has promised forgiveness and an immense reward.

Surah al-Hujurat begins with the address, 'O you who have believed!' to draw the attention of the believers. In the first verse, it is commanded not to put oneself forward before Allah and His Messenger. The word 'taqdim' means to put something forward. This prohibition forbids acting hastily in word and deed without observing the Sunnah of the Prophet and the ruling of Allah. The verse encompasses every kind of disrespect and behavior contrary to the Sharia.

There are various narrations regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse: In one narration, it is stated that it was revealed upon the dispute that arose between Abu Bakr and Umar when the delegation of Banu Tamim arrived. According to another narration, some people had slaughtered their sacrificial animals before the Prophet on the Day of Eid al-Adha. Furthermore, it is also narrated that it was revealed when some said words such as 'if only it were like this'.

In the second verse, the believers are commanded not to raise their voices above the voice of the Prophet and not to speak loudly to him. When this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr and Umar lowered their voices before the Prophet. Thabit ibn Qays, on the other hand, worried because he thought his voice was naturally loud; however, the Prophet gave him the glad tidings that he was among the people of Paradise.

In the third verse, it is reported that those who lower their voices in the presence of the Prophet possess piety and will receive a great reward. In the fourth and fifth verses, those who call out from behind the private chambers are reproached. It is narrated that these verses were revealed concerning a delegation from the tribe of Banu Tamim. They called out, disturbing the Prophet, and this conduct of theirs was criticized.

In the sixth verse, it is commanded that if a corrupt person (fasiq / a sinful person) brings news, its accuracy must be investigated. The occasion of revelation of this verse concerns al-Walid ibn Uqbah being sent to the Banu al-Mustaliq as a collector of zakah and his bringing false news that they had apostatized from the religion. The verse counsels against believing news immediately and causing harm.

In the seventh verse, the believers are reminded that the Messenger of Allah is among them. The importance of following the Prophet is emphasized, and it is stated that if he were to follow them in many matters, they would surely fall into hardship. Then, it is stated that Allah has endeared faith to them and made disbelief, defiance, and disobedience hateful to them. This demonstrates that faith is grounded upon love and is a grace from Allah.

By Allah's grace and favor, those who remain steadfast on the path of faith and obedience are those who heed the Prophet's warnings and refrain from corruption and rebellion. These individuals are the distinguished servants whose hearts Allah has tested for piety. They are the ones rightly guided. Allah knows all things and bestows favor through His wisdom.

If two groups among the believers fight, reconciliation must be made between them immediately. This command was revealed concerning an incident that took place between Abdullah ibn Ubayy and Abdullah ibn Rawahah. If one of the parties attacks unjustly, that transgressing group must be fought until it returns to the command of Allah. When the fighting ceases, judgment must be made with justice. Although this ruling is primarily directed at those in authority, it is a collective obligation (fard al-kifayah) that concerns all believers.

All believers are brothers. For this reason, making peace between two brothers is a requirement of brotherhood in religion. Fearing Allah and preserving peace is part of piety. If there is no peace among believers, their strength to struggle against the disbelievers weakens, and they may be deprived of Allah's mercy.

O you who have believed! Let not a people ridicule another people; perhaps the ridiculed are better than those who ridicule. Nor let women ridicule other women. Do not insult yourselves, and do not call each other by offensive nicknames. These prohibitions are meant to reinforce respect and brotherhood among believers. Ridicule means insult and contempt; this is contrary to the spirit of Islamic brotherhood.

Avoid much suspicion, for indeed, some suspicion is a sin. Do not spy—that is, do not seek out faults—and do not backbite one another. Backbiting is saying something behind a person's back that they would dislike; this is an abhorrent act, like eating the flesh of one's dead brother. Fear Allah, for He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.

O mankind! We created you from a male and a female, and made you into nations and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is Knowing, All-Aware.

The Bedouins said, 'We have believed,' but faith had not yet settled in their hearts. True believers are those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives. The reward of those who obey Allah and His Messenger is not diminished. Allah is Forgiving, Most Merciful. They should not hold their becoming Muslim as a favor; rather, they should realize that they attained faith through Allah's grace.

Allah commands: O mankind! We created you from a male and a female. That is, you are all of the same origin; therefore, there is no meaning in boasting of your lineage or looking down upon others. We made you into nations and tribes that you may know one another—that is, so you may know your lineage and cooperate accordingly, not to quarrel and boast. The most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most advanced in piety. That is, the one among you whose consciousness of responsibility toward Allah and sense of vigilance is the strongest is the most worthy.

Piety (taqwa) literally means protection. It is a person's shielding themselves from sin and the punishment of Allah. Taqwa has degrees: its lowest degree is avoiding polytheism (shirk), while its highest is turning toward Allah with one's entire being and refraining from everything other than Him. To be a person of piety, avoiding the unlawful (haram) is not enough; one must also keep away from doubtful matters. For circling around the unlawful may cause a person to fall into it. Our Prophet (peace be upon him) said regarding this: What is lawful is clear, and what is unlawful is clear; and between the two are doubtful matters. Whoever avoids doubtful matters safeguards his religion and his honor.

Regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse, the following narration is reported: Salman al-Farsi used to serve two Companions. One day, because he overslept, they sent him to ask for some condiment from the Prophet. When they learned that the Prophet had nothing with him, they said between themselves about Salman something like, 'If we sent him to a well, its water would run dry.' Later, when they came into the presence of the Prophet, the Messenger of Allah remarked that he saw the greenness of meat in their mouths, whereupon they stated that they had not eaten meat. Upon this, the Prophet said, 'You must have backbitten,' and this verse was revealed.

Then the verse draws attention to the difference between faith and Islam. The Bedouins said, 'We have believed.' Say to them: You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted in Islam.' For faith is the affirmation of the heart; it has not yet entered your hearts. True believers are those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. They are the truthful ones. Allah's knowledge encompasses all things; whatever is hidden and whatever is open, He knows. Therefore, He will judge you according to your intentions.

Finally, addressing those who held their becoming Muslim as a favor over the Prophet, it is declared: Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has conferred a favor upon you, for He has guided you to faith. If you are truthful, this is a great blessing. Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth; He sees everything you do. Be upright, then, from inside out, and protect yourselves through piety.

Surah Qaf, like Surah Sad, begins with a letter and an oath by the Quran. These letters are allegorical (mutashabih); their meaning is known only to Allah. According to Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, these letters serve as an alert to draw the listener's attention, and just as the rationale behind certain acts of worship cannot be grasped by human intellect, reciting these letters is an act of submitting to the divine command purely with the intention of worship. Allah swearing by these letters confers a distinct honor upon them.

Al-Razi lists five points regarding oaths sworn by letters: that oaths are taken either by things or by letters; that in oaths sworn by letters the oath particle is not mentioned; that the oaths are sworn by simple letters rather than by composite entities of things; that oaths sworn by letters occur in 28 surahs, whereas oaths sworn by things occur in 14 surahs; and that while oaths sworn by letters appear throughout, oaths sworn by things generally occur in the latter part.

The narration stating that the letter Qaf is the name of a mountain is considered weak. Al-Razi and al-Alusi oppose this view; according to al-Razi, the existence of this mountain has not been empirically observed, and al-Alusi shares the same opinion. Since the narration regarding Mount Qaf does not trace back to the Prophet (peace be upon him), it is more appropriate to consider the letter allegorical (mutashabih) and regard it as a symbol of Allah's omnipotence. However, according to a narration from Ibn Abbas, Qaf is a mountain encircling the earth and can be interpreted as the atmosphere.

Turning to the exegesis of the verses, it is stated that Allah swore by the glorious Qaf (Qaf al-Majid), that the disbelievers were astonished that a warner had come to them from among themselves, and that they deemed resurrection after death far-fetched. It is expressed that Allah's knowledge encompasses what the earth diminishes of man and that everything is preserved in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). This knowledge demonstrates that resurrection is not impossible.

Allah commands looking at the sky and the earth; it is recounted that the sky is without rifts, that the earth is spread out and stabilized with mountains, and that every beautiful pair of plants is brought forth. All of these serve as a lesson and a reminder for every servant who turns to their Lord. The sending down of blessed water from the sky to revive dead land is an analogue to the emergence of the dead from their graves.

It is recalled that earlier nations—Noah, al-Rass, Thamud, 'Ad, Pharaoh, Lot, and Tubba'—suffered punishment as a result of denying the prophets. It is emphasized that there was no incapacity in the initial creation, and thus re-creation is entirely possible. The idea of the continuous renewal of creation at every moment influenced thinkers such as Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi and Descartes.

Because Allah created man, He knows the whisperings of his soul; He is closer to him than his jugular vein. Two angels on the right and left record every word. When the stupor of death arrives, it is said, "This is what you used to evade." The Trumpet (Sur) is blown, and every soul arrives with a driver and a witness. On that day, the veil of heedlessness is lifted, and vision becomes sharp. The companion angel says, "This is ready." Allah commands that obstinate ingrates be cast into Hell; Satan pleads that he did not cause him to transgress. Allah declares that disputing in His presence is of no avail.

Allah knows everything that a person's soul whispers to him. Whispering (waswasah) encompasses hidden emotions, memories, and misgivings passing through a person's inner self. Allah knows even these most concealed thoughts, for He is the Creator. He is closer to man than his jugular vein. This closeness is in terms of knowledge and power; it is not a spatial proximity. Scholars have interpreted this expression as a proximity of knowledge or power. Al-Raghib states that closeness is used in the sense of power. Ibn Jarir reports that Arabic linguists disagreed over the meaning of this verse.

There are differing views regarding the expression habl al-warid. Warid is the vein in the neck, while habl means rope or cord. In anatomy, al-warid is the vein that carries dark blood to the heart, whereas al-watin is the aorta. This vein swells in moments of anger. Al-Zamakhshari states that habl al-warid can also be understood as the base of the neck. Al-Raghib, on the other hand, notes that what is meant by habl al-warid is the soul (ruh). The arrival of dark blood to the heart pertains to purification and a new creation, pointing toward the states of the Hereafter.

The views of Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi regarding Allah's closeness are relayed. According to him, the presence of the Closest One is with His essence for the people of mystical unveiling (kashf). Yet this closeness entails distance for the sinner. Allah is closer to us than we are to ourselves, for union is only through Him. The servant draws near to Allah through supererogatory devotions (nawafil) and becomes His hearing and His sight. However, this does not mean that the servant becomes Allah; there remains an essential distinction between them. In the concept of the Unity of Existence (Wahdat al-Wujud), the Creator and the creation are not identical; everything belongs to Allah, but being Allah is something entirely different.

In the continuation of the verse, mention is made of two angels who record every word of man. They sit on the right and on the left, keeping record. Every word, whether good or evil, is recorded by an observer beside him. However, the whisperings within the soul—inner speech that has not reached the level of intent and decision—are not written down. On this matter, Imam Malik stated that everything is written down, whereas some scholars noted that only matters entailing accountability are recorded. The style of the verse depicts man like an interrogated criminal or a patient on the verge of death.

Thereafter, death and the Hereafter are depicted. When the stupor of death comes in truth, Allah is closer than the jugular vein. The Trumpet is blown, and this is the Day of Retribution. Every soul arrives accompanied by a driver and a witness angel. On that day, it is said to the disbeliever: 'You were in heedlessness of this.' Satan says, 'I did not lead him astray; rather, he was in his own deep misguidance.' Allah commands: do not dispute in My presence; the word is not altered, and He is not unjust to His servants.

Finally, Hell and Paradise are depicted. Allah says to Hell, 'Are you full?' and it asks, 'Are there any more?' Paradise, on the other hand, is brought near to the righteous. It is for those who turn to Allah, fear the Most Merciful (al-Rahman) unseen, and come with a penitent heart. It is said to them, 'Enter it in peace; this is the Day of Eternity.' There they will have whatever they desire, and with Us is yet more.

As described in verse 30, Hell will be questioned on that day as to whether it has been filled, and it will ask, 'Are there any more?' This marks the fulfillment of Allah's promise: 'Surely I will fill Hell entirely.' Hell will be filled with those cast into it in groups from among the jinn and mankind, yet its momentum will not slacken; out of fury and severity toward sinners, it will crave even more. This question and answer depict the terror of Hell. While some scholars regard this as literal reality, others, such as al-Alusi, share this view. In a hadith narrated from Anas in Bukhari and Muslim, it is recounted that Hell repeatedly asks, 'Are there any more?' until its Mighty Lord places His foot, whereupon it contracts and cries, 'Enough, enough!' In Paradise, there remains continual surplus space, and Allah creates a new creation to dwell there.

In verses 31–33, it is stated that Paradise is brought near for the righteous (al-muttaqun) and is not far off. This refutes the claim of the disbelievers who said, 'This is a far-off return.' The righteous are those who come with a heart turned to Allah, who fear the Most Merciful unseen, and who preserve His limits. 'Awwab' means one who turns repeatedly in repentance. These verses emphasize that Paradise promised to the righteous is near at hand.

In verses 34–35, it is conveyed that the righteous will be told, 'Enter in peace and security,' and that they will abide therein eternally. That day is the Day of Eternity; it has no end. In Paradise, they will have whatever they wish, and with Allah there is yet more; this surplus consists of blessings no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever conceived. This means that the inhabitants of Paradise will be granted more than they desire, or that they will be lavishly honored in the presence of Allah.

Verses 36-38 remind that earlier generations who were mightier than them were destroyed. They had traversed throughout the lands, seeking a place of escape from death. In what is recounted in this surah, there is indeed a lesson for anyone who possesses a heart or listens attentively. It is stated that Allah created the heavens, the earth, and all that is between them in six days and was not touched by weariness; this refutes the claims of the Jews.

In verses 39-40, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is commanded to be patient and to glorify his Lord with praise by performing prayer before the rising of the sun (the morning prayer), before its setting (the noon and afternoon prayers), and during the night (the evening and night prayers). Furthermore, glorifying Him after the prayers is recommended. This points to the appointed times of prayer and to glorification (tasbih).

In verses 41-44, the day when a caller will call out from a nearby place is described. This caller is Israfil or Gabriel (Jibril). On that day, everyone will hear this call and emerge from their graves. The earth will split open, and people will rush forth swiftly. This gathering is easy for Allah. According to al-Baydawi, the Day of Emerging is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection. The splitting of the earth is open to different interpretations: it cracks open either from beneath them or from above them. This gathering is tremendous, yet it is easy for Allah.

In verse 45, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is commanded not to act as a compeller over what the disbelievers say, but rather to remind with the Quran those who fear Allah's warning. Thus, they may strive to protect themselves for that Day, come with a heart turned toward Allah, and enter the Abode of Eternity in peace.

At the beginning of the surah, Allah swears by the winds scattering dust, the clouds carrying heavy burdens, the ships sailing smoothly, and the angels distributing commands, emphasizing that the promised matters (resurrection, reckoning, punishment) will inevitably come to pass. These oaths draw attention to the importance of the order in the universe and reinforce the certainty of the warnings to be described in subsequent verses.

Then, an oath is taken by the sky, which is likened to a firmly and beautifully woven fabric (Zatü'l-hubük). This simile expresses the firm structure of the sky, adorned with stars and orbits. Following this oath, it is stated that people utter differing words and stray from the right path. While some worship idols, others call the Prophet mad or a sorcerer; and because of these contradictory attitudes, they are turned away from.

The surah answers those who ask about the Day of Retribution: that day is the day they will be tormented in the Fire. As for the righteous (muttaqin), it is related that they sleep little at night, seek forgiveness in the pre-dawn hours, and allocate a rightful share of their wealth for the beggar and the deprived. According to some exegetes, this right is the obligatory zakat, while according to others, it is voluntary charity. In either case, the importance of goodness and mutual assistance is emphasized.

It is declared that on the earth and within yourselves there are many signs (proofs) demonstrating Allah's power and the truth of the religion. In the heaven, too, are provision and that which is promised. Swearing by heaven and earth, it is stated that the promise is as certain as your own speech. Then, the story of the angels, who were the honored guests of Abraham, is related: they give Abraham the glad tidings of a son and then announce that they will destroy the people of Lot.

Following the story of Abraham, a lesson is urged to be drawn from past nations: Moses (Musa) and Pharaoh, the barren wind that destroyed the people of 'Ad, the thunderbolt that struck the people of Thamud, and the flood of the people of Noah. All of these are examples of the disasters that befell the deniers. The belief in tawhid (the oneness of Allah) is reinforced by reminding that Allah built the heavens with power, spread out the earth, and created all things in pairs. At the end of the surah, a warning is issued that the jinn and mankind were created only to worship Allah, that He has no need of provision, and that the wrongdoers will suffer an inevitable punishment.

Allah is the Provider and the Possessor of power. His vastness bears two meanings: the first is vastness of power, meaning He was not exhausted by creating the heavens and can expand them even further. The second is vastness in wealth and the granting of blessings; He relieves distress and answers prayers.

We spread out the earth and furnished it with blessings. Live there for a time and take your share. We created pairs of everything. Some understood this as male and female, while others interpreted it as opposites such as motion and rest, or night and day. Al-Baydawi, on the other hand, interpreted it as 'two kinds of every species.' This also encompasses the diversity in the external and internal worlds. There is a duality in everything Allah created so that you may reflect.

Creating everything in pairs pertains not only to opposites in the external world, but also to perceptions in the mind. There is a duality in every perception, and without this duality, nothing can be known. However, this expression 'everything' encompasses created beings; Allah is not included. For there is nothing like unto Him, and He is transcendent above having a counterpart.

Therefore, flee to Allah, protect yourselves from His punishment, and be with the righteous. Indeed, I am a clear warner to you. Do not take another deity along with Allah. Previous nations also called the messengers 'a sorcerer' or 'a madman.' This is a consolation to you. They did not enjoin this upon one another, yet because they were united in transgression, their words resembled one another.

Now turn away from them, but continue to remind, for the reminder benefits the believers. I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me. This is the purpose of creation. Some have interpreted it as 'so that they may know Me.' Worship is for the benefit of the servants; Allah has no need of it.

Allah is the Provider and the Possessor of power. Serving Him is so that one may benefit from His strength and attain reward. For the wrongdoers, there is a large share of punishment. Let them not be in haste; the promised day will surely come. Woe, on that day, to those who disbelieve!

The surah begins with an oath by Mount Tur. Tur means 'mountain' in Syriac and is Mount Sinai, where Moses (Musa) heard the word of Allah. It also symbolizes the flight from matter to meaning. Next, an oath is sworn by an inscribed book written on outspread parchment. This book is neatly written on fine parchment called 'raqq'. Some have considered it to be the Torah, some the record of deeds, and others the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) or the Quran. The soundest view, based on verse 13 of Surah al-Isra, is that it is the record of deeds. Furthermore, an oath is sworn by the Inhabited House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur)—that is, a house in the heavens. This house is visited every day by seventy thousand angels. According to Hasan al-Basri, however, this is the Kaaba. Al-Baydawi says it is the heart of the believer. An oath is sworn by the elevated ceiling—that is, the sky or the Throne—and by the swelling sea (al-Bahr al-Masjur). Masjur means inflamed, filled, mixed, or empty. It is also said that this sea is the one in which Pharaoh drowned.

The answer to these oaths is that the punishment of your Lord will inevitably take place. On that Day, the heaven will sway violently, and the mountains will move from their places and turn into particles of dust. On that Day, woe to those who deny the Hereafter! They amuse themselves in a mire they have plunged into, engaging in vain pursuits instead of believing and preparing. On that Day, they will be thrust violently into Hell, and it will be said to them, 'This is the Fire that you used to deny.' They had called the revelation that foretold this Fire magic; now they are asked, 'Is this magic, then, which has actually come to pass?'

The righteous (muttaqin), on the other hand, will be in gardens and bliss. Those who believe, and whose offspring follow them in faith, are raised to the rank of their forefathers in Paradise along with their offspring. This occurs by virtue of the offspring's own faith, not merely through the earning of their fathers. Allah will not deprive them of anything from their deeds. Every person is bound to what they have earned. The righteous will be abundantly provided with fruits and meat of their desiring. There they will pass a cup to one another, wherein there is no vain talk nor inducement to sin. Circling around them will be youthful servants, as if they were hidden pearls. Turning to one another, they will say: 'Indeed, we used to be in fear earlier among our families. But Allah was gracious to us and protected us from the scorching punishment (samum). Indeed, we used to supplicate Him. Truly, He is the Beneficent, the Merciful.'

O Muhammad! Remind and give counsel. By the grace of your Lord, you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman. The polytheists say, 'He is a poet; we await for him the calamities of time.' Say: 'Wait, and I too am waiting with you.' Is it their intellect that commands them to do this? Or are they a transgressing people? Or do they say, 'He invented it'? Nay, they do not believe. Let them produce a discourse like it, if they are truthful! Or were they created without a creator? Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Nay, they do not reflect and comprehend the truth.

Or are the treasures of your Lord with them? Or are they the controllers of everything? Or do they have a ladder by which they eavesdrop? Then let their eavesdropper bring a clear proof! Is it that daughters belong to Him and sons to you? Or are you asking them for a fee, so that they are weighed down by a burden of debt? Or is the unseen with them, and they write it down? Or do they intend to set a trap? It is those who disbelieve who are trapped! Or do they have a deity other than Allah? Exalted is Allah far above whatever they associate with Him!

Even if they were to see a fragment falling from the sky, they would say, 'It is just clouds stacked in heaps.' So leave them until they meet their Day in which they will be struck down. On that Day, none of their ploys will avail them, nor will they be helped. And surely, for those who do wrong, there is a punishment besides this, but most of them do not know. So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, for indeed you are before Our eyes. And glorify your Lord with praise when you arise. And glorify Him during a portion of the night and at the setting of the stars.

The phrase 'when you arise' mentioned in verse 49 commands glorifying and praising Allah when rising from a gathering. In a hadith narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i, whenever the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) was about to rise from a gathering, he would supplicate: 'O Allah, I declare Your transcendence above every imperfection and praise You. I bear witness that there is no god but You, I ask Your forgiveness, and I turn to You in repentance,' and he would state that this prayer serves as an expiation for those present in the gathering.

Some scholars have stated that what is meant by 'when you arise' in this verse is the time when you get out of bed and stand for prayer. According to this view, the verse points to a supplication to be recited upon standing for prayer: 'O Allah, I declare Your transcendence above all imperfections and praise You alone. How exalted is Your name, and how sublime is Your majesty! There is no god but You.'

The subsequent expression 'and glorify Him during the night' commands worshipping during a portion of the night. 'At the setting of the stars' points to the end of the night, the pre-dawn time (sahar). Scholars among the Companions and Successors, such as Umar, Ali, Abu Hurairah, and Hasan al-Basri (may Allah be pleased with them), stated that what is meant by night glorification is supererogatory worship, while what is meant by glorification at the setting of the stars is the two-rak'ah sunnah prayer of the dawn prayer (fajr).

Surah at-Tur concludes by pointing to the arrival of morning with the phrase 'the setting of the stars,' and there is a beautiful correlation between this ending and Surah an-Najm beginning with the verse, 'By the star when it descends.' This link between the two surahs demonstrates the mutual harmony of the verses of the Quran.

These verses emphasize that a believer must remember Allah at every moment of life. Glorifying Him upon rising, while worshipping at night, and during the pre-dawn hours is a requirement of faith. Moreover, these glorifications serve as expiation for sins and bring a person closer to Allah.

The surah begins with the expression 'by the star.' Here, the word 'necm' has different meanings: a star, stemless plants, that which descends piecemeal (such as the Quran), or specifically the Pleiades (Ülker) star cluster. Based on the expression 'the Lord of Sirius (Şi'ra)' mentioned in verse 49, some exegetes have stated that 'necm' here is Sirius. The word 'heveyân', on the other hand, means the rising or setting of a star, something descending rapidly, or shooting upwards. The oath may have been sworn upon this movement of the star or upon the descent of the Quran.

The second verse is: 'Your companion has neither strayed nor erred.' 'Dalal' is the opposite of guidance (hidayah), while 'gayy' is the opposite of right judgment (rushd) and signifies losing the intellect's rectitude. By 'sahib' (companion), the Prophet (peace be upon him) is meant. This address is directed to the Quraysh, who said of him, 'He fabricated the Quran himself.' It is emphasized that the Prophet has neither strayed nor erred—that is, he has neither lost his way nor lost his reason. He does not speak out of whim (hevâ, according to the desire of his lower self); what he says is nothing but revelation.

In the third through seventh verses, the nature of revelation is described. The one who taught the Quran revealed to the Prophet is an angel 'of mighty power' (şedidü'l-kuvva), who is Gabriel (Cebrail). Although some say that the teacher is Allah, the majority hold the view that it is Gabriel. Gabriel is characterized as 'zûmirre' (possessor of soundness: strong, robustly built, sound in intellect). He stood erect (istivâ) on the highest horizon, and then drew near and descended downwards (tedellî). This describes the manner in which revelation arrived. Some commentators consider istivâ and tedellî to be an indication of the Prophet's Ascension (Mirac).

The eighth and ninth verses depict closeness: 'He became distant two bow-lengths or nearer.' 'Kavs' means a bow, and 'kâb' is the distance between the grip and the bowstring. When making an alliance, the Arabs would join the grips of two bows together, which symbolized the tightest intimacy. This expression denotes the supreme degree of spiritual proximity between the Prophet and Allah. The tenth verse states that Allah revealed unto His servant. It is narrated that among the matters revealed directly to the Prophet without an intermediary during the Mirac were the five daily prayers and the concluding verses of Surah al-Baqarah.

The eleventh verse states: 'The heart did not deny what it saw.' What the Prophet saw was not an illusion, but a reality attested to by the heart. In the twelfth verse, the polytheists are rebuked for disputing over what was seen. The thirteenth verse notes that the Prophet saw Gabriel once more; this occurred while descending from the Mirac. 'Sidre-i Münteha' (Sidrat al-Muntaha), mentioned in the fourteenth verse, means the lote tree of the utmost boundary. 'Sidre' is a tree resembling the Arabian jujube, and 'münteha' denotes the final destination. This tree represents the ultimate boundary in Paradise, and it is narrated that the Prophet met Gabriel there.

Sidre-i Müntehâ is a lote tree (nebk) located in the seventh heaven. This tree is the source from which the rivers of Paradise promised to the righteous emerge. Our Prophet (peace be upon him) likened its fruit to the tassels of a crown and its leaves to the ears of elephants. According to narration, even if a rider were to travel in its shade for a hundred years, he could not traverse it, and a single leaf of it would cover the entire community. In a narration from Ibn Mas'ud, it is stated that the sidrah is at the outer edges of Paradise, and upon it are Sündüs and İstebrak (fine and heavy silk). In al-Kashshâf, it is likewise expressed that it is situated at the terminus of Paradise. According to Ibn Abbas and Ka'b, the sidrah is a tree beneath the Throne; the knowledge of angels, prophets, and scholars ultimately reaches it, and beyond it is the unseen (gayb). Dahhâk states that every command of Allah reaches the sidrah and does not pass beyond it.

Fakhr al-Din al-Râzî interpreted sidre-i müntehâ in the sense of 'the utmost bewilderment': at a station where intellects are astonished to an unimaginable degree, the Prophet was not overcome by bewilderment, was not confused, and saw what he saw. However, Râzî accepts the first narration as sound. Abu's-Su'ud, on the other hand, relying on the verse 'And that to your Lord is the final goal,' states that what is meant by müntehâ is Allah, and that sidrah, through annexation (izafet) to Allah, means 'the sidrah of Allah.' Jannat al-Ma'wa (Cennetu'l-Me'vâ) is beside this sidrah, and it is the Paradise to which the righteous and the martyrs will arrive.

As related in the hadiths of the Mirac, when the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) saw the sidrah, an abrupt transformation occurred when there covered it from Allah's command that which covered it, and it entered a state that no one could describe. In Ibn Jarir's narration, the Prophet saw that a golden moth covered it and that an angel on every leaf was glorifying Allah. In the narration from Ibn Abbas, it is related that Allah covered it and that Muhammad saw the greatest of the signs of his Lord. Rabi' states that the light of the Lord and the angels enveloped the sidrah; Abu'l-Aliyah states that it was enveloped in the light of Allah; and Mujahid states that Muhammad saw both the sidrah and, with his heart, saw Allah.

The verse 'The sight did not swerve' reports that the Prophet's gaze did not waver, did not swerve to the right or left, and did not exceed the limit of vision. Even while beholding astonishing things that would baffle intellects, he neither swerved nor transgressed the boundary. This demonstrates his adab and fortitude. Râzî contrasts this circumstance with Moses (Musa): the mountain that Moses saw was leveled to dust and Moses fainted, whereas the sidrah stood firm and Muhammad was not shaken. The verse 'He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord' expresses certainty. 'Âyet' carries the meaning of marvels. Here, the meanings of 'the greatest sign' or 'the greatest among the signs' are present. During the Mirac, the Prophet saw the greatest sign among the signs of Lordship (rububiyyet) and the wonders of the dominion (mülk)—wonders that cannot be confined within the bounds of verbal speech and can only be attained through direct witnessing (müşahede). In this verse, it is not said that he saw his Lord, but rather that he saw the greatest of His signs; for this reason, the meaning of seeing Allah does not outwardly appear possible.

It is narrated in al-Bukhârî from Aisha: 'Whoever says that Muhammad saw his Lord has told a lie.' She then recited the verses al-An'âm 6/103 and Luqmân 31/34. However, in the narrations transmitted from Ibn Abbas, it is reported that the Prophet saw Allah. Al-Ash'arî and a group of scholars are of the opinion that the Prophet saw Allah with his physical eyes. Qâdî 'Iyâd states that seeing Allah in this world is rationally permissible and that there is no definitive proof against it in the sacred law (sharia). Râzî, however, indicates that the verse signifies that the Prophet saw Allah's signs rather than Allah Himself, yet points out that there is consensus that beatific vision (rü'yet) is permissible. Alî al-Qârî states that the proofs affirming rü'yet pertain to the manifestation of Allah's attributes, whereas the proofs negating it pertain to the manifestation of His essence (zât), and that manifestation of the essence is impossible. Ultimately, the sequence of the verses depicts the Prophet being taught through Gabriel, then ascending and surpassing Gabriel, and beholding the greatest signs.

Afterwards, the idols worshiped by the polytheists are censured: Lât, Uzza, and Menat. These are nothing but names that you and your fathers have given; Allah has sent down no authority for them. They follow nothing but conjecture and the desires of their souls, even though guidance has already reached them from their Lord. Lât was located in Tâif, Uzza in Nahle, and Menat in Kudeyd. There were special shrines and caretakers for each of them. The Quraysh regarded Uzza as the greatest idol, visited it, and offered gifts and sacrifices to it. During the conquest of Mecca, the Prophet (peace be upon him) dispatched Khâlid b. al-Walîd, had the trees where Uzza was situated cut down, and had the idol destroyed. In this event, Khâlid encountered Dübeyye, the keeper of the idol, and killed him.

Elmalılı recounts the history of the idols Lat, Uzza, and Manat mentioned in these verses. Lat was the name of a rock in Ta'if; Uzza was an idol consisting of three trees near Mecca; and Manat was an idol erected at Qudayd between Medina and Mecca. All of these idols bore feminine names, and the polytheists regarded them as the daughters of Allah. During the time of the Prophet (peace be upon him), these idols were demolished one after another.

Dwelling on the feminine names the polytheists gave to their idols, Elmalılı states that the expression 'the male for you and the female for Him' conveys reproof. The polytheists had given feminine names to their idols because they believed that the angels were the daughters of Allah. This is described as 'a most unjust division.' In terms of Arabic grammar, it is explained that the word 'diza' means 'most unjust.'

The verses emphasize that the idols are 'nothing but mere names.' The idols that the polytheists praised as 'exalted cranes' (gharaniq) are in fact nothing at all. At this point, Elmalılı addresses the famous 'story of the Gharaniq' and proves that it is a fabrication. He states that it is impossible for the Prophet to utter anything outside of revelation and that this story has been rejected by the exegetes.

Allah proclaims that there are numerous angels in the heavens, yet their intercession will be of no avail except by His permission. Those who do not believe in the Hereafter follow mere conjecture by giving feminine names to the angels. Conjecture, however, is of no avail against the truth. For this reason, the Prophet is asked to turn away from those who turn away from the Quran and desire nothing but the life of this world.

Those who do good avoid major sins; minor faults are forgiven. Allah's forgiveness is vast. He created human beings from the earth and already knew them while they were in their mothers' wombs. Therefore, we should not claim purity for ourselves. Allah knows best those who guard against evil.

The verses point to individuals like al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, who turned away, gave a little, and then withheld stubbornly. The principles written in the scriptures of Moses (Musa) and Abraham are recalled: No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another, and man shall have nothing except what he strives for. The ultimate return is to Allah. It is He Who makes one laugh and weep, Who causes death and gives life, and Who enriches and impoverishes. He is the Lord of Sirius (Shi'ra). The earlier nations were destroyed.
The word 'kudyah' refers to hard rock that is difficult to dig. It is also used in meanings such as stinginess and harsh withholding.
In verse 35, it is questioned how the deniers could agree to take on sins even though they possess no knowledge of the unseen and have not witnessed the Hereafter.

In verses 36–37, the rulings found in the scriptures of Moses and Abraham are recalled. Abraham (peace be upon him) was a faithful prophet. According to Abu Hayyan, between Noah and Abraham, people used to assume one another's sins; Abraham stood against this.

In verse 38, the principle 'No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another' is emphasized. In Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh), this is grounded in the rule 'There is no representation/proxy in punishments' (al-niyabah la tajri fi al-'uqubat). Everyone bears the punishment for their own crime.

In verse 39, it is stated that a person will have nothing except the reward for what they have striven for. A person cannot earn spiritual reward through anything other than their own deeds. However, there are also gifts bestowed through Allah's grace. Things such as intercession and supplication depend on a person's faith. This verse has not been abrogated; according to the majority of scholars (jumhur), it is definitive (muhkam).
In verses 40–42, it is explained that a person will see the result of their striving in the Hereafter, that the fullest recompense will be granted, and that the ultimate destination is to Allah.

In verses 43–47, it is emphasized that Allah is the One Who makes one laugh and weep, Who causes death and gives life, Who creates male and female, and Who undertakes the second creation. This serves as evidence for the reality of the Hereafter.
In verse 48, it is stated that Allah is the One Who enriches and provides wealth.
In verse 49, it is stated that Allah is the Lord of Sirius (Shi'ra). In the pre-Islamic period of ignorance (Jahiliyyah), this star was worshipped; this belief is refuted by the verse.

In verses 50–54, the destruction of past nations is recalled: 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Noah, and the overturned cities (the people of Lot). These destructions were the consequence of the people's own sins.
In verses 55–56, human beings are asked which of their Lord's favors they doubt, and it is stated that these warnings are like the warnings of the earlier prophets.
In verses 57–58, the approaching Hour of Resurrection is described, and it is explained that none besides Allah can disclose or avert it.

In verses 59–62, it is recounted that the deniers marveled at the Quran, laughed instead of weeping, remained defiantly haughty, and were called to prostrate. The surah concludes with a verse of prostration (sajdah). According to narration, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) prostrated here.

In the first verse of Surah al-Qamar, it is stated that the Hour of Resurrection has drawn near and the moon has split. This is one of the greatest miracles of the Prophet (peace be upon him). By the consensus of the commentators (mufassirun), this verse reports the event of the splitting of the moon, which took place in Mecca upon the polytheists' demand for a miracle. The event was narrated by many Companions.

In hadith sources such as al-Bukhari, Muslim, and al-Tirmidhi, narrations from Companions such as Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Anas, and Hudhayfah report that the moon split into two parts, one part being seen in front of the mountain and the other behind it, and that the Messenger of Allah said, "Bear witness!" The polytheists described this as sorcery; however, when those arriving from other regions also stated that they had seen it in the same manner, they were astounded.

In some narrations, the expression "twice" (marratayn) appears. While some scholars interpreted this as two separate splittings, the majority stated that it means "two parts" (firqatayn), and that the splitting occurred once but opened and closed swiftly. Hafiz Ibn Hajar states that he knows of no hadith scholar who said there was more than one splitting.

It has been narrated that some scholars, such as al-Hasan al-Basri and 'Ata', said, "The moon will split on the Day of Resurrection." However, this does not mean that they denied the miracle; rather, they intended to emphasize that the past splitting was a sign of the great splitting on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, the continuation of the verse reports that whenever they see a miracle, they turn away and call it "sorcery," which demonstrates that the event occurred in the past.

Among the philosophers, Ibn Sina argued that the splitting of celestial bodies was impossible, yet this view of his was based on Aristotelian physics. Today, it is scientifically accepted that the moon can break apart. Miracles occur through the power of Allah and are rationally possible. The Quran's reporting of this event is the strongest evidence of its truthfulness.

Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi compares the splitting of the moon to the emergence of the perfect human (al-insan al-kamil). According to him, the moon is a celestial body that changes between crescent and full moon, and its splitting points to the manifestation of divine commands. This event witnessed by the Companions is a physical miracle proving the truth of the Prophet.

In conclusion, the miracle of the splitting of the moon is established through mutawatir (mass-transmitted) reports and accepted by the vast majority of commentators. Metaphorical interpretations, on the other hand, contradict the context (siyaq) of the verse and authentic narrations. This miracle demonstrates that the Day of Resurrection has drawn near and that Allah has power over all things.

The verse mentions the miracle of the splitting of the moon at the beginning of Surah al-Qamar. When the polytheists saw this miracle, they said, "continuous sorcery." They would only believe in what they clearly saw. Even though the miracle took place, they still did not believe and characterized it as sorcery. The Prophet's duty is to display miracles, not to compel belief. When they saw the moon split, they asked travelers coming from other places, and when those travelers also stated that they had seen it, they said, "this is continuous sorcery."

Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi mentioned the possibility that the splitting of the moon took place in the eye of the beholder. However, this does not mean that he denied the miracle. He merely described the perspective of the polytheists. Ismail Fenni Ertugrul criticizes this interpretation, stating that such an explanation would reduce the miracle to the level of sorcery. He believes that the splitting of the moon truly took place and notes that it is established by mutawatir hadiths. The majority of commentators are also of this view.

In the verses that follow, it is explained that the polytheists rejected the Prophet and what he brought, and followed their desires. Every matter has an appointed goal and is determined with Allah. News of past nations and warnings regarding the Hereafter came to them. These warnings are profound wisdom, yet they still did not believe. The Prophet is commanded to turn away from them and await the Day of Resurrection. On that Day, the caller (Israfil) will call to a terrifying thing, and people will emerge from their graves like swarming locusts. The disbelievers will say that this is a very difficult day.

The people of Noah also denied their prophet and called him "mad." When Noah was overcome and prayed to Allah, Allah opened the gates of heaven with pouring water, caused the earth to burst forth with springs, and the waters met. As for Noah, He carried him on an ark made of planks and nails, which sailed under Allah's watchful eyes. This was done as a reward for Noah. Allah left the ark as a sign (ayah). Yet how few people reflect and take heed?

The people of 'Ad also denied the warnings. Allah sent against them a furious, roaring wind (sarsar) on a day of continuous ill fortune. This wind plucked people away as if they were uprooted trunks of palm trees. How terrible were Allah's punishment and warnings! The Quran has been made easy to understand, yet there are so few who take heed.

The people of Thamud also denied the warnings and said, "Shall we follow a human being from among ourselves?" They envied that revelation was given to Salih instead of one of them, and accused him of lying. Allah announced that He would send a female camel (naqah) as a trial. This she-camel was to be a miracle for them. However, they were warned not to harm the camel. Thus, the destruction of each nation came about on account of their own disbelief.

The she-camel sent to the people of Thamud was released as a trial. Here, the word "fitnah" means test or trial. According to al-Razi, the primary purpose was to confirm the prophet; for the she-camel was a miracle by being brought forth from a rock, and a trial by being released to roam among them and by the division of water. Through these two aspects, it was a test distinguishing between those who would earn reward and those who would incur punishment.

The water was apportioned in turns between the she-camel and the people. One day the she-camel would drink, and one day they would take water. The people would draw water on their turn, and on the she-camel's turn, they would benefit from her milk. This she-camel was a magnificent creature that brought both a burden and a blessing; being called "the camel of Allah," it was managed like an endowed property (waqf). However, this apportionment and burden became too heavy for them, and they could not endure it.

Qudar ibn Salif, one of the notables of the people, hamstrung the she-camel and killed it. Salih (peace be upon him) warned them of punishment within three days: their faces would turn yellow, then red, then black, and on the fourth day, punishment would befall them. When they saw the signs, they sought to kill Salih, but he was saved along with the believers. On the fourth day, they were destroyed by a violent blast and earthquake; they became like the trampled, dry twigs of an enclosure builder.

The people of Lot also denied the warnings. We sent against them a wind showering stones; Lot and his believing family were saved, except for his wife. Lot had warned them of the terror of the punishment, but they sought to do evil to his guests (the angels). Thereupon, We obliterated their sight and said, "Taste My punishment and My warnings!" Early in the morning, an abiding punishment seized them.

Warnings also came to the people of Pharaoh, but they rejected all Our signs. So We seized them with the seizure of One Mighty and Powerful. Are your disbelievers now better than those? Or do you have an exemption written in the scriptures? Or do they say, "We are a victorious assembly"? That assembly will be defeated, and they will turn their backs and flee. This is a miracle that took place on the day of Badr. Yet the Hour of Resurrection is their appointed time, and that Hour is far more catastrophic and bitter.

The criminals are in error and madness. On that Day, they will be dragged on their faces into the Fire, and it will be said, 'Taste the touch of Hell!' We have created everything according to a destiny. Our command is but one, like the blinking of an eye. Indeed, We destroyed your likes; is there anyone who will take heed? Everything that is done is present in the books; small and great, all is written down. The righteous are in gardens, in light, and on seats of truth in the presence of an all-powerful Sovereign.

Surah ar-Rahman begins with Allah's name ar-Rahman. ar-Rahman means the One whose mercy and boundless favor surge forth in abundance. In this verse, it is emphasized that Allah is ar-Rahman. In the second verse that follows, it is stated that ar-Rahman taught the Qur'an. The verb 'ta'lim' denotes the teaching of the Qur'an; this teaching encompasses the entirety of teaching to Gabriel, to the Prophet, and to the ummah. Some scholars have stated that this verb means 'to make a sign'; according to this, the Qur'an was made a sign for those who take admonition and a miracle for prophethood.

In the third verse, it is stated that ar-Rahman created man. What is meant by man could be Adam, Muhammad (peace be upon him), or the human species; the most correct view is the human species. In the fourth verse, it is expressed that man was taught clear expression (bayan). Bayan means a person's clear expression of the feelings and thoughts within them to others. This is the blessing of speech and language; the acquisition of knowledge and the teaching of the Qur'an become possible through this. The teaching of the names of things to Adam was also by virtue of the knowledge of bayan.

In the fifth verse, it is stated that the sun and the moon move according to a precise calculation. This indicates that people should understand calculation well and be prepared for the Day of Reckoning. In the sixth verse, it is recounted that plants and trees prostrate, submitting to the will of Allah. In the seventh verse, it is expressed that the sky was raised and the balance (mizan—the law of equilibrium) was established. Mizan is the universal law of balance and justice; it is the foundation of gravity and measuring instruments such as scales, and it ensures that everything stands in accordance with its due right.

In the eighth verse, the reason for establishing the balance is so that injustice is not committed in weighing. In the ninth verse, it is commanded to maintain the weight with justice and not to make the balance deficient. In the tenth verse, it is stated that the earth was laid low for creatures, that is, the earth was made suitable for living beings. This is a manifestation of Allah's mercy.

In the eleventh verse, it is stated that there are fruits and date palms with spathes on the earth. In the twelfth verse, husked grains (such as wheat and barley) and fragrant plants (rayhan) are mentioned. Rayhan also means provision. In the thirteenth verse, the address 'Which of the favors of your Lord will you twain deny?' is directed to humans and jinn. This verse emphasizes that favors must not be denied; at each of its repetitions, it is recommended (mandub) to say, 'No, we do not deny any of Your favors, O our Lord; praise be to You.'

In the fourteenth verse, it is explained that man was created from sounding dry clay (salsal), and in the fifteenth verse, that the jinn (jann) were created from a smokeless flame of fire. The human and jinn species are mentioned separately. Marij fire has been interpreted as a smokeless pure flame or a fire that penetrates all things. This difference in creation reflects the characteristics of both types of beings.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth verses, it is emphasized that ar-Rahman is the Lord of the two easts and the two wests. This expression may refer to the rising and setting points of the sun and the moon, the summer and winter solstices, the spherical shape of the earth, or material and spiritual lights. In the nineteenth verse, it is related that the two seas were released and meet each other. These seas have been interpreted in various ways, such as sweet and salty, the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean, or the heavenly sea and the earthly sea. The meeting of the two seas has also been understood as an allusion to the opening of the Suez Canal.

There is a barrier (barzakh) between the two seas. Barzakh means the boundary and separating barrier between two things. In geography, it is also applied to the land between two seas. Thanks to the barrier between them, these two seas do not mix with each other, and the water of one does not impair the characteristic of the other. This is an evidence of Allah's power.
From these seas emerge pearls and coral. Pearls and coral are used both as ornaments and as blessings of commerce. In particular, large pearls and red coral are valuable.

Ships floating like mountains upon the sea are also among Allah's blessings. The expression 'jawari al-munsha'at' means ships that are constructed or whose sails are unfurled. Although these ships are made by human beings, in reality they exist through Allah's creation. Furthermore, this expression also alludes to celestial bodies flowing along by Allah's power.

Everything on earth is mortal and perishing. Only the Face (Essence) of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor, remains enduring. The word 'wajh' (face) is in the meaning of Allah's Essence. This attribute demonstrates both Allah's grandeur and His grace. The expression 'Dhu al-Jalali wa'l-Ikram' is an exclusive name belonging to Allah and is used as a great supplication.

Everyone in the heavens and the earth asks of Allah. Every day He is upon a new affair. This affair is related either to majesty or to honor. At every moment, Allah creates, destroys, raises, or lowers whatever He wills. The expression 'every day upon a new affair' means either that He is engaged in a new work at every moment, or that He has two distinct affairs: this world and the Hereafter.

O company of humans and jinn! When the Day of Reckoning arrives, Allah will direct His attention to you and settle your account. You are called 'thaqalan' because you are like heavy burdens borne on the earth. On that day, if you had the power to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, you would flee, but you can only pass through with permission from Allah. If you attempt to flee, a flame of fire and smoke like molten brass will be sent upon you, and you will neither be able to defend yourselves nor be saved.

When the Resurrection takes place, the sky will split asunder and turn into a crimson rose like molten oil. The terror of that day cannot be described. On that day, there will be no need to interrogate the criminals about their sins, because they will be recognized by their marks; they will be seized by their forelocks and feet and cast into Hell. They will circulate between Hell and boiling water. Which of the favors of your Lord will you twain deny?

On the Day of Resurrection, the sins of the guilty will not be questioned, because they will be recognized by their faces. The sinful and the sinless will not be confused; everyone's state is determined. The terror of that day, separating the obedient from the disobedient and exacting retribution from the disbelievers, is also a blessing. When the sky splits asunder and becomes like a red rose, terrifying upheavals will occur.

The criminals will circle round between the fire of Hell and scalding hamim (boiling water). They will suffer the punishment for their disbelief and ingratitude. After the manifestations of majesty belonging to the Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor, have been thus expounded, the manifestations of His honor are recounted.

For those who fear the station of their Lord, there are two gardens. The word 'maqam' (station) means Allah's sovereignty over all things or the standing of mankind before Him for reckoning on the Day of Resurrection. Fear is not merely a palpitation of the heart, but abstaining from disbelief and obeying with faith and gratitude. These two gardens may be physical and spiritual; their details are not known.

Both gardens possess diverse trees, fruits, and two flowing springs. Of every fruit there are pairs. They recline on couches lined with rich brocade, and the harvest of the fruits hangs within reach. Therein are maidens who restrain their glances solely to their spouses, whom neither human nor jinn has touched before them. They are like rubies and coral.

Besides these two gardens, there are two other gardens; they are dark green, with two gushing springs, and all kinds of fruit, date palms, and pomegranates. Within them are women of noble character and lovely countenances, houris secluded in pavilions with their eyes turned toward their husbands. Neither human nor jinn has touched them before either. The people of Paradise will recline on green cushions and beautifully embroidered couches.

The reward of goodness is nothing but goodness. In the narrations concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, it is reported that Abu Bakr, pondering the terror of the Day of Judgment, said, 'If only I were greenery,' and that during the time of Umar, when a young man died of his passionate love, Umar said, 'For you there are two gardens.' This demonstrates the importance of fearing Allah and acting with ihsan (excellence in worship and virtue).

The reward for the one who attains the blessing of Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) is Paradise. The expression 'kâsırâtu't-tarf' means beauties who direct their glances only toward their husbands, or who draw the gaze of the beholder to themselves. As for 'tams,' it means virginity or not having been touched. Our Lord is the Lord of Generosity; how exalted is His name!

In the 62nd and 63rd verses, Allah Almighty informs that, besides the two gardens mentioned earlier, there are two more gardens on this side of them or beyond them. According to Ibn Zayd, the earlier gardens are for the muqarrabun (those brought near to Allah), whereas these subsequent ones are for the ashab al-yamin (the companions of the right), whose records of deeds are given in their right hands. Hasan al-Basri also stated that the former are the Companions, and the latter are the Successors (Tabi'un). According to both views, the second gardens are lower than the first in honor and rank. The former are described with more concise and mature attributes.

In the 64th and 65th verses, the color of these gardens is described as 'lush green.' The word 'müdhâmmetân' is derived from 'dühme,' which means the darkness of night and the color of a dark horse. Here, it denotes an intense, deep dark-green color. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and others interpreted this word as 'hadrâvân,' that is, lush green. According to the narration of Abu Ayyub (may Allah be pleased with him), the Prophet (peace be upon him) also stated that this word means hadrâvân.

In the 66th and 67th verses, it is stated that in these gardens there are 'two gushing springs.' 'Nadh' means the gushing of water; the form written with a dotted 'hâ' indicates a more vigorous gushing. These gushing fountains are considered more artistic and beautiful than flowing springs.

In the 68th and 69th verses, it is described that in both gardens there are various kinds of fruits, date palms, and pomegranates. The nunation (tanwin) indicates that these fruits are of an unprecedentedly superior nature. The specific mention of date palms and pomegranates is because, in addition to being fruits, they possess benefits such as sustenance and medicine. The seedless pomegranate is also particularly noteworthy here.

In verses 70–75, the houris, who are the spouses of Paradise, are depicted. The word 'hûr' means a beauty whose eye-whites are intensely white and whose pupils are intensely black. They are chaste maidens inside pavilions (tents), gazing only upon their husbands. In a hadith of the Prophet (peace be upon him), it is reported that these pavilions are made of a hollow pearl and their height is sixty miles. According to al-Razi, this expression shows that in Paradise items move toward the believers, and that they attain every blessing without fatigue.

In the 76th verse, it is described that the people of Paradise recline on green refrefs and beautiful abkaris. 'Refref' carries various meanings such as fine fabric, a mattress, a spread, or green meadows. 'Abkarî,' on the other hand, refers to embroidered and precious fabrics attributed to the settlement of Abqar, once located in China or Yemen. Although some scholars attributed abqari to the jinn, it actually denotes bedding and carpets of superior quality.

The commentators have expressed various views regarding the meanings of the words abkari and refref. For refref, meanings such as green fabric, mattress, bedsheet, spread, curtain, cushion, raised couch, and a garden of Paradise have been given. As for abkari, it has generally been used in the sense of beautiful and high-quality fabric; in one narration it was attributed to a region in China, while some interpreted it as a place where the jinn reside.

Regarding the origin of the word abkari, al-Farra defined it as thick fabric, Mujahid as silk fabric, Qatadah as carpets and rugs, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as antique furnishings. These narrations indicate that abqari is not attributed to a place, but is a noun in its own right. In conclusion, refref can be considered as the meadows of Paradise, and the abkaris as the fine garments of the people of Paradise.

In Surah ar-Rahman, the same verse is repeated thirty-one times. Eight of these occur after the subjects of creation and the worldly life and the Hereafter, seven after the warnings concerning Hell, and eight after the descriptions of the first two gardens. These numbers indicate that the gates of Hell are seven and the gates of Paradise are eight. Thus, whoever believes in and acts upon the first eight matters enters both gardens and is protected from Hell.

At the end of the surah, the name of your Lord is mentioned as tabaraka (blessed and exalted). The expression 'Zü'l-celali ve'l-ikram' (Possessor of Majesty and Generosity) emphasizes that Allah is the Possessor of greatness and bounty. The word tabaraka here signifies exaltedness, abundance of good, and blessing. Al-Alusi states that the attribution of this verb to the name of Allah is permissible, because mercy is sought through its honor.

The expression 'they recline' in the verse indicates that the people of Paradise are perpetually in tranquility and rest. According to al-Razi, while people in this world find themselves in varying states, in Paradise there is no fatigue or exertion. For this reason, in the verses, ittika (avoidance/caution) is mentioned sometimes earlier and sometimes later. In addition, words such as refref and abqari are meant to convey the indescribable beauty of the blessings of Paradise.

At the beginning of Surah al-Waqi'ah, the event of the Resurrection is described. The word 'al-Waqi'ah' means an event that is bound to happen. When the Day of Resurrection occurs, no one will be left to deny it, for it is an event so immense that it will compel everyone into helpless affirmation. This event humbles some and exalts others; the earth is shaken with a violent shaking, and the mountains are crumbled into dust. Then people are divided into three groups: the Companions of the Right (ashab al-maymanah), the Companions of the Left (ashab al-mash'amah), and the Foremost (al-sabiqun). The Companions of the Right are those endowed with auspiciousness and blessing, whereas the Companions of the Left are wretched and worthless individuals. The Foremost are those who have preceded others in good deeds and are the ones brought near (al-muqarrabun) to Allah.

For the Foremost (al-sabiqun), there are in Paradise thrones encrusted with jewels, youthful attendants, wine that neither causes headaches nor intoxicates, varied fruits, and fair houris. Most of them are from the earlier communities, and a few from later generations. The blessings of this group are described by likening them to the highest pleasures of this world. In Paradise, they hear no vain talk, only words of peace (salam). These blessings are a reward for their deeds.

The Companions of the Right (ashab al-yamin) are the felicitous ones who follow the Foremost and are given their records of deeds in their right hands. The description of their Paradise is depicted in a manner that would particularly appeal to bedouins: thornless lote-trees (sidr), clustered bananas, extended shade, pouring waters, and unfailing fruits. For them, there are raised couches and houris created anew, formed by restoring elderly women to youth. These houris are of equal age, loving, and beautiful women. These blessings of the Companions of the Right are entirely by the grace of Allah; for regarding this group, the expression 'as a reward for what they did' is not mentioned.

The Companions of the Left (ashab al-shimal) are the wretched who are given their records in their left hands. Their punishment consists of a scorching fire, boiling water, and a shadow of black smoke that is neither cool nor beneficial.
