The reason for this is that while in the world, they indulged in luxury, committed sins, and persisted in the great sin (shirk or false oaths). They used to deny the Resurrection. In the Hereafter, they will eat from the tree of Zaqqum, fill their bellies with it, and drink boiling water on top of it, drinking insatiably like thirst-stricken camels. This will be their hospitality on the Day of Recompense.

In the continuation of the surah, attention is drawn to the power of Allah against the disbelievers' denial of the Resurrection: the creation of man (from semen), the bringing forth of vegetation from the soil, the sending down of water from the clouds, and the creation of fire are cited as examples. These proofs demonstrate that those who know the initial creation ought to accept the Resurrection as well. Had Allah willed, He could have rendered the semen futile, turned the crops into dry chaff, made the water salty, and extinguished the fire. Therefore, human beings must show gratitude and exalt the name of their Lord, the Magnificent (al-Azim). These verses emphasize human helplessness and Allah's absolute power.

The expression 'that We may change your forms' mentioned in verse 61 has been interpreted differently by commentators. The word 'amthal' can be taken either as the plural of 'mithl' (like/similar) or as the plural of 'mathal' (attribute, form). In the first case, the meaning is: 'We have decreed death among you so that We may bring your likes.' In the second case: 'We are able to eliminate you and create you in another form.' Hasan al-Basri interpreted this verse as pointing to a worldly transformation, taking it as a threat of being transformed into apes and swine. The verse encompasses both worldly transformation and resurrection in the Hereafter.

In verses 62–63, human beings are urged to reflect on their first creation. Man, who was created from dust stage by stage, should realize that the same Power is capable of resurrecting him. Then the subject turns to provision, and attention is drawn to the seed that is sown: 'Have you seen the seed that you sow? Is it you who cause it to grow, or are We the Grower?' According to al-Qurtubi, it is commendable (mustahabb) for anyone sowing a crop to recite this verse and state that it is Allah who makes it grow.

In verses 64–66, it is emphasized that it is Allah who causes the seed to grow. The word 'hutam' means dry debris; when the crop is broken down and turned into dry chaff, people say in bewilderment, 'We are ruined, we are undone.' This is an expression of ingratitude and despair.

In verses 68–70, attention is drawn to the water that is drunk. It is reminded that Allah is able to make the water sent down from the rainclouds (muzn) salty and bitter (ujaj). While gratitude should be shown for these blessings, people immediately fall into despair at the moment of deprivation.

In verses 71–74, fire and its tree are addressed. It is Allah who created the tree of fire; this fire is both a reminder and a means of utility for travelers. In conclusion, one is commanded to glorify their Lord, who bestows all these blessings, by His name 'al-Azim' (the Magnificent).

In verses 75–82, an oath is sworn by the positions of the stars. It has been debated whether the particle 'la' is redundant (za'id), emphatic (ta'kid), or negative, and preferably it has been given a negative meaning. The Quran is an honorable and well-preserved Book; none can touch it except the purified. The disbelievers belittle this discourse and make their livelihood consist solely of denial.

In verses 83–87, the moment of death is depicted. When the soul reaches the throat, people look on helplessly. Yet Allah is nearer to the dying person than they are. If they are truthful in their claims, let them bring the soul back! This demonstrates their utter helplessness.

In verses 88–96, the ultimate end of the three groups is explained: for those brought near (al-muqarrabun), there is rest, bountiful provision, and a Garden of Delight (Jannat al-Na'im). The Companions of the Right greet one another with peace. For the deniers who went astray, there is boiling water and Hellfire. All of this is absolute truth (haqq al-yaqin), that is, certain reality. Finally, it is once again commanded to glorify one's Lord by His name 'al-Azim'.

At the beginning of the surah, it is declared that whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah. Glorification (tasbih) means declaring Allah free of all imperfections. This glorification is understood literally in words for the angels and the believers, and metaphorically for other beings through inspiration or by way of their pointing to Allah through the order in their creation. Allah is the Almighty (al-Aziz) and the All-Wise (al-Hakim).

Allah is the Owner of the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He gives life to whom He wills, causes to die whom He wills, and He is capable of all things. He is the First (al-Awwal) and the Last (al-Akhir), the Manifest (al-Zahir) and the Hidden (al-Batin). That is, He is before all things and after all things; just as His existence is manifest in everything, it is also hidden beyond the perception of the senses. One must consider these attributes as a whole and not fall into the error of wahdat al-wujud (unity of existence).

Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself above the Throne (istiwa). He knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the heaven and what ascends into it. Wherever you are, He is with you; His knowledge and power never part from you. He merges the night into the day and merges the day into the night, and He knows what is in the hearts.

The believers are commanded to believe in Allah and His Messenger and to spend (in His cause) from the wealth over which Allah has made them trustees. This spending (infaq) encompasses both zakah and voluntary expenditures. Moreover, although those who spent and fought before the victory hold a greater rank, Allah has promised the best reward to all of them. Here, 'victory' refers to the conquest of Mecca or the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. The Prophet (peace be upon him) stated that those who came later could never attain the level of the earlier believers.

Giving a goodly loan to Allah (qard al-hasan) means giving from lawful and the best of one's wealth, with sincerity, secretly, and without reproach, to the one who is most in need. On the Day of Resurrection, the light of the believers will race before them and on their right, according to their deeds. The hypocrites will seek to benefit from this light, but they will be told to turn back and seek light. A wall will be erected between them, inside which is mercy and outside of which is punishment.

To the believers: Has the time not come for their hearts to submit in reverence to the remembrance of Allah and the truth that has been revealed? They should not be like those who were given the Scripture before; a long time passed over them, so their hearts grew hard, and many of them were defiantly disobedient. Just as Allah revives the dead earth, He revives hearts. For the charitable men and women and those who lend Allah a goodly loan, there is a manifold reward. Those who believe in Allah and His Messenger are, in the sight of their Lord, in the rank of the truthful (siddiqin) and the martyrs; as for those who disbelieve, they are the companions of Hellfire.

When the hypocrites see the light of the believers racing before them and on their right on the Day of Resurrection, they will plead, 'Give us light too.' The believers or the angels will rebuke them, saying, 'Turn back behind you—that is, go back to the world—and seek light there.' A wall (a dividing barrier) will be erected between them. Scholars have offered different interpretations regarding this wall: some said it is al-A'raf, while others said it is a barrier between Paradise and Hell. This wall has a gate; its inner side contains mercy, and its outer side contains punishment.

The hypocrites will say, 'Were we not with you?' The believers will answer: 'Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation (fitnah), waited for misfortune to befall the believers, doubted, and false hopes deceived you. In the end, you remained conceited until Allah's command (death) came, and the Deceiver (Satan) deceived you concerning Allah.' Today, no ransom will be accepted from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your abode is the Fire, and what a wretched destination it is.

Addressing those who believe, it is asked: 'Has the time not come to revere the remembrance of Allah and the truth that has been revealed?' Do not be like the people of the Scripture before, whose hearts hardened as a long time passed over them. Know that just as Allah revives the earth after its death, He can also revive hardened hearts. This is the reason the verses are made clear, so that perhaps you may reflect, understand, and not fall into hardness of heart despite the passage of time.

The charitable men and women and those who believe in Allah and His Messenger—they are the truthful and the martyrs. In the presence of their Lord, they have their reward and their light. As for the disbelievers who deny Allah's verses, they are the companions of Hellfire and will abide therein eternally. The life of this world is nothing but play, amusement, adornment, mutual boasting, and rivalry in increasing wealth and children. Just like vegetation produced by rain, it initially pleases, then dries up and becomes chaff. And in the Hereafter, there is severe punishment, or forgiveness and pleasure from Allah.

Race toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Paradise whose width is like the width of the heaven and the earth. This Paradise is prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers. Allah bestows His bounty upon whom He wills. Every calamity that occurs on the earth or in yourselves is already recorded in a Book before We bring it into being. This is so that you do not grieve over what you have lost, nor exult over what has been given to you. Allah does not like anyone who is self-deluded and boastful. As for those who are stingy and command people to stinginess, Allah is indeed free of need and worthy of praise. The messengers were sent with clear proofs, and with them the Scripture and the balance (measure of justice) were sent down. And We sent down iron, wherein is great military might and benefits for mankind. This is so that Allah may make evident those who support His religion and His messengers. Indeed, Allah is Powerful, Almighty.

To those who abandon the transient pleasures of worldly life and race toward forgiveness and Paradise in the Hereafter, Allah announces that no calamity occurs on the earth or in your souls except that it is recorded in a Book. A calamity (musibah) is a disaster that severely strikes a human being; calamity on the earth includes disasters such as drought, famine, and earthquakes, while calamity in one's soul encompasses afflictions like death, illness, and hunger. Just as pleasant successes are Allah's bounty, all calamities are a decree recorded in His eternal knowledge. This writing was inscribed before the calamity was created, and that is easy for Allah. Since escaping a destined calamity by fleeing from it is impossible, both those who enter the race and those who flee are subject to the same destiny. This belief imparts strength and steadfastness to the heart in the face of calamities.

The wisdom of the decreed record is that you may not grieve over what you have lost, nor become arrogant with what you have been given. Those who believe in Allah's decree, even though they naturally feel human emotions in the face of bitter and sweet events, succumb neither to the anguish of grief nor to the pride of joy. Knowing that everything comes from Allah and bears hidden wisdoms, they attend to their duties with humility. Allah does not love the conceited and arrogant; therefore, one must beware of overconfidence, arrogance, and pride.

Those who are stingy both refrain from spending their wealth in the cause of Allah themselves and enjoin stinginess upon others. Whoever turns away from spending in the cause of Allah should know that Allah is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani) and the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid); He has no need of anything, and He alone is worthy of all praise. Their turning away does not harm Allah; the harm is only to themselves.

Allah sent His messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance. The Scripture is the divine guide that distinguishes truth from falsehood; the balance is the measure that ensures justice and equilibrium. These were sent down so that humanity might stand firm in justice. In addition, iron was sent down, in which there is both great might (instruments of war) and many benefits for humanity. Iron is used in every field, from industry to agriculture, and is indispensable for humanity. Allah has made the things that are most needed abundant and easily accessible; since the need for air is the greatest, it is the most abundant, while water and food, being less urgently needed, are found with greater difficulty. This is a trace of Allah's mercy.

As stated in Fakhr al-Din al-Razi's tafsir, there is a profound relationship among the Scripture, the balance, and iron. The Scripture is the means for theoretical knowledge and arriving at the truth; the balance ensures justice in action; and iron is the instrument to compel tyrants and wrongdoers back onto the right path. People are either people of truth who act in accordance with the Scripture, or they are on the middle path and need the balance, or they are obstinate and are disciplined with iron. These three elements represent the aspects of the foundations (usul), branches (furu'), and discipline of the religion.

Noah and Abraham were sent, and prophethood and scripture were granted to their descendants. While some among them accepted guidance, most of them became transgressors (fasiqun). Following them, Jesus was sent and was given the Gospel, and tenderness and mercy were placed in the hearts of those who followed him. As for monasticism (monastery life), they invented it themselves; Allah had not prescribed it for them, yet they deemed it necessary for the sake of seeking Allah's pleasure. But they did not observe it with its due observance, and most of them strayed from the path. Those who believed were granted their rewards.

O you who believe! Fear Allah and believe in His Messenger, that Allah may grant you a twofold share of His mercy: one share for believing in the previous prophets, and one share for believing in Muhammad. May He grant you a light by which you will walk, and forgive you. Allah is the Forgiving (al-Ghafur), the Merciful (al-Rahim). Let the People of the Book know that they can obtain nothing of Allah's bounty; all bounty is entirely in Allah's Hand, and He grants it to whom He wills. Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.

This verse questions the reason why the People of the Book do not believe. The commentators have put forward different views regarding the connection between this verse and the preceding one. Some scholars have stated that the particle 'an' in the verse is redundant and have interpreted the meaning in an affirmative sense as 'not because they do not know'.

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, summarizing a well-known view, states: The People of the Book used to claim that revelation and messengership belonged exclusively to them. After commanding them to believe in the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and promising great rewards, Allah sent down this verse, declaring that the virtue of prophethood was not exclusive to them alone. The meaning is as follows: This address and declaration is meant to warn the People of the Book.

Some commentators, such as Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, took the particle 'an' in a negative sense and referred the pronoun to the Prophet and his Companions. According to them, the verse corrects the erroneous belief of the People of the Book that 'the Prophet and his Companions would not have power over Allah's bounty.' Al-Razi favored this view.

Elmalılı Hamdi Yazır states that he does not agree with either of these two views. According to him, the verse is a warning directed at the People of the Book who disobeyed the command 'Fear Allah and believe in His Messenger.' The meaning is as follows: 'Do the People of the Book not know that they have no power over anything of Allah's bounty? On the contrary, they know, but they do not believe out of envy and obstinacy.' According to what Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah, the verse was revealed because the People of the Book envied the Muslims.

Our Prophet (peace be upon him) explained this situation through a parable: A man hires laborers to work until nightfall; they work until tomorrow and then quit; he employs others until the late afternoon (asr); then he hires other laborers for a wage of two qirats to finish the remaining work. When the laborers' wages differ, they object, and the man says, 'The property is mine, I give it to whomever I wish.' This demonstrates the condition of our ummah and the bounty of Allah.
Thus Surah al-Hadid has ended. Surah al-Mujadilah will follow. May my Lord not make it difficult, but make it easy, and grant that it be completed with goodness.

The opening verses of the surah were revealed concerning the situation of Khawlah bint Tha'labah, whose husband Aws ibn Samit had pronounced zihar upon her. Zihar is a man's saying to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother." In the pre-Islamic period of ignorance (Jahiliyyah), this statement was considered a cause of definitive separation. Since no ruling had been revealed on this matter, the Prophet (peace be upon him) followed custom and told Khawlah that she had become unlawful to her husband. However, Khawlah persistently presented her grievance to Allah, and eventually the verses were revealed. Allah hearing her voice and answering her plea demonstrates that He hears all things and is responsive to the problems of His servants.

In Islam, zihar is described as an abominable and false statement. This is because comparing a woman to one's mother does not reflect reality and injures the woman's dignity. However, when this statement is uttered, it does not remain devoid of legal consequence; it leads to a state of prohibition. To make amends for this sin, Allah has prescribed the path of expiation (kaffarah). Expiation, for a man who wishes to revoke the zihar before touching his wife, consists in this order: freeing a slave; if he lacks the means for this, fasting for two consecutive months; and if he is unable to do this, feeding sixty poor people. These three options are ordered according to the individual's means. While the Hanafis do not stipulate that the slave to be freed must be a believer, the Shafi'is have made being a believer a condition.

These rulings are the limits ordained by Allah. Whoever transgresses these limits and opposes Allah and His Messenger will suffer disgrace in this world and be subjected to a humiliating punishment in the Hereafter. At this point, the verse both warns the believers and threatens the disbelievers. It is emphasized that Allah knows all things and takes count of everything that is done, one by one.

Starting from the seventh verse, the topic of secret counsels (najwa) is addressed. Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth; there are no three persons in secret counsel but He is their fourth, nor five but He is their sixth. No matter how few or how many they may be, Allah is with them at all times. This verse was revealed upon the polytheists' question, "Does Allah know what we talk about?" Furthermore, it also points to the situation where Companions engaged in private conversation with the Prophet (peace be upon him).

In the eighth verse, those who secretly conspire in sin, aggression, and disobedience to the Messenger—despite having been forbidden from doing so—are condemned. The Jews and the hypocrites are criticized for greeting the Prophet with phrases such as "Death be upon you." Their conduct is an insolence that invites the punishment of Allah. In the ninth verse, the believers are commanded to make righteousness and piety (taqwa) the foundation of their private conversations, and to avoid sin and aggression. The tenth verse states that such secret counsels stem from Satan and are intended to cause grief to the believers, yet Satan cannot harm them in any way except by Allah's leave.

The eleventh verse concerns making room for one another in gatherings and showing respect to those possessed of knowledge. In the twelfth and thirteenth verses, it was commanded that those who wished to consult the Prophet privately should offer a charity beforehand; later, this ruling was eased and pardoned. The believers are commanded to establish prayer, give zakah, and obey. All these verses aim at organizing social life and purifying hearts from evils.

According to the narrations concerning the occasions of revelation of the verses, when the Jews greeted the Prophet (peace be upon him), they used to say, "Death be upon you." Our Prophet (peace be upon him) would respond to them, "And upon you." Aisha became very angry at this and cursed them, but our Prophet (peace be upon him) cautioned her. The Jews would say, "Why does not Allah punish us for what we say?" It was upon this behavior of theirs that this verse was revealed. The punishment of Hell is sufficient for them; what a wretched destination it is!

Addressing the believers, it was made known that secret counsels (najwa) are not forbidden entirely, but that they must not be regarding sin, aggression, and disobedience to the Prophet. Private conversations must be based upon goodness, righteousness, and piety (taqwa). Furthermore, when three people are together, two whispering to one another may cause grief to the other; this has been forbidden. Likewise, speaking in a language that the person next to them does not understand is not permissible if it saddens them.

In the verse concerning making room in gatherings, the believers were commanded to make space when told to "spread out." According to a narration, when a group from among the veterans of Badr arrived, they were not given room in the assembly; this distressed the Prophet (peace be upon him), and he had some individuals stand up. When the hypocrites criticized this, this verse was revealed. In addition, when told to rise or move up, they were commanded to rise promptly; it was declared that Allah will raise those who believe and those who have been given knowledge in degrees. This verse is evidence for the virtue of knowledge. In the hadiths, it is emphasized that scholars are superior to worshippers and that knowledge is the inheritance of the prophets. However, those who do not act upon their knowledge are condemned.

Those who wished to consult privately with the Prophet were commanded to give charity before their consultation. This was to demonstrate sincerity and to bring joy to the poor. However, this ruling was abrogated (naskh) shortly thereafter. Ali stated that he was the first and the last person to act upon this verse. Subsequently, Allah granted permission to consult the Prophet without giving charity, while prayer, zakah, and obedience were commanded.

The hypocrites who take as allies a people with whom Allah is angry (the Jews) are condemned. They belong neither to the believers nor to the Jews. They knowingly swear false oaths, taking their oaths as a shield to turn people away from the path of Allah. For them is a humiliating punishment. Satan has overtaken them and made them forget the remembrance of Allah. They are the party of Satan, and they are the losers. Those who oppose Allah and His Messenger are among the most abased. Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers shall surely prevail."

Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not take as allies those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kinsfolk. Allah has inscribed faith in their hearts and strengthened them with a spirit from Himself. He will admit them into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. They are the party of Allah; it is they who are the successful.

The expression "Do you not see" in verse 16 expresses astonishment and condemnation. Allah condemns the hypocrites for aiding and abetting a people with whom He is angry (the Jews), conveying the secrets of the believers to them, and knowingly taking false oaths. In the narrations concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, it is recounted that our Prophet (peace be upon him) said to those with him, "A man with the eyes of a devil will come to you now," and that a blue-eyed man arrived and swore an oath denying that he and his companions had cursed the Prophet. It is reported that the verse was revealed upon this incident.

The same theme is repeated in verse 17. It is emphasized that the hypocrites aided the Jews, that they belonged neither to the believers nor to the Jews, and that they wavered continuously between the two parties. Again within the context of the same narration, it is related that this verse was revealed upon the oaths taken by the hypocrite named Abdullah ibn Nabtal and his companions. There is no contradiction among the narrations; therefore, it can be said that the remainder of the surah was revealed on account of this event. Although there are differing views regarding the identity of Abdullah ibn Nabtal, there are narrations indicating that he was among the hypocrites or that he later repented.

In verse 18, the state of the hypocrites is likewise described with the same expressions, and the same narration is repeated once again. The repetitions in these verses aim to emphatically highlight the evil state of the hypocrites. The fact that the narrations come from different sources reinforces the authenticity of the incident.

In verse 19, it is stated that hypocrites possessing these characteristics are the party of Satan (hizb). Having been overtaken by Satan and having forgotten Allah, these people are Satan's partisans and will certainly suffer loss. For they have brought ruin upon their own souls by forfeiting eternal bliss and plunging themselves into punishment.

In verse 20, it is stated that those insolent ones who attempt to contend against Allah and His Messenger are counted, both in the past and the future, among the most wretched of people, those most deserving of humiliation. The greater the honor and might of the side they oppose, the more their own baseness increases in proportion.

In verse 21, it is stated that Allah decreed victory in pre-eternity in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). According to Qatadah, this statement serves as an oath. Allah has decreed: "Assuredly, I and My messengers shall prevail." Even if prophets are killed, they prevail in their cause through clear proof and the sword. For Allah is All-Powerful, has no equal or partner, aids His messengers, and can never be defeated.

In verse 22, it is emphasized that those who believe in Allah and the Last Day cannot love those who oppose Allah and His Messenger. Such love signifies affection for disbelief and is incompatible with faith. Believers do not love these enemies even if they are their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their relatives. Allah has inscribed faith in the hearts of these believers and strengthened them with a spirit from Him. He will admit them into Gardens beneath which rivers flow; He will be pleased with them, and they will be pleased with Him. They are indeed the party of Allah, and it is only they who are the successful. The surah concludes in this manner, and Surah al-Hashr follows it.

This surah begins by declaring that everything in the heavens and on earth glorifies Allah. Allah is al-Aziz (the Almighty), meaning the Absolute Victor and Prevalent; He grants honor to whomever He wills and abases whomever He wills. He is also al-Hakim (the All-Wise), meaning that He does everything with wisdom. This introduction is in harmony with the content of the surah: for the event of the expulsion of the Jews of Banu Nadir, which is to be recounted, is a manifestation of Allah's might and wisdom, and it is emphasized that there was no injustice or wrongdoing in this incident, but rather a purification.

Allah's might and wisdom expelled from their homes those who disbelieved among the People of the Book—namely, the tribe of Banu Nadir. They had come to await the final Prophet, yet when he arrived, they disbelieved. This expulsion is called the 'first gathering' (a minor resurrection) and is an example of the great gathering in the Hereafter. Neither the believers nor the disbelievers anticipated that they would be expelled; they relied upon their fortresses and their strength. But Allah defeated them from where they did not anticipate, by casting terror into their hearts, so much so that they began to destroy their homes with their own hands. This event is a great lesson for those who have eyes to see: the consequence of disbelief, oppression, and relying solely on material causes is bitter; whereas faith and sincere reliance on Allah bring His help.

According to the legal theorists (usul scholars), the command 'take admonition' in the ayah indicates that analogical reasoning (qiyas) is a valid proof. Taking admonition (ibrah) is the transition from an observed situation to understanding an unobserved one. Here, proceeding from the punishment of Banu Nadir because of their oppression and disbelief, the conclusion is drawn that every act of oppression and disbelief certainly merits punishment. This punishment may be in this world or in the Hereafter; by Allah's wisdom, it is sometimes deferred and sometimes inflicted immediately. From this perspective, analogical reasoning is valid.

Had Allah not decreed exile (jala') for them, He would have inflicted upon them a greater punishment in this world. Jala' means the forcible expulsion of a community from their homeland. Banu Nadir were punished with exile, whereas Banu Qurayzah, who took no admonition, were killed. In either case, the punishment of the Fire awaits them in the Hereafter. Even if they escape worldly punishment, they cannot escape the punishment of the Hereafter.

Regarding whether or not to cut down date palms during war, it is stated: 'Whatever date palms you cut down or left standing on their trunks, it was by Allah's permission.' This permission was granted in order to disgrace those transgressors. The word 'linah' mentioned in the ayah means date palm; some scholars have stated that it refers to the most prized kind of date palm. This dispensation was granted for the purpose of weakening the enemy.

The ruling regarding the spoils acquired from Banu Nadir is different. Allah granted these properties to His Messenger as fay'. Fay' refers to spoils obtained without fighting and without spurring horses. These were properties for which the Muslims spurred neither horses nor camels; therefore, they belonged solely to the Messenger of Allah. He, in turn, spent them in the cause of Allah after setting aside a year's maintenance for his family. Ganimah (war booty), on the other hand, is obtained through fighting, and its ruling is subject to the one-fifth division explained in Surah al-Anfal. Fay' is broader than ganimah; it also encompasses revenues such as land tax (kharaj) and poll tax (jizyah).

In the subsequent ayah, a general ruling is declared with the expression 'the spoils that Allah granted to His Messenger from the people of the towns.' This encompasses all revenues obtained from conquered cities. After the conquest of the lands of Iraq, Umar cited these verses as evidence to argue that the lands should not be distributed among the Muslims but should instead be retained as kharaj-bearing lands, and the Companions adopted this view. Thus, future generations were also able to benefit from these revenues.

This ayah indicates that the spoils are divided into six shares: Allah, the Prophet, near relatives, orphans, the needy, and wayfarers. Some scholars made it six shares, allocating Allah's share to be spent on the repair of the Kaaba and mosques. According to another view, it is divided into five shares by counting a single share for Allah and His Messenger. Although it bears similarity to the verse in Surah al-Anfal, the stipulation of one-fifth is not explicitly mentioned here.

There are different views regarding the share of the Messenger of Allah. According to the Hanafis, this share ceased after the demise of the Prophet, because the Rightly Guided Caliphs acted in this manner. According to one view of al-Shafi'i, this share is given to the imam (leader), because the Prophet took this share in his capacity as head of state. The majority of the Shafi'is hold that this share must be spent on matters that serve the benefit of the Muslims.

What is meant by 'near relatives' (dhu al-qurba) is the Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib. The Prophet did not allocate a share from the spoils to relatives outside these two clans. This matter is explained in a hadith: the Prophet considered Banu al-Muttalib as part of his own family, as they had aided him during the pre-Islamic era of ignorance (Jahiliyyah) as well. The Hanafis stated that this share is to be given only to needy relatives, not to the wealthy.

An orphan is a poor child whose father has passed away; the destitute (miskin) is an impoverished person who possesses nothing; and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil) is a traveler stranded on the road. These categories must be both Muslim and poor. There are differences of opinion among scholars regarding the definitions of the poor (faqir) and the destitute (miskin). According to the Hanafis, the poor is one who does not possess the nisab threshold of wealth, whereas the destitute is one who has nothing at all.

The wisdom behind distributing the spoils in this manner is so that wealth does not become a commodity circulating only among the rich. The word 'dulah' mentioned in the ayah signifies wealth and bounty. It is commanded to take whatever the Prophet gives, to refrain from whatever he forbids, and to fear Allah. The distribution of the spoils was left entirely to the Prophet; obedience to those in authority (ulu al-amr) also falls within this scope.

Although this command was revealed specifically concerning the spoils, as the exegetes have pointed out, its meaning encompasses all commands. In a hadith narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, and al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Mas'ud stated that Allah has cursed women who practice tattooing and those who have it done, those who pluck facial hair, those who file their teeth for beauty, and those who alter Allah's creation. When a woman named Umm Ya'qub claimed that this was not in the Quran, Ibn Mas'ud reminded her of the verse: 'Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, abstain from it.' This demonstrates that what the Messenger of Allah forbids is also regarded as Allah's command.

It is narrated from Imam al-Shafi'i that he said he could answer every question posed regarding the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger; he then stated that Umar's order to kill hornets (zanbur) was binding because the Messenger of Allah commanded obedience to Umar, and the Book of Allah commanded obedience to the command of the Messenger of Allah. This is not an analogy in the form of 'The order of the commander is the order of the commander of the commander's commander,' but rather drawing a deduction directly from the supreme proof. Obedience to those in authority who do not contradict Allah and His Messenger is also declared in verse 59 of Surah an-Nisa.

As stated in the works of jurisprudence (fiqh), if the head of state so chooses, he may divide a territory conquered by force ('anwatan) among the Muslims and impose the tithe ('ushr) upon it, as the Messenger of Allah did at Khaybar, or he may leave the inhabitants in place and collect jizyah and kharaj, as Umar did in the lands of Iraq. According to the Hanafis, this fay' (jizyah and kharaj) is not divided into five; the entirety of it is spent for the benefit of the Muslims, such as on soldiers, workers, judges, and imams. In the distribution of the portion of the spoils other than the one-fifth, the Messenger of Allah and the head of state likewise possess the discretion to choose through legal reasoning (ijtihad) that takes into account the needs of the Muslims.

In the eighth ayah, it is stated that the spoils are for the poor Emigrants (Muhajirun). These are the ones who were expelled from their homes and wealth, seeking Allah's bounty and pleasure, and aiding Allah and His Messenger. It is they who are the truthful—that is, upright and faithful people who prove their words through their deeds. According to Qatadah's narration, the Emigrants suffered such hardships that some tied stones to their stomachs out of hunger, while others slept in pits without bedding. They abandoned worldly pleasures, persevered for the sake of religion, and strived in jihad.

The ninth ayah is about the Ansar (Helpers). Before the Emigrants, they prepared Medina, embraced faith, loved those who emigrated, and felt no longing or covetousness in their hearts for what was given to them. Even if they themselves were in need, they gave preference to the Emigrants over themselves (îsâr). This is the highest station of morality. The Messenger of Allah distributed the spoils of Banu Nadir among the Emigrants, giving only to three needy persons among the Ansar, and they accepted it with pleasure. Furthermore, in a narration reported from Abu Hurayrah, a man from the Ansar went without the meal meant for his own daughter and stayed hungry in the dark in order to host the guest of the Messenger of Allah.

The word 'shuhh' mentioned in the ayah refers to the soul's disposition toward jealousy and stinginess. Ibn Mas'ud defined shuhh as 'unjustly consuming one's brother's wealth,' whereas Ibn Umar described it as 'coveting what one does not possess.' Being protected from stinginess is a condition for attaining salvation. Many hadiths emphasize the evil of stinginess. For example, it was stated: 'Nothing ruins Islam other than stinginess.' However, being protected from stinginess does not require being generous in everything; paying zakat, hosting guests, and helping in times of need are sufficient. Ali also said, 'Whoever pays the zakat on his wealth has been protected from the stinginess of his soul.'

The tenth ayah describes those who came after the Emigrants and the Ansar. These are the Successors (Tabi'un) and all believers who follow them in good conduct. This ayah shows that they, too, are partners with the earlier ones in the ruling on the spoils. Umar stated that the ayah encompasses all Muslims, saying, 'If I live, the share of the shepherd tending his flock will reach him without breaking a sweat.' Moreover, Umar acted prudently in the division of conquered lands with future generations in mind.

The other half of Khaybar was set aside for future hardships that might arise and matters such as visiting envoys. This portion was conceived as a fund for unforeseen emergencies that Muslims might encounter. The Messenger of Allah leased these lands to the Jews in return for half of the produce; this arrangement was in the form of musâkât (sharecropping of orchards in exchange for fruit) and müzârea (sharecropping of farmland). This practice continued during the caliphate of Abu Bakr. When Umar became caliph, as the number of Muslim laborers increased, the Jews were expelled to Syria (Sham) and the lands were distributed among Muslims. This practice of Umar shows that it is not obligatory to partition lands conquered by force of arms; indeed, Mecca was conquered by force, yet it was not partitioned. Imam Malik held the view that lands taken entirely through conquest should be placed in endowment (waqf) on behalf of the Muslims.

Umar did not divide the lands of Iraq (Sawad) as war spoils, but left them in the hands of the local inhabitants, imposing on them kharaj (land tax) and jizya (poll tax). In doing so, he cited verses 7–10 of Surah al-Hashr as evidence, maintaining that these verses command the preservation of the rights of all Muslims, including future generations. Although some of the Companions, such as al-Zubayr, Bilal, and Salman, initially favored division, they too accepted this view following Umar's lengthy address and his substantiation with verses from the Quran. Thus, the lands of Iraq were left to the local population in return for kharaj and jizya: for every dunam, one dirham and one qafiz; for vineyards, ten dirhams; for clover fields, five dirhams of kharaj; as for individuals, a jizya of 48 dirhams for the wealthy, 24 for those of average means, and 12 for the poor was assessed. Eighty million dirhams were collected in the first year, and one hundred and twenty million in the second year.

Imam al-Ghazali states in his work al-Ihya: It is not permissible to give wealth from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) to the wealthy who are of no benefit to the public. Although scholars have differed on this matter, this is what is correct. Even though Umar's practice indicates that every Muslim has a right to the public treasury, he distributed wealth only to those possessing specific attributes. Accordingly, it is permissible, and indeed necessary, to provide a sufficient stipend to those who work for the benefit of Muslims and are occupied with earning their livelihood (such as scholars, teachers, muezzins, students of knowledge, administrators, soldiers, scribes, and financial officials). They may be paid even if they are wealthy, for the Rightly Guided Caliphs gave even to those who were not in need. The amount depends on the discretion (ijtihad) of the head of state; depending on the situation, an amount is given that will make them wealthy or suffice them.

The 10th ayah does not use an absolute expression like 'those who came after'; rather, it describes their state as follows: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and leave no rancor in our hearts toward those who have believed. Our Lord, You are indeed Kind and Merciful." This ayah indicates that Muslims must not harbor rancor toward one another, must respect their elders, and must pray for the forgiveness of shortcomings. Ibn Umar heard a man reviling the Emigrants and recited to him verses 8, 9, and 10 in succession; when the man reached the last verse and asked, "Am I among these?", he replied, "No, whoever reviles them cannot be among them." Citing this ayah as evidence, Imam Malik also said that whoever reviles or hates one of the Companions has no share in the spoils.

Turning to the condition of the hypocrites: In the 11th ayah, the promises made by the hypocrites to their disbelieving friends among the People of the Book (the Jews of Banu Nadir) are described. Hypocrites such as Abdullah ibn Ubayy told the Jews, "If you are expelled, we will surely leave with you; we will never obey anyone against you; and if you are fought against, we will help you." Allah bears witness that they are liars. In the 12th ayah, it is reported that these promises will not be kept: If they are expelled, they will not leave with them, and if they are fought against, they will not help them; even if they were to help them, they would turn their backs and flee, and they themselves will not be helped. The 13th ayah states that they fear you in their hearts more than they fear Allah, because they are a people who do not understand.

In the 14th ayah, it is stated that they cannot fight you united except in fortified towns or from behind walls; that there is intense discord among themselves; and that although they appear united, their hearts are divided. This is because they are a people who do not use their intellect. The 15th ayah likens them to the polytheists who met their punishment at Badr, or to the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa, who tasted the evil consequences of their deeds. The story of Banu Qaynuqa is related: they broke the treaty, exposed the private parts of a woman, then retreated into their fortresses, and eventually surrendered and were expelled. In verses 16–17, the state of the hypocrites is likened to Satan: he first says to man, "Disbelieve," but once man disbelieves, he says, "I am free of you; indeed, I fear Allah." In the end, both are in the Fire eternally. This is the recompense of all wrongdoers. Both the one who commands and the one who commits the act are responsible; and deeming wrongdoing permissible is disbelief.

In verse 18, the believers are addressed: "Fear Allah, and let every soul look to what it has prepared for tomorrow; indeed, Allah is aware of what you do." In verse 19, it is commanded not to be like those who forgot Allah, and so Allah made them forget themselves; they are the defiantly disobedient (fasiqun). In verse 20, it is emphasized that the companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise are not equal, and that the companions of Paradise are the attainers of their desires. In verse 21, the majesty of the Quran is described: Had it been sent down upon a mountain, it would have humbled itself and split apart out of fear of Allah. These parables are given so that people may reflect.

In verses 22–24, Allah's beautiful names and attributes are enumerated: He is the One besides Whom there is no deity, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. He is the Sovereign, the Pure, the Source of Peace, the Granter of Security, the Guardian, the Almighty, the Compeller, the Supremely Great; the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner. To Him belong the most beautiful names. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him. He is the Almighty, the All-Wise. These verses conclude the surah with a magnificent proclamation of tawhid and glorification.

In these verses, it is indicated that the life of this world is one day and the life of the Hereafter is one day. It means 'today is the worldly life, tomorrow is the Hereafter.' Man must consider every day what he has prepared for tomorrow. Although the command 'Fear Allah!' may appear to reinforce the preceding command, the former expresses fulfilling commands out of love for Allah, whereas this one expresses avoiding prohibitions out of fear of Allah. Allah is aware of everything you do and will grant punishment or reward tomorrow accordingly.

In verse 19, we are commanded not to resemble those who forgot Allah, and so Allah made them forget themselves. These people do not know what they are doing, do not understand human worth, and do not contemplate good and virtue. On the Day of Resurrection, they are subjected to terrible tragedies. Even those who claim there is no soul are such self-forgetting people. The innate nature (fitrah) of those heedless of consciousness has become corrupted. They are indeed the defiantly disobedient (fasiqun)—a corrupted group that has departed from obedience and plunged into rebellion. Believers must not resemble them.

In verse 20, it is emphasized that the companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise are not equal. The transgressors who abandoned Allah and indulged in sin deserved Hell, while those who feared Allah and protected themselves became worthy of Paradise. Those who attain salvation are only the people of Paradise. To avert this danger and attain this great goal, believers must protect themselves from sins, reckon every day what they have prepared for tomorrow, and not forget Allah and become like the transgressors.

In verse 21, it is explained that had the Quran been sent down upon a mountain, that mountain would have bowed down and cleaved asunder out of fear of Allah. It is recalled that the mountains did not accept the trust; the Quran was revealed to human beings. While people ought to be even more deeply moved by this impact, most unjust and ignorant people are not affected by it. These parables are given so that people may reflect and take heed. Reflection (fikr) consists of arranging pieces of knowledge in order and connecting the conclusion to what preceded it.

In verses 22–23, the attributes of Allah are described: There is no deity except Him; He knows the unseen and the witnessed; He is the Most Gracious (al-Rahman) and the Most Merciful (al-Rahim). He is al-Malik, al-Quddus, al-Salam, al-Mu'min, al-Muhaymin, al-Aziz, al-Jabbar, al-Mutakabbir. He is far exalted above the partners that the polytheists associate with Him. The attributes al-Rahman and al-Rahim express two kinds of mercy: the Rahmaniyyah encompasses everyone, whereas the Rahimiyyah is granted to those who strive. These verses instill fear and hope together.

In verse 24, it is stated that Allah is al-Khaliq, al-Bari, and al-Musawwir. To Him belong the most beautiful names. Creation (khalq) means determining and bringing into existence; al-Bari is the One Who creates purely and soundly; al-Musawwir is the One Who shapes forms as He wills. Attributes are divided into three: essential (dhatiyyah), active (fi'liyyah), and qualitative (ma'nawiyyah). The names of Allah are ninety-nine; whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise. These names should be invoked with reverence, mentioning good and evil together.

According to what al-Jami' al-Saghir records, the names of Allah Almighty established in the Book and the Sunnah explicitly or by allusive indication are not limited to ninety-nine. In the Quran, there are many more names and attributes such as Rabbu'l-alamin, 'alimu'l-ghaybi wash-shahadah, and ghafiru'dh-dhanb. These are of such nature that they cannot be attributed to any other than Allah. Likewise, names mentioned in supplications in al-Bukhari and Muslim, such as munzilu'l-kitab and mujri's-sahab, belong exclusively to Allah.

In a hadith narrated from Abdullah b. Mas'ud, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'If any Muslim is afflicted with distress or grief and says: "O Allah, I am Your servant, the son of Your servant, and the son of Your maidservant. My forelock is in Your hand. Your judgment over me is prevailing, and Your decree concerning me is just. I ask You by every name that belongs to You, which You have named Yourself with, or revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or preserved in the knowledge of the unseen with You, that You make the Quran the spring of my heart, the polish of my sorrow, and the dispeller of my grief and anxiety," Allah Almighty will dispel his distress and grant him relief in place of his grief.'

In the hadith narrated by al-Bayhaqi from Aisha, Aisha wanted to learn from the Messenger of Allah the name of Allah through which supplications are accepted, and the Messenger of Allah told her to perform ablution, pray two rak'ahs, and then make supplication. In her supplication, Aisha said: 'O Allah, I ask You by all Your beautiful names, those we know and those we do not know, and by Your supreme name, with which when someone supplicates You, You are pleased, and with which when one asks You, You grant,' and the Messenger of Allah said: 'You have struck the truth.'

The statement in the previous hadith, 'Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise,' does not mean that the names are limited to ninety-nine. This indicates that whoever enumerates ninety-nine of the known most beautiful names will enter Paradise. The fact that an even one hundred was not counted and one was excluded is to show that observing an odd number is recommended (mustahabb). Indeed, the fact that in the glorification prayers (tasbih) 'Subhan Allah', 'al-hamdulillah', and 'Allahu Akbar' are recited thirty-three times each, totaling ninety-nine, is based on this wisdom.

There are various narrations regarding the virtue of the final verses of Surah al-Hashr. In the hadith narrated from Ma'qil b. Yasar, it is reported that whoever says 'A'udhu billahi minash-shaytanir-rajim' three times in the morning and recites the last three verses of Surah al-Hashr, seventy thousand angels will invoke blessings upon him, and if he dies on that day, he will die as a martyr. In al-Daylami's narration, it is stated that Allah's greatest names are in the last six verses of Surah al-Hashr. Moreover, it is narrated that these verses are a cure for headache, and that Gabriel (Jibril), when bringing down this verse, said: 'Place your hand upon your head.'

However, the purpose of these verses is not merely reciting them or practicing incantations, but placing one's hand on one's head and reflecting, being filled with the fear of Allah, and preparing for tomorrow in accordance with the verse 'O mankind, fear Allah, and let a person look to what he has sent forth for tomorrow.' One must fear offending the majesty of Allah, work for the future with faith and piety (taqwa) by glorifying and sanctifying Him, and attain the salvation heralded by His mercy. O my Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise, the Compassionate, and the Most Merciful! Enable us to attain our goal through Your forgiveness, leave no malice in our hearts toward our believing brothers, and increase our faith and love.

The occasion of revelation for the initial verses of Surah al-Mumtahanah was that a Companion named Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah secretly sent a letter to the polytheists during the preparations for the conquest of Mecca. Since Hatib had no kinship ties to the Quraysh, he wrote a letter informing them of the Prophet's preparations for war in order to protect his relatives in Mecca; however, Allah informed the Prophet of the situation through Gabriel (Jibril). Thereupon, Ali, Zubayr, and Miqdad were dispatched and intercepted the letter; Hatib was interrogated and pardoned on the basis of the hadith in which the people of Badr were given glad tidings of forgiveness.

Upon this incident, the first verse states: 'O you who have believed! Do not take My enemies and your enemies as allies.' What is meant here are the disbelievers who are the enemies of Allah and the enemies of the believers. The verse forbids the believers from harboring affection for them and disclosing secrets to them. For they have disbelieved in the truth (the Quran and faith) that has come to you, and have expelled the Prophet and yourselves from your homeland simply because you believe in Allah, your Lord. If you have gone out to strive in the cause of Allah and to seek His pleasure, do not take those enemies as allies.

With the expression 'you show affection to them,' the verse refers to sending letters or harboring affection in the heart. Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare. Whoever violates this prohibition has strayed from the right path and led himself to ruin.

In the second verse, it is described what the enemies would do should they overcome you: they would stretch out their hands and their tongues against you with evil, seek to kill and capture you, and moreover wish that you would disbelieve. This is a frightening warning demonstrating how far their hostility could go.

The third and fourth verses inform that relatives and children will be of no benefit on the Day of Resurrection, and that Allah will judge you according to your deeds. For this reason, believers must not take the enemies of Allah as allies and must strictly refrain from disclosing secrets to them in times of war.

In the fifth verse, a prayer is taught: 'Our Lord, make us not a trial for the disbelievers.' That is, do not cause us to be defeated by them lest they look down upon faith. In the sixth verse, it is commanded to take Abraham (Ibrahim) and his companions as an example; they had clearly declared enmity to their people. One should not pin one's hopes on anyone other than Allah.

In the seventh and eighth verses, the glad tidings are given that if one stays completely away from enemies and strives (engages in jihad), Allah may turn hostility into friendship. Indeed, after the conquest of Mecca, many enemies became Muslims. However, the ninth verse strictly forbids establishing friendship with those who fight against you, expel you from your homes, and aid in your expulsion; those who do so are the wrongdoers.

From the tenth verse onward, it is commanded that migrating believing women be tested, that they not be sent back to their disbelieving husbands, and that their mahr (dowries) be refunded. It is stated that believing men should not hold disbelieving women in marriage bonds and should ask back the mahr they spent. In the final verses, the terms of allegiance for women (not associating partners with Allah, not stealing, not committing adultery, not killing their children, not bringing slander, and not disobeying the Prophet in what is good) are explained, and Allah's forgiveness is emphasized.

In the 10th verse of the surah, it is commanded that believing women who have migrated be tested. Allah knows best about their faith. If it is recognized that they are believers, they must not be sent back to the disbelievers. For these women are not lawful for the disbelievers, nor are the disbelievers lawful for them. What their husbands gave as mahr must be returned. Believing men may marry these women once they have given them their mahr. It is not permissible to retain disbelieving women in marital bonds; the mahr spent on them should be demanded, and they too may demand what they spent. This is the judgment of Allah.

In the 11th verse, if any of the wives of the believers flee to the disbelievers and the believers prevail in battle, it is commanded that those whose wives fled be given from the spoils of war an amount equal to what they had spent as mahr. Believers must be mindful of Allah. These rulings constitute the foundation of Islamic international law and relations.

In the 12th verse, the conditions for believing women who pledge allegiance (bay'ah) to the Prophet are listed: not associating anything with Allah, not stealing, not committing adultery, not killing their children, not producing a slander fabricated between their hands and feet (that is, not attributing an illegitimate child to the husband), and not disobeying the Prophet in any good deed. The pledge of those who pledge allegiance under these conditions is accepted, and forgiveness is sought for them from Allah.

In the 13th verse, believers are forbidden from allying with people who have incurred Allah's wrath. Just as the disbelievers have despaired of the occupants of the graves, they have likewise despaired of the Hereafter. Moreover, befriending those who fight on account of religion, expel you from your homes, and assist in your expulsion is also forbidden. This prohibition requires not displaying love and friendship toward them.

In these verses, there is a subtlety in specifically mentioning 'those who aided in your expulsion': the intention was not to sever ties immediately with those who aid enemies, but rather to allow an opportunity for political initiatives to dissuade them from assisting. Thus, these two verses determine important rules in Islam's international relations. The verses present believers with a test of recognizing friend and foe, and staying away from enemies.

In this section, the verses addressing the believers that begin with Allah Almighty's command, "O you who believe!" are examined. In his tafsir, al-Razi notes that there is a beautiful connection in the arrangement of these verses: An obstinate person either persists in their obstinacy, abandons it, or shows submission. These verses inform the believers how to treat them according to each situation: (60/4) points to the first, (60/7) to the second, and (60/10) to the third situation. Then, it is commanded to examine the believing women who arrive having migrated. This examination is intended to reveal the sincerity of their faith. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) would have them swear an oath in this manner: "Do you swear that you did not set out out of hatred for a husband, nor desiring one place over another, nor for any purpose other than love for Allah and His Messenger?"

The reason for this examination is that the primary condition of faith is the affirmation of the heart, and only Allah knows the secrets in the heart. The believers conduct this test to attain outward knowledge. If, as a result of the examination, the women are found to be believers, they must not be returned to the disbelievers. For believing women are not lawful for disbelievers, nor are disbelievers lawful for believing women. This verse specifically protects women from this prohibition and commands the compensation of the expenses (mahr) incurred by the disbelieving husbands. However, this compensation applies to parties that have concluded a treaty, such as the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. Indeed, throughout the treaty's duration, the Messenger of Allah returned the men who came from Quraysh, while regarding the women, this verse was revealed.

In the continuation of the verse, it is stated that there is no sin upon you in marrying believing women, provided you give them their dowers (mahrs). As for disbelieving women, do not hold fast to marital bonds with them ('ismah); that is, do not maintain the bond of marriage with them. Furthermore, it is commanded to mutually claim and exchange the dowers spent on the migrating believing women. According to the majority of exegetes, the expression "if you have your turn (mu'aqib)" means "if the turn comes to you." That is, if your women flee to the disbelievers and then their women migrate to you, the turn to compensate falls upon you, and you pay this compensation from the spoils of war or similar means. Fear Allah and abide by His judgment.

Next, the verse regarding the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) of the believing women (60/12) is explained. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) accepted the pledge from women upon the following conditions: not to associate anything with Allah, not to steal, not to commit adultery, not to kill their children, not to bring forth a slander they have fabricated between their hands and feet, and not to disobey the Messenger of Allah in any good deed. During this pledge, the Prophet (peace be upon him) did not shake hands (musafahah) with women; he used a piece of cloth or water. What transpired during the pledge of Hind bint 'Utbah is recounted: Hind raised certain objections, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) smiled and pardoned her.

In the final section of the surah, the verse, "O you who believe! Do not take as allies a people with whom Allah is angry" is addressed. This phrase describes the disbelievers who have despaired of the Hereafter. The phrase, "just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves" has been interpreted in two ways: First, that the disbelievers who enter the grave completely lose hope upon seeing their place in Hellfire; second, that the disbelievers have despaired of the resurrection of the dead. Despair is disbelief (kufr) and invites the wrath of Allah. Following this, Surah as-Saff is introduced: It was revealed in Medina, and is also known as "al-Hawariyyun" and "Surah 'Isa". It contains fourteen verses, two hundred and twenty words, and nine hundred and twenty-six letters. There are three narrations regarding its occasion of revelation: the Companions asking which deed is most beloved, certain young men speaking of things they had not done, and the actions of the hypocrites contradicting their words.

Surah as-Saff encourages the believers to strive (jihad) in the way of Allah with truthfulness and loyalty. At the end of the previous surah, Surah al-Imtihan, hope in the Hereafter was strengthened by warning against despair. In this surah, in order to prove the supremacy of the religion of Islam before all the worlds, Muslims are commanded to align themselves in ranks like a solid structure and take their place on the fields of jihad. Everything that glorifies Allah proclaims that He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.

"O you who believe! Why do you say what you do not do?" There are various narrations concerning this verse: in the narration of 'Abdullah ibn Salam, it is emphasized that vows must be fulfilled; in the narration of al-Dahhak, lying is condemned; and in another narration, the hypocrites are rebuked. The most correct view is that it refers to vows made regarding the future. That is, when a legitimate act is vowed, it becomes obligatory (wajib); once vowed, it must certainly be fulfilled.

Allah loves those who fight in His way, lined up in ranks as though they were a solid structure cemented together. When Moses (Musa) said to his people, "Why do you hurt me?", as they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate. Jesus ('Isa) likewise heralded to the Children of Israel a messenger to come after him whose name would be Ahmad. But when clear proofs came to them, they said, "This is obvious magic." There will be those who wish to extinguish the light of Allah, but Allah will complete His light and make His Messenger prevail over all religions.

"O you who believe! When believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them. Have them take an oath to ascertain that their hearts match their tongues. If you are satisfied of their faith, do not return them to the disbelievers; for believing women are not lawful for disbelievers, nor are disbelievers lawful for believers. Pay them the dower that the disbelievers spent on those women. This ruling pertains to the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. Allah judges between you, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."

"O Prophet! When believing women come to you to pledge allegiance, take their pledge upon the conditions that they will not associate anything with Allah, will not steal, will not commit adultery, will not kill their children, will not bring forth a slander they have fabricated between their hands and feet, and will not disobey you in what is right." The Prophet (peace be upon him) did not shake hands with women. What occurred during the pledge of Hind bint 'Utbah is an example of the implementation of this verse. Ask forgiveness from Allah for the women who pledge allegiance.

"O you who believe! Fear Allah and abide by His decree." Allah Almighty states in a hadith qudsi: "O My servants! I have forbidden injustice to Myself, so do not wrong one another. I conceal your sins with My forgiveness; seek forgiveness from Me so that I may forgive you. I preserve your deeds; whoever finds good, let him praise Allah, and whoever finds evil, let him blame no one but himself." Indeed, the meaning of this surah is sincerity and being like a solid structure.

The believers must not take as allies a people who have incurred Allah's wrath. Although this expression is generally used for the Jews, the hypocrites or the polytheists of Quraysh may also be intended here. What is most important is that those who have despaired of the Hereafter can commit every kind of evil; therefore, the believers must beware of such despair.

Despairing of the Hereafter is disbelief (kufr) and incurs the wrath of Allah. Indeed, it is also stated in Surah Yusuf: "For none despairs of Allah's mercy except the disbelieving people." The believers must remain hopeful of Allah's mercy and be filled with the joy of faith.

Surah as-Saff was revealed in Medina and consists of 14 verses. There are three narrations regarding the occasion of the surah's revelation: First, that it was revealed when the Companions asked which deed was most beloved to Allah; second, that certain youths spoke of things they had not done; and third, the hypocritical behavior of the hypocrites. The most authentic narration is the first one, which comes from Abdullah b. Salam.

The primary objective of the surah is to encourage striving (jihad) in the cause of Allah with truthfulness and devotion, and to illuminate the future of Islam. The believers must fight interlocking together like "bunyan marsus," that is, a solid structure. This metaphor expresses both physical order and unity of heart; behaviors that disrupt love and solidarity among the believers must be avoided.

The verse, "Why do you say that which you do not do?" warns particularly regarding vows. Believers should not vow what they cannot do, and when they do make a vow, they should fulfill it immediately. This is to avoid lying, which is a major sin in the sight of Allah.

Allah loves those who fight in His cause standing in ranks. This rank must be as solid as a wall joined together with lead. The name of the surah, "as-Saff" (The Rank), also points to this unity. The mujahideen must unite around the same objective and act in this manner to earn Allah's love.

Moses asked his people why they hurt him even though they knew he was Allah's messenger to them. When they did not turn toward the truth, Allah caused their hearts to deviate. This demonstrates that the transgressors (fasiqun) will not be guided to the right path. Muslims must be prepared to fight against such corrupted communities.

Jesus stated that he was sent to the Children of Israel, confirming the Torah, and heralding the glad tidings of a messenger to come after him whose name is Ahmad. The Jews rejected him, and the Christians altered this glad tidings. The name Ahmad means praiseworthy and is among the names of the Prophet Muhammad.

The word 'Paraclete' (Faraklit) mentioned in the Gospels points to Ahmad or Muhammad. Although Christians translate this as 'the Comforter', in reality, this word derives from the root hamd and heralds the Prophet Muhammad. In the face of this clear declaration of the Quran, it is understood that the Gospels have been corrupted.

Jesus (peace be upon him) had announced the glad tidings to the Children of Israel that a messenger named Ahmad would come after him. However, just as the Jews refused to heed this glad tidings, most of the Christians also concealed it or corrupted and denied it. Finally, when that heralded messenger (Muhammad, peace be upon him) came with clear proofs, the Jews and Christians deviated into denial, saying, 'This is obvious magic.' Furthermore, fabricating lies against Allah, they invented falsehoods such as attributing a son to Him and presented these as the word of Allah.

Who can be more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or fabricates falsehoods concerning Him? Allah does not guide such wrongdoers to the right path, nor does He grant them success. Indeed, the injustices of these deniers are among the reasons that necessitate the believers' preparing for war in the way of Allah and make striving a beloved deed. They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah will perfect His light, even if the disbelievers dislike it.

Allah has sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to cause it to prevail over all religions. Addressing the believers, it is proclaimed: Shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment? That transaction is: to believe in Allah and His Messenger, and to strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if you only knew. Striving may feel difficult, but something you dislike may be good for you.

Through this faith and striving, Allah forgives your sins and admits you into Gardens beneath which rivers flow and into pleasant dwellings in the Gardens of Eden (Adn). That is the supreme triumph. Moreover, there is another blessing that you will love: help from Allah and an imminent conquest. So give these glad tidings to the believers!

O you who believe! Be supporters of Allah. Just as Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, 'Who are my supporters for Allah?' and the disciples replied, 'We are the supporters of Allah.' Thereupon, a group from the Children of Israel believed, while another group disbelieved. Allah supported those who believed, and they became victorious. So be like that as well.

The disciples (Hawariyyun) were the distinguished first disciples of Jesus who believed, numbering twelve individuals. This name was given to them on account of their sincerity and purity. Some scholars have stated that they received this name because of the white garments they wore, or because they cleansed people with religion and knowledge. The disciples were sent to various regions and spread the message of Jesus (peace be upon him). Later figures like Paul, who deviated into false beliefs, are not counted among the disciples.

The Companions of our Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) became supporters of Allah just like the disciples, and in a short time they overcame the polytheists and the Christians, causing Islam to prevail. This superiority is not confined solely to that era, but encompasses all believers who act in this manner until the Day of Resurrection. The help of Allah is with those who help His religion. In order to prevail over their enemies, believers must rely on this divine promise and seek their shortcomings in their own sins.

Everything in the heavens and on the earth glorifies Allah. This is a reality inherent in the creation of every existent being. Human beings, too, by using their freedom of will, must declare Allah free from every flaw and deficiency, and refrain from associating partners with Him. As stated at the end of the previous surah, they should not be deceived in moments of victory and deviate into excess, but knowing that victory comes from Allah, they should continue to glorify and exalt Him. Allah is al-Quddus, that is, entirely pure and far removed from every imperfection. He is in need of nothing. The mention of glorification (tasbih) and sanctification (taqdis) together at the beginning of this surah indicates the rejection of excesses such as Christians falling into the Trinity following victory. Allah is also the Almighty (al-Aziz, the Exalted and Prevailing) and the All-Wise (al-Hakim, the Possessor of wisdom).

Allah has sent from among the unlettered a messenger from their own midst. The word 'ummi' means one who cannot read or write, and here it refers to the Arabs. This messenger recites Allah's verses to them, purifies them (cleansing them of evil beliefs and traits), and teaches them the Book and wisdom. Whereas previously, they were in clear misguidance. This messenger has been sent not only to the Arabs, but also to all other people who have not yet joined them.

The sending of this messenger is a grace of Allah; it cannot be acquired through labor. Allah gives it to whomever He wills. Following this, those who were given the Torah but did not act in accordance with it are rebuked. Their condition resembles that of a donkey carrying books on its back without being aware of what they contain. Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people who deny His verses.

Addressing the Jews, it is said: 'If you claim that you are the allies of Allah, then wish for death!' But on account of the sins their hands have put forth, they will never wish for death. Yet death will inevitably come and return them to the presence of Allah, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. At that time, everything they did will be made known to them, and they will receive their recompense.

O you who believe! When the call to prayer is made on Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah (the sermon and the prayer) and leave off trading. That is better for you. Once the prayer is completed, disperse throughout the land and seek your share of Allah's bounty. And remember Allah much so that you may attain salvation. Regarding the 'call' mentioned here, the view preferred by the Hanafis is that the obligation begins with the first external adhan. As for 'hastening' (sa'y), it does not mean running in a panic, but rather proceeding promptly and striving with intention.

One of the conditions of the Friday prayer is the sermon (khutbah). The sermon falls under the scope of 'the remembrance of Allah' (dhikrullah) and is delivered before the prayer. According to the Great Imam (Abu Hanifah), the obligatory component of the sermon is the shortest utterance that can be called dhikrullah (such as praising Allah [hamd], declaring His oneness [tahlil], or glorifying Him [tasbih]). Preaching, admonition, and supplications are Sunnah. Among the other Sunnah acts of the sermon are ritual purity, delivering it standing, facing the congregation, commencing with praise, and reciting from the Quran.

When the believers saw some merchandise or amusement, they dispersed immediately toward it and left you (the Messenger of Allah) standing. Say: 'That which is with Allah is better than amusement and merchandise. And Allah is the best of providers.' This verse emphasizes that worldly gains hold no value alongside the blessings of the Hereafter.

During the sermon, it is Sunnah for the preacher (khatib) to recite three short verses or one long verse from the Quran, to offer praise and glorification to Allah, to invoke blessings upon the Prophet, and to supplicate for believing men and women. It is necessary to sit between the two sermons for the duration of reciting three verses; if this sitting is omitted, the preacher incurs sin. That the sermon be short and the prayer long is in accord with jurisprudence (fiqh) and the Sunnah. It is recommended (mustahabb) for the preacher to raise his voice, and it is recommended to soften it in the second sermon compared to the first. Mentioning the four caliphs, Hamzah, and Abbas in the sermon is regarded as commendable. It is an essential condition that the preacher be qualified to lead the prayer.

When the imam ascends the pulpit, it is not permissible to speak, eat, or drink; the congregation must also remain silent. Listening to the sermon is obligatory (wajib), and being close is more virtuous, but stepping over people's shoulders to move forward is disliked (makruh). The essential substance of the sermon is dhikrullah; the prayer is likewise a form of remembrance. In accordance with the verse, 'O you who believe, when the call to prayer is made on Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trading,' engaging in commerce once the call to prayer is made is forbidden (haram). A sale concluded at the time of the call is not invalid (batil) provided there is no defect in the item sold or the contract itself, but it is prohibitively disliked (tahriman makruh); because the prohibition is not due to the transaction in its essence, but due to the proximity of the time.

Friday is the weekly festival (eid) of Muslims and the master of days. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Every Friday, Allah frees six hundred thousand people from the Fire.' Whoever dies on Friday is granted the reward of a martyr. Furthermore, there is an hour on that day (the hour of response, sa'at al-ijabah) such that if a Muslim coincides with it while supplicating, Allah grants what he asks. There are various narrations regarding which hour this is; the strongest is that it spans from the moment the imam ascends the pulpit until the prayer concludes. On Friday, the angels stand at the door of the mosque, recording those who arrive early; the one who comes earliest receives a reward as though having offered a camel, then an ox, then a ram, then a chicken, then an egg in charity.

The first Friday prayer in Medina was performed before the Migration (Hijrah) by As'ad ibn Zurarah with forty men.
