Mus'ab ibn Umayr, on the other hand, led twelve people in the Friday prayer by order of the Prophet. When the narrations are reconciled, it is understood that As'ad gathered the congregation while Mus'ab served as the imam. In the hadith of Jabir regarding the obligation of the Friday prayer, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Allah has made Friday [prayer] an obligation upon you in this year, in this month, on this day, and in this place until the Day of Resurrection. Whoever abandons it out of disregard, may Allah not bless his affairs.'

When the Prophet (peace be upon him) migrated to Medina, he stayed in Quba for several days and then set out on a Friday. When the time for the Friday prayer entered in a valley belonging to the Banu Salim ibn Awf, he delivered a sermon and led the first Friday prayer. Later in Medina, he ordered a pulpit (minbar) to be constructed; it is narrated that he prayed upon the pulpit built by the carpenter slave of a woman and demonstrated prayer upon the pulpit to serve as an example for the people. The introduction of the pulpit ensured that the sermon was conducted in a more orderly manner.

According to the narration of Jabir ibn Abdillah, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) initially used to deliver the sermon leaning against a palm trunk. When the pulpit was built, that trunk began to moan like a she-camel separated from her calf. The Messenger of Allah stepped down from the pulpit and placed his hand upon it, whereupon it fell silent. This event is known as the miracle of 'the moaning of the palm trunk' (Hanin al-Jidh'). The first Friday prayer outside Medina was performed at the mosque of Abd al-Qays in Jawatha, Bahrain.

The conditions of the Friday prayer are divided into two categories: conditions of obligation (wujub) and conditions of performance (ada'). The conditions of obligation are: freedom, being male, residency (not being a traveler), good health, having the ability to walk, and safety (the absence of blindness, fear of an enemy, torrential rain, and similar conditions). For whoever lacks these conditions, Friday prayer is not obligatory, but if they perform it, their prayer is valid.

The first of the conditions of performance is the 'misr al-jami',' that is, a major city possessing administrative institutions. According to the Hanafis, this is a place where there is a judge to enforce legal rulings and an authority to ensure security. Imam al-Shafi'i, however, did not stipulate this as a condition, stating that the Friday prayer may be performed anywhere forty free resident men reside. In addition, it is a condition that the Friday prayer be performed within its proper time (the time of Dhuhr); if its time expires, it is not made up as Friday prayer, but rather the Dhuhr prayer is performed.

Another condition of valid performance is that the head of state (the imam) or a person authorized by him leads the prayer. This is called "izn-i sultan" (permission of the ruler). As for the condition of the congregation, it is at least three men along with the imam; Abu Yusuf considers three people including the imam sufficient. The Great Imam Abu Hanifa, however, stipulates four people along with the imam. Although there are many opinions regarding the size of the congregation, the most virtuous is to pray in a crowded mosque.

Performing ghusl (ritual bath) on Friday is commanded in many hadiths. Hanafi scholars state that this ghusl is sunnah or recommended (mustahabb). Ghusl should be performed after dawn and before going to Friday prayer; additionally, wearing pleasant perfume, using a miswak, and putting on one's finest clothes are recommended. In hadiths narrated from Abdullah ibn Salam and Abu Dharr, it is reported that whoever performs this purification and goes to Friday prayer will have their sins forgiven between the two Fridays.

One Friday, while the Messenger of Allah was delivering the sermon (khutbah), a trade caravan arrived, and upon hearing the sound of drums, most of the congregation left the mosque and headed toward the caravan. Only twelve people remained with the Messenger of Allah. Thereupon, Allah the Exalted revealed the ayah, "When they saw a transaction or amusement, they left you standing." In the ayah, the believers are reminded that the reward with Allah is better than trade and amusement.

The surah relates that when the hypocrites came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), they bore witness saying, 'Truly you are the Messenger of Allah,' yet they did so not with sincerity, but merely to appear Muslim on the outside. In response to their false testimony, Allah Almighty states that He knows the Prophet is indeed His messenger, but Himself bears witness that the hypocrites are liars. A hypocrite is someone whose inward does not match their outward, who is outwardly a Muslim and inwardly a disbeliever. Those meant here are Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his supporters. The emphatic expressions in their words are in fact an effort to convince the Prophet that they believe; yet they swear oaths even though they know they are lying.

The hypocrites take their oaths as a shield. By appearing outwardly Muslim, they seek through these oaths to protect their lives and wealth in this world. In this way, they turn away from the path of Allah or strive to bar others from the true religion. How evil an immorality is this conduct of theirs!

When you see them, their outward appearance pleases you; and when they speak, the beauty of their words affects you. Yet they are like hollow timbers propped up; they fear every loud shout, thinking it is against them. Because they are treacherous, they are in constant anxiety. May Allah curse them; how they are turned away from truth to falsehood!

When it is said to them, 'Come, let the Messenger of Allah ask forgiveness for you,' they turn their heads away and act arrogantly. It is all the same whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them. For Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people. This ayah was revealed after the Messenger of Allah said he would ask forgiveness more than seventy times, following the verse previously revealed in Surah at-Tawbah.

The hypocrites say, 'Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah so that they will disperse.' However, to Allah belong the treasures of the heavens and the earth; He is the Provider of sustenance. These words of theirs stem from their ignorance. Regarding the occasion of revelation of this ayah, the narration of Zayd ibn Arqam is significant. Zayd heard this statement from Abdullah ibn Ubayy and informed the Messenger of Allah; however, when Abdullah denied it under oath, Zayd felt grief until revelation descended.

The hypocrites also say, 'When we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humiliated from it.' Yet honor (izzah) belongs only to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. The hypocrites do not know this; they mistake their arrogance for honor. Whereas true honor lies in a person knowing their soul and not debasing it. As for the believers, they prostrate to none other than Allah; therefore, true honor belongs to them.

O you who believe! Let not your wealth or your children distract you from the remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that, they are the losers. And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you and he says, 'My Lord, if only You would delay me for a short while so that I might give charity and be among the righteous.' But never will Allah delay a soul when its appointed term has come. And Allah is fully aware of what you do.

In the ninth ayah, addressing the believers, Allah commands that neither wealth nor children should distract them from remembering Allah. Here, preoccupation with wealth and children—which are the fleeting adornments of worldly life—must not cause one to forget the remembrance of Allah, which is the primary objective. The purpose is not to have no concern for them at all, but rather that concern for them should not become so excessive as to make one forget Allah and His pleasure.

The remembrance of Allah (dhikrullah) entails acts of worship such as prayer, as well as contemplating Allah and bearing in mind His commands and prohibitions. Whoever becomes preoccupied with the pursuit of wealth and children and forgets Allah, those are the ones who are in loss. For worldly life passes away, and in the Hereafter only enduring righteous deeds are of benefit.

In the ayah, two qualities are emphasized for believers to attain honor: not being negligent of the remembrance of Allah and spending (infaq) from the sustenance He has provided. These two matters bring to mind a hadith concerning the discussion among the angels: the angels confer over the expiations (kaffarat, deeds that expiate sins) and degrees (darajat, deeds that elevate ranks).

The expiations are walking to good deeds, remaining seated in the mosque after prayer, and performing ablution. The degrees are feeding others, spreading the greeting of peace, and praying at night. The Messenger of Allah commanded us to learn these deeds as a lesson. Infaq (spending in Allah's cause) in particular is the bridge that leads a person to true honor; after obligatory dues are paid, supererogatory charities elevate ranks.

True honor lies not in consuming food, but in feeding others. Those who spend their wealth solely on themselves and give no thought to others are at a low level. Noble societies, on the other hand, race with one another in spending in charity; the angels' discussions are also about expiations and degrees. The religion of Islam has commanded the remembrance of Allah and spending in His cause in order to raise believers to this high honor.

In the eleventh ayah, it is stated that Allah will never delay any soul when its appointed term comes, and that He is fully aware of all that you do. Therefore, before death arrives, we must not forget Allah and we must spend in His way. This ayah reminds us that gain and loss will become manifest on the Day of Reckoning; Surah at-Taghabun elaborates further on this subject.

Everything in the heavens and on earth constantly glorifies Allah. This glorification demonstrates that sovereignty and praise belong to Him alone, and that He is capable of all things. Serving as an introduction to matters such as death and resurrection, this verse proclaims the truths that the disbelievers fail to comprehend.

Allah created you; yet some among you are disbelievers, and some are believers. Both disbelief and faith are by Allah's creation, but the servant's will and choice play a role in this creation. The verse reflects both fatalistic and moderate views; in contrast to the Jabriyyah, the responsibility of the servant is emphasized. Allah sees what you do and requites everyone according to their deeds.

Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in truth, fashioned man in the finest form. As a requirement of this noble creation, man ought to choose goodness and turn toward Allah. The return is to Allah, and everyone will receive the recompense for what they have done.

Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and on earth; everything open and hidden is encompassed by His knowledge. The catastrophes that befell past nations show that deniers are punished in this world. To those who suppose they will not be resurrected, it is said: "Nay, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected."

That day is the Day of Taghabun (mutual loss and gain); the day when mutual deception will be brought to light, and profit and loss will become manifest. Those who believe and do righteous deeds will enter Paradise to abide therein eternally; while those who disbelieve will suffer eternal punishment in Hell. That indeed is the ultimate triumph.

No calamity strikes except by Allah's leave. Whoever believes in Allah, Allah guides his heart to what is right. Obey Allah and obey the Prophet; if you turn away, the messenger's duty is only to convey the message clearly. There is no deity except Allah; let the believers rely upon Him alone.

Among your spouses and your children are enemies to you; so beware of them. If you pardon and overlook, Allah is also forgiving. Your wealth and your children are a trial; the immense reward is with Allah. Fear Allah as much as you are able, obey, and spend. Whoever is saved from the stinginess of his own soul—they are the ones who attain success. If you lend Allah a goodly loan, He will multiply it manifold and forgive you. Allah knows the seen and the unseen; He is the All-Mighty, the All-Wise.

No calamity befalls except by Allah's permission. Whether one is a disbeliever or a believer, every kind of hardship that befalls anyone is by Allah's leave. Even though some calamities stem from a person's own self, they still do not occur without Allah's decree and permission. Allah guides the heart of whoever believes in Him, consoling him by reminding him that the calamity comes from Him and will return to Him. The patient are granted their reward without measure. Therefore, believe in Allah, His Messenger, and the Quran. Obey Allah, and obey the Prophet.

O you who believe! Among your spouses and your children are enemies to you; so beware of them. This verse was revealed regarding some Muslims who wished to emigrate to Medina but were prevented by their spouses and children. Spouses and children, intentionally or unintentionally, may hold a person back from good deeds and even harm religion. For this reason, the man as the head of the family should be vigilant toward his family, raise them with religious upbringing, and not spoil them with excessive affection and indulgence. Along with this, he should pardon, overlook, and show tolerance toward their shortcomings. Allah is indeed the Forgiver of sins and the Merciful.

Your wealth and your children are a fitnah (a trial and a source of hardship). By binding you to themselves, they may keep you away from righteous deeds and lead you into sin. Yet the great reward is with Allah. For this reason, one should prefer love for Allah, His remembrance, and obedience to Him over love for wealth and children; and while attending to concerns regarding wealth and children, one should not compromise the worship and obedience due to Allah.

Fear Allah as much as you are able, and hold to the path of piety (taqwa). Hear the commands, obey, and spend. Give zakah and charity from the provision Allah has granted you. Do good for your own souls. Seek refuge in Allah, and guard yourselves against greed and stinginess. Those who are preserved from the stinginess of their souls are the ones who achieve salvation. Do not forget Allah and fall behind in doing good out of anxiety over wealth and children.

If you lend Allah a goodly loan (spend your wealth for the sake of Allah), Allah will multiply its reward for you and forgive your sins. Allah is Shakur (the Most Appreciative, who rewards goodness manifold) and Halim (the Forbearing, who does not hasten to punish). He is the All-Mighty (Aziz) and the All-Wise (Hakim). He knows both the unseen (ghayb) and the seen (shahadah); He knows the secret and the manifest. When He wills, His reckoning is swift, yet He often grants respite. There is wisdom in everything He does.

At the end of the surah, a warning is issued regarding family matters: spouses and children can sometimes be enemies, so beware of them. The marital bond can be dissolved, but the parent-child bond is enduring. Through this wisdom, divorce was made permissible, and this surah is followed by Surah at-Talaq.

The address to the Prophet at the beginning of the surah serves as a reminder and an indication of the importance of conveying the rulings in these verses to the ummah. The ruling of divorce is not exclusive to the Prophet, but is for all Muslims. Allah Almighty says: when you divorce women, divorce them taking into account their waiting period (iddah). That is, calculating the number of days of the woman's menstrual cycle, divorcing her during a period of purity without having had sexual intercourse, by a single pronouncement of divorce (talaq), is the manner conforming to the Sunnah.

Since it is commanded to keep away from women during menstruation, divorcing during menstrual days is forbidden (haram). Likewise, divorcing during a period of purity after having had sexual intercourse is disliked (makruh). Issuing three divorces all at once is even more abhorrent and sinful. Such forms of divorce are innovations (bid'ah); while the divorce is valid, the person who executes it incurs sin. For divorce is a right entrusted to the will of men, and even though the act is sinful, the divorce takes effect.

The purpose of marriage is to establish a family based on the love and mercy that Allah has created between husband and wife. Even if there are discords or resentments, as long as natural desire and peace continue, the family should not be destroyed. However, if desire and tranquility cease and malice and hatred emerge, then divorce becomes a legitimate necessity. On the other hand, a divorce carried out in anger or out of lustful indulgence is ingratitude and often brings about regret.

Although divorce has been made legitimate, there are manners of it that conform to the Sunnah. The best of these is to divorce the woman with a single pronouncement of divorce during a period of purity without having had sexual intercourse. This is called ahsan (the best). Issuing one divorce in each period of purity until reaching three divorces is considered hasan (good). In contrast, divorcing during menstruation or after sexual intercourse is an innovative divorce (talaq al-bid'ah); issuing three divorces at once is the severest innovation.

The expression 'divorce them taking into account their waiting period' mentioned in the verse was interpreted by Companions such as Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas as 'while in a state of purity, before intercourse' or 'at the start of their waiting period.' Mujahid, Qatadah, and other scholars also supported this view. According to the Hanafis, the waiting period consists of the days of menstruation, whereas according to the Malikis and Shafi'is, it is the period of purity. However, all of them agreed that the woman must be divorced at a time when she is in a state of purity and no sexual intercourse has taken place.

The right of divorce belongs to the man. The woman does not have the direct authority to divorce; however, if this authority is granted by the man during or after the marriage contract, she may exercise it. Otherwise, the woman may seek separation through khul' (by offering a ransom). According to the Hanafis, the judge seeks reconciliation by appointing arbiters from the families of both parties; according to the Shafi'is, the judge has the right of annulment (faskh). The Hanafis accept annulment only in cases where the husband is incapable of sexual intercourse or in the event of illnesses such as leprosy.

It is forbidden to expel divorced women from their homes during their waiting periods. In the verse, it is stated: 'Do not expel them from their houses, nor should they leave.' This prohibition prevents the husband from casting the woman out due to anger or need, and it also encompasses the woman leaving on her own accord. However, if the woman commits open indecency and immorality, she may then be expelled from the house. This exception includes major sins such as adultery (zina), theft, and causing harm to family members. Most scholars have stated that 'fahishah' refers to any major sin.

Fearing Allah means observing the commands and prohibitions concerning divorce and the waiting period. It is not permissible to undercount or artificially prolong the waiting period. Harming women must be avoided. Acting in accordance with the Sunnah during divorce prevents regret and delays the dissolution of the family. It must not be forgotten that divorce is among the most detestable of permissible things in the sight of Allah, and it should only be resorted to in cases of necessity.

These verses are the limits set by Allah for His servants. Whoever exceeds these limits has wronged himself. Perhaps Allah will bring about a new situation thereafter, and when one regrets and wishes to return, it will be too late. For this reason, in the process of divorce, it is necessary to observe the waiting period, pronounce divorce during a state of purity, and count the waiting period. As long as it does not reach three, the divorce is revocable (raj'i); that is, reconciliation is possible during the waiting period. Because of these wisdoms, do not exceed the limits, count the waiting period, and fear Allah; do not expel women from their houses, nor should they leave.

When the waiting period reaches its end, either retain them with kindness or separate from them with kindness. Retention can also take place through an act; this is the view of the Great Imam (Abu Hanifah). When separating, release them gracefully and call to witness two just men. The command to bring witnesses has generally been understood as recommended (mandub). Although al-Shafi'i argued in his earlier view that it was obligatory, in his later view he stated it was recommended. Al-Alusi finds Tabarsi's view—that this command makes bringing witnesses obligatory at the moment of divorce—to be weak. The apparent meaning of the verse requires witnessing to take place at the time of retention or separation; the claim that it is a condition for the validity of divorce is far-fetched. This is because such a condition would contradict the benefit provided by revocable divorce and the Sunnah manner of divorce. Moreover, a contradiction would arise where a divorce would be invalid if witnesses were not present during the divorce but were brought afterward. For this reason, all mujtahids are in agreement that the command to bring witnesses upon separation is recommended. Then, uphold the testimony uprightly for Allah. All these commands are an admonition to those who believe in Allah and the Last Day; they are the ones who benefit.

Whoever fears Allah, Allah creates a way out for him and provides for him from where he does not expect. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) recited this verse and said: 'Allah creates a way out from the doubts of this world, the agony of death, and the severity of the Day of Resurrection.' Narrated from Abu Dharr: 'If all people held fast to this, it would suffice them.' Whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him. Allah accomplishes His purpose; He has destined a measure for all things. Relying on worldly causes is finite, while relying on Allah is infinite. Reliance upon Allah (tawakkul) means performing one's duty to the best of one's ability and leaving the outcome to Allah. First piety (taqwa), then reliance is commanded. Our Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Tie your camel and put your trust in Allah.' Just as Allah has set a measure for everything, He has also set limits for the waiting period, maintenance, and other matters.

The waiting period of women who have passed menopause is three months. Those who have not menstruated also wait three months. This includes those under seventeen years of age who have not yet reached puberty, or those who have reached puberty but do not menstruate. This ruling also applies to those who menstruated once or twice and then stopped. In the case of continuous cessation of menstruation, it is said that 'the period of purity has lengthened'; the Hanafis state that such a woman must wait until the age of menopause. However, since the primary purpose of the waiting period is to eliminate any doubt of pregnancy, waiting up to the maximum duration of pregnancy appears more appropriate in such cases. As for pregnant women, their waiting period ends when they deliver their burden. This applies both in the case of divorce and upon the husband's death. Although Ali and Ibn Abbas initially thought this verse applied only to divorced women and accepted the longer of the two terms (four months and ten days or childbirth), the ruling of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) became known through the hadith of Umm Salamah: 'When you have given birth, you have become lawful.' This hadith, authentically narrated in al-Bukhari and other sources, indicates that Surah at-Talaq was revealed after the verse concerning the mourning waiting period upon death in Surah al-Baqarah, and that it abrogated the ruling regarding pregnant women.

These rulings are the command of Allah. Whoever fears Allah, Allah will expiate his sins and magnify his reward. In the surah, recommendations of piety (taqwa) are repeated, drawing attention to the importance of family law and the dangers of carelessness regarding divorce. Divorce is the most hateful of permissible things (halal) in the sight of Allah. For this reason, when divorce is necessary, it is commanded to observe the waiting period (iddah), not to expel them from their homes, and then either to retain them with kindness or separate from them with kindness.

Lodge the divorced women where you live according to your means, and do not harass them in order to distress them. If they are pregnant, spend on them until they deliver. If they breastfeed for you, give them their payment and consult among yourselves in a fair manner. If you encounter difficulties, another woman may breastfeed for him. Let the wealthy person spend according to his abundance, and let the one whose provision is restricted spend from what Allah has granted him. Allah does not burden any soul beyond what He has given it. Allah will bring about ease after hardship.

In matters pertaining to women such as menstruation and pregnancy, and in circumstances like the cessation of menstruation or pregnancy, the woman's statement is taken as the basis. As stated in verse 228 of Surah al-Baqarah, it is not lawful for women who believe in Allah and the Last Day to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs. The waiting period (iddah) of a divorced woman is to determine whether she is pregnant; if it becomes known that she is pregnant, she does not need to wait for three menstrual periods, but waits until she gives birth, and maintenance (nafaqah) is provided during this time. The duration of pregnancy is at least six months, and at most two years according to the Hanafis and four years according to the Shafi'is. The condition 'if they are pregnant' here is not the reason for the command of maintenance, but rather the justification for spending throughout the period leading up to childbirth. This condition does not mean that non-pregnant divorced women will not receive maintenance; on the contrary, it indicates that spending is obligatory (wajib) even during short waiting periods.

The command in the verse 'Do not expel them, lodge them' indirectly conveys that spending (infaq) is also one of the requisites of lodging, alongside the prohibition of expelling them from the home. There are several points of wisdom in specifying the condition of pregnancy: First, to show that the primary purpose of the waiting period and maintenance is pregnancy. Second, to dispel doubt against the possibility of a prolonged pregnancy. Third, it points to the need for showing special care toward pregnant women. Fourth, to explain the rulings regarding the breastfeeding and care of the child after birth. After the child is born, if the mother breastfeeds on the father's account, the father must pay the breastfeeding fee. If the mother breastfeeds on her own account, the father covers only clothing and other expenses. In both cases, it is necessary to reach an agreement through kind and proper mutual consultation. If a dispute arises, the father is obliged to hire another wet nurse. However, if the child refuses the breast of another woman, the mother may be compelled to breastfeed by a judicial arbitrator's ruling.

In the 7th verse, it is commanded that the one of abundance should spend according to his abundance, and the one whose provision is restricted should spend from what Allah has granted him. This is a ruling applicable to all maintenance matters. The person obligated to spend is responsible according to his wealth if he is rich, according to his modest means if he is middle-class, and according to his poverty if he is poor. Allah does not burden anyone beyond his capability. One who can borrow may spend by borrowing in good faith. Allah will bring about ease after hardship. For this reason, the poor and their families should be patient and never despair of Allah, and the wealthy should not neglect them but look after them through zakat and charity (sadaqah).

In verses 8-10, it is reported that many a city that rebelled against the command of Allah and His messengers was called to a severe account and subjected to an unprecedented punishment. These societies tasted the consequence of their deeds, and the outcome of their affair was ruin. Allah has prepared a severe punishment for them. O people of understanding who have believed! Fear Allah, for Allah has sent down to you a reminder (the Quran or a messenger).

In the 11th verse, it is stated that Allah sent a messenger reciting the clear verses of Allah to bring those who believe and do righteous deeds out of darkness into light. Whoever believes in Allah and does righteous deeds, Allah will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever. Allah has indeed granted him an excellent provision. What is meant by the messenger is our Prophet Muhammad Mustafa (peace be upon him). The tanwin (nunation) in the word 'Rasul' expresses grandeur.

In the 12th verse, it is reported that Allah created seven heavens and of the earth a similar number, and that the command descends between them. This is so that we may know that Allah is capable of all things and that His knowledge encompasses everything. While the expression 'seven heavens' is definite, it does not mean there is nothing beyond them. The contrary implication of numbers (mafhum al-mukhalafah) is not valid unless there is corroborating evidence. Ayat al-Kursi and the hadiths show that the Kursi (Footstool) is vaster than the heavens and is like a ring within the Throne (Arsh). The seven heavens may also be understood as regions demarcated by the orbits of the seven known planets; however, this number does not preclude the existence of other planets.

The similarity in the phrase 'and of the earth, their like' pertains to number and certain attributes. According to the majority of commentators, just like the seven heavens, there are seven earths, and between each of them there is a distance equivalent to that between heaven and earth. In each earth, there are living creatures created by Allah. Some commentators, however, stated that it refers to the strata of the earth or the seven climes. Sound hadiths also support the existence of seven earths. The wisdom behind the Quran usually mentioning 'the heavens and the earth' in other verses and using the singular 'of the earth' here is that the earth serves as a single gravitational center, whereas the sky, as an expanse of ascent, is manifold. This demonstrates that Allah's knowledge and power encompass all things.

If the 'lam' (definite article) in the expression 'al-Ard' in the verse denotes the genus (jins), it is understood as a resemblance of the terrestrial genus to the seven heavens—meaning that planets, like the earth, are centers of gravity and habitations. If the 'lam' denotes specific reference (ahd), it indicates a resemblance to the seven heavens solely in terms of the continents, strata, and regions of our own earth. All of these interpretations may be correct, and each offers a distinct perspective in understanding Allah's power.

Here, it is noted that the word "in" may have two different meanings. One of these is that the word is an "ibtidaiyyah" particle, that is, a preposition denoting inception. In this case, the verse describes the creation of human beings from dust and their subsequent coming into existence with the command "Be". Indeed, similar expressions are found in verses Al-i Imran 3/59 and Ta-Ha 20/55. This interpretation encompasses the creation of the human being in both body and soul.

According to the second interpretation, what is meant is the descent of divine commands between the seven layers of heaven and the earth. As stated in Fussilat 41/12, He revealed its command to each heaven. These commands regulate the movement and rest, as well as the events and affairs, of all beings. In this way, divine revelation regarding divine decree and destiny (al-qada' wa'l-qadar) descends continuously.

The point to be noted here is that all events in systems of celestial bodies, such as the solar system, do not occur by their own nature, but by the command of Allah. As expressed in al-Isra 17/85, the soul (ruh) is also from the command of the Lord. In the same way, the Quran was also sent down into the heart of our Prophet as a light descending from above the heavens.

All these acts of creation and command are so that we may know that Allah has power over all things. He is also fully capable of fulfilling what He has promised to those who believe and perform righteous deeds. Moreover, Allah's knowledge encompasses all things; the creation and order of the universe stand as proof of His power and knowledge.

Surah at-Talaq ends here. In connection with the subject of prohibition, which is one of the consequences of divorce (talaq), Surah at-Tahrim will follow next. This surah also pertains to oaths and family matters.

The surah begins in its first verse with the address “O Prophet!”, primarily emphasizing an expression of veneration (ta'zim). This address indicates that the admonition is directed not to the Prophet's person himself, but to convey a ruling that must be communicated to the ummah by virtue of his status of prophethood. The subsequent question, “Why do you make unlawful?”, carries both present and future tense meanings through its imperfect verb form (mudari'); hence, it can be understood as “why do you make unlawful” or “why will you make unlawful.” Since the interrogative particle conveys an element of disapproval/denial (inkar), the verb actually signifies prohibition (nahy); that is, it means “do not do so, it is not good.”

The concept of “tahrim” (making unlawful) in the verse can be creedal, verbal, or practical. To deem what Allah has made unlawful as lawful, or what He has made lawful as unlawful, is unbelief (kufr) or a prohibited act; this also applies to the Prophet. The tahrim meant here is in the nature of an oath, whether practical or verbal. According to the Hanafi school, saying “may what is lawful be unlawful to me” is considered an oath; depending on the intention, the ruling of ila, zihar, or talaq (divorce) is applied. Al-Shafi'i, however, did not consider tahrim to be an oath, stating only that it requires expiation (kaffarah) with regard to wives. Different opinions have been transmitted from the Companions and the Successors (tabi'un).

In the second verse, the expression “Allah has ordained for you” appears. While the word “fard” here carries the meaning of an absolute obligation when used with “'ala”, when it comes with “lam” it means both “to ordain” and “to explain/clarify.” Muqatil interpreted this verse as “Allah has explained,” while others said “He has ordained”; both meanings are correct. Next, the word “tahillah” (tahlil) is explained: The lawful dissolution of an oath occurs either by fulfilling it properly, or by means of an exception (saying insha'Allah), or by breaking it and offering expiation. Although the Prophet's tahrim was related to an oath, the verse commands not the breaking of an oath, but its preservation. However, in oaths that are harmful, it is more virtuous to offer expiation and break them.

In the third verse, it is recounted that the Prophet confided a secret to one of his wives (Hafsah), and she disclosed this secret to another wife (Aishah). Allah informed His Prophet of this situation through revelation, and the Prophet confronted his wife with part of the secret while refraining from reproaching her with another part. Reports differ as to what this secret was: The most authentic report mentions the oath regarding honey syrup, another mentions the tahrim of Mariyah, and yet another mentions the glad tiding of the caliphate of Abu Bakr and Umar. Although harmonizing these reports does not seem possible, commentators of the Quran state that the primary incident was the Prophet's making ila from his wives (a month of seclusion) and the events that unfolded during this period.

In the continuation of the verse, it is emphasized that the Prophet sought the pleasure of his wives in the face of this incident. However, Allah informs His Prophet that it is not appropriate for him to make unlawful what He has made lawful for him merely to please his wives. This admonition is not a condemnation of the Prophet, but a cautionary reminder (tanbih) pointing to the loftiness of his station. Following this, the sentence “Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful” serves to alleviate the Prophet's sorrow and provide consolation. In conclusion, these verses offer important lessons regarding the safeguarding of family secrets, the importance of trust between husband and wife, and the responsibilities of the Prophet's wives.

In the commentary on the 4th verse, it is stated addressing Aishah and Hafsah, the wives of the Prophet (peace be upon him), that your hearts have swerved, meaning you fell short in sincerity toward the Prophet. If you repent, your hearts will be set right. Here, the word 'saghat' means inclining to one side. Commentators have stated that the particle 'fa' in the sentence indicates causation, and that the inclination is a deviation from the truth. Furthermore, the plural usage in the phrase 'your hearts' points to the Prophet's wives grouped into two sides: Aishah and Hafsah on one side, and Zaynab and the others on the other side.

In the 5th verse, the address is directed to all wives: 'Perhaps his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him wives in your place better than you.' The attributes of these better wives are listed as follows: Submitting to Allah (muslima), believing (mu'mina), steadfastly obedient (qanita), repenting (ta'iba), worshipping ('abida), fasting (saiha), previously married and virgins. The word 'sahat' (saihat) is a metonymy for fasting; for a fasting person resembles a traveler who has no provisions with them. The distinction between previously married and virgins recalls that among the Prophet's wives, only Aishah was taken as a virgin.

The 6th verse addresses all believers: 'O you who have believed! Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire.' The head of the family is responsible for directing his household toward Allah's commands. The fuel of that Hellfire is people and stones; over it are assigned harsh angels (zabaniyah) who do not disobey Allah's command. In the 7th verse, it is addressed to the disbelievers: 'Make no excuses today; you are only being recompensed for what you used to do.' This is in the context of encouraging believers to repent and orienting the Prophet against the disbelievers.

In the 8th verse, sincere repentance (tawbah nasuh) is commanded. The word 'nasuh' means either 'most pure and sincere' or 'most rectifying.' Nasuh repentance is to abandon sin purely because of its ugliness and to firmly resolve never to return to it. In the hadith, it is described as 'not returning to sin just as milk does not return to the udder.' According to Ali, there are six conditions of repentance: remorse, making up missed obligations, returning rights to their owners, seeking mutual forgiveness and clearing liabilities, firmly resolving never to return, and melting the ego through obedience. Allah conceals the sins of those who repent and admits them into Paradise; on that day, the light of the believers will run before them and on their right.

The 9th verse: 'O Prophet! Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them.' This verse is a warning against those who spread false rumors and caused corruption during the tahrim incident. While jihad against hypocrites is carried out by presenting proof and conveying the message, armed jihad is also commanded against disbelievers. In the 10th verse, Allah sets forth the wives of Noah and Lot as an example for those who disbelieve. Even though these two women were under the marriage bond of righteous prophets, they betrayed them; they disbelieved and leaked revelation secrets to the enemies. The betrayal here is hypocrisy in religion, not adultery.

In the 11th and 12th verses, good examples are presented to the believers: Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, prayed, 'My Lord! Build for me a house near You in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and the wrongdoers.' As for Mary (Maryam), she guarded her chastity, Allah breathed into her from His spirit, and she testified to the truth of the scriptures. These examples demonstrate that believing women can remain on the straight path even in an evil environment.

The wives of the prophets Noah and Lot failed to possess the faith and obedience demanded by the honor of being their wives; they inclined toward disbelief and ingratitude, causing harm to their husbands. They even betrayed their trust by conveying secret intelligence to the enemies of Allah. For this reason, they incurred the wrath of Allah, and not even their prophet husbands could save them from the punishment. This is a cautionary lesson for the disbelievers; everyone is accountable for their own deeds.

For those who believe, Allah gave Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, as an example. Despite Pharaoh's tyranny, Asiya believed and asked Allah to build for her a house in Paradise and to deliver her from Pharaoh and his evil deeds. Allah accepted her prayer, took her soul as a martyr, and raised her to the high stations of Paradise. This is glad tidings for righteous women who preserve their faith despite having a wicked husband.

Another example is Mary, the daughter of Imran. She guarded her chastity, and through the breathing of Allah's spirit, she became pregnant with Jesus. Mary affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures, persevered in worship, and was counted among the qanitin (the obedient). This shows that she attained an exalted station combining both female and male qualities.

The use of the pronouns in this ayah indicates that the Arabic word 'farj' is used metonymically (kinayah) and that the act of breathing was from above. Mary's preservation of her chastity and her belief in the words of Allah served as the means for her conceiving Jesus in an extraordinary manner. This is a miracle demonstrating Allah's power.

While Allah condemned the wives of Noah and Lot to Hell on account of their disbelief, He exalted Asiyah and Mary because of their faith and chastity. These examples are an instructive lesson for the believers and their families. Everyone will be recompensed according to their own deeds. This surah serves as a complement to Surah at-Talaq regarding family law and moral upbringing, and prepares the transition to Surah al-Mulk.

In the first verse of Surah al-Mulk, Allah's majesty and the fact that everything is in His dominion are emphasized. He possesses eternal perfection and is supreme above all things with His endless goodness and blessings. Dominion (mulk)—that is, disposal, creation, annihilation, governance, and punishment in the earth and the heavens, in this world and the Hereafter—is entirely in His hand of power. He gives dominion to whom He wills and takes it away from whom He wills; He has no partner and is powerful over all things.

In the second verse, the wisdom behind Allah's creation of death and life is explained: to test people and reveal which of them will do better deeds. Here, it is understood that death, like life, is a created entity. The majority of Ahl al-Sunnah scholars accept that death is not mere non-existence, but an occurrence pertaining to existence. Death is the opposite of life and a transition carrying human beings to another realm.

The mention of death before life reminds us that man came into life from non-existence, and will eventually die again and be resurrected. This emphasizes that the life of this world is transient and that the true life is the Hereafter. Death is a punishment for the disbelievers, whereas for the believers it is a gate of salvation and grace. The verse encourages people toward good deeds and reminds them of the recompense in the Hereafter.

At the conclusion of the test, it is declared that Allah is the Almighty (al-Aziz) and the All-Forgiving (al-Ghafur). He vanquishes those who do evil, elevates those who do good, and forgives those who repent. This verse shows that the purpose of the creation of human beings is to worship Allah and to know Him. This is also in harmony with the verse in Surah adh-Dhariyat: 'I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.'

In the third verse, the creation of the seven heavens is described. The number 'seven' can express both a specific count and multiplicity. These heavens encompass the orbits of the planets in the solar system and the realm of stars beyond them. The seven heavens are layers that can be counted when viewed from our earth; these layers are conceived as nested concentric circles.

According to modern astronomy, our earth is the first heaven, Mars (Merih) the second, Jupiter (Mushtari) the third, Saturn (Zuhal) the fourth, Uranus the fifth, Neptune the sixth, and beyond the Milky Way is the seventh heaven. This order demonstrates Allah's power and the order of the universe. The creation of the seven heavens and the earth reveals the magnificence of Allah's knowledge and power.

In Allah's dominion, the number seven holds great significance. For the concept of a physical body (jism), seven points must come together. The earth and sky are conceived as seven through the six directions and one central point. This is expressed in the verse: 'So turn your vision again: can you see any flaw?' (al-Mulk, 67:3). Through material sight, seven heavens are seen, but what lies beyond is grasped through reason and revelation.

From a spiritual perspective, there are seven windows in the human heart: the five senses, intellect and logic, inspiration and revelation. The spirit ascends and descends through these windows. Satan and the jinn, on the other hand, are evil forces that attempt to obstruct these spiritual currents. Through this realm of seven senses, human beings attain truth and attain faith.

Beyond the material heavens, there are spiritual heavens. Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Furthest Boundary) is the ultimate point situated in the sixth and seventh heavens. In the hadiths of the Ascension (Mi'raj), it is related that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) crossed the seven heavens both bodily and spiritually and reached the presence of Allah. This was an ascension accomplished with both body and soul.

Allah's Essence (Dhat) is transcendent above both the material and spiritual realms. Some look solely from a material viewpoint and imagine Allah as a physical body, while others look from a spiritual viewpoint and suppose Him to be a universal spirit. Both views are false. Allah's Essence encompasses all things and is exalted above everything. In His dominion, spirit and body are like two wings that testify to His existence.

The concept of a physical body is not limited to three dimensions. Four-, five-, six-, and seven-dimensional realms can be conceived. In this way, our realm may be envisioned as a point, and the other realms as higher dimensions. However, this line of thought carries the risk of causing one to lose oneself. The primary purpose is to grasp Allah's oneness and attain the truth.

These verses invite mankind to reflection (tafakkur) upon Allah's dominion. The harmony between the material and spiritual realms demonstrates Allah's power. Seeing the order in these realms, man ought to strengthen his faith and act with the consciousness of servitude. Indeed, in the continuation of Surah al-Mulk, Allah's mercy and power are recounted.

Elmalılı explains that moving beyond the three-dimensional physical realm is a mental exercise, and that in this way one delves into the spiritual realm. He states that the notion of a four-dimensional body consists merely of spiritual dimensions, and that in reality one leaves the physical realm and passes into the realm of imagination. He emphasizes that rather than limiting or increasing the conception of physical bodies to reach the Truth, rising to the encompassment of both realms is a firmer path.

Dwelling on whether a four-dimensional physical realm is possible, Elmalılı states that it may be hypothesized and imagined, but cannot be judged to exist in reality. Nevertheless, he expresses that this supposition is beneficial in prompting those accustomed to the physical realm to reflect on the expanse of the spiritual realm and the vastness of Allah's dominion. He adds that for consciousness to surrender to its Creator, it is sufficient for a person to be sensible of oneself and one's creation.

He notes that those who are conscious of their consciousness see the proof of the Creator in every consciousness and attain the secret of the verse: 'He is with you wherever you are' (al-Hadid, 57:4). He states that believers strive to increase their knowledge and deeds by recognizing the blessings in Allah's dominion, that understanding the physical realm in three dimensions is sufficient, and that upon stepping out of it, one enters the realm of spirituality. He emphasizes that it is possible to conceive the seven heavens as being in mutual conformity or layer upon layer, but that Allah's creation of seven heavens is certain.

He explains that the word tibaq can be a verbal noun (masdar) or a plural, and that most exegetes have preferred the meaning of mutabaqah (conformity). He explains with examples that the meaning 'layer upon layer' is also fitting, and that the planets and realms of perception exist in layers. In commenting on the verse, 'You see no disparity in the creation of the Most Merciful,' he indicates that tafawut means disparity and lack of order, and that Allah created the heavens in harmony as a manifestation of His mercy.

Explaining the word futur (fissure/cleft), Elmalılı indicates that the verse is not proof that the heaven cannot be cleaved; rather, cleaving is indeed possible, but Allah's power encompasses all things. Regarding the turning back of the gaze, he emphasizes the necessity of looking repeatedly, noting that the two perceptions of the eye are one. He gives the meanings of the words khasi'an and hasir: the former means driven away in humiliation or dazzled, while the latter means fatigued and exhausted. Through these expressions, he states that the gaze returns in bewilderment and impotence without being able to find any flaw in dominion, and that in this way a person will come to understand Allah's oneness and power and believe.

Addressing the subject of the lowest heaven (the nearest heaven), Elmalılı states that this expression is an adjectival phrase and that 'dunya' can mean the lowest or nearest heaven. He explains that it is the first of the seven heavens, beginning from the lunar orbit, but because it is adorned with stars, some commentators have interpreted this more broadly. Quoting the view of Baha' al-Din al-Amili, he notes that the claim that the stars are gathered within the lunar orbit is not necessary, and that meteors (shihabs / flaming projectiles) can fall from the stars. He expresses that the qualification 'dunya' in the verse does not mean that the lamps (masabih) belong solely to the first heaven, but perhaps points generally to the visible stars.

Elmalılı states that there are two views regarding what the lowest heaven is. The first view is that the lowest heaven is the lowest tier, being one of the seven heavens. The second view is that the lowest heaven is the celestial sphere seen from the earth that encompasses all the stars. Elmalılı says that the second view, preferred by verifying scholars, is more accurate. According to him, the lowest heaven is the inner surface of a sphere—what we call the sky—that accommodates everything we see within it, whose outer surface is known only to Allah. This view is compatible both with the apparent meaning of the ayah and with the hadiths.

Citing al-Alusi, he explains that the word 'masabih' is the plural of 'misbah', meaning lamp. It is debated whether calling stars lamps is metaphorical or literal. Elmalılı argues that calling stars lamps in terms of giving light is not metaphorical, and that they can be regarded as literal lamps. He also states that 'masabih' being brought in the indefinite form is for magnification (ta'zim)—that is, ordinary lamps are not intended, but great and precious lamps. He emphasizes that these lamps are stars that illuminate the surroundings at night like lanterns.

Comparing the views of ancient and modern astronomers, Elmalılı explains that ancient astronomers conceived of the heavens as solid spheres, whereas modern ones view them as bodies moving in space through gravitational forces. He expresses that Quranic verses (for instance, Ya-Sin 36/40, Ar-Rahman 55/7, and Ar-Ra'd 13/2) are understood more easily through modern astronomy, and therefore it is possible to understand the verses in their apparent meanings without needing strained interpretations. However, he adds that no science or philosophy can fully comprehend the sublime truths pointed to by the Quran, and that it is not right to restrict tafsir to the knowledge of a specific era.

Stating that the sources of human knowledge are the senses, reason, and true report, Elmalılı says that the senses do not deceive within their own domain, and that errors arise in reasoning when attributing things to causes beyond sensation. He gives the example of a ship passenger who supposes the shore to be moving; in reality, it is the ship that is moving, but through an error of reason, the shore is assumed to move. Similarly, he emphasizes that when interpreting the movements of celestial bodies, it may not be our senses, but our ideas that are mistaken. He explains that the visible sky is a domain that encompasses our senses, and that beyond this domain can be reached only through faith.

Elmalılı renders the meaning of the verse as follows: 'By My Majesty, We adorned that lowest heaven with material and spiritual lamps that delight eyes and hearts, and We made them missiles against devils.' Here, he notes that lamps can be understood both as material sources of light (stars) and as spiritual lights (knowledge and faith). He says that the primary purpose is for these lamps to awaken faith in hearts by pointing to divine power and beauty. He recalls that the matter of shooting at devils is also related to this spiritual dimension, and that stars are used to drive devils away.

In this section, two main meanings of the word 'rujum' are emphasized first. The first meaning signifies physical projectiles cast from the sky to drive devils away, namely flaming fires (shihabs). This is supported by verses found in Surah al-Hijr and Surah as-Saffat. Accordingly, devils cannot listen to the exalted assembly of angels; yet if they attempt to eavesdrop, they are pelted and driven away by a flame of fire that pursues them. What is important here is that it is noted that while this physical occurrence may be connected to spiritual events, this physical meaning is not the interpretation most fitting to the apparent meaning of the ayah.

The second meaning is that 'rujum' is a spiritual stoning. That is, the stars serve as spiritual projectiles against devils. Prophets, Companions, and scholars are likened to these spiritual projectiles. As also stated in Surah al-Jinn, after the Prophet (peace be upon him) was sent, jinn and devils could no longer approach the heaven. In this interpretation, devils encompass both devils among jinn and devils among humans. Human devils are those who deceive the public by casting stones into the unseen, such as astrologers and soothsayers. The verse encompasses both meanings; in the first, jinn devils are described, and in the second, human devils.

In this context, astrology (ahkam al-nujum), which attempts to derive decrees from the stars, is severely criticized. As Ibn Sina also stated, knowing the unseen belongs exclusively to Allah. It is not possible to derive definitive judgments concerning the future from the positions of stars, because events are formed not merely through celestial factors, but through the combination of many factors on earth. For this reason, the claims of astrologers consist mostly of falsehood. Islamic scholars have reached consensus that believing in the influence of the stars is disbelief and polytheism.

Then the verse describes the condition of the disbelievers in Hell. When they are cast into Hell, they hear its terrifying roar. Hell is almost bursting with rage. As each group is cast in, the keeper-angels (zabaniyah) ask them sternly: 'Did no warner come to you?' The disbelievers then confess the truth: 'Yes, a warner came to us, but we denied him and said, "Allah has not sent down anything; you are in nothing but great error."' Thus, they confess their own error.

This confession reveals the true nature of disbelief: not only denying the existence of Allah, but also not believing in His prophets, His scriptures, and His miracles is disbelief. The disbelievers, paying no heed to the warnings, condemned themselves to eternal punishment. Here, it is stated that those who say 'Allah has not sent down anything' are in fact deists who deny prophethood. The Quran is more exalted and protected than all divine scriptures; it has suffered no corruption whatsoever.

The polytheists characterized the Quran, which is the word of Allah, as a fabrication of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Yet the Quran rejected these claims of theirs and demanded that they produce the like of it. Even Western writers have admitted that the Prophet (peace be upon him) could not have founded such a moral and revolutionary religion. In his tafsir, Razi states that there are two possibilities regarding whether the expression 'You are in nothing but great error' is a word spoken by the disbelievers to the prophets or a word that the keepers of Hell will say to them. According to the preferred view, this is the word of the disbelievers, and 'dalal' denotes their error in this world or the destruction that is its consequence.

When the disbelievers are interrogated in Hellfire, they say: If only we had listened or reasoned, we would not have suffered punishment. According to them, there were three reasons for their falling into disbelief: not listening, not using their intellect, and being in a bad environment. Hearing and intellect are man's two most precious guides; those who do not use them are lower than animals. However, those who lack any capacity whatsoever are not held accountable. As for the disbelievers, because they possessed hearing and intellect yet failed to use them, they deserve the punishment.

The disbelievers confess their sins and realize that there is no deficiency in Allah's grace or justice. Allah has adorned the lowest heaven with lamps, sent down stars and verses, and tested people with glad tidings and warnings. (In verse 12) For those who revere their Lord unseen—that is, who guard themselves in sincere fear—there is forgiveness and a great reward. Those who do not fear until they see the punishment, or those who are hypocrites, are deprived of this.

Whether speech is secret or open makes no difference to Allah; He knows it all. He knows the innermost essence of all breasts. Does He who created not know? He is al-Latif (the Subtle, Most Kind) and al-Khabir (the All-Aware). Latif means exceedingly gracious or subtle; Khabir means aware of all things. According to al-Razi, these attributes belong to the Creator, and His creation is realized through knowledge and power. Created beings have nothing that is concealed from Him.

Allah made the earth subservient (zalul) for mankind. It is commanded to walk upon its shoulders (manakib). Commentators have offered different views regarding manakib: according to Qatadah, mountains and hills; according to al-Hasan, roads and sides; and according to al-Zamakhshari, this expression is a metonymy for the earth being so docile that it can be trodden like the shoulders of a camel. According to the most comprehensive view, manakib encompasses all parts of the earth—east, west, north, and south. This ayah encourages Muslims to study geography and other earth sciences and to make explorations.

The commands 'walk' and 'eat' in Surah al-Mulk, verse 15, have generally been interpreted by commentators as indicating permissibility (mubah). However, Elmalılı states that these commands are not merely permissible, but also convey a divine grace and a warning. When a person must secure their livelihood and eat enough to stay alive, these commands take on the status of an obligation (wajib). Moreover, the purpose of these actions is also essential; one must act without forgetting Allah, mindful of being called to account, and staying away from evil intentions. In this respect, the verse serves as both an individual and a social warning.

The commands 'walk' and 'eat' in the same verse encompass all kinds of beneficial endeavor in the struggle of life, such as working and earning, jihad, commerce, and agriculture. They also include such objectives as traveling the earth to take heed, acquiring knowledge, and seeking spiritual sustenance. These commands are primarily directed toward society, encouraging Muslims to hasten toward good deeds and to perform the best of works in the arena of trial. The word 'provision' in the phrase 'eat of His provision' encompasses not only material sustenance, but also spiritual blessings such as knowledge, pointing to the connection between the earth and the heavens.

There are three views concerning 'manakib' (shoulders) in the phrase 'walk upon its shoulders': the first is mountains and hills; the second is paths and sides; and the third is a metonymy for extreme submissiveness, as the most compliant part of a mount. Elmalılı states that the most comprehensive interpretation is 'all regions of the earth', which covers every direction—east, west, north, and south. In addition, this verse encourages the pursuit of sciences such as geography and the earth sciences.

Allah's making the earth 'zalul' (subservient) indicates that it is readily usable like a docile mount. 'Zalul' is distinct from 'zalil'; being zalul does not imply being humiliated or abased. Walking upon the shoulders of the earth expresses both physically walking upon the earth and advancing toward the sky by means of transport. This is a journey in which worldly and otherworldly purposes converge. In this journey, the believer must seek the pleasure of Allah and never forget that the final return is unto Him.

The expression 'Do you feel secure that He who is in the heaven...?' in verse 16 is a matter of discussion. While some maintain this refers to the angels, the majority hold the view that it refers to Allah. However, since Allah is free from any need for a physical body or a place, the expression 'the heaven' denotes absolute transcendence and supremacy. The scholars of the Salaf regarded this verse as mutashabih (allegorical) and did not venture into figurative interpretation (ta'wil), consigning its ultimate reality to Allah. Elmalılı notes that 'heaven' here does not signify a material body, but rather refers to the Exalted Being who is above all things.

The transcendence of Allah means that He is supreme over all things and nothing is like unto Him. The statement 'Allah is in heaven' indicates not that He is in need of space, but rather His absolute transcendence and that He is omnipresent and omniscient. This is in accord with the verse: 'He is the only God in the heavens and on earth' (al-An'am 6:3). Saying 'Allah is on earth,' however, is not permissible because it implies lowliness; whereas saying 'Allah is in heaven' is correct in the sense of grandeur and highness. Even so, it must not be understood that His Essence is contained within the heavens and the earth; He is the deity worshipped in the heavens and on the earth.

In verses 16–17, those who defy Allah's power are warned: Are the people walking upon the earth secure from His punishment? Allah could destroy them by shaking the earth beneath them or by sending a storm of stones upon them. Earlier nations (Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, Pharaoh, etc.) denied the messengers and suffered a terrible punishment. This is a lesson and warning for the deniers.

In verse 19, the state of the birds flying above them is brought to attention: none holds them as they fly with wings outspread and folded except the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). They move according to Allah's ordained system. In the same way, human beings, as they walk upon the earth, remain upright only by Allah's power. Lessons must be drawn from the birds, and the commands of Allah must be obeyed. No matter how high or far they fly, they cannot escape His forces.

In verse 21, the question is asked: 'Who is it that can provide for you if He withholds His provision?' If Allah were to cut off provision, no one could provide water, air, or food. Therefore, we must recognize that provision comes only from Allah, and we must work while offering gratitude to Him. The disbelievers, on the other hand, flee from the truth, veering away sideways in obstinacy.

In verse 22, the condition of one who walks fallen prone on his face is compared with that of one who walks upright on a straight path. Those who crawl face-down look only toward baseness and deviate into falsehood; those who walk upright follow the path of tawhid (divine unity). Man should not crawl like an animal; rather, he ought to walk on the straight path, within the bounds of morality and the Shariah, and build up and cultivate the earth.

In verse 23, it is emphasized that Allah has granted human beings hearing, sight, and hearts, and that they must listen, see, and reason with them. Sadly, people show little gratitude for these blessings and use them wrongfully. Yet these faculties were bestowed specifically to perceive Allah's warnings and to find the right path.

Allah has granted human beings senses such as hearing, sight, and hearts. These are His warning messengers. Through these faculties, people see, hear, and reflect upon Allah's signs. Most people, however, fail to fulfill their gratitude for these blessings and use them on wrongful paths. Had they listened and reasoned, they would have been saved from the punishment of Hell. Ears and eyes warn a person by signaling dangers from afar, whereas senses like touch and taste only perceive what is immediate, at which point it is already too late to protect oneself.

Allah is the One Who created people and spread them across the earth. He settles each of you in a place, multiplies you, and scatters you. In the end, all of you will be gathered into His presence. This promise of gathering is certain. Why, then, do you worship others and not turn to Him? If you were to heed His tidings and obey, you would understand that you cannot escape death and that you are in need of Him at every moment. It is then that you would turn your face to Him, fear Him alone, and be grateful to Him.

The disbelievers ask, 'When will this promise of gathering be fulfilled?' O Muhammad! Say: The knowledge of it is only with Allah. I am only a clear warner. Knowing its appointed time does not belong to me. I am only informing you that it will happen. This warning is to caution against the punishment of the Hereafter.

Say: Whether Allah destroys me and the believers with me or has mercy on us and grants us life, in either case there is none who can save the disbelievers from a painful punishment. As long as you do not believe, the death of the Prophet will bring you no benefit. The punishment is due to your disbelief and ingratitude. As for the believers, they do not fear death; they depart gladly to eternal life.

Say: The One Who grants us mercy is the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). We have believed in Him and in Him alone have we put our trust. Soon you will know who it is that is in clear misguidance. Consider: If your water were to sink into the ground, who could bring you flowing water? Only the Most Merciful can bring it. Therefore, those who rely on other than Him are in clear misguidance. We have believed in the Most Merciful, submitted to Him, and to Him we shall return.

The surah begins with the disjointed letter (huruf al-muqatta'at) "Nun". This letter is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses in the Quran; that is, its meaning cannot be fully known. The scholars of recitation (qira'ah) mostly recited this letter with izhar (clear pronunciation), while some recited it with idgham (assimilation), either with or without ghunnah (nasalization). The letter Nun, in terms of its script, is in the shape of a dot and a circle. This letter points to the source of speech and writing in human nature (fitrah) and emphasizes its value. The primary purpose here is to demonstrate human helplessness and to test those who are deeply rooted in knowledge.

The word Nun in Arabic also conveys meanings other than the familiar letter "nun". Among these are meanings such as "fish" (as in Prophet Jonah [Yunus] being called Dhu al-Nun), "inkwell", and the blade of a sword. According to an opinion narrated from Ibn Abbas, it is a great fish upon which the earth rests; this fish is called "Yahmut". In another narration, it is related that the first thing Allah created was the pen, then He created the Nun upon the water and spread the earth's crust over it.

These narrations point to the beginning of creation. First, the "Supreme Pen" (al-Qalam al-A'la) was created, and everything that would occur until the Day of Resurrection was written. Then matter was created, after which the heavens were formed from gaseous matter, and the terrestrial globe from its liquid state. This Nun at the center of the earth moves like a fish and causes earthquakes. As for the mountains, they were created to quell this motion, serving as pegs for the earth. These descriptions coincide with certain findings of modern geology.

Exegetes (mufassirun) have put forward differing views regarding whether the "Nun" here is a letter or a noun. Scholars like al-Zamakhshari stated that it is one of the disjointed letters of the alphabet and cannot be a noun because its ending does not take grammatical inflection (i'rab). Others, relying on narrations from Ibn Abbas, accepted that it means "fish" or "inkwell". After citing these disagreements, Elmalılı states that the most sound path is to accept this letter as ambiguous (mutashabih) and entrust its ultimate interpretation (ta'wil) to Allah.

The expression "Wal-Qalam" (By the pen) in the surah is also dwelt upon. The pen may be the divine pen that wrote the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or it may refer to the genus of pens used by human beings. The first created pen wrote everything that will take place until the Day of Resurrection. The human pen, on the other hand, is the foundation of knowledge and civilization. By teaching humanity to write with the pen, Allah bestowed a great blessing. This oath emphasizes the value of the pen and of writing.

In summary, the "Nun" at the beginning of the surah and the oath taken by it draw attention to the importance of creation and knowledge. This ambiguous letter prompts intellects to deep reflection. The pen, on the other hand, is a symbol of both divine power and human intellect. The surah, by stating that the Prophet (peace be upon him) is upon an exalted character, counsels him to have patience. This introduction serves as a preparation for the main themes of the surah.

The surah begins with an oath by "Nun" and the pen. What is meant by the pen here is the divine pen that writes the truth and what is right. The oath encompasses not only the pen, but also those who write and what is written. What does the writing is not the pen itself, but the beings endowed with intellect who use it; these are the angels or human consciousnesses. This oath is meant to emphasize that the Prophet (peace be upon him) is not mad and that he has been favored with divine blessings.

As the response to the oath, it is proclaimed to the Prophet (peace be upon him) that, by the grace of his Lord, he is not mad. He has been endowed with sublime qualities such as prophethood and intellect. Furthermore, it is stated that he is upon an unending reward and an exalted character. This exalted character is the etiquette of the Quran and divine morality; Aisha stated that the character of the Prophet was the Quran.

In the continuation, with the words "You will see, and they will see," it is indicated that it will become clear who is afflicted with madness. It is emphasized that your Lord knows best who has strayed from His path and who is rightly guided. For this reason, the Prophet (peace be upon him) is commanded not to obey the deniers. They wished for the Prophet to be lenient and to compromise, yet he never ceased to speak the truth.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) is asked not to obey individuals who possess certain vile traits: those who swear many oaths, the contemptible, slanderers, hinderers of good, sinful, coarse, and ignoble (zanim)... These qualities do not target a specific person alone, but generally address such people. They boast of having wealth and sons, yet they are morally base.

When the verses are recited to them, these wicked individuals say, "Fables of the ancients." Allah declares that He will brand their snouts (noses) to humiliate them. This is a punishment that will disgrace them in this world or in the Hereafter. Believers must not conform to such people, but should persevere on the path of truth with patience and good character.

Allah had given the deniers in Mecca wealth and children as a trial. This was a test for them. The Prophet (peace be upon him) prayed for the affliction of famine upon the tribe of Mudar; they were punished with a famine that lasted seven years. This verse transitions to the story of the owners of the garden: In Yemen, a righteous man had a vineyard; when he died, his children acted stingily and deprived the poor. They 'swore to harvest the garden in the morning, but did not make an exception (by saying insha'Allah).'

While they were asleep, Allah sent a calamity upon the garden, and by morning the garden was reduced to ashes. In the morning, they called out to one another, saying, 'Go early to harvest your produce.' As they went, they whispered secretly to each other, 'Let no poor person enter upon you today.' They acted with tyranny and greed.

When they reached the garden and saw it devastated, they said, 'We must have lost our way; rather, we are ruined.' The most moderate among them (awsat, meaning the most prudent and best), whose counsel had previously not been heeded, spoke up: 'Did I not tell you, why did you not glorify Allah? Exalt Allah above all deficiencies, uphold what is right, and make an exception (by saying insha'Allah)!' he said.

They repented in regret, saying, 'O our Lord, truly we were wrongdoers,' and turned in repentance. They began to reproach one another. They said, 'Perhaps our Lord will give us better than this in its place; indeed, we turn to Him.' Such is the punishment of this world; it awakens. Yet the punishment of the Hereafter is far greater; to be protected from it, one must believe beforehand.

For the righteous (the people of taqwa), there are Gardens of Delight (Na'im) with their Lord. Would We ever treat Muslims like criminals? Is it written in their book that 'whatever you choose shall be yours'? On the Day of Resurrection, matters will become severe, and they will be summoned to prostrate, but they will not be able to do so. I grant respite to the deniers; indeed, My plan is firm.

The Prophet is told to be patient and not to be like the companion of the fish (Jonah [Yunus]). He had prayed in anger, but the grace of his Lord reached him. When the disbelievers heard the Quran, they almost knocked you down with their eyes and said, 'He is indeed mad.' Yet the Quran is nothing but a reminder to all the worlds.

In verses 38–41, the polytheists' claim that "Whatever we desire shall be ours" is refuted. Allah has not granted His authority of judgment to anyone. There is neither a book nor a covenant supporting these claims of theirs. If there were such a rule, the tyrants and nations of the past would have remained in this world. Ask them: Which of you can guarantee the truth of this statement? Or do they have partners they associate with Allah? Then let them bring their partners; but they can never alter the truth.

The word "saq" mentioned in verse 42 literally means the shin or the origin of something. Here, it is a metaphor expressing the intensification of the decree of truth on the Day of Resurrection. In a hadith found in al-Bukhari and Muslim, it is narrated that on that day Allah will uncover His "saq" and the believers will fall down in prostration. This allegorical (mutashabih) expression has been interpreted as the uncovering of the truth and the mounting of terror. Scholars such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi have stated that this word is used to convey the severity and difficulty of calamity. It is not correct to derive any meaning that likens Allah to physical bodies.

In verse 43, it is related that on the Day of Resurrection the guilty will be called to prostrate, yet they will not be able to do so. While they were safe and sound in this world, they had been invited to prostrate, but they did not accept it. On that day, however, they will desire to prostrate, but will be unable to do so. This is a matter of profound regret and humiliation for them.

In verses 44–45, it is commanded to leave those who deny the Quran to Allah. They will be led to punishment gradually without realizing it; they will be granted a long respite, and then seized with a firm plan. This shows that what they deem to be good is in fact evil.

In verses 46–47, it is emphasized that the Prophet does not ask for a reward in return for conveying the message, and that they are not weighed down under debt. Knowledge of the unseen (ghayb) is not in their possession, nor is the pen that writes everything in their hands. Therefore, the judgments they render are false.

In verses 48–50, the Prophet is advised to be patient and not to be hasty like Jonah (Yunus, peace be upon him). Jonah departed from his people in anger and fell into the belly of the fish, but through Allah's mercy he was saved and became one of the righteous. This story teaches the importance of patience and of being content with Allah's decree.

Here, with reference to the story of the Prophet Jonah (Yunus), it is related that because of a momentary anger he was confined in the belly of the fish, but thanks to the blessing his Lord bestowed upon him, he was delivered and became a righteous servant.
