This indicates that everything occurs through the writing and decree of Allah, who knows the unseen; there is an order within His determination, and within this order, human beings have also been granted a certain authority.

States such as anger or patience depend on one end upon Allah's decree and on the other upon human will. Our Prophet (peace be upon him), the possessor of that magnificent character, is commanded not to show impatience like Jonah, but to bear the decree of his Lord with patience and continue his duty. He must look to the judgment of tomorrow and await what the sublime Pen has written in the unseen.

When the disbelievers heard the Quran, they would almost strike you down with their eyes. Out of their envy, they were as if ready to cast the evil eye upon you, wishing to destroy you through the malice of their sinister glances. Just as anger has an effect upon the body, the eyes likewise carry a good or bad influence depending on how they gaze.

Much has been said concerning the evil eye (nazar); some have denied it, while others have accepted it. However, without delving into details, let us state this: the evil eye is real, and, may Allah protect us, being conspicuous is dangerous. Allah makes a shield against the evil eye for those servants whom He wills to protect. The polytheists envied the beauty of the Quran and the Prophet's attaining it; they glared at him as if they would devour him, and then fell into contradiction by claiming, 'He is a madman.'

Yet the Quran does not belong to them alone; it is a reminder to all the worlds. Those endowed with pure intellect benefit from it, whereas those who are not bring harm upon themselves. In the end, they depart, groaning in anguish. Surah al-Qalam concludes, just as it began, with 'Nun'. May Allah, the Lord of the worlds, grant success in remembrance and reflection to those who write, read, and listen.

At the beginning of Surah al-Haqqah, the word "al-Haqqah," which is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection, is dwelt upon. Twelve different views have been transmitted regarding the meaning of this word. Among these are interpretations such as "the Hour whose occurrence is inevitable," "that which reveals the reality of things," and "the Day on which every deed is requited." However, all of them emphasize that al-Haqqah cannot be fully known through reason and contemplation, but can only be known through Allah's notification.

The question "What is that Haqqah?" is asked to demonstrate the magnitude and horror of the event. This question emphasizes the dreadfulness of al-Haqqah and expresses that it can only be made known by Allah, beyond the grasp of human intellect. For this reason, since the disbelievers cannot comprehend it with their intellects, they attempt to deny it.

The past nations that denied al-Haqqah are described. The peoples of Thamud and 'Ad denied "the striking calamity (al-Qari'ah)," that is, the tremendous event that strikes people. Thamud was destroyed by al-Taghiyah (the overwhelming cataclysm); as for 'Ad, they were annihilated by rih sarsar (a furiously howling, intensely cold gale). This storm was "husum," that is, an ill-omened wind that cut off their roots.

Those before Pharaoh and the people of Lot were punished in a similar manner. All of them denied the verses of Allah through wrongdoing (deliberately committing sin). Allah punished them with an increasingly overwhelming seizure. However, during the time of the Flood of Noah, He protected those who believed by carrying them in the floating Ark.

These events serve as a reminder and a lesson for people. Allah desires that these reminders be listened to and learned by attentive ears and that their requirements be fulfilled. Following this, the description of the Great Resurrection begins: the Trumpet (Sur) will be blown, the earth and mountains will be lifted and crushed against each other, and on that Day the Inevitable Event (al-Waqi'ah, the Resurrection) will take place.

Different interpretations have been made regarding the condition of the earth and the mountains. According to one view, the mountains fly into the air and turn into dust and smoke, and the earth becomes completely flat. According to another view, the earth breaks apart earlier, while the mountains melt and flow away. A third view is that both perish simultaneously and equally. In any case, on that Day everything undergoes transformation in order to appear before Allah.

On that Day, the heaven will be split apart with clouds, and the angels will descend in succession. The sun and the moon will be eclipsed, the stars will disappear, and the sky will take on a mournful and sorrowful state. (Al-Haqqah, 16)

In the continuation of the verse, it is stated that the angels are lined up in ranks at the split edges of the heaven. The term 'malak' (angel) mentioned here is a generic noun referring to all angels. Scholars have debated the difference between 'malak' (angel) and 'mala'ikah' (angels); some have said that 'malak' is more comprehensive, while others have stated that 'malak' is more specific than 'mala'ikah.' In conclusion, the use of 'malak' in the verse points to the angels charged with a special duty on that Day. (Al-Haqqah, 17)

On that Day, eight angels will bear the Throne ('Arsh). There are various narrations regarding the number, nature, and identity of these eight. In a hadith, it is reported that they are four today and will be eight on the Day of Resurrection. Since we do not possess definitive knowledge on this matter, the most correct approach is to say 'Allah knows best' and not exceed the bounds of what has been transmitted. (Al-Haqqah, 17)

On the Day of Resurrection, everyone will be presented before Allah to give account. This presentation is such an exposition that nothing hidden will remain. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) informed that people will be presented three times: in the first two, there will be dispute and presentation of excuses, and in the third, the record books of deeds will fly into hands. (Al-Haqqah, 18)

The believer who is given his book in his right hand says with joy, 'Here, read my book; for indeed, I knew that I would meet my account.' He leads a pleasing life in an elevated Paradise; its fruits hanging low, he eats and drinks as he pleases. These blessings are the reward for what they sent forth in the cause of Allah while in the world. (Al-Haqqah, 19-24)

Islaf is to offer and present beforehand with the return coming on credit; in commerce, it is called salaf or salam. In this verse, the expression "what you advanced" alludes to this transaction, to giving a goodly loan to Allah, and to the benefit derived from serving an elder. And this can be done not during times of hardship, but in unoccupied and opportune days, especially in the prime of youth. According to a narration, on that Day Allah will proclaim: "O My friends! In the world, I often looked upon you while your lips were parched with thirst in My way, your eyes sunken, and your bellies clinging to your loins. Today, eat and drink in return for what you offered and advanced in those bygone days."

The one who is given his book in his left hand says: "Ah, would that that first death had been the end of it all!" This wishing to die once more is not due to the pain of death, but because of the horror of the catastrophe he witnesses. He neither dies nor lives anymore; his wealth avails him nothing, and his dominion vanishes. This regret is for those who relied on power and wealth in this world and miscalculated their account. Indeed, Fana Khusraw, known by the title 'Adud al-Dawlah, went mad while boasting of being "ghallab al-qadar" (the overcomer of destiny) and constantly repeated these verses as he gave up his soul; in the end, he was crushed beneath the foot of destiny.

Allah the Almighty commands the angels of punishment (zabaniyah): "Seize him, shackle him, then cast him into the Blazing Fire (Jahim), then bind him in a chain seventy cubits long." Seventy cubits may be a metonym for great quantity, or it may indicate that it is far-fetched for those who do not believe until the age of seventy to ever reform. The reason for this punishment is two things: first, that person did not believe in Allah the Almighty; second, he did not encourage the feeding of the destitute. He did not look after the poor, did not offer aid, and was not even humble enough to be present at a meal with the poor.

On that Day, there will be for him neither a hamim (a close friend or cool water) nor any food, except for ghislin (a foul substance like purulent discharge). None eats this except the great sinners whose sole preoccupation is committing errors and crimes, especially those who associate partners with Allah. This recalls the end of deniers such as Pharaoh and the people of Lot.

Then Allah swears by what you see and what you do not see, declaring that the Quran is the word brought by an honorable messenger. Here, attention is drawn to the error of positivists and sophists; believing only in what is seen and denying what is unseen is a grave mistake. Yet experience demonstrates that what lies beyond the visible also exists. Knowledge obtained through reliable transmission, especially revelation coming from a trustworthy messenger, conveys realities that lie beyond reason and empirical experience.

The Quran is not the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor is it the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect! It is a revelation sent down from the Lord of the worlds. If the Prophet had attempted to fabricate any sayings falsely attributed to Allah, Allah would have seized him by the right hand and severed his aorta; then none of you could have shielded him.

The Quran is an unforgettable reminder for the righteous (people of taqwa). Nevertheless, Allah knows that there are deniers among you. It is indeed a source of regret for the disbelievers; truly, it is knowledge beyond any doubt. So glorify the magnificent name of your Lord.

In the 43rd verse of Surah al-Haqqah, Allah states that the Quran has been sent down from Allah the Almighty, the Lord of all the worlds. In previous verses, it was said, "It is the word of an honorable messenger"; here, it is emphasized that both the meaning and the words of the Quran were revealed by Allah. Thus, the misconception that it is the messenger's own speech is prevented.

In verses 44–45, it is stated that if the messenger had fabricated lies in the name of Allah, Allah would seize and punish him. The word 'yamin' can be interpreted either as the oaths sworn by the prophet or as the power of Allah. In any case, it is related that the messenger who swears falsely would be disgraced.

Verses 46–47 explain the extent of this punishment: Allah cuts the aorta (or spinal cord) of the liar, meaning He destroys him. At that point, no one can save him. Yet the reality is that the messenger is a trustworthy prophet, far removed from falsehood, and the Quran has truly been sent down from Allah.

Verses 48–50 touch upon the wisdoms of the Quran: It is an admonition and a reminder for the people of taqwa (the God-conscious). However, there are deniers among us; they will face their punishment. The Quran is a source of bitter regret for the disbelievers; on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the reward of the people of taqwa, they will feel boundless remorse.

Verse 51 declares that the Quran is haqqu'l-yaqin (absolute certainty), meaning there is no doubt whatsoever about its reality. It possesses a higher degree of certainty than 'ilmu'l-yaqin (certainty by knowledge) and 'aynu'l-yaqin (certainty by sight). In the final verse, the messenger is commanded to glorify the exalted name of his Lord.

The word 'sa'il' mentioned in the first verse means asking, inquiring, or flowing. There are three views regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse. According to the first, Nadr ibn al-Harith said, 'O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky,' whereupon this verse was revealed. According to the second view, the polytheists said to one another, 'Ask Muhammad, for whom is this punishment?' According to the third view, the Prophet (peace be upon him) asked for swift punishment, and Allah commanded him to be patient. The first view is considered more sound.

In the second and third verses, it is emphasized that the punishment is for the disbelievers and that it comes from Allah. The word 'ma'arij' means instruments of ascent, stairs, or degrees. Commentators have interpreted this word in four ways: the first is the heavens and high degrees; the second is virtues and blessings; the third is ranks in Paradise; and the fourth is spiritual and immaterial ranks. According to this last interpretation, ma'arij refers to the ranks to which angels and souls ascend.

In the fourth verse, it is stated that the angels and the Spirit (Gabriel) ascend to Allah. This ascent takes place in a day the measure of which is fifty thousand years. Some scholars have said that this day is the Day of Resurrection, which will be long and distressing for the disbelievers and light for the believers. Here, by the Spirit, Gabriel (peace be upon him) is predominantly understood.

Beginning with the fifth verse, gracious patience is commanded to the Prophet (peace be upon him). While the disbelievers consider the punishment distant, Allah sees it as near. On that Day, the sky will be like molten metal, and the mountains will be like tufts of colored wool. A person will abandon his closest relatives (his brother, his mother, and his father), and everyone will be preoccupied with their own plight. In the fifteenth verse, 'laza' (blazing fire), and in the sixteenth verse, 'shawa' (stripping away skins), are described as attributes of Hell.

In the twentieth and twenty-first verses, it is stated that man is 'halu'' (fretful): when evil touches him, he is fretful, and when good touches him, he is stingy and withholds good. Only the believers who perform prayer are exempted from this bad disposition. They are described with seven qualities: they are constant in their prayers; there is a recognized right (zakah) in their wealth; they affirm the Day of Recompense; they fear the punishment of their Lord; they guard their chastity; they are faithful to their trusts and covenants; and they are upright in their testimonies. These qualities render them worthy of Paradise.

Almighty Allah states, as the eighth characteristic of the believers, that 'they guard their prayers.' Commentators have explained the difference between being constant in prayer and guarding prayer as follows: the expression 'they are constant in their prayers' signifies never abandoning prayer at any time, whereas the expression 'they guard their prayers' signifies performing it in the most perfect manner by paying meticulous attention to what must be observed before, during, and after prayer. The matters before prayer are paying attention to the times, ablution, cleanliness, covering the 'awrah, seeking the qiblah, clean clothing and place, congregational prayer and mosques, and purifying the heart from misgivings to attain humility (khushu'). While performing prayer, one should contemplate that prayer is an ascension (mi'raj), and recite and remember Allah with presence of heart without turning right or left. The matters after prayer are abstaining from idle talk and sin. Alongside these, remaining ready for sentinel duties and jihad with the awareness that a secure Islamic homeland and society are necessary so that prayer does not become a 'fear prayer' and subject to enemy attack is also part of guarding prayer. Indeed, in Surah at-Tawbah (9:18), it is stated that only those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakah, and fear none but Allah shall maintain the mosques. This eighth characteristic demonstrates that in Islam, social order, public security, governance, and military affairs are connected to the objective of guarding prayer. Even though the command to fight had not yet been revealed in Mecca, these principles were in the preparatory stage.

It is seen that the beginning and end of these eight qualities are framed by prayer, all of them are summarized as attributes of the person who performs prayer, and it is thus explained that prayer is the pillar of religion. In verse 35, by the statement 'These will be honored in gardens,' it is indicated that these eight traits correspond to the eight gates of Paradise.

In verses 36–39, the state of the deniers is described. The polytheists were gathering around the Prophet (peace be upon him) in circles and separate groups, mocking what he said and declaring, 'If these people enter Paradise as Muhammad says, we shall enter before them.' Thereupon, these verses were revealed. The expression 'in separate groups' means divided and scattered, each belonging to a faction. Allah asks whether each one of them expects to be admitted into a Garden of Delight; nay, He states that He created them from what they know (from a sperm-drop).

In verses 40–44, Allah swears by the Lord of the easts and the wests, declaring that He is able to replace them with others better than them, and that no one can outstrip Him. So let them converse vainly and amuse themselves until they meet their Day which they are promised (the Day of Resurrection). On that Day, they will emerge swiftly from the graves, rushing as though they were racing toward idols, with their eyes cast down, disgrace covering them. That is the Day they were promised.

Surah al-Ma'arij concludes with a warning, explaining that Allah has the power to change things belonging to the future, as described in the verse of Surah al-Haqqah (69:38–39): 'So I swear by what you see and what you do not see...' Surah Nuh will follow in order to explain this power through an example seen in the past. The word translated as 'separate groups' in the verses is the plural of 'izah' and derives from the root 'azw,' meaning 'to be affiliated with.' These warnings against the mocking attitude of the polytheists serve as a reminder of Allah's omnipotence and the fate of the deniers.

At the beginning of Surah Nuh, it is stated that the word Nuh is not Arabic, but means "calm" (sakin) in Syriac. Although some reports state that Noah's actual name was Abdulghaffar and that he was called Nuh because he wept excessively, this is not authentic. According to the famous report, Noah's lineage is Ibn Melek b. Methuselah b. Ahnukh. Ahnukh is the name of Idris (peace be upon him). According to this, Noah came after Idris; however, some Companions stated that Noah came before Idris.

It is reported that there were approximately one thousand years between Adam and Noah. However, the fact that the people of Noah possessed an industry advanced enough to fashion idols (Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, Nasr) raises doubts regarding the brevity of this period. This circumstance brings to mind the possibility that the dating regarding Adam's creation may be inaccurate, or that the Adam referred to here might not be the father of humanity. Elmalılı states that nothing definitive can be said on this matter, and that only Allah knows.

Since it is stated in the ayah, "We sent [him] to his people," Noah was sent as a prophet not to all mankind, but only to his own people. The distinction of being sent to all humanity belongs exclusively to our Prophet (peace be upon him). Although it is not known with certainty where the people of Noah lived, it is reported that they were in the region of Kufa in Iraq. In light of this information, it can be understood that the Deluge of Noah also did not encompass the entire world, but only the region where that people lived. Al-Alusi also favored this view.

There are differing views regarding the universality of the Deluge. The Zoroastrians (Majus) do not acknowledge the Deluge; some say it occurred only in the region of Babylon. Countries such as India, Persia, and China do not accept the Deluge. What is correct is that everyone living on earth is descended from Noah's children. Indeed, it is stated in Surah as-Saffat: "And We made his descendants the survivors."

Regarding the forgiveness of sins, it is stated that past sins are wiped away by Islam. As for the rights of fellow human beings (kul hakkı), they can only be pardoned by obtaining their consent and settling the grievance. The expression in the verse, "and delay you until a specified term," is contingent upon the condition of faith and worship. When the term decreed by Allah arrives, it cannot be postponed; however, before it arrives, it may be delayed due to certain causes. Although this may appear contradictory at first glance, what is actually postponed is the person himself, not the appointed term.

According to al-Zamakhshari, Allah decreed that if the people of Noah believed, their lifespan would be a thousand years, and if they disbelieved, nine hundred years. In this case, the expression "that He may delay you" indicates that upon believing, they would be granted life until the furthest appointed term. Other commentators have supported this view, yet they stated that in reality the appointed term is one, though two different possibilities exist. Ibn 'Atiyyah, on the other hand, criticized the Mu'tazilite concept of two appointed terms, stating that the verse serves as no evidence for their claim.

Although saying 'that He may delay you' on the one hand while stating 'when it arrives, it cannot be postponed' on the other might appear at first glance to be a contradiction, upon deeper reflection it becomes clear that there is no contradiction. For the expression 'that He may delay you' means delaying people, not the appointed term itself. That is, you are granted respite and forgiven until the appointed term, whereas the term itself is never postponed. For this reason, there is no contradiction; one must prepare before the appointed term arrives.

The appointed term may be delayed through causes such as faith and obedience to Allah. However, once the decreed term arrives, it is no longer possible for it to be postponed. In this case, by believing and performing righteous deeds before the appointed term arrives, it may be possible to reach that longer term. Otherwise, the shorter term comes upon one, and there is no deliverance.

Al-Zamakhshari offers the following interpretation on this matter: Almighty Allah decreed that if the people of Noah believed, their lifespan would be a thousand years, but if they persisted in disbelief, they would be destroyed at nine hundred years. According to this decree, those who believe attain the furthest specified term, while those who disbelieve are doomed to the shorter term. Al-Razi also adopted the same view.

Al-Qadi, Abu al-Su'ud, and al-Alusi, in addition to this interpretation, state that the term which cannot be postponed is not only the specified term (ajal musamma); rather, neither of the two terms can be postponed once it arrives. According to them, the expression in the verse, 'when the term of Allah arrives, it cannot be postponed,' pertains to the shorter term in the event that one does not believe. For if you do not worship, you will not be delayed until the longer term; your shorter term will arrive, and that, too, cannot be postponed.

What is understood from these views is that the appointed term has two phases: The first is the phase of possibility, which can lengthen or shorten depending on causes according to the nature of things. The second is the phase of the term that actually occurs, in which no one has two terms. Divine decree encompasses the true term known in pre-eternity that will inevitably come to pass. However, before this appointed term occurs, none knows it except Allah.

In his tafsir, Ibn 'Atiyyah states that the verse has been cited as evidence for the Mu'tazilite claim that 'man has two appointed terms,' yet there is nothing in the verse to support their position. For Noah (peace be upon him) did not know whether their term would be postponed or not; he was merely promising that if they believed, they would attain a long term. As for Allah, by virtue of His pre-eternal judgment, He decreed a long term for those who believe and a short term for those who disbelieve. In conclusion, faith and worship are prerequisites for the forgiveness of sins and for attaining the specified term (ajal musamma); the respite granted must be seized as an opportunity.

Allah's forgiveness of past sins is possible through a person's entry into Islam. For Islam severs the disbelief and sins committed prior to it. However, regarding sins related to the rights of fellow human beings (kul hakkı), Allah's forgiveness is contingent upon reconciling with and obtaining the consent of the rightful parties.

The expression in the verse, "that He may delay you until a specified term," demonstrates that the term decreed by Allah cannot be postponed once it arrives, yet before it arrives, lifespan can be lengthened through faith and righteous deeds. The apparent contradiction is resolved by the fact that what is postponed is not the appointed term, but the individuals themselves: a person is delayed and forgiven until the appointed term—that is, he attains the term.

Among the commentators, al-Zamakhshari states that Allah decreed two conditional terms for the people of Noah: one thousand years if they believed, and nine hundred years if they remained in disbelief. Scholars such as al-Razi, al-Qadi, Abu al-Su'ud, and al-Alusi state that in reality the appointed term is one, but before it occurs, different possibilities exist. Ibn 'Atiyyah, however, rejects the Mu'tazilites taking this verse as evidence for two appointed terms, for Noah (peace be upon him) did not know whether their terms would be postponed or not.

The word "waqar" in the verse, "Why do you not expect majesty from Allah?" has been interpreted either as a warning in the sense of not fearing Allah's greatness, or as an encouragement in the sense of not expecting honor and dignity from Allah. Subsequently, it is stated that Allah created man in stages: first from the basic elements, then foodstuffs, then sperm-drop, embryo, a lump of flesh, bones, and finally fashioned him into an entirely different creation.

It is recounted that Allah created the seven heavens in tiers, made the moon a light and the sun a lamp, made man grow from the earth like a plant, and will then return him to the earth and bring him forth anew. The word "nabatan" is construed as an absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq); this points to the wondrous and extraordinary manner of growth in man's creation. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi stated that this phrasing is more suited to grasping Allah's power through reason.

Noah complains to his Lord, stating that his people have rebelled against him and followed an oppressor whose wealth and children have only increased him in ruin. This person was one of the notables of the people of Noah who incited the populace against Noah.

The notables of the people urged the public to remain devoted to their idols, telling them not to abandon the idols named Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, and Nasr. These idols were the greatest entities worshipped by the people, and there was a difference of degree among them. Noah notes that these idols have led many astray and asks Allah to increase the confusion of the wrongdoers.

Exegetes explain that these idols were originally the names of righteous individuals, and that after their deaths, statues were erected at the instigation of Satan and over time turned into idols. For instance, while Wadd was a beloved Muslim among his people, after his death Satan deceived the people by fashioning an image of him, and generations later this image came to be worshipped. Al-Alusi states that the view of the idols being in human form is more sound.

Noah prays for the destruction of his people: "Do not leave a single one of the disbelievers upon the earth. For if You leave them, they will lead Your servants astray and will beget only immoral, ungrateful disbelievers." He then seeks forgiveness for himself, his parents, whoever enters his house as a believer, and all believing men and women, and asks that the destruction of the wrongdoers be increased.

Upon these prayers, the people were drowned on account of their sins and then cast into the Fire. This has been interpreted as the punishment of the Barzakh (the intermediate realm). There is an eloquent expression in mentioning water and fire together. Noah's prayer encompasses not only that community but also subsequent wrongdoers, while the believers seek forgiveness.

Following Noah's prayer, those in the ark came ashore in safety, and believing generations spread across the earth. However, there would also be communities of wrongdoers in the future; though they may enjoy worldly provisions for a time, they will ultimately suffer a painful punishment. This opens the door to Surah al-Jinn with a transition to the jinn, who do not belong to the lineage of Adam and Noah.

At the beginning of this surah, it is recounted that the jinn listened to the Quran and believed. The word 'nafar' denotes between three and ten individuals, yet it can also be used for a greater number. Since it is also used for the jinn, it is not exclusive to human beings. The verb 'we listened' mentioned in the verse is passive and is read with an upper vowel mark (fathah) in the recitations. The sentence 'They said: Indeed, we' is read with a kasrah, because it indicates reported speech.

The word 'hidayah' means the truth and the upright path. The connection between the verses varies according to the differences in recitations. While in some recitations it is connected to 'we heard', in the Hafs recitation it is read with a fathah, yielding the meaning 'we believed in it'. In the expression 'Exalted is the majesty of our Lord', 'jadd' means greatness, glory, and sublimity. Here, Allah's sublime attribute is intended. The expression 'our foolish one' describes the rebellious jinn or Iblis; 'shatat', on the other hand, means exceeding the boundary and swerving from the truth.

Certain individuals among humankind used to take refuge in certain individuals among the jinn. This seeking of refuge took place through practices such as talismans and incantations. The word 'rijal' (men) is used here for males of both humankind and jinn. According to the majority of scholars, this demonstrates that the jinn also consist of males and females. The word 'rahaq' conveys meanings such as covering, frivolousness, and transgression; humans seeking refuge in the jinn increased the jinn's arrogance and transgression.

The jinn had assumed that Allah would never send a messenger. However, when they probed the heaven, they found it filled with formidable guards and flaming fires. 'Shihab' means a flame of fire. These flames prevented the jinn from eavesdropping on tidings of the unseen. In reality, this symbolizes the light of the Quran and prophethood obliterating falsehood. Through this occurrence, the jinn realized that Allah may send a messenger to whomever He wills.

The jinn said: 'We do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether good is willed for them.' They admitted that there were righteous and base individuals among them, and that they were divided into distinct factions. They recognized that they could never frustrate Allah nor flee from Him. They listened to the Quran and believed; whoever believes will neither be wronged of their due nor fall into humiliation. Those who submit as Muslims are worthy of goodness, while the deviators are deserving of Hell.

Allah declares: 'If humans and jinn had remained steadfast on the upright path, We would have provided them with abundant sustenance. This is a trial. Whoever turns away from the remembrance of their Lord, He will thrust into an arduous punishment.' 'The places of worship (masajid) belong to Allah; so do not supplicate anyone alongside Him.' Masajid signifies sanctuaries. Some scholars have interpreted this as the entire earth or the places of prostration. Allah commands that worship be devoted exclusively to Him.

When the servant of Allah (the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him) stood up supplicating to Him, the jinn or the polytheists crowded around him so densely that they were almost pressing into one another. The Prophet was instructed: 'Say: I pray only to my Lord and associate no partner with Him. I possess no power to cause you harm or benefit; I only convey the messages and embassies of Allah. Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, the fire of Hell belongs to them. I do not know whether that which is promised is near or far; only Allah knows the unseen. He discloses His unseen to no one except His chosen messengers.'

Allah Almighty commands His Prophet: Say, no one can protect me from Allah. That is to say, there is no power that can shield against the punishment of Allah. If I were to associate partners with Allah or supplicate to other than Him, neither human, nor jinn, nor angel could save me. For this reason, I supplicate only to Allah, and there is no sanctuary besides Him. Nor should you fear me or anyone else; fear only your Lord and take refuge in Him. This verse might lead one to presume that it is impermissible to place any hope in or ask anything of the Prophet; however, if this judgment is passed without taking the exception into account, it would be mistaken. Indeed, although the Wahhabis considered taking the Prophet as a means of mediation (wasilah) to be associating partners with Allah, this is not correct.

In verse 23, an exception is introduced: "Except for notification from Allah and His messages." This is an exception to the preceding statement, "I possess no power to cause you harm or guide you of my own accord." That is to say, the Prophet can do nothing of his own accord; rather, he is charged with conveying Allah's commandments. This is precisely what is expected of the Prophet. At the same time, he serves as a means for the supplication of the servants, for Allah has commanded, "Pray for them, so that it may bring peace to their hearts." Just as believers are not forbidden from requesting supplication from one another, asking for supplication from the Prophet is not forbidden either. This exception has conferred great honor and authority upon the Prophet.

For those who disobey Allah and His Messenger, there is the fire of Hell, wherein they will abide eternally. This warning encompasses those who disbelieve by associating partners with Allah. In verse 24, it is stated that when they behold the punishment promised to them, they will come to know who is weaker in supporters and fewer in number. On that day, the rebellious among humans and jinn, who deemed themselves mighty and numerous, will see how feeble they truly are. In verse 25, when asked when that punishment will come, the Prophet answers: "Without a notification from my Lord, I cannot know. Whether that which is promised to you is near or far is not known; the knowledge thereof is solely with Allah."

Allah knows the entirety of the unseen (ghayb). The unseen denotes that which is not present to sensory perception or acquired knowledge. The absolute unseen cannot be known by any created being; however, Allah discloses aspects of His unseen to those messengers whom He chooses. This disclosure pertains to the proofs of messendership, legal rulings, and sanctions. The messenger knows only what has been disclosed to him; he does not know the absolute unseen. Matters such as the timing of the Hour are exclusively within the knowledge of Allah. When Allah reveals His unseen, He posts guardian angels before and behind His messenger to protect him, thereby preventing the jinn and devils from interfering with the revelation. They are driven away with flaming meteors (shihab); this is a miracle exclusive to the prophethood of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).

The reason Allah posts these guardian watchers is so that the messenger may know with certainty (yaqin) that the revelation reaching him is truly from Allah. Thus, the messenger realizes that he has conveyed the word of his Lord precisely as it is, and that Allah encompasses all things in His knowledge. Following the elucidations concerning "what you see and what you do not see" sworn to in Surah al-Haqqah, and after describing the Prophet's sublime character and the manner in which revelation descends, this surah will continue with Surah al-Muzzammil.

The word al-Muzzammil means 'the one wrapped up, the one shrouded.' This title was given because the Prophet (peace be upon him), frightened by the intensity of the revelation he received in the cave of Hira, lay down saying to his wife, 'Cover me, cover me.' Some scholars, however, stated that this title means the one who bears the burden of prophethood. According to Ikrima, al-muzzammil, derived from the root 'ziml', means 'the bearer of a heavy load' and indicates that the Prophet took upon himself this heavy duty.

Allah's address, 'O you wrapped up!' is, according to some exegetes, a severe warning, while according to others, it is an affectionate gesture and an encouragement. According to what Abu Hayyan narrated from al-Suhayli, the Arabs, in order to comfort someone without reproach, would address them with an adjective describing their current state. For this reason, the address takes into account the state the Prophet was in, aiming to awaken him and prepare him for his duty.

The night prayer (qiyam al-layl) is commanded in this surah. In the initial period, this prayer was made obligatory for the Prophet and his Companions, but it was later lightened. Regarding the duration, an option was offered in the verse by saying 'half the night, or a little less than that, or a little more.' This flexibility provides the possibility of making adjustments according to the length of the nights and the strength of the individual.

Reciting the Quran with tartil is commanded. Tartil is to recite by giving each letter its due, distinctly, properly, and reflecting upon the meaning. This encompasses reciting in accordance with the rules of tajwid, with a slow or moderate cadence. The primary goal is to understand the Quran and act upon it. Rising at night and reciting with tartil serves as a preparation for the heavy responsibilities to come.

In the verse, it is stated: 'We shall send down upon you a heavy word.' This word is the Quran and the duty of prophethood. Just as the descent of revelation was materially heavy, implementing the rulings it contains is also arduous. Night worship is a training to grant the endurance to withstand this heavy duty. The tranquility of the night allows the heart to be more sincere and attentive; for this reason, it has been said that 'the rising by night is more potent and more upright for recitation.'

The Prophet was commanded to remember his Lord and dedicate himself completely to Him, detached from everything else (tabattul). Tabattul is detaching oneself from worldly occupations and concentrating on worshiping Allah. Afterwards, he was asked to place his trust in Allah, the Lord of the East and the West, to be patient with the disbelievers, and to depart from them in a graceful manner. This signifies a period of patience and forbearance that applied before the command to fight.

At the end of the surah, the severe punishments prepared for the disbelievers are described: ankal (fetters), jahim (blazing fire), food that chokes, and a painful punishment. Al-Razi interpreted these punishments both physically and spiritually. In the spiritual interpretation, the soul's entanglement in worldly attachments is considered ankal, the pain of being deprived of these attachments is jahim, and being deprived of the divine light is regarded as the greatest punishment.

In the fourteenth verse, it is recounted that on the Day of Resurrection the earth and the mountains will shake, the mountains will become a heap of poured-out sand, and the surface of the earth will be leveled flat. In this transformation, there is an indication that especially the great mountains will be demolished.

From the fifteenth verse onward, the address turns toward the disbelievers. Allah informs them that He has sent them a messenger. This messenger will be a witness over what they do. An analogy is drawn with the messenger sent to Pharaoh (Moses [Musa]). There are three meanings in this comparison: First, to clarify that this is the messenger foretold in the Torah addressing Moses regarding the final prophet; second, to indicate that the polytheists of Mecca are oppressors like Pharaoh; and third, to explain the ultimate outcome by recalling that Pharaoh was dreadfully punished when he rebelled.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth verses, it is asked how the disbelievers will protect themselves from that terrible day. From the dread of that day, the sky will crack, and children will turn into gray-haired elders. The nineteenth verse states that these warnings are a reminder, and whoever wills may take a path to his Lord.

The twentieth verse is the verse upon which there is consensus that the command to rise at night given at the beginning of the surah was lightened and modified. According to a narration from Aisha, this verse was revealed eight months after the initial command, turning the night prayer from obligatory (fard) into supererogatory (nafl). According to a narration from Ibn Abbas, however, this command, which had become difficult for the believers, was lightened after one year. There are similar narrations from Qatada and Hasan as well. In some narrations, it is reported that the Prophet worshiped in this manner for ten years, after which it was lightened.

There is disagreement over whether this verse was revealed in Mecca or Medina. The mention of subjects such as zakah and jihad has been considered evidence that it was revealed in Medina. However, taking into account that zakah was also made obligatory in Mecca, whereas permission for warfare was granted in Medina, the view that at least a portion of this verse may have been revealed in Medina outweighs the other. In conclusion, this verse lightened the duration of night worship, and after the five daily prayers were made obligatory, the obligation of the tahajjud prayer was converted into a supererogatory act.

Regarding the expression 'recite what is easy of the Quran' in the verse, there are three matters: First, is the intent of recitation (qira'ah) the prayer, or merely reciting the Quran? The majority holds the view that the prayer is meant here. Second, the ruling expressed by this command: whether it denotes obligation (wujub/fard) or recommendation (nadb/mustahabb) is disputed. Third is the quantity of the phrase 'what is easy.' While some say at least fifty verses, narrations from al-Imam al-A'zam state that at least one short verse or three short verses must be recited. Imam Malik and al-Shafi'i, on the other hand, stated that reciting Surah al-Fatihah is obligatory. In the continuation of the verse, establishing the prayer, giving zakah, lending Allah a goodly loan (infaq) are commanded, and seeking forgiveness from Allah is recommended.

Surah al-Muddaththir begins with an address meaning "the one enveloped in his cloak." This word is originally "mutadaththir," meaning one who wraps himself in an outer garment (dithar). It is narrated that the cloak the Prophet wrapped himself in was made of velvet. According to 'Ikrimah, this means the one enveloped in prophethood and spiritual perfections. This address conveys that the time for sleep and comfort has passed, and that the time has come to awaken, proclaim the truth, and endure hardships. Verse 2 contains the command "arise and warn," while verse 3 contains the command "and magnify your Lord." According to a narration, when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah said "Allahu akbar," and Khadijah also rejoiced by uttering the takbir. The letter "fa" signifies attachment to the preceding command.

In verse 4, the command "keep your garments clean" encompasses both physical and spiritual cleanliness. The word "thiyab" (garments) here has been interpreted as a metaphor for the soul, the heart, or moral character. Furthermore, it is also noted that "thiyab" denotes the community that surrounds a person, which points to the verse "and warn your nearest kinsfolk." In verse 5, "rujz" or "rijz" means impurity and punishment, as well as idols and statues. In verse 6, "do not confer favor" is explained in two ways: reproaching someone with a favor, or doing good while expecting something in return. Verse 7 gives the command "and for your Lord, be patient."

Verses 8–10 describe the blowing of the Trumpet: "When the horn is blown, that day will be a difficult day for the disbelievers." Naqur means horn. The difficulty of that day is a hardship that steadily increases and never becomes easy. Verses 11–17 contain a warning specifically concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah: "Leave Me with him whom I created alone." He was granted abundant wealth, sons present by his side, and vast means, yet he desired even more. Saying "Nay!" Allah declares that He will drive him up a steep ascent (Sa'ud). Sa'ud is a mountain of fire in Hell; the disbeliever climbs it for seventy years and then falls.

Verses 18–25 describe Walid's obstinate attitude: He thought and plotted, frowned and scowled, turned his back and waxed proud. Concerning the Quran, he said it was "magic handed down from of old" or "dazzling magic." According to the details of the incident, Walid listened to the Quran from the Prophet and was moved, but under pressure from Quraysh, he rejected it. He reached his verdict by saying, "This is nothing but the word of a human being."

Verses 26–31 introduce the Hell of Saqar: "I will cast him into Saqar." Saqar means scorching; it leaves nothing remaining and spares nothing. "Incessantly scorching the skins" (lawwahah). Over it are nineteen (angels). Allah made the keepers of the Fire angels and made their number a trial for the disbelievers. Abu Jahl's objection or the questioning of the Jews is narrated as the occasion of revelation. The expression "none knows the soldiers of your Lord except Him" emphasizes that the mystery of this number requires faith.

In verses 32–39, Allah swears by the moon, the night, and the morning, declaring that Saqar is one of the greatest calamities and that it has come to warn humanity. "Every soul is bound to what it has earned, except the companions of the right." They are in Paradise and ask the criminals: "What led you into Saqar?"

In verses 40–56, the answer of the criminals is related: "We were not of those who prayed, we did not feed the poor, we engaged in vain discourse with those who indulged, and we denied the Day of Recompense, until death finally came." The intercession of intercessors will no longer benefit them. They turn away from the Quran; they are like frightened wild asses. Each of them wants unrolled scrolls given to him, but they do not fear the Hereafter. Yet the Quran is an admonition; whoever wills may take heed, but they cannot take heed unless Allah wills. He is the Protector and the Forgiver.

The oaths sworn by the moon, the night, and the morning in verse 34 point not only to these entities, but also to the dawning of the light of Prophethood from the darkness of ignorance (jahiliyyah) and the approach of the sun of Islam.
Saqar (Hell) is one of the momentous matters; it is recounted to warn people. Every soul is pledged to its earning; whoever does good is saved, and whoever does evil suffers its punishment.

However, those who are given their record of deeds from the right (ashab al-yamin) are an exception to this general rule. Rather than being tied solely to their own earnings, they attain higher ranks through Allah's grace. This is a grace that, like Prophethood, is not acquired through effort. Ashab al-yamin has been interpreted in two ways: those who are on the right side in destiny, or those who remain true to their covenant.

The companions of the right in Paradise ask the criminals, 'What led you into Saqar?' The criminals say: 'We were not of those who prayed, we did not feed the poor, we joined with those who engaged in vain pursuits, and we denied the Day of Recompense. We were like this until death came upon us.'

The intercession of intercessors will no longer benefit them, because they died in disbelief. Those who turn away from Allah's admonition flee from a lion like frightened wild asses. Yet they are fleeing from salvation and running toward ruin.

They demand that pages specifically for them be sent down, but the real issue is that they do not fear the Hereafter. The Quran is an admonition; whoever wills reflects. Yet no one reflects unless Allah wills. He alone is the One to be feared and the One to forgive. In hadiths, it is narrated that Allah said, 'I am the One to be feared and the One to forgive.'

The surah begins with the statement, "Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection." The particle "lâ" here before the oath is not for negation, but for emphasis; it signifies the greatness of the matter being sworn by. Most scholars consider this "lâ" to be a silā (emphatic particle), though some state that when it occurs at the beginning of speech, it denotes negation. In that case, it carries a meaning like "nay, by Allah" and enhances the significance of the oath. Swearing by the Day of Resurrection and the self-reproaching soul emphasizes the certainty of these realities.

Man thinks that We cannot assemble his bones. Yet Allah is able to gather them together; He can even restore his very fingertips. This points to the subtleties in the creation of man. Man wishes to continue sinning and mockingly asks about the Day of Resurrection. When that day arrives, the sight is dazed, the moon is eclipsed, and the sun and the moon are joined together. In horror, man says, "Where is the place to flee?" but there is no refuge; on that day, the final destination is to your Lord alone.

On that day, man will be informed of everything he sent forward and kept back. Because man is a clear witness (basirah) against himself, he knows in his conscience what he has done. Even if he pours out his excuses, he is a witness against his own self. This describes the true inner nature of man and his condition on the Day of Reckoning.

Addressing the Prophet (peace be upon him), it is stated: "Move not your tongue therewith to make haste with it." For the collecting and reciting of the Quran belongs to Allah. When it is recited, it should be followed, and its explanation should be left to Allah. This is an instruction for the preservation and comprehension of revelation.

People love the immediate world and leave the Hereafter. On that day, some faces will be radiant, looking toward their Lord; and some faces will be gloomy, expecting a back-breaking calamity. Then, the moment of death is depicted: the soul reaches the collarbones, and it is said, "Who can cure him?" The person realizes the parting, leg intertwines with leg, and on that day the drive is to your Lord alone.

In the concluding verses, the person who did not give charity, did not pray, denied the truth, and turned away is condemned: "Woe to you, and woe!" Does man think he will be left aimless? He was created from a drop of sperm, then became an embryo, then was proportioned and made into male and female. Is Allah, Who did this, not able to bring the dead back to life? Indeed, He is surely able.

The expression "did not confirm" in verses 31–33 of Surah al-Qiyamah means, according to most commentators, that he did not believe. However, some scholars such as Abu Hayyan interpreted this word as meaning he did not give charity. According to Elmalılı, the second interpretation is more meaningful because while the immediately following phrase "denied the truth" would merely remain an emphasis under the first interpretation, a broader meaning emerges that encompasses both the refusal to give charity and denial of faith. This interpretation is also in harmony with the verses in Surah al-Muddaththir: "We were not among those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor."

The letter "fa" in the verses explains the state of the sinner who indulges in worldly pleasure and questions the Day of Resurrection: That person neither affirmed the future, nor performed any deed for the sake of Allah, nor gave charity, nor prayed. On the contrary, by denying Allah, the Prophet, the Quran, and the Hereafter, he turned away from the truth and abandoned obedience.

Following this defiant attitude, that person went to his family strutting in arrogance. Yet, in the end, he will depart from this world and arrive before his Lord. On that day, his face will not smile, his back will be broken, and he will meet his doom. The concise and succinct expressions of the verses strikingly convey these meanings.

The expression in verses 34–35, "Woe to you, and woe!" is a malediction in Arabic, meaning "serves you right" or "may the greatest disaster befall you." Although it has been narrated that these verses were revealed concerning Abu Jahl, it is evident that they encompass everyone in a similar condition.

In verse 36, man's assumption that he will be left aimless is challenged. The following verses, 37–39, prove that this assumption is invalid by reminding that man was actually created from a simple drop of emitted semen. Verse 40 emphasizes that Allah, Who created these, is also capable of bringing the dead back to life. Regarding saying "Yes" at the end of the surah, there is a hadith narrated from the Prophet (peace be upon him).

The word hal in this verse expresses affirmation; it has the meaning of "came" or "drew near." This conveys in definitive terms that the creation of man occurred after the creation of the universe. Subsequently, it is stated that man was created to be tested, and that the grateful will attain salvation, while the ungrateful will suffer punishment.

The human species was created after the beginning of time. Dahr is the span of time that elapses from the existence of the universe until its end. Hin, on the other hand, is an unknown duration of time within this span prior to the creation of man. During that period, man was not something mentioned; that is, man in today's sense did not exist.

Man was created from a mixed drop of fluid (nutfah). Nutfah is the pure seed, which is a drop of semen. The word amshaj means "mixed"; it has been interpreted either as a single mixture or as a combination of various mixtures. According to Ibn Mas'ud, they are the vessels of the nutfah, and according to Qatadah, its colors and states. This demonstrates that man underwent a gradual and complex creation, rather than a simple one.

Man was created to be tested and was made hearing and seeing. Allah showed him the right way; choosing this way and being grateful, or being ungrateful and denying, was left to his own choice. This guidance was realized through rational and transmitted proofs supported by the verses of the Quran and the signs in the universe.

Chains, shackles, and a blazing fire have been prepared for the disbelievers. The righteous (abrar), however, will drink in the Hereafter from a cup whose mixture is camphor (kafur). The mixture of this cup is camphor; this is either the name of one of the fountains of Paradise or a characteristic of the drink. Unlike worldly wine, this drink does not cause intoxication; it provides complete joy and peace.

The expression 'camphor' in the sixth verse is mentioned as an additive to the drink of Paradise, and it is stated that this additive is a spring. This spring is a source from which the 'servants of Allah' drink and cause to gush forth wherever they wish. Some commentators have said that this source has gold pipes. In the seventh verse, it is stated that the good servants 'fulfill their vows.' Nadhr is a good deed that a person makes obligatory upon himself; this verse emphasizes that they consistently fulfill Allah's commandments and the promises they made to themselves.

In the eighth verse, it is narrated that these good servants 'feed food out of love for it.' Even if they are in need themselves, they give food to the needy, the orphan, and the captive. Special attention is drawn to treating captives well. In the ninth verse, it is stated that they do this feeding solely for the sake of Allah and expect no reward. In the tenth verse, it is expressed that they fear a grim and distressful day, that is, the terror of the Day of Resurrection.

In the eleventh and twelfth verses, glad tidings are given that Allah will protect them from the evil of that Day and bestow radiance upon their faces and joy upon their hearts. In reward for their patience, they will be given Paradise and garments of silk. In the thirteenth and fourteenth verses, they are depicted as reclining upon couches, seeing neither excessive heat nor bitter cold.

In the fifteenth and sixteenth verses, crystal vessels and cups of silver are mentioned. These vessels are a unique depiction combining the whiteness of silver with the clarity of crystal. In the seventeenth verse, another cup whose mixture is ginger is offered. In the eighteenth verse, a spring named 'Salsabil' is mentioned; this word denotes water that flows smoothly and is easy to drink.

In the nineteenth verse, it is stated that immortal youths circulate around them. In the twentieth verse, it is explained that wherever one looks in Paradise, the eye sees great bliss and a vast realm. In the twenty-first verse, it is expressed that upon them are garments of fine green silk and brocade, that they are adorned with bracelets of silver, and that their Lord gives them a pure drink. This drink is interpreted as a spiritual drink that purifies from malice and impurity.

In the twenty-second verse, the people of Paradise are addressed: 'Indeed, this is a reward for you, and your striving has been appreciated.' Subsequently, in the twenty-third verse, it is recalled that the Quran was revealed gradually in stages. In the twenty-fourth verse, the Messenger of Allah is commanded to be patient and not to obey the sinners and the ungrateful. In the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth verses, he is asked to remember Allah morning and evening, to prostrate at night, and to perform the tahajjud prayer.

In the twenty-seventh verse, it is stated that the disbelievers love this fleeting world and leave a heavy Day behind their backs. In the twenty-eighth verse, it is expressed that Allah created human beings and bound their joints firmly, and that whenever He wills, He will replace them with others like them. The twenty-ninth verse states: 'This is indeed a reminder; so whoever wills, let him take a path to his Lord.' In the thirtieth verse, it is emphasized that human will is dependent upon Allah's will by stating: 'And you cannot will except as Allah wills.' In the thirty-first verse, it is declared that Allah admits whomever He wills into His mercy, and that for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment.

Surah al-Mursalat begins with Allah swearing by the dispatched entities. The response to this oath is the verse, "Indeed, what you are promised is bound to occur." The entities sworn by are mentioned by their attributes: Mursalat (those sent forth), Asifat (those sweeping violently), Nashirat (those spreading), Fariqat (those separating), and Mulqiyat (those delivering). There is disagreement regarding what these are: they could be angels, winds, Quranic verses, the sending of prophets, or inspirations that come to human beings. The clearest view is that all of them are spiritual powers—that is, angels—and that they are sent by Allah.

The letters "waw" and "fa" prefixed to these attributes indicate the sequence between the actions. While there is a sequence in those that begin with "fa", sequence is not a condition for those that begin with "waw". For example, "sweeping violently" (asifat) comes after being sent forth, yet "spreading" (nashirat) may be concurrent with sweeping violently or separate from it. "Separating" (fariqat) comes after spreading, and "delivering the reminder" (mulqiyat) comes after all of them.

The word "urf" means "in succession / one after another" and is a metaphor derived from a horse's mane. It also carries the meaning of "goodness" or "custom" (urf / a recognized good deed). "Nashirat" means to spread or to resurrect the dead (nushur). "Fariqat", on the other hand, means to separate, to distinguish between truth and falsehood.

"Mulqiyat-i zikr" (those that deliver the reminder) may be the angels who bring revelation, or they could be the angels of inspiration who instill admonition in people, or events. In al-Kashshaf, these verses are interpreted by dividing them into two groups: one group of angels brings the commands and sweeps violently through whatever comes before them; the other group of angels spreads the revelation, revives dead souls, separates truth from falsehood, and delivers the reminder to the prophets. This reminder is divided into two categories, being for "udhr" (excuse / justification) and "nudhur" (warning). Udhr means accepting the excuse of those who embrace the truth, while nudhur means warning those who accept falsehood.

In al-Kashshaf, it is also stated that oaths are sworn by the winds of punishment and the winds of mercy. The winds of punishment sweep violently, while the winds of mercy bring life to dead earth and distinguish between the grateful and the ungrateful. Those who recognize Allah's blessing and give thanks seek pardon, while the ungrateful are warned. The most comprehensive and sound interpretation is that these attributes refer to forces sent in succession—that is, the angels.

Subsequently, the "messengers" (prophets) and their awaited time, the Day of Resurrection, are mentioned. This day is the Day of Decision, when truth will be separated from falsehood. The verse repeated at the end of each section of the surah, "Woe that Day to the deniers!", emphasizes the terror of this day. The word "wayl" means the descent of calamity, destruction, torment, or a valley/gate in Hell. With each repetition, it emphasizes a different aspect according to the preceding subject: the first addresses the Day of Decision, the second torment, the third Allah's knowledge and power, and the fourth human helplessness and the denial of Allah's blessings.

In this section, the expression 'wayl' is used to convey the severity of the terrifying state on that day. The word 'mukadhdhibin' (the deniers) is repeated in each verse and is linked each time to a different subject: such as the Day of Decision, torment, Allah's knowledge and power, human helplessness, and the denial of blessings.

In verses 21–25, the creation of man is addressed: a 'firm lodging' (the womb), a determined term (birth), and a 'receptacle / gathering place' (kifat) are described. The word 'kifat' means 'gathering place' or 'receptacle'; Elmalılı interprets this as the 'tokat' in Anatolia where stray livestock are penned. Furthermore, Allah's blessings are recalled through the establishment of firm mountains and the provision of sweet water on earth.

In verses 29–34, the disbelievers are addressed: they are told, 'Proceed to that which you used to deny,' and the expression 'a three-pronged shadow' is explained. This expression points to the Christian belief in the Trinity (father, son, holy spirit); while some commentators state that it is the shadow of the smoke of Hell, according to Ibn Abbas they are commanded to seek shelter in the three prongs of the cross. That shadow neither provides shade nor protects from the flame; the sparks of Hell are as huge as castles and as numerous as yellow camels.

In verses 35–40, the frequently repeated expression 'woe that Day to the deniers' draws a contrast between those who deserve this punishment and the state of the believers. The righteous (people of taqwa) are rewarded under shades and among springs, with whatever fruits they desire. They are told, 'Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you used to do.' The criminals, on the other hand, are left for a brief time with the words 'Eat and enjoy yourselves a little,' and then they face torment. When they are commanded to bow down (in ruku'), they do not submit.

The surah concludes with the question, 'Then in what statement after this (the Quran) will they believe?' Elmalılı points out that Surah al-Mursalat ends here, but that the disbelievers will not be let off on the Day of Decision, and that this subject will continue in Surah an-Naba'.

At the beginning of the surah, it is described what great news the deniers ask one another about. This news is Prophethood and, in particular, the Day of Resurrection. They have fallen into disagreement regarding this news; some believe, some deny, and some hesitate. Allah rejects their denial and disagreements, emphasizing that the news is certain and that they will come to know in the future.

It is stated that the earth was created as a bed and the mountains as pegs. This analogy conveys that the earth is like a bed prepared for human beings, and the mountains are like pillars holding it steady. The wisdom behind the creation of mountains includes numerous benefits, such as protecting the earth from tremors, separating the seas and landmasses, and ensuring the flow of rivers.

The creation of human beings in pairs, sleep being made a rest and cessation, the night a covering, and the day a time of livelihood are described. Sleep is described as a cessation and rest; the night covers like a garment, and the day is a time for work and livelihood.

The creation of the heaven as seven strong structures, the sun as a radiant lamp, the pouring down of abundant water from the clouds, and thereby producing grains, plants, and luxuriant gardens are described. All of these are proofs demonstrating the power and blessings of Allah.

It is announced that the Day of Decision is an appointed time, that the Horn (Sur) will be blown, and people will come in crowds. On that day, the heaven will be opened and the mountains will be set in motion, becoming a mirage. Hell has been prepared as a place of ambush for the transgressors, and they will abide therein for ages.

Elmalılı states that the word 'ahqab' is the plural of 'huqb', and that huqb means an epoch comprising consecutive years. There are different interpretations of this word, such as eighty-some years or seventy thousand years. However, the fact that 'ahqab' denotes a finite duration does not mean that the punishment of Hell will come to an end; because the meaning of succession can extend indefinitely. Furthermore, it is explicitly stated in other verses that the disbelievers will abide in Hell eternally.

As a punishment for the transgressors, there is boiling water and purulence. 'Hamim' is scalding water, and 'ghassaq' is the purulent discharge flowing from the bodies of the dwellers of Hell. This punishment is a fully fitting recompense for their denial in the worldly life. The verse declares that the torment is continuous and will be increased: 'So taste, we will never increase you in anything except torment.'

For the righteous, however, there is triumph, gardens, vineyards, maidens of equal age with swelling breasts, and full cups. In Paradise, neither vain talk nor falsehood is heard. These blessings are granted as a sufficient gift from their Lord. The word 'Lord' emphasizes that Allah is the Lord of the heavens, the earth, and whatever is between them; no one can address Him.

On the Day of Resurrection, the Spirit and the angels will stand in ranks. No one will speak except those permitted by the Most Merciful. Those who are permitted will speak the truth. There are different interpretations regarding who the Spirit is: Gabriel, an angel appointed over the souls, or another creation. Knowledge concerning these details is with Allah.

That day is the True Day. Whosoever wills, let him take a path toward his Lord. This path consists of speaking the truth and obeying through faith and righteousness. Allah warns people of an imminent punishment. On that day, a person will look at what his hands have sent forth, and the disbeliever will say, 'Would that I were dust!' According to some narrations, animals will be resurrected, and after their dues are settled, they will become dust; and the disbeliever will desire to be like them.

In the first five verses of Surah an-Naziat, an oath is sworn by the entities that perform five acts: pulling out violently, drawing out gently, swimming/gliding along, racing ahead, and arranging affairs. The response (jawab) to this oath is not explicitly stated because it is understood from the subsequent verses, meaning: 'The Day of Judgment and the resurrection after death will certainly come to pass.'

Because words such as "nazi'at", "gharq", "nashit", and "nasht" in these verses carry multiple meanings, it is not possible to translate them with a single meaning. Therefore, it is necessary to seek to understand them through tafsir (exegesis).

The word "gharq" carries meanings such as plunging into water, filling a vessel, and drawing a bow vigorously. As for "nazi'at", it is derived from the root "naz'" and possesses meanings such as death throes, drawing a bucket from a well, bending a bow, and galloping horses. It also carries the meaning of yearning for something by deriving from the root "nuzu'". Accordingly, nazi'at may be the angels that take souls, fighting forces, or souls that yearn for their bodies.

"Nashitat", on the other hand, comes from the root "nasht", which means gently pulling or untying a knot. For this reason, nashitat has been interpreted as the angels who take the souls of the believers with ease, or the planets moving from one constellation to another. If it is derived from "nashat", it means joy and cheer of the heart, in which case it indicates that the souls of the believers depart in peace.

Commentators have offered different interpretations regarding the entities mentioned in these verses: First, all of them are angels; angels of punishment who violently extract the souls of the disbelievers, angels of mercy who gently take the souls of the believers, and angels who traverse by divine command and manage affairs. According to the second interpretation, they are human souls; virtuous souls departing from the body or perfected human beings engaged in spiritual struggle against the lower self (nafs). The third interpretation is that they are warriors (ghazis) or their horses. The fourth is the stars, though acting as managers of affairs is not fitting for them.

The clearest interpretation is that these are angels, virtuous souls, or forces. By swearing upon these entities, it is emphasized that the Day of Judgment and the resurrection will surely occur. The manner in which the verbs in the verses are connected is also noteworthy; the first three verbs are connected with "waw" (and), whereas the last two verbs are connected with "fa" (then/so), indicating that the final two actions are the result of the preceding ones.

The words appearing at the beginning of Surah an-Naziat, such as nazi'at, gharq, nashitat, and nasht, have multiple lexical meanings, so it is impossible to translate them with a single meaning. For this reason, one must endeavor to understand them through tafsir. While gharq means plunging into water to submerge/drown, or drawing a bow fully; nazi'at can derive from the roots 'naz'' (to pull, pluck, tear out) or 'nuzu'' (to incline toward, yearn).

The word nazi'at has been interpreted in various ways, such as angels violently snatching souls, dying souls in their death throes, forces extracting souls by pulling from the depths, warriors drawing their bows, or galloping horses. In addition, likened to an exile yearning for their homeland, the meaning of souls separated from their bodies has also been given to it. As for nashitat, it stems from the roots 'nasht' (to pull gently, to untie a knot) or 'nashat' (joy of the heart); it has been interpreted as the angels of mercy who gently extract the souls of the believers or as the souls departing from the body with joyful contentment.

Commentators have transmitted four main interpretations regarding these words: First, they are all angels; nazi'at are the angels of punishment, nashitat are the angels of mercy, sabihat are the angels traversing by divine command, sabiqat are the angels conveying souls to Paradise or Hell, and mudabbirat are the angels managing affairs by Allah's command. The second interpretation is that they are human souls; the virtuous souls of the deceased or souls progressing along the spiritual path. The third interpretation is that they are warriors or their horses. Although the fourth interpretation is the stars, the attribute of 'arranging/managing affairs' is not suitable for them; the most accurate view is that they are angels or virtuous souls.

The response to the oath made with these five actions (pulling violently, drawing gently, gliding along, racing ahead, and arranging affairs) has been concealed; however, it is emphasized that the Day of Judgment and the resurrection after death will definitely take place. Then, the terror of the Resurrection is described: 'The quaking commotion (al-Rajifah) and the second commotion that follows it (al-Radifah).' Al-Rajifah has been interpreted as the first blast (of the Trumpet), and al-Radifah as the second blast.

The deniers, saying, 'Shall we indeed be returned to our former state? Even after we have become decayed bones?', deem resurrection impossible and mock it. In response, Allah states, 'It will be but a single cry, and behold, they will be awakened in the open plain.' Here, as a lesson regarding the end of the deniers, the narrative transitions to the story of Moses (Musa); recounting Pharaoh's claim, 'I am your supreme lord,' and Allah commanding Moses to ask, 'Do you have the will to purify yourself?' This narrative was elaborated in earlier surahs and is presented here in a concise and brief manner.

Allah the Almighty asks, rebuking the disbelievers: Is it harder to create you, or to create the heaven? He built the heaven, raised its canopy, and proportioned it. He darkened its night and brought forth its morning brightness. This demonstrates the greatness of His power.

After that, He spread out and leveled the earth. From it He drew forth its water and its pasture, and firmly set the mountains. All of this is for the provision of you and your livestock. Creation is not in vain; it possesses a wisdom and a purpose.

But when the great, overwhelming calamity (the Resurrection) arrives, man will realize what he was striving for. On that day, Hell will be made plainly visible for all who see. Everyone will see it and witness its terrifying state.

Then, as for whoever transgressed and preferred the life of this world, indeed, Hell will be his refuge. That person did not obey Allah's commands while in this world, but followed the desires of his lower self.

And as for whoever feared standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from vile desires, indeed, Paradise will be his refuge. This person walked the straight path in the world with concern for the Hereafter.

They ask when the Hour will arrive. How could you know of it? The knowledge of it belongs to your Lord alone. You are only a warner for those who fear it. On the day they see it, it will seem to them as if they had not tarried in this world except for an evening or a morning thereof.

The surah begins with our Prophet (peace be upon him) frowning and turning his back. It is understood that the pronouns in the verbs 'he frowned' and 'turned away' here refer to the Messenger of Allah; however, with the transition from the third person to the second person (the art of iltifāt / shift of perspective), attention is drawn to the fact that warning and admonition must first begin with the warner himself. The reason is the arrival of a blind Companion (Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum) to him. The attribute 'blind' emphasizes his excuse and his need for guidance; it is pointed out that frowning and turning away was not appropriate.

In the verses, it is expressed that the blind one might perhaps be purified from sins or take heed and benefit. The Prophet's turning toward the wealthy who deem themselves self-sufficient rather than toward this needy person is criticized. The expression 'you attend to him' means giving excessive importance to the guidance of those wealthy individuals. Yet, he is not responsible if the self-sufficient one does not purify himself; the true responsibility is to turn toward those who are eager, like the blind man who comes striving and fearing Allah. The words 'you pay no heed to him' reinforce the impropriety of this neglect.

Next comes the warning, 'No, indeed, do not do so!' For the Quran is an admonition, a reminder. Whoever wills may ponder it and take heed. Here, the expression 'whoever wills' does not mean leaving the person free, but rather conveys a warning and a threat. The Quran is in noble, exalted, and purified sheets, in the hands of scribes (angels or writers). These scribes are noble and righteous; they are called 'safara'. The dignity and purity of the sheets demonstrate the majesty of the Quran and that it is worthy of reverence.

Human ingratitude is condemned: 'Cursed is man; how ungrateful he is!' Man must not forget that Allah created him from a drop of fluid and proportioned him in the finest form, then eased his way, caused him to die and be buried, and will resurrect him whenever He wills. In spite of this, man has not fully carried out Allah's command. This deficiency is a general characteristic of humankind; grateful servants are few.

Let man look at his food: Allah pours down water abundantly, splits the earth open, and causes crops, grapes, clover, olive groves, date palms, dense gardens, fruits, and pastures to grow there. These are beneficial for humans and animals. These blessings serve as a reminder of Allah's power and His favors that require gratitude.

When that deafening noise (the Day of Resurrection) arrives, a person will flee from his brother, his mother, his father, his spouse, and his sons. For on that Day, every person will have a concern sufficient to preoccupy him. On that Day, there are faces that will be shining, laughing, and rejoicing; and there are faces that will be dust-stained and covered in darkness. It is these latter faces that belong to the disbelievers and the transgressors.

Allah causes various blessings to grow on the earth for humans and animals: grains, grapes, fresh clover, vegetables, olives, date palms, and dense, tangled gardens. It is Allah the Almighty who grows and matures all of these. The word "abb" mentioned in these verses means meadow, pasture, vegetables, or animal fodder; it inherently carries the meaning of preparation and being prepared.

According to what is narrated from Abu Bakr and Umar, when they were asked about what the word "abb" was, they preferred, without going into excessive detail on this matter, to act upon what the Quran has clearly stated and to entrust what is unknown to Allah. Umar emphasized that delving into the details of such words is burdensome and an undue strain, and that what is truly important is to give thanks for the blessings.
