Three important points can be drawn from these narrations: First, there are concise/general (mujmal) words in the Quran whose meanings not everyone can comprehend at all times, and one must believe in them in brief. Second, the word "abb", like "mar'ā" (pasture) in the previous surah, is a comprehensive expression encompassing many plants that humans and animals benefit from. Third, the meaning of 'preparation' inherent in this word points to the necessary preparations for the life of the Hereafter.

When the Day of Resurrection arrives, a deafening, violent sound called "al-Sakhkhah" will burst forth. This sound is defined by two characteristics: first, making itself heard and perceived above all else; second, deafening the ears due to its intensity in such a way that no other sound can be heard. This is an unparalleled example of eloquence expressing the terror of the Resurrection.

On that Day, everyone falls into their own concern; a person flees from his brother, his parents, his spouse, and his children. For everyone has a matter sufficient to keep them occupied. As stated in the hadith, people are gathered naked, barefoot, and bathed in sweat; each person looks only to their own state.

On the Day of Resurrection, some faces are bright, smiling, and joyous. These are the faces of those who have been purified through reverence for Allah, faith, and righteous deeds. In some commentaries, it is stated that this radiance is the result of acts of worship such as the night prayer, ablution, or jihad. Other faces, however, are covered in dust, dark, and miserable; these are the disbelievers and the wicked. Before that Day arrives, man should believe, refrain from sin, and strive to attain salvation with an untarnished face.

Surah at-Takwir was revealed in Mecca and consists of 29 verses, 139 words, and 533 letters. The end-rhyme (fasila) of the surah consists of letters. According to what Imam Ahmad, at-Tirmidhi, and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Umar, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever wishes to look upon the Day of Resurrection as if seeing it with their own eyes, let them recite Surahs at-Takwir, al-Infitar, and al-Inshiqaq.' In the opening verses of the surah, twelve events that will occur on the Day of Resurrection are mentioned, and it is said, 'Every soul shall know what it has brought.' These events are: the folding up of the sun, the clouding of the stars, the setting of the mountains in motion, the abandonment of prized possessions, the gathering of wild beasts, the setting ablaze of the seas, the pairing of souls, the questioning of the girl buried alive, the opening of the records of deeds, the stripping away of the sky, the kindling of Hellfire, and the bringing near of Paradise. Some of these will take place in this world, and some in the Hereafter.

There are different views regarding the folding up of the sun (takwir al-shams). Takwir means folding, wrapping, and gathering together, as well as casting down, throwing away, and blinding. According to a narration from Ibn Abbas, the sun is joined to the Throne; it has been interpreted from Mujahid, Qatadah, and Hasan as the departure of its light; from Rabi' b. Khuthaym as its being cast away; and from Abu Salih as its being turned upside down. Al-Qurtubi states that the sun will be wound up like a turban and, after its light is removed, it will be cast away. The clouding/dimming of the stars (inkidar) has been explained in two senses: the extinguishing of their light or their falling down. Al-Bukhari narrated the view of their falling, and commentators have mostly preferred this. As for the setting of the mountains in motion, it is described as the shaking of the earth, the mountains being carded like wool, and their being hurled into the sky.

In the expression 'the abandonment of prized possessions' (ta'til al-'ishar), 'ishar' is the name given to ten-month pregnant camels and represents the most valuable property. In the face of the terror of the Day of Resurrection, their owners leave these possessions unattended. Some scholars have interpreted this expression as the drying up of clouds or as lands from which the tithe ('ushr) is collected. The gathering of wild beasts has been interpreted in three ways: their coming together out of fear, their perishing through death, or their being resurrected for retribution (qisas) and gathered at the place of assembly (mahshar). In the hadith, it is reported that the hornless sheep will claim its right from the horned one. The setting ablaze of the seas (tasjir) has been interpreted as the receding of waters through volcanoes, their being filled with fire, or waters overflowing and invading the earth. Some narrations state that the first six events take place in this world, and the last six in the Hereafter.

The pairing of souls (tazwij al-nufus) has been understood primarily in two senses. According to the first view, the good are brought together with the good, and the wicked with the wicked, and classified. This is supported by verses in Surahs as-Saffat and al-Waqi'ah. According to the second view, souls are restored to their bodies and reunited. The first view is considered stronger and denotes the classification at the place of assembly. The questioning of the girl buried alive (al-maw'udah) deals with the custom during the pre-Islamic period of ignorance (Jahiliyyah) of burying female children for various reasons. In the verse, this girl will be asked for what sin she was killed. This custom was practiced due to beliefs such as poverty, fear of shame, or regarding angels as the daughters of Allah.

Islam took a severe stance against the custom of burying female children alive. In Surahs al-An'am and al-Isra, killing children out of fear of poverty was forbidden. The Prophet (peace be upon him) commanded Qays b. Asim, who had committed this act, to free a slave or sacrifice a camel for each girl buried. Scholars have stated that this command indicates recommendation (mandub), not obligation (wujub). Furthermore, it is narrated that regarding coitus interruptus ('azl, discharging semen outside during intercourse), the Prophet (peace be upon him) stated that it was 'concealed infanticide.' In jurisprudence (fiqh), 'azl is considered disliked (makruh). These verses and hadiths indicate that abortion and deliberately induced miscarriage are likewise major sins.

One of the scenes of the Day of Resurrection is asking the girl buried alive in the earth for what crime she was killed. Rather than interrogating the killer directly, directing this question to the oppressed victim carries the meaning of a severe rebuke and silencing (tabkit) in order to torment the killer's conscience and make him confess his wrongdoing. Here, bringing forward the innocent little girl as the plaintiff is an effective warning that no defense will be valid on that day.

The opening of the records of deeds has been interpreted in two ways: First, that the deceased person's record is rolled up and then opened on the Day of Resurrection for the reckoning. Second, that after the reckoning, the pages announcing the results are distributed, which is called 'the flying of the pages.' While the believer's page falls into their hand declaring 'in an exalted garden,' the disbeliever's falls declaring 'in Hellfire.' The first meaning is more suitable here; the verses in the subsequent surah also explain this.

The stripping away of the sky (kasht) is the removal of the covering of the sky, just like skinning an animal. Rather than annihilation, this signifies the full manifestation of realities in the new realm. Indeed, al-Nisaburi states that when the sky is opened and removed, Paradise and the Throne above it will appear. On that day, the Throne of the Truth (al-Haqq) becomes manifest, and human souls remain between the manifestations of divine wrath and mercy.

The kindling of Hellfire, its being stoked ablaze for the transgressors, and the bringing near of Paradise to the righteous take place during the phase of final judgment. When these twelve events (the folding up of the sun, the clouding of the stars, the setting of the mountains in motion, etc.) occur, every soul will know what it has prepared. Every deed, good or evil, will be found in the record of deeds and placed on the scale, and the person will see the recompense for what they did. This knowledge occurs after the opening of the records and the stripping away of the sky.

Some commentators have stated that lessons may be drawn from these verses for the minor resurrection (death) as well as the major Resurrection. For example, the folding up of the sun has been interpreted as the soul's separation from the body, and the falling of the stars as the loss of bodily faculties. However, the primary meaning belongs to the major Resurrection. Such interpretations do not harm faith; rather, they enhance the lesson. In the Quran, there are exoteric (zahir) and esoteric (batin) meanings; while believing in the manifest meaning is essential, it is also permissible to benefit from allusions and interpretations (ta'wil) that do not contradict it. It is necessary to avoid excess (ifrat) and negligence (tafrit) and find the middle path.

There are different narrations regarding the interpretation of the expression "al-khunnas al-kawnas" mentioned in these verses. According to what is transmitted from al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatadah, and Ali, this expression refers to stars in general. However, it is also narrated from Ali that it was interpreted specifically as the five planets. The word "kunnas" has been associated with "kunus," which indicates the places where wild cattle and gazelles conceal themselves. For this reason, it is narrated from Ibn Abbas, Sa'id b. Jubayr, and al-Dahhak that it means gazelles, and from Ibn Mas'ud that it means wild cattle.

After transmitting the narrations, Ibn Jarir stated that it is more appropriate to interpret this expression generally. According to him, Allah swore by things that sometimes disappear, sometimes course along, and return to their places. In Arabic, the word "kunnas" refers to the places where wild cattle and deer enter. It is also possible that it is used for the positions of the stars by way of metaphor (isti'arah). It would be more accurate to say that everything bearing these attributes is intended in the verse. In this case, a general metaphor is involved, and this metaphor is supported by the fact that the disappearing and coursing of the stars conforms to the flow of the verses.

In verses 17 and 18, oaths are sworn by the night and the morning. The word "As'ase" means both to come and to depart. The majority preferred the moment of the night's departure, which is the harbinger of morning. The breathing of the morning points to the pleasantness of the morning breeze. These oaths promise the Prophet (peace be upon him) and the Muslims that the Hereafter is better than this world. For them, this world is like a night turning toward morning, and the Resurrection is like an approaching morning.

In verses 19–25, it is emphasized that the Quran was brought by a noble messenger. This messenger is Gabriel (peace be upon him). He is an angel who is esteemed, powerful, trustworthy, and obeyed in the presence of the Lord of the Throne. It is stated that the Prophet (peace be upon him) is not mad; rather, he saw him on the clear horizon. It is narrated that Gabriel was seen in his original form twice. The Prophet is not withholding of the unseen; he receives the revelation with complete trust and conveys it. The Quran is not the word of outcast devils.

In verses 26–29, people are addressed: "Where then are you going?" The Quran is a reminder for all the worlds, especially for those who wish to be on the straight path. However, a person's willing to be on the straight path is contingent upon Allah's will. You cannot will unless Allah wills. This shows that human will is subordinate to Allah's will. One must not attribute success to oneself, but view it as Allah's favor. The verses contain both a warning and a consolation.

The expression "you cannot will unless Allah wills" in the final verses of Surah at-Takwir, though appearing absolute at first glance, actually contains a hidden object (maf'ul). The fact that the verb is transitive (muta'addi) indicates the presence of this object. From the context of the previous verse, "for whoever among you wills to be on the straight path," it is understood that this object is "to will to be on the straight path." That is, the meaning is: "Unless Allah wills that you will to be on the straight path, you cannot will it." Verifying scholars have preferred this explanation.

Nevertheless, some have regarded the verb as intransitive (lazim) to preserve the generality of the address, understanding it as "you cannot will anything." In this case, it is explicitly expressed that without Allah's willing, the servant can have no willing whatsoever, which is the precise view of the Ahl al-Sunnah. However, the specific restriction regarding being on the straight path is understood not through explicit expression, but through implication. The first explanation is more direct and accords better with the flow of speech.

This verse does not support a determinist view (jabr) that completely negates the will of servants. By virtue of the rule of "istithna-i mufarragh" (vacuous exception), the phrase "unless Allah wills" does not entirely eliminate the servant's willing; rather, it indicates that without Allah's willing, no willing can take place. The servant can will by Allah's will, and can even possess a willing that requires what is desired to come to pass. This is called "cebr-i mutavassit" (intermediate determinism). The Maturidi school states that although the servant's universal will (iradah kulliyyah, the power of will) is created, their particular will (iradah juz'iyyah) is an evaluated, subjective matter (amr i'tibari).

In a narration transmitted regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse, when Abu Jahl heard the verse "for whoever among you wills to be on the straight path," he said, "So the matter has been left to us; if we wish, we will be on the right path, and if we do not wish, we will not." Thereupon, this verse was revealed and showed that there is no absolute autonomy. The verse encourages not fatalistic compulsion, but asking Allah for guidance to the straight path. The warning and the necessity of willing are understood through implicit indication.

People must seek the truth by willing to be on the straight path and benefit from this reminder. However, those who attain success must recognize it as coming from Allah and not forget that He has the power to remove and extinguish that willing. By the statement "for whoever among you wills to be on the straight path," one should not fall into the delusion that every desire is rightful and true, but remember that the responsibility lies with themselves. In conclusion, without Allah's will, neither the servant's will nor their purpose is realized; therefore, humility and reliance upon Allah (tawakkul) are essential.

Surah al-Infitar was revealed in Mecca and consists of nineteen verses, eighty words, and three hundred and twenty-seven letters. The surah addresses the terror of the Day of Resurrection and human responsibility.

In the first four verses, the portents of the Day of Resurrection are enumerated: when the sky is cleft asunder, when the stars are scattered, when the seas are burst forth, and when the graves are overturned. These events depict the moment the cosmic order is disrupted. In the fifth verse, it is stated that everyone will know what they have sent forth and what they have left behind in this world. This means that a person will see the recompense for the good or evil they have done.

In the sixth verse, addressing man, it is said: 'O man! What has deceived you concerning your Generous Lord?' This question challenges man's falling into rebellion by relying on Allah's grace. In the seventh and eighth verses, this generosity is recalled by recounting Allah's creating man, giving him a proportionate form, and fashioning him in whatever shape He willed. Man ought to be grateful for these blessings of creation and must not succumb to pride.

In the ninth verse, by the statement, 'Nay, but you deny the Judgment,' people's denial of the reckoning in the Hereafter is criticized. In verses ten through twelve, it is stated that there are guardian angels over every person who record everything that is done. These angels are described as 'kiraman katibin,' meaning noble scribes.

In the thirteenth and fourteenth verses, it is stated that the righteous will be in bliss and the wicked will be in Hell. Verses fifteen and sixteen emphasize that the wicked will enter Hell on the Day of Judgment and will not be able to escape from it. This shows that the recompense for the good and evil deeds done will certainly be rendered.

In the last three verses, the gravity of the Day of Judgment is emphasized through questioning: 'And what will make you realize what the Day of Judgment is?' In the nineteenth verse, the characteristic of that day is explained: no soul will have the power to help another, and the command will belong entirely to Allah. This recalls the dread of the Day of the Hereafter and the absolute sovereignty of Allah.

Surah al-Mutaffifin is the last surah revealed in Mecca, and according to some narrations, the first surah revealed in Medina. Woe to those who defraud in measure and weight! When they take measure from people, they take it in full, but when they measure or weigh for others, they give short. These verses sternly warn those who make a habit of cheating in measure and weight.

The word "Wayl" means severe punishment, a valley in Hell, and similar meanings. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Wayl is a valley in Hell down which a disbeliever falls for forty years before reaching its bottom." This warning shows that even one who cheats ever so slightly in measure and weight deserves a severe punishment. Indeed, a Bedouin said to Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan: "If a defrauder (mutaffif) is threatened like this for stealing a tiny amount, then what will your state be when you take the property of Muslims without measure?"

Cheating in measure and weight shakes the foundation of right and justice. The heavens and the earth stand upon a measure and balance. Two things are required for accurate measurement: the measuring instrument being complete, and the conscience of the measurer being upright. People cannot be free from fraud unless they view the rights of others as their own rights. This is why Allah commands the rectification of measure and weight first.

Do those who commit this fraud not think that they will be resurrected for a tremendous Day? On that Day, people will stand before the Lord of the worlds, and everyone will receive their due right. It is this belief that prevents fraud. The record of the wicked is in Sijjin. Sijjin is a sealed book; the deeds of the wicked are recorded there. Woe that Day to the deniers! They deny the Day of Recompense and call Our verses "tales of the ancients."

Their hearts have rusted with the sins they have earned. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "When a servant commits a sin, a black spot appears on his heart. If he repents, it is erased; if he repeats it, the spot grows until it covers his heart. That is what Allah refers to as 'ran'." For this reason, they will be deprived of seeing their Lord in the Hereafter and will enter Hell.

The word Sijjin means "constricting, confining" or "dungeon." The record of the wicked is recorded in a book beneath the seventh earth, where Iblis is located. This book is sealed and accepts no alteration whatsoever. The record of the righteous, on the other hand, is in Illiyyun, which signifies elevation. Sijjin, however, symbolizes abasement and humiliation.

In verse 17, it is stated that on that Day it will be said to the deniers: 'This is what you used to deny.' The word 'Kalla' (Nay) at the beginning of verse 18 warns against defrauding in measure and weight, encourages goodness, and reminds that one must turn away from the path of the wicked. For the record of the righteous is surely in Illiyyun.

The word Illiyyun has been explained differently by lexicographers and commentators. Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni states that it is the plural of the word 'illiyy', while al-Zajjaj says that its grammatical inflection (i'rab) is like a plural. In tafsirs, meanings such as the seventh heaven, the right leg of the Throne, Sidrat al-Muntaha, and 'infinitely higher and higher' have been given. According to some, Illiyyun is the place where the angels' registers of deeds are kept and, as the opposite of Sijjin, the register in which good deeds are inscribed. In verses 19-21, it is stated that Illiyyun is a sealed book, witnessed by the angels brought near to Allah.

In verses 22-28, it is described that the righteous are in bliss in Paradise. They are served a pure drink, rahiq. Rahiq is a wine that has no mixture, is clear, delicious, and does not cause a headache. Its vessel is sealed with musk. The mixture of this wine is from Tasnim; Tasnim is the highest of the springs of Paradise. While the servants brought near to Allah (al-muqarrabun) drink it pure, the other righteous servants (al-abrar) drink it mixed. This is also connected to the command to compete in the verse.

Verses 29-33 describe how the criminals used to mock the believers in the world. The polytheists of Mecca would laugh at the poor believers, wink at one another when they passed by them, and amuse themselves when they returned to their homes. They would accuse them of being astray. Yet, they were not sent as keepers over the believers; they had no right to these judgments.

In verses 34-36, it is stated that on the Day of Resurrection, the believers will laugh at the disbelievers. Seated on couches in Paradise, the believers watch the disbelievers enter Hell. The question asked, 'Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?', is the retribution for their mocking in the world. This is also to mock them in return. In conclusion, everyone receives the recompense of their deeds.

In the first verse of Surah al-Inshiqaq, it is stated: "When the sky has split open." The word "inshiqaq" mentioned here means the cracking of the sky by divine command and ultimately its being rolled up. Initially, there is a splitting with clouds, which points to the verse in Surah al-Furqan: "The day when the sky will split open with clouds." This splitting occurs through the terror of the Day of Resurrection and is accompanied by events such as the scattering of the stars when the sky cracks. According to a narration from Ali, this splitting will begin from the region of "majarrah"; majarrah has been interpreted as the gate of heaven. The splitting consists of several stages: the initial cracking, followed by splitting with clouds, then the sky melting and becoming like a rose, and finally being rolled up. Thus, this verse encompasses all these stages together.

In the second verse, the expression "When it has listened to its Lord" occurs. This shows that the sky accepted the command to split open submissively and willingly. Just as the sky said "We come willingly" during its initial creation, it obeys now as well. The statement "and it was made fit for it" conveys that this obedience is what befits the nature of the sky. According to another interpretation, Allah made obedience obligatory upon the sky. That is to say, the sky is destined to split open due to the terror of the Day of Resurrection. These verses are of a complementary nature to the event of the sky splitting. Furthermore, the expression "haqqat" (it was fulfilled) means the realization of the Day of Resurrection or the prevailing of truth.

In the third and fourth verses, it is stated that the earth is stretched and expanded, casts out what is within it, and becomes completely empty. The earth is leveled completely, and the mountains are destroyed. The expression "casts out what is within it" means that it casts forth the dead and also pours out the heavy burdens (treasures and minerals) within it. While some scholars intend by this only the bringing forth of the dead, Qatadah accepted both meanings. As for the emptying of the earth, as stated in a hadith according to al-Alusi's narration, it is the earth's casting out what is within it and returning to the state it was in when there was nothing.

In the fifth verse, it is stated once again: "When it has listened to its Lord and was made fit for it." This indicates the two stages of the events in the heavens and the earth. The words "idha" here have been interpreted as conditional or temporal particles. Some stated that the apodosis is omitted, while others stated that the answer is found in the verse: "At that time everyone will know what they have done" or "you will meet your Lord." In the sixth verse, humanity is addressed: "O human being! Indeed, you are laboring toward your Lord with great exertion." The verb "kadh" means to scratch and to exert serious effort. Man strives toward his Lord through death and what follows, and ultimately meets Him. According to some commentators, this verse is considered the answer to the preceding conditional clauses.

In the seventh and eighth verses, it is stated that those who are given their record in their right hand will be subjected to an easy reckoning. "An easy reckoning" (hisab yasir) means glancing over the record without an interrogation and passing through. In a hadith narrated from Aisha, the Prophet (peace be upon him) stated that this reckoning is merely a presentation (ard) and that a contested reckoning will lead to ruin. In the ninth verse, it is described that this person will return to his people (his family, friends, and the houris in Paradise) in joy. In the tenth verse, as for the one who is given his record behind his back, it is stated that he will cry out, "Come, O destruction!" This expression indicates that they will enter Hell. In the eleventh verse, the cause of this punishment is explained: while in the world they were joyful among their people, they assumed they would never return to the Hereafter. The word "hawr" expresses returning to decrease after completeness; they thought they would never die.

In the twelfth to fifteenth verses, it is emphasized that this assumption of the disbelievers is false. In the section beginning with "Nay," it is conveyed that they will return to their Lord and that everything they did was observed. Then Allah swears by the twilight, by the night, and by the moon when it is gathered full. These oaths remind us of the continuous change in the universe and that human beings are also subject to this change. In the nineteenth verse, it is stated: "You shall surely embark from stage to stage." The expression "tabaqan 'an tabaq" means passing from state to state, generation to generation, or degree to degree. This reinforces the truth that life in this world is not static and that one will pass into the Hereafter through death. The same verse has also been recited addressing the Prophet, "you shall surely embark," and has been considered an allusion to the Night of the Ascension (Mi'raj). Both recitations carry the promise of elevation for the believers and a descent toward punishment for the disbelievers.

From the twentieth verse onward, it is questioned why the deniers do not believe in the face of these truths. In the twenty-first verse, it is stated that when the Quran is recited to them, they do not prostrate. The occasion of revelation for this verse is that the polytheists clapped their hands and whistled when the Prophet prostrated. Abu Hanifah (al-Imam al-A'zam) stated that the prostration of recitation (tilawah) is obligatory in this verse, whereas al-Shafi'i stated that it is Sunnah. In the twenty-second and twenty-third verses, it is expressed that the deniers reject the Quran and that Allah knows what they conceal within themselves. The verb "yu'un" means storing and hiding hidden thoughts within a vessel in their hearts. In the twenty-fourth verse, he is commanded to give the disbelievers tidings of a painful punishment. In the twenty-fifth verse, it is stated that those who believe and perform righteous deeds are exempted from this punishment and that for them is an uninterrupted reward. This exception generally represents the separation of the believers from the disbelievers, and it also includes those among the disbelievers who come to faith.

The surah begins by swearing by the constellations, that is, the sky adorned with star clusters. Constellations (burūj) means visible lofty mansions and refers to the twelve zodiac constellations in the sky. Then, an oath is sworn by the promised day, namely the Day of Resurrection, and by the witness and what is witnessed. These oaths indicate that the believers must persevere with patience and that the oppressors will be punished.

The story of the Companions of the Pit (Ashab al-Ukhdud) is recounted: Cursed are the companions of the ditch. These are the people who dug trenches filled with fire to turn the believers away from their faith and burned them. The Quran narrates this event without attributing it to a specific people; what matters is that the oppression and the suffering endured for the sake of faith serve as a universal example. The believers are praised for persevering steadfastly in their faith, while the oppressors are condemned.

Allah is witness to the torture inflicted upon the believers, and He sees and knows all things. For those who persecute believing men and believing women and then do not repent, the punishment of Hell and the punishment of burning await them. As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, there are gardens beneath which rivers flow; that is the supreme triumph.

Indeed, the grip of your Lord is severe. He is the One who originates creation and restores it, the All-Forgiving, the All-Loving, Owner of the Throne, the Glorious, and the Doer of whatever He wills. These verses emphasize the greatness of Allah's power and the severity of His retribution against the oppressors. No creature can escape His grasp.

Has there reached you the story of the hosts of past nations such as Pharaoh and Thamud? They too denied the messengers and were ultimately seized by Allah's grip. Those who disbelieve persist in denial, yet Allah encompasses them from behind. This Quran is an exalted book preserved in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz); its glory is lofty and it is far removed from any kind of corruption.

At the beginning of the surah, Allah swears by the sky and by al-Tariq. The oath is meant to draw attention to the importance of the truth about to be explained. Just as the sky refers to the known heaven, it can also encompass everything in the heights. Al-Tariq means that which comes by night, knocks at the door, or strikes the heart; here, the bright star that rises toward morning is meant.

In the second and third verses, what al-Tariq is is asked and answered: It is the star piercing the darkness (necm-i sâkıb). Sâkıb means to pierce or to ascend; this star cleaves the darkness with its light. Some commentators have said that this is the Morning Star, while others have said it is the Pleiades (Süreyya) or another star. Moreover, in a spiritual sense, it can also represent divine guidance that imparts light to the heart.

In the fourth verse, it is stated that over every soul there is a protector (hâfız). This protector is primarily Allah; furthermore, the angels accompanying man also record his deeds and protect him. No human being is left unattended; everyone is under surveillance at every moment. This demonstrates Allah's power and mercy.

In the fifth verse, man is commanded to look at what he was created from. Man was created from an insignificant fluid, that is, an ejected semen. While this reminds him of how humble his origin is, Allah's creating him from this simple matter and elevating him is also evidence of His power to create anew.

In the sixth and seventh verses, the nature of that fluid is described: An ejected fluid (mâin dâfik) that emerges from between the backbone (sulb) of men and the ribs (terâib) of women. Sulb is the spine, while terâib is the ribcage. This expression points to the region where the reproductive organs are located.

Commentators present two views regarding this verse: According to the first view, only the semen of the man is meant. According to the second view, both the male and female fluids should be considered together, because the child is formed from the union of both. The woman's fluid is thin and yellow, lacking the characteristic of being ejected with force, yet it plays a role in fertilization.

After this initial stage of creation, man sequentially passes through the stages of nutfe (drop), alaka (embryo), mudga (morsel of flesh), bones, and being clothed with flesh, reaching an entirely different creation in the seventh stage. By showing these stages, Allah emphasizes that He has the power to resurrect man once again.

In summary, these verses call upon man to reflect on the wisdom in human creation. Even though man was created from a simple fluid, there is a constant protector over him. This should distance him from arrogance and direct him toward Allah. Furthermore, he should believe in Allah's power to resurrect after death.

Elmalılı addresses the objections raised against the expression "emerges from between the backbone and the breastbones" in Surah al-Tariq. These objections are based on the misunderstanding that semen is formed directly in the testicles. However, the expression carries a broad meaning encompassing the entire reproductive process, such as the formation, differentiation, and ejection of semen for fertilization. Elmalılı states that these objections are empty sophistries, because the expression in question is the most comprehensive description embracing all the relevant organs and the nervous system in both the male and female bodies.

The expression "ejected fluid" in the verse implies not only the ejection of the fluid, but also that it must be discharged toward the womb for fertilization. The maturation of semen and its discharge for fertilization takes place between the backbone and the breastbones in both man and woman. Therefore, this stage of creation is an important proof demonstrating Allah's power and man's helplessness.

The creation of man from a nutfe reveals the power of the Supreme Creator, Who made him a thinking, reasoning being. It also proves that resurrection in the Hereafter is possible. For Allah, Who created a human being from scattered parts, is also able to bring them together again. This is evidence of the resurrection after death and the Day of Reckoning.

The day when secrets will be examined is the day when the beliefs, intentions, and deeds hidden in hearts will be exposed. On that day, a person will have neither power nor helper. If the revealed secrets are pure, there is salvation; if they are defiled, there is punishment. Therefore, man should reflect upon what he was created from and keep his secrets pure during worldly life.

The surah begins by swearing by the returning sky and the earth that splits open. The expression "the returning sky" points to the rotational movements of the sky, rain, or the descending and ascending of the angels. As for "the earth that splits open," it refers to meanings such as the emergence of plants, valleys, or the cleaving open of graves. These oaths recall the cycle in human creation and the resurrection in the Hereafter.

The Quran is not a joke or amusement, but a decisive word that distinguishes truth from falsehood. Even if the disbelievers devise plots to invalidate the Quran, Allah's plan is stronger than theirs. What falls upon the believers is to heed this solemn word and strive to enter Allah's presence with a sound heart on the day when secrets are disclosed. As for the disbelievers, they have been granted a brief respite.

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) loved Surah al-A'la very much. He named this surah 'the most virtuous of the surahs describing the glorification of Allah.' According to a narration from Aisha, the Prophet would recite al-A'la in the first rak'ah of the witr prayer, al-Kafirun in the second, and al-Ikhlas along with the Mu'awwidhatayn in the third. In addition, he would recite Surah al-A'la and Surah al-Ghashiyah during the Eid and Friday prayers.

At the end of Surah at-Tariq, there was a promise that the Messenger of Allah would prevail against the plots of the disbelievers. In this surah, however, this promise is reinforced with the verse, 'We shall ease you unto the easiest way,' and guaranteed through the Lord's name 'al-A'la' (the Most High). Following this, an invitation is made to glorify the lofty name of the Lord, and it is emphasized that the Hereafter is better and more enduring.

The surah consists of 19 verses. In the first verse, it is commanded, 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.' Tasbih (glorification) is to hold Allah free from any defective attributes. The name 'al-A'la' expresses that Allah is transcendent above all things in His Essence and attributes. Just as it is impermissible to bestow this name upon anyone else, it is likewise necessary to mention the names used for Allah with reverence, keeping them far from meanings unworthy of Him.

Granting respite to the disbelievers at the end of the previous surah, along with the reminder of the Lord's majesty here, serves as an assurance that the promise will be fulfilled. The command to glorify is simultaneously an invitation to the duty of gratitude. Although there are different views regarding the word 'name' (ism), it is understood that the primary intent is to declare the transcendence of the Possessor of the name.

When verse 74 of Surah al-Waqi'ah was revealed, the Prophet commanded saying it in bowing (ruku'), and when verse 96 was revealed, he commanded saying 'Subhana Rabbiya'l-A'la' in prostration (sujud). This shows that glorification can be performed through words and actions. Although it has also been suggested that what is meant by 'name' is the trace or work of creation, there is no need for this interpretation; because a name is the expression that identifies its possessor and is clearly understood.

In the second verse, it is stated that Allah created and proportioned, and in the third, that He determined and guided. Creation is a requirement of the name Rabb (Lord). Determining (taqdir) is to assign a measure and destiny to everything, while guidance (hidayah) is to direct them toward their purposes of creation. This also encompasses the guidance of intellect and religion given to humanity. All of these are the works of Allah's Lordship (Rububiyyah), and none other than He can accomplish them.

In the fourth verse, it is stated that it is Allah who brings forth the pasture, and in the fifth verse, that He turns it into black stubble like flood-scum. This points to plants drying up and decaying over time to turn into compost and coal. Attention is likewise drawn to the formation of coal. The end of those who seek humanity solely in material pleasures will also be like such a blackened heap.

In the sixth and seventh verses, it is stated that the Qur'an will be recited to the Messenger of Allah and that he will not forget, except what Allah wills. In the eighth verse, it is said, 'And We shall ease you unto the easiest way.' In the ninth verse, he is commanded to remind, if the reminder benefits. In the tenth and eleventh verses, it is stated that the one who has reverence will take heed, while the wretched one will avoid it.

In the twelfth and thirteenth verses, it is stated that the wretched will enter the greatest Fire, where he will neither die nor live. In the fourteenth verse, it is declared that whoever purifies himself will attain prosperity, and in the fifteenth, that whoever remembers the name of his Lord and prays will be saved. In the sixteenth and seventeenth verses, it is emphasized that people prefer the worldly life, whereas the Hereafter is better and more enduring. In the last two verses, it is recalled that these truths are also found in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses (Musa).

Addressing His Prophet (peace be upon him) with the words 'We will make you recite,' Allah informs that He will reveal and teach the Qur'an through Gabriel (Jibril) and grant him success in reciting it. This recitation is in the sense of reciting from memory, and our Prophet will no longer forget. However, if Allah wills, He can cause him to forget; this demonstrates that His power cannot be restricted. This exception draws attention to the fact that the Prophet's not forgetting is not due to his own power, but to the grace of Allah. Scholars such as al-Farra have stated that this exception was actually intended to emphasize that forgetting would never occur at all. Indeed, Allah stated that if He willed, He could take away the revelation entirely, yet He did not will it. This promise is one of the miracles of the Prophet; occasional minor forgetfulness occurring for a divine wisdom does not harm the permanence of this promise.

Then, by saying 'We shall ease you unto the easiest way,' Allah promises to grant His Prophet the easiest path in every matter. This signifies ease in knowledge, teaching, action, and guiding to truth. In every domain of religion, attaining even the most difficult goals with ease will be the characteristic of the Prophet and his community (ummah). The source of this ease is Allah's bestowal of success (tawfiq). Receiving both manifest and hidden revelation and comprehending the lenient rulings of the Shariah also fall within the scope of this ease.

By stating, 'Remind, if the reminder benefits,' Allah commands His Prophet to preach and advise in situations where reminding will be of benefit. This condition is not actually a restriction, but rather for emphasis and mitigation; for in reality, reminder inevitably provides benefit to the recipients. In some cases, however, reminding may increase the intransigence of stubborn disbelievers; in such circumstances, giving advice may not be obligatory. Those who show reverence take heed, while the most wretched avoid it. Those wretched ones will be cast into the great Fire, where they will neither die nor live.

The wretched who will be cast into the greatest Fire will suffer eternal punishment of Hell in the Hereafter. They will neither die and be relieved, nor will they find a beneficial life. This expresses the severity and permanence of the punishment. Sinful believers, however, will die after remaining in Hell for a time and will be saved through intercession (shafa'ah). For the disbelievers, there is no death; the torment is eternal.

In contrast, with the declaration, 'He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself,' whoever is cleansed of evils, purifies their heart from polytheism (shirk) and bad character, pays zakah, and performs prayer has attained salvation. Purification (tazakki) here encompasses both internal and external purification, such as faith (iman), sincerity (ikhlas), major ritual ablution (ghusl), and minor ritual ablution (wudu). Although some scholars have said that the prayer in this verse refers to the Eid prayer and zakah refers to the fitr charity (sadaqat al-fitr), these rulings may have come later since the revelation of the verse took place in Mecca. Essentially, the verse encompasses all bodily and financial acts of worship.

Yet instead of this purification and acts of worship that bring salvation, people prefer the life of this world. They prioritize the ornaments, amusements, and pleasures of the world and cast the Hereafter behind them. This preference is either the state of the disbelievers who reject the Hereafter entirely, or the state of heedless or disobedient believers who, despite believing in the Hereafter, prioritize this world. Yet the Hereafter is better and more enduring than this world.

These reminders were also present in the scriptures of earlier prophets. Especially in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses, there were fundamental principles such as declaring the oneness of Allah (tawhid), purifying oneself, performing prayer, and that the Hereafter is better than this world. This demonstrates that the religion of Islam carries the same fundamental message as previous religions. The Prophet being granted success in the easiest path and the triumph of his religion were also heralded in these scriptures.

Surah al-Ghashiyah takes its name from the word 'al-Ghashiyah', which means 'the covering, the all-encompassing' and refers to the terrifying event of the Resurrection that will engulf everything. This surah urges attentive listening to that momentous news and explains what a great calamity the Resurrection will be for the disbelievers, and what an eternal bliss it will be for the believers.

On that Day, some faces will be humbled, downcast in humiliation. These are people who did not strive in the world upon the path commanded by Allah, but instead wore themselves out for falsehood and labored in vain. According to different interpretations, this fatigue and distress is either the very torment of Hell in the Hereafter, or the retribution for their wasted deeds in the world. In the end, all of them are in loss.

These people will enter a scorching Fire and be made to drink from a boiling spring. Their food will be a poisonous, thorny plant called 'dari'', which neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger. This punishment is the bitter consequence of their having toiled in vain and failed to strive in the way of truth.

Other faces on that Day, however, will be in bliss and joy. These are those who strove in the world in accordance with the pleasure of Allah, saw the reward of their deeds, and were well-pleased with what they had done. They will be in an elevated Paradise; no vain or futile talk is heard therein, but only peace and happiness.

In Paradise, there is a flowing spring, raised couches, cups filled with drink, cushions arranged in rows, and splendid carpets spread out. These blessings have been prepared for the believers who performed righteous deeds in the world and earned the pleasure of Allah.

Allah invites people to look at the lessons in creation: Do they not look at the camel, how it was created; at the sky, how it was raised high; and at the mountains, how they were set firm? These beings are a means to contemplate Allah's power and the Day of the Hereafter. Through this reflection, man can find the right path and attain eternal happiness.

Almighty Allah asks people to look at the earth and the order upon it. They are commanded to ponder how the earth has been spread out, how the mountains, plains, and seas were created, and how it was made suitable for human life. This perspective is at the same time a means to comprehend that resurrection after death, reckoning, and retribution are real, and to recognize the power of Allah.

People will live on the earth for a while, then die and be resurrected. For this reason, they must know the place in which they dwell, observe the fate of past nations, and spend their lives in faith, spiritual discernment, and righteous deeds. By commanding that one look at such physical evidence, the Quran points to the importance of engaging in rational and empirical sciences such as astronomy and geology. However, these sciences should not be used solely for worldly purposes, but to recognize Allah's signs and prepare for the Hereafter.

The expression 'Do they not look?' occurring in the verse reproaches those who do not pay attention to such admonitory matters. Allah has left the details of creation in this universe to human investigation, having provided a comprehensive reminder. This reminder opens the door to attaining deeper knowledge by employing reason and empirical observation.
O Muhammad! You are only a reminder; you are not tasked with compelling them to believe. Give counsel and admonition, but do not compel; for ruling over the hearts belongs to Allah.

Whoever turns away from the reminders and persists in disbelief, Allah will punish him with the greatest torment. This torment is the eternal punishment in the Hereafter, compared to which the punishment of this world is minor. In the end, everyone will return to Allah and give account; there is no escape from this reckoning.

The surah begins with an oath by the dawn (fajr). Fajr is the cracking open of the night's darkness and the emergence of the first whiteness of morning. With this oath, attention is drawn to the transition from darkness to light and to the Lordship of the Creator. The prefixed 'lam' may denote genus (jins) or specific reference ('ahd); if it denotes genus, it signifies every dawn, and if it denotes specific reference, it signifies a blessed dawn, such as the morning of the Feast of Sacrifice (Eid al-Adha).

The second oath is by the 'ten nights.' The strongest view is that these are the first ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah. The proof for this was narrated from Jabir via a hadith of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him). There is also the possibility of them being the last ten nights of Ramadan or the tenth of Muharram. The purpose is to emphasize the value of arduous hours of worship that end in celebration and joy.

The third oath is by 'the even and the odd.' Shaf' means even, and watr means odd. There are many interpretations regarding this expression. According to Mujahid, the even is everything created, and the odd is Allah. In another hadith, the even and the odd are interpreted as the even and odd rak'ahs of prayer. According to the narration from Ibn Abbas, however, the even is the day of the Feast of Sacrifice, and the odd is the day of Arafah. This is the most consistent both with the order of the verses and with the oath by the ten nights.

The fourth oath is by 'the night as it departs.' It points to the time of dawn (sahar), when the darkness of the night is about to come to an end. It has also been said to be the night of Muzdalifah. All these oaths constitute a momentous oath for those of understanding, because they point to Allah's oneness and Lordship.
The answer to the oath is the verse, 'Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful.' Allah will punish the disbelievers. To see this, it is sufficient to look at the stories of 'Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh.

How did Allah destroy the people of 'Ad? They were the dwellers of the city of Iram. The epithet 'Zat al-'Imad' means possessors of pillars. The people of 'Ad were a tall, powerful people who constructed immense buildings. The city of Iram is also recounted as a legendary paradisiacal garden built by Shaddad, but this is a fabrication.

As for the people of Thamud, they used to carve out houses from the rocks in the valley. They too were subjected to torment. Pharaoh, on the other hand, is referred to as 'the owner of stakes'; this is an allusion to the pyramids and to his might. All of this shows that those who transgress in this world cannot escape Allah's watchful surveillance.

Human beings misunderstand Allah's test. Whenever Allah honors a person and bestows favors upon him, he says, 'My Lord has honored me.' And whenever He restricts his provision and brings him distress, he says, 'My Lord has humiliated me.' In truth, both are tests; worldly blessing is not an absolute honor, nor is hardship an absolute humiliation.

O you people! You do not honor the orphan, nor do you encourage feeding the poor. You consume inheritance voraciously, and you love wealth with an exceeding love. All of this stems from not reflecting upon the Hereafter.

Yet when the earth is violently shaken and leveled, when your Lord comes with the angels rank upon rank, and when Hell is brought forth, man will understand. On that Day, he will say, 'If only I had sent forth good deeds for my life!' but it will be of no avail. None can punish as Allah punishes, and none can bind as He binds.

As for the reassured soul (al-nafs al-mutma'innah) that devotes itself to Allah and finds serenity in Him, it will be addressed: 'O reassured soul! Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing to Him, and enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise.'

In these verses, it is stated that the reassured soul (al-nafs al-mutma'innah) is addressed on the Day of Resurrection. According to the flow of the discourse, while on that Day the disbelieving person laments, saying, 'If only I had sent forward something for my life,' Allah the Exalted will call out to those who believed and attained peace of heart: 'O reassured soul!' This rhetorical style is one of the aspects of the Quran's inimitability (i'jaz) and instantly prepares the listener for that moment.

In verses 28–30, this soul is told: 'Return to your Lord, both well-pleased and pleasing [to Him].' The concepts of 'radiyyah' and 'mardiyyah' mean that the person is pleased with Allah and Allah is pleased with him. Then follow the commands: 'enter among My servants' and 'enter My Paradise.' Commentators have explained this entering as joining the company of sincere, righteous servants and entering Paradise alongside them. According to another interpretation, it refers to pure souls reflecting upon one another, thereby augmenting their radiance and ultimately attaining Paradise.

The concept of 'nafs' mentioned in the verse has been examined in detail. The nafs is the essence and reality of man by which he says 'I'; it has two dimensions: the perceiver (sha'ir) and the perceived (mash'ur). These two dimensions can separate from each other in states such as sleep, heedlessness, or death. A person's full harmony with his soul is possible only within the reality of Allah, which transcends him. Indeed, the verse 'Allah intervenes between a person and his heart' points to this. As for the spirit (ruh), it is by the command of the Lord and is taken by Allah in death and sleep. For this reason, al-nafs al-mutma'innah means the reassured essence or spirit.

Regarding the definition of al-nafs al-mutma'innah, al-Razi presents three aspects: First, it is the taste of believing in the Truth with absolute certainty (yaqin) without any doubt. Second, it is attaining a security that cannot be shaken by fear and grief. Third, it is the heart finding rest solely through the remembrance of Allah. This serenity is attained either by reaching the Supreme Cause in intellectual reasoning and settling upon it, or by realizing that the servant's infinite need can only be fulfilled by Allah's infinite perfection. Whoever chooses Allah not for anything else but purely for Himself, that is the reassured soul.

Regarding when this address will be made, there are three views: at the moment of death, at the time of resurrection after death, or when the reckoning is completed. According to the context of the discourse, the most apparent view is that it occurs on the Day of Reckoning. However, it is reported in traditions that an angel will recite this verse to Abu Bakr at the moment of death. A narration from Zayd ibn Aslam states that good tidings are given to the reassured soul in all three places: at death, at resurrection, and on the Day of Gathering. These views can be reconciled; indeed, the day of death is also considered a part of the Resurrection.

Sufis have classified the stages of the soul: the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammarah), the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah), the reassured soul (al-nafs al-mutma'innah), the pleased soul (al-nafs al-radiyyah), the pleasing soul (al-nafs al-mardiyyah), the inspired soul (al-nafs al-mulhamah), and the purified soul (al-nafs al-zakiyyah). In this surah, first the condition of the commanding soul and the self-reproaching soul is described, followed by the salvation of the reassured soul. Some commentators have stated that the command 'return' applies at every moment in this world as well. According to this, in every matter, the believer should turn back to Allah being pleased with Him and His decree, thereby joining the company of righteous servants in this world and becoming worthy of entering Paradise in the Hereafter.

The surah begins with the expression, "I swear by this city." What is meant by this city is the Sacred City (al-Balad al-Haram), namely Mecca the Honored (Makkah al-Mukarramah). Commentators are in consensus on this matter. Naming Mecca as "al-Balad" indicates that it is a blessed, well-known city worthy of reverence. Allah swore by this city, and subsequently by the father and the son, to emphasize that man was created amidst hardship.

The phrase "While you are free of restriction in this city" addresses the Prophet (peace be upon him). The word "hill" carries meanings such as being lawful, leaving the state of ihram, or settling in a place. Here, it indicates that fighting in Mecca was made lawful for the Prophet for a brief period. Indeed, on the day of the conquest, permission was granted to kill a few individuals, after which the sacred inviolability of Mecca continued. This demonstrates the virtue of the Prophet and the honor of that city.

There are various interpretations regarding the expression "I swear by the father and his children" mentioned in the third ayah. According to one view, the father (walid) is Adam (peace be upon him), and what he fathered (ma walad) is his offspring. According to another view, Abraham (peace be upon him), his son Ishmael, and his descendant Muhammad (peace be upon him) are intended. The most comprehensive interpretation is that every father and his child are included. This oath draws attention to the importance of the human lineage and the purpose of creation.

The ayah stated as the response to the oaths, "Indeed, We created man in hardship and toil," explains that human life is full of difficulties. The word "kabad" derives from the word for liver and means hardship and fatigue. From the mother's womb until death, man faces various hardships. These difficulties are for the trial of worldly life and preparation for the hereafter.

Then, it is narrated that man, presuming himself strong, says, "I have squandered heaps of wealth." This refers to arrogant individuals who waste their wealth or spend it out of hostility toward the Prophet. Allah asks that person: "Does he think that no one has seen him?" That is to say, Allah has seen everything he did and will call him to account.

Allah reminds of the blessings He has bestowed upon man: two eyes, a tongue, and two lips. These meet man's basic needs such as seeing, speaking, and eating. Then it is stated, "And We showed him the two paths." These two paths are the path of good and the path of evil. Man has been given the ability to do both good and evil, and the choice of which one to take has been left to him.

The arrogant man could not attempt that steep ascent. This steep ascent, called "al-Aqabah", refers to demanding deeds of goodness. Overcoming this steep ascent is to free a slave, or to feed an orphan or a destitute person on a day of famine. These are deeds that require great sacrifice and heroism.

Those who believe and counsel patience and compassion are the people of happiness; their books will be given from their right side. As for the disbelievers who deny Our verses, they are the people of ill omen; they will be cast into the Fire in Hell, and the Fire will be closed in over them. This symbolizes their eternal punishment.

Allah begins by swearing by the sun and its bright morning light. 'Duha' means the time when the sun has risen high and its light has spread out. With this oath, attention is drawn to the sun itself and to its most prominent feature, its light. For the sun is the source of light for the world, and by virtue of its light we see things and comprehend Allah's power.

Next, an oath is sworn by the moon as it follows the sun. 'Tuluw' means to follow. The moon rises after the sun sets and reflects its light. Commentators have pointed to different aspects of this following: such as the moon following the sun in rising, following it in setting, receiving light from it, and being like a second sun when it is a full moon. Its clearest meaning is the time during full moon nights when the moon resembles the sun the most. This oath also draws attention to a different manifestation of light.

An oath is sworn by the day and the night. The day is the time when it reveals the sun clearly, while the night is the time when it conceals the sun. These two contrasting states emphasize the importance of light and the transience of darkness. While the brightness of the day demonstrates the presence of the sun, the darkness of the night makes one feel the value of light. There is also an allusion here to the luminous and dark states of the soul (nafs).

An oath is sworn by the sky and the One Who built it, and by the earth and the One Who spread it out. That is, Allah has raised the sky and placed the stars; and He has made the earth habitable and spread it out. Here, there are two views regarding whether the particle 'ma' is a relative pronoun (mawswl - 'who/the one who') or an infinitive/verbal noun (masdar - 'the building/spreading'). Its being a relative pronoun is more evident: 'He' is Allah. Although the earth is a sphere, the expression 'spread out' describes its being extended in such a way that one can live comfortably upon it.

An oath is sworn by the soul and the One Who proportioned it. That is, an oath by Allah, Who created the human soul, breathed the spirit into it, and fashioned its organs. Allah has inspired every soul with its wickedness and its righteousness (taqwa). Inspiration (ilham) means to cast something into the heart. Fujur means sin and rebellion, while taqwa means piety, caution, and goodness. Thanks to this inspiration, human beings can distinguish between good and evil.

The response to the oaths is this: Whoever purifies his soul has succeeded, and whoever corrupts and buries it has suffered loss. 'Tazkiyah' means to purify and develop; 'tadsiyah' means to corrupt and bury. This can occur through a person's own striving, just as it occurs through Allah's decree. While the Mu'tazilites emphasize human effort, Ahl al-Sunnah accepts both aspects. When the Prophet recited this verse, he would pray for the purification of his soul.

The story of the people of Thamud is an example of this. Thamud denied their prophet Salih because of their transgression. Salih (peace be upon him) told them to leave Allah's she-camel alone, but the most wretched among them killed the camel. Thereupon, Allah destroyed them with a mighty blast, an earthquake, or a thunderbolt, leveling them all equally. Allah is not questioned about what He does; He has no fear. This story demonstrates the end of those who corrupt their souls.

The oaths at the beginning of this surah are like a summary of the oaths in the previous surah. There, the path leading from darkness to light, and from non-existence to knowing Allah and the soul, was shown. Here, however, attention is drawn to darkness by swearing by the night and the moment it envelops. Then an oath is sworn by the day as it shines forth, and by the One Who created the male and the female. These oaths point from transient non-existence to permanence, unity, and the order in creation.

Then it is stated, 'Indeed, your efforts are diverse.' The word 'shatta' means scattered and separate. This indicates that people's intentions and deeds differ, with some striving toward good and others toward evil. The primary objective is to caution against disunity as in the Age of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah) and to guide toward order through tawhid and action. The divergence of efforts stems from the variation of whims and desires within the souls.

'As for he who gives, is mindful of Allah (has taqwa), and affirms the best (husna), We will ease him toward the easiest path.' Here, spending one's wealth in the way of Allah, guarding against evil, and believing in the finest outcome (Paradise, the pleasure of Allah) are praised. 'Husna' has been interpreted as the most excellent trait, word, or reward. With the help of Allah, such a person finds ease on the path of goodness and attains happiness.

'But as for he who is stingy, considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best, We will ease him toward the hardest path.' A person who acts stingily and does not give from his wealth, deems himself self-sufficient, and denies the Hereafter is dragged toward a harsh end. When that person perishes, his wealth will not benefit him. Amassing wealth cannot save him.

'Indeed, it is incumbent upon Us to show guidance. And surely to Us belong the latter and the former.' Allah shows guidance through the prophets and the books. The Hereafter and this world belong to Him. No one is independent of His guidance. Then comes the warning of 'a blazing Fire.' Into that Fire will enter only the 'most wretched,' namely, the one who denied the Truth and turned away.

'But the most righteous will be kept far away from it—the one who gives his wealth to purify himself, and harbors no favor from anyone to be repaid, seeking only the countenance of his Lord, the Most High. And he will surely be well-pleased.' It is narrated that these verses were revealed concerning Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) on account of his freeing slaves like Bilal. The most righteous person, having attained the pleasure of Allah, reaches contentment in this world and the Hereafter.

The surah begins with an oath by the morning brightness and by the night when it grows still. Duha is the moment when the sun rises and begins to shine brightly—the youth of the day. Night, on the other hand, is the time when it fully settles, becomes calm, and is cloaked in silence. These two contrasting states recall the fluctuations of life, such as joy and sorrow.

O Muhammad! Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He become displeased. The pause in revelation was not an abandonment, but a moment of rest necessitated by mercy and wisdom. Just as in the stillness of the night, this interval is a source of tranquility and a herald of forthcoming joys.

For you, the end of every state is better than its beginning. The life of prophethood, the arrival of revelation, its pause, and its resumption; the life of this world and the Hereafter—at every stage, there is a continuous ascent. You will advance from good to greater good day by day.

Your Lord will bestow such favors upon you that you will be well-pleased. This promise also encompasses the station of intercession. The Prophet will intercede for his community and, by Allah's leave, satisfy them.

Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? The Prophet was born fatherless and also lost his mother and grandfather. Allah protected him under the care of his uncle Abu Talib and reared him in an incomparable manner.

Did He not find you unaware of the way and guide you? The Prophet was far removed from polytheism, yet before divine revelation arrived, he did not know the details of the true religion. Allah showed him the right path by granting him the Book and wisdom.
Did He not find you poor and make you rich? While materially poor, he became enriched through blessings in trade and the wealth of Khadijah. Spiritually as well, he brought richness to his community.

Therefore, never oppress the orphan, nor look down upon him considering him weak. Protect his rights and treat him with compassion. Do not chide the petitioner, whether asking for material aid or for knowledge—help him to the best of your ability or turn him away with gentle words.
Proclaim the blessing of your Lord. Give thanks through word and deed, and let others benefit as well. Recognize the value of these blessings and spread them.

Reciting the takbir at the end of this surah is Sunnah. It has been narrated from the Prophet that 'Allahu Akbar' is said at the conclusion of each surah. This practice is an expression of joy following the pause in revelation.

At the conclusion of this blessed surah, following the sorrow felt over the interruption of revelation, glad tidings are given that with the relief brought by the brilliance of the morning sun and the continuation of the Lord's help, the end is better than the beginning. Ultimately, by awakening feelings of compassion for the orphan and mercy for the needy, the surah concludes with the command to recount the blessing one possesses. It conveys what a beautiful compliance with the command, what a delightful declaration of peace of heart, and what a profound sense of gratitude it expresses to hasten to proclaim this blessing with complete faith and inner tranquility by pronouncing the takbir, 'Allahu Akbar'.

To avoid giving the impression that this takbir is part of the Quran, and to indicate that it is not obligatory but left to the sentiments of those who experience that spiritual delight and meaning, it was not transmitted through successive narration (tawatur) in the recitations; rather, it was narrated as a specific practice and, in one respect, a command of the Messenger of Allah, such that omitting it is permissible. As a result, it has come to be practiced customarily as recommended (mandub) and desirable (mustahabb).

In current practice, it is mostly said as 'Allahu Akbar'; frequently, it is also recited as 'Allahu Akbar, la ilaha illallahu wallahu akbar wa lillahi'l-hamd'. For extensive information on the subject, one should consult al-Jazari's 'an-Nashr al-Kabir'.

Upon this relief and peace of heart that dispels sorrows, one should not fall into indolence under the presumption that no hardship or trouble remains in the world. Knowing that along with every hardship there is ease, one must strive even harder to proclaim the blessing possessed. The importance is emphasized not merely of seeing the blessing, but of looking to the Essence of the One who bestows that blessing, directing all longing toward Him, and striving to journey toward Him.
For this reason, this surah is followed by Surah al-Inshirah. Surah al-Inshirah reinforces the same theme, teaching that the believer must turn to Allah and give thanks in every circumstance.

Surah al-Inshirah begins by recalling the great blessings bestowed upon the Prophet. In the first ayah, it is stated, 'Did We not expand your breast for you?' Here, the expression 'sharh al-sadr' (expansion of the breast) signifies bringing relief to the heart, strength to the soul, and joy, rather than a physical opening of the chest. As Raghib also stated, what is in question here is a divine light and tranquility of heart.

Lexicographers elaborate on this expression. According to the author of Shihab, while 'sharh' originally meant cutting open flesh, over time it came to be used in the sense of removing the heart's distress and bringing joy. Alusi, on the other hand, states that the origin of sharh is dispersing and expanding, and that it may be regarded as conventionally literal in the sense of the soul's relief. These explanations help us understand the spiritual expansion in the ayah.

Exegetes mention two main views regarding 'sharh al-sadr': The first is the physical operation mentioned in the narrations, in which the chest was opened and the heart removed and filled with faith and wisdom during childhood, at the onset of prophethood, or on the night of the Mi'raj. The second is that this was a spiritual opening, which is the meaning agreed upon by all. The essential purpose is the unfolding of the truth through faith and wisdom. The event in the hadith of the Mi'raj is also an example of this spiritual opening.

In the second ayah, it is stated, 'And did We not remove from you your burden?' 'Wizr' means a heavy burden; although some have interpreted it as sin, the majority understand it as the difficulties, perplexity, and anxiety of responsibility prior to or at the beginning of prophethood. This burden was so heavy that it weighed down the Messenger of Allah's back and made his bones creak. Allah Almighty lifted this burden with the revelation of Surah ad-Duha and brought relief to his heart.

In the fourth ayah, it is stated, 'And did We not raise high your mention?' Here, 'dhikr' signifies fame and honor. The name of the Prophet is mentioned alongside the name of Allah; in the adhan, in prayer, and wherever Allah is mentioned, he is mentioned as well. In a hadith, Gabriel reported that Allah said, 'Whenever I am mentioned, you too will be mentioned with Me.' This is the highest station of honor.

In the fifth and sixth ayahs, it is stated, 'For indeed, with hardship comes ease.' This statement is emphasized by being repeated twice. 'Hardship' ('usr) appears as definite, while 'ease' (yusr) appears as indefinite. This indicates that following or alongside every hardship there is ease, and indeed two eases. According to a narration, when this ayah was revealed, the Prophet said, 'One hardship cannot overcome two eases.'

In the seventh ayah, it is stated, 'So when you are free, still toil.' That is, when you finish one task, immediately occupy yourself with another act of worship, and do not turn to comfort. When the obligatory acts are finished, move on to the supererogatory; when the prayer is finished, stand in supplication. In the eighth ayah, there is the command, 'And to your Lord alone turn your attention.' In all your strivings, aim only for Allah; do not turn to anyone other than Him. See the Bestower of blessings in the blessing and walk toward Him.

The maxims derived from these surahs are as follows: 'When there is constriction, expansion follows', 'Blessing corresponds to burden', 'The judgment of an action is according to its intended purpose', and 'Whoever strives for the sake of Allah reaches Allah.' These two surahs (ad-Duha and al-Inshirah), by describing the condition and glory of the Prophet, recall the diffusion of spiritual grace, and then, by turning from the blessing to the Bestower of blessings, remind us of yearning for Allah alone. Following them comes Surah at-Tin.

Regarding al-Tin (the Fig) and al-Zaytun (the Olive), commentators have put forward two main views. According to the first view, what is meant here are the well-known fruits, the fig and the olive. Those who maintain this view state that figs and olives provide immense benefits for human life in terms of food, fruit, medicine, and trade, and that an oath may therefore have been sworn by these blessed fruits. Some, on the other hand, have stated that these two fruits symbolize the male and the female.

The second view is that Tin and Zaytun are proper nouns and point to blessed places. Those who prefer this view cite as evidence their mention alongside Tur-i Sinin (Mount Sinai) and al-Balad al-Amin (the Secure City) in the verse. Three different interpretations have been made regarding the nature of these places: mountains, mosques, or towns. For instance, it has been said that Tin is the mountain of Damascus or the mosque of Noah, while Zaytun is the mountain or the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Furthermore, according to a narration from Ibn Abbas, Tin and Zaytun mean 'Mount Tin' and 'Mount Olive' in Syriac, and these mountains are the lands where Jesus and other prophets were raised.

Tur-i Sinin is the blessed mountain upon which Moses spoke with Allah. 'Tur' means a mountain covered with vegetation. It has been narrated that the word 'Sinin' signifies beautiful or blessed, and that it carries the meaning of beautiful in the Ethiopic language. Some scholars have explained the expression 'Tur-i Sinin' as 'the blessed, beautiful mountain,' stating that this designation is in harmony with such Quranic expressions as 'the Sacred Valley' (al-Wadi al-Muqaddas) and 'the blessed spot.'

Al-Balad al-Amin, on the other hand, has been interpreted by consensus as Mecca. Mecca being designated as the 'secure city' rests on such reasons as Allah making the Kaaba a safe sanctuary for mankind, making it abundant and blessed upon the prayer of Abraham, and its being protected from chastisement due to the presence of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) within it. These oaths express an ascent from material nourishment toward spiritual security, underscoring the vital importance of security for humanity.

Following the oaths, Allah proclaims that He created the human being in the finest form. 'Ahsen-i takvim' (the finest composition) signifies that man was created in the best configuration, both physically and spiritually. This encompasses not merely outward physical beauty, but also spiritual capacities such as intellect, discernment, and moral aptitude. The human being possesses the potential to attain this sublime state. Yet, despite this initial creation, man can in time decline to the lowest of the low; this may take the form of bodily deterioration, moral degeneration, or plunging into Hellfire.

However, those who believe and perform righteous deeds are saved from this degradation. Their reward is uninterrupted, and they attain the most excellent outcome. This constitutes the essence of religion: that Allah creates the human being in the finest form, after which one either preserves and elevates this beauty through faith and righteous action, or sinks into degradation through disbelief. The true meaning of religion is epitomized in this law of reward and punishment.

Following these explanations, the verse asks: 'What, then, causes you to deny the religion?' In other words, in the face of such clear proofs and with Allah's promise and retribution so manifest, how can a person possibly deny religion or call it a lie? This question serves as a warning directed both to the human being himself and to the Prophet.

In the final verse, it is declared: 'Is not Allah the most just of judges?' He is above all sovereigns, ruling with absolute justice. Hence, His religion is the truth; He will grant reward to the believers and inflict punishment upon the disbelievers. Man must not forget this reality, must not give the lie to religion, and ought to attain eternal salvation through deeds that earn divine reward. This surah stands as a summary of the preceding surahs and a preparation for those that follow.

The first five verses of this surah are the first verses of the Qur'an to be revealed. Surah al-Fatihah, on the other hand, is the first to be revealed as a complete surah. The first revelation came to our Prophet in the cave of Hira; Gabriel said to him 'Read,' and he replied 'I cannot read.' This repetition occurred three times, and finally the verse 'Read in the name of your Lord!' was revealed. That these five verses were the first to be revealed is established by authentic narrations. The remainder of the surah was revealed later, specifically upon the transgression of Abu Jahl.

The first five verses are as follows: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created! He created man from an alaq (embryo). Read! And your Lord is the Most Generous. Who taught by the pen. Taught man what he did not know.' In these verses, Allah's creation, teaching, and generosity are emphasized. Although our Prophet was unlettered (ummi—unable to read and write), Allah granted him the ability to read and revealed the Qur'an to him. The teaching of writing with the pen is also among Allah's great blessings.

From the sixth verse onward, the warning begins: 'No! Indeed, man transgresses, because he sees himself self-sufficient (free of need). Indeed, to your Lord is the return.'
