Here, it is reminded that man transgresses by considering himself self-sufficient, but in the end he will return to Allah. This address is directed first to our Prophet, and then to all people.

Afterward, Abu Jahl's preventing our Prophet from performing prayer is recounted: 'Have you seen the one who prevents a servant when he prays? If he is upon guidance, or commands righteousness? What if he denies the truth and turns away? Does that man not know that Allah sees him?' The verses condemn this transgression of Abu Jahl and issue a warning to him. Scholars of tafsir mention Abu Jahl's attempt to prevent the Prophet (peace be upon him) from prayer as the occasion of revelation for these verses.

Allah the Almighty directs a severe threat toward Abu Jahl: 'No, no! If he does not desist, We will surely drag him by the forelock—that lying, sinning forelock. Then let him call his associates; We will call the angels of torment (zabaniyah).' The zabaniyah are the angels of punishment who are the keepers of Hell. Here, the power of Allah is emphasized in contrast to the power of the prominent figures of the age of ignorance (Jahiliyyah).

The final verse of the surah is a comfort and a command to our Prophet: 'No, never obey him! Prostrate and draw near.' That is, do not comply with transgressors like Abu Jahl, continue your servitude to your Lord, and draw near to Him through prostration. Prostration is the moment when the servant is closest to Allah. This verse also requires a prostration of recitation (tilawah); our Prophet also prostrated when he recited this surah.

This surah begins with the expression, "Indeed, We sent it down." According to the majority, the pronoun "it" here refers to the Quran. The greatness of the One who sent it down and the glory of what was sent down are emphasized. Although some commentators have stated that the pronoun refers to the command "read" in Surah al-Alaq or to the word "sef'" pointing to the victory of Badr, the strongest view is that it refers to the Quran. This verse informs that the Quran was sent down on the Night of Qadr (Laylat al-Qadr).

The Night of Qadr carries the meanings of "the night of decree", "the night of honor", or "the night of constriction". As stated in Surah ad-Dukhan, every wise matter is distinguished on this night. All three of these meanings are valid, and the mention of "the Night of Qadr" three times in the surah points to this.

"The Night of Qadr is better than a thousand months." This expression conveys that deeds performed on that night are more virtuous than the deeds of a thousand months that do not contain the Night of Qadr. A thousand months equals eighty-three years and four months. In some narrations, this has been interpreted as referring to the thousand months of worship of a person from the Children of Israel, or to the duration of the Umayyad state. However, the essential meaning is to emphasize the boundless goodness of this night.

"The angels and the Spirit (Gabriel) descend therein by permission of their Lord for every matter." According to the majority, what is meant by the Spirit is Gabriel (Jibril). The descent is to the lowest heaven or to the earth. The expression "for every matter" encompasses all affairs that are decreed or to be executed on that night.

"That night is peace until the break of dawn." Salam signifies the angels greeting the believers, protection from evil, or complete peace and tranquility. Supplicating on this night is a Sunnah; the supplication taught to Aisha is: "O Allah, You are Pardoning, You love to pardon, so pardon me." Prayer, reciting the Quran, and contemplation are also recommended.

The Night of Qadr is likely to occur concealed each year in Ramadan, especially in the last ten days, and most probably on the twenty-seventh night. Although some have said that it was a one-time event because it was the night when the first revelation descended or when the victory of Badr occurred, the majority hold the view that it recurs every year. Whoever spends this night in worship attains a reward better than a thousand months. In connection with the command "read" in the preceding surah, the surah counsels prostrating and worshipping Allah, who sent down this magnificent Book.

In the first verse of the surah, it is stated that the disbelievers from among the People of the Book and the polytheists would not depart from their state of disbelief until a clear proof (bayyinah) came to them. This 'clear proof' is a Messenger sent by Allah. That Messenger recites purified pages, and within these pages are valuable, upright scriptures (the Quran).

While the first verse states that 'they would not depart,' the fourth verse states, 'The People of the Book did not divide until after the clear proof had come to them.' There is an apparent contradiction between these two statements. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi relates five different interpretations to resolve this contradiction. The finest of these belongs to the author of al-Kashshaf: Before the Prophet came, those disbelievers had promised, 'We will not depart from our religion until he comes.' Allah first recounts this statement of theirs, and then states, 'The People of the Book did not depart' (that is, they did not keep their word). From another perspective, Elmalılı adds this: That era was an interregnum (fatrah); they were considered excused until the clear proof arrived. However, once the clear proof arrived, those who remained obstinate had no excuse left.

The fifth verse explains what was actually commanded to the People of the Book: to worship Allah alone, making religion purely sincere to Him as hanifs (those who turn away from false beliefs and incline toward truth), to perform the prayer, and to give zakah. This is the upright and steadfast religion (din al-qayyim). These are the fundamental principles brought by all prophets.
In the sixth verse, it is stated that the disbelievers who deny the clear proof after it has come will abide eternally in the fire of Hell. They are the worst of creatures.

In the seventh verse, those who believe and perform righteous deeds are characterized as the best of creation. Righteous deeds do not consist solely of obligatory duties such as prayer and zakah; they also encompass every good deed conforming to Allah's pleasure and avoiding the forbidden.

In the eighth verse, it is stated that the reward of these believers is the Gardens of Eden (Adn) beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide eternally. Furthermore, glad tidings are given that Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Allah. This immense reward and pleasure are exclusive to those who fear their Lord (having khashyah). Khashyah is proportional to knowledge and spiritual discernment (ma'rifah); scholars have a greater fear of Allah.

The word 'zalzalah' mentioned in the first ayah of Surah az-Zilzal refers to the violent shaking of the earth. This shaking is the great earthquake that will occur on the Day of Resurrection. The terror of this earthquake is also described in Surah al-Hajj, Surah al-Waqi'ah, and other surahs.

In the second ayah, the earth bringing forth its burdens has been interpreted in two ways: first, the resurrection of the dead from their graves; second, the emergence of the treasures and minerals within the earth. Scholars who combine both views have stated that the word 'athqal' encompasses both the dead and the treasures. Whether this bringing forth occurs at the first blowing of the Trumpet or the second is disputed.

In the third ayah, it is described that man, in the face of this terrifying event, is bewildered and asks, 'What is the matter with this earth?' This expression emphasizes the horror of the earthquake and the bringing forth. In this situation, the disbelievers are gripped by fear, while the believers realize that Allah's promise has been fulfilled.

In the fourth and fifth ayahs, it is stated that on that Day the earth will recount all its news, because its Lord has inspired it. This recounting may be metaphorical, or it has also been interpreted as Allah literally causing the earth to speak. As narrated from the Prophet (peace be upon him), the earth will bear witness to the deeds that everyone committed upon it.

In the sixth ayah, it is stated that people will emerge in scattered groups, in various states: some with honor and some in disgrace; some mounted and some on foot; some felicitous and some wretched. Every community will be summoned with their leaders, or every individual will arrive alone.

In the seventh and eighth ayahs, it is explained that deeds will be displayed and that an atom's weight of good or evil will be recompensed. The purpose is to demonstrate that even the smallest good or evil is not lost in the sight of Allah. The atom (zarrah) is an exceedingly small entity and represents the lowest limit of accountability.

The letter 'waw' at the beginning of the surah is a particle of oath (qasam). 'Adiyat' means those that run swiftly; they can be horses, camels, or warriors. 'Dabh' is the panting sound of breath while running. 'Kadh' means striking sparks repeatedly, that is, striking sparks from stones with hooves. This indicates that the horses run swiftly at night. Even though some commentators interpreted this as tongues that kindle the fire of war or deceitful schemes, its most evident meaning is horses carrying out a night raid. Modern motorized vehicles also fall within this scope.

'Mugirat' means those that raid in the morning. 'Nak'an' means raising clouds of dust. This verbal clause, being coordinated with the preceding participles, yields the meaning: 'horses running breathlessly, striking fire from their hooves, launching a morning raid, raising clouds of dust.' The most widely accepted commentary on these verses is that they are the horses of cavalrymen. However, there are also those who state they are the camels of the pilgrims. In addition, it has been narrated that 'kadh' refers to enmity with the tongue, and 'mugirat' refers to bayonets.

As the response to the oath: 'Indeed, mankind is truly ungrateful to his Lord.' 'Kenûd' means one who denies blessings, a miser, and a faultfinder. In a hadith, it is described as: 'He eats alone, beats his slave, and withholds his due.' Man is himself a witness to this ingratitude; he either knows it in his conscience or will confess it in the Hereafter.

And man is exceedingly stubborn due to his intense love of worldly wealth. 'Khayr' ('hayır') here means wealth. 'Sedîd' means stingy or strong. That is, man loves wealth presuming it to be good, acts stingily, or is greedy in acquiring it. Yet in the Hereafter, when that which is inside the graves is overturned and that which is in the breasts is brought forth, everything will be exposed and man will understand what he has done.

On that Day, their Lord is fully aware of everything concerning them. The wealth hoarded in this world will be heated in the fire of Hell, and their owners' foreheads, flanks, and backs will be branded with it. This is stated in Surah at-Tawbah, verse 35. Its worldly example is the war raids described at the beginning of the surah. However, the punishment of the Hereafter is eternal. As al-Razi said: 'O man, while you make preparations for worldly benefit, what are you preparing for your Lord?' It is with this warning that people are encouraged to spend in the way of Allah.

The word Kâria is derived from the root 'kar'', meaning to strike violently. In the lexicon, it carries meanings such as a mallet, knocking on a door, and clashing with swords. Over time, it became a name for great calamities and especially for the Resurrection. In the Quran, in the form 'el-Kâria', it is a proper name expressing the terror of the Resurrection.

Several reasons have been put forward as to why Kâria was given this name: First, that it is the initial terrifying cry (the blowing of the Trumpet [Sur]) that will bewilder people's minds. Second, the violent collision of celestial and terrestrial bodies during the destruction of the cosmos. Third, that it strikes people with terror. Fourth, that it strikes the enemies of the truth with punishment and torment. This last view of Muqatil has been considered stronger.

The expression 'What is that kâria?' in the verses is not an actual question, but is intended to instill fear. The repetition of the name 'kâria' three times reinforces this intimidation. According to some scholars, this expression is a warning in the sense of 'beware, there is the kâria!' The true nature of kâria cannot be fully known by anyone until it is actually witnessed.

On the Day of Resurrection, people are likened to scattered and fluttering moths (butterflies). This simile depicts the bewilderment and wretchedness arising from the terror of that day. Although it has also been stated that they are likened to locusts, the simile of moths is more widespread.

The mountains, on the other hand, will become like carded colored wool. First they crumble, then they turn into a heap of sand, and then, dispersing like clouds, they turn into carded wool. This resembles a volcanic eruption of the earth. This first stage of the Resurrection encompasses the period between death and resurrection.

Those whose scales are heavy—that is, those whose good deeds outweigh their sins—will be in a pleasing life. The word 'mevâzîn' (scales) may be the plural of 'mîzân', just as it may be the plural of 'mevzûn' (the deeds weighed). The weighing of deeds is a reality, but there are different views regarding how it will be carried out: According to some, the record books of deeds are weighed, while according to others, the weighing is done by good and bad deeds taking physical form. It is obligatory (wajib) to believe in the reality of the scale, but knowing its exact manner is not a condition.

The destination of those whose scales are light is 'hâviye' (the abyss). 'Hâviye' is one of the names of Hell and denotes a deep abyss. The expression 'His mother is hâviye' has been interpreted in different ways: as being a refuge like a mother's embrace, as an expression of a curse, or as meaning the crown of his head. Ultimately, this conveys being cast into the bosom of Hell or falling headlong.

After asking what hâviye is, it is answered: 'It is a blazing fire.' This fire is fierce and scorching, forming the lowest level of Hell. This very fire is the eternal abode of those whose scales are light.

The surah addresses worldly wealth and the delusion of abundance that distracts people from their true purpose. The word 'alha' means distraction, occupying oneself with futile things and being diverted from important matters. 'Takathur', on the other hand, means boasting of abundance and competing for superiority against one another.

This boasting occurs through worldly things such as wealth, children, lineage, or tribal numbers. The verse is stated unconditionally; therefore, it encompasses boasting of every kind of abundance. However, what is specifically intended is boasting of worldly matters that divert a person from obedience to Allah.

There are different narrations regarding the reason for revelation: According to one narration, the Banu Abd Manaf and Banu Sahm, and according to another, two Ansar tribes of Madinah, competed over which was more numerous by counting even their dead. In another narration, greed for wealth is emphasized.

Three different meanings have been given to the expression 'until you visit the graves' in the verse: First, boasting of the number of the dead and physically visiting the graves; second, remaining in this heedlessness until the moment of death and awakening with death; and third, tasting the punishment of the grave.

The verse does not condemn boasting of abundance in an absolute sense, but rather taking pride in worldly wealth that diverts one from servitude to Allah. Competing in good deeds and taking pride in righteous actions is praised. What matters is sincerity and devotion (ikhlas).

Visiting graves is permissible and even a Sunnah if done to take heed and remember the Hereafter. However, visits made for the purpose of boasting and pride are condemned. Our Prophet first forbade visiting graves, and later permitted it for the sake of taking heed.

In summary, the surah warns people against being preoccupied with worldly wealth and the delusion of abundance, and reminds them of the Hereafter. When visiting graves, the primary purpose must be to take heed and awaken from heedlessness.

In this section, it is stated that boasting of abundance distracts a person until they reach the graves. Visiting graves was actually made permissible to take heed and remember the Hereafter. However, some have abused this visit to boast of the great number of their dead, and to take pride by using their names and fame. Such behaviors deserve the condemnation and rebuke of the verse. It is not correct to deny the lawful aspect of visiting graves; extensive information on this subject is found in books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

According to books of jurisprudence, visiting graves is permissible, and even a Sunnah. In works such as al-Durr al-Mukhtar, Imdad, al-Mujtaba, al-Bahr, and Radd al-Muhtar, it is explained that there is no objection even for women, through the Prophet's hadith: 'I had forbidden you to visit graves, so go and visit them.' The most virtuous days for visiting are Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday, and Thursday. It is Sunnah to supplicate while standing during the visit; when the Prophet went out to Baqi', he would say: 'Peace be upon you, O inhabitants of the abode of believers! We, if Allah wills, shall join you.' Furthermore, the Quran may be recited at the head or feet of the deceased; reciting al-Fatihah, the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah, Ayat al-Kursi, Amanar-Rasul, Ya-Sin, al-Mulk, Surah at-Takathur, and Surah al-Ikhlas is recommended.

In Ibn Abidin's Radd al-Muhtar, it is stated that gifting reward to the deceased is permissible, and that the rewards of deeds such as prayer, fasting, and charity can be bestowed upon others. In fact, in charity, intending for all believing men and women is more virtuous. Although some scholars wished to forbid gifting the reward of reciting the Quran to the Prophet, the majority argued that there was no need for such a restriction.

In his bequest to Abu Yusuf, Imam al-A'zam advises that in the face of the ruler's conduct contrary to knowledge, one should remind him of the truth while obeying, debate if he is an adherent of innovation, and take refuge in Allah if he does not accept. He also counsels visiting graves, shaykhs, and blessed places. All of this shows the legitimacy and wisdom of visiting graves; the essence is not to ask for help from the dead, but to give greetings of peace, pray to Allah, and gift rewards.

The concept of 'yaqin' (certain knowledge) mentioned in the verse is emphasized. Yaqin is knowledge free of doubt. It has three degrees: 'ilm al-yaqin (knowledge through reason and evidence), 'ayn al-yaqin (knowledge through seeing with the eye), and haqq al-yaqin (knowledge through direct personal experience). The expression 'ilma'l-yaqin' in this verse means either certain knowledge, or what is known in an absolute sense, or knowledge of death. Commentators are in agreement that the response to 'in' has been elided; it is estimated either as 'had you known, you would not have done so' or as 'what you would have done cannot be described.' The second view is preferred.

This verse contains a grave warning for scholars. For those who know with certainty the calamity at the end of boasting of abundance desist from this conduct. Thus, there is no certain knowledge in those who do not abandon boasting. The condition of those who bear the title of scholar yet do not act upon their knowledge is dire. Knowledge must be the most powerful motivator for righteous deeds. Otherwise, on the Day of Resurrection, there will be grief and regret.

In the next verse, it is declared: 'By all means, you shall surely see Hellfire.' This statement is not the response to the preceding 'in', but an independent threat in its own right. The 'lam' is for an oath. Hell is a blazing fire. Commentators state that this verse is not the response to 'in', because 'in' expresses impossibility; here, the aim is to inform that Hell will certainly be seen in the future. Although some have estimated it as 'had you known, you would have seen it,' this is more convoluted.

Then, it is declared: 'Then you shall surely see it with the eye of certainty.' 'Ayn' means either the eye, that is, seeing clearly; or essence, meaning certainty itself. The second meaning points to the degree of haqq al-yaqin; and this occurs by entering Hell. According to this interpretation, the first seeing is at the Gathering, and the second seeing is after entering Hell.

In the final verse, it is declared: 'Then, on that Day, you shall surely be questioned about the blessings.' 'Na'im' encompasses every kind of blessing: life, health, well-being, even a single sip of water. The address is directed at those who are distracted by their worldly life; and the questioning is by way of rebuke and punishment for those who misuse these blessings. Some commentators have said that the questioning applies only to disbelievers, while others have stated that it encompasses everyone, both believer and disbeliever. Narrations indicate that this questioning is general. Indeed, the Prophet (peace be upon him) informed us that we will be questioned about blessings, even if it be a single date and water.

It is well known that the Prophet (peace be upon him) and his Companions avoided ostentation to the utmost in their livelihood and spent blessings in the way of Allah. Accountability is proportional to the abundance of blessings. Therefore, boasting of abundance is a great heedlessness. The expression 'except for those who believe and do righteous deeds' in Surah al-Asr serves as an explanation of this verse.

The letter waw in the expression "Wal-'Asr" at the beginning of the surah is for an oath. In the dictionary, the word "'asr" has meanings such as: dehr (night and day/time), the two ends of the day, particularly the late afternoon, a group of people, and rain. As a verbal noun, it means to confine, to forbid, and to press and squeeze out juice. The specific time of something is also called "'asr". Commentators have primarily focused here on the following meanings: the 'Asr prayer, the late afternoon time, dehr and time, especially the era of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the end times. Ibn Jarir stated that the correct view is that "'asr" encompasses all these meanings. For "'asr" is a homonymous term (lafz mushtarak), and there is no contextual clue specifying any single one; therefore, it is most correct to apply it to all of them.

The first view: The 'Asr prayer. Muqatil stated that Allah Almighty swore by the 'Asr prayer. For the "middle prayer" (Al-Baqarah 2:238) is the 'Asr prayer and is of great merit. In a hadith, it was stated: "Whoever misses the 'Asr prayer, it is as though his family and his wealth were destroyed." Since the late afternoon is the time when people are most deeply engrossed in worldly affairs, an admonition was made by swearing an oath by this prayer.

The second view: The late afternoon time. Qatadah stated that just as Allah Almighty swore by the forenoon (duha), He also swore by the late afternoon. In terms of being the end of the day, the late afternoon resembles the final stages of a person's life. If a person does not gain anything at this time, they suffer loss. For this reason, after the deceptiveness of boasting in worldly increase was explained in the previous surah, swearing an oath by the late afternoon while describing the loss of mankind in this surah is of great significance.

The third view: Dehr (time). Those who say that asr means dehr draw attention to the importance of time. Time encompasses bitter and sweet events, and changes. In a narration from 'Ali, "asr" was interpreted as dehr, and by swearing an oath by time, it was recalled that man constantly encounters afflictions. Time itself is full of wondrous things; it is a process between non-existence and existence. Human lifespan is the most precious capital, and every moment of it brings profit or loss. Therefore, by swearing an oath by asr, the value of life is emphasized.

The fourth view: The era of the Prophet (peace be upon him). This era is the era of prophethood. It encompasses the Era of Bliss from the sending of the Prophet until his passing, as well as the end times that follow. This era is like the summary and the late afternoon of all times. In a hadith, it is related that this Ummah is compared to the late afternoon in relation to the other communities. For this reason, swearing an oath by asr indicates the virtue and importance of this era.

In conclusion: O Muhammad! By asr in all its meanings, particularly the final era, mankind is in absolute loss. Man's capital is his lifespan; every breath is running out and the reckoning is drawing near. Excepted, however, are those who possess the following four qualities: 1) Those who believe, 2) Those who do righteous deeds, 3) Those who advise one another to truth, 4) Those who advise one another to patience. These are not in loss, but in profit. Faith and righteous deeds are for a person's self-perfection, while advising to truth and patience is for perfecting others as well. Patience is divided into two: enduring pain for obedience and struggle, and refraining from forbidden things. These four qualities are the signs of complete faith in the Truth. Those who do not have these attributes are in ruin; and those who believe but do not act are also in a kind of loss. The explanation of the surah encompasses the entire Quran. The Companions would not part upon meeting without reciting this surah. How great indeed is our need to reflect upon our era and advise one another to truth and patience!

The words humazah and lumazah are intensive forms derived from the roots "hamz" and "lamz". "Hamz" means to pinch with the hand, prod, or break; while "lamz" means to reproach or disparage. These two words denote people who backbite, slander, mock, and gossip about others. According to some commentators, humazah refers to an assault committed with the hand, and lumazah to one committed with the tongue; while according to others, humazah denotes what is done to a person's face, and lumazah what is done behind their back. In general, these attributes are used for those who have made it a habit to wound people's honor and dignity, find fault, and mock.

One of the primary characteristics of those who adopt this habit is their fondness for amassing wealth and constantly counting it. They think that their wealth will make them immortal. Yet true salvation lies in faith and righteous deeds. By Allah, these arrogant and mocking individuals will surely be cast into the Hell called "Hutamah".

Hutamah is a specially kindled fire symbolizing Allah's wrath. It is unlike ordinary fires; it does not merely burn physical bodies, but penetrates right into souls and hearts. The closing of that fire over the people of Hell is depicted as its doors being shut tight with long pillars and props. This emphasizes the permanence and severity of the torment.

On the Day of Resurrection, after the disobedient believers are taken out of the Fire, the doors of Hell will be closed upon the disbelievers with covers, nails, and pillars of fire, leaving neither a breath of air nor an escape route. Allah will abandon them as if having forgotten them; the people of Paradise will be amidst bounties, while the people of Hell will be unable to ask for any help, and only their groans will be heard. O Allah, protect us from the fire of Hell and admit us into Paradise along with the righteous!

The question "Have you not seen?" at the beginning of the surah addresses the Prophet (peace be upon him) and expresses seeing with the heart's eye, that is, certain knowledge. The Incident of the Elephant was seen by many people living in that era, a universally known event that took place even while figures such as the famous poet Labid were alive. As narrated from Aisha, two of those who led the elephant were seen begging in Mecca, blind and crippled. Because this event was a sign portending the birth of the Prophet, he was specifically addressed.

Allah's asking "how He dealt" is to draw attention to the quality of the action. For the astonishing aspect of the incident is how it occurred. It was not an ordinary destruction, but took place in an extraordinary manner. With this question, Allah reminds people of the wonder of His treatment of the companions of the elephant and warns them against heedlessness. Theologians call this "the aspect of proof" (wajh al-dalil); that is, those who are heedless of the subtleties of the qualities cannot fully grasp the truth.

The companions of the elephant were the Abyssinian army under the command of Abraha, who had invaded Yemen. Relying on Mahmud, a large elephant, they came to destroy the Kaaba, but were unsuccessful and were devastated. This event is known among the Arabs as the "Year of the Elephant," and the Prophet was born in this year—according to reports, fifty days after the incident. When calculated according to the Hijri calendar, it is stated that this event corresponds to the 880s CE.

Allah rendered their plots futile. He ruined their secret plans, termed "kayd," by abandoning them to straying and error. Their aim was to demolish the Kaaba and replace it with the church of al-Qullays. Yet they were devastated before they could even drive their elephants into Mecca. Then Allah sent upon them the ababil birds. Ababil means flocks of birds coming in successive groups and droves. These birds were strange birds never seen before; some were large, some small, in black, green, and white colors.

These birds threw stones of baked clay (sijjil) at the companions of the elephant. Sijjil refers to stones of mud hardened like tiles, derived from the Persian words "sang" (stone) and "gil" (mud). According to reports, these stones were the size of lentils, chickpeas, or hazelnuts. It is related that each bird carried three stones—one in its beak and two in its claws—and that whichever person was struck, the stone pierced straight through their body. Thus, the army was torn to shreds like eaten straw. The expression "asf ma'kul" likens them to fresh crop leaves eaten and scattered by animals, describing how they were destroyed.

This event is a clear proof of Allah's power. As Fakhr al-Din al-Razi also noted, this incident took place so recently and before so many witnesses that had it been a fabrication, the Meccan polytheists would have immediately denied it. Yet none of them denied it; on the contrary, many poets recounted this incident in their poems. Therefore, rather than attempting to explain this story through natural causes, one must accept it as an extraordinary act of Allah and take heed.

Even if extraordinary events recorded in history do not conform to normal laws, science does not deny them; rather, it records and examines them, however rare they may be. The Quran's account of the Incident of the Elephant is just like this: this incident is an exceptional event demonstrating Allah's power and has been transmitted through mutawatir (successively reported, definitive knowledge) chains. The Prophet (peace be upon him) lived in the aftermath of this event and grew up hearing of it from his surroundings. For this reason, he was addressed with: "Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?"

The Incident of the Elephant begins during the Abyssinian rule in Yemen, when Abraha set out to destroy the Kaaba. Abraha had built a grand church in Sana'a and intended to redirect the pilgrimage of the Arabs to it. Enraged when the Arabs desecrated the church, Abraha marched upon Mecca with a vast army and elephants. Realizing they could not resist, the Quraysh withdrew to the mountains. Abd al-Muttalib went to Abraha, demanded the return of his camels, and stated that the protector of the Kaaba was Allah.

As Abraha was preparing to enter Mecca, the great elephant among them named Mahmud refused to move forward. At that very moment, Allah Almighty sent flocks of birds from the sea. Each bird carried stones like chickpeas and lentils in its beak and claws. These stones rained down upon the Abyssinian army, and whomever was struck was destroyed. The army was routed, and the fleeing soldiers trampled one another on the roads. Abraha was also wounded, his limbs falling off piece by piece, and he died.

In some reports, it is said that following this event, smallpox and measles were seen in Arabia for the first time. However, these reports are weak (da'if) and isolated. In a narration transmitted from 'Ikrimah, it is stated that smallpox broke out in the people struck by the stones thrown by the birds. But this too does not rely on a reliable chain of transmission. In the face of the clear account of the Quran and the widely accepted reports, such narrations carry little weight.

Certain orientalists and contemporary writers have attempted to portray this incident as an ordinary epidemic of disease. However, Elmalılı criticizes such interpretations. In particular, he sternly rejects Abduh's attempt to obscure the miraculous aspect of the incident by elevating a weak narration to the rank of mutawatir. He emphasizes that the Incident of the Elephant was a manifest divine punishment and that the birds' stones were an integral part of it. Attempting to explain the event through natural causes diminishes its extraordinary nature and its instructive value.

When commenting on this surah, Abduh first states: The surah reminds us of the greatness of Allah's power. A people, relying on their elephants, wished to harm the servants of Allah, and Allah destroyed them, thwarting their plans. Understanding this much is sufficient for drawing an admonition.

Abduh then states that it is permissible to delve into details regarding the Incident of the Elephant. For this incident is a well-known and mutawatir report. Indeed, the Arabs used to date events according to the Year of the Elephant. For this reason, detailed elaboration is permissible.

However, Elmalılı points out that there is an error in this detailed elaboration by Abduh. Under the classification of 'mutawatir,' Abduh relates only this: An Abyssinian commander came with a large army to demolish the Kaaba, reached the vicinity of Mecca, and sent an envoy. Yet Abduh says, 'On the second day, smallpox and measles spread in the Abyssinian army,' which is not mutawatir.

Elmalılı refutes this claim of Abduh. The narrations of 'Ikrimah and Ya'qub ibn 'Utbah are weak, and in reality, their destruction by the birds throwing stones is what is mutawatir. Abduh distorted these narrations to fit his own view, ignored the expressions 'birds' and 'stones,' and reduced the incident to a disease.

Abduh goes even further, asserting that the birds were flies or disease-bearing creatures, and the stones were mud clinging to their feet. Elmalılı emphasizes that this is contrary to the clear declaration of the Quran. The surah explicitly speaks of 'flocks of birds' and stones of 'sijjil' (baked clay). Interpreting these as flies and dust is distortion.

Elmalılı states that the correct course is to believe as conveyed by the Quran and authentic narrations. Explaining the incident as a normal epidemic of disease diminishes divine power. Allah does whatever He wills, and it is not right to confine extraordinary events within the limits of human reason.

In this section, Elmalılı addresses a controversial issue regarding the commentary of Surah al-Fil. He strongly rejects the view of certain commentators that the stones cast upon them by the birds were the agents of smallpox or measles. In his view, this interpretation contradicts both the wording and the spirit of the verse, because the verse explicitly mentions stones called 'sijjil' (hardened clay). There is neither a rational nor a textual proof to restrict these stones to an illness such as smallpox. Furthermore, such an interpretation limits Allah's power and imposes conditions on His act of creating as He wills.

Elmalılı specifically criticizes the interpretation of Abduh. Abduh interpreted the birds as invisible microbes and explained the stones as microbe-bearing stones. According to Elmalılı, this interpretation is weak from the standpoint of both traditional narration (riwayah) and analytical reasoning (dirayah). He states that during the period when the surah was revealed, the Arabs did not derive the meaning of microbes from these verses; rather, they understood the event as visible birds and stones. He maintains that this interpretation of Abduh distorts the plain meaning of the verse and weakens the message of the surah.

Elmalılı emphasizes that the most admonitory aspect of the Incident of the Elephant is that the army, coming to demolish the Ka'bah relying on its own might, was routed by Allah in an entirely unexpected manner. The verse, 'Did He not make their plan go astray?' constitutes the core of the event. The sending of birds and stones, on the other hand, are secondary verses that explain the nature of this divine intervention. In the face of such a clear event, the fact that even the polytheists attributed it to Allah shows that the event was no ordinary occurrence.

He cites a question posed by Fakhr al-Din al-Razi: 'Even though the disbelievers of Quraysh filled the Ka'bah with idols, why did Allah punish not them, but those who sought to demolish the Ka'bah?' Elmalılı also relays the answer given by al-Razi: 'Because filling the Ka'bah with idols is a violation of Allah's right, whereas demolishing it is a violation of the people's right. Worldly punishments are predominantly inflicted for violations committed against the rights of servants. The punishment for violating Allah's right, however, fundamentally belongs to the Hereafter.' Furthermore, the wisdom behind this event was that it served as a preparation for the birth and prophetic call of the Messenger of Allah.

To defend the historical reality of the Incident of the Elephant, Elmalılı provides examples from poems composed during that period. He notes that in the poems of poets such as Abdullah ibn al-Ziba'ra, Abu Qays Sayfi, and Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, they recount the destruction of the army with birds and stones. These poems demonstrate that the event was acknowledged even by adversaries and transmitted through successive reporting (tawatur). In light of these proofs, Elmalılı opposes those who deny or allegorically interpret (ta'wil) the event, emphasizing that at the time the surah was revealed, no one contradicted these accounts.

Lastly, as Elmalılı continues his critique of Abduh's interpretation, he remarks that the fine ideas in his work lose value due to such weak interpretations. He also draws attention to the error of certain translators who render the verse as 'they threw microbe-bearing stones.' In his view, such interpretations are unacceptable in the face of the surah's explicit wording. He states that well-intentioned people of knowledge must exercise caution in this regard.

The surah begins by mentioning the îlâf of Quraysh. The spelling of the word 'îlâf' varies according to different recitations (qira'at); in some it is written with a hamzah, and in others with the letter 'ya'. These differences point to the different pronunciations and meanings of the word. The original spelling in the mushafs of 'Uthman is without an 'alif' and with a 'ya', and this form encompasses all three recitations simultaneously.

Îlâf derives from the root 'ulfah'. In the if'al form, it means 'to accustom, to make inclined', and in the mufa'alah form, it means 'to agree, to enter into a covenant'. It expresses both Quraysh's mutual agreements among themselves and their commercial and political agreements with those around them. It is not correct to reduce this word to a single meaning; it encompasses the meanings of both familiarity (ulfah) and covenant-making.

Quraysh is the great Arab tribe to which the Prophet (peace be upon him) also belonged. Its lineage traces back to Fihr b. Malik b. al-Nadr b. Kinanah. Its name is derived from the word 'taqarrush', which means 'gathering, coming together' or 'engaging in trade'. This diminutive expression is actually intended to denote greatness and honor. Thanks to leaders such as Qusayy and Hashim, Quraysh distinguished itself from the other tribes in Mecca and attained a preeminent position.

The letter 'lam' at the beginning of the surah has been interpreted in three ways. First, it is for ta'ajjub (wonder/astonishment): expressing surprise that Quraysh fails to give thanks despite these blessings. Second, it is for ta'lil (expressing cause/reason): it is linked either to the action in the preceding surah (the destruction of the companions of the elephant) or to the command 'let them worship'. The preferred view is that the 'lam' serves as ta'lil for the command 'let them worship'. Third, this lam recalls the past and future îlâf of Quraysh, especially the treaties that ensured the security of the pilgrimage and trade routes.

The winter and summer journeys of Quraysh were travels undertaken for the purpose of trade. In winter they would go to Yemen, and in summer to al-Sham (Syria). Hashim and his brothers made agreements with neighboring kingdoms for the safety of these journeys, securing immunity for the merchants of Quraysh. These agreements were virtually in the nature of capitulations. The Event of the Elephant reinforced this order and enhanced the prestige of Quraysh.

Allah bestowed favor upon Quraysh by both saving them from hunger (nourishment through trade) and granting them security from a great fear (the attack of the elephant army). In return for these blessings, Quraysh must worship the Lord of this House (the Kaaba), abandon polytheism (shirk), and adhere to the religion of tawhid (monotheism). In connection with the preceding surahs, the surah serves as a reminder of the fundamental principles of Islam and transitions to Surah al-Ma'un.

Surah al-Ma'un criticizes a life that leaves religion merely in words and is devoid of mercy and responsibility. Here, Elmalılı emphasizes that religion must be understood together with morality, worship, and social sensitivity.

Pushing the orphan away and not encouraging the feeding of the poor is the sign of a heart that does not take accountability in the Hereafter seriously. The surah reminds us that faith must be visible in one's conduct toward the weak and vulnerable in society.
Those who perform prayer yet are heedless of their prayer are also warned. The problem here is not prayer itself, but detaching prayer from its spirit and turning it into ostentation or mere habit.

'Preventing ma'un' means withholding even seemingly small acts of assistance. According to Elmalılı, true religious devotion also encompasses everyday kindnesses and small gestures of support in times of need.
In short, the surah states that worship must be completed with mercy, sincerity, and assistance.

In this surah, Allah the Exalted addresses the Messenger of Allah, saying: "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar." In Arabic, Kawthar is derived from the root kathrah, meaning abundance, and denotes something that is exceedingly abundant. In the lexicon, it signifies the majority of something, an extraordinarily benevolent man, a most generous giver, and a specific river in Paradise. Here, the fact that what is given is mentioned by Allah with immense majesty demonstrates that it indeed signifies an eternal and infinite abundance. The first obvious meaning understood is 'khayr-i kesir', that is, abundant good.

Regarding what Kawthar is, the commentators have enumerated up to twenty-six opinions. One of the most famous is that Kawthar is a river in Paradise. This meaning is established through sound hadiths. In the hadiths, it is reported that this river is whiter than milk, sweeter than honey, its width is as vast as the distance between the east and the west, and the Ummah will drink from it on the Day of Resurrection. Furthermore, a basin belonging to our Prophet is also mentioned, which some say is located on the Gathering Plain. However, belief in these basins is not obligatory; yet, because the hadiths concerning our Prophet's basin are well-known, belief in it has been deemed obligatory by the Ahl al-Sunnah.

According to the second opinion, Kawthar is the honor of prophethood. Prophethood is an abundant good that encompasses happiness in this world and the Hereafter. The third opinion is the scholars of the Ummah. As the inheritors of the prophets, the scholars draw grace from the source of revelation and teach good to the Ummah. The fourth opinion is the great number of the Ummah. Allah has granted the Messenger of Allah so many noble Companions and such an abundant Ummah that more than half of the people of Paradise will be from his Ummah. The fifth opinion is the abundance of our Prophet's descendants. This surah was revealed as an answer to his enemies who called him 'abtar' (one cut off from lineage) when his son died. Allah gave the glad tidings that his lineage would not be severed, but rather that He would grant him an abundant progeny.

The majority of commentators have accepted Kawthar as 'abundant good' because this is its broadest lexical meaning. The other meanings are also included within this concept of 'abundant good'. The famous view narrated from Ibn Abbas is likewise that Kawthar is the good that Allah bestowed upon His Messenger. The description of the river in the hadiths can be understood as the most prominent example of this good. For this reason, while accepting the hadiths about the river, commentators have preferred the meaning of 'abundant good' by considering all the possibilities of the wording.

That Kawthar is a river in Paradise is supported especially by the hadiths of the Mi'raj. This river was shown to our Prophet during the Mi'raj, and great manifestations occurred near the Sidrat al-Muntaha. This meaning points to eternal and sacred objectives of good. However, interpreting it as 'abundant good' in a way that everyone can understand is more comprehensive and beneficial. Allah's expression of the verb 'We have given' in the past tense shows that this bounty was an accomplished fact realized while in this world. All future goods are also evaluated within this giving. Kawthar is an uninterrupted and infinite gift encompassing the goods of both this world and the Hereafter.

Kawthar is a bounty specific to the Prophet and the source of the rivers of Paradise. In this surah, the statement 'We have given you al-Kawthar' in the past tense carries the meaning of an announcement from pre-eternity, an establishment in the present, and a commitment for the future. This gives the glad tidings that all goods in this world and the Hereafter—blessings such as knowledge, wisdom, prophethood, the Quran, and sublime character—have been bestowed upon the Prophet and his Ummah. This favor is continuous, and the Prophet's family, his Companions, and the Followers (tabi'un) will also partake in this grace.

As gratitude for this blessing of Kawthar, the Prophet was commanded to perform prayer. The letter 'fa' indicates that this command is connected to the preceding favor. Prayer is the foremost of acts of worship, encompassing every form of gratitude. The qualification 'pray for your Lord' emphasizes that the prayer must be performed purely for Allah's pleasure, with sincerity. This is the essence of prayer and requires staying away from ostentation.

Along with the command of prayer came the command of sacrificial slaughter. It carries the meaning of 'pray for your Lord, and sacrifice for your Lord,' and it is a condition that both acts of worship be performed solely for Allah. The sacrifice is an act of worship requiring financial sacrifice and was made obligatory specifically for the Prophet. This command also encompasses sacrificing after the prayer and may point to the Eid prayer.

There are differing views regarding which prayer the command refers to: the obligatory prayers, supererogatory prayers, the Eid prayer, or the mid-morning (duha) prayer. In addition to the five daily prayers, the tahajjud and duha prayers were also obligatory for the Prophet. Since the Eid prayer had not yet been made obligatory in Mecca, it can be considered that this command was directed toward the duha prayer. However, there are also those who state that the surah is Medinan.

Regarding the command to sacrifice, it has been narrated that while it was obligatory for the Prophet, it was not made obligatory for the Ummah. In the Hanafi school, sacrifice is considered wajib. This command refers to the udhiyyah sacrifice slaughtered after the Eid prayer. The word 'nahr' means slaughtering, and the principle that this worship must be performed for Allah is a requirement of Islam's understanding of tawhid.

The word "nahr" in the second verse of Surah al-Kawthar has generally been interpreted as "to sacrifice an animal." Elmalılı states that beyond the slaughter of camels, this word encompasses all cattle and small livestock, though it is more commonly used for camels. Furthermore, he emphasizes that the command in the verse entails performing prayer along with sacrificing an animal for the pleasure of Allah.

Hadiths concerning the sacrificial practices of our Noble Prophet are cited: his slaughtering of a ram, his slaughtering the sacrifice himself while saying "Bismillahi wallahu akbar," and matters such as a camel sufficing as a sacrifice for seven people. Elmalılı notes that the most virtuous sacrifice is a ram, yet points out the camel's great size.

Although some scholars have interpreted "nahr" as raising the hands to the chest in prayer or facing the qiblah, Elmalılı rejects this view. According to him, the clear meaning of the verse is sacrificial slaughter; contrary interpretations rely on reports with weak chains of narration and do not accord with the context of the verse.

The words "shani'" (the one who hates) and "abtar" (docked, cut off) mentioned in the third verse are explained. Elmalılı states that this verse signifies that those who harbor animosity toward the Prophet are the ones who are truly cut off, and that their lineages and good fortunes will be severed. The verse is an answer to those who called the Messenger of Allah 'abtar' due to the death of his sons.

At the end of the surah, gratitude and worship to Allah are emphasized with the command, "Pray for your Lord and sacrifice." Elmalılı expresses that these verses are connected to similar commands in Surahs al-Duha and al-An'am, and that Kawthar is an uninterrupted good. He also dwells upon the wisdom behind the Prophet's lineage continuing through his daughter.

Surah al-Kafirun was revealed in the Meccan period and consists of six verses. This surah is also called 'al-Muqashqishah'; this name means that which cures or rids one of diseases such as polytheism (shirk) and hypocrisy (nifaq). It is also referred to as the 'Surah of Worship' and the 'Surah of Sincerity'. Together with Surah al-Kawthar, they are described as 'al-Ikhlasayn' (the two surahs of sincerity). In hadiths, the virtue of this surah has been emphasized, and it has been stated that it is equivalent to a quarter of the Quran.

As for the occasion of revelation, the following incident is narrated: The notables of Quraysh came to our Prophet (peace be upon him) and proposed, 'You worship our gods, and we will worship your God; whichever is better, we will all attain it together.' The Prophet rejected this offer, saying, 'Allah forbid that I should associate partners with Allah!' and upon this, Allah Almighty revealed this surah.

The surah begins with the command, 'Say: O disbelievers!' This address is specifically directed toward those who are known in the sight of Allah as never coming to faith. Our Prophet did not utter these words of his own accord, but conveyed them by the command he received from Allah. This call is a decisive refutation of the polytheists' proposal and a warning that exposes their persistence in disbelief.

In the second and third verses, it is stated: 'I do not worship what you worship. Nor do you worship what I worship.' Here, our Prophet declares that he will never worship the idols of the polytheists and that they will never properly worship Allah. For the condition of worship is sincerity (ikhlas); worship performed by associating partners with Allah is invalid.

Although the fourth and fifth verses appear to be a repetition, they actually point to different periods of time. The expression 'Nor am I going to worship what you have worshipped' indicates that he did not worship idols in the past either, while the expression 'Nor are you going to worship what I worship' indicates that they will not worship with sincerity in the future either. These repetitions serve to dash the hopes of those who persist in disbelief.

The sixth verse: 'For you is your religion, and for me is my religion.' This carries the meaning that their religious choices are not interfered with, but believers will not compromise on their own religion either. The verse is not a proposal for a treaty, but a rejection and a warning. For this reason, there is no abrogation (naskh) in the surah; all of it is clear and decisive (muhkam). The surah teaches believers to stay away from disbelief and hypocrisy, and to worship with sincerity.

In this section, emphasis is placed on the use of the word "âbid" (worshipper) in the verse as an active participle (ism al-fa'il) and on the meaning of the particle "mâ". Although al-Kisa'i accepted that the active participle could govern a conjunctive "mâ" (al-mawsulah) carrying a past-tense meaning, the majority of scholars reject this. Although it is mentioned in al-Kashshaf that this view of al-Kisa'i was adopted, it was considered improbable. For this reason, it is more appropriate for "âbid" in the first verse to convey a future meaning and in the second to convey a present meaning. However, the use of the past tense form "you have not worshipped" in the third verse provides a clue to considering a past-tense connotation by way of allusive indication in "âbid" here as well. Therefore, neither the present and future meaning nor the past meaning should be neglected. This grammatical governance occurs either by way of formal correspondence (mushakalah) with the preceding, or because "mâ" is interpreted in the sense of worship, functioning like a masdariyyah (verbal noun) in place of an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). In this case, treating "mâ" in the subsequent verses as masdariyyah and directing it toward an absolute active participle so as to encompass all three—past, present, and future—in negation is more fitting for the comprehensive inclusion (istighraq) of an indefinite noun occurring in a negative context (siyaq al-nafy), and serves as the strongest of emphatic reinforcements.

Here, many subtle nuances are pointed out through the various conjugations of the verb of worship. Numerous interpretive forms emerge depending on the meanings of the particles "mâ" and the ways the conjunctions "waw" connect them. The verbs carry a present-tense meaning; however, since it is not possible in Turkish to form a relative clause directly from the present and imperfect verb, expressions such as "that which you worship / worshipped, that which I worship" have been used in the translation. Yet this distinction is important; for while both "that which you are worshipping" (present) and "that which you worshipped" (past) are used for the addressees, only the expression "that which I worship" (present) is used for the portion pertaining to the Prophet, and the past is passed over silently. This serves as a reminder that the action of the Prophet that must be followed is his worship from the onset of his prophethood onward.

In the exegesis of the sixth verse, emphasis is placed on the statement "Lekum dinukum veliye din" (For you is your religion, and for me is my religion). According to the majority of commentators, this is a reinforcement of the earlier statements "I do not worship what you worship" and "Nor am I a worshipper of what you worship." That is to say, this is the proclamation of steadfastness. The Prophet's religion is the true religion of Islam, which consists of worship and obedience to Allah with tawhid (monotheism) and sincerity. There are many interpretations of this verse: First, it is a threat, like "Do whatever you will" (Fussilat 40/40). Second, it is a statement uttered by the Prophet to dissuade them from inviting him to polytheism. Third, it encompasses the dimensions of belief and deeds of religion: Your religion is for you, and mine is for me. Fourth, religion here means recompense; that is, the requital for your religion is upon you, and the requital for mine is upon me. Fifth, religion means supplication (du'a); your supplication is futile, while mine is accepted. Sixth, religion means custom; your custom of polytheism is for you, and my custom received through revelation is for me.

Al-Razi addresses three issues. The first issue: Does this verse permit disbelief? No, because the Prophet was sent to forbid disbelief. What is meant is a threat, deterrence, or saying: 'If being destroyed is good for you, then remain upon your religion.' The second issue: The statement "For you is your religion" carries the meaning of restriction (takhsis, belonging exclusively to you). This points to the verses "And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives" (al-Najm 53/39) and "No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" (al-Isra 17/15). That is, everyone is responsible for their own deeds. The Prophet's duty is conveyance, and your persistence in disbelief will not harm him. Al-Razi explains this restriction as 'it belongs to you, not to me; and it belongs to me, not to you.' Abu al-Su'ud expresses it even more clearly: 'Your religion is assigned exclusively to you and does not pass over to my side; and my religion is assigned exclusively to me and does not pass over to you.'

The third issue: Al-Razi states that it is not permissible for people to use this verse as an illustrative citation (tamthil) during treaties, because the Quran was not revealed for casual quotation, but to be reflected upon and acted upon. However, al-Alusi objects to this; quotation (iqtibas) is permissible, and there are examples of it in the words of the Prophet, the Companions, and scholars. Yet it must not be forgotten that quoting is not appropriate everywhere, but only in contexts that are suitable and not contrary to reverence. Whether this verse is abrogated (mansukh) has also been debated. Qadi al-Baydawi says that there is neither permission for disbelief nor prohibition of jihad here; its abrogation by the verse of fighting could only be in question if it were interpreted as a treaty. The fact that this surah is followed by Surah al-Nasr indicates that this is not of the category of the abrogated, but rather of the nature of struggle (mujahadah).

The surah announces that when the help of Allah and the conquest come, the Prophet will see people entering the religion of Allah in waves. Here, 'nasr' means victory against the enemy, and 'fath' means the conquest of lands such as the conquest of Mecca. Some commentators have stated that this help and conquest are not limited to Mecca alone, but point to all future conquests. Indeed, after the conquest of Mecca, Islam spread rapidly, and tribes embraced Islam in throngs.

The expression 'you saw the people' in the verse signifies seeing with the eye or knowing with the heart. The verb form 'entering' indicates that the entry was not yet complete, but would continue gradually. 'Fawj fawj' (fevc fevc), on the other hand, means in groups, troop by troop. This denotes that entering Islam was like a procession, and that this process, which began with the conquest of Mecca, continued until the passing of the Prophet.

When these events took place, the Prophet was commanded to glorify his Lord with praise. Tasbih means declaring Allah free from every kind of deficiency, while hamd means praising Him. Here, tasbih and hamd are mentioned together, which signifies commemorating Allah's attributes of majesty (jalal) and bounty (ikram) together. That is, one must exalt Allah by remembering both His power and His grace.

Furthermore, the Prophet was commanded to make istighfar, that is, to seek forgiveness from Allah. This was to be done both for himself and for his community (ummah). Istighfar entails regretting sins and resolving not to commit them again. Merely uttering words of forgiveness is not enough; heartfelt remorse and repentance (tawbah) are required. It is conveyed that Allah is ever-accepting of repentance.

At the end of the surah, it is narrated that these commands came at a time close to the passing of the Prophet. It is reported from Aisha that when the Prophet heard this surah, he began to make tasbih and istighfar abundantly. This shows that the religion had reached perfection and the Prophet's mission was completed. Drawing from this example, believers too should give thanks to Allah and seek forgiveness in moments of success and victory.

Al-Alusi says: No matter how hard a servant strives, he cannot be free of shortcomings in fulfilling what is truly due to the majesty of the Worshipped. For this reason, istighfar has been prescribed following many acts of worship, such as seeking forgiveness three times after the obligatory prayer, the one who performs the night prayer (tahajjud) seeking forgiveness in the pre-dawn hours, and the pilgrim seeking forgiveness after the Hajj. It has been narrated that this command of istighfar pointed to the news of his death; with the religion reaching perfection, it was understood that the mission of calling to Islam was nearing its end.

At the beginning of the surah, with the promise of help and conquest, it was announced that the people would enter Islam in droves, after which tasbih, hamd, and istighfar were commanded. This command is a sign that the passing of the Prophet was near and that his mission would be completed. Indeed, this surah was revealed shortly before the passing of the Prophet, and Companions such as Abbas and Umar understood this.

In Razi's tafsir, it is noted that there are two paths for travelers of truth: The first is the path of those who say, 'I have not seen anything without seeing Allah after it'; and the second is the path of those who say, 'I have not seen anything without seeing Allah before it.' The second path is more perfect. This surah points to this superior path by mentioning first tasbih and hamd (directed toward the Creator), and then istighfar (directed toward the creation). Tasbih indicates the attributes of majesty, while tahmid indicates the attributes of beauty; istighfar, on the other hand, is to recognize the shortcomings of the self and seek pardon from Allah.

Following the conquest and victory, the Prophet was given the choice between worldly blessings and meeting Allah, and he chose meeting Allah. This surah signifies that he would now engage in tasbih and hamd, leave the religion to his community, and meet his Lord. In the tenth year of the Hijrah, the Farewell Pilgrimage was performed, the final verses were revealed, and then the Prophet fell ill and passed away on Monday, the twelfth of Rabi' al-Awwal. His last words were: 'Nay, the highest companion (al-rafiq al-a'la).'

After the passing of the Prophet, the conquests of Islam did not cease, and its enemies still failed to achieve their desires. To convey this, Surah al-Tabbat was revealed, reporting that the Prophet's uncle, Abu Lahab, was ruined by persisting in disbelief. This surah demonstrates the end of those who do not believe.

Surah Tebbet foretells the ruin of Abu Lahab and his wife. The word "tebbet" bears the meaning of both the report that 'he perished' and the curse of 'may he be ruined'. Due to his hostility toward our Prophet, Abu Lahab died in despair after the Battle of Badr, and thus the surah's prophecy was fulfilled. His two hands—that is, all his means and efforts—came to naught, and he was ruined.

The reason Abu Lahab is specifically mentioned in the surah is that, despite being the Prophet's uncle, he persisted in disbelief and therefore deserved the severest condemnation. Furthermore, the name "Abu Lahab" literally means 'father of flame'; this indicates that he is destined for Hell and represents all fire-spitting disbelievers. Lineage and honor could not save him, and this served as an admonition to other people.

Abu Lahab's wealth and what he earned (his children, commerce, his hostilities) availed him nothing and did not save him from destruction. The word 'kesb' mentioned in the verse encompasses all these gains. Along with all of these, he will enter a blazing fire—Hell.

Abu Lahab's wife, Umm Jamil, will also enter Hell and be depicted as a 'carrier of firewood'. This expression is an allusion to her carrying thorns in the worldly life to torment the Prophet or to her spreading malicious gossip. Furthermore, it should be remembered that the firewood of Hell is the disbelievers. His wife sharing in the punishment will increase Abu Lahab's suffering.

Around her neck, instead of a necklace, there will be a sturdy rope called "mesed". This rope is a strong cord twisted from palm fibers. For a woman who lived in adornment and honor in this world to be humiliated in the Hereafter as a carrier of firewood with a rope around her neck is the bitter consequence of disbelief and ingratitude. The surah concludes with this exemplary scene.
Surah al-Ikhlas is one of the shortest and most concise surahs introducing Allah. Elmalılı states that the surah explains tawhid (the oneness of Allah) in a simple yet very profound manner.

The command 'Say' demonstrates that this knowledge is not our Prophet's own words, but the truth revealed by Allah. The believer also comes to know Allah through this divine declaration and proclaims it as such.

The expression 'Allah is One' proclaims that Allah has no peer, partner, likeness, or second deity. This oneness is not merely in terms of number, but in the sense of being unique in His Essence and divinity.
The name 'al-Samad' conveys that everyone is in need of Allah, while Allah is in need of nothing. All needs are directed to Him; He is flawless, complete, and not dependent on any being.

The expression 'He neither begets nor is born' refutes notions of lineage, ancestry, and physical comparisons regarding Allah. Allah does not resemble created beings; He is not limited by a beginning or an end.
The sentence 'Nor is anything equal to Him' completes the culmination of tawhid. According to Elmalılı, the surah exalts Allah above both having partners and resembling created beings.
In short, Surah al-Ikhlas teaches knowing Allah as One, unique, absolutely free of need, and far removed from all imperfections.

The surah begins with the command "Say." The Prophet (peace be upon him) was commanded to say "Say." This command is addressed not only to the Prophet, but to all believers until the Day of Resurrection. For this reason, the surahs were recorded verbatim in the copies of the Quran (mushafs) and reciting them in this manner became obligatory (wajib). As Imam al-Maturidi also stated, the one charged with this command is not solely the direct addressee, but every accountable individual. Whoever recites it does so as though commanding both himself and everyone else to utter this supplication.

The word falaq derives from the root falq, meaning 'to split' or 'to cleave.' In the lexicon, it bears numerous meanings, such as a fissure, a crack, the light of dawn, creatures, or a pit in Hell. Its most comprehensive meaning encompasses all creatures that have been cleaved out of nonexistence. In this sense, falaq stands in contrast to the divine attribute of al-Samad. That is to say, falaq denotes everything that is created and destined to perish. As for the meaning of daybreak, it symbolizes the light that emerges after darkness and the relief that follows distress. In this respect, the expression 'Rabbi'l-falaq' bestows a promise of deliverance and hope upon the one seeking refuge.

The use of the name al-Rabb (the Lord) here indicates that the one seeking refuge is in need of the Lord in every state. The servant can never be independent of the Lord in any matter. Furthermore, saying 'the Lord of falaq' signifies that He is the Lord of both the one sought refuge in and the one seeking refuge. This emphasizes the need for protection against both external and internal evils. As Ibn Sina also pointed out, there is a subtle secret here: the servant is commanded to seek refuge in his Lord, which serves as a reminder that perfection and good come from Allah, whereas evil stems from one's own lower self.

In the second verse, by stating, 'From the evil of what He has created,' it is commanded to seek refuge in Allah from every kind of evil that He has created. This evil encompasses every sort of harm, whether material or spiritual, worldly or otherworldly, originating from outside or arising from one's own soul. All kinds of creatures and phenomena—such as humans, jinn, animals, insects, microbes, fire, and poison—as well as the evil of sins, desires (hawa), the lower self (nafs), and corrupt deeds, fall within this scope. All evils directed against the one seeking refuge are covered by this verse. The evil of the self is also included, for the greatest enemy lies between a person's two sides.

In the third verse, it is stated, 'And from the evil of ghasiq when it enters/overtakes (waqaba).' Ghasiq carries meanings such as the night, the moon, the Pleiades (Thurayya), a snake, or the groin. The most renowned interpretation is the darkness of the night. Waqab, on the other hand, means to enter, descend, fall, or set. Accordingly, the verse means, 'from the evil of the night when its darkness settles.' Evils that occur at night and sudden afflictions fall under this evil. The eclipse or setting of the moon has also been interpreted within this scope. This verse teaches seeking protection especially against perils that emerge during dark and hidden times.

According to a view cited by al-Razi, Surah al-Falaq and Surah al-Nas explain the ranks of created beings. Evil occurs in the corporeal realm. Bodies are either ethereal (subtle, orderly) or elemental (dense, corruptible). There is no disorder in ethereal bodies; they are entirely good. Elemental bodies, on the other hand, can be inanimate, plant, or animal. In inanimate objects, there is no appetitive faculty; utter darkness prevails. This is precisely what the expression 'from the evil of the night when it darkens' points to. Plants possess the faculty of growth. Animals possess faculties such as sensation, lust, and anger, and these deter the human soul from being devoted to Allah. The verse 'and from the evil of an envier when he envies' also depicts this animalistic faculty. After this level remains the human soul (nafs), whose degrees are mentioned in Surah al-Nas.

The word 'ghasiq' has been interpreted in various ways. While al-Razi specifies it as inanimate bodies (pure darkness), Ibn Sina interpreted it as the animalistic faculty (a turbid dark power). In our view, in accordance with the progression of the verses from the general to the specific, it is more accurate to understand ghasiq as elemental bodies in an absolute sense (including plants and animals), and then to specify the vegetative faculty followed by the animalistic faculty. In this case, the evil of ghasiq encompasses all the evils of the material realm in its state of generation and corruption; it points to the scourge of every kind of dark force or phantom confronting human beings, and even to the grim end of the mortal body condemned to enter the grave.

According to another interpretation, ghasiq refers to every sort of dark calamity that strikes a person; material or spiritual evil, grief, and sorrow are described as darkness. In this case, 'waqub' means to assault or attack. Ibn Jarir, on the other hand, conveys the following view: Allah Almighty commanded His Prophet to seek refuge from the evil of ghasiq. Ghasiq is that which is dark; when the night grows dark, when a star sets, or when the moon is eclipsed, it is called ghasiq. Allah did not single out any of these, but generalized it. Therefore, refuge is sought from the evil of anything that can be called ghasiq at the moment of its occurrence.

The phrase 'naffathati fi'l-ukad' in the fourth verse means 'those who blow onto knots.' 'Nafth' (to blow) means blowing with a slight amount of saliva or without saliva at all. The author of al-Kashshaf states that it involves blowing with saliva, whereas the author of al-Lawami' notes that it may also be without saliva. Al-Raghib states that nafth is casting out a little spit and that it is less than spitting. Sorcerers use their vile breaths when performing magic. In contrast to this, there is also ruqyah (reciting and blowing) performed for good; beautiful words such as sermons, admonitions, and spiritual healing fall within this category. However, what is commanded to be sought refuge from here is the vile, venomous blowings of male and female sorcerers.

The word 'ukad' is the plural of 'ukdah.' Numerous meanings are enumerated in al-Qamus: a knot, a knotted place; guardianship over cities; a covenant concluded for governors; property; a densely wooded and tangled place; sufficient pasture; that upon which a person's livelihood depends; fertile land; an animal forced to browse on trees; binding obligation (such as the bond of marriage or a sales contract); a belief, resolve, or intention in the heart; and malice and anger. Al-Raghib notes that ukdah is the name of that which is tied or concluded, and that it is also used for marriage, oaths, and an impediment of speech. The sorcerer's knots are the symbols of his demonic resolves and intentions. 'Azimah' (firm resolve) is the heart's resolute commitment to a matter, and the sorcerer's resolve is directed toward evil and deviltry.

The occurrence of 'naffathat' in the feminine plural form is interpreted in three ways: First, with the implied noun being 'nisa'' (women), it means 'the blowing women/witches,' because witchcraft is predominantly the craft of women, and the spellbinding effect of female guile is potent. Second, with the implied noun being 'nufus' (souls), it means 'the blowing souls,' which is the most preferred opinion since it encompasses both male and female. Third, with the implied noun being 'jama'at' (groups/communities), it means 'the blowing groups,' as spells performed collectively by sorcerers are more potent.

In the books of tafsir, the primary meaning given to the verse is: From the evil of the sorceresses (or souls, or groups) who practice incantations and charms by tying and blowing onto knots of thread. Reports from Companions and Successors such as Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid, and Ikrimah are to this effect. Ruqyahs that are free from sorcery and performed solely to seek refuge in Allah and ask for healing are permissible. The prohibition of ruqyah in the hadiths applies to those carrying the potential of polytheism (shirk) and sorcery. In conclusion, this verse commands seeking refuge in Allah from evil breaths of the kind associated with witchcraft and magic.

In this section, first of all, the subject of warning against satanic incantations and succumbing to delusions is addressed. Most commentators have concentrated the meaning here on sorcery and stated that one must particularly beware of incantations (ruqyah) mixed with magic. They considered reciting while tying knots in thread to be a type of sorcery; indeed, some scholars such as Ikrimah even viewed blowing and stroking with the hand as suspect. However, what is meant here are spit-filled blowings and smearings that shatter the nerves; otherwise, the existence of sacred and divine (rahmani) blowings is not denied. In accordance with the hadith that there is a cure for everything, just as treatment for spiritual illnesses through spiritual means and for physical illnesses through physical means is lawful, mixed treatment is likewise lawful for mixed conditions. On condition that the effect is known to come not from the means, but from Allah, and that all kinds of intrigue, sorcery, charlatanry, deception, and causing harm are avoided.

There are many hadiths demonstrating the legitimacy of ruqyah (recitation and blowing). Among the hadiths recorded by al-Razi, there are examples such as Gabriel (Jibril) reciting over the Messenger of Allah, the prayers of seeking refuge recited over Hasan and Husayn, and Uthman ibn Abi al-As reciting over himself. Although there is no indication of blowing in these, the commands in the Quran for supplication and seeking refuge, together with these surahs, are sufficient. It is also established that every night the Messenger of Allah recited the Mu'awwidhat, blew into his hands, and wiped his face and body. While these narrations show that ruqyah is permissible, it is emphasized that the requirement of true piety is for a person to pray directly to Allah and not to seek the mediation of another.

In the principles of Islamic jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), treatment and ruqyah are divided into three categories: definitive (maqtu'), probable (maznun), and illusory (mawhum). Ruqyah is considered part of the illusory category. According to Hanafi jurisprudence, treatment is permissible on condition that healing is recognized as coming from Allah; however, in those that are illusory like ruqyah, abandoning them is more in keeping with reliance upon Allah (tawakkul). It is forbidden (haram) to abandon definitive treatments, permissible to practice those based on probable conjecture, and more virtuous to abandon those based on illusion. This distinction does not change with the advancement of medicine, because in every era there exist degrees of certainty, presumption, and illusion. Indeed, even in modern medicine, one-hundred-percent certainty cannot be claimed.

The expression "the women who blow on knots" (naffathat fi al-'uqad) has been interpreted in different ways. According to one view, these are sorceresses or women who lead men into temptation (fitnah). Another view, favored by Ibn Sina and some gnomic scholars (arifs), is that this points to powers in fundamental bodies, such as the vegetative soul and the power of growth. According to this interpretation, certain faculties in the human body, such as the power of lust, act like blowing on knots. Furthermore, it has been stated that the word 'uqdah (knot) can also be used for spiritual and legal ties, such as the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) or guardianship (wilayah). However, the general consensus is that this expression means seeking refuge from the evil of male and female sorcerers.

The definition of envy (hasad) and seeking refuge from its evil are addressed in the commentary on the fifth verse of the surah. Envy is wishing for a blessing to disappear from its possessor.
