While the believer feels harmless emulation (ghibtah), the hypocrite envies. When an envier envies, he brings forth his evil; at this time, evil looks or physical assaults may occur. For this reason, seeking refuge in Allah is commanded. Envy is often mentioned together with the evil eye, and the soul of the envier takes on an ugly state at that moment. All kinds of trickery may be resorted to in order to harm the envied person. However, as long as envy remains in thought, it causes no harm; but when it is put into action, one must protect oneself from its evil.

Envy means wishing for a blessing possessed by another to disappear. In addition, wishing for a deficiency in another to persist is also called envy. The common meaning is the first one. The envier is in an unloved state in the sight of Allah and His servants, and it has been counted among the major sins. However, if one does not act upon the innate feeling of envy—that is, the disposition stemming from creation—and struggles against one's ego (nafs) and treats one's brother well, it is not a sin; in fact, one earns a reward. Ghibtah, on the other hand, is wishing for the same blessing to be in oneself without wishing for it to disappear from the other, and there is no harm in this.

Envy should not be confused with jealousy. Jealousy is mostly expressed in Arabic as 'ghayrah' and carries the purpose of protecting values such as honor and dignity. This type of jealousy is praised. However, being unable to tolerate another's spouse, wealth, beauty, or any blessing, and wishing for its destruction, is envy and is condemned. In this case, the word 'jealousy' is used metaphorically. True jealousy is protective zeal (ghayrah) and sense of honor (hamiyyah), and as long as it is not taken to excess, it is commendable.

Envy is at the same time a form of injustice (dhulm). Wishing for a blessing to disappear from its rightful owner is envy. However, wishing for a blessing in the hands of an usurper to disappear or striving to deliver what is due to its owner is not envy, but zeal and justice. As long as the feeling of envy remains inside, it harms only the envier and touches no one else. But if this feeling is translated into action and an attempt is made to destroy the blessing, then it becomes injustice and transgression, and one must seek refuge in Allah. Ibn Sina states that the evil of the envier stems from the struggle between body and soul.

In this surah, by enumerating the evils that could harm the human soul, seeking refuge in Allah is commanded. First, by saying "from the evil of what He created," the origin of all evils is briefly mentioned. Then, the dark night, the blowers (incantation-makers), and enviers are specifically mentioned. These three explain the most important evils or their ranks. At the end of the surah, by specifically mentioning the evil of the envier, the protection of the human soul against evils that may come from outside is aimed at.

The words 'ghasiq' and 'hasid' occurring in the surah are brought in the indefinite (nakirah) and singular form, whereas 'naffathat' is brought in the definite (ma'rifah) and plural form. Some scholars have stated that not every ghasiq and hasid is evil, but every blower is evil. In our view, while the evil of the ghasiq and the hasid generally occurs in secret and in darkness, the blowers commit evil more openly. For this reason, 'naffathat' appears as definite and plural. This surah, being completed by Surah an-Nas, teaches seeking refuge in Allah from evils coming from both outside and inside.

The names 'Rabb' (Lord and Sustainer), 'Malik' (Sovereign), and 'Ilah' (God) mentioned in this surah express three distinct relationships of Allah with human beings. 'Rabb' means the one who nurtures, fosters, and educates, encompassing the entire process from a person's creation until they attain intellect. 'Malik' means ruler and king, denoting the governance of rational beings through commands and prohibitions. 'Ilah', on the other hand, is the sole Being worthy of worship. These three names reflect the ascending degrees of humanity's devotion and attachment to Allah.

Elmalılı explains several wise aspects regarding the threefold repetition of the word 'nas' (people/mankind). According to al-Zamakhshari, this repetition serves as an explanatory apposition (atf al-bayan), emphasizing a distinct aspect of each divine name. Al-Razi, however, states that this repetition elevates the honor of mankind, as it signifies that Allah introduces Himself in relation to humanity. Al-Baydawi similarly indicates that this repetition points to the various spiritual ranks and stations of man.

Ibn Sina (Avicenna) and certain gnostics associate the three mentions of 'nas' with the three levels of the human soul. The first level (the material intellect / al-aql al-hayulani) is the state wherein man does not yet possess knowledge and is in need of nurturing and cultivation, which is designated by the name 'Rabb'. The second level (the intellect in habitu / al-aql bi'l-malaka) is the phase in which self-evident knowledge is acquired and the faculty to transition into theoretical sciences is formed, a level signified by the name 'Malik'. The third level (the actualized intellect / al-aql bi'l-fi'l) is the state wherein theoretical sciences are translated into actuality and the soul reaches perfection, to which the name 'Ilah' points.

Al-Razi summarizes the progression of these three names as follows: Man first observes the blessings of his Lord and recognizes Him as the Nurturer (Rabb). He then realizes that his Lord is entirely free of need from all things, knowing Him as the Sovereign (Malik). Finally, realizing that he is obligated to worship Him, he accepts Him as his God (Ilah). Al-Baydawi also notes that this sequence corresponds to the servant's stages of contemplation, while simultaneously reflecting the customary etiquette of seeking refuge: first appealing to an elder, then to a ruler, and ultimately to Allah.

The mention of Allah, to whom refuge is sought in this surah, by three distinct attributes—unlike in Surah al-Falaq—points to the gravity of the evil against which protection is sought. Whereas in Surah al-Falaq refuge is sought solely with 'the Lord of the daybreak', here the attributes of Rabb, Malik, and Ilah are cited together. This demonstrates that the evil sought refuge from (whispering / waswasah) is the most perilous affliction: an evil that springs from within man, pollutes his soul, and entails moral accountability.

The concepts of waswasah (whispering) and khannas are explained as follows: 'Waswas' is an epithet of Satan meaning 'one who whispers incessantly'; he continually strives to deceive humankind. 'Khannas' refers to one who retreats, slinks away, and then returns to whisper again. This depicts Satan's method of surreptitiously approaching and leading man astray. It is precisely against the evil of this whispering that seeking refuge in the three attributes of Allah has been commanded.

In elucidating the word 'waswasah', Elmalılı notes, citing al-Kashshaf and al-Raghib, that it fundamentally denotes a whisper or a faint, concealed sound. It is for this reason that the faint jingling of jewelry is called 'waswas al-huliyy', and the quiet rustlings of hunters and their hounds are referred to as waswasah. Over time, this term came to be used for the vile, futile thoughts cast into the heart by the lower self (nafs) or by Satan. Verse 16 of Surah Qaf is cited as an example of the whispering of the self, while verse 120 of Surah Ta-Ha exemplifies the whispering of Satan.

'Khannas' is derived from the root 'khunus', meaning one who frequently conceals himself, slinks away, and retreats. Exegetes have generally interpreted khunus as lagging behind and cowering. For this reason, Elmalılı deemed it appropriate to translate 'khannas' as 'insidious'. In al-Kashshaf, it is related that when a person remembers his Lord, Satan flees back, and when he falls into heedlessness, Satan resumes his whispering. Al-Raghib likewise states that al-khannas is the devil who falls back when Allah is mentioned. Thus, 'al-waswas al-khannas' became an established description of Satan.

The whisperer (al-waswas) has become a title for Satan, as his entire preoccupation is whispering and seduction. Abu Hayyan notes that waswasah is also applied to the inclinations of the lower self whispered by carnal desires. At the close of the verse, the expression 'mina'l-jinnati wa'n-nas' (from among the jinn and mankind) generalizes that the whisperer may be from either the jinn or humans. This encompasses both the unseen devils and human devils. According to Ibn Sina, waswasah is a thought linked to the imaginative faculty; others interpret it as the power of illusion and delusion. Elmalılı emphasizes that such interpretations do not impede the understanding of the verse, but rather represent a necessary aspect of deeper reflection.

The whispering devil or the lower self introduces whispers into the breasts (the inner beings) of people. Exegetes explain that there are three syntactic possibilities in the parsing (i'rab) of the clause 'alladhi yuwaswisu fi suduri'n-nas': as an adjectival description (sifah), as an independent inception clause (isti'naf), or in the accusative of censure (mansub ala'dh-dhamm). Elmalılı indicates that 'nas' here refers to heedless people, and may even be linked to 'nasi' (one who forgets). The verse clarifies that whispering originates from both jinn and human devils, both of which drag man toward evil.

Exegetes have proposed different interpretations regarding the preposition 'min': first, that 'min' is explanatory (al-bayaniyyah), setting forth the categories of whisperers as jinn and humankind; second, that it denotes origin (al-ibtidaiyyah), marking the starting point of the whispering; and third, that it explains 'nas', according to which view the jinn may also be referred to as 'nas'. The author of al-Kashshaf rejects this third view. Elmalılı states that the most evident interpretation is the first. In conclusion, mankind is commanded to seek refuge in Allah—the Lord, Sovereign, and God of humanity—from the evil of every whisper stemming from jinn and men. This refuge is in complete harmony with the supplication in Surah al-Fatihah: 'You alone do we worship and You alone do we ask for help.'
